title: A Plantation Witch
summary: Collected by Joel Chandler Harris in the Uncle Remus stories, 'A Plantation Witch' tells of supernatural occurrences on the plantation. Uncle Remus recounts that witches on the plantation could transform into animals, particularly haunts and hags that rode people at night. According to the tale, a young enslaved man named 'Toby' was ridden by a hag every night and would wake up exhausted. An old conjure woman told him to sprinkle salt and pepper around his bed before sleeping. When the hag came that night, she could not approach him. In a rage, she revealed herself as a woman from the neighboring plantation who had been jealous of Toby's good fortune. She promised to leave him alone if he never revealed her secret. Toby agreed, and the hag never troubled him again. But from that night on, Toby kept a container of salt and a Bible under his pillow, just in case. The tale illustrates the deeply held African American folk belief in night-hags and the practical, protective measures used against them.

title: Ababinili and the Creation of Humans (Chickasaw)
summary: Ababinili (also spelled Aba' Binni'li'), meaning 'One Who Sits Above' or 'Dwells Above,' is the Creator god of the Chickasaw people. According to legend, Ababinili created the first humans from the clay of the earth and breathed life into them. He taught the people how to live, hunt, farm, and conduct ceremonies. Ababinili established the sacred fire as a symbol of his presence and instructed the people to keep it burning always. He created the sun, moon, and stars to give light and mark the passage of time. Ababinili also appointed the thunder and lightning to bring rain. The Chickasaw believe that Ababinili watches over all creation and that humans must live in harmony with nature to maintain his favor.

title: Abai Geser the Mighty (Buryat Epic)
summary: The Buryat version of the great Central Asian epic of Geser (Geser), focusing on his battles with various demons rather than military campaigns. The epic begins with a unique prologue: the great Tengri Khormusta of the western celestial tribes wars with Atai Ulan, lord of the eastern evil gods. After victory, Khormusta dismembers Atai Ulan and throws his body parts to Earth, where they become monsters and demons that nearly destroy humanity. The middle son of Khormusta, Bukhe Belligte, is sent from heaven as Abai Geser to save the world. The Buryat version contains nine branches or song episodes, each devoted to defeating a different enemy including giant rats, steel ravens, a sun-eating monster, and various multi-headed demons.

title: Abaia the Magical Eel
summary: Abaia is a huge, magical eel from the mythology of Fiji, the Solomon Islands, and Vanuatu. This enormous freshwater eel is said to dwell at the bottom of deep lakes and rivers, acting as a guardian spirit of the waters. In Fijian tradition, Abaia is associated with Degei and is considered a powerful spirit being that can control fish and water creatures. Fishermen who respect Abaia and offer proper rituals are blessed with abundant catches, while those who disrespect the waters face misfortune. Some stories describe Abaia creating lakes by thrashing its enormous body, forming depressions that filled with water. The eel is a totemic animal for some clans, and killing a large eel is considered taboo as it may be an incarnation of Abaia.

title: Ableegumooch: How Rabbit Lost His Tail
summary: Ableegumooch the Rabbit was once the most vain of all animals, boasting constantly about his beautiful long tail. He teased Otter for having only a small, stubby tail. Annoyed, Otter challenged Rabbit to a fishing contest. Rabbit, who knew nothing about fishing but would never admit it, agreed. Otter caught fish after fish by diving into the river, while Rabbit sat on the bank with a line, catching nothing. In desperation, Rabbit tied his line to his tail and cast it far into the water, but instead of catching a fish, a giant turtle grabbed his tail and pulled. Rabbit escaped but his magnificent tail was snapped off, leaving only the short stub rabbits have to this day. Otter laughed at Rabbit's vanity, and Rabbit learned that pride comes before a fall. Glooscap, watching from his lodge, declared that Rabbit's new tail would remind all creatures of the dangers of vanity.

title: Abu Zayd al-Hilali and the Banu Hilal Epic
summary: The Epic of the Banu Hilal (Taghribat Bani Hilal) is one of the great oral epics of the Arab world, particularly celebrated in Egypt and North Africa. It recounts the migration of the Bedouin Banu Hilal tribe from the Arabian Peninsula into North Africa in the 11th century. The hero, Abu Zayd al-Hilali, is a legendary warrior-poet and trickster, born with black skin to Arab parents—a detail that creates dramatic tension throughout the epic. The story follows the tribe's journey across the Nile, their conquest of Tunisia, and their eventual downfall through betrayal. The epic features supernatural elements: magical horses, prophetic dreams, jinn interference, and heroes with superhuman strength. Abu Zayd's main antagonist is Khalifa al-Zanati, the Berber king of Tunisia, who eventually defeats the Hilali invasion. The epic was inscribed in 2008 on UNESCO's Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity, and it remains performed by poet-singers (sha'ir) throughout Egypt and the Maghreb.

title: Abuk, the Mother of Seed
summary: In the beginning, the goddess Abuk held all the seeds of the earth within her body, and the sky god demanded she surrender them to humanity. Her defiance and eventual sacrifice shaped the eternal bond between women and the soil.

title: Adaro: The Sea Spirits of the Solomon Islands
summary: In the mythology of Makira (San Cristobal) in the Solomon Islands, the Adaro are powerful sea spirits that dwell in the ocean. They are described as half-human, half-fish beings who can travel along rainbows and sunlight beams. Adaro are said to have gills on their bodies and fins on their arms and legs. They can be both benevolent and malevolent, sometimes helping fishermen by guiding them to abundant fishing grounds, and other times causing shipwrecks and drowning. The Adaro are closely associated with the shark cults of the Solomon Islands, particularly on Malaita where sharks are considered sacred manifestations of ancestral spirits. Offerings were made to Adaro before long sea voyages to ensure safe passage.

title: Adbar: The Spirit Guardians of Ethiopia
summary: In Ethiopian folk belief, every mountain, river, forest, and crossroads is protected by a spirit called an Adbar. These guardian spirits are ancient beings who existed before humans and serve as the intermediaries between God and the natural world. Each Adbar has a specific territory and responsibility: some protect travelers on dangerous roads, others guard the fertility of farmlands, and still others watch over water sources. Before embarking on a journey or planting a harvest, Ethiopians traditionally offer coffee beans, incense, or bread to the local Adbar, asking for safe passage or a bountiful yield. The Adbar are neither good nor evil — they are ancient forces of nature who demand respect. Offending an Adbar can bring misfortune, while honoring it brings protection and prosperity. The tradition of Adbar reflects the deep Ethiopian reverence for the spiritual dimension of the natural world.

title: Adonis and the River of Blood
summary: A beautiful youth killed by a boar, whose blood flows every spring through the rivers of Lebanon — turning them red with his memory, and the women weep because beauty does not last.

title: Adventure With a Tie-Snake (Natchez)
summary: The Tie-Snake (u'lax daxgi'ilu in Natchez) is a water spirit common to Southeastern Native American folklore. Though the size and shape of an ordinary snake, Tie-Snakes possess immense strength and can coil around a human with crushing force. In the Natchez story, a man encountered a Tie-Snake while fishing. The snake rose from the water and tried to drag him under. The man fought bravely, remembering the teachings of his elders, and managed to cut the snake in half with his knife. The two halves of the Tie-Snake transformed into eels and slithered away into the water. The story teaches that knowledge and courage can overcome even supernatural threats, and it explains the origin of eels. Tie-Snake legends are found across the Southeast, from the Cherokee to the Creek to the Natchez.

title: Adze: The Vampiric Firefly
summary: A witch-spirit takes firefly form, entering homes to drain the blood of sleepers.

title: Agneta and the Sea King
summary: Agneta, daughter of a lord, encounters the Sea King by the lake at sunset. Enchanted by his music, she forgets her former life and becomes his queen beneath the waters for seven years, bearing him seven sons. When church bells reach her underwater realm, she begs to attend church. Above the surface, memories of her father and former life overwhelm her. When the Sea King comes to reclaim her, she refuses, choosing her own freedom over returning to her children.

title: Agnete og Havmanden
summary: A merman woos Agnete to leave her children behind and come and live with him in the sea. She does so and has several children by him. But one day she hears the ringing of church bells and with the merman's permission returns to land to visit the church. In most variants, she then abandons the merman and the children she bore by him, choosing to remain with her former family.

title: Ah Puch and the Moon Child
summary: A young Maya girl ventures too close to the entrance of Xibalba and encounters Ah Puch, lord of death, who tests her courage and teaches her the boundary between the living and the dead.

title: Ahoeitu and the Founding of the Tupou Dynasty
summary: Ahoeitu was born to a Tongan chiefess and the god Eitumatupua, who descended from heaven on a great tree. The jealous half-brothers of Ahoeitu conspired against him, murdering him and cutting his body into pieces. When Eitumatupua discovered the crime, he restored Ahoeitu to life and punished the treacherous brothers. Ahoeitu became the first of the Tu'i Tonga line, establishing the sacred dynasty that ruled Tonga for over a thousand years. His descendants held supreme temporal and spiritual authority, their mana legitimized by direct divine ancestry. The story reinforces the sacred nature of Tongan kingship and the consequences of defying divinely ordained rule.

title: Aina-Kizz and the Black-Bearded Bai
summary: Aina-Kizz, an incredibly clever young girl from Samarkand, helps her widowed mother by using her intelligence to outwit a greedy black-bearded bai (rich man). The bai boasts of impossible feats — that he once grew a wheat field so vast that a whole caravan got lost in it, and that the caravan emerged from his mouth when he ate bread. Aina-Kizz cleverly exposes his lies and reveals that he is the murderer of her uncle, whose silk robe the bai still wears. Through her wit and careful trap-setting, she forces the bai to confess and returns justice to her family. The story celebrates feminine intelligence over male arrogance and remains one of the most popular Uzbek folk tales.

title: Aisha Qandisha, the Demoness of the Waters
summary: Aisha Qandisha is among the most famous mythological figures in Moroccan folklore—a beautiful woman with the legs of a goat or camel who lures men to their doom. She is said to live near water sources: the sea at Tangier, the Martil River at Tetouan, the Sebou River among the Beni Ahsen. Using her enchanting beauty, she seduces young men, then drives them mad or kills them. Some historians trace her origins to a 16th-century Moroccan resistance fighter who seduced Portuguese soldiers before they were killed by her ambush party; snip after her death, her spirit lingered. Other theories connect her to the ancient Phoenician goddess Astarte or the Canaanite Qetesh. The Hamadsha and Zar societies conduct rites of voluntary possession by her. She is associated with Hammu Qayyu, her consort. She remains a potent figure in Moroccan popular culture, referenced in Gnawa music and contemporary horror films.

title: Aisha Qandisha: The Jinn of the Moroccan Rivers
summary: A beautiful jinn with goat hooves seduces men at rivers and drives them to madness.

title: Akbaatatdia the Creator
summary: Akbaatatdia (One Who Has Made Everything) is the supreme Creator in Crow religion. Also known as Iichíkbaalee (First Doer) and Isáahkawuattee (Old Man Coyote), this singular omnipotent god created the universe. The Crow believe the universe consists of three worlds: the physical world (the smallest), the spirit world (the intermediate realm), and the third world where God alone dwells. Akbaatatdia is omnipresent and omnipotent, and Crows believe they are in contact with God during every aspect of daily life. Because God created everything, all of nature is sacred, and all religions are considered valid paths to the same Creator.

title: Akbar and Birbal — The Farmer's Well
summary: A poor farmer bought a well from a rich man, but the rich man later refused to let him draw water, claiming he had sold only the well, not the water. The farmer brought his case to Emperor Akbar's court, who handed it to his wise advisor Birbal. Birbal told the rich man: 'Since you sold the well and not the water, you must either remove all your water from the well or pay rent to the farmer for keeping your water in his well.' The rich man realized his scheme had backfired and allowed the farmer to use the well freely, teaching that clever deceit can be defeated with even cleverer logic.

title: Al, the Underworld Dweller
summary: A demonic being who lives in the depths of the earth, luring the living underground with promises of treasure, because in Georgia the earth itself hungers.

title: Al-Khidr and the Sultan of Petra
summary: When a greedy sultan attempts to claim the treasures of Petra for himself, Al-Khidr appears as a humble guide to teach him that the city of stone holds no wealth for those who do not understand its meaning.

title: Ala and the Sacred Earth (Igbo)
summary: Ala is the great earth goddess of the Igbo people, the most revered deity in Odinani. She is the goddess of fertility, morality, death, and the ancestral realm. The Igbo believe that the earth is Ala's living body, and that all who die return to her womb. Killing, incest, theft, and the birth of twins were considered 'nsọ Ala' (desecration of the earth) and required elaborate purification rituals. The royal python is considered Ala's messenger; killing one requires a full human burial. In Igbo cosmology, Ala maintains order in the universe and punishes wrongdoers through her power over the land's fertility. Each village maintains an Ala shrine (ihu Ala) where community decisions are made and justice is dispensed. The Ala shrine is both a court of law and a place of worship.

title: Aladdin and the Magic Lamp
summary: In a far city of China, though the tale itself comes from the sands of Arabia, there lived a poor tailor named Mustapha and his wife, who had one son.

title: Aladdin and the Wonderful Lamp
summary: A poor young ne'er-do-well in a Chinese city is recruited by a Maghrebi sorcerer to retrieve a magic lamp from a booby-trapped cave. When the sorcerer betrays him, Aladdin discovers a genie bound to the lamp that grants wishes. He becomes wealthy, marries Princess Badroulbadour, and builds a magnificent palace. The sorcerer returns to steal the lamp by trickery, but Aladdin uses a magic ring to recover it. Though added to the Arabian Nights by Antoine Galland from Syrian storyteller Hanna Diyab, it became one of the most famous Middle Eastern tales worldwide.

title: Aldar Qose the Trickster
summary: Aldar Qose is the beloved Kazakh trickster figure, analogous to Nasreddin Hodja in other Turkic traditions. He is a poor but clever wanderer who uses his wit to outsmart greedy bais (wealthy men), corrupt officials, and even devils. In one famous tale, Aldar convinces a miserly bai to give him almost all his possessions — including his beautiful daughter — through elaborate verbal tricks. In another, a devil who comes to take possession of Aldar ends up outsmarted and humiliated. Aldar Qose stories serve as social satire, exposing the hypocrisy of the powerful while celebrating the cunning of the common people.

title: Ali Baba and the Forty Thieves
summary: In a town in Persia, there once lived two brothers.. The elder, Cassim, married a wealthy woman and became the richest merchant in the marketplace.

title: Ali, the Mountain Demon
summary: A monstrous demon who dwells in the high mountains, stealing livestock and children, because in Georgia the peaks belong to things older than faith.

title: All I Possess!
summary: A miserly farmer marries a woman who supposedly eats almost nothing. Suspicious, he spies on her three times—down the chimney, inside a feather bed, and in a beer barrel. Each time she outwits him (with smoke, beating, and scalding lye). On his deathbed, his cries of 'All I possess!' are interpreted as his final wish that she inherit everything.

title: Alpamysh Batyr
summary: Alpamysh (Alpamıs in Kazakh) is one of the most important Turkic epic heroes, shared across Kazakh, Uzbek, Karakalpak, and Altai traditions. The epic tells of the hero's miraculous birth to elderly parents after years of prayer, his childhood exploits, and his marriage to the beautiful Barchin after defeating rival suitors in contests. When Barchin's father moves the clan to the land of the Kalmyks, Alpamysh follows and wins her through heroic feats. After returning home, he fights the usurper Ultantaz who has persecuted his people and tried to force Barchin into marriage. The epic ends with the reunification of the divided Kongrat tribe under Alpamysh's heroic leadership.

title: Amadioha, the God of Thunder (Igbo)
summary: Amadioha is the Igbo god of thunder, lightning, justice, and the sky. His name means 'free will of the people' in Igbo. Amadioha represents divine justice and collective will, striking down those who break oaths and commit crimes. His color is red, his sacred animal is the ram, and his day is Afọ. The main shrine of Amadioha is at Ozuzu in Rivers State, Nigeria. Amadioha is the expression of divine wrath against taboos and crimes; in oaths he is sworn by and strikes down those who swear falsely with thunder and lightning. He is also associated with Anyanwu, the sun deity. In many Igbo communities, Amadioha is considered the consort of Ala, the earth goddess. Together they maintain the moral and cosmic order of the universe, punishing the wicked and rewarding the righteous.

title: Amaterasu and the Cave
summary: Amaterasu, the Sun Goddess of Shinto, is the most important deity in the Japanese pantheon.

title: Amirani, the Chained Hero
summary: A Titan-like hero who defied the gods and was chained to a mountain for eternity, his chains binding him until the day a greater hero comes to free him.

title: Amleth
summary: Prince Amleth's father, King Horvendill, is murdered by his uncle Feng. Amleth fakes madness to survive and eventually kills Feng by burning down his palace during a feast, avenging his father's death and reclaiming his kingdom.

title: Amma and the Cosmic Egg: The Dogon Creation
summary: In the beginning, Amma, the supreme creator god of the Dogon people, existed alone. He created the universe from a cosmic egg called aduno tal, which contained all future matter and motion. Amma attempted to create the world but the first being, Ogo (also called Yurugu the Pale Fox), was born prematurely and without a twin, embodying incompleteness and disorder. He stole seeds and introduced chaos. To restore balance, Amma created the Nommo, twin amphibious fish-beings who represent water, speech, and cosmic order. One Nommo was sacrificed and dismembered, his body scattered across the universe, establishing the ritual order. The Nommo descended to Earth in a spinning copper ark from Sirius, bringing the first ancestors, seeds, weaving, and the sacred word.

title: Anansi and the Dispersal of Diseases (Ashanti/Akan)
summary: Anansi once tricked Nyame, the Sky God, by taking one of his sheep and promising a beautiful maiden in return. Nyame discovered the deception and took all of Anansi's wives, leaving only a sick woman. Following her advice, Anansi bathed her and kept the water in a gourd, and she became beautiful. When Nyame saw her and demanded she be brought to him, Anansi crafted a drum from the gourd containing the disease-water. During a celebratory dance, Anansi opened the drum and released the disease-water, unleashing sickness upon the world. This is why illnesses exist among humanity, and the tale serves as a cautionary story about the consequences of deception, even when intended to right a wrong.

title: Anansi and the Pot of Wisdom
summary: Anansi tricks humans into giving him all the world's wisdom—but discovers it cannot be kept.

title: Anansi and the Pot of Wisdom (Ashanti/Akan)
summary: Anansi the Spider gathered all the wisdom in the world into a pot, planning to hoard it for himself. He decided to hide the pot at the top of a tall tree, but each time he tried to climb the tree with the pot tied in front of him, he kept sliding down. Anansi's young son, Ntikuma, watched and asked, 'Father, wouldn't it be easier if you tied the pot on your back instead?' Furious that his son had outsmarted him, Anansi threw the pot down in anger. The pot shattered, and the wisdom scattered everywhere, carried by rain into the rivers. That is why wisdom is now spread across the world and accessible to all. The moral teaches that wisdom is only valuable when shared, and that even children can teach their elders.

title: Anansi and Tiger in the Pit
summary: Anansi hears Tiger roaring and finds him trapped in a deep pit. As Tiger claws his way up inch by inch, Anansi taunts him from above. When Tiger reaches near the top, gasping that he has no more strength, Anansi mockingly advises him to pray — to put his paws together and pray for strength. The moment Tiger puts his paws together, he slides all the way back down into the pit while Anansi runs off laughing. This classic Anansi trickster tale demonstrates how the spider uses cunning and psychological manipulation to defeat a much stronger opponent, a theme that resonated deeply with enslaved Africans in Jamaica.

title: Anansi and Turtle (Ashanti/Akan)
summary: Anansi once invited Turtle to dinner, but when Turtle arrived after a long journey, Anansi told him that custom required Turtle to wash his hands before eating. As Turtle walked to the river and back, Anansi ate all the food. Turtle, realizing he had been tricked, invited Anansi to dinner at the bottom of the river. Anansi jumped into the water but floated to the surface, unable to sink. Turtle told Anansi to fill his pockets with stones to weigh himself down. Anansi did so and reached the river bottom, but Turtle had already eaten all the food. When Anansi tried to leave, the stones made him sink back down. Turtle mocked him, saying that just as Anansi had tricked him with hand-washing, Turtle had returned the favor with stones. The story teaches poetic justice and that deceivers will eventually be deceived.

title: Anansi Boys
summary: Anansi's sons—Fat Face and Small Head—continue their fathers trickery in the Caribbean.

title: Anansi: The Spider Who Owns All Stories
summary: A clever spider uses his wits to capture the world's most dangerous creatures and win all the stories in existence.

title: Anarteq the Salmon Spirit
summary: A man named Anarteq undergoes a spiritual transformation after a series of events that lead him to merge with the essence of the river. He becomes a salmon spirit, possessing the ability to move between the human and aquatic worlds. This myth explains the spiritual connection between hunters and their prey, suggesting that some humans are destined to protect the animal realms.

title: Andaokut Rescues the Children (Nuu-chah-nulth)
summary: A woman whose children had been stolen by Malahas, a malicious forest goddess, wept uncontrollably. From her mucus or tears, a child was born — Andaokut. This miraculous birth child grew with extraordinary speed and possessed supernatural abilities. Andaokut set out to rescue the stolen children, tracking Malahas to her remote forest lair. Using courage and cleverness, he confronted Malahas and defeated her, freeing all the children she had captured. He killed Malahas and returned the children safely to their families. This story from Nuu-chah-nulth tradition exemplifies the theme of miraculous birth and the triumph of good over evil. Andaokut represents hope born from despair, showing that even from a mother's tears, salvation can emerge. The defeat of Malahas demonstrates that even the most powerful evil beings can be overcome by determination and courage.

title: Antar and Abla
summary: The epic romance of Antarah ibn Shaddad, a 6th-century pre-Islamic Arab poet-warrior born a slave to an Ethiopian mother and Arab father in the tribe of Banu Abs. Despite his dark complexion (one of the 'Arab crows'), Antar rose through courage and poetry to win his freedom and the hand of his cousin Abla. His poem became one of the Seven Hanging Odes (Mu'allaqat) displayed in the Kaaba. The romance spans his heroic battles, his eloquence, and his enduring love for Abla against tribal opposition. The saga, comparable to Arthurian legend, remains central to Arab oral tradition and is still recited in coffeehouses across the Middle East.

title: Anubis
summary: Anubis is the most ancient of Egyptian funerary gods — the jackal-headed guardian of the dead whose dark form has watched over tombs and necropolises since the earliest dynasties.

title: Anulap: The God of Knowledge in Chuuk
summary: Anulap is a powerful god of magic and knowledge in the mythology of Chuuk (Truk) in the Federated States of Micronesia. He is revered as the deity who taught humanity the arts of magic, navigation, medicine, and all forms of sacred and practical knowledge. Anulap is the husband of the creator goddess Ligobubfanu and may himself be a creator deity. In the Chuuk creation story, Anulap established the cosmic order, separating the sky from the sea and creating the first islands. He is the grandfather of the trickster god Olifat and serves as the supreme authority in the Micronesian pantheon. Anulap's wisdom was essential for navigators who needed to read the stars, currents, and winds to travel between the scattered islands of Micronesia.

title: Anzar and the First Rain
summary: Anzar, the god of rain and thunder in Berber mythology, fell in love with a beautiful mortal woman who refused his love. In his grief, Anzar withheld the rain from the earth, causing a terrible drought that parched the land. The woman eventually relented and agreed to marry him. When she finally accepted his hand, Anzar brought the rain back to the earth, ending the drought and making the land fertile once more. This story still underpins rain-calling rituals in Kabyle and other Berber communities, where women sing to Anzar during times of drought, coaxing clouds with ritual and song. The Tale of Anzar and the First Rain is among the most enduring Berber myths, explaining the life-giving power of water in the arid Maghreb landscape.

title: Apwoyo the Trickster Hare
summary: Among the Luo, Apwoyo the hare is the most cunning creature in the animal kingdom, constantly outsmarting larger and stronger animals through pure wit. In one famous tale, Apwoyo tricked the mighty elephant into a tug-of-war contest against a python, pitting them against each other while pretending each was tied to him. In another, he escaped being eaten by the lion by claiming to be the messenger of Were, sent to inspect the animals' behavior. When the hyena tried to copy Apwoyo's tricks, disaster always followed — the hyena's stupidity and greed leading to beatings, lost tails, or worse. The Apwoyo stories teach Luo children that intelligence and quick thinking are more valuable than brute strength, but also that trickery used for selfish ends eventually catches up with the trickster.

title: Arash the Archer
summary: An Iranian hero sacrifices his life force to shoot an arrow that defines the nation's border.

title: Areop-Enap: The Spider Who Created the World
summary: In Nauruan creation mythology, the primordial being was Areop-Enap, an ancient spider who existed alone in darkness on an endless sea. Searching for food, Areop-Enap found an enormous clam that swallowed him. Inside the darkness, he discovered two snails. He slept three days transferring his power to each snail, then sent the smaller snail to open the clam, leaving a phosphorescent trail. In the light, he found a white worm called Rigi. Areop-Enap cast a strength spell on Rigi to pry open the clam. The clam died from the effort, and Areop-Enap made the lower shell into Earth and the upper into the sky. He placed the smaller snail in the west to become the Moon and the larger snail in the east to become the Sun. Rigi drowned in his own sweat and was hung in the sky as the Milky Way. Humans were created from stones to support the sky.

title: Arwe: The Serpent King of Ethiopia
summary: A giant serpent ruled Ethiopia for four centuries until a clever hero defeated it with poisoned food.

title: Asema, the Vampire of the Rainforest
summary: A vampire-like spirit from Surinamese folklore who sheds her skin at night and flies through the forest in search of blood.

title: Ask and Embla
summary: In the time before time, when the world was young and the great void of Ginnungagap had only recently given birth to the first living things, Odin and his brothers Vili and Vé walked along the shore of the newly made world.

title: Aswang: The Shapeshifter
summary: The most feared creature in Philippine folklore—a shapeshifter that eats human flesh, especially unborn children.

title: Atabey, Mother of Waters and Creation
summary: Atabey (also Atabex) is the supreme mother goddess of the Taino people, the indigenous inhabitants of the Greater Antilles. She is the goddess of fresh water, fertility, the earth, and the moon. According to Taino creation myth, Atabey gave birth to herself from all the elements before creating the world. She then produced twin sons: Yocahú (also called Yucaju), the god of cassava and the sea, and Guacar, who became Juracán, the god of storms and chaos. After creating the world, Atabey found it empty and lonely, so she and Yocahú filled it with living beings, plants, and natural wonders. Guacar grew jealous of their bond and became Juracán, conjuring hurricanes to dismantle their creations. Atabey is depicted in a birthing position in petroglyphs found at Caguana, Puerto Rico, and Taino women called upon her during childbirth.

title: Atargatis, the Fish Goddess
summary: A goddess who dove into a lake and became half-fish, her scales shimmering in the deep water — because in Lebanon, the boundary between gods and monsters is thinner than the surface of the sea.

title: Atira—Mother Corn
summary: Atira is the Pawnee goddess of the Earth and wife of Tirawa, the creator god. Her name literally means 'Mother Corn,' and she is associated with the corn that sustained the Pawnee people. Atira is a nurturing figure who provides food and life from the earth. In the Hako (Calumet) ceremony, a symbol representing Atira was created, showing corn painted so that the Rainstorm, Thunder, Lightning, and Wind are represented. The South Bands of the Pawnee particularly honored Atira through agricultural ceremonies, giving thanks for the harvest and praying for continued fertility of the soil.

title: Auriaria and Nei Tituaabine: The Origin of Trees
summary: In Kiribati mythology, Auriaria was a red-haired giant chieftain who fell in love with the beautiful red-haired woman Nei Tituaabine. Despite their love, they had no children. When Nei Tituaabine died, Auriaria buried her with great sorrow. From her grave grew three trees: a coconut tree from her head, a pandanus tree from her heels, and an almond tree from her navel. Nei Tituaabine became a tree goddess, and these three trees became the most important plants for the people of Kiribati. The coconut provides food, drink, and materials for shelter; snip the pandanus provides leaves for weaving; snip and the almond provides nutritious nuts. This story explains the sacred origin of the plants essential to survival on the low-lying atolls of Kiribati and connects human love and mortality with the bounty of nature.

title: Aztlán — The Mythical Homeland of the Aztecs
summary: Aztlán is the mythical ancestral homeland of the Aztec (Mexica) peoples, a legendary island paradise from which they began their long migration southward to central Mexico around 1064 CE. According to the Codices Aubin, Boturini, and Azcatitlan, the Mexica left Aztlán guided by their god Huitzilopochtli, who forbade them from calling themselves Azteca and commanded they be known as Mexica. The 200-year journey brought them to Lake Texcoco where they saw the prophesied sign: an eagle on a cactus holding a serpent. There they built Tenochtitlan, which became the capital of the Aztec Empire. In the 1960s, the Chicano Movement reclaimed Aztlán as a symbol of cultural identity and territorial heritage. The 1969 'Plan Espiritual de Aztlán,' drafted at the National Chicano Youth Liberation Conference in Denver, declared the US Southwest territories conquered in the Mexican-American War as 'Aztlán' — the ancestral homeland of the Chicano people. For Chicanos, Aztlán represents not just a physical territory but a spiritual concept of belonging, indigenous sovereignty, and the right to cultural self-determination. It remains a powerful symbol in Chicano art, literature, and political activism.

title: Baal, Lord of the Storm
summary: The storm god who defeated Yamm, lord of the sea, to become king of the gods — but his victory was bought with blood, and every thunderstorm is a reminder of the war he fought.

title: Baaxpée and the Vision Quest
summary: Baaxpée is the sacred power of God (Akbaatatdia) in Crow belief, meaning 'power transcending the ordinary.' To acquire Baaxpée, a Crow must go on a vision quest (bilisshíissanne—'to fast from water'). The quester goes alone to an isolated peak, usually in the Wolf Mountains, fasting without food or water for two to three days. Self-mortification, including finger removal, is sometimes offered to show devotion. When a spirit pities the quester, it induces a vision, adopting the Crow as a child and bestowing Baaxpée. The spirit becomes a 'Medicine Father' who guides the Crow throughout life. The quester creates a Xapáaliia (medicine object) to represent the bond.

title: Baba Yaga
summary: A brave girl is tested by the forest witch Baba Yaga and discovers that kindness and guidance can overcome the most terrifying forces.

title: Baba Yaga: The Witch of the Woods
summary: A fearsome witch lives in a hut standing on chicken legs deep in the forest—children must complete tasks to escape her.

title: Backoo, the Barnacle Spirit
summary: A mischievous water spirit of Guyanese folklore, the Backoo is a small, hairy creature covered in barnacles that lives in rivers and canals.

title: Badang the Strongman
summary: Badang is the legendary Malay strongman from ancient Singapura (pre-colonial Singapore) whose feats of strength are celebrated in the Malay Annals (Sejarah Melayu). Originally a slave, Badang gained superhuman strength after consuming the regurgitated vomit of a river spirit — a grotesque but powerful magical substance he had declined to eat before being tricked into it. His strength became legendary: he could lift boats single-handedly, uproot trees, and hurl massive boulders. The Raja employed him as the royal strongman, and he famously defeated a champion from India in a strength contest by lifting an impossibly heavy stone. This stone, known as the Singapore Stone, once stood at the mouth of the Singapore River.

title: Bahram Gur (Bahram V, the Hunter King)
summary: The Sassanid king Bahram V (Bahram Gur), renowned for his love of hunting (especially onager, giving him the epithet 'Gur' meaning onager), is the subject of numerous Persian legends. His exploits include hunting with a lion and an onager as companions, his romance with the Indian princess Sapinud (whom he marries after killing a lion and a dragon), and his building of the seven pavilions for his seven princesses (the subject of Nizami's Haft Paykar). Bahram embodies the ideal Sassanid king: martial prowess, justice, and cultural patronage. The story of 'Bahram and the Dragon' recounts his killing a dragon to save a beautiful maiden.

title: Bai Ze: The Beast of Infinite Knowledge
summary: A mythical beast appears to the Yellow Emperor, revealing all knowledge of spirits and monsters in the world.

title: Baiame the Sky Father
summary: Baiame is the supreme creator god and sky father in the mythology of several Aboriginal Australian peoples of southeastern Australia, including the Kamilaroi, Wiradjuri, and Eora nations. In the Dreamtime, Baiame descended from the sky world to create the land, plants, animals, and humans. He gave the people their laws, customs, and ceremonies before returning to the sky, where he remains watching over the world from his home in the Milky Way. Baiame established the rules of marriage, the totem system, and the proper relationships between people and land. His wives include Birrahgnooloo (associated with fertility and floods) and Cunnembeillee. Baiame is portrayed in rock art and carvings, often depicted with enormous size and radiating headgear suggesting divine power. His son Daramulum acts as an intermediary between Baiame and humans.

title: Baiame: The Sky Father
summary: The great creator spirit who descended from the sky to shape the land and give law to the people.

title: Bakru, the Forest Spirit Child
summary: A small, childlike forest spirit who can bring wealth to those who capture it but demands terrible sacrifices in return.

title: Bakunawa: The Moon-Eating Serpent
summary: In Visayan mythology, Bakunawa is a massive sea serpent or dragon believed to cause eclipses by attempting to swallow the moon. Originally a beautiful sea goddess, Bakunawa was transformed into a serpent as punishment for falling in love with a mortal. Each night she rises from the ocean depths to chase the moon across the sky. When she catches it, the people must make loud noises with pots and pans to frighten her away, causing her to release the moon. This ancient myth explains lunar eclipses and reflects the deep connection between Filipino ancestors and celestial observation.

title: Bamboo Hat Guardian
summary: Three mysterious strangers reward a kind couple with golden statues, while a greedy merchant finds that stolen blessings bring only ruin.

title: Banshee
summary: In Ireland, there is no sound more feared than the wail of the Banshee—the washerwoman of the dead.

title: Baron Samedi, Lord of the Dead
summary: Baron Samedi (Baron Saturday) is one of the most iconic lwa of Haitian Vodou, the master of death, tombs, graveyards, and resurrection. He is depicted wearing a top hat, black tail coat, dark glasses, and cotton plugs in the nostrils like a corpse prepared for burial. Often shown as a skeleton, he speaks in a nasal voice and is known for disruption, debauchery, and his fondness for tobacco and rum. As head of the Gede family of lwa, he has the final say on death itself and is also a healer and protector of souls. His consort is Maman Brigitte. Baron Samedi can grant resurrection as well as death, making him a figure of both fear and respect.

title: Barong and Rangda
summary: On the Caribbean island of Trinidad, where the heat is thick enough to drink and the nights pulse with the music of crickets and frogs, the old folks tell stories of the Soucouyant.

title: Basilisk
summary: The Basilisk, known throughout the ancient and medieval worlds as the King of Serpents, is one of the most feared creatures in all of folklore.

title: Basilisk: The King of Serpents
summary: A rooster-born king of serpents with a deadly gaze is defeated by his own reflection, proving that the greatest power can be its own undoing.

title: Batu Belah Batu Bertangkup
summary: A classic Malay folktale from Perak about a mother who abandons her children after being seduced by a forest spirit. The story follows two siblings, a brother and a sister, left to fend for themselves when their mother disappears into the jungle with a mysterious man. The children wander alone until they encounter a massive split rock called Batu Belah Batu Bertangkup — a sentient stone that opens and closes like a mouth, devouring anyone who passes too close. The sister is swallowed by the rock, but the resourceful brother uses trickery and the help of forest animals to rescue her. The story teaches children about responsibility, family loyalty, and the dangers of trusting strangers.

title: Bawang Merah Bawang Putih (Shallot and Garlic)
summary: A popular Javanese folktale of two stepsisters: Bawang Putih (Garlic), who is kind, diligent, and beautiful, and Bawang Merah (Shallot), who is spoiled, lazy, and cruel. After their father dies, Bawang Putih is mistreated by her stepmother and stepsister. While washing clothes in the river, she accidentally loses a garment and meets an old woman who returns it after Bawang Putih helps her with chores. The old woman rewards her with a pumpkin containing jewels. Greedy Bawang Merah replicates the journey but behaves rudely, receiving a pumpkin filled with snakes and scorpions. The story teaches that kindness is always rewarded while greed and cruelty bring misfortune.

title: Bayajidda Slays the Serpent of Daura
summary: The foundational legend of the Hausa people tells of Bayajidda (Abu Yazid), a prince from Baghdad who traveled across Africa to Daura, where a fearsome serpent named Sarki guarded the town's only well, the Kusugu well. The serpent only allowed the people to draw water on Fridays. Bayajidda, unaware of the danger, went to the well on a Thursday. When the serpent attacked, he cut off its head with his sword. As a reward, Queen Daurama offered him half her kingdom, but Bayajidda instead asked for her hand in marriage, ending the tradition of celibate queens. Their son Bawo fathered six sons who, along with Bayajidda's first son Biram, became the founders of the seven Hausa states: Daura, Kano, Katsina, Zaria, Rano, Gobir, and Biram.

title: Beaivi: The Sun Goddess's Journey
summary: The myth of Beaivi, the Sámi sun goddess who travels with her daughter through the sky in an enclosure covered with reindeer bones and antlers, bringing spring. In winter, she disappears below the horizon for two months in the far north. On the winter solstice, white female reindeer were sacrificed to ensure her return. Butter was smeared on doorposts to strengthen her. Madness was believed to result from her absence during the dark winter months.

title: Beauty and the Beast
summary: A beautiful young woman agrees to live with a beast to save her father. Through her kindness and growing love, the beast transforms into a handsome prince.

title: Beauty and the Beast (Swedish)
summary: Helena Nyblom's Swedish adaptation of the classic French fairy tale. A merchant's daughter sacrifices herself to live with a hideous Beast to save her father's life. Over time she learns to see past appearance and grows to love the Beast, whose love breaks an enchantment and reveals a handsome prince. Nyblom's version appeared in Bland tomtar och troll (1911) with illustrations by John Bauer.

title: Behula and Lakhindar — The Serpent Goddess's Trial
summary: Chand Saudagar, a wealthy merchant and devotee of Shiva, refused to worship the serpent goddess Manasa. In revenge, Manasa killed his six elder sons by snakebite. His last son, Lakhindar, was married to Behula in a specially constructed iron chamber meant to protect him from snakes. But on the wedding night, Manasa sent a snake that entered through a tiny crevice and killed Lakhindar. Refusing to accept her husband's death, Behula placed his body on a banana-leaf raft and floated down the river for nine months, enduring storms and dangers, until she reached the court of the gods. Her unwavering devotion moved Manasa, who restored Lakhindar and all his brothers to life. Chand finally acknowledged Manasa's divinity. Behula is celebrated in Bengali culture as the epitome of wifely devotion.

title: Behula: The Faithful Wife of Bengali Legend
summary: A woman sails her dead husband's body down a river to win his life back from the snake goddess.

title: Belliegħa, the Water Witch
summary: A water-dwelling spirit from Maltese folklore who guards the freshwater springs and punishes those who waste water.

title: Belt il-Għasel, the Witch of the Honey Ravine
summary: A mysterious witch who lives in a ravine filled with wild honey, luring children with her sweet treats and teaching them hard lessons.

title: Berggeist, the Mountain Spirit
summary: A nature spirit of the Alps that lives in the mountains of Liechtenstein, the Berggeist guards the mineral wealth and punishes greedy miners.

title: Bergsrå's Secret
summary: A respectful miner earns the favor of the Bergsrå, the mountain spirit, discovering that humility and honor are the true keys to unlocking the earth's riches.

title: Bhil Origin Story — The Birth of the Bhil People
summary: The Bhil tribe, one of India's largest Adivasi groups, traces its origin to the god Mahadev (Shiva). According to the myth, Mahadev was roaming the forest when he created a bow and arrow to teach humanity survival. The first Bhil was born from the sweat of Mahadev's brow. Another version tells that the goddess Parvati created the first Bhil woman from her combings, and Mahadev created the first Bhil man from his nail parings. The bow and arrow (dhanush and teer) is central to Bhil identity — every Bhil is traditionally a skilled archer. The legend of Bhilna Dev and the tiger, in which a Bhil hero tames a man-eating tiger using only his bow and his wits, remains a central cultural story. The Bhil goddess Bhadbhavi is the protector of forests and is invoked before hunting expeditions.

title: Bieggolmmái: The Wind God's Shovels
summary: Bieggolmmái (the Wind Man) is the god of wind who lives in a cave. He holds two shovels—one to release wind from his cave and one to put it back. According to the Nærøy manuscript, he had a club in his left hand to chase the wind back. He was crucial for reindeer herding because reindeer travel into headwinds to avoid mosquitoes. Sacrifices of horns were made at Piegg-oaivadz fells. Tiny birch-bark boats with offerings were set adrift as sacrifices.

title: Big Peter and Little Peter
summary: Two brothers of vastly different sizes—one a giant and one tiny—set out to seek their fortune. Though they are opposites in physical stature, they find that their differing abilities complement each other perfectly, allowing them to succeed where others failed.

title: Big Water Creature and the Great Flood
summary: In the Third World, after the reunion of men and women, a mother and her two daughters missed the raft crossing and swam the river. Big Water Creature (Tééhoołtsódii) seized the daughters and dragged them underwater. Talking God and Water Sprinkler created bowls of white and blue shell that spun an opening to an underwater house. First Man and First Woman rescued the girls while Coyote (First Angry) stole Big Water Creature's own two children. In retaliation, Big Water Creature sent a great flood from all directions. The people fled to the sacred mountain Sisnaajiní, where First Man planted the Male Reed. Woodpecker hollowed the reed, and the people climbed into the Fourth World through its passage, just ahead of the rising waters.

title: Bigorn the Forger of Chains
summary: An iron chain spirit called Bigorn haunts the old colonial smithies, binding the wrists of those who enslaved others and forging unbreakable links of conscience.

title: Bijan and Manijeh
summary: Bijan, a knight of Iran and son of Giv, is sent to drive wild boars from Armenian fields. Afterward, the envious knight Gorgin tempts Bijan to cross into enemy Turan by describing the beautiful gardens of Afrasiab. Bijan meets Manijeh, the daughter of Afrasiab, and they fall in love. She drugs him and smuggles him into her chambers, but Afrasiab discovers them and chains Bijan in a dungeon. Manijeh is exiled to wander the wilderness. The Iranian king Kay Khosrow sees Bijan in his crystal cup and sends Rostam disguised as a merchant into Turan. With Manijeh's help, Rostam frees Bijan and returns him to Iran, where Manijeh becomes his wife.

title: Birth of the Harp
summary: Wainamoinen creates the first kantele from the jawbone of a giant pike. When he plays the instrument, the music is so hauntingly beautiful that all of nature, animals, and even the gods are moved to tears by the sound.

title: Birth of the Nine Diseases
summary: In a moment of cosmic imbalance or divine punishment, the nine diseases are created. These ailments spread across the world, bringing suffering, sickness, and death to humanity for the first time.

title: Birth of the Second Harp
summary: A second, more powerful harp is fashioned, symbolizing a new era of music and magic. This instrument allows for even deeper insights into the mysteries of the universe and the will of the gods.

title: Birth of Wainamoinen
summary: In primeval times, the Daughter of the Ether descends to the ocean. A duck nests on her knee, laying six golden eggs and one iron egg. These eggs break, forming the earth, sky, sun, moon, and stars. Wainamoinen is born and spends years in the womb before emerging as an old, wise singer and enchanter who shapes the early world.

title: Bishop Svedberg and the Devil
summary: Bishop Svedberg's wagon loses a wheel on the way to Brunsbo but he calmly continues the journey. Upon arrival he reveals the devil himself had been serving as the missing wheel. The devil later burns down Brunsbo in revenge and the bishop banishes him to hell.

title: Blockhead Hans
summary: A story about a man who is considered a fool by society, but whose simple, honest nature and unwavering kindness lead to an unexpected positive outcome and the realization of his true worth.

title: Blue Jay Finds a Wife (Chinook)
summary: Ioi decided it was high time for Blue Jay to quit his playful trickery and settle down with a wife. She told him he must select a wife from the land of the dead, from the Supernatural People. Ioi recommended that Blue Jay choose an old woman and suggested the recently deceased wife of a chief. Blue Jay went to the ghost town and courted the ghost woman. True to his nature, he behaved foolishly, misinterpreting the customs of the dead and acting disrespectfully. He made inappropriate jokes and did not understand that the ghosts perceived reality differently than the living. Despite Ioi's warnings, Blue Jay's behavior caused chaos in the ghost village. The story highlights Blue Jay's inability to mature and learn from experience, making him a comic but ultimately tragic figure. It is also one of several Chinook stories that explore the relationship between the living and the dead, suggesting that the boundary between worlds must be approached with humility and respect.

title: Blue Jay Visits Ghost Town (Chinook - Ioi and Blue Jay)
summary: Blue Jay's sister Ioi was bought by ghosts as a wife and disappeared to the land of the dead. After a year, Blue Jay went searching for her. He asked all the trees and birds where people go when they die. He journeyed to the ghost town, which appeared to him as a place of bones and decay, but the ghosts saw it as beautiful. Ioi warned Blue Jay not to laugh at the ghosts or behave disrespectfully, but Blue Jay could not control himself. He kicked skulls, laughed at the skeletons, and shouted at the ghost people who were only skeletons to his eyes. When the ghosts went to butcher a whale, Blue Jay saw only a beached skeleton. When they brought in firewood, he saw only bark. Ioi kept explaining that his eyes saw differently because he was alive — the ghosts saw everything as beautiful. He tried to join the ghost dances, but when the ghosts danced gracefully, Blue Jay stood on his head. He died a second time and remained in the ghost world forever. This haunting story explores the boundary between life and death and the dangers of lacking respect for the supernatural world.

title: Bluebeard
summary: Once there lived a man of immense wealth who owned fine houses in town and country, with silver and gold plate, embroidered furniture, and gilded coaches.

title: Bodu Naga: The Serpent Spirit of the Lagoon
summary: Bodu Naga is a great serpent spirit in Maldivian folklore inhabiting lagoons, reefs, and deep channels between islands. In pre-Islamic Maldives, Nagas were revered as powerful nature spirits associated with the waters that surrounded the atolls. Fishermen offered prayers and small offerings before venturing into waters believed to be guarded by Bodu Naga to ensure safe passage and abundant catch. The entity is part of a broader Maldivian tradition of spirit beings (handi, fureytha, dhevi) that could appear in human form — often as beautiful women or well-built men — to lure humans. The Bodu Naga legend reflects the ancient Dravidian naga worship that existed in the Maldives before Buddhism and Islam, and shares similarities with serpent traditions across South India and Sri Lanka. The nagas were said to have been subdued as Buddhism spread through the Indian Ocean, but their stories persist in folklore about dangerous waters and forbidden reefs.

title: Bonbibi – The Lady of the Sundarbans Forest
summary: Bonbibi is the guardian spirit of the Sundarbans mangrove forest, worshipped by both Hindus and Muslims in Bengal and Bangladesh. According to legend, she was sent by Allah to protect forest-dwellers from the demon-king Dakkhin Rai, who ruled the forest in the form of a tiger and demanded human sacrifices. Bonbibi, accompanied by her brother Shah Jangali, fought and defeated Dakkhin Rai, forcing him to agree never to harm those who called upon Bonbibi's name. Before entering the forest to collect honey or wood, locals pray to Bonbibi for protection against tigers, and her shrines are found throughout the Sundarbans. She represents the syncretic folk traditions of Bengal where Hindu and Muslim practices blend seamlessly.

title: Bonbibi: The Guardian of the Sundarbans
summary: A goddess revered by both Hindus and Muslims protects the people of the Sundarbans from the tiger demon.

title: Boots and His Brothers
summary: Three brothers try to win a princess by felling a magical oak and digging a well. The older brothers fail and are exiled, but the youngest, Boots, uses magical tools to succeed.

title: Boots and the Troll
summary: A poor boy who is ridiculed for wearing oversized boots discovers that the footwear possesses magical properties that allow him to outsmart a greedy troll. Through wit and the strange power of his boots, he manages to secure a fortune and prove his worth to the community that once mocked him.

title: Boots Who Made the Princess Say 'That's a Story'
summary: A king offers his daughter's hand to anyone who can make her admit a story is a lie. Boots wins by telling an increasingly absurd tale of exaggeration that eventually forces the princess to concede.

title: Boukhencha: The Ogre of the Moroccan Mountains
summary: In the villages of the Rif and the Atlas Mountains, where the Berber traditions run deep and the night air carries the scent of mint and cedar, parents tell their children about Boukhencha.

title: Bouki the Hyena's Greed (Wolof)
summary: Bouki the Hyena found a field of ripe watermelons and decided to eat them all. But each time he took a bite, the vine made a creaking sound that terrified him because he thought it was a farmer approaching. Bouki became so paranoid that he refused to eat alone and begged Leuk the Hare to join him. Leuk agreed on one condition: Bouki must close his eyes and not open them until Leuk said so. Leuk then ate all the best watermelons while Bouki sat with his eyes closed. When Bouki finally opened his eyes, only the rotten rinds remained. Bouki complained, but Leuk shrugged and said that greedy creatures do not deserve good things. The story serves as a cautionary tale about greed and the importance of sharing. Bouki's constant hunger and foolishness represent the consequences of selfishness in Wolof moral teaching.

title: Bouti, the Red Sea Demon
summary: A malevolent sea demon of Djiboutian folklore, Bouti rises from the depths during storms to capsize boats and drown sailors.

title: Brer Cooter (Terrapin) and the Deer: The Great Race
summary: In this Gullah Geechee variant of the classic trickster race tale, Brer Cooter (the terrapin) and Brer Deer are both courting the same young lady. She declares she will marry whichever one wins a ten-mile race. Brer Deer laughs at the slow-moving terrapin, but Brer Cooter is clever. He stations nine members of his family at each mile marker along the race course, and he himself waits at the start right in front of the young lady's door. At nine o'clock, the race begins. Brer Deer springs forward while Brer Cooter disappears. At the first mile marker, Brer Deer calls out, 'Brer Cooter!' A voice answers from the broomgrass, 'I'm here too!' At every mile post, the same thing happens: Brer Deer calls out, and a terrapin voice answers. By the ninth mile, Brer Deer believes he is about to tie with Brer Cooter. But at the finish line, Brer Cooter is already there, having won the race and the young lady's hand. The tale reinforces that speed alone does not win—strategy, family, and preparation are just as important as raw ability.

title: Brer Rabbit and the Briar Patch (Bred and Bawn)
summary: After Brer Fox captures Brer Rabbit using the Tar-Baby, he declares his intent to kill and eat him. Brer Rabbit pleads for his life, begging not to be thrown into the briar patch, suggesting instead that he be roasted, hanged, drowned, or skinned. The more Brer Rabbit begs to avoid the briar patch, the more determined Brer Fox becomes to throw him there. Finally, Brer Fox snatches Brer Rabbit by the hind legs and flings him deep into the briar patch. To Brer Fox's astonishment, Brer Rabbit appears on a hillside, picking burrs from his fur, and shouts back: 'Bred en bawn in a brier-patch, Brer Fox—bred en bawn in a brier-patch!' The briar patch, which would tear the skin of any other creature, was Brer Rabbit's ancestral home.

title: Brer Rabbit and the Moon in the Millpond
summary: A classic African American trickster tale in which Brer Rabbit, feeling thirsty, goes to the millpond to drink and sees the moon reflected in the water. Mistaking it for a golden cheese wheel, he tries to retrieve it. Unable to reach it from the bank, he tricks Brer Fox into helping him by claiming there is a valuable treasure in the pond. Brer Fox ties a rope around Brer Rabbit's waist and lowers him down, but Brer Rabbit only stirs up the water, making the reflection disappear. He claims the treasure sank and convinces Brer Fox to jump in after it, leaving Brer Fox cold and humiliated while Brer Rabbit laughs and feasts on the cheese he finds elsewhere.

title: Brer Rabbit Finds His Match at Last
summary: Brer Rabbit, overconfident after countless successful tricks, encounters a creature he cannot outsmart. In some versions, it is Old Man Tarrypin (the terrapin) who turns the tables on Brer Rabbit; snip in others, it is a wise old woman or a young girl who matches wits with him. Brer Rabbit tries every trick in his repertoire—false friendliness, reverse psychology, flattery, and fear—but nothing works. The creature remains calm, sees through every deception, and ultimately traps Brer Rabbit in a situation where his cleverness fails him. Brer Rabbit must humble himself, admit defeat, and negotiate his release. This tale serves as a caution that even the most cunning trickster may eventually meet his match, reminding listeners that overconfidence is the trickster's own greatest vulnerability.

title: Brer Rabbit Nibbles Up the Butter
summary: Brer Rabbit, Brer Fox, Brer Possum, and Brer Coon together churn butter and set it aside to share later. Brer Rabbit grows hungry and secretly eats all the butter. When the friends discover the butter is gone, Brer Rabbit blames Brer Possum and suggests they test who is guilty by having each lie down in the sun and see whose belly the butter melts from. Brer Rabbit arranges things so that Brer Possum ends up sitting on the butter smear, and when the sun warms him, the butter appears on his fur. Brer Possum is punished for Brer Rabbit's crime, while Brer Rabbit escapes blame through clever manipulation. The story explains why the possum plays dead when caught—he learned to be wary of being tricked again.

title: Brer Rabbit Rides Brer Fox
summary: Brer Rabbit, seeking to prove his superiority, convinces Miss Meadows and the girls that he can ride Brer Fox like a horse. Brer Fox overhears this boast and vows revenge. The next day, Brer Rabbit pretends to be sick and asks Brer Fox to carry him to Miss Meadows's house. Once on Brer Fox's back, Brer Rabbit digs in his heels and rides Brer Fox straight to the gathering, where he shows off by declaring: 'This is the way I ride Brer Fox!' Humiliated, Brer Fox shakes him off, but Brer Rabbit escapes into a hollow tree. Brer Fox enlists Brer Wolf to help dig him out, but Brer Rabbit tricks them by claiming enemies are approaching and sends them fleeing. The tale is part of a cycle of African trickster stories also found in the Caribbean and South America.

title: Brer Rabbit's Laughing Place
summary: Brer Fox catches Brer Rabbit and declares he will finally kill him. Brer Rabbit, always quick-witted, says he does not care about dying but begs to be allowed to visit his 'laughing place' one last time to die happy. Curious, Brer Fox agrees and follows Brer Rabbit into the woods. Brer Rabbit leads him to a hollow tree filled with a swarm of angry bees. Brer Rabbit points to the tree and whispers that his laughing place is inside. When Brer Fox peers into the hollow, the bees swarm out and attack him furiously. While Brer Fox flees in agony, Brer Rabbit laughs himself silly and escapes once again, proving that his most dangerous weapon is his clever tongue.

title: Brer Terrapin Outruns Brer Rabbit
summary: Brer Rabbit, proud of his speed, mocks Brer Terrapin for his slow, plodding pace. Brer Terrapin challenges Brer Rabbit to a race. Knowing he cannot win on speed alone, Brer Terrapin stations his wife and several family members at intervals along the race course. At each mile marker, Brer Rabbit calls out 'Brer Terrapin!' and one of the terrapin family calls back, 'Here I am!' After several such exchanges, Brer Rabbit grows exhausted and confused, unable to understand how the slow terrapin keeps ahead of him. When Brer Terrapin crosses the finish line first, Brer Rabbit collapses from exhaustion. The story—a variant of the tortoise and hare theme—is a cornerstone of African American animal folklore, reinforcing that patience and strategy triumph over arrogance.

title: Briar Rose (Sleeping Beauty)
summary: In times long past, a king and queen ruled a prosperous kingdom. Centers on Fairy,  from Europe. nature-spirit associated with forest and meadow..

title: Brother Martin
summary: Set during Sweden's Christianization, Brother Martin, a monk from Sigtuna, travels into the remote Bergslagen region to missionize among pagan forest dwellers. The deep woods are still ruled by the old beliefs, and he finds himself unable to convert the stubborn, idolatrous people. As he pushes deeper into the wilderness, he is set upon by trolls, elves, and other supernatural beings that guard the ancient ways. Despite his unwavering devotion, Brother Martin is overwhelmed by the hostile forces and suffers martyrdom, receiving the martyr's crown in heaven.

title: Bruin and Reynard
summary: A series of encounters between Bruin the Bear and Reynard the Fox, where the fox's superior intelligence and deceptive nature allow him to repeatedly outsmart the stronger but slower-witted bear, often leading the bear into ridiculous and embarrassing situations.

title: Bu Darya, the Father of the Sea
summary: A powerful sea demon who rules the waters of the Arabian Gulf, demanding respect and tribute from every sailor who ventures into his domain.

title: Bu Draya of the Deep Channel
summary: A fleet of pearl divers encounters the Bu Draya, a massive sea creature that guards the deepest channel between Bahrain and the mainland, and must negotiate safe passage.

title: Bukha Noyon the Bull God
summary: A Buryat myth about Bukha Noyon, the sacred bull god who descended from the sky to create the world. In the beginning, the sky god sent Bukha Noyon, a massive celestial bull, down to the primordial waters. The bull dredged up mud from the bottom with his horns, which the creator used to form the earth. Bukha Noyon then became the progenitor of the Buryat people, particularly the western Buryat clans. He is associated with fertility, strength, and the mountains of the Baikal region. Sacred sites dedicated to Bukha Noyon still exist in Buryatia, where traditional offerings are made. The bull is considered the totemic ancestor and protector of the Buryat people, and his legend reinforces the strong pastoral traditions of Buryat nomadic culture.

title: Bukit Shahbandar (The Warning Hill)
summary: A Bruneian legend about Datu Mansur, a corrupt Shahbandar (harbor master) who abused his authority by overtaxing merchants and stealing from the Sultan's treasury. The people suffered under his greed, but none dared speak against him. An elderly village bomoh (shaman) named Nenek Fatimah warned him that the ancestors would not tolerate his corruption. When Datu Mansur dismissed her and increased his oppression, supernatural storms gathered over his hilltop settlement. Lightning struck the ground, the earth trembled, and the entire settlement — including Datu Mansur — was transformed into stone. The hill became a permanent warning to those who abuse power. Today, Bukit Shahbandar stands as a reminder of divine justice and the consequences of corruption in leadership.

title: Bukwus the Wild Man of the Woods (Kwakwaka'wakw)
summary: Bukwus is the male counterpart of D'Sonoqua, the Wild Man of the Woods in Kwakwaka'wakw mythology. He is a hairy, giant being who lives in the deep forests and is associated with the spirits of those who died by starvation or exposure. Bukwus roams the woods calling out in a hollow voice, trying to lure humans into the forest with promises of food. He is particularly dangerous because he appears as a starving, pitiful figure who begs for help, but anyone who follows him becomes lost forever and joins his ghostly company. Unlike D'Sonoqua, who is more easily outwitted, Bukwus is treacherous and deceptive. However, like D'Sonoqua, he is also associated with great wealth and can bestow supernatural powers upon those who manage to survive an encounter with him. Bukwus appears in both the T'seka (Red Cedar Bark Ceremonies) and the Tła'sala (Peace Dances), where dancers wear masks depicting his gaunt, haunted features.

title: Bunyip
summary: In the billabongs, swamps, and deep waterholes of Australia, there dwells a creature of ancient legend—the Bunyip.

title: Bushy Bride
summary: A man marries a woman who appears bushy and strange in form, much to the surprise of his family. However, her outward appearance hides a magical nature and a virtuous heart, which eventually bring prosperity and joy to the household.

title: Buttercup
summary: A plump and fond-of-good-things boy named Buttercup is captured by a wicked witch. Despite her terrifying nature, Buttercup uses his quick wit and appetite to outmaneuver her, eventually escaping her clutches to find wealth and freedom.

title: Butu, the Sierra Leonean Spirit
summary: A forest spirit of Sierra Leone, Butu is a mysterious being that haunts the dense jungles, punishing those who harm the sacred groves.

title: Buzz Buzz, the Modern Spirit
summary: A mysterious spirit of the modern era, Buzz Buzz is said to manifest through electronic devices, a digital-age counterpart to traditional nature spirits.

title: Bwiti, the Sacred Path
summary: Bwiti is a central spiritual tradition of Gabon, a sacred practice involving the iboga plant that connects initiates to the spirit world.

title: Bárðar Saga - The Guardian of Snæfell
summary: Bárðr, born of a human mother and a father who was half-giant and half-troll, settles in Snæfellsnes. After a series of family conflicts involving his brother and children, Bárðr gives away his land and vanishes into the Snæfellsjökull ice cap. He becomes the guardian spirit of the region, appearing in a grey cowl to help those in need during times of great difficulty.

title: Bárðar Saga - The Mound of King Raknarr
summary: Gestr, the son of Bárðr, journeys to the far north to challenge the undead King Raknarr. With the help of a priest and a magic candle, Gestr enters Raknarr's burial mound and beheads the king and his 500 undead crew. However, the magic candle fails, and Gestr is only saved by the divine light of King Olaf, who drains the undead of their strength.

title: Calon Arang the Witch
summary: Before the Maori arrived in New Zealand, the islands were already inhabited by mysterious beings whose stories predate human memory. Calon Arang is one such tale — a story of dark magic and the terror it unleashed upon an ancient kingdom.

title: Capture of the Fire-fish
summary: To restore light and warmth, the heroes embark on a perilous journey to the depths of the ocean to capture a magical fire-fish, which is the only source of fire remaining in the world.

title: Capture of the Sampo
summary: The heroes of Kalevala successfully infiltrate Pohjola and steal the Sampo. A thrilling and dangerous chase ensues as Louhi, the Mistress of Pohjola, pursues them with all her might to reclaim the magical mill.

title: Cedar Woman (Ts'uu Jaas) and the Cedar Tree (Haida)
summary: In Haida worldview, the Cedar Tree is considered an Ancient Sister called Ts'uu Jaasas. She is a SGaana Kiidads (Supernatural Being) and a physical manifestation of the Haida people's interconnected relationship with the land and sea. The cedar tree is regarded as every woman's older sister, known as Ts'uu K'waayGa. This supernatural being taught the Haida people how to use cedar for clothing, shelter, canoes, and baskets. The cedar tree's importance in Haida culture cannot be overstated: it provided the material for the great houses, the seagoing canoes, the bentwood boxes, and the ceremonial regalia. The Haida legal framework, called the Ts'uu JaasGalang HlGaajuu (Older Cedar Sister) Framework, derives from the teachings of this supernatural being, emphasizing the interconnectedness of all life and the responsibility humans have to care for the natural world.

title: Cerberus
summary: At the gates of the Underworld, where the River Styx flows black and cold and the souls of the dead drift like shadows in the mist, there stands a guardian that has never been bribed, never been tricked, and never been defeated.

title: Chang Er on the Moon
summary: A very long time ago, in the age when gods still walked among mortals, there were ten suns in the sky.

title: Changer and the Creation of the World (Coast Salish)
summary: In Coast Salish tradition, dukʷibəɬ the Changer (also known as Xe'las or Xelas) walked the earth when the world was not yet as it is today. Sometimes he appeared as a brilliant light from the East, sometimes as a young man, sometimes as several young men, and sometimes as an invisible old person who knew everything. The Changer went everywhere, preparing the world for the First People who were yet to come. He transformed inappropriate things into useful ones: he turned rocks that beat people over the head into hammers, sticks that struck people into fish spears, and dangerous beings into animals, birds, and landscape features. The Changer also sent a flood to cleanse the earth when things went wrong. All living things were destroyed except one woman and one dog, who fled to the top of Tacobud (Mount Rainier). From them, the next race of people was born. The Changer's work established the Coast Salish understanding of the world as a place shaped by a powerful transformer who continues to watch over the land and its people.

title: Changó, the Lord of Thunder and Fire
summary: Changó (Shangó) is the powerful orisha of thunder, lightning, fire, and war in Cuban Santería/Lucumí, syncretized with Saint Barbara in Catholic tradition. According to myth, Changó was once a king of the Yoruba city of Oyo who was deified after death. He wields a double-headed axe and dances with fiery intensity. Changó's legends tell of his battles, his many lovers including Oshún and Oyá, and his terrible temper. The batá drums are sacred to him, and his number is 6. A famous patakí (sacred story) tells how Changó received his powers from Obatalá and how he used thunder to defeat his enemies. In Cuba, Changó became a symbol of resistance and masculine power for enslaved Africans.

title: Charcoal Nils and the Troll-Woman
summary: A Swedish tale of Nils, a charcoal burner, who encounters a troll-woman in the forest. He outwits her through cleverness and escapes her supernatural traps.

title: Charonda the Blood-Drinker
summary: In the villages of the Karpas Peninsula, the Charonda rises each night to drain the vitality of the living, leaving only hollow shells where people once stood.

title: Chata and Chicksah: The Separation of the Choctaw and Chickasaw (Choctaw/Chickasaw)
summary: Two brothers named Chata and Chicksah led their people from the west, following a sacred pole. Each night they planted the pole in the ground, and each morning they traveled in the direction it leaned. After an immensely long journey, they finally reached a place where the pole stood perfectly upright. There, they laid to rest the bones of their ancestors, which they had carried in buffalo-hide sacks from the original land in the west. The great earthwork mound of Nanih Waiya grew from that burial. Afterward, the land could not support all the people. Chicksah took half the people and departed north, becoming the Chickasaw tribe. Chata and the others remained near Nanih Waiya and became the Choctaw. This shared origin story explains the close relationship between the two tribes.

title: Cheval Mal Fet, the Cursed Steed
summary: A ghostly black horse that appears on the roads of Wallonia, carrying a demonic rider who tempts travelers into deadly bargains.

title: Cheyenne Creation Story
summary: In the beginning, all was water and nothing existed but the Creator Ma'heo'o and aquatic birds. The Creator sent various waterbirds—the loon, otter, beaver, and turtle—to dive to the bottom of the endless water to bring up mud. After several failures, the turtle succeeded in bringing up the primordial mud. From this mud, the Creator formed the earth. Then he created grass, trees, animals, and finally human beings. The Cheyenne emerged from beneath the earth onto the surface, guided by the Creator. The story teaches that all creation is interconnected and that humans must respect the earth as their mother.

title: Chhinnamasta — The Self-Decapitated Goddess
summary: Goddess Chhinnamasta (the 'Self-Decapitated One') is a powerful Tantric deity worshipped primarily in Bengal and parts of eastern India. The legend tells that once, while bathing in the Mandakini River with her attendants Dakini and Varnini, Parvati (in her form as Chhinnamasta) was overcome by a ravenous hunger that her attendants also felt. When asked to satisfy their hunger, Parvati severed her own head with a sword and held it in her hand. Three jets of blood spurted from her severed neck — one feeding her own mouth, and two feeding her attendants. The iconography shows her standing in a battlefield, holding her severed head, drinking her own blood. The myth symbolizes the goddess's power to transcend death and her role as both destroyer and sustainer of cosmic energy (Shakti).

title: Chickasaw Creation and the Sacred Pole (Chickasaw)
summary: The Chickasaw creation story tells of their emergence as a people guided by a sacred pole. According to tradition, the Chickasaw and Choctaw were originally one people who migrated from the west. They carried a sacred pole (sometimes described as a dogwood pole) which they planted each night. Each morning, they would travel in the direction the pole leaned. After a long journey, the pole stood perfectly upright at the site of Nanih Waiya mound in Mississippi. There they divided: the Chickasaw, led by Chicksah, traveled north, while the Choctaw, led by Chata, remained. The Chickasaw settled in northern Mississippi, western Tennessee, and northwestern Alabama. Before arriving at Nanih Waiya, they had emerged into this world from a hole in the ground at a place where the sun rises.

title: Chickasaw Flood Myth (Chickasaw)
summary: The Chickasaw flood myth tells of a time when the earth was covered by a great deluge. As the waters rose, the people climbed to the highest ground, but the water continued to rise. Ababinili, the Creator, instructed a man and a woman to build a raft and take on board pairs of all the animals. The flood covered even the tallest mountains for many days. When the waters finally receded, the man and woman found themselves at Nanih Waiya, the sacred mound. From them, the Chickasaw people were reborn. The flood myth shares elements with the Choctaw flood legend, reflecting their shared origins. The story emphasizes renewal and divine mercy — the Creator preserved a remnant of life to begin anew.

title: Chimera
summary: The Chimera was not one monster but three, all wrapped into one terrible form.. Its head was the head of a lion—the king of beasts—but wrong, changed.

title: Chimi Lhakhang and the Divine Madman Drukpa Kunley
summary: Chimi Lhakhang (the Fertility Temple) in Punakha district, Bhutan, is associated with Drukpa Kunley (1455–1529), the 'Divine Madman' — a Buddhist monk famous for his outrageous methods of teaching. When three demonesses terrorized the Dochula Pass, Drukpa Kunley pursued them to Lobesa Hill, where the chief demoness Loro Duem transformed into a dog. Kunley subdued her using his phallus — called the 'Flaming Thunderbolt of Wisdom' — and buried her under a black chorten, naming the site 'Chimi' (meaning 'no dog'). The temple, built in 1499, is a fertility pilgrimage site where childless couples receive blessings by being struck on the head with a 10-inch ivory and wood phallus. Drukpa Kunley is credited with introducing phallus paintings on Bhutanese houses to drive away evil spirits. His dog Sachi is also enshrined with him in the temple.

title: Chinthe: The Lion Guardians of the Burmese Pagodas
summary: Half-lion half-dragon guardians protect the entrances of pagodas across Myanmar.

title: Chitapo of the Silent Lake
summary: A woman grieving the loss of her child wanders to a lake in the Bangweulu wetlands and encounters Chitapo, a lake spirit who offers to return what was taken but demands a price measured in memory.
