title: Chiuta, the Spider Who Wove the World
summary: Before the world had form, Chiuta the Spider sat upon the void and spun the first web — and from that web, the rivers, the mountains, and the people were born.
themes: the interconnectedness of all living things
the divine present in the humble

title: Chiwara: The Antelope Spirit Who Taught Agriculture
summary: The Bambara people of Mali revere Chiwara, a mythical half-human, half-antelope being who taught humans the fundamentals of agriculture. Chiwara used its antlers and a pointed stick to dig into the earth, making it possible for humans to cultivate the land. The people watched the antelope and followed its example to create their own farms, becoming expert farmers. Their harvests grew so bountiful that they began wasting the grain, taking abundance for granted. Disappointed, Chiwara buried itself deep into the earth and disappeared. The elders, regretting the loss of their great teacher, ordered that masks be made in Chiwara's memory. To this day, Bambara dancers wear Chiwara headdresses in ceremonies that honor the agricultural spirit, leaping and turning like antelopes to keep the teaching alive.

title: Choctaw Creation: The Emergence from Nanih Waiya (Choctaw)
summary: In the beginning, there was a great mound called Nanih Waiya. The Creator fashioned the first people from the earth within this mound. These first Choctaw emerged from a long, dark cave that led from the center of the mound into daylight. After emerging, they scattered across the land to populate the earth. When a great flood arose, the Choctaw people fled by canoe to an island, guided by a dove. They prospered there but eventually overpopulated the island. They traveled back to the coast of Turtle Island and journeyed for hundreds of years, eventually reaching the Yucatan and finally settling in what is now Mississippi. They rebuilt their sacred Nanih Waiya and found a home for the bones of their ancestors that they had carried throughout their long migration.

title: Chuhayster: The Windy Grandfather of the Carpathians
summary: A cheerful forest spirit protects travelers from the dangerous mavkas in the Carpathian Mountains.

title: Chupacabra: The Goat Sucker
summary: A creature that drains the blood of livestock, appearing after strange lights in the Puerto Rican night.

title: Chura-Batyr: The Hero of Kazan
summary: Chura-Batyr is the heroic epic of the Tatar people, set in the mid-16th century during the Kazan Khanate's struggle against the expanding Moscow state. Chura is a batyr (hero) who defends Kazan against Russian invasion. The epic contains ancient motifs including Chura's miraculous birth to elderly parents after years of childlessness, his heroic childhood, his journey to Kazan with the blessing of a holy elder, and his service to the khan. The Tatar version emphasizes Chura's resistance against Ivan the Terrible's forces. In the most moving section, Chura is betrayed and killed through treachery, but his sacrifice inspires the Tatar people to continue fighting. The epic is a powerful expression of Tatar national identity and resistance, surviving in multiple versions among Kazan Tatars, Crimean Tatars, Nogais, and Kazakhs.

title: Chyskhaan, the Snow Spirit
summary: The Yakut legend of Chyskhaan, the powerful spirit of winter and cold who rules over the frozen landscape of Siberia. Chyskhaan is depicted as a towering figure with icy breath that can freeze anything instantly and a heart made of permafrost. He is both feared and respected by the Sakha people, as he governs the long, brutal winters that define life in Yakutia. Offerings are made to appease him before the onset of winter. In modern Sakha culture, Chyskhaan has been adopted as a regional Father Frost figure (similar to Ded Moroz) while retaining his ancient animistic origins as the personification of the extreme cold that can reach -60°C.

title: Cinderella
summary: A mistreated girl goes to the ball with magic help. Centers on Fairy,  from Europe. nature-spirit associated with forest and meadow..

title: Comanche Creation: The Dust People
summary: The Great Spirit collected swirls of dust from the four directions—north, south, east, and west—and molded them into strong, powerful figures. He breathed life into them, and the Comanche people were born from the earth itself, infused with the strength of mighty storms and the spirit of the wind. However, a shape-shifting demon formed in the shadows, envious of the people's power. It tormented the Comanche by taking many forms. The Great Spirit cast the demon into a bottomless pit, but before falling, the demon shattered into countless pieces that took refuge in the fangs and stingers of rattlesnakes, scorpions, and spiders, continuing to harm people to this day.

title: Corn Woman (Creek)
summary: Corn Woman is a central figure in Muscogee Creek mythology. Her origin story varies across traditions: in one version, corn fell from a woman's feet after she rubbed them together; in another, corn poured from her thigh after she scratched it. Many legends end with Corn Woman sacrificing herself to allow corn crops to grow, symbolizing how life comes from death. Corn Woman is closely associated with female fertility and the agricultural cycle. The Green Corn Ceremony, the most important Muscogee ritual, honors her gift and marks the beginning of the new year. The story emphasizes the sacred nature of agriculture and the interconnectedness of women's creative power and the growth of corn, the tribe's staple food.

title: Corn Woman and the Origin of Corn (Natchez)
summary: The Natchez legend of Corn Woman (also known as Corn-Woman's Son) tells how agriculture came to the people. According to the story, Corn Woman gave birth to a son and from her body came the first corn. In one version, corn poured from her thigh when she scratched it. In another, she sacrificed herself so that corn would grow from her burial place. Her son became the first Great Sun, the divine ruler of the Natchez. The story establishes the connection between female fertility, sacrifice, and agricultural abundance. Corn was the staple crop of the Natchez, and its cultivation was surrounded by ritual and ceremony. The legend teaches that food is a gift that comes through sacrifice and that the people must honor that gift through proper ceremonies.

title: Coviella
summary: In the sun-drenched hills of the Italian countryside, where olive groves stretch across terraced slopes and the scent of rosemary and thyme drifts on the warm breeze, there once lived a young woman named Coviella.

title: Coyote and Eagle Steal the Sun and Moon
summary: A Zuni story explaining the origin of day and night and the changing seasons. In the beginning, the Sun and Moon were kept locked in boxes by a powerful being who would not release them. The world was in perpetual twilight. Coyote and Eagle, two of the most clever animals, devised a plan. Eagle flew to the being's home with Coyote hidden in his feathers. While the being slept, Coyote crept out, opened the boxes, and Eagle seized the Sun and Moon with his talons. They fled, pursued by the angry being. Eagle rose higher and higher into the sky, placing the Sun and Moon in their proper positions. But in the chaos, Coyote dropped the box containing half the daylight, which shattered. This is why days are shorter in winter than in summer, and why daylight decreases after the summer solstice. The story reflects the Zuni understanding of astronomical cycles and the partnership between sky and earth creatures.

title: Coyote and the Creation of the Tribes (Chinook/Chelan)
summary: Long ago, the Great Chief Above made the world, then the animals and birds. After twelve moons, the animal people gathered. Bluejay, Meadowlark, and Coyote complained about their names, but the Creator declared that names would stay as given. The Creator told Coyote he would be the head of all creatures and given power to keep peace. As the Creator foretold, things became bad — mountains swallowed creatures, winds blew them away. Coyote stopped the mountains and winds, rescued the creatures, and made laws for natural forces. When Coyote's work was done, the Creator told Coyote he would not make the first human. Instead, the four Wolf Brothers took over. The youngest Wolf Brother killed Beaver and cut it into twelve pieces according to the Creator's instructions. The pieces were given to different animal people who carried them to different regions, where each piece became a different Indian tribe: the Nez Perce from the liver, the Spokane, Lake people, Flathead, and others from different organs. The blood became the Blackfeet. This story explains the origin of the twelve tribes of the Columbia Plateau region.

title: Coyote Helps Decorate the Night
summary: In this Hopi story about the origins of the night sky, the animals were decorating the darkness. Various animals placed stars and patterns in the sky, but Coyote, growing impatient with the slow, careful work, grabbed a handful of stars and threw them carelessly across the sky. This explains why some stars are scattered randomly while others form orderly patterns. Another version tells that Coyote was given the task of placing the stars but became distracted or deliberately did a poor job, resulting in the Milky Way and the chaotic scattering of stars. The story warns against impatience and the consequences of rushing sacred work.

title: Coyote the Comanche Trickster
summary: Coyote is the central trickster figure in Comanche folklore. Unlike the spider tricksters of other Plains tribes, Coyote is a clever but flawed creature who often helps humans while constantly getting into trouble due to greed, dishonesty, and recklessness. Many Comanche storytellers refer to Coyote affectionately as the brother of the Comanches. In one tale, Coyote tries to steal fire from the fire people and is burned, explaining his singed fur. In another, he tricks prairie dogs into leaving their holes so he can catch them, but is himself outwitted by Skunk. Coyote stories teach social values through humor.

title: Crab Water-Spirit of the Mangroves
summary: A water spirit in crab form guards the mangrove forests and coral reefs, dragging fishermen who poison the water into the tides to learn the sea's lessons firsthand.

title: Crane and Changer (Coast Salish)
summary: As told by Snoqualmie Charlie, this story recounts how dukʷibəɬ the Changer came upon a man with very long legs standing by the shore, getting hit over the head by rocks. The Changer asked what he was doing, and the man explained he was trying to get food but the rocks kept hurting him. The Changer took the rocks, declared they would be hammers for the people, and knocked them together, transforming them into useful tools. Then the long-legged man picked up a stick to use as a fish spear, but it too hit him over the head. The Changer took the stick, broke it in two, and declared they would be fish spears. He gave the transformed items to the man and walked away, continuing his journey of preparing the world. The long-legged man was transformed into the Crane, who to this day stands on long legs at the water's edge, using his beak as a fish spear. This is one of many stories showing how the Changer shaped the world by transforming flawed ancestors into the animals and birds we know today.

title: Creation of the Sun and Moon
summary: In the Fourth World of Navajo tradition, First Man, First Woman, and Great Coyote planned the creation of the sun and moon. They summoned Black God (Fire God) from beneath the earth along with Water Sprinkler, House God, and Talking God. Turquoise Boy agreed to become the Sun and White Shell Girl the Moon, but demanded payment: the lives of all beings on earth. First Man heated turquoise on a buckskin with Black God's fire and Turquoise Boy entered it, becoming the Sun (Jóhonaaʼéí, 'The One Who Rules the Day'). White Shell Girl entered white shell and became the Moon (Tłʼéhonaaʼéí, 'The One Who Rules the Night'). They established twelve months with White Shell Girl's whistle of twelve holes. First Angry Coyote, excluded from planning, cursed the arrangement so the moon's months would not match the sun's, bringing irregular seasons and occasional frost and drought.

title: Crow Morning Star
summary: In Crow belief, the Morning Star (Aapisowaahs) is a heroic figure who lights the night sky. He is the son of Naato'si (the Sun) and Ko'komiki'somm (the Moon), created by the first being Apistotoke. Old Man Coyote traveled to the sky world and brought knowledge of the Morning Star back to the people. The Morning Star is associated with new beginnings, hope, and guidance. In Crow ceremonies, the Morning Star is honored at dawn with prayers and songs. The star's appearance signals the time for certain rituals and serves as a reminder of the Crow's connection to the celestial realm.

title: Cunjah Maum and the Healing Roots
summary: On a rice plantation along the South Carolina coast, an old Gullah woman named Cunjah Maum was known as the most powerful rootworker in the Lowcountry. When the master's daughter fell ill with a mysterious fever that no doctor could cure, the master reluctantly sent for Cunjah Maum. She came to the big house and asked for three things: a lock of the girl's hair, water from the spring that flowed east, and privacy. Cunjah Maum ground roots and leaves into a paste, mixed it with the spring water, and sang songs in an African language over the mixture. She rubbed it on the girl's forehead and feet and prayed to ancestors she could see standing in the corners of the room. Within three days, the girl recovered completely. The master offered Cunjah Maum money, but she refused—she asked instead that her grandson be taught to read. The master, grateful, agreed. Cunjah Maum's story embodies the Gullah belief in the power of rootwork to heal not just the body but to negotiate justice in a world where Black people had little power. Her refusal of money and demand for literacy represents the deeper value of knowledge over wealth.

title: Curupira: The Forest Guardian of Brazil
summary: A forest spirit with backward-facing feet protects the Amazon from those who would destroy it.

title: Cú Chulainn and the Salmon of Knowledge
summary: In the green, rolling hills of ancient Ireland, beside the silver waters of the River Boyne, there lived a poet named Finegas.

title: D'Sonoqua (Dzunukwa) and the Children (Kwakwaka'wakw)
summary: D'Sonoqua, also known as Dzunukwa or Tsonokwa, is the Wild Woman of the Woods, a giant cannibal ogress in Kwakwaka'wakw tradition. She is black in color with messy hair, pendulous breasts, pursed red lips, and carries a huge basket on her back. She wanders the forests calling 'Hu! Hu!' - a sound that children are told is the wind blowing through cedar trees. She captures children who misbehave or wander too far from home, stuffing them into her basket and carrying them to her remote house in the woods to eat them. However, D'Sonoqua is dim-witted with poor eyesight, and children frequently outwit her. In many versions, a clever child tricks her into sitting on a hot fire or into falling into a pit, killing her and taking her treasures. From the ashes of one burned D'Sonoqua came the first mosquitoes. Despite her fearsome reputation, she is also associated with wealth and is venerated as an ancestor of the Namgis clan through her son Tsilwalagame.

title: Dag and Daga, and the Flying Troll of Sky Mountain
summary: Dag and Daga are orphaned siblings who live alone in a forest cottage after their parents die. Despite being young, they manage to survive through their own resourcefulness: Dag hunts with his bow, and Daga gathers herbs, berries, and mushrooms. They live happily until one day Dag goes hunting and does not return. Daga waits in vain, then discovers only his hat and quiver left behind. Despite the warnings of neighbors who tell her to abandon hope, Daga sets out alone to find her brother. She travels through vast forests and over high mountains, facing dangers and exhaustion. Unbeknownst to her, her loyal house tomte follows and protects her. She encounters a prince who falls in love with her and offers her fine clothes and a golden crown, but when she realizes his servants are not actually searching for Dag, she leaves the finery behind and continues alone. She reaches Sky Mountain, where the terrible Flying Troll dwells. Inside, she finds Dag encased in rock — the troll imprisoned him for failing to learn gold-forging. The troll offers a bargain: if Daga can produce a queen's crown of pure gold before he counts to three, he will free Dag. As the troll begins counting, Daga produces the golden crown the prince gave her and throws it onto the troll's clawed hand. Stunned, the troll must keep his word, and Dag is freed. The reunited siblings return home, and the prince, having punished his dishonest servants, finds Daga and marries her, valuing her loyalty and bravery above all. The story celebrates sibling devotion, courage, and the power of keeping one's word.

title: Dakuwaqa the Shark God
summary: Dakuwaqa is a fearsome shark deity in Fijian mythology who appears as a fierce sea monster guarding the islands. He was greatly respected by fishermen for protecting them from danger at sea. In one creation myth, Dakuwaqa attempted to conquer Kadavu Island by swimming up a river, but the goddess Rokobakaniceva challenged him in the form of a great octopus. After a titanic battle, the octopus pulled out Dakuwaqa's teeth with her eight arms, forcing the shark god to promise never to attack Kadavu again. He became the protector of Kadavu and can shapeshift into any form, but his true form is a muscular Fijian man with the upper torso of a shark.

title: Dame Soåsan
summary: A powerful female troll named Dame Soåsan lives in the hills near Eksjö. She punishes those who insult her and rewards those who show kindness. A poor woman who spins yarn for her grows rich but becomes greedy, cheats the trolls, and loses everything. A servant girl who is kind to troll children is rewarded with cows that return home milked each night.

title: Dangun: The Founder of Korea
summary: A divine being descends from heaven and marries a bear to found the first Korean kingdom.

title: Davy Crockett
summary: The legendary king of the wild frontier, folk hero of American expansion and tall-tale tradition.

title: Death of Lemminkainen
summary: While attempting to kill the swans in the river of the underworld (Tuonela), Lemminkainen is ambushed and killed. His body is brutally torn to pieces and scattered across the river, symbolizing the ultimate price of his hubris and reckless ambition.

title: Degei the Serpent God
summary: The creator god who brought humans from the mountains. Centers on Degei,  from Fiji. deity associated with Polynesian heavens and Polynesian sacred sites..

title: Degei the Serpent God and the Creation of Fiji
summary: Degei, the supreme god of Fijian mythology, is a great serpent who created the world, fruits, and the first humans. He hatched an egg from which the first human couple emerged. Degei lives in a cave near the summit of Mount Uluda in the Nakauvandra Range. Earthquakes and thunder are caused by his uneasy turnings within the cave. He judges newly dead souls who pass through one of two caves, Cibaciba or Drakulu, sending a few to paradise (Burotu) and casting most into a lake to sink to Murimuria for reward or punishment. He is also a god of wrath who punishes by destroying crops or sending floods, and is connected to the snake cult throughout Fiji.

title: Departure of Changing Woman
summary: In Navajo tradition, after the monsters were defeated and the world was made safe, Changing Woman decided to leave the earth. She gathered the Holy People and announced her departure to the West. She created a beautiful floating house made of turquoise, abalone shell, white shell, and jet, located on an island in the western ocean. Before leaving, she blessed the Navajo people and gave them the corn, sheep, and knowledge they would need to prosper. She taught them the ceremonies that would protect and heal them. Changing Woman decreed that she would live in the west forever, aging through the winter and rejuvenating each spring — thus establishing the cycle of seasons. She promised to watch over the Navajo people from her western home and to send her blessings whenever the proper ceremonies were performed.

title: Devi, the Mountain Giant
summary: A race of giants who once ruled the mountains of Georgia before humans drove them into the deep caves, where they still wait to reclaim the surface.

title: Dharumavantha Rasgefaanu: First Convert to Islam
summary: Dharumavantha Rasgefaanu (Sultan Dhovemi) was the king of the Maldives who converted to Islam in 1153 CE, marking the nation's transformation from Buddhism to Islam. According to Maldivian tradition, the king's conversion was triggered by the miracle of Abu'l-Barakat al-Barbari, who vanquished the sea demon Rannamaari by reciting the Quran. The king built the first mosque in the Maldives, the Hukuru Miskiiy (Friday Mosque) in Malé, and declared Islam the state religion. Known for his piety and justice, he was given the name Dharumavantha ('the Pious/Righteous One'). He established the Sultanate and ruled for 29 years. The Isdhoo Loamaafaanu copper plates, one of the oldest written records in Maldivian history, document these events. The conversion of the Maldives is celebrated annually as the Day of Conversion to Islam (2 Rabi'ul Akhir).

title: Dhegdheer: The Cannibal Woman with Long Ears
summary: Dhegdheer ('Long-Ears') was once a normal woman whose selfishness and greed cursed her into a monstrous form. Her ears grew enormous, granting her supernatural hearing — she could detect the faintest heartbeat from miles away. She developed an insatiable hunger for human flesh, particularly children, and would creep silently into villages at night, listening for the sounds of playing or laughing children. Her long ears allowed her to hear whispers through mud walls and locate hidden children. The people lived in constant terror until one brave girl confronted Dhegdheer. The girl realized that the monster's ears, though powerful, were also her weakness. She tricked Dhegdheer into sticking her ears through a small hole in a door, then set the ears on fire. The monster fled, shrieking, never to be seen again. The story teaches Somali children about courage, cleverness, and the consequences of greed.

title: Didibri, the Rainbow Dragon
summary: A great dragon-like serpent associated with the rainbow, sometimes a bringer of destruction and other times a protector of hidden treasure.

title: Diné Bahaneʼ: The Four Worlds
summary: The Navajo creation epic describes four worlds through which the Diyin Dineʼé (Holy People) journeyed. The First World (Niʼ Hodiłhił, Black World) was small with a floating island in four seas, inhabited by Air-Spirit People, insect people, and the four rulers of the seas. First Woman (Áłtsé Asdzą́ą́) and First Man (Áłtsé Hastiin) were formed from clouds and wind. The Second World (Niʼ Hodootłʼizh, Blue World) held blue-gray mammals and swallow people. The Third World (Niʼ Hałtsooí, Yellow World) had two crossing rivers, six sacred mountains, and the Holy People including Talking God, Water Sprinkler, House God, and Black God. A great flood forced emergence into the Fourth World (Niʼ Hodisxǫs, White World) where the current world was shaped and monsters (anaye) roamed until the Hero Twins defeated them.

title: Ditaolane Slays the Devourer Khanyapa
summary: In Basotho mythology, the monstrous Khanyapa (also called Kholumolumo or Kgodumodumo) went about swallowing every living thing in its path, devouring entire villages until only one pregnant woman survived by hiding in a stable, her scent masked by ashes. She prayed to Modimo and gave birth to a son named Ditaolane, who emerged from the womb wearing a necklace of divination bones and instantly grew into a fully grown man. Ditaolane took a knife and went to confront Khanyapa. The monster swallowed him, but inside its belly Ditaolane was unharmed. He slashed the monster's entrails from within, killing it, then carved an opening through which thousands of humans and animals emerged alive. The people he rescued grew to fear him and plotted his death. Ditaolane turned himself into a stone, escaping their treachery. The myth symbolizes the triumph of a single righteous hero over overwhelming darkness.

title: Div (Daeva), the Demon of the Waste
summary: A powerful demon from Zoroastrian tradition who brings drought, disease, and despair to the people of the Afghan highlands.

title: Div-e Sepid, the White Demon
summary: A legendary white demon from Persian epic tradition, the Div-e Sepid is a monstrous being of immense strength who terrorized the heroes of old.

title: Djinn
summary: Before humans, before the world was made as it is now, there were beings made of smokeless fire—beings that did not burn, because they were the fire itself.

title: Doll i' the Grass
summary: A tiny, fairy-like girl discovered in the grass is initially seen as a curiosity. Through her bravery, intelligence, and helpfulness, she becomes indispensable to the royal family, demonstrating that even the smallest among us can possess the greatest strength of character.

title: Don Pedrito Jaramillo — The Healer of Los Olmos
summary: Don Pedro Jaramillo (1829–1907) is the most famous curandero (traditional healer) and folk saint of South Texas. Born to Purépecha parents in Guadalajara, Mexico, he received his healing calling after a vision during a three-day treatment for a nose ailment with mud and water. He moved to the Los Olmos Creek area near Falfurrias, Texas, where for decades he treated thousands of people without charging, living on donations. His cures often involved water — bathing, drinking, or applying water in specific quantities for specific durations — and the number nine played a prominent role in his prescriptions. He was known for his clairvoyance, able to detect if someone was lying about their illness. At the height of his fame, families traveled from as far as New York City to seek his help. His shrine at his burial site in Falfurrias remains a pilgrimage destination, and the Texas State Historical Marker dedicated to him in 1971 was the first bilingual marker in the state. Don Pedrito embodies the tradition of curanderismo that continues to serve Hispanic communities in the borderlands, blending Indigenous healing knowledge with Catholic faith.

title: Doña Sebastiana — The Skeleton in the Cart
summary: Doña Sebastiana is a folk figure from New Mexican Hispano culture, depicted as a skeleton riding a wooden cart or chariot, carrying a bow and arrow. She is the northern New Mexican variant of the Grim Reaper, brought by Spanish colonists and merged with Indigenous death imagery. Unlike the anonymous European Death, Doña Sebastiana has a name and personality — she is said to be vengeful toward sinners but merciful to the faithful. Her image appears in the santero tradition of New Mexican folk art, particularly in the bultos (wooden carvings) of the penitentes. In some stories, she is the same figure as Santa Muerte, while in others she is a separate entity — a skeletal woman who appears to those about to die, giving them a final chance to confess their sins. Her cart is said to be heard rattling through the mountain villages of northern New Mexico on the night before someone dies. The figure of Doña Sebastiana represents the unique religious synthesis of Spanish Catholicism and Puebloan spirituality that characterizes the Hispano culture of New Mexico, a tradition that has endured for over 400 years.

title: Drakaina of the Copper Mines
summary: Beneath the ancient copper mines of Skouriotissa, a dragon守护 the veins of ore and punishes those who take more than the earth can spare.

title: Draugar of the Barrow
summary: A wicked Viking warrior is cursed to remain as an undead draugr, haunting his burial barrow and punishing those who seek his stolen silver.

title: Draugur (Faroese Revenant Legends)
summary: In Faroese folklore, the draugur (dreygur) is a malevolent undead being or revenant, akin to the Norse draugr. Draugar are described as large in build, wearing grey clothes with black hair—the same description given for Huldufólk in Faroese tradition. They are said to inhabit graves, mounds, and coastal areas, often guarding treasure or haunting the living. Unlike ghosts, draugar have physical bodies—animated corpses that can swell to enormous size. In Faroese sea folklore, drowned fishermen may become sea-draugar who haunt the waters where they died. The draugur embodies the thin line between the living and dead in isolated island communities where death at sea was a constant reality.

title: Drukpa Kunley Subduing the Demoness of the Pass
summary: The most famous legend of the Divine Madman Drukpa Kunley recounts his confrontation with the three demonesses of Dochula La. Two lesser demonesses merged into the body of the chief demoness Loro Duem and fled to Punakha. When Loro Duem reached the hillock of Lobesa, she disguised herself as a red dog. Drukpa Kunley, undeterred, caught the dog by the ear and used his 'Thunderbolt of Flaming Wisdom' (his phallus) to subjugate her. He buried the demoness under a giant rock and built a black chorten atop it. The color black symbolized her evil intent. Loro Duem was then transformed into Chhoekim, the local guardian deity (Chos-skyong) of Chimi Lhakhang, vowing to serve the Buddha. The round hillock where the monastery sits is said to 'resemble the breast of a woman.' This legend established Drukpa Kunley's reputation as the 'fertility saint' and the phallus as a protective symbol throughout Bhutan.

title: Duende of the Ceiba Cathedral
summary: A young boy who befriends a forest Duende learns that the small spirits of the Belizean jungle guard the ancient ceiba trees, and their friendship comes with a duty to protect what cannot protect itself.

title: Duende, the Forest Guardian
summary: A small, dwarf-like forest spirit who protects the animals and trees of the Ecuadorian highlands.

title: Dukher Boro — The Great Sorrow of Bengal
summary: Dukher Boro (literally 'Elder Brother of Sorrow') is a tragic figure from the Maimansingha Gitika, a collection of Bengali folk ballads from the Mymensingh region of Bangladesh. The ballad tells of a virtuous man who experiences immense suffering and loss through no fault of his own — losing his family, property, and social standing through a series of cruelly ironic events. The narrative explores themes of social injustice, poverty, and the arbitrary nature of fate in rural Bengal. Unlike the romantic ballads of the collection, Dukher Boro presents a stark, realistic portrayal of peasant life. The ballads were collected by Chandrakumar De in the early 20th century and edited by Dinesh Chandra Sen, published as Eastern Bengal Ballads (1923-1932).

title: Dullahan
summary: The headless rider of Irish folklore who heralds death with his grim procession.

title: Dullahan: The Headless Horseman
summary: A headless warrior who rides at night, carrying his own head—and anyone who watches is marked for death.

title: Duppy: The Restless Spirits of Jamaica
summary: Duppies are restless spirits in Jamaican folklore, believed to be the souls of the dead who have not found peace. Good duppies appear in dreams (called 'dream you') to give advice or information from deceased family and friends. Bad duppies can cause harm and may be set on someone through obeah (sorcery). Duppies are said to speak in high-pitched nasal voices. Signs of a duppy's presence include a feeling that one's head is growing or unexplained heat. Protection methods include eating salt (which duppies despise), wearing clothes inside out, cursing, or exposing oneself to shame the spirit. Specific duppies include the Three-Footed Horse and Rolling Calf.

title: Durga
summary: Long before the age of men, when the cosmic forces of good and evil were locked in an eternal struggle, there arose a demon unlike any the universe had seen before.

title: Dutchman, the Guyanese Phantom
summary: The ghost of a Dutch colonist who wanders the plantations and canals of Guyana, forever searching for the treasure he buried and never reclaimed.

title: Dwen and the Spirit of the Hidden Valley
summary: A grieving mother is led by a mysterious spirit into a hidden valley where the boundaries between the living and the dead grow thin, and learns that love does not end at death.
themes: the boundary between life and death

title: Dwenn: The Stone That Remembers
summary: A stonemason building a church in the hills above St. David's encounters the Dwenn, a spirit of the land itself, and learns that some stones hold the memory of everything that has ever happened upon them.

title: Dybbuk, the Clinging Spirit
summary: A dybbuk is a restless spirit in Jewish folklore that possesses the living to resolve unfinished business, clinging to its host until exorcised.

title: Dze-temi, the Night Hunter
summary: A spectral hunter who rides through the night sky, chasing the souls of the dead, because in Georgia the hunt never ends.

title: Dzudzerume, the Mountain Witch
summary: A mountain witch who steals children and replaces them with changelings, because in Georgia the mountains take what they want.

title: Džambas, the Macedonian Demon
summary: A demonic creature of North Macedonian folklore, Džambas haunts the forests and mountains, leading travelers astray with eerie lights.

title: Each Uisge
summary: In the Scottish Highlands, the water spirits called Each Uisge haunt the fords and bridges of the wild rivers.

title: East of the Sun and West of the Moon
summary: A courageous girl journeys to the ends of the earth to rescue her love from a cruel enchantment.

title: Ebbe Skamelson
summary: Knight Ebbe Skamelson betroths the beautiful Malfred before departing for the Crusades for seven years. Believing him dead, Malfred's mother betroths her to another. Ebbe returns during the wedding feast and in rage kills Malfred, her mother, and the bridegroom. He seeks papal absolution but cannot find peace, and is sentenced to visit all 365 islands in Lake Bolmen in chains. Upon hearing a ballad of his own story, his chains fall off and he dies.

title: Egle: The Queen of Serpents
summary: A young woman marries a serpent king and must choose between her husband and her family in Lithuania's greatest folk tale.

title: El Aro, the Spectral Ring
summary: A ghostly apparition in Honduran folklore, El Aro is a spectral ring that rolls through the streets at night, foretelling death or disaster.

title: El Bacá: The Demonic Familiar of Dominican Folklore
summary: A shapeshifting demon brings wealth to its master in exchange for blood sacrifices.

title: El Boyo: The Mournful Ghost
summary: El Boyo is a sorrowful ghost haunting the rivers and swamps of Nicaragua, the restless spirit of a drowned man whose eerie wailing warns travelers away from dangerous waters.

title: El Cadejo and the Drunkard
summary: A drunkard who mocked the Cadejo and was found dead on the road the next morning, because in Panama the things you laugh at are the things that laugh last.

title: El Cadejo, the Dog of the Night
summary: A large spectral dog that appears at night, sometimes white and protective, sometimes black and deadly, because in Panama every traveler needs a guardian or a grave.

title: El Cadejo, the Honduran Spirit Dog
summary: A legendary spirit dog of Honduras, El Cadejo appears as a large shaggy beast with glowing eyes, alternately a protector and a portent of doom.

title: El Caleuche: The Ghost Ship of Chiloé
summary: A brilliantly lit ghost ship crewed by witches and demons sails the canals of southern Chile, luring sailors to their doom.

title: El Chupacabra
summary: The goat-sucking creature of Puerto Rican legend, blamed for mysterious livestock deaths.

title: El Chupacabra in the Texas Borderlands
summary: Throughout the 2000s and 2010s, dozens of alleged Chupacabra carcasses were reported across Texas, particularly in San Antonio, Cuero, Hood County, and Coleman County. Ranchers described finding livestock with puncture wounds and drained of blood, often attributing the attacks to a strange, hairless creature. In Cuero (2007), a hairless carcass named the 'Cuero Chupacabra' gained national attention before DNA tests revealed it was a coyote-wolf hybrid with severe mange. In Hood County (2010), animal control officers shot a creature later identified by Texas A&M as a coyote-dog hybrid. These sightings reflect the blending of ancient Mexican folk belief with modern American cryptozoology, creating a uniquely borderlands legend that continues to evolve with each new discovery.

title: El Chupacabra — The Goat-Sucker
summary: The Chupacabra is a legendary cryptid that first appeared in Puerto Rico in 1995, blamed for mysterious livestock killings in which animals were found drained of blood. Descriptions vary: in Puerto Rico and Latin America it is often depicted as a reptilian, alien-like creature with spines along its back, standing 3-4 feet tall and hopping like a kangaroo, while in the US Southwest it is described as a hairless, dog-like animal with a pronounced spinal ridge, fangs, and claws. The legend spread rapidly through Mexico and the border states of Texas, New Mexico, and Arizona during the late 1990s, with hundreds of alleged sightings and attacks. Scientific investigations have consistently identified the creatures as coyotes, dogs, or raccoons suffering from severe sarcoptic mange, which causes hair loss, thickened skin, and a ghastly appearance. The first eyewitness's description was inspired by the alien creature 'Sil' from the 1995 science-fiction film Species. Despite the debunking, El Chupacabra remains deeply embedded in modern Hispanic folklore throughout the Southwest, representing the mysterious and unexplained in rural life.

title: El Coco — The Boogeyman of the Spanish-Speaking World
summary: El Coco, also known as El Coco Man or El Hombre del Costal (the Sack Man), is a bogeyman figure used throughout the Spanish-speaking world to frighten children into good behavior. The figure likely has Moorish origins, derived from the Arabic word for 'fear.' In the Mexican-American and Chicano communities of the Southwest, El Coco is described as a dark, shadowy creature with glowing red eyes who hides in closets, under beds, or in dark corners. Parents warn children: 'Duérmete mi niño, duérmete mi sol, si no viene el Coco y te come el dedo gordo del pie' (Sleep my child, sleep my sun, or the Coco will come and eat your big toe). Some versions describe him as a hunchbacked figure who carries a sack to collect misbehaving children. Unlike many other Hispanic folklore figures, El Coco is purely a disciplinary tool, rarely appearing in narrative stories but persisting as a cultural touchstone across generations of Hispanic families in the United States.

title: El Cuchubo, the Shadow Thief
summary: A small hairy creature that steals shadows, leaving its victims alive but without a shadow, because in Panama even your shadow can be taken.

title: El Cucuy — The Monster Under the Bed
summary: El Cucuy is a distinctly Mexican and Mexican-American variant of the bogeyman legend, particularly prevalent in the US Southwest among Chicano families. Unlike the more generic El Coco, El Cucuy is specifically described as a small, hairy, goblin-like creature who lives under children's beds or in dark closets, waiting to grab ankles or drag away children who refuse to sleep. Some accounts describe him as having red or yellow eyes, long claws, and a mischievous grin. The legend serves dual purposes: as a parenting tool to enforce bedtime and as a cultural rite of passage where children learn to face their fears. In recent decades, El Cucuy has been reimagined in Chicano literature and art as a symbol of the fears faced by immigrant children — the unknown terrors of a new country, border crossing, and cultural displacement.

title: El Cuellado, the Long Neck
summary: A creature with an impossibly long neck that peers into windows at night, watching families sleep, because in Panama even the walls have eyes.

title: El Dorado
summary: High in the cold, windswept plateau of the Colombian Andes, there lies a lake of dark, still water, ringed by ancient mountains and shrouded in mist.

title: El Duende — The Gnomelike Trickster
summary: El Duende is a small, gnomelike creature from Spanish and Latin American folklore who has a prominent place in Mexican-American oral tradition. Described as a tiny old man or child-like figure wearing a large hat and often carrying a walking stick, El Duende lives in forests, caves, or abandoned buildings. He is known for playing tricks on people — stealing food, hiding objects, and leading travelers in circles through the woods. In some versions, El Duende tries to capture children to keep as his own, especially those who wander away from their parents. In curanderismo, encounters with duendes are believed to cause illness, particularly susto (fright sickness), requiring a limpieza (spiritual cleansing) from a curandero. The duende is also said to have backward feet, making it easy to identify his tracks. Among Hispanic families in the Southwest, stories of El Duende serve to keep children close to home and to explain the mysterious sounds and occurrences of rural life.

title: El Duende, the Costa Rican Trickster
summary: A small, mischievous forest spirit of Costa Rica, El Duende leads travelers astray and plays pranks on those who wander into his domain.

title: El Jinete Sin Cabeza del Valle — The Headless Horseman of the Valley
summary: While the headless horseman is a figure known in many cultures, the Hispanic version from the Rio Grande Valley and northern Mexico has unique characteristics. Known as El Jinete Sin Cabeza, this specter is said to be the ghost of a Spanish conquistador or a Mexican rancher who lost his head in battle — either during the Mexican War of Independence or the Mexican-American War. He rides a black horse through the moonlit mesquite at midnight, carrying his head under his arm. Unlike the more playful Halloween version, this headless horseman is a fearsome omen: to see him foretells death, war, or disaster. In some versions, he is searching for his head, which was cut off by Comanche raiders. If you encounter him, you must not look into the eyes of his severed head, or you will be doomed to ride beside him forever. Some Chicano versions of the legend place him at the Battle of the Alamo or at the Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo, connecting the supernatural figure to the traumatic history of Mexican dispossession in Texas.

title: El Lobizón: The Argentine Werewolf
summary: In the vast plains of Argentina, where the pampas stretch to the horizon and the cattle graze beneath a sky that seems too large for the world, there is a curse so deeply believed that the government passed a law to protect its victims.

title: El Nahual — The Shapeshifting Witch
summary: El Nahual (or Nagual) is a shapeshifting witch or sorcerer in Mesoamerican and Hispanic folklore, with a strong presence in Mexican-American tradition. The belief, originating with the Aztecs and other Nahua peoples, holds that certain individuals have the spiritual power to transform into animals — most commonly jaguars, coyotes, dogs, owls, or turkeys. Each person is born with a tonal (animal spirit companion) linked to their birth date in the Mesoamerican calendar, but only those with special power can actually assume the animal's form. Nagualism was practiced by pre-Columbian shamans and integrated with European witchcraft beliefs during the colonial period. In Mexican-American folklore of the Southwest, nahuales are feared for their ability to cause illness, steal livestock, and harm enemies while in animal form. However, in some Indigenous communities, the nahual is seen as a protector of the people and natural resources. The concept was popularized in English by Carlos Castaneda's books, though these accounts are controversial. Today, belief in nahuales persists alongside curanderismo as part of the living folk religion of the borderlands.

title: El Niño Fidencio — The Child Healer of Espinazo
summary: El Niño Fidencio (José de Jesús Fidencio Sintora, 1898–1938) is a Mexican folk saint and curandero whose cult center is in Espinazo, Nuevo León, and whose devotion extends into Mexican-American communities in Texas and California. Orphaned at a young age, Fidencio began performing healings at age 14 and gained fame for his extraordinary cures, which included surgery performed without instruments, trance-channeling of spirits, and the use of mud baths and herbs. He was known for his childlike demeanor — playing with toys, speaking in a high voice, and having his followers call him 'Niño' (child). His healing sessions often included theatrical elements: he would dress as a woman, a doctor, or a bullfighter. After his death in 1938, his devotees established the Fidencista Christian Church. Pilgrimages to Espinazo on his feast day (March 19) draw tens of thousands. In the US, Fidencio altars are maintained in Chicano communities, and his tradition of 'cajones' (trance sessions) continues among espiritista and curanderismo practitioners. His story represents the fusion of folk Catholicism with Indigenous healing traditions that characterizes borderlands spirituality.

title: El Pacto con el Diablo — Faustian Legends of the Borderlands
summary: Pact-with-the-devil legends are widespread in Hispanic folklore of the US Southwest and northern Mexico, reflecting the deep Catholic influence on borderlands culture. These stories typically involve a desperate or ambitious person who sells their soul to the devil in exchange for wealth, power, love, or musical talent. One famous variant tells of a musician at a border cantina who makes a pact with a mysterious stranger to play the guitar like nobody else — only to find his shadow disappears and his soul is claimed at midnight. In another, a farmer in the Rio Grande Valley trades his soul for a well that never runs dry during drought, a deal that eventually costs him his entire family. The most famous Faustian figure in Hispanic folklore is Juan de Dios, who reportedly signed a contract with the devil in blood to become the greatest charro (horseman) in Jalisco. These legends serve as morality tales about the dangers of pride, greed, and the pursuit of worldly success at the expense of spiritual salvation. They also reflect the harsh economic realities of the borderlands, where poverty often tempted people toward desperate bargains.

title: El Pombero: The Goblin of the Argentine Forest
summary: A nocturnal forest spirit punishes those who harm nature and rewards those who show respect.

title: El Silbón — The Whistling Specter of the Plains
summary: El Silbón (The Whistler) is a terrifying specter from the folklore of Mexico's northern plains and the US Southwest borderlands. He is described as a tall, thin figure dressed in white, carrying a bundle of bones on his back. His most distinctive feature is his whistle — a melody that begins softly and grows increasingly louder, signaling his approach. Those who hear his whistle must not move; snip if the whistle sounds close, the Silbón is far away, but if it sounds distant, he is right behind you. According to legend, the Silbón was a young man who murdered his father after the father killed the young man's wife in a fit of rage. The grandfather, as punishment, set the dogs on him and cursed him to wander forever carrying his father's bones. In Mexican-American ranching communities, El Silbón is a warning to those who would harm their families, and his story is told to keep children from wandering out at night. His legend has evolved in the borderlands into a uniquely bi-cultural ghost story, blending Mexican spectral traditions with the open landscapes of the American Southwest.

title: El Sombrerón — The Goblin with the Big Hat
summary: El Sombrerón is a small, mischievous goblin figure from Guatemalan and southern Mexican folklore who also appears in Mexican-American storytelling. He is described as a tiny man — no taller than a child — wearing an enormous hat, a red tie, and riding a tiny horse or mule. El Sombrerón is known for braiding the manes and tails of horses, donkeys, and mules into intricate patterns that cannot be undone. He also bothers women by serenading them under their windows with a tiny guitar, causing them to fall into a deep melancholy or sleeplessness. His enchantment can only be broken by someone who feeds him or by making the sign of the cross. The legend traveled to the US Southwest with Central American and Mexican immigrants, where it persists as a cautionary tale about vanity and the dangers of nighttime wandering. In some versions, El Sombrerón is said to stuff his victims with food and sugar until they die of sweetness.

title: El Tesoro de los Jesuitas — The Jesuit Gold of the Border
summary: The legend of the Jesuit Treasure is one of the most enduring treasure myths of the US Southwest and northern Mexico. When the Spanish Crown expelled the Jesuits from New Spain in 1767, the order was said to have hidden vast stores of gold and silver throughout the Sonoran Desert rather than let it fall into royal hands. The most famous hiding place is said to be in the Sierra Madre, near a cave marked with a cryptic Jesuit symbol — a heart pierced by an arrow above three crosses. Over the centuries, countless treasure hunters — Mexican, Anglo, and Native — have searched for this gold. Some claim the treasure is guarded by the spirit of a Jesuit priest who appears as a ghostly figure in black robes near the hiding place. Others say the treasure tunnels form a network connecting Jesuit missions across the Southwest. In Mexican-American folklore, the legend speaks to the history of Spanish colonization, the power and mystery of the Jesuit order, and the enduring hope of discovering hidden wealth in the desert. The story also reflects the painful history of dispossession, as the treasure rightfully belonged to the Indigenous and Hispanic peoples of the region.

title: El Tigrillo, the Spirit of the Jungle Cat
summary: A spirit animal of the Costa Rican jungles, El Tigrillo is a spectral ocelot that guards sacred places and guides the worthy through the forest.

title: El Trauco — The Cursing Dwarf of the Forest
summary: El Trauco is a legendary figure from the folklore of Chiloé, Chile, but his legend has traveled through Latin American diaspora communities into the US Southwest. Described as a small, ugly, deformed dwarf — no more than three feet tall — who wears a hat made of a type of vine, has no teeth, and carries a wooden club or axe. He lives in deep forests and is known for two terrifying powers: his gaze can deform or curse those who meet his eyes, and his breath is believed to possess the power to impregnate young women who wander alone in the woods. According to legend, if a young woman has an unexplained pregnancy, it is blamed on El Trauco. Despite his fearsome reputation, he is also said to be a protector of the forest who punishes those who destroy trees and wildlife. In Chilean-American communities in the US, El Trauco serves as a cautionary figure against premarital sex and as a guardian of old-world traditions in a new environment. His story represents the persistence of rural folklore in urban immigrant communities and the adaptation of Latin American legends to the American landscape.

title: El Trauco: The Forest Dwarf of Chiloé
summary: A grotesque dwarf-like creature with powers of irresistible seduction haunts the forests of Chiloé.

title: Eleggua, the Trickster Messenger
summary: Eleggua (Elegbara) is the trickster orisha of crossroads, doors, opportunities, and fate in Cuban Santería. He is the messenger between humanity and the other orishas, syncretized with the Holy Child of Atocha. Eleggua opens and closes paths, and no ceremony can begin without his permission. He is depicted as a mischievous child who carries a hooked staff and wears a red and black beaded necklace. His number is 3, multiplied by 21. One legend tells how Eleggua created confusion among the orishas by wearing a hat of two colors, causing arguments about which way he was walking — teaching that perspective and truth are often deceptive. Eleggua is considered the first orisha that initiates receive, making him fundamental to all of Santería practice.

title: Elvehøj
summary: A young man falls asleep beside an elf-mound and is wooed by elf-maidens who sing beautifully. He resists their enchantments, grasping his sword, and is ultimately rescued by the crowing of a cock at dawn, which awakens him from the spell.

title: Encantada, the Andorran Fairy
summary: A beautiful fairy of Pyrenean lore, the Encantada of Andorra appears at mountain springs and punishes those who betray promises of love.

title: Enkai and the Gift of Cattle
summary: In the beginning, Enkai, the supreme god of the Maasai, lived on earth with the first people. One day, Enkai decided to give the Maasai a gift more precious than any other — cattle. He lowered them from the sky on a leather thong, and they landed on the green plains below. Enkai instructed the Maasai that they were to be the sole guardians of all cattle in the world, and that these animals would provide them with milk, blood, and meat for eternity. This sacred bond between the Maasai and their cattle remains the cornerstone of Maasai identity to this day.

title: Enkai and the Rainbow Serpent
summary: In the time when Enkai still walked among the people, a great drought struck the land. Rivers dried up, grass turned to dust, and the cattle began to die. The Maasai begged Enkai for rain, but their prayers went unanswered. One day, a young girl saw a magnificent rainbow serpent emerge from a dry riverbed. The serpent spoke, saying it would carry a message to Enkai if the people would honor it as a messenger of the divine. The Maasai agreed, and the serpent slithered up the rainbow into the sky. When it reached Enkai, it sang the people's plea. Enkai was moved and sent rain that restored the land. Since then, the rainbow has been seen as a bridge between earth and sky, and the serpent as a sacred messenger between Enkai and the Maasai.

title: Epic of Gesar of Ling
summary: The great Tibetan epic of King Gesar, the longest living epic in the world with over one million verses and 120 volumes. The story recounts the miraculous birth of Gesar, son of deities sent to earth to vanquish demons, depose the powerful, and aid the weak. He has a despised childhood where he appears as an ugly, snotty child called Joru before winning a horse race at age 12 to become king and marry the beautiful 'Brugmo. Mounted on his celestial steed Kyang Go Karkar, he wages campaigns against demon kings, retrieves his kidnapped wife from the King of Hor, and in his eighties descends to Hell before ascending back to heaven. Rooted in pre-Buddhist Bon traditions and dated to the 12th century, it is sung by bard-shamans across Tibet, Mongolia, and Central Asia.

title: Er Sogotokh (The Lonely Man)
summary: A foundational Yakut Olonkho epic about Er Sogotokh, the first human hero created by the supreme deity. Born alone in the Middle World, he must contend with the hostile Abaasy spirits from the Lower World who seek to destroy him. After achieving victory over the evil forces, he finds a wife from the Upper World and establishes the first human tribe. The epic explores themes of solitude, divine purpose, and the establishment of human society in a hostile cosmos. It contains some of the oldest layers of Yakut mythology, predating the northward migration of the Sakha people.

title: Erdlaveersissok the Entrail-Seizer
summary: Erdlaveersissok is a terrifying spirit who haunts the celestial path leading to the moon. She targets travelers who lack composure or discipline. Her most disturbing trait is her habit of stealing the entrails of anyone she can trick into laughing. She serves as a guardian of emotional restraint and a symbol of the perils of the spiritual journey.

title: Erect Horns and the Sacred Buffalo Hat
summary: Erect Horns (Tomȯsévėséhe) was the prophet of the Só'taeo'o people who later merged with the Cheyenne. He received the Ésevone (Sacred Buffalo Hat) at Tȯhóonévose (Stone Hammer Mountain) near the Great Lakes in Minnesota. The sacred hat represents female power, while the Sacred Arrows represent male power—together they form the two great covenants of the Cheyenne Nation. Erect Horns gave the people the Sun Dance ceremony and convinced the tribe to abandon their sedentary agricultural lifestyle, adopt the nomadic Plains horse culture, and rely on buffalo for survival. His vision transformed the Cheyenne from earth-lodge dwellers to tipi-dwelling Plains warriors.

title: Erkei-Mergen and the Seven Suns
summary: Long ago, seven suns rose in the sky simultaneously, drying up all rivers and vegetation on earth. Men and animals struggled to survive in the unbearable heat. A famous archer named Erkei-Mergen stepped forward to save the world. Using his divine bow, he shot down the extra suns one by one, restoring balance to the world. The story explains the origin of the single sun and moon in the sky and is one of the most widespread Mongol folktales about the regulation of celestial bodies, reflecting the ancient Mongols' interest in natural phenomena and their origins.

title: Erlig Khan and the Palace of the Dead
summary: Erlig Khan (also Erlik Khan) is the Mongol and Turkic god of death and ruler of the underworld. In one of the most famous Mongol tales, 'The Woman Who Sought Her Husband in the Palace of Erlik Khan,' a brave woman descends into the underworld to rescue her dead husband. She navigates past guardian spirits and offers tribute at the court of the terrifying Erlig Khan, who sits in judgment over the souls of the dead. Through her courage and devotion, she wins her husband's soul back. The story reflects the Mongol belief in a multi-layered cosmos where the underworld is a place of judgment but accessible through shamanic journey and pure intent.

title: Esben and the Witch
summary: Esben is captured by a witch who intends to cook him. Using his wit and bravery, he manages to escape her clutches and outsmart her, eventually returning home safely.

title: Eshu the Trickster and the Two Friends (Yoruba)
summary: Eshu, the divine messenger and trickster, once walked between two farmers who were best friends, wearing a hat that was red on one side and white on the other. The two friends saw him from opposite fields and later argued about the color of the passerby's hat, each insisting on what they had seen. Their argument escalated until they drew weapons against each other. Only then did Eshu reveal himself, explaining that he was teaching them that truth has many sides and that human perception is limited. As the god of crossroads, chance, and communication, Eshu taught the Yoruba that ambiguity is part of life and that patience and humility are essential before judgment. Eshu serves as the messenger between humans and the Orishas, carrying sacrifices to the gods.

title: Excalibur
summary: In the time of kings, there was a boy named Arthur who pulled a sword from a stone—proving he was the rightful ruler of Britain.

title: Eyrbyggja Saga - The Guest Thorgunna
summary: The wealthy and sickly Thorgunna is buried with a specific request that her bedding be burned. When a friend, Thorodd, keeps her bed sheets as a gift for his wife, Thorgunna returns as a ghost. She appears in the middle of the night at a farmstead, setting the table and preparing a meal for the living before vanishing back into the grave.

title: Eyrbyggja Saga - The Haunting of Thorolf Halt-Foot
summary: Thorolf Halt-Foot returns as a malevolent draugr after his death, terrorizing the area around Þórsnes. He is buried, reburied, and even burned, yet he continues to return, even manifesting as a bull. Eventually, his son Arnkel manages to lay him to rest by building a high stone wall around his grave to prevent him from escaping.

title: Eyrbyggja Saga - The Seal of Frodis-water
summary: The house at Frodis-water is haunted by a group of undead fishermen and their leader, Thorir Wooden-leg. The hauntings escalate until a seal's head begins to emerge from the floorboards. Despite the inhabitants' attempts to smash it back down, the seal keeps rising until a young man uses a sledgehammer to drive it back, temporarily ending the phenomenon.

title: Faithful and Unfaithful
summary: Two brothers — one faithful, one unfaithful — set out into the world; the faithful brother wins a princess through kindness while the unfaithful one schemes and falls to ruin. This tale is a distant offshoot of the Tristan legend cycle.

title: Falak, the Serpent of Purgatory
summary: A colossal serpent that guards the bridge between life and death, biting the souls that try to cross — because in Lebanon, the journey to the afterlife is not a gift, but a test.

title: Falcone, the Sammarinese Winged Guardian
summary: A monstrous winged creature said to inhabit Mount Titano, Falcone is a guardian of San Marino who protects the republic from invasion.

title: Farmer Weathersky
summary: Farmer Weathersky possesses a unique ability to interact with the weather. When opportunistic neighbors try to exploit his gift or cheat him out of his land, he uses his cleverness to turn the tide in his favor, ensuring justice and prosperity.

title: Faroese Chain Dance and Kvæði (Ballad Tradition)
summary: The Faroese chain dance (Føroya Dansur) accompanied by kvæði (ballads) is the national dance and a living tradition that preserves folklore. Dancers form a circle holding hands, moving rhythmically while a kvæðamaður (ballad singer) recites verses recounting tales of legendary heroes, folklore figures, and historical events. Many kvæði date to the Middle Ages and preserve stories otherwise lost, including the Sjúrðar Kvæði (cyclic ballads about Sigurd the Dragon-Slayer from Norse mythology) and ballads about Finnur hin Fróði and other Faroese figures. The tradition was instrumental in preserving the Faroese language during centuries of Danish rule and continues as a living cultural practice at festivals and gatherings.

title: Father Bruin in the Corner
summary: A humorous tale about Father Bruin, a bear who believes himself to be superior but is repeatedly tricked by the cunning Reynard the Fox. The story highlights the contrast between Bruin's strength and Reynard's intelligence.

title: Finkingo: The Stickball Game (Choctaw)
summary: The Choctaw game of stickball, known as Finkingo or kabocha, is featured in many Choctaw legends. According to tradition, the game was given to the Choctaw by the spirits to resolve conflicts without warfare. Stickball is played with two small rackets and a ball, and it is extremely fast and violent. The game was often played between villages, with hundreds of players on each side, goals miles apart, and games lasting from sunrise to sunset. One legend tells of a young warrior who won the hand of a chief's daughter by scoring the winning goal in a legendary match. Another story describes how stickball settled a territorial dispute between the Choctaw and a neighboring tribe, avoiding a bloody war. The game remains central to Choctaw culture today.

title: Finn, the Giant, and the Minster of Lund
summary: A giant named Finn builds Lund Cathedral in exchange for Saint Lawrence's eyes, but the saint overhears Finn's name in a lullaby and Finn turns to stone in the crypt. This world-famous master-builder legend is connected to several European cathedrals; Finn's petrified form can still be seen grasping a pillar in the crypt of Lund Cathedral.

title: Finnur hin Fróði and Faroese Wizard Legends
summary: Faroese folklore includes tales of powerful wizards and cunning folk (wise men and women) who could control weather, heal sickness, and ward off trolls. One of the most famous is Finnur hin Fróði (Finn the Wise), a legendary figure associated with magical knowledge and runic wisdom. These wizard legends blend Norse pagan traditions with later Christian elements—wizards were said to possess books of black magic (the 'Black Book' tradition) that could only be passed on to a willing successor. The island of Svínoy and the village of Sumba are particularly associated with wizard lore. These tales reflect the historical tension between official Christianity and older folk beliefs that persisted for centuries.

title: First Born, First Wed
summary: A king's son and a queen's daughter, promised to each other at birth, must overcome separation, enchantment, and a wicked stepmother before they can fulfill their destiny. This is a purely Swedish treatment of the redemption motif.

title: First Man and First Woman
summary: In the First World, Black Cloud and White Cloud came together in the East, and from their breath First Man (Áłtsé Hastiin) was formed, carrying white corn and crystal. Blue Cloud and Yellow Cloud came together in the West, forming First Woman (Áłtsé Asdzą́ą́) with yellow corn, white shell, turquoise, and yucca. First Woman made a fire with turquoise and First Man with crystal. Seeing each other's light, they joined together, establishing the pattern of life. Great Coyote (Mąʼiitoʼí Áłchíní) appeared, claiming to know all under water and sky. Then First Angry (Áłtsé Hashké) appeared, claiming seniority and bringing witchcraft into the world. Conflict among the Air-Spirit People led to their expulsion from the First World.

title: Flat Pipe and the Arapaho Creation
summary: In the beginning, there was nothing but water covering everything. A man carrying a Flat Pipe walked on the water for six days, weeping and fasting, searching for a safe place to rest his pipe. On the seventh day, he called to the four directions and summoned seven cottonwood trees and all the creatures. One by one, various animals dove into the water to bring up mud—Grebe, waterfowls, Kingfisher, Otter, Beaver, Coot, Garter Snake, Black Snake, ducks, goose, crane—all failed. On the seventh dive, Turtle and the Man (who transformed his Flat Pipe into a Red-headed Duck) succeeded in bringing up mud. The Man cast the mud in four directions, creating the Earth.

title: Foam Woman and Ice Woman (Haida)
summary: Among the SGaana Kiidads (Supernatural Beings) of Haida tradition are Kalga Jaad (Ice Woman) and GaayhllGa Jaad (Flood-Tide-Woman). These female supernatural beings are part of the Raven Traveling narratives, also known as Xuuya Kaagang.ngas, which tell of Raven traveling the earth and transforming it to make it suitable for humans. Kalga Jaad controls ice and winter forces, while GaayhllGa Jaad governs the tides and the boundary between land and sea. These beings embody the Haida understanding of the interconnected relationship between land and sea. They are among the many supernatural entities that Raven encountered during his travels across Haida Gwaii, and their stories teach respect for natural forces and the balance required for human survival on the islands.

title: Food for Kings: Oatcake and Herring
summary: When King Charles XI confiscated most noble properties in the Great Reduction of 1680, his aunt Countess Maria Eufrosyna of Höjentorp was affected. When the king came to visit, she greeted him with a box on the ear, then served him nothing but a herring's tail and an oatcake. When the king offered to return her property, she cut him off and gave him a second box on the ear. The king hastily commanded that she keep her property.

title: Found-in-the-Grass
summary: Found-in-the-Grass is a rags-to-riches hero of Arapaho folklore. In some versions, he is an orphan abandoned as an infant and found by villagers in the tall grass. In others, he is the magical twin Spring-Boy grown older. Despite his humble beginnings, Found-in-the-Grass rises to become a great warrior and leader through courage, wit, and the help of spirit allies. He performs incredible feats, defeats enemies, and brings prosperity to his people. His story embodies the Arapaho value that one's origins do not determine one's destiny, and that perseverance and spiritual strength can overcome any disadvantage.

title: Friar Tuck
summary: Of all Robin Hood's Merry Men, none was more surprising than the holy man who could fight like a soldier and laugh like a drunkard.

title: Friends in Life and Death
summary: Two inseparable friends swear to remain loyal even after death. When one passes away, the other visits the grave and journeys into the afterlife. There, he observes the symbolic representations of human greed and contentment, learning a profound lesson about the soul.

title: Fumo Liongo: The Warrior Poet of the Swahili Coast
summary: Liongo Fumo was a legendary Swahili prince, warrior, and poet who lived on Pate Island sometime between the 9th and 13th centuries. He was a giant of a man, nearly invulnerable except for his navel, and a master archer whose bow no other man could draw. Despite being the rightful heir, his brother Mringwari usurped the throne, forcing Liongo into exile. Liongo became a heroic outlaw, fighting against injustice and defending the Swahili people from Oromo invaders. He composed poems and songs that are still sung at weddings and gungu dances along the coast. His death came through betrayal — his own son was bribed to stab him in the navel with a copper needle. Mortally wounded, Liongo staggered to a well, dying upright with his bow in hand, his body so fearsome that no one dared approach until his mother confirmed his passing. His poetry remains the oldest surviving Swahili literature.

title: Funkwe the Devourer of Rivers
summary: When a Tonga village's river begins to vanish overnight, a young girl discovers that the Funkwe, a giant water serpent, has been drinking the river dry as punishment for the village chief's arrogance.

title: Gamarala: The Foolish Farmer of Sri Lankan Folktales
summary: A simple village farmer is constantly outwitted by his clever wife and the animals around him.

title: Ganesha
summary: Ganesha, the elephant-headed god of wisdom, remover of obstacles, lord of beginnings, is one of the most beloved deities in the Hindu pantheon.

title: Garang of the Reed Weapon
summary: A mortal hero named Garang forged a weapon from river reeds and bone, then ventured into the spirit marsh to rescue his village's stolen cattle from the water spirits who guarded the flood plain.

title: Garcis, the Giant Who Built the Hills
summary: Garcis, a colossal giant of Latvian legend, shaped the rolling hills and river valleys of the Baltic countryside before retreating into the earth as the age of men began.

title: Gashadokuro: The Giant Skull
summary: A massive skeleton fifteen times bigger than a human appears at night, searching for living people to bite.

title: Gbahali, the Liberian Sea Monster
summary: A fearsome sea monster said to inhabit the waters off Liberia's coast, the Gbahali drags unwary fishermen and swimmers to a watery grave.

title: Genghis Khan and the Golden Whip
summary: According to Mongol legend, the young Temüjin (later Genghis Khan) was riding alone in the steppe when he discovered a golden whip lying on the ground. When he picked it up, the sky thundered and Tengri spoke, telling him that this whip was a sign that he would unite all the Mongol tribes under one banner. The whip had the power to command the loyalty of all who saw it. Genghis Khan kept the golden whip as his personal standard (the nine-tailed white banner) and carried it into every battle. The whip became a sacred symbol of Mongol unity and imperial authority, kept to this day as a national relic of Mongolia.

title: Gertrude's Bird
summary: A young girl named Gertrude receives a mysterious bird that possesses the ability to speak and provide guidance. The bird helps her navigate a series of trials and obstacles, leading her toward a destiny of happiness and nobility through kindness and perseverance.

title: Ghost of the White Deer (Chickasaw)
summary: The Ghost of the White Deer is a Chickasaw legend explaining why the white deer is considered sacred. A young hunter once encountered a pure white deer in the forest. The deer spoke to him, revealing itself as a spirit sent by Ababinili to test the hunter's character. The hunter chose not to kill the deer, showing mercy and respect for the spirit world. Because of his compassion, the hunter was blessed with success in future hunts and prosperity for his family. From that day, the Chickasaw have regarded the white deer as a sacred being that should never be hunted. Killing a white deer brings bad luck and spiritual contamination. The story teaches that mercy and respect for all living things bring blessings, while greed and disrespect have spiritual consequences.

title: Ghoul, the Desert Devourer
summary: A shape-shifting desert demon that feasts on the flesh of the dead and leads travelers astray in the wilderness of Palestine.

title: Gikuyu and Mumbi: The First Parents
summary: Ngai, the supreme god who dwells on Mount Kenya (Kirinyaga), created the first man, Gikuyu, and placed him at the center of the land beneath the mountain. Ngai showed Gikuyu a place where a magnificent fig tree (Mukuyu) grew and told him to build his homestead there, naming it Mukurwe wa Gathanga. To Gikuyu, Ngai gave a wife named Mumbi, meaning 'creator' or 'molder.' Together they had nine beautiful daughters: Wanjiru, Wambui, Njeri, Wanjiku, Nyambura, Wairimu, Waithira, Wangari, and Wangui. When it was time for the daughters to marry, Gikuyu prayed to Ngai beneath the fig tree, and the next morning nine young men appeared, marrying the nine daughters and becoming the founders of the nine Kikuyu clans.

title: Gizo the Spider Trickster and the Wisdom Bird
summary: Gizo is the spider trickster of Hausa folklore, a clever but overconfident schemer whose plans often backfire. In one well-known tale, Gizo tries to outwit the Wisdom Bird but fails spectacularly, teaching that intelligence without humility leads to ruin. Another story tells of him building a luxury lagoon home through trickery, convincing the animals to build it for him by claiming a magical competition. Gizo's character embodies both the cleverness and the folly of human nature, serving as a moral compass for Hausa communities. His stories, told by griots across Nigeria and Niger with drumming and call-and-response, teach the dangers of greed, the value of community, and the lesson that deception ultimately fails.

title: Glooscap and the Evil Frog Monster
summary: In the days of the Mi'kmaq ancestors, a monstrous frog spirit had swallowed all the water in the world. Rivers dried up, lakes vanished, and people and animals were dying of thirst. The great being Glooscap took pity on his people. He tracked the enormous frog to its lair and engaged it in a titanic struggle. He struck the frog with such force that it coughed up all the water it had swallowed. Water gushed forth, refilling the rivers and lakes. Some of the animals present were so relieved and joyful that they leaped into the water and were transformed into fish and other aquatic creatures. The lesson of this story is that even a small creature (the frog should not be underestimated in its power to do harm, but that goodness and determination will ultimately prevail. The foam of Glooscap's battle can still be seen in the whitecaps of the Bay of Fundy.

title: Glooscap and the Great Beaver: The Five Islands
summary: Glooscap once transformed himself into a giant beaver to create a safe haven for his people. Swimming in the Bay of Fundy, he slapped his enormous tail against the water with such tremendous force that it churned up the earth from the seabed, creating the Five Islands of Nova Scotia. When Glooscap slept, Nova Scotia was his bed and Prince Edward Island his pillow. In another tradition, when Glooscap finished painting all the splendor of the world, he dipped his brush into a blend of all the colors left over and created Abegweit, meaning Cradled on the Waves, his favorite island — Prince Edward Island. The Annapolis Valley was also shaped by Glooscap's hand. These landscape features are constant reminders to the Mi'kmaq of their culture hero's presence and his love for the land and its people.

title: Gluskabe and Dzeedzeez (The Baby Who Outmatched the Hero)
summary: Gluskabe, the great culture hero, was resting in his lodge after his many labors when he heard a baby crying. The baby was Dzeedzeez (Wasis in Passamaquoddy), whose mother had left him alone while she gathered firewood. Gluskabe, confident in his powers, decided to quiet the baby himself. He tried using his magic, but the baby only cried louder. He sang his most powerful healing songs, but Dzeedzeez screamed. He tried every trick he knew — shapeshifting, illusions, promises of gifts — and Dzeedzeez simply stared at him and continued wailing. Finally, the great Gluskabe, who had defeated monsters and giants and even his evil twin brother, was utterly defeated by a baby. He left the lodge humbled, realizing that some challenges cannot be overcome by strength or magic. The story teaches that wisdom sometimes comes from recognizing one's own limitations.

title: Gluskabe and the Monster Frog
summary: A devastating drought struck the land of the Wabanaki. Rivers dried to dust, the lakes shrank, and the people were dying. A giant frog monster had swallowed all the water and held it captive in its bloated body. The people called to Gluskabe for help. Gluskabe found the giant frog sunning itself on a rock, swollen with all the water of the world. He approached carefully and, using his magic, made the frog laugh. As the frog's great mouth opened, a flood of water poured forth, refilling the rivers and lakes. Some of the animals that had been trapped in the frog's belly leaped out transformed — those who had been four-legged became fish, and those who had been birds became waterfowl. Gluskabe then shrunk the frog down to its present size and declared that from then on, frogs would live near water but never again swallow more than they needed.

title: Gluskabe and the Wind Eagle
summary: Gluskabe (Glooscap) was annoyed by the constant wind that made life difficult for his people. He traveled to the great mountain where the Wind Eagle — a colossal bird whose wingbeats created all the wind in the world — was perched. Gluskabe climbed the mountain and captured the Wind Eagle, tying its wings together so they could not move. Immediately the wind stopped. At first, everything was calm and pleasant, but soon the air grew hot and still. The water became stagnant, the people could not breathe, and the world began to suffocate. Gluskabe realized that the wind was necessary for life. He returned to the mountaintop and untied the Wind Eagle's wings — just a little — allowing a gentle breeze to flow. He learned that while too much wind is destructive, no wind at all is even worse. The Wind Eagle's wings have been tied ever since, which is why we have breezes but not constant gales.

title: Gluskonba and the Four Wishes
summary: Gluskonba (Glooscap) offered four Abenaki men a single wish each.
