The first man wished to be powerful and rich, and was turned into a great pine tree — tall and strong, but rooted in one place forever. The second man wished to be feared by everyone, and was turned into a bear — powerful but alone. The third man wished to live forever, and was turned into a rock — eternal but without feeling or movement. The fourth man listened to the fate of the others and asked only for the wisdom to accept whatever Gluskonba gave him. Gluskonba blessed this man with a long, happy life, many children, and the love of his community. The first three had received what they asked for, but found their wishes brought misery instead of happiness. The story teaches that true wisdom lies not in seeking power or wealth, but in accepting the gifts of the Creator with gratitude.

title: Golden Treasure
summary: A story focusing on the pursuit of wealth and the moral lessons learned through the acquisition or loss of a legendary golden treasure, emphasizing that true value is not material.

title: Golem, the Creature of Clay
summary: A being of mud and clay animated by Kabbalistic magic, the Golem of Prague is the most famous artificial creature in Jewish tradition.

title: Gond Creation Myth — The Lizard That Made the World
summary: According to the Gond tribe of central India, in the beginning there was only water. The supreme god Bhagavan created a tortoise and a lizard to work together to create land. The tortoise dived deep into the waters and brought up mud on its back. The lizard spread this mud across the surface, forming the first solid ground. Bhagavan then breathed life into clay figures to create the first humans, but his first attempts were imperfect. He made a man and woman from clay, but they refused to bear children. Angered, Bhagavan sent termites to eat away the edges of the earth, threatening to sink it back into the waters. The first humans were terrified and agreed to reproduce. Thus, the world was saved, and humanity began. The lizard remains a sacred creature in Gond cosmology.

title: Goosey Grizzel
summary: A housekeeper named Grizzel is made to look like a monster by her employer. She joins a band of thieves and uses her frightening appearance to scare others, eventually encountering a priest who tries to 'bind' her.

title: Goubet Monster, the Red Sea Cryptid
summary: A fearsome sea monster said to dwell in the Gulf of Tadjoura off the coast of Djibouti, dragging fishermen to their doom.

title: Grandmother Spider Steals the Fire (Cherokee)
summary: In the beginning, the only fire belonged to the Thunders in the sky world. The animals held a council to decide who would bring fire to the people. Many brave animals volunteered but failed: Raven tried to carry an ember but his feathers turned black; Screech Owl's eyes were burned red; Hooting Owl's eyes were singed white. Finally, the tiny Water Spider, Dilsdohdi, volunteered. She spun a bowl-shaped web, placed it on her back, and crossed the water to the sky world. She placed a small ember in her web-basket and carried it safely back across the water to the people. This is why the Water Spider has black downy hair with red stripes — the smoke and fire marked her. Fire became the sacred gift that transformed human life.

title: Grettis Saga - The Fight with Glámr
summary: Grettir Ásmundarson, a man of extraordinary strength, is hired to protect a farm haunted by a wight. He eventually faces the undead shepherd Glámr in a brutal battle. Although Grettir triumphs, Glámr uses his final breath to curse him, leaving Grettir forever unlucky and terrified of the dark, which leads to his eventual exile and lonely death on the island of Drangey.

title: Gryphon
summary: In the distant lands of Scythia, beyond the borders of the known world, there lived creatures of such terrible beauty that they became legend even before Greeks reached them.

title: Grímur Kamban (The First Settler)
summary: Grímur Kamban is recorded in the Færeyinga Saga as the first Scandinavian settler in the Faroe Islands, arriving around 825 AD—decades before the main Norse colonization of Iceland. He settled at Funningur on Eysturoy. The name 'Kamban' may be of Gaelic origin, suggesting he was a Norse-Gael from the British Isles (possibly the Hebrides or Ireland). According to legend, he was a feared Viking who fled Norway after committing murder. His settlement at Funningur marks the beginning of continuous habitation in the Faroes. The story bridges history and folklore, representing the arrival of humans into a landscape already inhabited by trolls, giants, and hidden people.

title: Gudbrand on the Hill-side
summary: Gudbrand, a poor and humble youth, embarks on a journey and helps various animals and spirits along the way. His kindness and selflessness are rewarded when he is guided to a hidden treasure and the heart of a beautiful princess, proving that a good heart is the greatest asset.

title: Guinevere at the Trial by Fire
summary: Accused of treason, Queen Guinevere faces the ordeal by fire at the court of King Arthur, where her innocence must be proven by divine judgment or consumed by flame.

title: Guri Kunna: The Sea Witch of Hitra
summary: A dangerous sea witch lures fishermen to their doom along the Hitra and Fosen coast.

title: Göroglu: The Son of the Grave (Turkmen Version)
summary: The Turkmen epic of Göroglu ('Son of the Grave') — also known as Köroğlu — is the national epic of Turkmenistan, recognized by UNESCO as Intangible Cultural Heritage. Unlike the western versions, the Turkmen Göroglu was born miraculously in his mother's grave after she died, giving him his name. He was raised by his grandfather Jygalybek and aunt Gülendam, grew up with superhuman strength, and captured the magical winged horse Gyrat. With his forty jigits (warriors), Göroglu built the fortress of Chandybil and defended the Turkmen people against foreign oppressors. He married the peri (fairy) Agaýunus after seeing her in a dream. The epic combines heroic battles, romance, and deep mythological motifs including the wise figure Hızır who guides the hero.

title: Güije: The River Goblin of Cuba
summary: Small black-skinned goblins haunt Cuban rivers, playing tricks on those who disturb their waters.

title: Haggs: The Twilight Wanderer
summary: A schoolteacher new to the island dismisses the village warnings about the Haggs, a malevolent spirit of the twilight hours, until she finds her classroom filled with the scent of burning herbs and the chalk has written itself on the board.

title: Hanako-San: The Bathroom Ghost
summary: A ghost girl haunts school bathrooms in Japan. Knock three times and ask if she is there—if she answers, you are marked.

title: Hansel and Gretel
summary: Children abandoned in the forest discover a witch's gingerbread house and must use their wits to survive.

title: Hanuman
summary: Hanuman was born to the wind god Vayu and the celestial nymph Anjana.. According to the Ramayana, his mother was a vanara — a divine monkey being — who had been blessed with a son possessing the strength of the gods.

title: Hatim al-Tai: The Legend of Generosity
summary: Hatim ibn Abdallah of the Tai tribe, a pre-Islamic Arab chief in 6th-century Yemen, became the enduring symbol of Arab generosity and chivalry. Countless legends recount his extreme hospitality: slaughtering his prized horse when no other food was available for guests, giving away his possessions until left with nothing, and offering his own life to an assassin sent by a jealous king rather than sending the man back empty-handed. Even after death, legend says he hosted travelers from beyond the grave. The name 'Hatim' remains synonymous with generosity across the Arab and Persian world, and his son Adi became a companion of the Prophet Muhammad.

title: Hatuibwari: The Dragon God of the Solomon Islands
summary: Hatuibwari is a powerful dragon-like being from the mythology of the Solomon Islands, particularly among the people of Guadalcanal. Described as a massive serpent with the features of a dragon, Hatuibwari is a creator and cultural hero who shaped the islands and taught humans essential skills. In some accounts, Hatuibwari is a dual-sex being who created the first humans from clay and gave them fire, tools, and knowledge of agriculture. The being is associated with both creation and destruction, capable of bringing rain and fertility but also earthquakes and storms when angered. Hatuibwari's serpentine nature connects it to the widespread Melanesian motif of powerful snake deities who play central roles in creation myths across the region.

title: Hatupatu and the Bird-Woman
summary: Hatupatu was a young Maori warrior who was captured by Kurangaituku, a fearsome bird-woman with sharp claws and a taste for human flesh. She kept him in her cave dwelling, but clever Hatupatu bided his time. When Kurangaituku relaxed her guard, he escaped, running across the rugged landscape of the central North Island. The bird-woman pursued relentlessly. Hatupatu called upon the gods for help and was saved by the hot springs and geysers of Rotorua, where the scalding waters repelled his pursuer. He hid in a narrow rock crevice that Kurangaituku could not reach, and she eventually gave up the chase.

title: He Who Could Ride in All Weathers
summary: A castle-dwelling daughter is brought home by her father to the castle in Tyrol. She does not give her hand to the richest or most handsome suitor, but instead chooses the one who defies all dangers and makes his way through all weathers. The tale carries a feminist message about a woman's right to choose her partner based on character rather than wealth or status.

title: Heer Ranjha — The Tragic Lovers of Punjab
summary: Heer, the beautiful daughter of a wealthy Jatt family in Jhang, fell deeply in love with Ranjha, a youngest son who tended cattle and played the flute. They met secretly for years until Heer's jealous uncle Kaido exposed them. Heer's family forcibly married her to another man. The heartbroken Ranjha became a wandering Jogi (ascetic), piercing his ears and renouncing worldly life. Traveling across Punjab, he eventually found Heer again. Her parents finally agreed to their union, but on the wedding day, Heer's uncle poisoned her. Ranjha, seeing her die, took the same poison and died beside her. The lovers are buried together in Jhang, where their tomb remains a pilgrimage site. Waris Shah's 1766 poetic rendition elevated this folk tragedy into the quintessential Punjabi romance.

title: Heitsi-Eibib Defeats the Ga-Gorib
summary: Heitsi-Eibib, the ancestral hero and trickster of the Khoikhoi people, confronted the fearsome monster Ga-Gorib who sat at the edge of a deep hole, challenging passersby to throw a stone at his forehead. The stone would bounce back and kill the thrower. Unlike his predecessors, Heitsi-Eibib refused the challenge and instead distracted Ga-Gorib long enough to strike him behind the ear. Ga-Gorib lost his balance and fell into his own pit, dying in the hole he had prepared for others. Heitsi-Eibib is a death-rebirth figure whose funeral cairns are scattered across southern Africa, where travelers throw stones for good luck.

title: Helhest
summary: A three-legged horse associated with the goddess Hel. It is seen in churchyards as a harbinger of death and illness, often appearing before a person dies. Legend says a living horse was interred in every churchyard before human burial, returning as the Hel-horse.

title: Heloha and Melatha: Thunder and Lightning Birds (Choctaw)
summary: In Choctaw mythology, Heloha (Thunder) and Melatha (Lightning) are two enormous birds responsible for the dramatic thunderstorms that sweep across the Mississippi region. Heloha, the female, lays her giant eggs high in the clouds, and the eggs rumble and roll around atop the clouds, creating the sound of thunder. Her mate, Melatha, is incredibly fast despite his huge size. As he streaks across the sky, he leaves a trail of sparks that become lightning. Together they create the powerful storms that bring rain to the land. The Choctaw respected these bird spirits and understood thunder and lightning as natural phenomena caused by living creatures, not abstract forces.

title: Hi'iaka's Journey to Bring Lohiau to Pele
summary: Pele fell in love with Lohiau, a chief of Kauai, during a spirit dream. She sent her beloved youngest sister Hi'iaka to retrieve him. Hi'iaka agreed on the condition that Pele protect her sacred lehua groves and friend Hopoe. On Kauai, Hi'iaka found Lohiau had died of heartbreak and spent thirty days chanting to revive him. On the journey back, Pele grew jealous of Hi'iaka's prolonged absence. In rage, Pele destroyed Hi'iaka's lehua groves and encased Hopoe in lava. Hi'iaka, seeing this through far-sight, defiantly embraced Lohiau at the crater's edge. Pele engulfed them in flames. Hi'iaka revived Lohiau again, and ultimately Pele allowed them to return to Kauai together.

title: Hi-nun and the Niagara Legend
summary: The Seneca tell of Hi-nun, the Thunderer, who fought a great battle with a monstrous serpent living in the Niagara River. The serpent had grown so large that it blocked the flow of the river, causing devastating floods. Hi-nun descended from the sky with his thunderbolt and struck the serpent, whose thrashing body carved out the shape of Niagara Falls as it died. The mist that rises from the falls is said to be the serpent's dying breath. The Spirit of the West Wind was honored thereafter by the Seneca for his role in the battle, and the thunder of the falls is Hi-nun's voice warning away other monsters. This legend explains both the origin of the falls and the reverence paid to the thunder beings.

title: Hiawatha and the Invention of Wampum
summary: When Hiawatha's three daughters were killed by the evil Tadodaho, he was consumed by grief and wandered the wilderness. The Great Peacemaker found him and taught him the Condolence Ceremony to ease his grief. As part of this ceremony, Hiawatha invented wampum — strings of purple and white shell beads — to record the laws and treaties of the growing Confederacy. He strung the white beads to represent peace and the purple to represent the grave matters of the law. The strings of wampum became the constitutional record of the Haudenosaunee, serving as mnemonic devices to help storytellers recall the exact words of the Great Law. The Hiawatha Belt, with its central symbols, depicts the five nations united under the Great Tree of Peace.

title: High John the Conqueror and the Devil's Daughter
summary: High John the Conqueror, an African prince sold into slavery who became a legendary trickster, falls in love with the Devil's beautiful daughter. The Devil, enraged, sets John a series of impossible tasks to keep them apart: John must clear sixty acres of forest in half a day, plow the land, plant it with corn, and harvest it all before sunset. The Devil's daughter, who loves John truly, secretly gives him a magical axe that fells trees on its own and a magical plow that turns the soil without effort. John completes every task with time to spare. The Devil then tries to kill John by setting his bed on fire, but John escapes by shape-shifting. John and the Devil's daughter steal the Devil's swiftest horses and flee. The Devil pursues them, but John and his lover transform themselves into various forms—a pond and a duck, a church and a preacher—evading capture at every turn until they escape forever.

title: High John the Conqueror Brings Freedom
summary: According to the lore collected by Zora Neale Hurston, High John the Conqueror was more than a trickster—he was a spirit of liberation who moved invisibly among the enslaved. Born an African prince, John was captured and sold into slavery, but his spirit could never be broken. When the whip fell, John would 'take the spirit of his people out of their bodies' so they could not feel the pain. He could be heard laughing in the slave quarters at night, a sound that reminded the enslaved that freedom was coming. John planted the idea of emancipation in the minds of white people and provoked the Civil War itself. After emancipation, John returned to Africa, but according to Hurston, 'He left his power here' and 'he waits to return when his people call him.' High John's root—a dried tuber carried in a mojo bag—remains a central talisman in Hoodoo practice, symbolizing unbreakable spirit and the certainty of victory over oppression.

title: Hikule'o, Tangaloa, and Maui Divide the Cosmos
summary: In Tongan creation myth, after the primordial god Taufulifonua fathered Hikule'o with his sister Havea Lolofonua, the three great powers divided the universe. Hikule'o received Pulotu, the underworld realm of spirits and the afterlife. Tangaloa took the vast sky and heavens, becoming ruler of the celestial domain. Maui received the underworld (the earth's foundation) and was tasked with fishing up the islands from the ocean. This tripartite division established the cosmic order—the sky above (Tangaloa's realm), the earth's surface (under Maui's influence), and the underworld of Pulotu (Hikule'o's domain where souls journey after death). The balance between these three realms governs Tongan spiritual beliefs.

title: Hina: The Woman in the Moon
summary: Hina (also called Sina or Ina across different Polynesian cultures) was a mortal woman who became the moon goddess. In the Maori version, Hina went to fetch water at night and cursed the moon when she stumbled in darkness. The moon descended, caught her, and lifted her into the sky. In Hawaiian tradition, Hina was the mother of Maui who escaped human troubles and found refuge in the moon. Cook Islands stories tell that the moon god Marama fell in love with Ina and carried her away. In Samoa, Hina makes tapa cloth in the moon, her form visible during full moon nights. Across Polynesia, Hina represents the divine feminine, the cycle of death and rebirth, and the celestial light that guides voyagers at night.

title: Hinemoa and Tutanekai
summary: Hinemoa, a high-born maiden from the shores of Lake Rotorua, fell in love with Tutanekai, a younger son of a chief who lived on Mokoia Island. Her family disapproved of the match. Tutanekai would play his flute across the lake each night, and Hinemoa listened from the shore. One night, spurred by her love, Hinemoa tied gourds to her body for buoyancy and swam across the cold lake in darkness. She reached Mokoia Island and found her way to Tutanekai by following his music. The lovers were reunited, and her family eventually accepted their union. This story is one of the most celebrated Maori love legends.

title: Hinnon, the Thunder Spirit
summary: The Huron believe in the Thunders, a group of powerful storm spirits who live in the sky and look like a cross between men and giant turkeys. Their leader is Hinnon, whom they call Grandfather. Hinnon and his warriors pursue and destroy the great horned serpents and other monsters that threaten the world. When lightning flashes, it is Hinnon throwing his thunderbolt; when thunder rolls, it is his voice. The Huron make offerings of tobacco to Hinnon before long journeys and during storms. In the Huron creation myth, the first thunderclap occurred when Aataentsic fell through the Sky Land, marking the beginning of the new world below. The Thunderers also gave the people tobacco and taught them the proper ceremonies to honor the Great Spirit.

title: Hiro the Trickster and the Magic Canoe
summary: Hiro, the Tahitian trickster god of thieves and the son of the god Ta'aroa, built a magical canoe that could sail faster than the wind. Using his cunning and his enchanted vessel, Hiro traveled across the Society Islands performing daring thefts and outsmarting chiefs and gods alike. He stole fish from the markets, food from the temples, and once even attempted to steal the island of Bora Bora itself. His exploits angered the other gods, who eventually unleashed a great storm to stop him. The story of Hiro's rebellion and eventual downfall teaches that even the cleverest trickster cannot escape divine justice, but his resourcefulness remains celebrated in Tahitian storytelling.

title: Hlakanyana: The Zulu-Xhosa Trickster Born from the Womb
summary: Hlakanyana (Uhlakanyana) is a cunning trickster figure in Zulu and Xhosa folklore, of weasel-like size and nature, who speaks from his mother's womb demanding to be born because the cattle of his father are being devoured. After birth, he embarks on a series of adventures: he tricks a cannibal by cooking the cannibal's mother and feeding her to him, escapes by turning into a stick, steals birds from traps, and outwits a hyena and a baboon. His stories emphasize the triumph of intelligence over brute strength and the importance of cunning for survival in a precarious world.

title: Hoklonote: The Shape-Shifting Spirit (Choctaw)
summary: Hoklonote is a malevolent Choctaw spirit who can assume any shape it desires. This bad spirit is believed to be able to read people's thoughts, making it nearly impossible to hide from. Hoklonote takes different forms to deceive and harm humans — appearing as a loved one, an animal, or even an inanimate object. The spirit's ability to change shape and read minds made it one of the most feared beings in Choctaw mythology. Shamans performed protective rituals to ward off Hoklonote, and people were taught to be suspicious of unexpected occurrences or unusual animal behavior. The story teaches that evil can take many disguises and that spiritual awareness is necessary for protection.

title: Holy Boy Makes the Sun and Moon
summary: In Apache tradition, Holy Boy was unhappy with the darkness in the underworld and decided to create a sun. He tried many materials without success. Cyclone, spying on the Hactcin, told Holy Boy that White Hactcin had the sun. Holy Boy went to White Hactcin who gave him the sun, and to Black Hactcin who gave him the moon. Black Hactcin taught Holy Boy how to make a sacred sandpainting on a buckskin to hold the sun and moon. Holy Boy, Red Boy, Black Hactcin, and White Hactcin held a ceremony with songs, and White Hactcin released the sun while Black Hactcin released the moon. Light grew stronger as the sun moved from north to south, becoming daylight. The medicine people immediately claimed credit for making the sun, arguing with each other. The Hactcin warned them about eclipses. When an eclipse came, the medicine people could not restore the sun — only the Hactcin could, teaching that humans should not claim divine powers.

title: Hotu Matu'a Discovers Rapa Nui
summary: King Hotu Matu'a lived in the mythical land of Hiva, which was sinking beneath the ocean. A prophet named Hau Maka appeared in Hotu Matu'a's dream and told him to search for a new island called Rapa Nui. Seven explorers were sent ahead in a canoe, finding the uninhabited island. They returned to report its location. Hotu Matu'a then sailed with two large canoes carrying approximately a hundred people, including his wife, children, and essential plants and animals. When they landed at Anakena Beach, Hotu Matu'a established the first settlement and divided the island among his descendants. His nine sons became the ancestors of the Rapa Nui clans, and he inaugurated the moai carving tradition to honor his lineage.

title: Hotuiyi (Antelope) and the Warning
summary: A Comanche hunting party was pursuing a herd of antelope across the plains when a strange antelope with glowing eyes appeared. The lead hunter recognized it as a spirit messenger and halted the chase. The antelope led the party to a hidden spring where they found water, then traced a path around a dangerous canyon where enemy warriors lay in ambush. The hunter realized the antelope had saved them from both thirst and attack. The Comanche gave thanks to the antelope spirit and thereafter considered antelope sightings as omens—if the antelope runs east, good fortune follows; if west, danger approaches.

title: Hou Yi and the Arrows
summary: Before there were emperors or dynasties, before history was written in bronze and bone, the world was ruled by gods, and among those gods were the ten suns.

title: How Anansi Got His Stories
summary: Long ago, all stories in the forest belonged to Tiger, and were called Tiger Stories. Anansi, tired of being mocked as the weakest creature, demanded that stories be named after him. Tiger set an impossible task: capture Snake. After failing with a noose, a pit trap, and a cage, Anansi tricked Snake by challenging his length against bamboo. Anansi tied Snake's head and tail to the bamboo, proving that brains can overcome brawn. From that day, all stories became Anansi Stories. The phrase "Jack Mandora, mi nuh choose none" is traditionally said at the end to absolve the storyteller of Anansi's mischievous deeds.

title: How Brer Rabbit Lost His Fine Bushy Tail
summary: In this pourquoi tale explaining why rabbits have short tails, Brer Rabbit once had a long, beautiful, bushy tail that he showed off constantly. Brer Fox grew tired of Brer Rabbit's vanity and devised a plan. During a cold winter, Brer Fox went ice fishing and called out to Brer Rabbit, showing him a string of fish he had caught. Brer Rabbit, greedy for the fish, asked how to catch them himself. Brer Fox told him to cut a hole in the ice, dip his beautiful tail in, and sit there until the fish bit—then pull up the tail with a mighty jerk. Brer Rabbit sat all day until his tail froze solid in the ice. When evening came, he gave a mighty jerk and his tail snapped off clean, leaving only the short stub rabbits have to this day. Brer Fox laughed heartily at the vanity that cost Brer Rabbit his finest feature.

title: How Death Came to Humanity (Yoruba/Benin)
summary: In the beginning, humans did not experience death. When they grew old, the god Olorun would rejuvenate them. A man named Iku (Death) was sent to test humanity. Iku appeared as an old man begging for food, but only one woman, a poor widow, shared her meal with him. Iku rewarded her by warning her that a plague would come and only those who stayed indoors would survive. When the plague struck, the disobedient died, and from that moment on, death entered the world. Iku was appointed as the one who carries souls to the afterlife. The Yoruba believe that death is not an end but a transition to the ancestral realm (Ọrun), where the dead join the ancestors and continue to influence the world of the living. This story explains the origin of mortality and the importance of hospitality in Yoruba culture.

title: How Fisher Went to the Skyland (The Big Dipper)
summary: Long ago, the giant lynx Mishipeshu had imprisoned all the summer birds in a cave beneath the earth, plunging the world into endless winter. The animals held a council and decided to free the birds. Fisher, the swiftest of them, led a band of animals to the cave. While the others distracted Mishipeshu, Fisher slipped inside and released the birds. Summer returned, but the enraged Mishipeshu pursued Fisher across the sky. As Fisher ran, the spirits lifted him higher and higher into the heavens, where he was transformed into the constellation we call the Big Dipper (which the Ojibwe call Ojiig, meaning Fisher). Every year, when the constellation appears in the northern sky, it signals the return of spring. The other animals who helped were also placed in the sky as stars.

title: How Fox Saved the People
summary: During a catastrophic famine, the cunning Fox discovers a hidden source of food. While Raven tries to take credit through tricks, Fox's genuine assistance saves the community. The tale serves as a lesson in humility and the value of practical wisdom over empty boasting.

title: How Glooscap Found the Summer
summary: In the long-ago time, there was no summer — only endless winter. The earth was covered in snow and ice, the people were freezing, and the animals suffered. Glooscap decided to find the spirit of summer and bring it back. He traveled to the far north where Winter, a powerful giant, held Summer captive in his ice lodge. Glooscap challenged Winter to a contest of power. They told stories for many days, and as Winter talked, frost grew thicker on the walls. But Glooscap's stories were of warmth, green leaves, and flowing water. He so charmed the spirit of Summer that she awakened and began to melt Winter's ice. Winter retreated north, and Summer followed Glooscap back to the people. Ever since, Summer and Winter alternate — Winter rules for half the year, but when his power wanes, Summer returns and the world thaws. The Mi'kmaq celebrate this cycle as the eternal rhythm of life.

title: How Gluskabe Stole Tobacco
summary: In the early days, tobacco was guarded jealously by Grasshopper (or a giant), who kept it hidden from humanity. The people prayed for tobacco to use in their ceremonies, as it was the sacred plant that carried their prayers to the Creator. Gluskabe heard their pleas and devised a plan. He transformed himself into a small, harmless creature — sometimes a rabbit, sometimes a mouse — and snuck into Grasshopper's lodge while he was away. He found the tobacco bundled in a pouch and escaped with it. Grasshopper pursued but Gluskabe was too swift. He distributed the tobacco among the Wabanaki tribes, teaching them how to plant and harvest it and how to offer it in sacred pipes. The smoke rising from the pipes carries the people's prayers directly to Gichi Niwaskw, the Great Spirit, and Gluskabe is honored for this gift that connects the people with the divine.

title: How Medicine Man Resurrected Buffalo
summary: During a terrible famine, all the buffalo had disappeared from the plains. The Arapaho people were starving. A powerful medicine man went into the mountains to seek a vision. After four days of fasting, the spirit of the Earth came to him and told him that the buffalo had gone underground because the people had been wasteful. Following the spirit's instructions, the medicine man gathered the tribe for a ceremony. Through songs, prayers, and the use of his medicine bundle, he opened a passage to the underground buffalo world. The buffalo emerged, and the people were saved. He taught them never to waste the buffalo's gift.

title: How One Went Out to Woo
summary: A clumsy but well-meaning man attempts to find a wife, encountering a series of absurd obstacles and eccentric characters. Through sheer luck and a refusal to be discouraged, he eventually finds a partner who appreciates his oddities.

title: How Pieraš Ánde Learned Noaidi Skills
summary: The initiation story of a Sámi noaidi named Pieraš Ánde who learned shamanic arts. The noaidi's calling often came through dreams, where an ancestor or ancient drum would call the initiate. The initiation involved withdrawal into solitude, metaphorical death and rebirth, and learning to navigate the three levels of the universe to retrieve souls, heal, and divine the future.

title: How Rabbit Brought Fire to the People (Creek)
summary: In this Muscogee Creek legend, the animals possessed fire but kept it hidden from humans. Rabbit, the trickster figure Chufi, decided to steal fire for the people. Rabbit crept to where the animals were guarding the fire and tricked them. He challenged them to a game and, while they were distracted, grabbed a burning ember. The animals chased Rabbit, but he was too quick and clever, passing the fire to the humans. This is why Rabbit is honored by the Creek people. The story differs from the Cherokee fire-bringing myth (which features Water Spider) but shares the theme of a small, clever creature overcoming larger, more powerful beings to bring the gift of fire to humanity. Rabbit's trickster nature is celebrated as ultimately benefitting the people.

title: How Smaland and Schonen Came to Be
summary: An etiological tale explaining why Småland is rocky and barren while Skåne is flat and fertile — because the Devil tried to create land but was foiled at every turn by God. This humorous origin legend was also used by Selma Lagerlöf in her writings.

title: How the Buffalo Were Released on Earth
summary: Long ago, all the buffalo were kept hidden in a cave deep beneath the earth by a powerful spirit who did not want to share them with humans. A young Comanche warrior, guided by a wolf spirit, discovered the cave entrance. Following the wolf's advice, he transformed into a buffalo calf and entered the herd. When the keeper opened the cave door to let the buffalo graze, the warrior-turned-calf stampeded the herd out of the cave. The buffalo poured across the plains, and the Comanche people had food and clothing. The wolf spirit taught the people how to hunt the buffalo with respect.

title: How the Coyote Joined the Dance of the Burrowing-Owls
summary: A Zuni trickster tale about Coyote who stumbled upon a sacred dance of the Burrowing-owls. The owls were performing a ceremonial dance in the moonlight, and Coyote, ever the opportunist, wanted to join. At first the owls were suspicious, but Coyote insisted he could dance as well as they. He joined their circle, but his clumsy, undisciplined dancing disrupted the sacred ceremony. The owls, annoyed by his foolish behavior, played a trick on him. When Coyote tired and wanted to leave, he found that the owls' dance had placed him under a spell — he could not stop dancing. He was forced to dance until dawn, exhausted and humiliated. The story explains why coyotes are often seen running in circles or acting strangely at night. It teaches the Zuni lesson that not all dances are for everyone and that sacred ceremonies require proper preparation and respect.

title: How the Moai Walked
summary: According to Rapanui oral tradition, the great stone moai statues were carved at the Rano Raraku quarry and then walked to their final ahu (ceremonial platforms) across the island. The moai walked at night, powered by mana from the ancestors channeled through the kahuna (priests). Using a system of ropes and rocking motions, teams would chant and coordinate to make the massive statues 'walk' upright, step by step, sometimes for miles. The largest moai, Paro, walked over 10 kilometers before taking its position at Ahu Te Pito Kura. One legend describes how a moai stopped mid-journey when the villagers broke a sacred tapu, and it remains fallen to this day, frozen by the broken taboo.

title: How the Rattlesnakes Came to Be What They Are
summary: A Zuni story explaining the origin of rattlesnakes and their relationship with humans. In the days of the ancients, rattlesnakes did not have their distinctive rattle or their dangerous venom. A man who had been saved by a rattlesnake or had made a pact with one became the founder of the Rattlesnake Society. The snake was given its rattle as a warning device so that humans could hear it and avoid being bitten. The venom was given as a defense but also carries healing power in the hands of those who know the proper ceremonies. The story teaches that rattlesnakes are not merely dangerous creatures but sacred beings with a role in the spiritual ecology of the world. Members of the Rattlesnake Society can handle rattlesnakes without harm and use them in healing ceremonies. The rattle is understood as a gift — a way for the snake to say 'I am here, please step carefully.'

title: How the Sky-God's Stories Became Anansi's (Ashanti/Akan)
summary: Anansi the Spider wanted to buy the stories of Nyame, the Sky God, who owned all the stories in the world. Nyame set a nearly impossible price: Anansi must bring him Onini the python, Mmoboro the hornets, Osebo the leopard, and Mmoatia the invisible dwarf. Through clever trickery, Anansi succeeded. He caught the python by pretending to argue about its length and getting the snake to stretch out on a branch, then tying it. He tricked the hornets into a gourd by convincing them rain was coming. He trapped the leopard in a pit by digging a hole and covering it. He captured the dwarf using a sticky doll. Nyame was so impressed that he declared all stories would henceforth be called Anansi stories. The Akan word 'Anansesem' (spider tales) refers to this collection of stories that Anansi won for humanity.

title: How the Stálos Were Tricked
summary: A classic Stállu trickster tale where a clever Sámi outwits one or more Stállu giants through cunning rather than strength. The story exemplifies the core pattern of Sámi Stállu narratives: a small, clever Sámi hero uses intelligence and knowledge of the landscape to defeat the much larger, stronger, but stupider Stállu. The Stállu's own knife must never be used against him as it gives him strength. After defeating Stállu, the hero must also kill Stállu's dog Rakke, which can lick wounds and resurrect its master.

title: How the Summer Birds Came
summary: A Zuni myth explaining the origin of small summer birds. In the days of the ancients, there were no little birds — only large birds like eagles, crows, and hawks. A Zuni man discovered a magical bundle of feathers left by the spirits. When he walked into a field of flowers, the bundle began to flutter, and small wings flew out from it, becoming the Sacred Birds of Summerland. The feathers were made living by the lives of the birds that had once borne them, and they came to life again in the environment of flowers and summer that they had loved. This is why, according to Zuni tradition, there are jaybirds, sparrows, finches, willow-birds, and all the beautiful little birds that herald summer and hover over flowers. The story concludes with the storyteller noting that Zunis have books too — not with marks but with words in their hearts from the ancients.

title: How Áhaiyúta and Mátsailéma Stole the Thunder-Stone and Lightning-Shaft
summary: In this Zuni myth, the twin war gods Áhaiyúta and Mátsailéma acquired the powerful weapons of thunder and lightning. The thunder-stone and lightning-shaft were kept by powerful beings who did not want to share their power. The twins, known for their cunning and bravery, devised a plan to steal these sacred weapons. Using their shapeshifting abilities and the help of their grandmother (Spider Woman often fills this role), they infiltrated the home of the thunder beings. They stole the thunder-stone (which creates thunder when struck) and the lightning-shaft (which shoots bolts of lightning). These weapons made them invincible in battle and allowed them to defeat enemies too powerful for ordinary weapons. The acquisition of thunder and lightning represents the transfer of cosmic power to the heroes who protect the Zuni people and maintain order in the world.

title: Huldra's Tail
summary: A skilled hunter falls for a beautiful Huldra, accepting her secret animal tail in a rare display of unconditional love that challenges the nature of forest spirits.

title: Huldufólk (The Hidden People)
summary: Huldufólk are supernatural beings in Faroese folklore described as large-built, grey-clad, dark-haired people who live in mounds, rocks, and cliffs—invisible to humans unless they choose to be seen. They are tricksters who dislike electricity, technology, crosses, and churches. According to legend, they left Suðuroy when electricity arrived in the 1950s. The Hidden People feature in Faroese nursery rhymes (skjaldur) such as 'Hulda, mulda, tulda' and traditional kvæði (ballads). They are said to fear knives and can be warded off with the sign of the cross. They coexist in a parallel society with farms, churches, and social structures mirroring human communities.

title: Huldufólk Captured by a Priest at Sørvágsvatn
summary: At Sørvágsvatn Lake on Vágar (the lake that famously appears to hang over the ocean), there is a stone mound where, according to legend, a priest trapped several Huldufólk (Hidden People). The priest used his spiritual authority to imprison the supernatural beings within the mound. Visitors to the area claim they can still hear the wailing and cries of the trapped hidden people emanating from the stone. The legend reflects Faroese beliefs about the power of Christian clergy over pagan supernatural beings, and the common motif of Huldufólk being afraid of crosses, churches, and Christian symbols.

title: Hushang Discovers Fire (Sadeh Feast)
summary: The second king of the Pishdadian dynasty in Persian myth, Hushang, grandson of the first man Gayomard, one day hurls his flint axe at a serpent blocking his path. He misses the snake but the axe strikes a rock, producing a spark. Curious, the king strikes two flints together and creates fire deliberately — the first controlled fire in human history. He proclaims it a divine gift, makes fire his altar, and establishes the Sadeh feast to celebrate the discovery. Hushang also teaches humanity metalworking (fashioning axes, saws, adzes), irrigation, agriculture, animal husbandry, and fur clothing, fundamentally transforming human civilization.

title: Hóu-koô-pô, the Tiger Spirit
summary: A protective tiger spirit who guards the mountains of Taiwan, appearing to those who are lost or in danger.

title: Iara: The River Mother of Brazil
summary: In the rivers of Brazil, where the water runs dark as tea and the piranhas flash silver in the sun, there is a voice sweeter than any bird.

title: Ibong Adarna (The Adarna Bird)
summary: The Ibong Adarna is a legendary magical bird from Philippine epic poetry whose song has the power to heal any sickness and whose droppings turn anyone they fall upon into stone. The tale follows three princes — Pedro, Diego, and Juan — who are sent by their dying king to capture the elusive Adarna Bird. Each prince falls asleep when the bird sings its enchanting melody, failing their quest until one discovers the secret: cutting oneself and applying lemon juice prevents sleep. After many trials involving shapeshifting, betrayal, and magical transformations, the youngest prince Juan ultimately succeeds, reclaiming his kingdom and finding love.

title: Ibonia: The Epic Hero of Madagascar
summary: A legendary hero conceived by magic undertakes a quest to rescue his betrothed from a stone monster.

title: Icarus: Wings Too Close to the Sun
summary: In the city of Athens, during the age of legends, there lived a master craftsman named Daedalus.

title: Iele, the Dancing Spirits of the Meadow
summary: Beautiful but dangerous fairy spirits who dance in moonlit meadows, luring travelers to join their fatal dance.

title: Ifrit
summary: The powerful djinn of the underground. Centers on Ifrit,  from Arabia. jinn associated with ruin..

title: Igbo Landing: The Flying Africans
summary: In May 1803, a group of 75 Igbo people from what is now Nigeria were captured and transported to Georgia. After surviving the Middle Passage, they were loaded onto a small vessel at Savannah and shipped to St. Simons Island to be sold at the slave market. Rather than submit to a life of bondage, the Igbo captives—led by their high-ranking warriors among them—rose up against their captors, took control of the ship, and forced it aground at Dunbar Creek. There, in a coordinated act of mass resistance, they walked deliberately into the water, singing in their native Igbo language, drowning themselves rather than accepting slavery. Some oral accounts say they did not drown at all but transformed into buzzards and flew back across the Atlantic to Africa. The site, Igbo Landing, became sacred ground in African American memory, birthing the enduring 'Flying Africans' mythos—the belief that those who refused to be enslaved could literally fly home to freedom.

title: Ijapa and the Sky Feast
summary: A clever Yoruba tortoise tries to attend a sky feast by tricking birds into carrying him, but his greed leads to a cracked shell.

title: Ikenga, the Horned God of Achievement (Igbo)
summary: Ikenga is the Igbo deity of achievement, success, war, and the right hand. He is depicted as a horned figure, often holding a sword and a severed human head, representing his power and victory. Every Igbo man traditionally owned a personal Ikenga shrine representing his individual chi (personal god) and his right to achievement through hard work. The horns symbolize strength and ambition. A man would pray to his Ikenga before important undertakings, and the shrine was passed down through generations. Ikenga is associated with the warriors, hunters, and men of title. When a man dies, his Ikenga is broken to release his spirit. The Ikenga cult reinforces the Igbo values of personal achievement, hard work, and the accumulation of wealth through one's own efforts.

title: Ikkyu: The Monk Child
summary: A precocious child monk uses his wit to outsmart greedy merchants and teach a lesson about the subjective nature of value.

title: Iktomi and the Boulder
summary: Iktomi the spider trickster wrapped himself in a fine robe and went walking. He came upon a large boulder and, feeling generous, offered it his robe. The boulder declined, but Iktomi insisted and placed the robe upon it. Later, when Iktomi wanted his robe back, the boulder refused. Iktomi grew angry and insulted the boulder, which chased him and crushed him flat. Bats came to help Iktomi, pecking at the boulder until it cracked open, freeing him. But the bats' faces were smashed flat in the effort, and Iktomi—ever ungrateful—scattered pebbles that became the stones covering the plains.

title: Iktomi the Spider Trickster
summary: Iktomi is the spider trickster of Lakota mythology, born fully grown with the body of a spider and the cunning of a man. He is known for his clever schemes and predictions, but his selfishness and mischievous nature often backfire. In one tale, Iktomi tried to keep a pot of fish soup for himself rather than share with a visitor, devising a race trick that ultimately failed. In another, Iktomi angered a boulder and was crushed, only to be freed by bats who were turned into stones. Despite his flaws, Iktomi is considered wise and his stories teach moral lessons about generosity and respect.

title: Ilmarinen Forges the Sampo
summary: Louhi, the powerful Mistress of Pohjola, demands that Ilmarinen forge the Sampo—a mythical mill that automatically produces salt, meal, and gold—in exchange for her daughter's hand in marriage. Ilmarinen succeeds in this monumental task, bringing immense wealth and prosperity to the land of Pohjola.

title: Ilmarinen's Bride of Gold
summary: Driven by loneliness, Ilmarinen forges a bride out of pure gold. However, he discovers that while she is physically perfect, she is cold and emotionless, lacking a human soul. This results in a hollow marriage and deep dissatisfaction.

title: Ilmarinen's Fruitless Wooing
summary: Ilmarinen attempts to find a real human bride to replace his golden creation. However, his efforts are consistently thwarted by fate and his own inability to form a genuine emotional connection with the women he pursues.

title: Ilmarinen's Wedding-feast
summary: Ilmarinen eventually marries the Daughter of Pohjola. The resulting wedding is a grand and opulent affair, but the celebration is overshadowed by the deep-seated tensions and long-standing rivalry between the peoples of Kalevala and Pohjola.

title: Ilmarinen's Wooing
summary: Ilmarinen attempts to woo the Daughter of Pohjola, bringing his skills as a master smith to the table. Like the other suitors, he is subjected to the capricious demands of Louhi, the Mistress of Pohjola, who tests his resolve and his abilities.

title: Imana and the First Rain
summary: When the world was dry and the rivers were empty, Imana struck the sky with his staff and the first rain fell — but the rain was a gift, not a right, and it can be taken back.

title: Imana Who Shaped the Land
summary: Imana, the supreme creator deity, sculpts the lakes and hills of Rwanda from raw earth and water, then breathes life into the first people, only to discover that free will brings both beauty and sorrow.

title: Imana, God of the Hills
summary: The supreme creator god who shaped the hills of Burundi with his hands, placing rivers in the valleys and forests on the slopes — and when the people forgot his name, the hills began to erode.

title: In the House of Ulda
summary: A young Sámi boy from Heahttá went cloudberry picking and took shelter from rain under a rock overhang. The earth opened and he found himself in the underground world of the Ulda. A beautiful Ulda girl with long hair offered him cloudberries on a gold-edged plate. The boy refused the food, remembering his parents' warning: if you eat Ulda food, you must stay forever. He saw strange round cases emitting sounds (radios), and walls with holes showing the sea.

title: Ina and the Shark
summary: The beautiful maiden Ina longed to reach the island of her lover Tinirau, the god of the ocean. A great shark offered to carry her across the sea. During the journey, Ina grew thirsty and cracked open a coconut, drinking its milk. Later, she struck a second coconut directly onto the shark's head to open it, hurting the shark badly. The shark tried to shake her off, but Tekea the Great, king of all sharks, rose from the deep and carried her safely to Tinirau's island. The dent on the shark's head from Ina's coconut blow remains visible to this day, and the story explains why sharks bear a distinctive indentation on their heads.

title: Inkarri and the Return
summary: The last Inca king, beheaded by the Spanish, regrows his body underground and will one day rise to restore the empire and reverse the world.

title: Innocence's Journey
summary: Princess Bella sets out on a solitary journey through the deep forest, a passage that strips away the trappings of civilization. A raven steals her crown for its nest. Undeterred, she continues deeper into the woods, shedding her garments as she becomes one with the wild. The story builds to a confrontation with a great dark eagle, and Bella reaches out her last garment to it in a gesture of complete trust. John Bauer's iconic illustration captures the tiny, pale princess facing the enormous bird in the twilight forest.

title: Inzoka the Serpent of the Lake
summary: A fisherman named Mugabo encounters Inzoka, the great serpent of the lake, who offers him untold riches in exchange for a promise he cannot keep, teaching him the cost of dishonesty.

title: Ioskeha and Tawescaron: The Twin Brothers
summary: After Aataentsic fell to the new earth, she gave birth to twin daughters. One of these daughters, Tekawerahkwa, became the mother of twin sons — Ioskeha and Tawescaron. The twins were opposites in every way. Ioskeha, the older twin, was the benefactor of the Huron people. He created the sun from his mother's body, brought light to the world, slew monsters, gave the people corn and tobacco, and taught them how to live. Tawescaron, the younger twin, was his antagonist. He created monsters, darkness, and winter, and constantly tried to undo his brother's good works. Ioskeha represented light, creation, and life, and was associated with the sun. Tawescaron represented darkness, destruction, and death, and was associated with the night and winter. Despite their opposition, both were necessary for the balance of the world.

title: Iram of the Pillars (Ubar, the Atlantis of the Sands)
summary: A legendary lost city in the Arabian desert mentioned in the Quran, built by the tyrannical King Shaddad son of Ad in an attempt to create an earthly paradise with gold and silver ramparts, pillars of chrysolite and ruby, and rivers flowing through channels of gold. God destroyed Shaddad and his entire army with a mighty sound when they were one day's march from the city, blotting out the road forever. The city became known as the 'Atlantis of the Sands.' In 1992, satellite radar imagery led to the discovery of a 2,000-year-old fortified trading site at Shisr in Oman, now identified by some with the legendary Ubar.

title: Isis and Osiris
summary: The Osiris myth is the most elaborate and influential story in ancient Egyptian mythology. Osiris, a wise and beloved king of Egypt, taught humanity agriculture, law, and civilization. His jealous brother Set conspired with 72 accomplices to murder him, tricking Osiris into a chest which was sealed with lead and cast into the Nile. Isis, Osiris's devoted wife and sister, searched tirelessly for her husband's body. She found the chest embedded in a tamarisk tree at Byblos, but Set discovered the body and dismembered it into fourteen pieces scattered across Egypt. Isis sailed through the papyrus marshes in a small boat, recovering every piece except the phallus. With the help of Thoth and Anubis, she reconstructed Osiris's body—making him the first mummy—and briefly revived him long enough to conceive their son Horus. Osiris became Lord of the Underworld, judge of the dead. Horus later challenged Set for the throne, and after a long contest confirmed by the gods, Horus prevailed, restoring maat (cosmic order) to Egypt.

title: Isokelekel: The Conqueror of Pohnpei
summary: Isokelekel, meaning shining noble or wonderful king, is a semi-mythical hero and warrior from Kosrae who overthrew the Saudeleur rulers of Pohnpei between the early 16th and early 17th centuries. According to legend, Isokelekel arrived at Pohnpei with a fleet of canoes and a band of warriors. The Saudeleur dynasty had ruled Pohnpei tyrannically for centuries, requiring the people to bring food and water by boat to the artificial island city of Nan Madol. Isokelekel defeated the Saudeleur rulers through a combination of military strategy and supernatural aid. After his victory, Isokelekel married a local woman and established the Nahnmwarki system of governance that continues in modified form today. He is considered the father of modern Pohnpei and resides in the oral history as the liberator who ended the oppressive Saudeleur regime.

title: Jab Jab: Carnival of Chains
summary: A young masquerader discovers that the Jab Jab who dances through the streets carries the memory of slavery in every clink of its chains, and that freedom is something you must choose to carry.

title: Jack and the Bean Tree
summary: The Appalachian African American version of the classic Jack and the Beanstalk tale. Jack, a poor mountain boy, trades his family's only cow for a handful of seemingly worthless beans. His mother, furious, throws the beans out the window. Overnight, a giant beanstalk grows all the way to the sky. Jack climbs the beanstalk and discovers a world above the clouds—a giant's castle. He meets the giant's wife, who hides him from her husband, who 'smells the blood of a Christian.' Jack steals the giant's gold, a hen that lays golden eggs, and a magical singing harp. When the giant pursues him down the beanstalk, Jack chops it down with an axe, killing the giant. In the Appalachian versions, the setting shifts to mountain terrain, and Jack's language reflects the regional dialect. African American tellers of the tale emphasized themes of economic survival and outwitting a powerful, deadly enemy—resonant with a community navigating a world where power was concentrated in hostile hands.

title: Jack and the Beanstalk
summary: A boy climbs a magic beanstalk to a giant's castle in the sky, risking everything for his family's survival.

title: Jack and the Robbers
summary: Jack leaves home seeking adventure and meets a group of robbers in the forest. Rather than fleeing, Jack cleverly ingratiates himself with them, pretending to be a fierce outlaw. He joins their band and joins them on a raid of a wealthy house. When the robbers send Jack in to check if the house is empty, Jack finds it full of people but convinces the robbers the house is safe by using ventriloquism and mimicry. During the robbery attempt, Jack deliberately makes noise to alert the householders, then blames the commotion on ghosts. The robbers flee in terror, leaving all the loot behind. Jack collects the abandoned treasure and returns home a rich man. The tale highlights Jack's hallmark traits: he is not particularly brave or strong, but he is quick-witted and lucky, always landing on his feet through a combination of clever words and fortunate circumstances. In Affrilachian versions, Jack's voice and humor are distinctly rooted in African American storytelling cadences.

title: Jack and the Varmints
summary: Jack is tasked with spending a night alone in a haunted cabin in the woods as a test of courage. The cabin is supposedly infested with 'varmints'—supernatural creatures that have driven away everyone who came before. Jack, being too lazy and stubborn to be properly scared, settles into the cabin for the night. As midnight approaches, he hears scratching at the door, howling from the chimney, and strange shapes moving in the shadows. Rather than fleeing, Jack bangs pots, shouts insults, and throws things at the darkness. His sheer orneriness and refusal to be intimidated somehow drives the varmints away. By morning, the cabin is peaceful, and Jack collects the reward. In some versions, the varmints are revealed to be pranksters in costume; snip in others, they are genuine supernatural beings defeated by Jack's audacious spirit. The story resonates in the African American Appalachian tradition as a tale of facing one's fears with humor and determination rather than weapons.

title: Jack in the Giants' Newground
summary: Jack, a lazy mountain boy, decides to seek his fortune after his mother grows tired of his idleness. He arrives at a king's house and learns that giants have overrun the king's 'newground' (newly cleared land) and will not let anyone farm it. Anyone who goes against them is eaten. Jack volunteers, armed only with his wits and a bag of tricks. He encounters the giants and, rather than fighting them directly, uses cleverness to turn them against one another. He convinces one giant that another has insulted his wife, leading the giants to fight among themselves. When the dust settles, the giants are either dead or fled, and Jack claims the reward. This tale originates from the European Jack Tale tradition but was carried into Appalachia by Scots-Irish settlers and preserved, particularly within African American communities of the Southern mountains, where Jack became a symbol of the clever underdog who overcomes overwhelming odds through wit rather than strength.

title: Jacky-My-Lantern
summary: In this African American version of the will-o'-the-wisp legend collected by Joel Chandler Harris, Jacky-My-Lantern is a wandering spirit who carries a flickering light through the swamps at night, luring travelers from the safety of the road into the treacherous marshland. According to Uncle Remus, Jacky-My-Lantern was once a man who made a deal with the Devil and was cursed to wander the earth with only a lantern made from a hollowed turnip and a coal of fire to light his way, never finding rest. When travelers see the bobbing light and follow it, hoping to reach shelter, they soon find themselves sinking into the bog, unable to find their way back. The only protection against Jacky-My-Lantern is to carry a Bible, wear your coat inside out, or avoid being out at night near the swamp. The legend blends African American folklore with European jack-o'-lantern traditions, creating a distinctively Southern cautionary tale about the dangers of the unknown and the consequences of making deals with dark forces.

title: Jaka Tarub and the Seven Heavenly Nymphs
summary: A Javanese folktale from Central Java about a young man named Jaka Tarub who spies on seven heavenly nymphs (bidadari) bathing in a forest lake. He steals the shawl of the youngest and most beautiful, Nawang Wulan, preventing her from returning to heaven. She marries him, and they have a daughter. Nawang Wulan possesses magical powers that allow her to cook a single grain of rice into a full meal. However, Jaka Tarub breaks her trust by lifting the cover of the cooking pot, breaking the spell. Nawang Wulan discovers her shawl, which Jaka Tarub had hidden, and returns to heaven. According to tradition, their descendants founded the great Mataram Kingdom.

title: Jataka — Prince Sattva and the Starving Tigress
summary: In this most famous Jataka tale of self-sacrifice, the Buddha in a past life was born as Prince Sattva (sometimes called Prince Mahasattva). While wandering in the forest with his brothers, he came upon a starving tigress too weak to nurse her newborn cubs, about to eat them out of desperation. Overcome with compassion, the prince sent his brothers ahead, then lay down before the tigress, offering his own body. When she was too weak to even bite him, he cut his throat with a sharp stick. The tigress and her cubs survived by eating his flesh, and the prince attained a higher spiritual state through his act of ultimate generosity.

title: Jataka — The Banyan Deer (Nigrodhamiga Jataka)
summary: In a past life, the Buddha was born as a golden deer named King Banyan Deer, leader of a herd of 500 deer in the forests near Benares. When the local king hunted deer excessively, the deer kings devised a lottery system where deer would sacrifice themselves in turn. One day, a pregnant doe from the Monkey Deer herd was destined to die, but her king refused to help her. King Banyan Deer took her place, laying his head on the chopping block. Moved by this extraordinary self-sacrifice, the human king granted the deer sanctuary and vowed to protect all animals in his kingdom.

title: Jesús Malverde — The Generous Bandit
summary: Jesús Malverde (1870–1909) is a legendary Mexican bandit turned folk saint whose devotion has spread to Mexican-American communities throughout the US Southwest. Born in Sinaloa, Malverde was said to rob from the rich and give to the poor, earning him the nickname 'The Generous Bandit' or 'The Robin Hood of Sinaloa.' He was hanged by government authorities in 1909, and his body was left to rot, but local people began to build a shrine at his grave. Today his shrine in Culiacán, Sinaloa, is visited by thousands who pray for protection, luck, and miracles. In the United States, Malverde is especially venerated by Mexican-American immigrants for his association with crossing borders, navigating danger, and surviving on society's margins. His image — a handsome man with a mustache wearing a white shirt and scarf — appears alongside Santa Muerte in botanicas from Los Angeles to Houston. Though the Catholic Church does not recognize him, his folk canonization speaks to the need for saints who understand the struggles of the poor, the criminalized, and the dispossessed. Malverde's legend raises complex questions about morality, justice, and who society chooses to sanctify.

title: Jinn (Genie), the Djiboutian Spirit World
summary: The jinn of Djibouti are powerful spirits of fire and air who inhabit the desert and the sea, interacting with humans through bargains and blessings.

title: Johan and the Trolls
summary: A servant named Johan is sent to catch a horse but is lured by a beautiful troll maiden into a mountain. He disappears for years, forced to steal food for the trolls using a magical red hat that lets him fly through locked doors. His master eventually rescues him by throwing his clothes up the cliff, but Johan is never the same, remaining gloomy and silent until his death.

title: John Henry
summary: In the years after the Civil War, as America stretched its railroads across the continent, a new kind of hero emerged from the sweat and labor of the nation's working men.

title: John Henry vs. the Steam Drill
summary: John Henry, the legendary steel-driving man, worked as a hammer-swinging laborer blasting tunnels through mountains for the expanding railroad. When a salesman brought a steam-powered drilling machine to the worksite, claiming it could outwork any man, the captain of the crew proposed a contest: man against machine. John Henry accepted the challenge to prove that human strength and dignity could not be replaced by cold iron. With his shaker holding the drill steady, John Henry swung his nine-pound hammer in great arcs, driving steel deeper and faster than the steam drill. For hours the contest raged, the rhythmic ring of John Henry's hammer against the drill echoing through the mountain. When the contest ended, John Henry had drilled fourteen feet while the steam drill had managed only nine. He had beaten the machine.

title: Jok, Lord of the Cattle Spirits
summary: Jok, the supreme sky spirit of the Nilotic peoples, sent his cattle spirits to walk among the herds of earth, teaching the people that every ox carries a fragment of divine will within its horns.

title: Jong Batu (The Legend of the Stone Ship)
summary: A beloved Bruneian legend about an unfilial son who was turned to stone, sharing the same moral motif as Malin Kundang and Si Tanggang. According to the tale, a wealthy young merchant named Awang or Si Untak returned to Brunei on his magnificent ship after making his fortune abroad. His elderly mother, who had raised him alone after his father's death, rushed to greet him at the shore. Ashamed of her simple appearance before his crew and wife, the son cruelly denied knowing his own mother, ordering his sailors to push her away. Heartbroken, his mother prayed for divine justice. A massive storm rose instantly, capsizing the ship and petrifying it into a rocky outcrop in Brunei Bay. The rock formation known as Jong Batu still stands today as a permanent warning against filial unfaithfulness.

title: Juan Bobo: The Folk Simpleton
summary: Juan Bobo (Simple John) is a beloved folk character in Puerto Rican and broader Caribbean folklore — a good-hearted but dim-witted boy whose adventures always go hilariously wrong. In one classic tale, Juan Bobo's mother asks him to watch the pot of rice while she goes to church. He decides to bathe the pig with the rice water, then feeds the rice to the chickens, explaining that he was keeping everything clean. In another, when told to mind the baby, he dresses the family dog in the baby's clothes. Despite his foolishness, Juan Bobo stories carry gentle moral lessons about honesty, kindness, and the importance of listening carefully to instructions. He represents the everyman who, through innocence rather than malice, reveals life's absurdities.

title: Juan Machete: The Fire-Vomiting Phantom
summary: A Colombian plainsman makes a pact with the devil but ends up cursed to guard his buried treasure for eternity.

title: Jumbie, the Restless Spirit
summary: In Antiguan folklore, a Jumbie is a restless spirit of the dead that haunts the living, often appearing at crossroads or near ancient trees.

title: Juoksáhkká: The Bow Woman
summary: Juoksáhkká (Bow Woman) is a goddess depicted with a bow on Sámi drums. One of the daughters of Máttaráhkká, she could change a child's sex from female to male in the womb if given enough offerings, as sons were more valued. She helped with development and birth, protected children from shots and falls, and helped women during menstruation. After a son was born, a small bow and arrow were placed in Sáráhkká's porridge.

title: Juracán, Lord of the Storm
summary: Juracán is the Taino god of storms and hurricanes, the origin of the English word 'hurricane.' In Taino mythology, Juracán was once Guacar, the twin brother of Yocahú, son of the mother goddess Atabey. While Atabey and Yocahú worked together filling the world with beautiful creations, Guacar grew jealous of their bond. His bitterness transformed him into Juracán, a destructive zemi of chaos who, alongside his wife Guabancex (goddess of storms), conjures devastating hurricanes to dismantle his mother's and brother's creations. The Taino believed Juracán dwelt in the mountains and unleashed storms when angered. The destructive power of Caribbean hurricanes was thus explained as divine conflict between creation and chaos. Cemí figures representing Juracán were carved with twisted, furious faces.

title: Jurate and Kastytis: The Amber Legend of the Baltic Sea
summary: A sea goddess falls in love with a mortal fisherman, and her shattered amber palace becomes the treasure of the Baltic shore.

title: Jábmiidáhkká: Ruler of the Underworld
summary: Jábmiidáhkká is the female ruler of Jábmiidaibmu, the Sámi underworld. The dead missed their relatives, so she sometimes allowed them to cause diseases among the living. If the dead caught a living person's soul and dragged it to the underworld, that person would fall into a coma or fatal illness. She could allow the soul to return if sufficient offerings were made. Black animals were sacrificed to her by being buried alive under piles of stones.

title: Kaang's Creation: The Great Tree and the First People
summary: The San creator god Kaang (also known as /Kaggen) created a wondrous tree whose branches stretched over the entire land. At its base he dug a hole reaching down to the underworld where people and animals lived in harmony. He led them up into the world, instructing them not to build fires. When the sun set, the people grew cold and afraid, disobeying Kaang's command. The fire frightened the animals, who fled to caves and mountains, and from that day forward humans lost the ability to communicate with animals. This myth explains the separation between humans and nature and the origin of animal wildness.

title: Kaats' and the Bear Woman (Tlingit)
summary: The Tlingit hunter Kaats' was hunting in the mountains near Glacier Bay when he encountered a bear who removed her skin and became a beautiful woman. He married her, and they had children who were half-human, half-bear. His bear wife provided for him and taught him about the forest, but Kaats' eventually grew homesick for his human village. When he tried to leave with their children, the bear wife pursued him. She called upon her bear relatives, and a great confrontation ensued. Kaats' escaped with the help of his human relatives, but the bear wife reclaimed her children and returned to the forest. The descendants of these children became the Bear Clan among the Tlingit. This story explains clan origins and the special relationship between the Tlingit Bear Clan and bears, who are considered ancestral relatives rather than mere animals. It also teaches profound lessons about cross-cultural marriage, identity, and belonging.

title: Kaguya-hime: The Princess of the Moon
summary: A celestial princess found in a stalk of bamboo brings wealth and beauty to her adoptive father, but must eventually return to her lunar home.

title: Kahausibware: The Creator Goddess
summary: Kahausibware is a creator goddess in the mythology of the Mono-Alu people of the Solomon Islands. She is a supreme female deity credited with creating the world, the islands, and all living things. In the beginning, Kahausibware created the land by pulling islands up from the sea. She then fashioned humans from clay and breathed life into them, teaching them how to build canoes, plant gardens, and fish. As a creator goddess, she represents the feminine creative principle and is associated with fertility, growth, and the abundance of the sea and forest. Her worship was central to Mono-Alu religious life, with offerings made to ensure good harvests and successful fishing expeditions.

title: Kaji, the Fire Spirit
summary: A spirit of fire and lightning that inhabits the hearth, protecting the home when respected and burning it when angered, because in Georgia fire is both hearth and hell.

title: Kalala Ilunga: The Founder of the Luba Empire
summary: Kalala Ilunga, son of Mbidi Kiluwe and Bulanda, was born with the destiny of a conqueror. From childhood, he showed extraordinary strength, intelligence, and mystical gifts far beyond his years — he was said to praise himself for future exploits on the very day of his birth. His uncle, King Nkongolo, grew jealous and afraid of the young prince's growing power. Nkongolo plotted to kill Kalala by digging a pit filled with spears and fetishes in the dance hall, hoping Kalala would fall in during a ceremonial dance. But the Mbudye priests warned Kalala, and he danced carefully, avoiding the trap. When Nkongolo's warriors attacked, Kalala defeated them and pursued Nkongolo. He caught the tyrant, beheaded him, and returned to the capital with his head and genitals as proof of victory. The people proclaimed him Mulopwe (Emperor). Kalala Ilunga expanded the Luba kingdom into an empire, establishing a sacred dynasty that would rule for centuries.

title: Kalanoro: The Forest Spirits of Madagascar
summary: Small, child-like spirits with backward feet haunt the remote forests of Madagascar.

title: Kali
summary: In the age when the devas, the gods of heaven, were locked in an eternal struggle with the asuras, the demons of the underworld, a terror arose that threatened to unmake the balance of the cosmos.

title: Kali and the Thugs
summary: In the frozen forests of Siberia, where the winter lasts nine months and the temperature can drop to sixty degrees below zero, there lives a creature that the Evenki reindeer herders have learned to respect.

title: Kalulu and the Pot of Wisdom
summary: Kalulu the Hare, the great trickster of Malawian lore, attempted to steal a pot of wisdom from the sky-god Chiuta, only to discover that wisdom cannot be hoarded — it must be shared to multiply.
themes: wisdom must be shared, not hoarded
storytelling as a vessel for knowledge
respect for the boundaries set by creators

title: Kalunga-Ngombe and the Bridge of Bones
summary: A river monster demands a toll from those who cross the water, and only a woman with the wisdom of her ancestors learns the true price of passage.

title: Kamata the Culture Hero of Vanuatu
summary: Kamata is a culture hero in Vanuatu mythology, particularly among the people of Ambrym and Malekula. He is credited with bringing fire, agriculture, and essential knowledge to humanity. Kamata journeyed across the islands performing great deeds, shaping the landscape, and teaching people how to cultivate yams, build houses, and conduct proper ceremonies. He is associated with the volcano spirits of Ambrym, a region known for its active volcanic activity. Kamata's exploits often involve tricking dangerous spirits and defeating monstrous beings. His stories are part of the larger cycle of Melanesian culture heroes who brought civilization to humanity and established social customs that continue to be observed.

title: Kanati and Selu: The Origin of Game and Corn (Cherokee)
summary: Kanati (The Lucky Hunter) and Selu (Corn) were the first Cherokee man and woman. Kanati would hunt by moving a rock at the entrance of a cave, releasing an animal and killing it. Their son befriended a Wild Boy born from the blood of slaughtered game. The boys secretly followed Kanati and discovered the cave; they opened it, allowing all animals to escape, which is why humans must hunt for food today. Selu would produce corn by rubbing her stomach, and beans by rubbing her sides. When the boys discovered her secret, Selu knew she would die. She instructed them to drag her body seven times around a cleared circle, then seven times inside it, and corn would grow by morning. The boys did not complete the ritual properly, which is why corn only grows in certain places. The story establishes the Cherokee relationship with hunting, agriculture, and the origin of food scarcity.

title: Kannagi and the Burning of Madurai (Silappadikaram)
summary: Kannagi, a virtuous merchant's daughter, married Kovalan in the Chola city of Puhar. When Kovalan fell for the courtesan Madhavi and squandered all his wealth, he eventually returned to Kannagi. The couple traveled to Madurai, where Kovalan tried to sell one of Kannagi's jeweled anklets to restart his life. The royal goldsmith, who had stolen the queen's similar anklet, falsely accused Kovalan of theft. The Pandya king ordered Kovalan's execution without proper trial. Kannagi stormed into court, broke open her anklet to reveal rubies (the queen's held pearls), proving her husband's innocence. The king died of shame, but Kannagi, in divine fury, tore off her breast and hurled it at the kingdom, cursing Madurai to burn to ashes — a curse that consumed the entire city.

title: Kappa: The River imp
summary: A water spirit that lives in rivers, respects honor, and can be fooled by a simple formality.

title: Karakoncolos: The Winter Goblin of Anatolia
summary: A hairy winter goblin challenges travelers with riddles during the coldest days of the year.

title: Kashehotapalo (Choctaw)
summary: Kashehotapalo is a creature from Choctaw mythology that is neither man nor beast. It has the legs and hooves of a deer but the body of a man. Its head and face are small and shriveled, and it is said that anyone who looks at it will be visited by evil. Kashehotapalo delights in frightening hunters who venture near the swamps it inhabits. It sneaks up behind them and lets out a loud call that sounds like a woman's scream before quickly fleeing into the darkness. Though it does not physically harm people, it takes great pleasure in their terror. Its name comes from 'kasheho' (woman) and 'tapalo' (call). The creature serves as a guardian of the wild places, warning against entering certain swamps and forests.

title: Katie Grey
summary: The Devil himself cannot sow discord between a loving couple, so he enlists the witch Katie Grey. She tricks the wife into trying a 'charm' (cutting hairs from her sleeping husband's beard) and convinces the husband that his wife will cut his throat. The misunderstanding leads to both spouses killing each other. Even the Devil is terrified of Katie Grey.

title: Katie Woodencloak
summary: Katie, a girl born with a wooden cloak that makes her an object of ridicule, endures hardship and loneliness. However, her resilience and the hidden magical properties of her cloak eventually lead her to a destiny of love and royalty, showing that true value lies beneath the surface.

title: Katrineholm Manor
summary: An old unoccupied manor in Småland is haunted because it was built on a mountain inhabited by troll spirits. The lady of the manor helps a troll queen in childbirth and receives a box of jewels, but warns that revealing the secret will bring disaster. When her husband discovers the treasure through their sons' curiosity, he rows to a mysterious island with the boys, where both children vanish forever.

title: Kaveh the Blacksmith and the Derafsh Kaviani
summary: Kaveh, a humble blacksmith, loses all but one of his sons to the daily sacrifice demanded by King Zahhak's serpent-shoulders. He storms the royal court, refusing the king's bribe of signing his remaining son's death warrant. Kaveh raises his blacksmith's leather apron on a spear as a battle standard and leads the populace in revolt. He seeks out Feraydun, the rightful heir, and guides him to overthrow Zahhak. The leather apron, embellished with jewels over centuries, became the Derafsh Kaviani, the legendary imperial standard of Iran used until the Arab conquest. Kaveh symbolizes righteous popular rebellion against tyranny.

title: Kawa the Blacksmith and Newroz
summary: The foundational Kurdish myth explaining the origins of Newroz (the Kurdish New Year on the spring equinox). The evil Assyrian king Zahhak (Zuhak) had serpents growing from his shoulders that demanded daily sacrifices of young men's brains. Kawa, a blacksmith who lost all but one of his sons to the sacrifice, rallied the people in revolt. He led them to the mountains, forged weapons, and stormed Zahhak's palace, killing him with his blacksmith's hammer. Kawa then lit a bonfire on the mountaintop to signal victory — a fire that spread across the land, melting winter and heralding spring.
