The Derafsh Kaviani (Kawa's leather apron on a spear) became the symbol of the uprising. Today Kurds celebrate Newroz by lighting bonfires and jumping over flames.

title: Kel Essuf, the Lonely Desert
summary: A Tuareg caravan leader learns why the Tuareg fear the Kel Essuf, the lonely spirits of the deep desert who lure travelers away from their caravans with false oases and phantom voices.

title: Kelpie
summary: Along the lonely shores of Scottish lochs, by the banks of dark rivers, and in the pools where the water runs deep and still, there dwells a creature both beautiful and deadly.

title: Kettil Runske
summary: Two rival kings on Vising Island hire troll-men to dig a dividing ditch. Gilbertil of Östergötland begins the work, but Kettil Runske of Vestergötland defeats him with a magical staff, leaving Gilbertil bound in a deep hole that still bears his name.

title: Khan Töölö the Hero
summary: The Tuvan epic of Khan Töölö, one of the most important figures in Tuvan oral tradition. The epic tells of a heroic warrior-prince who defends the Tuvan people against invading forces and monstrous beings from the Sayan and Altai mountains. Khan Töölö possesses supernatural strength granted by the sky spirits and rides a magical horse that can speak and fly. The epic is traditionally performed with throat singing accompaniment, with different vocal styles representing different characters — deep kargyraa for the hero, high sygyt for maidens, and rhythmic khoomei for battle scenes. The story reinforces Tuvan values of bravery, hospitality, respect for nature, and the sacred bond between a hero and his horse. The epic can take many hours to perform in its complete form.

title: Khanyapa the Forest Spirit of the Northern Province
summary: A Luvale boy lost in the forests of Zambia's Northern Province is guided to safety by Khanyapa, a forest spirit who tests whether travelers carry respect for the woodland in their hearts.

title: Khosrow and Shirin
summary: The Persian prince Khosrow Parviz falls in love with the Armenian princess Shirin through a portrait painted by his friend Shapur. Their love is thwarted by a series of obstacles: Khosrow's forced marriage to the Byzantine princess Mariam for political alliance, his dalliance with Shekar in Isfahan, and the tragic love of the sculptor Farhad who carves Mount Behistun for Shirin's sake (and dies upon hearing false news of her death). After Mariam's death, Khosrow finally marries Shirin. But Khosrow's son Shiroyeh, who also desires Shirin, murders his father. Shirin, to avoid marrying Shiroyeh, takes poison and dies on her husband's body. They are buried together.

title: Khun Borom: The Founding Myth of the Lao People
summary: The Khun Borom myth is the foundational creation story of the Lao and Tai peoples, detailing their origins after a great flood. According to the legend recorded in the Nithan Khun Borom chronicle, in ancient times humanity became wicked and corrupt. A powerful sky deity (Phaya Thaen) destroyed them with a great flood, sparing only three righteous chiefs who were preserved in heaven. The deity sent the chiefs back to earth with a sacred buffalo to help them cultivate the land. They descended at Muang Then (modern Dien Bien Phu in Vietnam). After the land was prepared for rice cultivation, the buffalo died, and from its nostril grew a bitter gourd vine. From the gourds emerged the new human race — darker-skinned peoples from gourds cut with a hot skewer, and lighter-skinned Tai peoples from gourds cut with a chisel. The gods taught the people to build houses, cultivate rice, and observe proper rituals. As the population grew, Phaya Thaen sent his son Khun Borom to rule as the first king of the Tai people. After 25 years, Khun Borom divided his kingdom among his seven sons, who became the founders of the major Tai kingdoms across Southeast Asia, including Lan Xang (Laos), Lanna (northern Thailand), Ayutthaya, and others.

title: Kianda and the Fisherman's Net
summary: A water goddess of the Angolan coast tests a fisherman's humility by offering him a net that catches everything beneath the waves — except what he needs most.

title: Kibo and Mawenzi: The Sister Peaks of Kilimanjaro
summary: Two sister peaks of Mount Kilimanjaro teach a lesson about preparation and generosity.

title: Kibuka: The War God of Buganda
summary: Kibuka is the fearsome war god of the Baganda people, the brother of the lake god Mukasa. According to legend, Kibuka was once a mortal man of extraordinary strength and military genius. When Buganda was threatened by invasion from the neighboring Bunyoro kingdom, Kibuka was called upon to lead the army. He fought with supernatural ferocity, invisible to his enemies, raining arrows down upon them from a cloud. The enemy could not see him but could feel his arrows, and they fled in terror. However, Kibuka grew overconfident. While resting in a fig tree, he boasted loudly about his invincibility. An enemy soldier heard him and shot an arrow into the tree, striking Kibuka in the chest. He fell dead, and his body was discovered by the Baganda. After his death, Kibuka was deified and his shrine at Butikkiro became a national sanctuary where kings prayed before battle. Kibuka's story teaches that even the greatest warrior can fall to pride and carelessness.

title: Kijuju: The Underwater People
summary: A secret people who live beneath African lakes, coming to trade with surface dwellers—but only at night.

title: Kikala: The First Fulani Shepherd and the Sacred Cattle
summary: According to Fulani legend, the first Fulani shepherd was Kikala, whose hand with six fingers contains the primordial genealogy of the Fulani people. Four fingers represent the four great Fulani aristocratic families (Dyal, Ba, So, and Bari), the fifth finger represents allied tribes, and the sixth represents those in symbiosis with the Fulani. Shortly before his death, Kikala divided his cattle among his first four sons by color, establishing the clan system. The Fulani believe cattle originated from water, and the annual Lotori ceremony drives herds to waterholes in remembrance of their watery origin. The number four governs Fulani cosmology: four elements, four cardinal directions, and four basic cattle hide colors.

title: Kilibob and Manup: The Two Brothers of Papua New Guinea
summary: In the mythology of northeastern Papua New Guinea, Kilibob and Manup are mythical brothers whose travels created the islands and peoples of the region. Kilibob traveled by canoe along the northern coast, creating islands and bestowing gifts like fishing nets, canoes, and knowledge of navigation. Manup followed a southern route and brought agriculture, domesticated animals, and ceremonial practices. Wherever they landed, the brothers left behind different languages and customs. Their journeys explain the cultural diversity of Papua New Guinea's coastal peoples. The brothers eventually became rivals, and their conflict is said to have created the distinct identities of the different language groups, as each brother favored different communities with different skills and knowledge.

title: King Dutugemunu and Elara: The Just Rivalry
summary: Elara (Ellalan), a Tamil Chola prince, ruled Anuradhapura with such famed justice that he earned the title Manu Needhi Cholan ('the Chola who follows justice') — he once executed his own son under a chariot wheel to give justice to a grieving cow. The young Sinhalese prince Dutugemunu, believing the island should be united under Buddhism, waged a campaign against the aging Elara. Their climactic battle took place at the south gate of Anuradhapura, where Dutugemunu killed Elara in single combat atop their war elephants (Kandula vs Maha Pabbatha). Despite victory, Dutugemunu honored his foe with royal cremation and a monument, decreeing that passing princes must silence their music out of respect.

title: King Erik XIV's Imprisonment at Kastelholm
summary: In the autumn of 1571, the deposed Swedish King Erik XIV was imprisoned at Kastelholm Castle by his brother Johan III. Erik had been dethroned in 1568 and was moved between various castles before being held on Åland. Local legend holds that Erik's ghost still wanders the halls of Kastelholm, his footsteps echoing through the stone corridors at night. The imprisonment at Kastelholm is part of a larger body of historical folklore surrounding the castle, which first appears in written records in 1388. The castle has witnessed sieges, royal visits, witch trials, and fires — and each layer of its history has contributed to its reputation as one of the most haunted places in Åland. During the restoration of the castle in the 20th century, workers reported unexplained sounds and cold drafts, which some attribute to the restless spirits of its many historical occupants.

title: King Lindorm
summary: A childless queen receives advice from an old woman: bathe in running water and eat two red onions. In her excitement, she eats one onion with the skin on, and peels the other. As a result, she gives birth first to a hideous lindorm (serpent), who is secretly thrown into the forest, and then to a beautiful prince. Years later, when the prince sets out to find a bride, the lindorm blocks the road and demands that a mate be found for him first. The king and queen try to appease the lindorm by forcing women to marry him, but he devours each bride. Finally, a shepherd's daughter is offered. She wanders into the forest weeping and meets a wise old woman who tells her exactly what to do: she must wear all her dresses, and for each dress she removes, demand that the lindorm shed one of his skins. On her wedding night, the girl follows this advice. The lindorm sheds one skin after another, until nine skins lie on the floor and he is revealed as a handsome prince beneath — the true eldest son, freed from the curse caused by the queen eating the onion with its skin. The story has a complex second part: King Lindorm goes to war, leaving his queen with his evil stepmother, who writes that the queen gave birth to 'whelps.' The faithful servant hides the queen and her twin sons. After years of wandering, she stays with a man who has made a pact with the Devil, which she rescues using three magical nuts from her mother's grave. Eventually, King Lindorm returns, discovers the truth, and the family is reunited.

title: King Lindworm
summary: A king is transformed into a serpent (lindworm) and can only be cured by a princess who agrees to a series of difficult tasks, eventually breaking the curse through her devotion.

title: King Solomon and the Jinn
summary: According to Islamic and Arabic folklore, Prophet Solomon (Sulayman) was granted dominion over all beings: mankind, jinn, birds, wild beasts, and the wind. He commanded armies of jinn and devils, imprisoned rebellious marids and ifrits in brass bottles sealed with molten lead and his signet ring, and cast them into the seas. He understood the speech of birds and animals, and his throne was carried by the wind. His vizier Asaf possessed the knowledge to bring the Queen of Sheba's throne instantly. Solomon's ring, bearing the Most Great Name of God, was the source of his power, and when lost to a demon named Sakhr, his kingdom was briefly usurped.

title: Kintaro: The Golden Boy of Mountains
summary: A supernaturally strong child raised by animals in the mountains becomes a legendary hero.

title: Kintu and Nambi: The First People of Buganda
summary: In the beginning, Kintu was the only man on earth, wandering the plains of Uganda alone with only a cow for companionship. One day, Nambi and her younger sister came down from the sky on a rainbow. Nambi saw Kintu and was curious about this strange creature she had never seen before. She fell in love with him and wanted to take him to meet her father, Ggulu (the Sky God). But Nambi's brother Walumbe, a jealous and destructive spirit, opposed the union. Kintu was subjected to five impossible trials by Ggulu — he had to eat a houseful of food in one night, chop an entire forest, and retrieve dew in a leaky pot. With Nambi's secret help, he passed them all. Ggulu gave his blessing, and Kintu and Nambi prepared to descend to earth. But Ggulu warned them: 'Do not return to the sky for anything forgotten.' Nambi had forgotten millet for her chickens and sent Kintu back — and Walumbe insisted on joining them, bringing death to humanity forever.

title: Kiranga, the Sacred Drum
summary: A drum that beats on its own at midnight, its rhythm echoing across the hills — because the drum holds the heartbeat of the first king, and as long as it beats, the kingdom endures.

title: Kishelamakank's Dream of Creation
summary: In the beginning, before there was anything, there existed only an endless void of darkness. Within this emptiness dwelled Kishelamakank (He Who Creates Us By Thought), the Great Spirit. While in the void, the Creator fell into a deep sleep and dreamed of the world as it would become — mountains, forests, animals, and people. Upon awakening, He brought His dream into reality. He created helper spirits: the Grandfathers of the East, North, and West, and the Grandmother of the South. Together, they shaped the earth. From a sacred tree, the first man emerged from the roots. When the tree bent and touched the ground, the first woman sprang forth. This story affirms the Lenape understanding that all creation began not with violence but with a divine dream.

title: Kitsune: The Fox Spirits
summary: Intelligent foxes with magical powers—they can shapeshift, possess humans, and serve as messengers of the gods.

title: Kitsune: The Fox Wife
summary: A fox spirit takes human form to marry a lonely farmer, proving that love can transcend the boundary between the human and spirit worlds, even if it cannot last.

title: Knös
summary: A boy born from an egg grows to giant size and becomes the strongest man at the king's court, defeating a fearsome sea troll to rescue three princesses and win the youngest's hand. This classic Swedish hero-tale draws on the Thor-like motif of the giant-slaying goblet found in the _Hymiskvida_ of the Poetic Edda.

title: Koimala: The First King of the Maldives
summary: According to Maldivian folklore, Prince Koimala was a prince from the Indian subcontinent (or Sri Lanka, in some versions) who sailed to the Maldives with two ships. The indigenous Giraavaru people — Dravidian fishermen who cleaned tuna on a large sandbank — spotted his vessel and welcomed him, allowing him to settle on the blood-tainted sandbank. Trees were planted there (the first being a papaya tree) and the island was named Maa-le (Malé, meaning 'big blood'). The islanders, impressed by his royal lineage, proclaimed him king. He unified the Maldives from Minicoy to Addu, establishing Malé as the seat of power. Koimala founded the House of Theemuge and the Lunar Dynasty. While some versions identify him as Dharumavantha Rasgefaanu (the first Muslim ruler), historical records show his successor Dhovemi actually converted to Islam in 1153. The Giraavaru are considered the original inhabitants of the Maldives.

title: Kolowa: The Hairy Ogre (Creek)
summary: Kolowa is a fearsome, hairy, man-eating ogre from Muscogee Creek mythology. Described as being covered in thick hair and possessing enormous strength, Kolowa lives in the deep forest and preys on humans who stray too far from their villages. Some modern Creek storytellers translate the name as 'gorilla.' Kolowa is particularly dangerous because it can imitate human voices to lure victims into the woods. Parents told stories of Kolowa to keep children from wandering off alone. The creature is one of several 'Man-Eater' figures in Creek mythology, along with Isti Papa, the Great Lion. Warriors and hunters who confronted Kolowa had to rely on their courage, cleverness, and spiritual protection to survive the encounter.

title: Komokwa and the Undersea Kingdom (Haida)
summary: In Haida tradition, the undersea world is ruled by powerful supernatural beings who control the wealth of the sea. The sea chiefs live in houses made of copper and abalone shell, surrounded by supernatural beings including the killer whale people, seal people, and halibut people. Those who drown do not truly die but are taken to live in the undersea kingdom, where they may acquire great supernatural power and wealth. The supernatural killer whales (SGaana) are the most powerful of the undersea beings; they can transform into human form and own houses, territories, and crests. The Haida people take their clan crests from these supernatural beings, copying their likenesses for use on totem poles, blankets, and ceremonial regalia. The relationship between the Haida and the undersea kingdom is reciprocal: humans show respect through proper protocols, and the supernatural beings provide salmon, halibut, seals, and whales for the people's survival.

title: Komokwa the Undersea Chief (Kwakwaka'wakw)
summary: Komokwa (also known as Qomoqua or Copper-Maker) is the powerful chief of the undersea world in Kwakwaka'wakw mythology. He lives in a magnificent copper house beneath the ocean, where he controls all the wealth of the sea, including seals, sea lions, salmon, and the precious copper that gives him his name. Komokwa appears as a figure with a large, bulbous head covered in feathers or hair, often depicted with a wide mouth and protruding tongue. He sometimes takes the form of a sea monster or appears riding a Sisiutl canoe. Humans who visit his underwater kingdom must undergo dangerous trials. In some stories, a person who drowns is taken to Komokwa's house and may return with great wealth and supernatural power. Komokwa is both feared and respected; he is a generous giver of wealth to those who treat him properly but also a dangerous being who can drown anyone who disrespects the sea.

title: Kongamato of the Falls
summary: A Lozi hunter ventures too close to a hidden cataract above Victoria Falls and encounters the Kongamato, a pterodactyl-like beast that guards the spray zones where the living are not meant to wander.

title: Korkut Ata and the Search for Immortality
summary: Korkut Ata (also Dede Korkut) is the legendary father of Kazakh music and the creator of the kobyz (horsehair string instrument). Unable to accept the inevitability of death, Korkut fled from human society into nature, seeking immortality. But every element of nature — the trees, mountains, steppes, and rivers — told him that they too were subject to decay and death. In his solitary anguish, Korkut hollowed out a tree called shirgay to make the first kobyz, pulled horsehair strings across it, and began to play. The music was so transcendent that it brought him immortality through art. His melodies still echo across the Kazakh steppe, and his burial place on the Syr Darya riverbank is a pilgrimage site.

title: Koschei the Deathless
summary: An immortal sorcerer hides his death inside a needle, inside an egg, inside a duck, inside a hare, inside an iron chest, buried beneath an oak tree on a distant island.

title: Koumen: The Fulani Initiation and the Mysteries of Pastoral Life
summary: In Fulani esoteric tradition, Koumen is the shepherd of the primordial cattle and the depositary of pastoral initiation secrets. He was entrusted by Gueno, the eternal creator, with the care of the land and all animals. Koumen can transform wild animals into domestic ones and vice versa, appearing to humans as a child between three and eleven years old. His wife Foroforodu assists him in transmitting secret knowledge. Those who complete the cycle of initiation gain the ability to understand animal language and become Silatigi, masters of ritual speech. The initiate learns that the universe was formed 'from a drop of milk' containing the four elements, which formed the 'hermaphrodite bovine,' symbol of all creation. The cow occupies the central place as the first creature, forming a mythical triad with woman and the universe.

title: Krakl, or Kratt, the Variant Servant
summary: A regional variant of the kratt, told in the dialects of southern Estonia, where the servant was made from straw and bound to a different master.

title: Krampus: The Christmas Devil
summary: On December 5th, Krampus comes for naughty children—while Saint Nicholas brings gifts to the good.

title: Kratt, the Hay and Firewood Servant
summary: A household servant constructed from hay and firewood, animated by dark bargains, who served his master until the price was collected.

title: Krishna
summary: Krishna is the eighth avatar of Vishnu, the preserver god who sustains the universe.

title: Krishna Tames the Serpent Kaliya
summary: Young Krishna, during his childhood in Vrindavan, discovered that the Yamuna River had become poisoned by Kaliya, a massive multi-headed serpent who had taken residence in its waters. The river boiled with venom, killing fish, birds, and trees along the banks, and the villagers could no longer drink or approach it. Without fear, Krishna dove into the deepest part of the river. The serpent wrapped him in his coils, but Krishna expanded his body, broke free, and began dancing on Kaliya's thousand hoods. As Krishna danced, each hood was crushed under his divine feet. The serpent, bleeding and exhausted, surrendered. His wives prayed for mercy, and Krishna spared Kaliya's life but banished him and his family to the ocean, restoring the Yamuna to purity.

title: Krsnik, the Slovene Daylight Hero
summary: A heroic spirit of Slovenian folklore, the Krsnik is a being of light who fights the dark forces of the Kurent, protecting villages from evil.

title: Kullervo and the Cheat-cake
summary: Kullervo is tricked into a situation involving a 'cheat-cake', which further cements his identity as a social outcast. The experience fuels his rage and his desire for revenge against those who have wronged him.

title: Kullervo As A Sheperd
summary: Kullervo is sent to work as a shepherd, a role he finds degrading. He uses his position to express his inner turmoil and resentment, causing trouble for his masters and further isolating himself from society.

title: Kullervo Finds His Tribe-folk
summary: Kullervo eventually discovers his biological family, but the reunion is tragic rather than joyful. Old misunderstandings and ingrained hatreds lead to a violent confrontation, proving that blood ties cannot always heal past wounds.

title: Kullervo's Evil Deeds
summary: In a fit of blind rage and despair, Kullervo commits a series of terrible crimes, the most heinous of which is the abduction and murder of his own sister, whom he had not recognized. This act marks the peak of his tragic descent.

title: Kullerwoinen Son of Evil
summary: Kullervo is born into a family marked by violence and hatred. Forced into slavery from a young age, he grows deeply resentful of the world and develops an intense hatred for all forms of authority, setting him on a path of destruction.

title: Kullerwoinen's Victory and Death
summary: After realizing the horror of his crimes, Kullervo finds himself unable to live with the guilt. He asks his sword if it will drink his blood, and upon the sword's agreement, he commits suicide, finally ending his cycle of suffering and violence.

title: Kulmking, the Frost King
summary: A spirit of the Estonian winter who ruled the frozen rivers and punishing cold, feared by travelers and honored by those who survived his season.

title: Kupe Discovering Aotearoa
summary: Kupe, a great Polynesian navigator and chief from Hawaiki, pursued the giant octopus Te Wheke-a-Muturangi across the Pacific Ocean after it stole his bait and caused chaos. His wife Hine-te-Aparangi sighted land and named it Aotearoa (Land of the Long White Cloud). Kupe and his crew landed at the Hokianga Harbour, where he battled and killed the giant octopus. He explored the coastline, named many landmarks, and returned to Hawaiki with tales of the new land, providing the first detailed navigational knowledge that later guided the great migration of Maori to New Zealand.

title: Kurupira, the Forest Guardian
summary: A small, green-skinned forest spirit with backwards feet who protects the trees and wildlife of Uruguay from those who take too much.

title: Kusillo, the Hairy Trickster
summary: A small, hairy creature with reversed feet leads travelers in circles through the highland puna, mimicking their laughter to lure them deeper into the fog.

title: Kuutkh (Raven) Creates the World
summary: The central creation myth of the Chukchi, Koryak, and Itelmen peoples of northeastern Siberia. Kuutkh, the Great Raven, is both creator and trickster who shaped the cosmos from primordial chaos. In the beginning, there was nothing but darkness and water. Kuutkh flew over the endless sea and, through his actions — purposeful and accidental — created land, mountains, rivers, and valleys. He brought light to the world, taught humans essential survival skills including fire-making, hunting techniques, and net-weaving. Kuutkh can shift between raven and human form and his unpredictable nature, blending divine intention with mischievous impulse, mirrors the volatility of the Arctic environment itself.

title: Kuveni: The Yakshini Queen
summary: Kuveni (also known as Sesapati or Kuvanna) was a Yakshini queen ruling in Lanka when Prince Vijaya arrived. Described as a shape-shifting demoness who could assume the form of a beautiful sixteen-year-old maiden, she initially imprisoned Vijaya's men in a chasm. After Vijaya overpowered her, she swore loyalty and helped him conquer the Yakkha city of Sirisavatthu. She bore him two children, Jivahatta and Disala. Vijaya later repudiated her saying 'men fear superhuman beings' and sent her away. When Kuveni returned to her own people, they killed her as a traitor. The Vedda people venerate her as Maha Loku Kiriammaleththo.

title: Kwanokasha: The Spirit Who Grants Powers (Choctaw)
summary: Kwanokasha is a powerful Choctaw spirit associated with caves and rock shelters, who appears to young children during vision quests. According to legend, Kwanokasha takes children who wander into certain caves into the spirit world, where they are tested. The spirit offers them three choices: a knife (representing the power to heal through surgery), herbs (representing the power to heal through medicine), or a pebble (representing the power to heal through prayer and ritual). The child's choice determines what kind of medicine person they will become. Those who choose nothing may be cursed with sickness or bad luck. The Kwanokasha legend underscores the Choctaw belief in the sacred nature of caves as gateways to the spirit world and the importance of choosing one's path wisely.

title: Kwatyat and Tihtipihin Rescue Their Mother (Nuu-chah-nulth)
summary: Two Nuu-chah-nulth brothers, Tihtipihin and Kwatyat, witnessed a great monster swallow their mother whole. Without hesitation, they willingly allowed themselves to be swallowed by the same monster so they could rescue her. Inside the monster's stomach, they found their mother alive along with other swallowed victims. Using their wits and supernatural strength, the brothers cut through the monster's stomach from the inside, freeing themselves, their mother, and all the other captives. They escaped safely as the monster perished. This story of filial devotion and brotherly courage is one of the most important Nuu-chah-nulth hero tales. Kwatyat, the younger brother, is particularly significant as he is recognized as a transformer figure in Nuu-chah-nulth mythology who later helped shape the world. The story emphasizes family loyalty, bravery in the face of overwhelming danger, and the power of cooperation between siblings.

title: Kwatyat the Transformer (Nuu-chah-nulth)
summary: Kwatyat is one of the most important transformer figures in Nuu-chah-nulth mythology. After his adventures with his brother Tihtipihin rescuing their mother from the monster, Kwatyat traveled the land transforming the world and making it ready for human beings. He changed dangerous beings into harmless animals, taught people how to fish and hunt, and established the proper relationship between humans and the supernatural world. Kwatyat also had a trickster aspect — he could be foolish and greedy, and many stories tell of his failed attempts to imitate others or his schemes backfiring. In one story, he tried to catch salmon by building a weir but was too impatient and it collapsed. In another, he tried to fly like an eagle and fell into the ocean. Despite his flaws, Kwatyat's transformations established the fundamental order of Nuu-chah-nulth life. He is sometimes paired with or compared to Raven, sharing the role of culture hero and trickster in a complementary way.

title: Kyllikki's Broken Vow
summary: Lemminkainen woos the beautiful Kyllikki, eventually winning her heart and promising her marriage. However, he betrays her vows to pursue other interests, leading a heartbroken Kyllikki to place a powerful curse upon him. This betrayal drives Lemminkainen into a life of further wandering and instability.

title: Kyys Debiliye (The Warrior Maiden)
summary: A rare Yakut Olonkho epic featuring a female warrior as its main protagonist. Kyys Debiliye is a powerful heroine who fights alongside and against male heroes, demonstrating the full range of martial prowess and determination. She defends her people against the evil Abaasy spirits and enemies that threaten the Middle World. The epic is notable for its strong female central character in a traditionally male-dominated genre and reflects the high status women could hold in Yakut mythology. It was published in the series 'Monuments of Folklore of the Peoples of Siberia and the Far East'.

title: Kääk, the Luxembourgish Forest Spirit
summary: A small, mischievous forest spirit of Luxembourg, Kääk dwells in the deep forests and delights in leading travelers astray.

title: Kópakonan (The Seal Woman of Mikladalur)
summary: A fisherman named Torkil from Mikladalur on Kalsoy Island watches a group of seal-people dancing on the shore after shedding their sealskins. He falls in love with the most beautiful seal-woman, steals her sealskin, and locks it in a chest. Unable to return to the sea, she marries him and bears his children. Years later, Torkil forgets the key to the chest while fishing; Kópakonan finds her skin and returns to the ocean, leaving her human family behind. She later appears in Torkil's dream begging him not to kill her seal husband and children, but he ignores her. Kópakonan curses the men of Mikladalur to die at sea and fall from cliffs until enough dead surround Kalsoy holding hands.

title: Kópakonan's Curse (The Seal Woman's Revenge)
summary: The darker sequel to the Kópakonan legend. After the seal woman returned to the sea, her human husband Torkil began sealing (hunting seals). Kópakonan appeared to him in a dream, begging him not to kill her seal husband and children. Torkil ignored her warning. When he killed her seal family, Kópakonan rose from the sea and pronounced a terrible curse: the men of Mikladalur would die at sea and fall from the cliffs until enough dead men could encircle the entire island of Kalsoy holding hands. The curse is said to still haunt the village, where the sea claims lives with unusual frequency. A 2.6-meter bronze statue of Kópakonan by Hans Pauli Olsen stands at the water's edge in Mikladalur since 2014.

title: L'Ankou, the Dark Coachman of the Low Countries
summary: A death omen spirit who drives a ghostly coach across the Belgian countryside, collecting the souls of those about to die.

title: La Cegua: The Shrouded Specter
summary: A young man encounters a beautiful woman on a dark road, only to discover she is La Cegua — a veiled spirit whose terrifying face beneath her shawl punishes the unfaithful and the arrogant.

title: La Ciguapa of the Dominican Mountains
summary: La Ciguapa is a legendary creature from Dominican folklore — a beautiful woman with long, flowing hair and dark skin who has her feet on backwards. She inhabits the remote mountainous regions of the Dominican Republic, particularly the Cordillera Central and Bahoruco Mountains. According to legend, La Ciguapa lures men into the wilderness with her stunning beauty, only to leave them hopelessly lost, confused, or dead. Her backwards footprints make it impossible to track her, as they appear to lead in the opposite direction. Some say the legend may have Taino origins, while others see influences from European mermaid myths. The Ciguapa embodies the danger and mystery of the Dominican wilderness, serving as a warning against wandering alone in remote areas and the perils of unchecked desire.

title: La Ciguapa: The Backward-Footed Woman of the Dominican Mountains
summary: A wild woman with backward-facing feet lures men into the mountains with an irresistible call.

title: La Culebra Mayor, the Great Serpent
summary: A monstrous serpent of Costa Rican legend, La Culebra Mayor is a winged snake that guards hidden treasures and devours anyone who seeks them.

title: La Curandera of the Llano — The Healing Woman of the Plains
summary: Across the Hispanic villages of New Mexico and Colorado, the figure of La Curandera — the wise healing woman — is both a historical reality and a legendary archetype. These women were the primary healthcare providers in isolated communities, using knowledge of medicinal herbs passed down through generations, prayer, and ritual cleansing (limpias). Legendary curanderas are remembered for miraculous cures: healing blindness with herbal poultices, setting broken bones by touch alone, and diagnosing illness by reading eggs or by feeling the patient's aura. One of the most famous is Doña María from Las Trampas, New Mexico, who was said to have healed a dying man by rubbing him with a live chicken and a raw egg while reciting Catholic prayers. Another, La Loba from the Llano Estacado, was known as a 'she-wolf' healer who could communicate with animals and knew the medicinal use of every desert plant. These legends preserve the vital role of curanderas as repositories of Indigenous and Spanish botanical knowledge, spiritual counselors, and community matriarchs. The curandera tradition remains alive today in Hispanic communities across the Southwest, where it coexists with modern medicine.

title: La Diablera of the Crossroads
summary: A seductive spirit of the crossroads offers travelers impossible bargains — wealth, knowledge, love — but always demands a price that cannot be paid until it is too late.

title: La Diablesse at the Crossroads
summary: A beautiful stranger appears at a rural crossroads to lure a young farmer to his doom, but his mother's warnings and an old obeah charm may yet save him.

title: La Diablesse of the Crossroads
summary: A charming stranger lures a proud young man down a moonlit road, but La Diablesse reveals her true nature only when he is far too late to turn back.

title: La Diablesse, the Devil Woman
summary: La Diablesse is a seductive she-devil from Trinidadian folklore who appears as a breathtakingly beautiful woman in an old-fashioned embroidered dress and wide-brimmed hat, smelling of expensive perfume. By moonlight, the perceptive may glimpse her true nature — one cloven hoof hidden beneath the hem. She lures unfaithful husbands, drunken braggarts, and morally weak men by catching their gaze and walking away, her petticoat making a rhythmic chac-chac sound. She leads them deep into the wilderness until she vanishes at the edge of a ravine, leaving them lost, injured, or dead. La Diablesse does not physically attack; she delivers men to their own punishment. On full moon nights, wise villagers keep close to home and company.

title: La Garita: The Goat Children
summary: La Garita (also known as the Goat Children or the Legend of the Garita) is a Puerto Rican folktale about two children who were transformed into goats as punishment or protection. The story is traditionally told to explain the presence of wild goats in the Puerto Rican countryside and to warn children against disobedience. The legend varies across the island, with some versions telling of children who mocked a holy figure and were turned into goats as a curse, while others speak of children who fled into the mountains and were transformed into animals by protective spirits. The garita itself — a sentry box or small structure — became associated with these mysterious goat-children who are said to still roam the island's remote hills, their bleating heard on quiet nights.

title: La Lechuza — The Witch-Owl of the Border
summary: La Lechuza is a terrifying figure in Mexican-American folklore, particularly along the Texas-Mexico border. She is described as a witch who transforms into a giant owl — specifically a great horned owl or barn owl — with a wingspan of up to ten feet and the face of an old woman. According to legend, a woman who makes a pact with the devil or practices black magic can become a lechuza, flying at night to attack enemies, steal children, or cause illness. In some versions, she appears as an enormous white owl that screeches a woman's cry, luring victims into the darkness. In South Texas and northern Mexico, it is said that if you hear an owl calling your name at night, you must never answer, or the lechuza will carry you away. Ranch hands and farmers tell stories of finding cattle mutilated by her talons. The lechuza is also associated with the nahual tradition, linking it to pre-Columbian shapeshifter beliefs.

title: La Llorona
summary: In Mexico, the rivers and canals hold a sorrow that never dies—that of La Llorona, the Weeping Woman.

title: La Llorona as La Malinche's Curse
summary: One of the most powerful variants of the La Llorona legend connects her directly to La Malinche, the Nahua woman who served as Hernán Cortés's interpreter, advisor, and mother of his son. In this telling, Malinche—cursed by her people for betraying the Aztec Empire—became La Llorona, condemned to wander forever weeping for her mestizo children. This version transforms the ghost story into a foundational myth of Mexican identity, embodying the trauma of conquest, the pain of cultural hybridity, and the complex legacy of the first Mexican mother. Chicana feminists like Gloria Anzaldúa and Sandra Cisneros have reclaimed this figure as a symbol of resistance, survival, and the power of the marginalized feminine voice.

title: La Llorona de los Ríos de Tejas — The Weeping Woman of the Texas Rivers
summary: In the South Texas borderlands along the Rio Grande, Mexican-American communities tell of La Llorona appearing near irrigation canals and arroyos where children have drowned. Unlike the classic Mexican version, the Texas variant often emphasizes her role as a protector of children rather than a predator — some say she appears to warn mothers of impending danger to their children. In Starr County and Hidalgo County, farm workers have reported hearing her cries mixing with the wind through the mesquite trees at dusk. The legend serves as both a cautionary tale about water safety in the agricultural landscape of the Rio Grande Valley and a symbol of maternal grief that transcends the border.

title: La Llorona — The Weeping Woman
summary: La Llorona is the vengeful ghost of a woman who drowned her children in a river after discovering her husband's infidelity, then drowned herself in grief. She now wanders along rivers and lakes across Mexico and the US Southwest, dressed in white with long black hair, weeping and wailing '¡Ay, mis hijos!' Those who hear her mournful cries are said to suffer misfortune or death. The legend has pre-Columbian roots in the Aztec goddess Cihuacóatl, who appeared before the Spanish conquest weeping for the fate of her people. During the colonial period, the story syncretized with Spanish folklore of white ladies and became associated with La Malinche, Cortés's interpreter who bore his child. Today La Llorona remains one of the most recognized figures in Hispanic folklore, told as a cautionary tale to children about wandering near water alone at night.

title: La Llorona: The Weeping Woman
summary: A woman who drowned her children now wanders near water, searching—and anyone who hears her cry is marked for death.

title: La Loba — The Wolf Woman of the Desert
summary: La Loba (The Wolf Woman) is a figure from New Mexican and Chicano folklore who protects the wild places and animals of the Southwestern desert. Older than any human, she is the guardian of wolf and coyote spirits, and it is said that when a wolf dies, La Loba collects its bones and sings over them until the animal is reborn. She is described as an ancient woman who lives in a cave in the mountains, surrounded by the skulls and bones of animals. Children who get lost in the desert are said to be guided home by her, and hunters who kill for sport rather than need find their guns mysteriously jammed. The figure was popularized by Clarissa Pinkola Estés in her book 'Women Who Run With the Wolves,' which linked La Loba to the archetype of the wild feminine. In Chicano folklore, La Loba represents the deep connection between Hispanic peoples and the land of the Southwest, the wisdom of curanderas, and the power of women as healers and protectors of nature. Her legend also connects to the nahual tradition of shapeshifting, as La Loba is sometimes said to transform between human and wolf form.

title: La Mano Pachona — The Disembodied Hand of the Border
summary: La Mano Pachona is a chilling legend from northern Mexico and the US Southwest about a disembodied, hairy hand that attacks travelers at night. The hand is described as large, dark, and covered in thick hair, with long fingernails. It is said to wander along lonely roads, scratching at windows and car doors, or reaching up from beneath vehicles to grab unsuspecting victims. Some versions claim the hand belongs to a man who was cursed for his evil deeds, while others say it is the hand of a murdered criminal that continues to seek revenge. In Mexican-American folklore of Texas and California, the story is often told around campfires and at sleepovers, serving as a tale of warning about traveling alone at night. La Mano Pachona represents the fear of the fragmented, disembodied threat — danger that comes not from a whole being but from something partial and inexplicable.

title: La Masa, the Honduran Monster
summary: A monstrous creature of Honduran folklore, La Masa is a shapeless, crushing entity that stalks the forests and crushes anyone who trespasses on sacred ground.

title: La Planchada — The Ghost Nurse in White
summary: La Planchada (The Ironed One, referring to her perfectly pressed uniform) is a ghost legend from Mexico City hospitals that has spread through Mexican-American communities in the US Southwest. According to the story, a beautiful nurse named Eulalia was deeply in love with a doctor who rejected her. Heartbroken, she took her own life, but her ghost now returns to the hospital where she once worked. Dressed in an immaculately starched white nurse's uniform, La Planchada appears in hospital wards at night, administering medicines and comforting patients. Some patients claim to have recovered miraculously after being visited by her, while others say she only appears to those who are about to die. The key warning is that if you see the hem of her dress or her feet, you will die within days — a version of the classic 'don't look at their feet' motif found in many ghost legends worldwide. La Planchada has been reported in Mexican-American hospitals and clinics along the border, where she is sometimes viewed as a benevolent guardian spirit of the sick and dying, particularly those without family to comfort them.

title: La Siguanaba — The Horse-Faced Woman
summary: La Siguanaba (or Sihuanaba) is a beautiful woman spirit from Mesoamerican folklore, particularly prevalent in El Salvador, Guatemala, and southern Mexico, with variants told in Mexican-American communities. She appears as a stunningly beautiful woman with long, flowing hair, seen bathing in rivers or washing clothes. She lures men — especially those who are unfaithful or have been drinking — by appearing as their lover or a beautiful stranger. When the man approaches, she transforms, revealing her true face: that of a horse or a skull, driving him mad with terror. Some versions say she then attacks and kills him. The legend has pre-Columbian origins among the Pipil and Maya peoples, where female water spirits were associated with both fertility and danger. In the US Southwest, the story is told as a warning against infidelity, drunkenness, and the dangers of trusting appearances, particularly to young men in Chicano communities.

title: La Silampa, the Forest Fire
summary: A ball of fire that rolls through the forest at night, burning everything in its path, because in Panama the forest holds grudges.

title: La Trola: The Deceiver
summary: La Trola is a cunning shapeshifting spirit who lures travelers into the wilderness with false promises, teaching a timeless lesson about the dangers of greed and trusting strangers.

title: La Tulivieja, the Drowned Woman
summary: A woman who drowned herself and her child in a river, now wanders the waterways searching for her baby, luring men to their deaths with her beauty.

title: Lady Barbro of Brokind
summary: The cruel Lady Barbro would bind her servants and place food before them they could not reach laughing at their suffering. After death her ghost haunted Linkoping cathedral until her body was impaled in a swamp. Yet even this did not quiet her spirit and strange lights still appear at Brokind.

title: Lady Guinevere
summary: She was said to be the loveliest woman in all the island.. Her name was Guinevere, daughter of King Leodegrance of Cameliard, and when Arthur first heard of her beauty, he knew he must have her as his queen.

title: Lafaek Diak (The Good Crocodile)
summary: The foundational creation myth of Timor-Leste, explaining why the island is shaped like a crocodile. A young boy discovered a baby crocodile struggling to reach the sea and compassionately carried it to the water. The grateful crocodile promised to repay the boy and invited him to ride on its back for many journeys. Despite its gratitude, the crocodile felt a predatory instinct to eat the boy. Seeking counsel from the whale, tiger, and water buffalo — all of whom said 'you cannot eat him' — and finally a wise monkey who cursed the crocodile, the crocodile resolved never to harm the boy. When the crocodile grew old, it offered its body as a final gift, transforming into the island of Timor so the boy and his descendants would have a homeland forever.

title: Lagahoo: Midnight on the Estuary
summary: A plantation-era overseer who abused his workers is cursed to become the Lagahoo, doomed to shapeshift each night and haunt the very roads he once patrolled.

title: Lakota Star Husband Story
summary: Two Lakota girls lay outside their tipi one night, and one pointed at the brightest star saying she wished to marry it. The next day the girls found themselves in the sky world, where the first girl became the wife of a star. She was told not to dig around a certain turnip-like root, but curiosity overcame her. When she pulled the root, she saw the Earth far below through the hole. Homesick, she and her husband wove a rope to descend, but it was too short and she fell. She survived and returned to her people, but the star husband remained in the sky and can be seen as the evening star.

title: Lalibela: The Rock-Hewn Churches
summary: In the 12th century, King Lalibela of the Zagwe dynasty was visited by a vision from God. In the vision, he was taken to heaven and shown magnificent churches built by angels. When he returned to earth, God commanded him to build a New Jerusalem in the rocky mountains of Ethiopia. King Lalibela gathered thousands of workers and began carving eleven churches directly from solid volcanic rock — each church a single monolith hewn from the mountain, carved from the top down. Angels worked alongside the humans at night, doing twice as much as the day crews. The churches were connected by a maze of tunnels and trenches, with hidden passages, crypts, and baptismal pools. The largest, Bet Medhane Alem (House of the Savior of the World), remains the largest monolithic church in the world. Lalibela became a pilgrimage site for Ethiopian Christians, a sacred city that rivals Jerusalem itself.

title: Lamia of the Dark Valleys
summary: A vengeful spirit with the body of a serpent and the face of a woman haunts the mountain passes of Cyprus, luring travelers with her weeping before revealing her true form.

title: Lamia, the Child Eater
summary: A beautiful woman who was once a queen, now a monster who steals children in the night — because in Lebanon, grief can turn love into hunger.

title: Language on a Mountain
summary: After a great flood swept through the land, Na'pi (Old Man) gathered all the people on top of a large mountain. He gave them water of different colors—black, red, yellow, and white—and told them to drink and then speak. Each group that drank the colored water spoke a different language. Only those who received the black water spoke the same language; these were the bands of the Blackfoot Confederacy: the Piegan, Siksika, and Blood (Kainai) people. This event was said to have taken place on the highest mountain in the Montana reservation.

title: Lars, My Lad!
summary: A spendthrift duke, reduced to poverty, discovers a scrap of paper in a hidden chest that summons a magical servant named Lars who grants every wish. He builds a palace, marries a princess, but foolishly gives the paper back to Lars and loses everything, ending up naked in a ruined hut and nearly hanged before tricking Lars into returning the paper.

title: Las Gorras Blancas — The Night Riders of the San Luis Valley
summary: Las Gorras Blancas (The White Caps) were a secret society of Mexican-American vigilantes who rode at night in northern New Mexico and southern Colorado between 1889 and 1891, terrorizing Anglo landowners and railroad companies who were stealing Hispanic land grants. Clad in white caps and masks, they cut down fences, burned barns, and destroyed railroad property, all while leaving notes signed 'Las Gorras Blancas.' Their legend has grown into folklore: said to appear on moonless nights as ghostly riders on black horses, their white caps glowing in the dark. Some stories claim they could disappear into the arroyos like spirits, or that their leader was a curandero with supernatural powers. The historical Gorras Blancas movement was a response to the systematic dispossession of Hispanic landholders after the Mexican-American War, when the Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo's land guarantees were violated. In Chicano folklore, the White Caps have become symbols of resistance against colonial dispossession and the fight for land rights, merging with the figure of El Justiciero — the righteous avenger — in borderlands storytelling.

title: Lasse, My Thrall!
summary: A ruined nobleman discovers a magic scrap of paper that summons a tireless servant named Lasse, who builds him a castle and wins him a princess — but losing the paper costs him everything until he learns wisdom. This popular Swedish tale is a distinctive Nordic variant of the Aladdin cycle, set down in the dialect of Nerike.

title: Lauma, the Spinning Fairy of Latvia
summary: Lauma, a luminous fairy of Latvian lore, haunts the spinning rooms and riverbanks, rewarding industrious maidens and punishing the idle with tangled thread and cold water.

title: Laumas, the Plural Spirits of the Meadow
summary: The Laumas are a chorus of meadow spirits who sing in the twilight, weaving fate into the flax and luring wanderers into the mist with their otherworldly voices.
themes: the power of music and song
the thin boundary between mortal and spirit worlds

title: Laxdæla Saga - The Curse of the Leg-Biter
summary: The sword 'Leg-Biter' (Fótbítur) is a legendary weapon that brings misfortune to those who wield it. It is stolen and recovered several times, eventually being used by Bolli to kill his foster-brother Kjartan, sealing a tragic fate for both and illustrating the theme of an inevitable, cursed destiny.

title: Laxdæla Saga - The Ghost of the Third Husband
summary: Guðrún Ósvífursdóttir, a woman of great beauty and ambition, suffers the loss of three husbands. Following the death of her second husband, she is haunted by his spirit, which serves as a reminder of the tragic consequences of her own pride and the cycle of vengeance that consumes her family and friends.

title: Layla and Majnun
summary: Based on the true 7th-century story of Qays ibn al-Mulawwah, a Bedouin poet of the Banu Amir tribe in Najd, who fell deeply in love with his cousin Layla. When her father refused the match due to Qays's obsessive behavior (seen as madness or jinn-possession, earning him the epithet 'Majnun' meaning 'crazy'), and forced Layla to marry another man, Qays fled to the desert, living among wild beasts and composing heartbroken poetry. He wasted away and was found dead among stones near Layla's grave. The story became the archetypal tale of unconsummated, spiritual love across Persian, Turkish, and Urdu literature, widely called the 'Romeo and Juliet of the East.'

title: Leap the Elk and Little Princess Cottongrass
summary: Princess Cottongrass (Tuvstarr) has lived her entire life in the Dream Castle, a sheltered world of safety and beauty. One day, a magnificent elk named Long-Leap (Skutt) appears. Enchanted by his stately bearing and crown-like antlers, she begs him to carry her out into the world. The elk warns her: 'The world is big and cold, little child, and you are so small. The world is full of evil and wickedness, and it will hurt you.' But she insists, and he relents. On their journey through the deep Swedish forest, the princess encounters a series of supernatural dangers. First, fairies lure her, and in her distraction, she loses her golden crown. Then the Lady of the Forest (Skogsrå) tricks her into letting go of the elk's antlers to show her dress — and snatches it away, leaving her naked. Each time, the elk warns her to hold tight to his antlers, but her innocent curiosity and trust lead her to lose more of herself. Finally, they reach a dark tarn deep in the forest. Mesmerized by the dark, still water, Princess Cottongrass leans forward to see her reflection, and the golden heart her mother gave her at birth slips from her neck and sinks into the depths. Despite the elk's desperate warnings, she cannot tear herself away from the water. The elk, heartbroken, leaves her there. The story ends with a poignant transformation: the princess becomes a small white cottongrass flower, forever leaning over the edge of the pool, gazing into the water for her lost heart. The elk returns now and then, the only one who remembers she was once a princess. John Bauer's illustrations for this tale are among the most famous in Swedish art.

title: Legba and the Divine Gate (Fon/Dahomey)
summary: Legba is the youngest son of Mawu-Lisa, the trickster god who serves as the gatekeeper between the human world and the spirit world. Unlike the other gods who dwell in distant heavens, Legba walks among humans. He is the master of languages, the interpreter of the gods, and the lord of crossroads. In one tale, Mawu gave each of her children dominion over a realm, but Legba was dissatisfied. He used his cunning to trick his mother into giving him the key to all the realms, making him the indispensable intermediary. Without Legba's permission, no message reaches the gods and no prayer is answered. Legba is depicted as a phallic figure, representing the creative force of life, and his shrines are placed at village entrances and crossroads throughout Benin and Togo.

title: Lemminikainen's Second Wooing
summary: Determined to find a new bride, Lemminkainen travels to Pohjola to woo the Daughter of Louhi. Louhi sets a series of nearly impossible tasks for him, including the requirement to kill the magical swans of Tuonela, which eventually leads to his downfall and death.

title: Lemminkainen's Lament
summary: The reckless and handsome warrior Lemminkainen enters a singing match with Wainamoinen, believing his charm and skill are sufficient. He is decisively defeated and humiliated by Wainamoinen's superior magic, leading him to lament his misfortune and seek a way to regain his lost honor.

title: Lemminkainen's Restoration
summary: Driven by maternal love, Lemminkainen's mother travels to the depths of Tuonela. She painstakingly retrieves every fragment of her son's body from the river and uses powerful magic to piece him back together. He is restored to life, though the experience leaves him forever changed.

title: Leuk the Hare and the Chief's Daughter (Wolof)
summary: A powerful chief announced that whoever could make him laugh would win his daughter's hand in marriage. Many tried and failed. Leuk the Hare presented himself and performed a series of absurd tricks, piling animals on top of each other in increasingly ridiculous ways. The chief finally burst out laughing, but then said Leuk must also complete three impossible tasks: find a talking cow, bring water in a sieve, and catch the wind. Leuk used his cleverness to succeed in all three tasks. He found a cow that 'talked' by having it moo at the right moment. He lined the sieve with clay to carry water. He caught the wind by trapping air in a bag. The chief, impressed by Leuk's intelligence, honored his word and gave Leuk his daughter. The story celebrates the Wolof value of wit over brute force and the belief that cleverness can overcome any obstacle.

title: Libahunt, the Werewolf of the Baltic
summary: The Estonian werewolf, a man cursed to become a beast under the full moon, caught between human guilt and animal hunger.

title: Ligaroo: Silver Teeth of the Mountains
summary: A boy in the high villages above St. George's encounters the Ligaroo, a vampiric shapeshifter who takes the form of someone you trust, and learns that silver and faith are the only weapons.
themes: the danger of cleverness without wisdom

title: Ligobubfanu the Creator Goddess
summary: Ligobubfanu is the creator goddess in the mythology of Chuuk, Micronesia, and the wife of the god Anulap. She is one of the supreme deities responsible for creating the world and all life within it. As a female creator, Ligobubfanu represents the fertile, nurturing aspect of the cosmos. She created the islands of Micronesia by scattering earth across the ocean and caused the first plants to grow. She is also associated with the tides, the moon, and the reproductive cycles of marine life. With Anulap, she governs the affairs of gods and humans, and their temple was said to exist in the sky world. Her name is invoked in traditional prayers and rituals, particularly those related to childbirth, agriculture, and fishing.

title: Lilith, the Night Demoness
summary: A powerful female demon from Jewish folklore, Lilith is Adam's first wife who refused to submit and became a night demon preying on infants and solitary men.

title: Linda-Gold and the Old King
summary: Long ago there lived an eccentric old king who had suffered great sorrow: his queen and children had died, and someone had torn his heart to pieces — someone 'with claws,' he said. Ever since, the king imagines that everyone has claws on their hands. No one is allowed to come within two arm's lengths of him. Servants must serve food at the farthest edge of the table, and anyone who steps closer spends a week in prison. Despite his oddities, he rules justly and is beloved by his people. But they worry because he refuses to remarry or name an heir. One day, a little girl named Linda-Gold arrives at the palace. Unlike everyone else, she is not afraid of the king. With the innocent audacity that only a child possesses, she approaches him and touches his hand. The king is so startled by her fearless touch that instead of ordering her imprisoned, he allows her to stay. Linda-Gold's pure-hearted love and her complete lack of fear gradually work their way into the king's wounded heart. She cuts her fingernails to show him she has no claws. Through her gentle presence, the king begins to heal from his trauma. His delusion fades, and he eventually adopts Linda-Gold as his daughter and heir, discovering that she truly has no claws — only the pure heart of a child. The story is a poignant exploration of grief, trauma, and the healing power of innocent love.

title: Liongo Fumo: The Birth of a Hero
summary: Liongo Fumo's birth was marked by supernatural signs. His mother, a secondary wife of the king of Pate, was childless for many years. Desperate, she prayed at the shrine of the sea spirits, offering her finest cloth and sweetest dates. That night, a spirit appeared in her dreams and told her she would bear a son of extraordinary power. When Liongo was born, he emerged fully formed with a bow in his tiny hand. As a child, he grew so fast that he reached adult size by his tenth year. His strength was legendary — he could bend a palm tree to the ground and could outrun a gazelle. But his true power was his voice: his poetry and songs could move listeners to tears, to laughter, or to battle. When his brother Mringwari usurped the throne, Liongo was cast into prison. But he sang such a beautiful song that the guards fell asleep, and he broke his chains with his bare hands. This tale establishes Liongo as the archetypal Swahili hero: part warrior, part poet, always defiant against injustice.

title: Little Annie the Goose-Girl
summary: A young woman is betrayed by her companions and forced to work as a goose-girl, hiding her royal identity. Through patience and the help of her animal friends, she eventually regains her status and finds true love.

title: Little Claus and Big Claus
summary: Little Claus outsmarts Big Claus through a series of tricks, including pretending to have a wizard in a sack and tricking him into paying for the skin of a dead horse. He eventually tricks Big Claus into being drowned in a river after convincing him he can get cattle from a mermaid.

title: Little Giver: The Corn Spirit (Seminole)
summary: Little Giver is the Seminole corn spirit who brought agriculture to the people. According to tradition, Little Giver appeared as a small, generous being who taught the Seminole how to plant, cultivate, and harvest corn. The spirit showed them the proper way to prepare the fields, the right time to plant, and the rituals to ensure a bountiful harvest. Little Giver is closely associated with the Green Corn Ceremony, the most important Seminole ritual, which marks the ripening of the corn and the beginning of the new year. Offerings are made to Little Giver during the ceremony to ensure continued blessings. The spirit embodies the principle of generosity — the name 'Little Giver' reminds the Seminole that even small gifts given freely are precious.

title: Little John
summary: When Robin Hood was about twenty years old and still gathering the men who would become his Merry Men, he grew restless after fourteen days without sport.

title: Little Red Riding Hood
summary: In Jamaica, when the sun goes down and the shadows grow long, grandmothers gather the children on their porches and tell them about Rolling Calf.

title: Ljungby Horn and Pipe
summary: At Trolle-Ljungby Castle in Scania, southern Sweden, a large glacial boulder called Maglestenen stands in the fields. Legend says that trolls live beneath this stone, and every Christmas Eve, the stone rises on golden pillars while the trolls feast and make merry beneath it. In the mid-16th century, the widowed Lady Sissela Ulfstand, mistress of Ljungby, grew curious about these tales and promised her best horse to any servant who would ride to Maglestenen on Christmas night and investigate. A brave stable hand took the challenge. When he arrived, he found the stone indeed raised on golden pillars, with trolls reveling beneath. They offered him a drinking horn and a pipe (whistle), urging him to drink the troll king's health and blow the pipe. As he was about to drink, a captive girl (a human taken by the trolls) secretly warned him. He threw the drink over his shoulder — the drops burned his horse's flank — and galloped away with the horn and pipe. The trolls chased him, but the girl had advised him to ride across a plowed field (forming a cross shape, which trolls cannot cross). The trolls were forced to run along the furrows, slowing them down. He reached the castle just in time, the drawbridge was raised, and the trolls could not enter. Furious, they cursed the estate: the horse and rider would die, the castle would burn three times, and if the artifacts were ever removed, the owner would face great misfortune. The horn (a drinking vessel with gilded silver mounts) and the pipe (carved from ivory, playable from both ends) remain at Trolle-Ljungby to this day. The curse is said to have come true: the horse died, the rider died three days later, and the castle burned three times.

title: Lodge-Boy and Thrown-Away (Creek)
summary: Lodge-Boy (or By-The-Door) and Thrown-Away are mythical twin heroes in Muscogee Creek (and Natchez) tradition. The twins were born after their pregnant mother was killed by a monster. One twin was found inside the lodge and the other was thrown away, giving them their names. They grew up with extraordinary strength and magical abilities. The twins are portrayed as rowdy monster-slayers who cause plenty of trouble during their adventures. They travel across the land defeating dangerous creatures, including giant serpents, man-eating monsters, and evil spirits. Each twin possesses complementary skills — one is physically powerful while the other is clever and resourceful. Their adventures teach the value of brotherhood, courage, and balance between strength and wisdom.

title: Lodge-Boy and Thrown-Away (Natchez)
summary: Lodge-Boy and Thrown-Away are twin culture heroes in Natchez mythology. The twins were born when their pregnant mother was killed by a monster — one was found inside the lodge (Lodge-Boy) and the other was found where he had been thrown away (Thrown-Away). They grew up in a single day, blessed with supernatural strength and abilities. The twins embarked on a series of adventures: they killed the monster that had murdered their mother, battled giant serpents, defeated man-eating ogres, and cleared the land of dangerous beings to make it safe for the Natchez people. They also brought important knowledge to the people, including hunting techniques and ceremonial practices. The twins are complementary — one uses brute strength while the other uses cunning — representing the balance needed to overcome life's challenges.

title: Lofa: The Stinking Ogre (Chickasaw)
summary: Lofa is a hideous, foul-smelling ogre from Chickasaw mythology, similar to the Choctaw Shampe. Lofa is a bigfoot-like creature that dwells in the remote swamps and forests of Chickasaw territory. It is covered in shaggy hair and emits an unbearable stench that can be smelled from a great distance. The creature's odor is so powerful that it can knock a person unconscious. Lofa preys on travelers who become lost in its territory. However, the creature is slow and clumsy, and an alert person can escape by running against the wind. Lofa stories served as warnings to children and hunters about the dangers of the wilderness and the importance of staying oriented and traveling in groups.

title: Long-Ears: The Wolf Monster (Seminole)
summary: Long-Ears is a wolf-like monster from Seminole folklore. This enormous, predatory creature is distinguished by its unusually long ears and its insatiable hunger for human flesh. Long-Ears dwells in the remote swamps and hammocks of Florida, emerging to hunt when food is scarce. The monster is said to be incredibly fast and cunning, able to track prey over long distances. Seminole hunters told stories of encounters with Long-Ears to young warriors as a test of courage. The creature also appears in stories as a cautionary figure, warning against venturing too deep into unknown territory unprepared. Like many Seminole monsters, Long-Ears represents the dangers of the wild Florida landscape that the Seminole learned to navigate and respect.

title: Lord Peter
summary: A story of a young man who overcomes the challenges set by a vengeful father-in-law to prove his worth. Through his courage and a series of magical quests, including defeating a dragon, he secures his marriage and attains great wealth and honor.

title: Los Aluxes — The Maya Trickster Spirits
summary: Los Aluxes (singular: Alux) are small, elf-like trickster spirits from Yucatec Maya tradition that survived into the Hispanic folklore of Yucatán and spread through Mexican-American communities. These mischievous beings, standing only knee-high, are said to inhabit ancient Maya ruins, cenotes, and forests. They are known to play pranks on humans — hiding tools, tangling hair, leading travelers astray, and making strange noises at night. However, if respected and offered small gifts (such as corn, honey, or balché), they can become protective guardians of homes and cornfields. In the Yucatán, farmers still build small houses called 'kahtal alux' to invite aluxes to guard their land. Among Mexican-American communities, the belief in aluxes persists especially in areas with Maya heritage, where they are seen as guardians of indigenous traditions and the natural world against modern development.

title: Lotan, the Seven-Headed Serpent
summary: A seven-headed sea serpent that served Yamm in the war against Baal, and whose heads were cut off by the storm god — but each head grew back, and the serpent still thrashes in the deep.

title: Lougawou: The Werewolf of Haiti
summary: A sorcerer removes their skin at night to transform into a beast that preys on children.

title: Louhi Steals Sun, Moon, and Fire
summary: As revenge for the theft of the Sampo, Louhi uses her dark magic to steal the sun, moon, and fire from the world, plunging the land of Kalevala into a terrifying and eternal darkness and freezing cold.

title: Loulou and the Stolen Moonlight
summary: A mischievous forest spirit called Loulou steals the moonlight from a fishing village, plunging the lagoon into darkness so the fish cannot find their way home.

title: Loundja the Sultan's Daughter
summary: An Algerian folktale in which a sultan's baby daughter, Loundja, is kidnapped from her crib by a female ghoul (ghoula) who raises her as her own daughter. Loundja grows up in the ghoul's cave home, unaware that her mother is a monster. When Loundja reaches maturity, she meets a handsome young man in the forest and falls in love. The ghoula immediately senses his ill intentions and follows the couple into the woods. When the young man lures Loundja deep into the forest, planning to take advantage of her and abandon her, the ghoula emerges to protect her adopted daughter. She entraps the man in an underground labyrinth and returns to prepare a feast. Loundja, kind-hearted, visits the man in his prison. He cunningly persuades her that if they marry immediately, the ghoula will forgive him. Loundja releases him, but the ghoula discovers their escape and confronts them. The tale subverts the typical fairy-tale archetypes: the ghoula is a loving, protective mother, while the charming young man is a predator. The story prepared Algerian girls to recognize danger beneath charming exteriors.

title: Lumiuk the Blind Boy
summary: Lumiuk is a blind boy who suffers extreme abuse from his family. He finds refuge in the sea, where the spirits of the ocean grant him sight and a new purpose. He returns as a powerful figure, proving that those cast out by society can find strength and redemption in the natural world.

title: Luna, the Flame Spirit of Flemish Hearths
summary: A gentle household spirit who protects Flemish hearths but punishes those who let the fire die out of laziness.

title: Luz de Yara: The Spirit Light of Hatuey
summary: The soul of a Taíno chief burned by Spanish colonizers wanders the Cuban coast as a mysterious light.

title: Lávrukaš and the Russian Chudes
summary: A legend about a Sámi woman named Lávrukaš who outwits Russian Chude attackers through bravery and cunning. This story from the coastal Sámi tradition features a female protagonist who saves her community from raiders. It reflects the strong women in Sámi storytelling tradition, particularly in Emilie Demant Hatt's collection.

title: Lạc Long Quân and Âu Cơ
summary: In the mountains of Papua New Guinea, where the jungle is so dense that villages can be separated by a day's walk and never know each other, the Kalam people tell stories of the Krim.

title: Mae Nak Phra Khanong
summary: The most famous ghost legend in Thai folklore tells the tragic love story of Mae Nak, a young woman who died in childbirth while her husband Mak was away at war. Upon returning home, Mak found his wife and newborn baby seemingly alive and well, unaware they were both ghosts. When Mak discovered the truth after witnessing Nak's arm extend through floorboards to retrieve a dropped lime, he fled in terror. Nak's heartbroken spirit terrorized the village until a powerful monk named Somdej Toh subdued her through compassion. Today, Mae Nak's shrine at Wat Mahabut in Bangkok remains a popular pilgrimage site where devotees seek blessings for love and protection from military conscription.

title: Mae Phosop: The Rice Goddess of Laos and Thailand
summary: Mae Phosop (Mother of the Rice Kernel) is the ancient rice goddess revered in Lao and Thai agricultural traditions. According to legend, Mae Phosop was a beautiful celestial maiden who descended to earth to become the spirit of rice — the essence that gives life to all who consume it. She is believed to possess a spiritual essence (khwan) that must be treated with the utmost respect. In one foundational myth, rice once grew as large as pumpkins and would fly directly into farmers' granaries by itself. However, a careless woman once struck a rice kernel with her broom in anger, and the offended rice spirit withdrew into hiding, causing famine. The people had to perform elaborate ceremonies to call Mae Phosop back. Today, before planting season, farmers perform the 'Rice Mother Calling' ritual (riak khwan khao), offering bananas, sugarcane, and flowers to Mae Phosop. During harvest, the 'Spirit of the Rice' ceremony involves selecting the most beautiful rice stalks and dressing them in silk as an offering. The legend teaches that rice is not merely food but a living, spiritual entity deserving of gratitude and respect. This agricultural animism coexists with Buddhism throughout the Lao world.

title: Maha Sona: The Great Graveyard Demon of Sri Lanka
summary: A decapitated warrior giant becomes the most feared demon in Sinhalese folklore, haunting graveyards and crossroads.

title: Mahogany Tree, the Sacred Sentinel
summary: The sacred mahogany tree of Antigua is believed to be inhabited by a powerful guardian spirit who protects the island's forests and punishes those who harm them.

title: Mahsuri of Langkawi
summary: The tragic legend of Mahsuri, a beautiful and virtuous woman from Kedah who lived on the island of Langkawi in the early 19th century. Falsely accused of adultery by a jealous rival, Mahsuri was found guilty by the village chief and sentenced to death by keris (ceremonial dagger). When executed, white blood flowed from her wound, proving her innocence. Before dying, she cursed Langkawi for seven generations — a curse that allegedly brought war, famine, and misfortune to the island. The curse was said to have been lifted seven generations later in the 1990s when Langkawi began to prosper. Today, Mahsuri's tomb is a major tourist attraction, and her story remains a powerful symbol of injustice and the consequences of false accusation.

title: Mahsuri: The Cursed Maiden of Langkawi
summary: A falsely accused woman curses the island of Langkawi for seven generations with her dying breath.

title: Maid Lena
summary: A story about a humble maid whose innate kindness, purity of heart, and resilience lead her to overcome adversity and find a happy ending.

title: Maid Marian
summary: Maid Marian was the heart of Sherwood Forest.. While Robin Hood was its soul and Little John its strength, Marian was the pulse that kept the Merry Men alive.

title: Maiden Bright-eye
summary: A tale of a maiden with extraordinary beauty and spiritual insight who positively influences the people around her, acting as a beacon of hope and purity.

title: Maiden of the Rainbow
summary: Wainamoinen encounters the elusive Maiden of the Rainbow, whose beauty is matched only by her distance. Their interaction involves a complex process of courtship and magical tests, further exploring the themes of longing, desire, and the inherent difficulty of finding a peer in love and magic.

title: Makemake and the Birdman Cult
summary: Makemake, the supreme creator god of Rapa Nui, shaped the world and gave life to the island. He created the birds, the fish, and the people, then withdrew to watch over them from the heavens. As Rapa Nui's society evolved, Makemake became associated with the Tangata Manu (Birdman) cult centered at the ceremonial village of Orongo. Each year, representatives of competing clans would descend the sheer cliffs, swim across shark-infested waters to the islet of Motu Nui, and retrieve the first Manutara (sooty tern) egg of the season. The successful competitor became the Tangata Manu, the Birdman of the year, gaining supreme temporal power for the tribe.

title: Malakas at Maganda (The First Man and Woman)
summary: According to ancient Tagalog creation myth, the world began as a vast emptiness with only the sea and sky. A huge bird grew tired of flying and stirred up the sea, causing an island to emerge. From a bamboo stalk split by the bird, the first man Malakas (Strong) and the first woman Maganda (Beautiful) sprang forth, becoming the ancestors of all humanity. This foundational Philippine myth explains the origin of the Filipino people and the islands of the archipelago.

title: Malin Kundang
summary: A tragic folktale from West Sumatra about a poor boy named Malin Kundang who leaves his mother to seek fortune overseas. After years of hardship, he becomes a wealthy merchant, marries a princess, and returns to his home village in a grand ship. His aging mother, overjoyed to see him, rushes to embrace him, but Malin Kundang, ashamed of his humble origins, cruelly denies knowing her and orders her driven away. Heartbroken, his mother kneels and prays to God to punish her ungrateful son. A violent storm immediately strikes, and Malin Kundang and his ship are turned to stone. The stone ship remains visible on the coast of Air Manis Beach in Padang as a warning against filial ingratitude.

title: Mam and Zin (Mem û Zîn)
summary: The Kurdish national epic, written down in 1692 by poet Ahmad Khani. Mem, a chivalrous youth of the Alan clan and heir to the City of the West, falls in love with Zin, the beautiful daughter of the governor of Botan (Cizre). They meet during a Newroz celebration. Their union is blocked by the jealous Bakr, who conspires against them. Mem is poisoned, and Zin, upon learning of his death, collapses and dies of grief at his grave.
