They are buried together, but a thorn bush grows between their graves, separating the lovers even in death — the roots of malice penetrating deep into the earth. Bakr is killed by Mem's friend Tacdin and buried nearby, his malice persisting as the thorn bush. The epic is foundational to Kurdish literature and identity.

title: Mama Cocha, Water Mother
summary: Mama Cocha, mother of all waters, commands the lakes and rivers, and the fishermen who forget her name find their boats overturned and their nets empty.

title: Mama D'Leau and the Lost Children
summary: Two children wandering near the mangroves encounter Mama D'Leau, the mysterious water woman, who tests their hearts before revealing the hidden path home.

title: Mama D'Leau of the River
summary: A water spirit of terrifying beauty guards the rivers of Dominica, punishing those who disrespect the water while rewarding those who approach with reverence.
themes: reverence for nature and water spirits
the dual nature of natural forces

title: Mama Dlo and the River Guardian
summary: A greedy fisherman ignores the warnings of the river spirits and takes more than his share from the waters, drawing the wrath of Mama Dlo.

title: Mama Dlo, Mother of the Waters
summary: Mama Dlo (also known as Mama D'Leau or Mama Glo) is a water spirit from Trinidadian folklore, the wife of Papa Bois. She is the mother of the waters, a beautiful woman from the waist up but a serpent or fish from the waist down — similar to a mermaid. Mama Dlo guards rivers, ponds, and wetlands, and is known to grant riches and favors to those who treat the waters with respect. She is notoriously protective of her domain and exacts revenge on those who pollute or overfish. Like many Caribbean water spirits, she combs her long hair by the water's edge, and anyone who captures her golden comb can demand a wish. However, dealing with Mama Dlo is dangerous — she may drown those who offend her or lure children too close to the water's edge. Her name comes from French Creole 'Maman de l'Eau' (Mother of the Water).

title: Mama Glo: Lights of the Lagoon
summary: A fisherman ignores his grandmother's warnings about the lagoon lights and is drawn beneath the water by Mama Glo, learning too late that some waters keep what they claim.

title: Mamba Muntu, the Dragon of the Kuilu
summary: A great dragon dwells in the Kuilu River, guarding the boundary between the living and the dead, and only those who carry no fear may pass its domain unharmed.

title: Mame Coumba Bang: The River Goddess of Saint-Louis
summary: A powerful river goddess controls the waters of the Senegal River and demands offerings from fishermen.

title: Mami Wata, the Liberian Water Spirit
summary: Mami Wata is a beautiful and powerful water spirit of West African tradition who lures men with her beauty and grants wealth to those who please her.

title: Mami Wata: The Water Spirit
summary: A beautiful water spirit of rivers and oceans brings wealth and beauty to those who honor her.

title: Mamlambo: The River Goddess Who Brings Wealth and Death
summary: Mamlambo is a shapeshifting water deity of the Zulu and Xhosa peoples, often depicted as a giant serpent with a horse's head or a beautiful woman who lures men to their doom. She controls the waters, causing floods when angered and droughts when she withdraws. Those who seek her out for wealth must make terrible sacrifices, and the riches she grants always come with ruin, illness, and death. In 1997 the Mamlambo gained notoriety when nine deaths near the Mzintlava River were attributed to her, with victims found with their brains sucked out, earning her the name 'brain sucker.' She represents the dangerous seduction of quick wealth and the unpredictable power of nature.

title: Manananggal: The Vampire Woman
summary: A beautiful woman who splits in half at night, flying to drink the blood of pregnant women—her upper torso flies while her lower body remains.

title: Manas: The Great Campaign and Death of the Hero
summary: The second major cycle of the Manas epic describes how Manas united the forty Kyrgyz tribes under the Tengrist sky-banner and led them to reclaim the Ala-Too mountains from Chinese and Kalmyk invaders. His magical white stallion Ak-Kula carried him through epic battles, advising him with human speech and prophetic warnings. After the great campaign against Chinese forces led by Konurbai, Manas was mortally wounded by treachery. His wife Kanykey buried him and built a mausoleum (Gumbez Manasa) over his grave in the Talas valley. To protect the tomb from grave-robbers, she inscribed a decoy woman's name on it. The mausoleum, dating from 1334, remains the most sacred pilgrimage site in Kyrgyzstan.

title: Mandukhai the Wise Queen
summary: Mandukhai Khatun (also known as Mandukhai Sechen Khongorjin) was a 15th-century Mongol queen who reunified the fractured Mongol nation after the fall of the Yuan dynasty. According to legend, she raised the orphaned Dayan Khan from childhood, then married him when he came of age. At age thirty-two, she led the Mongol army into battle against the Oirats while pregnant, wearing armor and carrying twin swords. She defeated the Oirat forces and secured Dayan Khan's rule. Her wisdom in statecraft and courage in battle made her one of the most revered figures in Mongol history, embodying the ideal of the warrior-queen.

title: Mangadhai: The Multi-Headed Dragons of Mongolia
summary: Terrible multi-headed serpent-dragons threaten the world in Mongolian epic folklore.

title: Mannegishi (Little People)
summary: The Mannegishi are small, bald humanoid beings in Crow mythology, described as having large, bulging eyes and tiny, tan bodies. They are tricksters who live in rocky areas and along riverbanks. These little people are known for playing pranks on humans, leading travelers astray, and causing mischief. Despite their troublesome nature, they are not considered evil. Some stories say they can be helpful to those who treat them with respect. The Mannegishi are similar to fairies in European folklore and are found in various forms across many Plains Indian traditions, often associated with mysterious sounds and disappearing objects.

title: Mariatta--Wainamoinen's Departure
summary: A virgin girl named Marjatta becomes pregnant after stepping on a rye grain. Her son is born and baptized as a Christian king. Realizing that the era of pagan magic is ending, Wainamoinen sails away into the sunset, leaving the world to the new order.

title: Marmennilin (The Merman of Elduvík)
summary: A farmer named Arnfinn from Elduvík encountered a Marmennil—a merman who lives at the bottom of the sea, smaller than a human with long fingers, who delights in teasing fishermen by stealing bait and snagging hooks. One day, the merman tried to stick Arnfinn's hook to the seabed but accidentally hooked his own hand and was pulled into the boat. The fishermen made the sign of the cross and brought him home. For years, they took Marmennilin fishing; when fish were below, he would laugh and play, and the men always caught plenty. But one day in rough waves, the men forgot to make the sign of the cross, and Marmennilin escaped into the sea forever. A statue by Hans Pauli Olsen was unveiled in 2020.

title: María Sabina — The Mushroom Shaman of Oaxaca
summary: María Sabina (1894–1985) was a Mazatec curandera and shaman from Huautla de Jiménez, Oaxaca, whose use of sacred psilocybin mushrooms in healing ceremonies gained worldwide fame. Her legend — part historical, part mythic — tells of a poor indigenous woman who discovered the sacred mushrooms as a child and was called by the spirits to become a healer. She conducted veladas (night ceremonies) in which she consumed the 'little saints' (as Mazatecs call the mushrooms) and channeled spirits who could diagnose and cure illnesses. In 1955, she was visited by American banker and amateur mycologist R. Gordon Wasson, whose Life magazine article 'Seeking the Magic Mushroom' (1957) introduced psychedelic mushrooms to the Western world. María Sabina later expressed regret about this exposure, saying it had broken the sacred tradition. In Chicano and Mexican-American folklore, María Sabina represents the profound healing knowledge of Indigenous Mexico, the power of women as spiritual leaders, and the tension between preserving sacred traditions and the outside world's hunger for indigenous wisdom. Her story continues to inspire spiritual seekers, artists, and activists in both Mexico and the United States.

title: Masalai: The Spirits of the Papua New Guinea Forest
summary: Shape-shifting place spirits guard sacred sites and punish those who break taboos in the jungle.

title: Master and Pupil
summary: A story exploring the complex relationship between a mentor and a student, focusing on themes of artistic growth, ambition, and the eventual surpassing of the master.

title: Master of Breath (Hesaketvmesē) (Creek)
summary: Hesaketvmesē, also called Epohfvnkv, is the supreme being in Muscogee Creek religion. Known as the 'Maker of Breath' or 'the One Above who holds life's breath,' Hesaketvmesē is a solar deity who spoke to and guided the Muscogee people on their journey from the west. The name emphasizes the belief that breath and life are one — Hesaketvmesē gives breath to all living things and can take it away. The Muscogee associated the Creator with the sun, which was central to their ceremonial life. Fire was considered the most striking representation of the sun on earth and was believed to have intelligence and to be in constant communication with Hesaketvmesē. The sacred fire in the square ground was maintained as a direct connection to the Creator.

title: Matlose the Hobgoblin (Nuu-chah-nulth)
summary: Matlose is the most feared hobgoblin spirit of the Nuu-chah-nulth people, described as a monstrous Caliban-like creature. His head resembles something that might have been human but is not, and his uncouth bulk is horrid with black bristles. His monstrous teeth and curved claws are like those of a bear, capable of rending prey into morsels with a single stroke. Most terrifying of all is his voice — whoever hears Matlose's terrible voice falls as if smitten, paralyzed by fear. He lurks in the deep forests and remote mountains of Vancouver Island, preying on anyone who ventures too far from the safety of the village. Shamans and warriors who successfully confront Matlose gain immense supernatural power. The Matlose legend serves as both a cautionary tale about the dangers of the wilderness and a testament to the power of the spirit world that surrounds the Nuu-chah-nulth people.

title: Matsieng's Footprints: The Tswana Creation
summary: According to Tswana tradition, Matsieng, a powerful one-legged giant considered the first ancestor of the Batswana people, emerged from a waterhole in southeastern Botswana. As he climbed out, he was followed by his people, domestic animals, and wildlife, all sinking their feet into the soft, unformed early earth. Their footprints hardened into stone over millennia, preserved as a sacred site now known as the Matsieng Footprints. The site contains over 170 carvings of human and animal footprints, which archaeologists date to the early second millennium and attribute to Khoe herders. To this day, the Tswana people visit the site for ritual purposes including rain-making ceremonies, maintaining the connection between the first ancestor and the living community.

title: Matsya
summary: In the dawn of the current cosmic age, before the world as we know it took shape, there lived a king named Manu.

title: Maui and Hine-nui-te-po: The Quest for Immortality
summary: Maui sought to conquer death itself by destroying Hine-nui-te-po, the goddess of death. He knew that if he could pass through her body unharmed, humanity would gain immortality. He took the smallest forest birds as his companions and found the goddess sleeping. Maui instructed the birds to remain silent while he crawled into her mouth and through her body. He warned them not to laugh. However, when only his legs remained visible, the tiny Tiwakawaka (fantail) could not contain its amusement at the sight. Its laughter woke Hine-nui-te-po, who snapped her obsidian teeth shut, cutting Maui in half. Thus Maui died and death became permanent for all humankind.

title: Maui and the Sun
summary: Long ago, when the world was young and the rhythms of nature were far more erratic than they are today, the sun, Tama-nui-te-rā, was a capricious and hurried deity.

title: Maui Fishing Up the North Island
summary: Maui's brothers refused to take him fishing, so he hid in their canoe and revealed himself at sea. Using a magical fishhook made from the jawbone of his ancestor Murirangawhenua, and chanting powerful incantations, Maui caught a gigantic fish. He instructed his brothers to wait until he had appeased Tangaroa before carving the fish, but they grew impatient and began cutting. The fish thrashed, forming the mountains, valleys, lakes, and rugged coastline of Te Ika-a-Maui (the North Island of New Zealand). Maui's canoe became the South Island, and Stewart Island became his anchor stone.

title: Maui Pulling Up the Tongan Islands
summary: Maui Kisikisi (Little Maui) sat in his canoe fishing but catching nothing. Growing frustrated, he reached down through the ocean with his powerful arms and grasped the sea floor. With tremendous effort, he pulled upward, bringing the Tongan islands to the surface. As he hauled, the coral, sand, and rock emerged from the depths, forming the archipelago. The story explains why Tonga's islands are relatively flat compared to volcanic islands—they were pulled up, not thrown up by volcanic force. This tale is part of a regional Maui cycle, adapted to explain Tonga's unique geography of low coral atolls and raised limestone islands.

title: Maui Slowing the Sun
summary: Maui observed that the sun, Tamanuitera, moved across the sky too quickly, leaving insufficient daylight for working, cooking, and fishing. He convinced his brothers to help capture the sun and force it to slow down. They traveled east to the pit where the sun rose, built a wall of clay to hide behind, and wove strong ropes from flax. When the sun rose, Maui chanted a karakia and the brothers threw ropes around the sun's body, trapping it. Maui struck the sun with his magic jawbone until it agreed to travel more slowly across the sky, giving humanity longer days for their labors.

title: Maui Stealing Fire from Mahuika
summary: After all fires in Hawaiki had been extinguished, Maui volunteered to visit his ancestress Mahuika, the goddess of fire, to obtain new flames. She pulled out one of her burning fingernails and gave it to him. However, Maui's trickster nature took over and he extinguished it, then returned for another. He repeated this deception until Mahuika had given away all but her last fingernail. Enraged, she threw her final nail at Maui, igniting a great forest fire. Maui transformed into a hawk to escape, then called upon his thunder god ancestors to send rain. Mahuika saved a few sparks which she threw into specific trees, explaining why certain woods are best for fire-making.

title: Mavka: The Forest Spirit of the Carpathians
summary: The spirit of an unbaptized child lures young men to their doom in the Carpathian forests.

title: Mawu, the Supreme Creator (Ewe/Fon)
summary: Mawu is the supreme creator god of the Ewe and Fon people, a lunar goddess who created the cosmos and all living beings. She is often paired with Lisa, the sun god, forming a dual-sexed creator deity (Mawu-Lisa). Mawu is considered distant from everyday human affairs, having delegated the running of the world to her children, the trɔwo (spirits or lesser gods). Each child received dominion over a specific domain: thunder, earth, sea, wind, and others. Mawu represents the feminine principle of creation and the moon's cool, nurturing light. Her day is Monday, and she is associated with peace, fertility, and the cycle of seasons. Shrines to Mawu are rare because she is considered too great for direct worship; instead, the Ewe venerate the trɔwo who serve as her intermediaries.

title: Mbatian the Great Laibon
summary: Mbatian was the most powerful laibon (spiritual leader) in Maasai history, a descendant of the Inkindongi clan. His prophetic powers were legendary — he could predict droughts, locate lost cattle, and communicate directly with Enkai. As he grew old, Mbatian had to choose which of his many sons would inherit his powers. His favorite, Senteu, was trained in the sacred arts, but his younger son Lenana proved more cunning. On his deathbed, Mbatian announced that whichever son he called to his bedside would inherit his powers. Lenana tricked a messenger into calling him first, usurping his brother's birthright. This sparked a bitter rivalry that would divide the Maasai and reshape their history during the colonial era.

title: Mbidi Kiluwe: The Culture Hero of the Luba
summary: Mbidi Kiluwe was a mysterious prince who came from the east, distinguished by his light skin and his refined, dignified manners. He arrived at the court of King Nkongolo Mwamba, the red-skinned ruler of the Luba. Where Nkongolo was crude and violent, Mbidi Kiluwe was gentle and wise. He introduced new customs: eating in private, using utensils, and the proper way to address royalty. Mbidi Kiluwe married Nkongolo's sister Bulanda, but when Nkongolo's tyranny became unbearable, Mbidi Kiluwe was forced to flee back to his homeland. Before leaving, he prophesied that his unborn son would return to overthrow Nkongolo. Mbidi Kiluwe's refined manners became the model for Luba kingship (bulopwe), establishing the sacred traditions of courtly behavior that would define Luba royal culture for centuries. He embodies the ideal of the cultured, wise ruler who governs through dignity rather than fear.

title: Mbona, the Rain Prophet
summary: Mbona was a powerful spirit of rain and water who could summon storms with a word and end droughts with a gesture. The people of the Shire River valley revered him as a living bridge between earth and sky.
themes: the power of the young to renew tradition

title: Mbwiri, the Gabonese Initiate
summary: The Mbwiri ceremony of Gabon is a sacred initiation where a possessed individual is purified through ritual dance and community support.

title: Meandash: The Celestial Reindeer Hunt
summary: In Kola Sámi tradition, Meandash also exists as a celestial reindeer hunted by the thunder god in the sky. The cosmic hunt is reflected in the constellations—Orion, the Pleiades, and Arcturus belong to the cosmic elk-reindeer hunt tradition. When the thunder god strikes Meandash down, everything falls apart: fire envelops the earth, mountains boil, ice boils, stars fall, the moon goes out, and the sun sinks. The myth describes an apocalypse.

title: Meandash: The Mythic Wild Reindeer
summary: The central creation myth of the wild reindeer from eastern Sámi (Kola Peninsula) tradition. Meandash is a shapeshifter—human inside his hut, wild reindeer outside. He is the son of a female noaidi. An earthly girl crosses a river of blood, lungs, and livers to reach him and becomes his wife. She bears his children, who are born human. She is forbidden from drying urine-soaked reindeer skins in the sun. When she breaks this taboo, Meandash transforms permanently into a wild reindeer and his children become reindeer calves, forming the first wild reindeer herds.

title: Medea's Vengeance
summary: A sorceress who sacrificed everything for love takes a terrifying and absolute revenge on her faithless husband.

title: Medusa
summary: In the ancient world, before the age of heroes faded into memory, there lived three sisters whose names struck terror into the hearts of all who heard them.

title: Melqart, the Tyrian Hercules
summary: The god of Tyre who died and rose again each year, his resurrection bringing the return of spring — because in Lebanon, even gods must die before they can be reborn.

title: Melusine: The Serpent Woman
summary: A woman who hides her serpent tail on Saturdays—until her husband discovers the truth.

title: Menes-Antti's Adventures in France
summary: An Inari Sámi humorous folktale collected by Koskimies and Itkonen about Menes-Antti traveling to France. He arrived in Paris in shabby clothing and went to a grand party building where he was almost thrown out. He overheard a king's daughter arranging a liaison, and pretending to be the suitor, he got into her bed. When discovered, he was paid 3000 gold talers to leave. The king's daughter became pregnant.

title: Merger the Hero (Nanai Epic)
summary: The central Nanai epic hero Merger, whose adventures form the core of Nanai oral tradition. The epic follows Merger as he journeys along the Amur River, battling evil spirits, demons, and rival clans to protect the Nanai people. He is aided by his shamanic powers, his supernatural strength, and the spirits of the Amur River and Siberian taiga. The story incorporates elements of shamanic initiation, shape-shifting (into tigers, birds, and fish), and journeys to the underworld. Merger's quests often involve retrieving stolen souls, restoring balance to the natural world, and defeating the 'water demons' that lurk in the deep pools of the Amur. The epic is traditionally performed by Nanai shamans during important ceremonies and can last for several nights of continuous recitation.

title: Merlin
summary: Long before Arthur drew the sword from the stone, before Camelot rose from the plains of Logres, there was Merlin.

title: Merlin's Madness in the Forest
summary: After foreseeing the destruction of Camelot, Merlin wanders the forest of Brocéliande in a madness born of knowledge he can never unlearn.

title: Metsavana, the Old Man of the Woods
summary: A forest keeper who punishes those who take too much from his woodland and rewards those who respect the sacred groves of hiis.

title: Mimi Spirits: The First Rock Artists
summary: In the Aboriginal Australian mythology of Arnhem Land in northern Australia, Mimi spirits (also called Mimih) are fairy-like beings with extremely thin and elongated bodies. They are so thin that they risk breaking in strong winds, which is why they spend most of their time living in rock crevices. According to tradition, the Mimi spirits had human form and lived in northern Australia before the Aboriginal people arrived. They were the first to make rock paintings, teaching the Aboriginal people how to paint, hunt, and cook kangaroo meat. Mimi are considered mischievous but generally harmless, sometimes playing tricks on travelers or leading people astray in the bush. The distinctive Mimi rock art style, characterized by dynamic stick-figure representations of hunting and dancing, can still be seen in the escarpments of Kakadu and Arnhem Land.

title: Mirza Sahiba — Elopement and Betrayal
summary: Mirza and Sahiba were cousins from the Jatt tribe of Punjab who fell in love. When Sahiba's parents arranged her marriage to another man, Mirza arrived at her wedding on horseback and eloped with her. As they fled across the countryside, Sahiba's brothers and their armed men pursued them. Mirza, a skilled archer, shot arrows to keep the pursuers at bay but eventually ran out. He asked Sahiba to fetch the quiver tied to the saddle. But Sahiba, afraid her brothers would be killed, deliberately brought the arrows slowly. In that fatal delay, her brothers caught up and killed Mirza. When Sahiba saw Mirza dead, she took his sword and killed herself. Unlike the other Punjabi romances, Mirza Sahiba highlights how hesitation and divided loyalties can lead to tragedy.

title: Mishipeshu, the Underwater Panther
summary: Mishipeshu, the Great Lynx, is one of the most powerful water beings in Ojibwe mythology, ruling the depths of Lake Superior from his home on Michipicoten Island. He has the head and paws of a giant cat but is covered in scales with dagger-like spikes along his back and tail. He is the master of all water creatures, including snakes, and can cause storms that capsize canoes and drown the unwary. Mishipeshu is the eternal opponent of the Thunderbirds who rule the skies. In one story, four Ojibwe warriors traveled to Mishipeshu's island home to take copper, but his eerie voice surrounded them and they barely escaped with their lives. Travelers traditionally made offerings of tobacco before crossing large lakes to appease the underwater panther and ensure safe passage.

title: Miss Cow Falls a Victim to Mr. Rabbit
summary: Brer Rabbit, hungry and with nothing to eat, approaches Miss Cow and asks her for some milk, claiming his children are starving. Miss Cow refuses, saying the milk is for her calf. Brer Rabbit then asks her to come to Miss Meadows's house where there is plenty of grass, but Miss Cow refuses again. Later, Brer Rabbit hides behind a bush and calls out in a deep voice, pretending to be a wild animal threatening to eat Miss Cow. He frightens her into running to Miss Meadows's gate, where he pretends to defend her. Grateful, Miss Cow offers him all the milk he wants. The next day, Brer Rabbit repeats the trick with variations, eventually milking Miss Cow dry. When Miss Cow realizes she has been tricked, Brer Rabbit is long gone.

title: Mlouka and the Strand of Hair
summary: An Algerian folktale from the west of the country, famous among Berber communities. Mlouka was a young peasant girl renowned for her extraordinarily long, strong, and beautiful hair—so long she could not wash it alone, and all the women of her family had to walk to the river to help her. A jealous cousin plucked a strand of Mlouka's hair, which was so long it curled and blocked the river's flow. When an honorable man of the village investigated the obstruction, he found the magnificent strand and was captivated. The hair became a symbol of desire, and Mlouka was forced into marriage with a man she did not love. But Mlouka refused to accept her fate. Using her intelligence and resourcefulness, she devised a plan to escape her forced marriage. The story subverts the traditional damsel-in-distress trope: Mlouka rescues herself through wit and determination, and the powerful knight who appears is revealed as selfish, not heroic. The tale teaches that a woman's worth lies in her intellect and courage, not her beauty alone.

title: Mockingbird Gives Out the Calls
summary: In this Hopi story, Mockingbird was responsible for distributing the languages and calls among all the peoples of the world. During the migrations after the emergence into the Fourth World, the people were all speaking the same language. Mockingbird called the people together and assigned different languages and dialects to different groups, effectively creating the diversity of tribes and nations. He gave various bird species their distinctive calls as well. According to some versions, Mockingbird received this task from Spider Grandmother or the Kachinas, and his imitative ability was used to create the range of human languages. The story explains why Mockingbird can mimic other birds and why there are so many different languages among the peoples of the earth.

title: Moddey Dhoo
summary: The phantom Moddey Dhoo, a spectral black dog, haunts the lanes of Peel, serving as a grim reminder of the boundaries between the living and the dead.

title: Modimo: The Supreme God of the Sotho-Tswana
summary: Modimo is the supreme deity in the traditional religion of the Sotho-Tswana people, recognized as the creator of all things, the source of life, and the controller of destiny. Intangible and all-pervasive, Modimo is addressed by praise names including Mme (Mother) and Lesedi (Light), but also Selo (Monster) for his dangerous powers beyond human comprehension. Modimo governs the elements, sending lightning, thunder, rain, or drought as signs of approval or discontent. However, Modimo is distant from daily human affairs, and the Tswana approach him through the Badimo (ancestors), who act as intermediaries. The Tswana say 'Motho ke modimo' (Man is modimo), expressing the profound interconnection between humans, ancestors, and the divine, with ancestors functioning as guardians of family morality and fertility.

title: Moko Jumbie: The Tall Guardian
summary: On the night before a village festival, a young stilt-walker named Corwin learns why the Moko Jumbie towers above the rooftops — not for spectacle, but to see the spirits that creep toward the sleeping village.

title: Mokélé-Mbembé, the Gabonese River Dragon
summary: The Mokélé-Mbembé is a legendary river creature said to inhabit the swamps and rivers of Gabon, resembling a long-necked reptile with a single tusk.

title: Momotaro: The Boy Born from a Peach
summary: In the province of Suruga, by a great mountain, an old woodcutter and his wife lived alone.

title: Momoy and the Firefly Dance
summary: A tiny fairy of the Venezuelan forests leads lost children through the trees with a trail of fireflies, guiding them home only when they promise never to return alone.

title: Mooin, the Bear's Child
summary: A young Mi'kmaq boy wandered into the forest and became lost. A great she-bear found him and, instead of harming him, adopted him as her own cub. The boy grew up among the bear people, learning their ways and understanding the language of animals. He became strong and brave, but he always remembered that he was human. When he was grown, the bear people told him it was time to return to his own kind. Before he left, the bears taught him the songs and ceremonies they used to honor the Great Spirit, and gave him permission to hunt them for food — but only if he always showed respect and gratitude. The boy returned to the Mi'kmaq people as a great hunter and medicine man, teaching them the ceremony for honoring the spirits of the animals they killed. This is the origin of the Mi'kmaq hunting ceremonies and the Bear Clan tradition.

title: Moremi Ajasoro and the Liberation of Ife (Yoruba)
summary: Moremi Ajasoro was a legendary queen of Ile-Ife who sacrificed her own happiness to save her people from repeated raids by the neighboring Ugbo people. The Ife warriors were unable to defend against the Ugbo, who were disguised as forest spirits. Moremi allowed herself to be captured and taken to Ugbo as a slave. There, she learned the secrets of their battle tactics and eventually escaped back to Ife. She revealed to the Ife warriors that the Ugbo were not spirits but men who could be defeated. The Ife won their freedom. However, as a result of her sacrifice, Moremi's only son, Oluorogbo, was taken by the gods as a blood price. The Yoruba honor Moremi to this day with the annual Edi Festival, celebrating her courage and maternal sacrifice for the survival of the Yoruba people.

title: Morgan le Fay
summary: Morgan le Fay was Arthur's half-sister and one of the most powerful enchantresses in all of British legend.

title: Morgan's Exile to Avalon
summary: After the fall of Camelot, Morgan le Fay departs Britain for the mystical isle of Avalon, carrying with her the last fragments of Arthur's broken crown.

title: Moso's Footprint
summary: The giant Moso was one of the first humans created by Tagaloa on the island of Savai'i. His enormous footprint can still be seen pressed deep into solid lava rock at the village of Salelologa. According to legend, Moso stood so tall that he could step from one island to another. His footprint was left when he stood on Savai'i and pushed the island of Upolu away to create the Apolima Strait between them. Moso also owned a legendary war club that could kill hundreds with a single swing. The footprint remains a sacred site, and the story explains the geographic separation between the two main Samoan islands while affirming the power of the original human inhabitants.

title: Mothman: The Prophet of Death
summary: A winged man with red eyes appeared before the Silver Bridge collapse in 1966—prophecy or coincidence?

title: Mount Cudi and Noah's Ark (Kurdish Tradition)
summary: According to Kurdish creation myths, Noah's Ark landed on Mount Cudi (Cudi Dagh) in southeastern Turkey, not Mount Ararat as in the biblical tradition. The Kurdish tradition holds that after the flood, Melik Kurdim, a member of Noah's tribe, established rule over Mount Cudi and built the first post-diluvian civilization. He created the Kurdish language, considered the first non-Semitic language. The city of Judi was the first town built after the Flood, followed by the castles of Sinjar and Silvan. This tradition is recorded by the 17th-century Ottoman traveler Evliya Çelebi. Mount Cudi has been a pilgrimage site for millennia, with Assyrian rock carvings 2,700 years old providing archaeological evidence of ancient pilgrimage.

title: Mountain God Nyenchen Thanglha
summary: The Tibetan legend of Nyenchen Thanglha, one of the most powerful mountain gods in Tibetan mythology. He is the spirit of the Nyenchen Thanglha mountain range in central Tibet, revered as a protector deity who commands armies of elemental spirits. In pre-Buddhist Bon tradition, he was a wrathful, dangerous spirit who demanded blood sacrifices. When Padmasambhava brought Buddhism to Tibet in the 8th century, he famously subdued Nyenchen Thanglha and bound him by oath to protect the Buddhist teachings. Today he appears in Buddhist iconography as a white-skinned warrior riding a white horse, holding a banner and jewel. He is considered the chief of all 'nyen' mountain spirits and is called upon for protection, success in endeavors, and favorable weather.

title: Mr. Bear Catches Old Mr. Bull-Frog
summary: Brer Bear, hungry and irritable, decides he will catch the enormous bullfrog that keeps him awake at night with its croaking. He finds the frog at the pond's edge and makes a grab, but the frog leaps into the water. Brer Bear decides to drink the entire pond dry. He drinks until his belly is swollen, but the pond level barely sinks. Then the bullfrog surfaces and teases him, telling him that he will never succeed. Brer Bear, in a rage, plunges his head underwater to catch the frog by force, but only gets his head stuck in the mud. Brer Rabbit and Brer Fox pass by and laugh at the sight of Brer Bear's enormous rump sticking up from the pond. They pull him out, but Brer Bear is so embarrassed that he retreats into the deep woods and never bothers the bullfrog again. The bullfrog is still there, croaking triumphantly. The tale illustrates that brute force and rage are futile against nature's defenses, and that the bully often ends up humiliated by those he sought to dominate.

title: Mr. Fox and the Deceitful Frogs
summary: Brer Fox, having not eaten for days, spots a large bullfrog at the edge of the pond and makes a grab for him. The frog dives deep, and Brer Fox, desperate, decides to drink the pond dry. He drinks until his belly swells enormously, but the pond level barely drops. Meanwhile, the frogs mock him from the safety of the water. The bullfrog surfaces and offers Brer Fox advice: tie a stone to his neck to sink himself, then he can catch all the frogs underwater. Brer Fox, not realizing he is being mocked, considers this seriously. Other animals pass by and laugh at the foolish fox attempting to drink an entire pond. Brer Fox eventually gives up, exhausted and humiliated, while the frogs continue their chorus of croaking laughter. The tale reinforces the cleverness of small creatures against larger predators.

title: Mukasa: The God of Lake Victoria
summary: Mukasa is the powerful god of Lake Victoria (Nalubaale) and the most important of the Lubaale (national deities) in Buganda tradition. According to legend, Mukasa was a human prince who was transformed into a lake deity because of his extraordinary wisdom and compassion. He lives in a magnificent palace beneath the waters of Lake Victoria, surrounded by his spirit attendants. Mukasa governs the lake's bounty — the fish, the calm waters, and the storms. Before setting out on the lake, fishermen make offerings of banana beer, coffee berries, and goat meat at his shrines along the shores. Mukasa also serves as an oracle who reveals the future through his priests (mandwa). The most famous shrine to Mukasa is on the Ssese Islands, where priestesses maintain a sacred fire that must never be extinguished. Mukasa is a merciful god who rarely punishes, preferring to guide humanity toward wisdom and prosperity through blessings rather than fear.

title: Mulan
summary: The ballad of Mulan was first sung in the northern dynasties of China, during a time when the Toba people ruled the north and the Rouran tribes pressed against the borders like a relentless tide.

title: Muldjewangk the Murray River Monster
summary: Muldjewangk is a malevolent water spirit from the Aboriginal Australian mythology of the Murray River region in South Australia. This powerful and dangerous creature dwells in the deep waters of the Murray River, particularly around Lake Alexandrina and the river's lower reaches. Muldjewangk is described as a large, dark creature that can capsize boats and drag people and animals under the water to drown them. The legend serves as a cautionary tale, especially for children, warning them about the dangers of swimming alone in deep or unknown waters along the Murray. The Muldjewangk story is one of many Australian Aboriginal water spirit legends that encode practical safety knowledge within mythological narratives, teaching respect for the powerful and unpredictable forces of nature embodied in the continent's river systems.

title: Munda Creation — The Egg That Became the World
summary: The Munda people of Jharkhand believe that before creation there was nothing but water. The supreme god Singbonga floated above this water and set a cosmic egg afloat on its surface. From this egg hatched the first beings: Horo, the tortoise, and Karakom, the crab. The tortoise dove into the waters and brought earth to the surface on his back, creating the first land. But the earth was too soft. Singbonga then created the great spider which spun a web across the landscape, hardening the earth. The first humans were born from the union of the sun and the earth. The Munda also revere bongas (spirits) who inhabit natural features like rivers, mountains, and forests. The Munda creation story emphasizes cooperative effort among animals and spirits rather than top-down divine command, reflecting the tribe's communitarian values.

title: Murdered Children: The Returning Spirits
summary: A dark Sámi legend from Emilie Demant Hatt's By the Fire collection about murdered babies who come back to haunt their parents. This reflects the Sámi belief that improperly buried souls become restless spirits (eahpáraš). They can cause illness, misfortune, or wail in the wilderness. The only remedy is to perform proper burial rites, even after death.

title: Muscogee Creation: Emergence from the Lower World (Creek)
summary: In Muscogee Creek belief, the cosmos is divided into three worlds: the Upper World (home of Hesaketvmesē, the Maker of Breath, along with the Sun, Moon, and Thunder), the Middle World (where humans live), and the Lower World (inhabited by the Tie Snake and the Horned Serpent). Human beings first emerged from beneath the earth in the West and journeyed eastward. The Creator, Hesaketvmesē, also called Epohfvnkv ('the One Above'), spoke to and guided the Muscogee on their journey. The Middle World exists as the balance between the order of the Upper World and the chaos of the Lower World. This tripartite cosmology emphasized balance and harmony, with humans playing a crucial role in maintaining equilibrium between the opposing forces.

title: Mvelincanti and the First Cattle
summary: The sky deity Mvelincanti sends the first cattle down to earth on a spider's silk thread, entrusting them to a humble woman who understands their sacred worth.

title: My Chau and Trong Thuy: The Tragedy of Co Loa Citadel
summary: One of Vietnam's most tragic love legends tells the story of Princess My Chau and Prince Trong Thuy against the backdrop of the fall of the Au Lac kingdom. King An Duong Vuong built the spiral-shaped Co Loa Citadel with the help of the Golden Turtle God (Kim Qui), who gave him a magic crossbow that could fire hundreds of arrows at once. The king's beloved daughter My Chau married Trong Thuy, the son of the Chinese invader Trieu Da. Trong Thuy discovered the secret of the magic crossbow — that its power came from a turtle claw trigger. He secretly replaced the claw with a fake, then told his father to attack. During the invasion, the magic crossbow failed, and King An Duong Vuong was forced to flee. The Golden Turtle God rose from the waters and told the king that his daughter was the traitor — she had revealed the secret to her husband. The king killed My Chau before following the turtle god into the sea. Trong Thuy, arriving to find his wife dead, threw himself into the well where he had hidden the crossbow claw. According to legend, My Chau's blood turned into precious pearls that could only be cleaned with water from Trong Thuy's well. The story serves as a cautionary tale about love, loyalty, and the dangers of foreign influence.

title: Myrkr
summary: The enchanted mist of Norse lore that causes travelers to become hopelessly lost.

title: Myrmidons: The Ant Soldiers
summary: On the sun-drenched shores of Aegina, where the Aegean Sea laps against white cliffs and the air smells of wild thyme and salt, there once ruled a king named Aeacus.

title: Mô-sîn-á, the Grass Spirit
summary: A mischievous grass spirit from Taiwanese Hokkien folklore who tangles the feet of travelers and leads them astray.

title: Na'pi Creates the Buffalo
summary: After Na'pi (Old Man) created the world and the first people, he saw that they were hungry. He went to a cave deep in the mountains where the buffalo were kept. Na'pi opened the cave and the buffalo poured out across the plains, providing food, clothing, and shelter for the people. He taught the Blackfoot how to conduct buffalo hunts with respect, using every part of the animal and giving thanks to the buffalo spirit. Na'pi emphasized that the buffalo were a gift from Apistotoke and must never be wasted, or they would disappear.

title: Nafanua: The Warrior Goddess
summary: Nafanua, daughter of Saveasi'uleo (god of Pulotu) and Tilafaiga, was born a female but hidden in the forest by her mother out of shame. She emerged as a fierce warrior when Samoa was oppressed by tyrannical rulers. Disguising her chest so enemies would not know she was a woman, Nafanua led rebellions that freed the people of Savai'i from bondage. She was relentless and merciful only in victory, bringing peace after winning the wars between the eastern and western districts. Nafanua established the matai (chiefly) system and is revered as Samoa's greatest war goddess. After her earthly exploits, she returned to Pulotu, the spirit underworld, and her legacy endures in Samoan ceremonial protocol.

title: Nag-drang and the River of Names
summary: A monster called Nag-drang haunts a river that carries the names of the dead, and a woman who has lost her son must trade her own name to retrieve his before it washes into forgetting.

title: Naga: The Serpent Kings
summary: Semi-divine serpents who guard treasures, live in underground palaces, and bless those who honor them.

title: Nakk, the Water Spirit of Estonia
summary: A shape-shifting water spirit who haunted Estonia's rivers and lakes, luring the unwary with beauty and song before dragging them beneath the surface.
themes: the hidden world beneath the surface

title: Nalusa Chito: The Soul Eater (Choctaw)
summary: Nalusa Chito, also known as Impa Shilup ('Soul Eater'), is a great black shadow being of Choctaw legend. If individuals allow evil thoughts, depression, or negativity to enter their minds, Nalusa Chito will creep inside them and devour their souls. Many Choctaw people will not speak its name aloud, for fear of summoning the spirit. The being represents the internal battle against despair and moral weakness. The legend teaches the importance of maintaining a strong, positive spirit and guarding one's thoughts against darkness. Nalusa Chito cannot harm those who keep their hearts and minds pure. Traditional healers perform rituals to protect vulnerable individuals from this soul-eating presence.

title: Nalusa Falaya: The Shadow Being (Choctaw)
summary: Nalusa Falaya, meaning 'Long Black Being,' is a terrifying shadow creature from Choctaw mythology. It resembles a man but with a shriveled face, very small eyes, long pointed ears, and an elongated nose. Nalusa Falaya is known to frighten hunters and can transfer its power to do harm. It prefers to approach people by sliding on its stomach like a snake. The creature has many children who, when quite young, possess the peculiar ability to remove their internal organs at night, becoming small, luminous bodies seen along the borders of marshes. Nalusa Falaya represents the danger of allowing negative thoughts to take hold and serves as a warning to maintain courage and a pure heart.

title: Nanabozho and the Creation of the World (Ojibwe)
summary: The Ojibwe creation story tells how Nanabozho, the son of Epingishmook (the West Wind) and a human mother, was born with great spiritual powers. After his mother died, he was raised by his grandmother Nokomis. When the underwater panthers and horned serpents killed his beloved wolf-brother, Nanabozho pursued them and in his rage caused a great flood that covered the earth. The waters rose until even the tallest mountains were submerged. Nanabozho and Nokomis floated on a log with the surviving animals. One by one, the animals tried to dive for earth — the loon, the otter, the beaver — until the muskrat finally succeeded, surfacing nearly dead with a pawful of mud. From this, Nanabozho created the new world on the back of the Great Turtle. He then filled it with plants, animals, and the first people.

title: Nanabozho and the Great Serpent
summary: The Great Horned Serpent Mishiginebig, ruler of the underwater world, had been devouring the people who lived near the Great Lakes. Nanabozho, the culture hero, vowed to destroy the monster. He transformed into a tree stump on the shore and waited. When the serpent surfaced, its antlered head rising like an island from the water, Nanabozho struck with his magical club. A terrible battle ensued, churning the waters of the lake into a furious storm. Nanabozho finally killed the serpent, but the dying monster's body caused a great flood that nearly destroyed the world. This flood led to the recreation of the earth from mud brought up by the muskrat. The story teaches the danger of disrupting the balance between the upper and lower worlds.

title: Nanabozho and the Theft of Fire
summary: In the beginning, fire belonged only to the spirits and the people shivered in the cold. Nanabozho, the culture hero, decided to steal fire for humanity. He traveled to the lodge of the Old Man who guarded the only flame, guarded by a fierce serpent. Nanabozho transformed himself into a rabbit to sneak past the serpent. He grabbed a burning brand and fled, with the Old Man and the serpent in pursuit. As he ran, the fire scorched the trees around him, which is why the birch tree still bears black marks on its white bark to this day. Nanabozho passed the fire to the animals who relayed it to the people. Ever since, the people have had fire for warmth and cooking, and the birch tree's scars are a reminder of Nanabozho's gift.

title: Nanapush and the Sacred Pipe
summary: After Kishelamakank created the world, the human tribes fell into conflict over a magical bear tooth, leading to wars and divisions between families. The Creator saw that the people had lost their way and sent the spirit Nanapush to restore harmony. Nanapush gathered the warring peoples together at a council fire. He introduced the sacred pipe ceremony, teaching them to smoke tobacco as a sign of peace. He declared that no pipe could be lit in anger, and that to smoke together was to call the Creator as a witness to one's peaceful intentions. The people accepted Nanapush's teachings and laid down their weapons. From that day forward, the Lenape used the sacred pipe to seal agreements, welcome strangers, and pray directly to Kishelamakank, a practice that continues to this day.

title: Nandi
summary: In every temple dedicated to Lord Shiva across the vast expanse of India, from the snowy peaks of the Himalayas to the sun-baked shores of Kanyakumari, there sits a stone figure of a great white bull.

title: Nang Kwak: The Cat-Calling Goddess of Prosperity
summary: Nang Kwak is a benevolent female deity in Thai folklore who is believed to bring good fortune, prosperity, and customers to businesses. She is depicted as a beautiful woman in traditional Thai dress, seated with her right hand raised in a beckoning gesture (the 'cat-calling' wave). According to legend, Nang Kwak was a virtuous woman who was granted supernatural powers by the Buddha to attract wealth and abundance to those who respected her. Her origins are linked to the Tai folk religion and the pre-Buddhist spirit traditions of Siam, though her image has been widely incorporated into Thai Buddhist practice. Nearly every shop, restaurant, and business in Thailand displays a statue of Nang Kwak near the entrance or cash register. The legend teaches that prosperity comes not from greed but from kindness, hard work, and generosity. Nang Kwak's imagery draws from both indigenous spirit beliefs and the Thai Ramakien character Suvannamaccha.

title: Napi and the Rolling Skull
summary: Na'pi was walking across the prairie when he kicked a buffalo skull and told it to get out of his way. The skull began to roll after him, chasing him across the plains. Na'pi ran to a tree and climbed it, but the skull called to the tree, asking it to bend down. The tree bent, and the skull rolled up to Na'pi's hiding place. Na'pi was trapped and the skull would have killed him, but he tricked it by saying he saw more buffalo over the hill. When the skull turned to look, Na'pi leaped down and escaped.

title: Narcissus
summary: In the frozen lands of the far north, where the aurora borealis paints the sky in ribbons of green and purple, the Inuit people tell stories of the Qallupilluq.

title: Natchez Creation: The People of the Sun (Natchez)
summary: The Natchez creation tradition centers on the Great Sun, the divine ruler who descended from the sun itself. According to legend, the first Great Sun was born of a woman who was impregnated by a ray of sunlight. This established the Sun lineage, which was matrilineal — the Great Sun was always the son of the Female Sun, and her daughter would be the mother of the next Great Sun. The Natchez believed they were the Children of the Sun, and their paramount chief was considered a living deity. The Natchez also have a flood myth in which the earth was covered by water, and a dog's sacrifice helped save the people. The sun, as the source of life and the symbol of divine authority, was central to all Natchez religion and governance.

title: Ndundiro and the Mountain of Gold
summary: The giant Ndundiro guards a hidden mountain of gold deep in the Rwandan wilderness, and a clever shepherd girl must use wit rather than force to pass him and save her starving village.

title: Neang Kakey: The Unfaithful Wife of Khmer Literature
summary: A beautiful but unfaithful wife meets a tragic end in this classic Khmer cautionary tale.

title: Ngabia Bate, the Marsh Monster
summary: A monstrous creature said to inhabit the marshlands of southern Chad, the Ngabia Bate is a serpentine beast that drags livestock and people into the water.

title: Ngai on Mount Kenya
summary: Ngai, also known as Mwene Nyaga (the Possessor of Brightness), made his home upon the snow-capped peak of Kirinyaga, Mount Kenya. He is the creator and giver of all things, the union of masculine and feminine principles, the divider of the universe who has no mother, no father, and no companion. From his mountain throne, Ngai watches over the Kikuyu people and all creation. When the Kikuyu need his guidance, they climb to sacred high places or gather beneath the mugumo (fig) tree, raise their hands toward Kirinyaga, and offer sacrifice. Ngai reveals himself through the sun, the moon, the rain, the rainbow, and the powerful lightning and thunder that shake the mountain's slopes. The mountain itself is considered sacred, a direct link between the divine and the earthly realms.

title: Ngake and Whataitai: The Taniwha of Wellington Harbour
summary: The great taniwha Ngake and Whataitai lived in Lake Rotoroa (now Wellington Harbour) when it was still an enclosed lake. Ngake heard tales of the vast ocean beyond the hills and grew restless. He threw his body against the land at the southern end, eventually breaking through at what is now the harbor entrance, creating Te Whanganui-a-Tara. Whataitai tried to follow but became trapped in shallow waters as the lake drained. He transformed into a hill, Mt. Victoria, where his spirit still watches over the harbor. The story explains the geological formation of Wellington Harbour and the Miramar Peninsula.

title: Niels and the Giants
summary: A story about a small boy named Niels who uses his ingenuity and quick thinking to outsmart towering giants and save his village from their threats.

title: Nihancan and the Dwarf's Arrow
summary: Nihancan the trickster was wandering when he encountered a small dwarf armed with a bow and arrow. Nihancan laughed at the dwarf, mocking his small size and tiny weapon. The dwarf challenged Nihancan to shoot the arrow at a target. Nihancan agreed, but when he tried to pull the bow, he found it impossibly heavy. The dwarf took back his bow and shot an arrow that flew with incredible power, splitting a boulder in half. Nihancan, humbled, realized that size does not determine power. The dwarf taught Nihancan to respect all beings, regardless of their appearance.

title: Nihancan the Spider Trickster
summary: Nihancan is the Arapaho trickster figure, a spider-like being similar to Iktomi of the Lakota and Wihio of the Cheyenne. He is both clever and foolish, often causing trouble through his greed and selfishness. In one tale, Nihancan tricked a bear family and killed the children, only to be outwitted himself. Another story tells of Nihancan encountering a dwarf with a powerful arrow; the dwarf taught Nihancan a lesson about humility and respect. Despite his flaws, Nihancan's stories serve as important moral lessons for the Arapaho people, teaching the consequences of antisocial behavior.

title: Nimba, the Guinean Protector
summary: A protective spirit of the Baga people of Guinea, the Nimba is a sacred guardian of fertility and motherhood, represented by a ritual mask.

title: Ninki Nanka: The Dragon of Rivers
summary: In the hushed whispers of the Mandinka people, passed down through countless generations beside the winding Gambia River, there lives a terror that no man dares speak of aloud after dark.

title: Nis Puk
summary: A legendary nisse (household spirit) who is mischievous but helpful. He interacts with humans in a trickster-like manner, often protecting the home while playing pranks on those who do not treat him with respect.

title: Nisse
summary: The general tradition of the household nisse, a small creature with a red cap who protects the farm and its animals. They are helpful if treated properly, particularly with a bowl of porridge and butter at Christmas, but cause chaos if offended.

title: Njáls Saga - The Burning of Bergþórshvoll
summary: A protracted blood feud culminates in the attack on the home of the wise Njáll. Despite Njáll's prophetic warnings and attempts to mediate, his enemies set fire to the building. Njáll, his wife Bergþóra, and their sons choose to perish in the flames rather than surrender, creating one of the most tragic and iconic scenes in the sagas.

title: Noion the Keeper of Hearths
summary: A household spirit called Noion watches over a family that has forgotten the old offerings, and when the youngest child falls ill, the grandmother must remember the ancient formula of barley, butter, and breath to restore the compact.

title: Nonoma the Spirit of Thunder
summary: Nonoma is the Cheyenne spirit of thunder, a powerful being who controls storms and brings rain to the plains. When Nonoma flaps his wings, thunder rolls across the sky. He is both feared and respected, as his storms can bring life-giving rain or destructive hail. The Cheyenne perform ceremonies to honor Nonoma and ask for his blessing on their crops and buffalo hunts. Thunder is associated with the renewal of life in spring, and the first thunder of the season signals the time for planting and the Sun Dance ceremony.

title: Norna-Gestr's Journey
summary: Norna-Gestr is a legendary traveler who possesses the gift of prophecy. His tales describe journeys to the edges of the known world and encounters with supernatural beings. He uses his foresight to navigate the dangers of the north, acting as a bridge between the human world and the realm of fate.

title: Not a Pin to Choose Between Them
summary: A humorous story about two brothers who are so identical in appearance and temperament that no one can tell them apart. This symmetry leads to a series of comical misunderstandings, eventually forcing them to find their own unique identities.

title: Nuckelavee
summary: If the Kelpie is a danger to individual travelers, the Nuckelavee is a terror to entire communities.

title: Nuckelavee: The Horse Demon
summary: A demon horse of the sea—its breath kills crops, its touch brings disease, and it appears during summer storms.

title: Num and Nga: The Duel of Creation
summary: The central Nenets dualistic creation myth about the sky god Num and his evil counterpart Nga. According to the legend, Num created the world out of chaos, shaping the land and sky, populating the earth with reindeer and people who lived in happiness. But Nga, the deity of destruction and death, constantly tried to undo Num's work, introducing disease, misfortune, and mortality into the human world. Their eternal struggle explains the coexistence of good and evil in the Nenets universe. Shamans play a crucial role in this cosmic battle, acting as intermediaries who can invoke Num's power to counter Nga's harmful influence through rituals, sacrifices, and journeys to the spirit world.

title: Nyabingi and the Last Rain
summary: Nyabingi, the ancient rain deity of the highlands, withdraws her blessing from the land after the people abandon their sacred rituals, and only a blind shepherd's faith restores the cycle of rain.

title: Nyamgondho Wuod Ombare
summary: Nyamgondho was a poor fisherman who lived on the shores of Lake Victoria. He owned nothing — no cattle, no goats, not even proper clothes. One morning, starving and desperate, he cast his net into the lake and pulled out a hideously ugly woman. Terrified, he tried to throw her back, but the woman spoke. She promised to make him wealthy beyond his dreams if he would take her as his wife and never reveal where she came from. Nyamgondho agreed. The lady of the lake worked tirelessly, and soon Nyamgondho became the richest man in the region, with vast herds of cattle and many wives. But wealth made him arrogant. One night, drunk and angry at being turned away from his wives' houses, he shouted at his first wife: 'Even you, ugly creature I found in the lake, refuse me?' Enraged, she revealed her true nature and walked back into the lake, all his cattle following her into the water until Nyamgondho was left with nothing.

title: Nyaminyami and the Breaking of the Dam
summary: When engineers came to dam the Zambezi, the Tonga people warned that Nyaminyami, the river god, would not tolerate the severing of his body, and the floods that followed proved them right.

title: Nyikang and the Bridge of Spirits
summary: The legendary Shilluk hero-king Nyikang built a bridge between the world of the living and the world of the spirits, ensuring that the ancestors would never abandon their descendants in times of need.

title: Nykur (The Nix of Sørvágsvatn)
summary: Nykur is a shapeshifting water spirit that inhabits lakes, most famously Sørvágsvatn on Vágar Island. It appears most often as a beautiful white horse that lures people onto its back, then gallops into the lake to drown them. A popular tale tells of two brothers playing at the lakeshore. The older brother climbed onto the horse, but the younger called his brother by name—'Nikkolas'—which sounded like 'Nix.' Hearing his own name, the water horse lost power and retreated into the lake, saving both boys. Nykur can also appear in other forms. An illuminated sculpture by Póla Skarðenni was installed at Sørvágsvatn in 2017 to commemorate the legend.

title: Nykur and the Brothers (Lake Vatnsdalsvatn Variant)
summary: A variant of the Nykur legend told around Lake Vatnsdalsvatn. Two children were playing by the lakeshore when they saw a beautiful white horse grazing nearby. The older brother, being tall enough, climbed onto the horse's back. Immediately the horse began galloping toward the deep water. The younger brother, who only wanted his sibling to come back and play, called out his brother's name. Because the Nykur loses its power when its name or the rider's name is spoken, the horse stopped and retreated, and the brother was saved. The tale serves as a warning to children about the dangers of lakes and the importance of knowing how to counter supernatural threats. Speaking a water spirit's name breaks its spell in Faroese folklore.

title: Nyurgun Bootur the Swift
summary: The most well-known Olonkho epic of the Yakut (Sakha) people, consisting of over 36,000 verses. It tells the story of the hero Nyurgun Bootur, a warrior of the Aiyy (good) tribe who protects the Middle World (human realm) from the evil Abaasy spirits of the Lower World. The epic explores the balance between three cosmic worlds — Upper (gods), Middle (humans), and Lower (devils) — and features elaborate descriptions of the hero's battles, his celestial origins, and his role as protector of the Uraankhai Sakha tribe. Recorded by Platon Oyunsky in the 1920s-1930s, it is considered a defining text of Yakut national identity and was recognized by UNESCO as a Masterpiece of Oral and Intangible Heritage.

title: Nzambi Mpungu and the Creation of the World
summary: In the beginning, there was only Nzambi Mpungu, the supreme creator, and the dark, formless waters. Nzambi Mpungu spoke the world into existence, separating the waters above from the waters below to create the sky and the earth. He created the sun, moon, and stars, then the plants, animals, and finally the first man and woman. Nzambi Mpungu gave humanity the laws of life and taught them how to live in harmony with nature. However, humans soon became disobedient, and Nzambi Mpungu grew weary of their constant quarrels. He withdrew from the world, leaving it to run on its own. But he left behind the Simbi spirits to guard the waters, the forests, and the mountains, and the Nzambi (earth goddess) to teach humanity arts, laws, and games. Though distant, Nzambi Mpungu still animates the natural forces of the world — the thunder, the rain, and the growth of crops.

title: Nzazi: The Thunder Spirit of the Kongo
summary: Nzazi is the powerful spirit of thunder and lightning in Kongo mythology, a fearsome being who lives in the sky and hurls bolts of fire at those who break the sacred laws. According to tradition, Nzazi was once a man who climbed too high in his ambitions and was transformed into a sky spirit as punishment. Now he patrols the heavens during storms, his flashing eyes creating lightning and his voice creating thunder. When a tree is struck by lightning, the Kongo say Nzazi has visited judgment upon someone hiding beneath it. But Nzazi is also a purifier — lightning strikes burn away impurities and clear the way for new growth. Those struck by lightning but left alive are considered chosen by Nzazi and often become nganga (spiritual healers). Lightning-struck wood is collected and carved into powerful protective talismans. Nzazi reminds the Kongo that the divine forces of nature demand both respect and awe.

title: Obatala and the Creation of Humanity (Yoruba)
summary: Obatala, the king of white cloth and the creator of human bodies, was given the task of molding the first humans from clay by Olodumare. However, Obatala grew thirsty during his work and drank palm wine, becoming intoxicated. In his drunken state, he molded some bodies imperfectly, creating people with physical disabilities. When Olodumare saw this, he forbade Obatala from ever drinking palm wine again and decreed that those with disabilities would be sacred and under Obatala's special protection. Obatala is thus the patron of those with physical differences, and his devotees wear white and are forbidden from drinking alcohol. He represents purity, justice, and the sanctity of all human life, regardless of physical form. His temple in Ile-Ife remains one of the most sacred sites in Yorubaland.

title: Ochi-Bala and Kan-Altyn
summary: Ochi-Bala and Kan-Altyn are two of the most important Altai heroic tales, recorded from the legendary kaichy (epic singer) Aleksei Kalkin in the 20th century. Ochi-Bala tells of a warrior woman of extraordinary skill who defends her people with a bow made of birch and arrows tipped with the teeth of defeated demons. Kan-Altyn ('Blood-Gold') recounts a hero who must retrieve a magical golden sword from the underworld to save his people from an ice demon that freezes the land. The hero travels through the underworld on a winged horse, receives aid from the spirit of his ancestor, and battles Erlik's ice minions. Both epics emphasize the reciprocal relationship between the Altai people and their landscape — the hero's power comes not from individual strength but from harmony with the spirits of mountains, rivers, and ancestors.

title: Odin and the Runes
summary: The Banshee is Ireland's most famous supernatural figure. Centers on Odin,  from Norway mythology. Known for astral projection and aquatic speed and energy manipulation..

title: Oduduwa and the Founding of the Yoruba Kingdoms (Yoruba)
summary: Oduduwa was the legendary progenitor of the Yoruba people and the first ruler of Ile-Ife. According to tradition, Oduduwa descended from heaven on a chain with a rooster, some soil, and a palm nut, completing the creation Obatala had begun. He became the first king and his sixteen sons became the founders of the sixteen principal Yoruba kingdoms, including Oyo, Benin, Ila, Ketu, and others. Each son carried a sacred staff as a symbol of authority. The story of Oduduwa establishes the divine right of Yoruba kings (Obas) and their connection to the spiritual realm. To this day, every crowned Oba in Yorubaland traces their lineage back to Oduduwa, and the Ooni of Ife is considered his direct descendant and the spiritual head of all Yoruba people.

title: Ogun Releases the Gods (Yoruba)
summary: After the creation of the world, the Orishas found themselves trapped between heaven and earth, unable to descend to the newly formed land. Ogun, the god of iron and war, used his machete to clear a path through the dense forest, creating the first road and allowing the other gods to reach the earth. He also taught humanity how to use tools and weapons, forging the first iron implements. Ogun's gift of metallurgy transformed human civilization, enabling agriculture, hunting, and warfare. To this day, Ogun is honored as the patron of blacksmiths, warriors, hunters, and all who work with metal, and his shrines are marked by iron tools and chains.

title: Okwa Naholo: White Water People (Choctaw)
summary: Okwa Naholo (or Oka Nahullo), meaning 'White people of the water,' are supernatural beings from Choctaw mythology who dwell in deep pools, rivers, and springs. They have light-colored skin like the underside of trout, which makes them almost invisible in the water. These powerful water spirits sometimes capture human beings, converting them into beings like themselves. Children were warned not to swim alone in deep water for fear of the Okwa Naholo dragging them under. They represent the dangerous yet beautiful aspects of the water realm, and their stories serve both to teach respect for the dangers of deep water and to explain mysterious disappearances near rivers and lakes.

title: Ol' Hige the Vampiric Witch
summary: Ol' Hige is a witch from Jamaican folklore who sheds her skin at night and flies through the air in the form of an owl or a ball of fire. She harms people — especially babies — by sucking their breath while they sleep. Her habit of shedding her skin makes her vulnerable: if someone discovers her empty skin and fills it with salt and pepper, she will be unable to put it back on, burning terribly, and can be killed at dawn. Babies are traditionally protected from Ol' Hige by placing an open Bible in their cribs or using special charms. The figure is of West African origin and is known in Trinidad as the Soucouyant.

title: Old Age, Cold, Poverty, and Hunger
summary: After the Hero Twins killed the major monsters, four lesser monsters remained: Old Age (Są́), Cold (Dǫǫh), Poverty (Téʼéʼį́), and Hunger (Báhí). When the twins confronted these beings, they pleaded for their lives. Old Age argued that without him, the world would become overcrowded and people would not appreciate youth. Cold said he was necessary to remind people of their mortality. Poverty claimed his existence motivated people to work and share. Hunger argued that without him, people would not appreciate food. The Hero Twins, acknowledging the necessity of balance in the world, allowed these four to remain in reduced form as part of the natural order of human existence, explaining why humans continue to experience aging, cold, poverty, and hunger.

title: Old Hopgiant
summary: A poor peasant shares his meager food with a strange old giant who rewards him with a magic mill that grinds anything — but the greedy neighbor learns that kindness cannot be stolen. Old Hopgiant is a genuine folk-tale figure who aids the poor against oppression.

title: Old Man Coyote Creates the World
summary: In the beginning, Old Man Coyote (Isáahkawuattee) was alone upon a great ocean. He saw two male ducks floating on the water and asked them what lay beneath. One duck dove deep and returned with a root in its beak; a second more dangerous dive brought up mud. Using this mud, Old Man Coyote built an island that grew into all the lands of Earth. He used the root to create plants and trees. Noticing the world was too flat, Old Man Coyote shaped mountains, rivers, and valleys. Then he molded man from clay, and created woman so that humans would be happy and multiply. He created female ducks so the ducks could be happy too.

title: Old Mr. Rabbit, He's a Good Fisherman
summary: Brer Rabbit, tired and hungry, finds his way to a creek where he sees Brer Fox and Brer Wolf fishing. Rather than asking for food, Brer Rabbit pretends to be a great fisherman himself. He cuts a willow branch, ties a string to it, and sits downstream, pretending to fish while actually eating the berries he finds nearby. When Brer Fox and Brer Wolf catch nothing and see Brer Rabbit with a full belly, they demand to know his secret. Brer Rabbit tells them the best fishing is done with a snare around one's tail—convincing them to tie their tails together and cast out. When a large fish tugs, they both pull, only to catch nothing while their tails are painfully tangled. Brer Rabbit wanders off, well-fed and amused at their gullibility.

title: Old Nick and the Girl
summary: A poor girl mad for dancing makes a deal with Old Nick (the Devil) for leather dancing shoes. After a year, she tricks him into a race around Lake Fryken by using her identical twin sister at both ends of the lake, wearing out Old Nick's shoes while proving her bark shoes superior.

title: Old Nick and the Pedlar
summary: A struggling pedlar makes a bargain with Old Nick: he will sell all he buys, but if his bags ever become empty he belongs to the Devil. Business booms until a buyer (Old Nick in disguise) purchases the entire lot. The pedlar escapes by claiming Katie Grey is in one of the bags, and Old Nick—terrified of her—flees.

title: Old Woman's Water and the Buffalo Cap
summary: An old woman who lived by a sacred spring found that her water had healing powers. She shared it with a young warrior who was wounded, and he was miraculously healed. The woman then revealed herself as a manifestation of the earth's power. She gave the warrior a buffalo cap made from the scalp of a sacred buffalo, which became the Ésevone (Sacred Buffalo Hat). The cap could summon buffalo herds and protect the people from harm. She taught the warrior the rituals needed to care for the cap and warned that if it was ever neglected, the buffalo would disappear and hardship would follow.

title: Ole Higue, the Guyanese Vampire
summary: A vampire-like spirit of Guyanese folklore, the Ole Higue is an old woman who sheds her skin at night and flies as a ball of light to drink blood.

title: Ole Lukøje
summary: The sandman who visits children at night, telling them beautiful stories through their eyelids to ensure they have sweet dreams, while those who are unkind receive empty stories.

title: Olifat the Trickster God
summary: Olifat is a trickster god in Micronesian mythology, particularly among the islands of Chuuk. He was the grandson of the great god Anulap, born to the god Lugeleng and the mortal woman Tarisso, daughter of the octopus goddess Hit. When Lugeleng's wife tried to prevent the union, Hit danced so lewdly that the wife fainted from arousal and had to be carried back to the sky, allowing Olifat's conception. Olifat is a mischievous and cunning figure who often disrupts the established order with his pranks. He is known for stealing food from the gods, playing tricks on humans, and introducing chaos into the world. Despite his troublesome nature, Olifat's adventures sometimes benefit humanity, as his chaotic actions occasionally lead to useful discoveries and innovations.

title: Olobit (Ukteni): The Great Serpent (Natchez)
summary: Olobit (also called Olobis or Intsiyacdoo'cgu, 'sharp-breasted snake') is a monstrous serpent from Natchez folklore. Similar to the Cherokee Uktena, Olobit is a giant serpent with supernatural powers and a deadly gaze. It also has a sharp, breast-like protrusion on its chest that can impale victims. Olobit dwells in deep water or remote forests and is extremely dangerous to encounter. The serpent is associated with the underworld and the chaotic forces that the Natchez believed existed beneath the ordered world of humans. Shamans performed rituals to protect against Olobit's influence. The Olobit legend reflects the widespread Southeastern belief in horned or crested water serpents that guard the boundary between the human world and the spirit realm.

title: Onditichiae: The Thunder Beings
summary: The Onditichiae are the Thunder beings of the Wyandot and related Tobacco Indians. They are a race of giant sky beings who control the storms. According to tradition, they were created to serve as the eternal enemies of all water monsters. Whenever a great serpent or underwater panther becomes too dangerous, the Onditichiae descend from the sky and hunt it down with lightning. Their leader Hinnon assigns each Thunder being a specific territory to protect. The noise of battle between Thunders and serpents is what people hear as summer thunderstorms. The Wyandot believe that if the Onditichiae ever stopped their vigilance, the water monsters would overrun the earth. Offerings of tobacco smoke are made to honor and strengthen the Onditichiae in their ceaseless war against chaos.

title: One Who Walks All Over the Sky (Tsimshian)
summary: This Tsimshian myth explains the origin of the sun, moon, and night sky. After Weeget (Giant/Raven) brought light from heaven, there was still the question of who would carry the sun across the sky each day and what the patterns of stars meant. The One Who Walks All Over the Sky is a supernatural being assigned to carry the sun on his daily journey from east to west. He walks across the dome of the sky, and his path determines the seasons. When he walks high, it is summer; when low, winter. The stars are his footprints or the campfires of other sky beings. This story is part of the larger Tsimshian astronomical tradition that interprets the night sky as a map of supernatural activities. The movements of celestial bodies are guided by the same social and spiritual principles that govern Tsimshian life on earth — chiefs, potlatches, journeys, and encounters with supernatural beings all have their counterparts in the sky world.

title: One's Own Children Are Always Prettiest
summary: A satirical look at parental bias through the eyes of several families who insist their children are the most beautiful in the world. A neutral judge is brought in to settle the dispute, leading to a lesson about the nature of love and perception.

title: Oochigeas and the Invisible Boy (The Mi'kmaq Cinderella)
summary: A great chief had a son who was invisible. Only a woman who spoke the truth could see him. Many vain young women tried and failed, always lying that they could see the Invisible Boy. In a nearby village lived Oochigeas, the youngest daughter, whose face and hands were scarred from tending fires because her cruel elder sisters forced her to do all the hard work. Her ragged clothes were made of bark. She decided to try her luck and walked to the chief's lodge in tatters. The Invisible Boy's sister asked her the question: Can you see my brother? Oochigeas answered truthfully that she could not. Then the sister gave her fine clothes and combed her hair. Oochigeas approached again, and this time she saw the Invisible Boy — a handsome young man sitting at the edge of the sky. They married, and her kindness and truthfulness were rewarded, while her cruel sisters were punished.

title: Origin of Iron
summary: Wainamoinen and the smith Ilmarinen seek to uncover the origin of iron, a material essential for tools and weapons. They discover that iron is a divine gift forged in the heavens. This story establishes Ilmarinen as the preeminent master smith, capable of working with the most challenging materials in existence.

title: Origin of Poison (Choctaw)
summary: Long ago, a poison vine grew in a pool where Choctaw people bathed. Everything that touched the vine would die. The vine loved the Choctaw people and did not want to hurt them, but it could not warn them when its poison would infect the water. It decided to rid itself of the poison and called the chiefs of the snakes, bees, and wasps, who had all been trampled by humans. The chiefs agreed to share the vine's poison among themselves as a defense. The bees took a small amount and promised they would die after stinging, showing they were not human enemies. The wasps took their portion and promised to buzz a warning before attacking. The snakes took the rest and promised to rattle before striking. From then on, only fools ignored these warnings.

title: Origin of the Chinook People (Chinook)
summary: When Old Man South Wind was traveling north, he met an Old Woman who was a giant. Hungry and tired, he asked for food. She gave him a net and told him to catch fish.
