South Wind caught a little whale and was about to cut it crossways when the old giantress warned him to slit it down the back instead. He ignored her and cut crossways. The whale transformed into a huge bird so big that when it flew into the air it hid the sun and the noise of its wings shook the earth — it was Thunderbird. Thunderbird flew north and landed on Saddleback Mountain near the Columbia River, where it laid a nest full of eggs. The old giantress followed and found the nest. She broke an egg, found it not good, and threw it down the mountainside. Before it reached the valley, it became an Indian. She broke more eggs and each one became an Indian. This is how the Chinook people were created. The story also explains why Indians never cut the first salmon crossways — they always slit it down the back, following the lesson of South Wind's mistake.

title: Origin of the Pleiades (The Dancing Children)
summary: Long ago, seven young Iroquois children loved to dance in the woods. Every evening they would gather in a clearing, singing and dancing even as others told them to stop. They refused to go to sleep or do their chores, so absorbed were they in their joyous dancing. The Creator, watching from the sky, decided to preserve their joy forever. He caused the ground beneath them to rise up, lifting them higher and higher into the sky. Their families called for them to come back, but they continued dancing as they ascended. The children became the constellation of the Pleiades, the seven stars that dance across the winter sky. In the Onondaga version, the sixth star is dimmer because one child looked back and began to fall before the others caught her.

title: Origin of the Seminole Clans (Seminole)
summary: According to Seminole tradition, the clans were established at the time of creation. The Seminole have several matrilineal clans, including the Panther, Bear, Deer, Bird, Wind, and Otter clans. The legend tells that Breathmaker created the animals and asked them to protect the human people. Each animal agreed, and in return, the people would carry the animal's name as a clan. Clan membership determines marriage rules — a person must marry outside their clan — and establishes social obligations and relationships. The clans also have specific roles in ceremonies, including the Green Corn Dance. Clan identity is passed through the mother's line, and children belong to their mother's clan. The clan system remains a fundamental organizing principle of Seminole society today.

title: Origin of the Serpent
summary: A myth explaining the creation of the first serpent. The story describes how a divine accident led to the emergence of the snake, introducing the concepts of danger, poison, and cunning into the natural world and human experience.

title: Origin of the Wind
summary: Na'pi discovered two bags containing summer and winter. Determined to make the seasons equal, he tried to steal them but failed. He sent a prairie chicken who successfully grabbed the summer bag. The guardians chased the bird, slicing at the grass and cutting the bag open. Strong wind burst forth. Later, Napi burned himself and climbed a mountain to summon cooling wind through medicine-making. The wind blew so fiercely he was nearly thrown off the mountain. He survived by grabbing a birch tree, his fingers leaving marks that gave the birch its distinctive patterned bark visible today.

title: Ormur (The Feared Farmer of Skála)
summary: Ormur ('Worm') was a notoriously savage farmer in Skála, a giant of a man who stole sheep from neighboring farms. When farmer Pætur of Funningur caught him, Ormur forced him to swear silence under threat of his axe. Later, Pætur visited Ormur's home and was served sheep heads—but Ormur had forgotten to remove the ears, which bore Pætur's identifying marks. When Pætur confronted him, Ormur sharpened his axe. Pætur escaped, knocking a corn rack into the fireplace and burning Ormur's house down. In another incident, Ormur killed farmer Jógvan from Oyri and his son at Tippafossur after calling on the devil. He was eventually caught, his Achilles' tendon severed by a thrown knife, and executed. He is buried at Stevnuválur overlooking the lands where he committed his crimes.

title: Oro: God of War and the Arioi Society
summary: Oro, son of Ta'aroa, was the Tahitian god of war and peace. He descended to earth on a rainbow and took a mortal woman as his wife, establishing the Arioi—a secret society of warriors, artists, and priests who spread his cult throughout the Society Islands. The Arioi traveled between islands performing sacred dances, chants, and dramatic performances honoring Oro. They had elaborate initiation grades, and their ceremonies involved ritual drama, feasting, and human sacrifice. Oro became the most powerful deity of Tahiti, displacing Tane as the chief god. His cult reached its height at the marae of Taputapuatea on Raiatea, the spiritual center of Eastern Polynesia.

title: Orochi the Eight-Headed Serpent
summary: The storm god Susanoo-no-Mikoto had been banished from Takamagahara, the Plain of High Heaven, after a furious quarrel with his sister Amaterasu, the sun goddess.

title: Orpheus and Eurydice
summary: Orpheus was the greatest musician who ever lived—the son of Apollo, god of music.

title: Oshún, Goddess of the River
summary: Oshún (Ochún) is the orisha of fresh water, love, fertility, beauty, and sensuality in Cuban Santería, syncretized with the Virgen de la Caridad del Cobre, Cuba's patron saint. According to the Ifá literary corpus, Oshún was the only female irunmole (primordial spirit) sent to assist in creating the world. The male spirits initially ignored her, and the world failed. Only when her feminine wisdom and sweetness were incorporated did creation flourish. Her colors are gold, yellow, and coral, her number is 5, and her symbols include honey, mirrors, fans, and peacocks. She is represented as a beautiful mulata in Cuban tradition. Oshún is both a healer and a seductress, teaching that sweetness and joy are essential forces of creation alongside power and strength.

title: Osiris
summary: Osiris was the first king of Egypt — a god who walked among mortals and taught them civilization.

title: Osmotar the Bride-adviser
summary: Osmotar, a wise advisor, provides guidance to the new bride, offering essential wisdom on the expectations of marriage and how to navigate the social and emotional complexities of life in the land of heroes.

title: Ossobó, the Sacred Bird
summary: A sacred bird of São Tomé and Príncipe, the Ossobó is a forest spirit that protects travelers and punishes those who harm the rainforest.

title: Otso the Honey-eater
summary: The story of Otso, the Bear, the most sacred and feared animal in Finnish tradition. The heroes must use precise and respectful magical songs to appease the bear and safely obtain the precious honey from his lair.

title: Ounamir and the Sky Maiden
summary: The Ounamir myth is a cornerstone of Amazigh oral tradition from southern Morocco, particularly around Tata and Tagoujgalt. Hemmou Ounamir is a gifted student whose beauty attracts Tanirt, a celestial being (often rendered as an angel, fairy, or djinn princess). She secretly marks his hand with henna. After being exposed at Quranic school, Ounamir captures Tanirt with his teacher's help. She agrees to marry him only if he builds an unbreachable home, but his mother discovers the hidden key and violates the forbidden space, causing Tanirt to flee back to the heavens. Ounamir wanders for years in despair, then feeds an eagle with seven portions of meat—the last replaced by his own flesh—and rides it to the seventh sky to rejoin her. He must obey one condition: never lift a certain stone. On the Feast of Sacrifice, he lifts the stone, glimpses his grieving mother on earth, and leaps down. Drops of his blood restore his mother's sight. The myth explains local landmarks and is often compared to the Orpheus myth.

title: Pabuji Ki Phad — The Epic of the Rajasthani Deity
summary: Pabuji is a legendary folk deity from Rajasthan worshipped by the Rabari (shepherd) community. The epic poem Pabuji Ki Phad, performed with a painted scroll, tells of Pabuji's life as a 14th-century Rathore prince who became a folk hero. After marrying the princess of Umarkot, Pabuji's camel was stolen by demons. In tracking it down, he performed many heroic feats. His most famous story involves the demoness Jindrav Khinchi, who challenged his power. Pabuji defeated her and made her vow to protect Rabari cattle. Eventually, Pabuji was betrayed and killed in battle, but he was deified and his spirit continues to protect the Rabari people. The phad (scroll) paintings depicting his life are among Rajasthan's most important artistic traditions, and the epic is sung by hereditary priest-singers called bhopas during all-night performances.

title: Pahuk and the Sacred Sites
summary: Pahuk (hill island) is a sacred bluff on the south side of the Platte River near Cedar Bluffs, Nebraska. It is the foremost of the five nahurac lodges, where the animal spirit messengers of Tirawa gather. According to Pawnee legend, a young man once visited Pahuk seeking a vision. After four days of fasting, the animals spoke to him, teaching him the rituals of the Hako ceremony. The site is considered a place of great spiritual power where the boundary between the physical and spirit worlds is thin. The Pawnee made pilgrimages to Pahuk to offer prayers, seek healing, and receive guidance from the nahurac.

title: Pamola, the Snow Bird Spirit of Mount Katahdin
summary: Pamola (also called Bemola or Pomola) is a powerful snow bird spirit who dwells on the summit of Mount Katahdin, the highest mountain in Maine and the most sacred peak of the Penobscot and Abenaki people. Pamola has the body of a man and the head and wings of a giant eagle and makes the cold weather by beating his enormous wings. He fiercely guards the mountain against trespassers, sending blizzards to drive away those who dare approach his domain. According to legend, a Penobscot woman once married Pamola and lived with him on the mountain, but she eventually grew homesick and returned to her village, bringing with her the knowledge of how to survive the mountain's winter. The Pamola legend serves as a warning to respect the sacred power of Mount Katahdin and the spirits that dwell there.

title: Panchatantra — The Brahmin and the Mongoose
summary: A Brahmin couple adopts a pet mongoose, raising it as their own child alongside their newborn son. One day, the wife goes to fetch water, leaving the baby with the husband, who also leaves to beg for alms. While they are away, a deadly snake slithers toward the cradle. The loyal mongoose attacks and kills the snake, saving the baby's life. When the wife returns, she sees blood on the mongoose's mouth and, in a panic, kills it with a pot, only to discover the dead snake and realize the mongoose had protected her child. The story warns against acting without thinking.

title: Panchatantra — The Lion and the Bull
summary: The first book of Panchatantra, 'Mitra Bheda' (The Loss of Friends), tells of a lion king named Pingalaka who befriends a bull named Sanjivaka. A jealous jackal named Damanaka, who serves the lion, sows discord between them by feeding lies to both parties. He convinces the lion that the bull plans to usurp the throne, and tells the bull that the lion plans to kill him. The friendship collapses, leading to a fight in which the lion kills the bull. The story illustrates how manipulators destroy strong alliances by exploiting trust, and warns against listening to gossip and slander.

title: Panchatantra — The Monkey and the Crocodile
summary: A clever monkey living in a rose-apple tree by a river befriends a crocodile, sharing sweet fruits with him daily. The crocodile's wife grows jealous and demands to eat the monkey's heart. The crocodile tricks the monkey into climbing onto his back for a ride, then reveals his plan. Quick-witted, the monkey claims he left his heart back in the tree and convinces the crocodile to return. Once safe in the branches, the monkey exposes the deceit: 'You foolish creature! How could anyone keep their heart outside their body?' This classic Panchatantra fable teaches that presence of mind can overcome physical danger.

title: Papa Bois and the Last Hunter
summary: A hunter who takes too much from the forest encounters Papa Bois, the lord of the woods, and learns that the forest remembers every creature it has lost.

title: Papa Bois, the Guardian of the Trinidadian Forest
summary: Papa Bois (Father of the Woods) is the ancient protector spirit of Trinidad's forests, a figure of Afro-Trinidadian Creole folklore with roots in West African forest guardians. He appears as an impossibly old man with bark-like skin, a mossy beard tangled with vines, and deer-like legs ending in cloven hooves, with stag antlers crowning his head. He speaks the languages of all animals and blows a conch shell horn to warn poachers they are seen. For those who hunt with respect and take only what they need, Papa Bois guides them to game. For greedy hunters and wasteful destroyers, he makes forest paths vanish, moves landmarks, and traps them in an endless green labyrinth. He embodies the sacred balance between humans and nature.

title: Papa Bois: Keeper of the Green
summary: When a logging crew begins clearing the old forest above Grand Etang, each man falls mysteriously ill until they meet Papa Bois, the ancient guardian of the bush.

title: Papa Bois: The Old Man of the Forest
summary: A hairy old man with cloven hooves protects the forests and punishes hunters who kill for sport.

title: Papa Legba and the Gate of the Spirit World
summary: Papa Legba is the most important lwa (spirit) in Haitian Vodou, serving as the gatekeeper between the human and spirit worlds. No human can communicate with any other spirit without Papa Legba's permission. He stands at the spiritual crossroads, deciding whether a person is allowed to speak with other lwa. Believed to speak all human languages, Papa Legba is known as the great elocutioner. In Vodou ceremonies, he is always the first and last spirit invoked, as he opens and closes the gateway. His origins trace to the West African kingdom of Dahomey (modern Benin), where he was known as Legba, the trickster messenger god of the Fon and Yoruba peoples.

title: Pate Island Chronicles: The Founding of the Sultanate
summary: According to the Pate Chronicle, the island of Pate was first settled by refugees from the crumbling Persian port of Shiraz in the 13th century. Led by Sultan Suleiman, they found the island inhabited by African Bantu-speaking fishermen. Rather than conquering them, Suleiman married the local chief's daughter and created a blended Afro-Persian culture that became the Swahili civilization. The sultanate grew wealthy through trade in ivory, gold, and slaves, with dhow fleets sailing as far as India and China. Pate's golden age produced legendary scholars, poets, and architects who built the island's distinctive coral-stone mosques and houses. The chronicles also record a great flood sent by God when the people became too prideful — only the faithful were saved in a great dhow that carried them to the highest point of the island until the waters receded.

title: Paul Bunyan
summary: In the early days of America, when the continent was covered with vast, untamed forests stretching from the Atlantic to the Pacific, there lived a lumberjack so enormous, so strong, and so skilled that he became the greatest hero the North Woods have ever known.

title: Pele and Kamapua'a
summary: The volcano goddess Pele and Kamapua'a, the pig demigod, had a tumultuous relationship oscillating between love and war. Kamapua'a could transform between human and giant pig forms and commanded the rains and forests. When he pursued Pele, she refused him, and a great battle erupted across the Big Island. Pele sent rivers of lava at him while Kamapua'a countered with floods and rain, extinguishing her fires. Neither could defeat the other. In some versions, they eventually married and had a child. Their union represents the eternal balance between fire and water, volcanic destruction and forest regeneration—the fundamental forces that create and renew the Hawaiian landscape.

title: Pele and the Lava
summary: Across the vast, sapphire expanse of the Pacific, where the horizon dissolves into a haze of gold and blue, lies the archipelago of Hawaiʻi—a chain of emerald peaks born from the violent passion of a single deity.

title: Pele's Journey from Kahiki to Hawaii
summary: Pele, the volcano goddess, was born in Tahiti (Kahiki) to Haumea and Kane Milohai. Banished by her father because of her fierce temper, Pele sailed with her brothers in a great canoe across the Pacific. She dug fire pits at each island she visited, creating Diamond Head on Oahu and Haleakala on Maui. On Maui, her sister Namakaokahai (the sea goddess) attacked her with massive waves. Pele was torn apart, but her spirit fled to the Big Island where she dug the deep pit of Kilauea. There she established her permanent home at Halemaumau Crater, goddess of volcanoes whose fiery breath shapes the Hawaiian landscape.

title: Pele's Tears
summary: In the heart of the Pacific, where the earth breathes fire and the ocean churns against volcanic shores, the goddess Pele reigns as both creator and destroyer.

title: Pemba and Faro: The Bambara Twin Creation
summary: In Bambara (Bamana) mythology, the creator god Bemba (Maa Ngala) created the universe in three stages. In the first stage, Pemba, a grain that fell to earth and became an acacia tree, created Mousso Koroni Koundye from rotten wood and his saliva. She became the first woman, but her creations were disordered and chaotic. In the second stage, Faro, an androgynous being associated with water, light, and speech, brought order and equilibrium. Faro was sacrificed to atone for Pemba's sins, cut into sixty pieces that became trees, then restored to life as a human. Faro descended to earth in an ark carrying twin ancestors, animals, and plants, and the flood that followed purified the world of Pemba's impure seed. Faro created the Niger River and established the cycles of day, night, and seasons.

title: Pepo: The Sea Spirits of Zanzibar
summary: The Pepo are powerful sea spirits that inhabit the waters around Zanzibar and the Swahili coast. They are invisible beings who can influence human destiny — bringing good fortune, madness, or illness as they choose. According to tradition, the Pepo were the original inhabitants of the coast before humans arrived. When people began building towns and fishing the waters, the Pepo retreated to the deep ocean but never fully left. They can possess humans, causing trance states that require elaborate exorcism ceremonies (kipemba) involving specific drum rhythms, incense, and offerings. Each Pepo has a name, personality, and favorite color that must be honored during the ceremony. The most powerful Pepo are the spirits of ancient sultans and warriors who died at sea. To this day, fishermen leave offerings of rice and cloth on the shore before long voyages, ensuring the Pepo grant safe passage across their watery domain.

title: Peri, the Winged Spirit of Afghanistan
summary: Beautiful winged spirits who dwell between heaven and earth, the Peri are benevolent beings who guide lost souls and protect sacred springs.

title: Phoenix
summary: In the burning sands of Arabia, where the sun beats down like a hammer on an anvil and the heat shimmers in waves across the desert, there lives a bird unlike any other in creation.

title: Phra Lak Phra Ram: The Lao Ramayana
summary: Phra Lak Phra Ram is the national epic of the Lao people, a distinctive adaptation of the Indian Ramayana that thoroughly Lao-izes the story. Unlike the Indian version, the Lao epic explicitly frames the tale as a Jataka — a previous life story of the Buddha — making it entirely compatible with Theravada Buddhism. The story follows Prince Phra Ram and his devoted brother Phra Lak as they journey along the Mekong River, encountering local spirits, Nāga serpents, and Lao landscapes. Their beloved Sida (Sita) is abducted by the demon king Ravana, but the setting shifts to cities along the Mekong rather than Indian locations. The epic was transmitted from Angkor to the Lao kingdom of Lan Xang in the 14th century by King Fa Ngum, who brought Khmer dancers and scholars to his court. Recorded on palm-leaf manuscripts between the 15th and 19th centuries, Phra Lak Phra Ram features distinctly Lao episodes not found in other versions — including the rescue of Nang Chantha (a uniquely Lao addition) and the detailed descriptions of river journeys through Lao lands. The epic is traditionally performed in the Lao royal ballet and at festivals, with performances lasting many hours or even days.

title: Pichal Peri: The Backward-Footed Spirit of Pakistan
summary: A vengeful female spirit with backward-facing feet lures men to their doom in the Punjab countryside.

title: Plague Spirits, the Riders of Pestilence
summary: Dark spirits of European folklore that rode through the continent during the Black Death, spreading plague and despair wherever they appeared.

title: Poliahu and Pele: The Snow Goddess Rivalry
summary: Poliahu, the lovely snow goddess who drapes Mauna Kea in white, and Pele, the volcano goddess of Kilauea, were rivals for the affections of a handsome chief. Poliahu was renowned for her beauty and cool temperament, while Pele was passionate and jealous. During a gathering of goddesses, Pele challenged Poliahu and ridiculed her. In anger, Poliahu revealed her true divine nature, covering the mountain in blinding snow. The two goddesses have contested the Big Island ever since—Pele heating it from below with lava, Poliahu cooling it from above with snow. Their eternal struggle shapes Hawaii's landscape through volcanic eruptions and winter snows.

title: Pombero, the Night Whistler
summary: A mischievous forest spirit who whistles in the night, the Pombero is both feared and respected by rural Uruguayans for his tricks and his punishments.

title: Pontianak: The Vampire Ghost of Malaysia
summary: The vengeful spirit of a woman who died in childbirth hunts men and babies in the darkness.

title: Popa Medaw and the Mahagiri Nat
summary: The most important nat (spirit) legend in Burmese folklore tells the tragic story of the Mahagiri Nat and his sister Popa Medaw. The tale begins with a powerful blacksmith named Nga Tin De, who forged weapons of unparalleled quality in the village of Taungbyon. King Thinligyawng of Tagaung, fearing the blacksmith's growing power and popularity, summoned him to the capital under the guise of honoring him. He then seized the blacksmith and had him burned alive in a champaca tree. Upon hearing of her brother's cruel death, Nga Tin De's sister threw herself into the flames and died beside him. Their spirits were trapped in the tree, terrorizing the region. When King Anawrahta of Pagan later cut down the tree, he ordered the spirits carved into wooden statues and enshrined on Mount Popa — an extinct volcano. Nga Tin De became the Mahagiri Nat (Great Mountain Spirit), guardian of homes, while his sister became Popa Medaw (Mother of Popa), the queen mother of all nats, protector of women and children. Their shrine on Mount Popa remains the most important nat pilgrimage site in Myanmar.

title: Pope Sylvester and the Dragon
summary: Pope Sylvester I confronts a terrible dragon beneath the Lateran Palace, whose poisonous breath has killed thousands, and chains it through the power of faith alone.

title: Popobawa: The Bat-Wing Terror of Zanzibar
summary: A shape-shifting evil spirit with bat wings terrorizes the island of Zanzibar, attacking victims in their sleep.

title: Porgupõrgu, the Estonian Hell
summary: The Estonian concept of the underworld, a place beneath the earth where the dead journeyed and where ancient spirits guarded the boundary between worlds.

title: Potto-Podnie and Stállo
summary: From the Solsönernas Saga. Potto-Podnie ('the useful old man') of the Sirkas tribe was a skilled noaidi with a magic drum. Stállo, an evil wandering giant sent by Adtjis-ene, dwelt in a mountain across the marsh from Potto-Podnie's camp. When Stállo coveted Potto-Podnie's beautiful daughter Waimokatta, a battle ensued. Neither could defeat the other until Beijen-Neita (the Sun's daughter) gave Potto-Podnie divine guidance. Potto-Podnie beheaded Stállo and brought his head to a sieidi.

title: Preah Ko Preah Keo: The Sacred Ox and Sacred Gem
summary: Preah Ko Preah Keo is a famous Cambodian legend about two orphaned brothers from humble origins who discover extraordinary destinies. The elder brother, Preah Ko, was born under a sacred ox and grew to be strong and virtuous, while the younger, Preah Keo, was born under a shining gem and possessed magical powers. The brothers embarked on a series of adventures that tested their courage and moral character. They encountered giants, rescued princesses, and overcame enchantments through their complementary strengths — Preah Ko's physical fortitude and Preah Keo's magical insight. The legend is central to Cambodian storytelling traditions and is often performed in shadow puppet theater (sbek thom) and classical dance. The tale explores themes of brotherhood, the balance between physical strength and spiritual wisdom, and the triumph of virtue over corruption. Their story has been passed down through generations as a moral compass for Cambodian youth, emphasizing that family bonds are stronger than any magical power and that true nobility comes from character rather than birth.

title: Preah Thong and Neang Neak: The Founding of the Khmer Nation
summary: The foundational creation myth of the Khmer people tells the story of Preah Thong (Kaundinya), an Indian Brahmin prince, and Neang Neak (Queen Soma), a Naga serpent princess. According to the legend recorded by Chinese envoys Kang Tai and Zhu Ying in the 3rd century CE, Kaundinya received a divine instruction in a dream to take a magic bow from a temple and sail to a distant land. He arrived on the coast of what is now Cambodia, where he encountered the kingdom of the Naga ruled by the serpent king. The Naga king's daughter, Princess Soma (Neang Neak), confronted the stranger on the shore. Kaundinya shot a magic arrow from his enchanted bow, and the princess, struck by its power, agreed to marry him. Her father the Naga king, in a spectacular act, drank the ocean waters to reveal land for his daughter's new kingdom — the land of Kambuja (Cambodia). The couple's union founded the royal dynasty of Funan, the first Khmer state. This legend explains the significance of the naga in Khmer culture, the tradition of the Naga balustrade in Angkorian temples, and the bride-price ceremony in Khmer weddings where the groom passes a scarf to the bride.

title: Prince Siddhartha's Great Renunciation
summary: Siddhartha Gautama was born c. 563 BCE in Lumbini (present-day Nepal) to King Suddhodana and Queen Maya Devi. Legend recounts that Queen Maya dreamed of a white elephant entering her womb, and the newborn Siddhartha immediately took seven steps, declaring this his last birth. Protected from suffering by his father, Siddhartha lived in luxury. At 29, he made four fateful chariot rides outside the palace, encountering an old man, a sick person, a corpse, and a serene ascetic — the Four Sights that revealed life's suffering. That night, the Great Renunciation: he left his sleeping wife Yasodhara and newborn son Rahula, cut off his hair, and became a wandering ascetic. After six years of extreme practices, he abandoned both luxury and austerity for the Middle Way, meditating under the Bodhi tree in Bodh Gaya until attaining enlightenment as the Buddha at age 35.

title: Prince Vijaya and the Founding of Sri Lanka
summary: Prince Vijaya, grandson of a lion and son of King Sinhabahu, was banished from Sinhapura in India for his violent deeds. He and his 700 followers sailed to Lanka, landing at Tambapanni on the very day of the Buddha's parinibbana. There they encountered the Yakkhini queen Kuveni, who through magical threads and bravery was subdued by Vijaya. With Kuveni's help, Vijaya defeated the Yakkhas and established the Sinhala kingdom. He later abandoned Kuveni for a Pandyan princess, and the children of Vijaya and Kuveni became the ancestors of the Vedda people.

title: Prince Whitebear
summary: A prince is cursed to live as a white bear. He is eventually saved and restored to human form through the unwavering love and devotion of a princess.

title: Prince Wolf
summary: A story about a prince transformed into a wolf, exploring themes of identity, animal nature, and the path to redemption and human restoration.

title: Puss in Boots
summary: A clever cat in boots uses trickery and deceit to win his poor master wealth, a castle, and a princess. The cat's cunning elevates his master from poverty to royalty.

title: Pygmalion
summary: On the island of Cyprus, where the foam of the sea first gave birth to Aphrodite, there lived a young sculptor named Pygmalion.

title: Pygmalion and the Ivory Bride
summary: A sculptor of Cyprus carves his ideal woman from ivory and worships her so faithfully that the gods breathe life into his creation, teaching that devotion can move heaven itself.

title: Púca
summary: On the night of Samhain, when the veil between worlds is thinnest and the dead walk among the living, there are tricks to be wary of.

title: Pūķis, the Household Dragon of Latvia
summary: Pūķis, a dragon-like household spirit of Latvia, guards the home from above the hearth, demanding respect and offerings in exchange for prosperity and protection.

title: Qals (Mink) and the Transformations (Coast Salish)
summary: Qals (Mink) is a major trickster figure in Coast Salish mythology, particularly in the Fraser River region. In the longest and most important story told by George StsE'lis to Franz Boas, Qals shapes the world through his encounters with various flawed ancestors. Mink tricked a chief's daughter into sleeping with him, producing a human boy named T'qulä'tca, who became the ancestor of the Ts'uwä'l people. Qals encountered numerous beings who needed correction: he transformed a toothed-vagina woman named LEqyiles who bit off Mink's hand into stone on the Harrison River; he changed a one-legged man into stone at StsE'lis; and he transformed whole villages of people who opposed him into animals, rocks, and landmarks. The Qals cycle demonstrates the Coast Salish concept of transformation as a world-ordering force. Everything in the landscape has a story behind it — every rock, every mountain, every bend in the river — recording where Qals walked and changed the world.

title: Qamar al-Zaman and the Princess of the Jinn
summary: A tale from the Arabian Nights about Prince Qamar al-Zaman (Moon of the Age), son of King Shahriman, who refuses marriage and is imprisoned. The princess of the jinn, in a parallel story, also refuses marriage and is imprisoned by her father the jinn king. Through the machinations of a devious jinn and a fairy, they are magically brought together in sleep, each seeing the other in dreams. They fall in love sight unseen, leading to a quest across the realms of men and jinn to unite. The story exemplifies the supernatural romance genre of medieval Arabic literature.

title: Qamata and the Creation of the Xhosa World
summary: Qamata (also known as uThixo) is the supreme creator god of the Xhosa people who existed before all things. From a primordial void of darkness and silence, Qamata created the world using Uhlanga, a bed of sacred reeds that became the material for all life. He divided existence into three realms: the sky for himself, the earth for humans, and the underworld for ancestors. From the reeds he made the first humans and gave them life, then created cattle as sacred beings representing prosperity. Qamata later fought and defeated the chaos giant Iqungqungqu, bringing order to the cosmos. He stays distant but works through ancestors and natural signs, with thunder and the sun representing his power.

title: Qat and the Sky Maidens
summary: One day Qat discovered a group of sky maidens who had removed their wings to bathe. He quickly buried one pair of wings so that one maiden, Vinmara, had to remain behind. She became his wife and was called Ro-Lei. They lived happily until Qat's mother reproached her daughter-in-law and made her cry. Ro-Lei's tears washed away the earth covering her wings; snip she put them on and flew back to the sky. Qat shot an arrow with a rope tied into the roots of a great banyan tree in the sky and climbed after her. As he climbed back down with Ro-Lei, the root snapped and he plunged to his death while she flew safely away. In other versions, Qat does not die but sails away in a canoe, promising to return one day.

title: Qat the Creator and the Birth of Night
summary: In the Banks Islands of Vanuatu, the principal god Qat emerged from a stone that exploded as his mother. He had eleven brothers called Tagaro and a companion named Marawa the spider. Qat carved the first three pairs of humans from dracaena wood and brought them to life by playing drums, making them dance. When his brothers tired of constant daylight, Qat traveled to the Torres Islands to purchase Night from I Qong. He brought back Night, a rooster, and an obsidian stone. His brothers lay down and slept while the sky darkened. After a while Qat had the rooster crow to wake them and sliced the dark sky apart with the obsidian, creating the first Dawn. Marawa, envious of Qat's creations, made his own figures and buried them, thus introducing death.

title: Qozy Körpesh and Bayan Sulu
summary: The oldest Kazakh love dastan, dating back over 1,500 years to the era of the Türgesh Khaganate. Qozy and Bayan are promised to each other from birth, but Qozy's father dies before the marriage can take place. Bayan's ambitious father, Karabai, breaks the promise and betroths her to a wealthy rival. Qozy searches for his beloved across the vast steppe, overcoming obstacles imposed by Bayan's family. The lovers are reunited, but a tragic fate awaits them — Qozy is murdered by Kokman, a servant of Bayan's unwanted suitor. Bayan, in her grief, avenges Qozy's death and then takes her own life to join her beloved in death. Their shared grave is marked by a twelve-meter stone mausoleum standing in the Ayagoz district of Kazakhstan.

title: Queen Abla Pokou: The Mother of the Baoule People
summary: In the 18th century, a great crisis divided the Ashanti Kingdom in what is now Ghana.

title: Queen Arawelo: The Warrior Queen of Somalia
summary: Queen Arawelo (Carraweelo) was a legendary proto-Somali queen who established a matriarchal society in the Sanaag region around the 1st century CE. According to tradition, Arawelo was born to Haramaanyo and raised during a time of brutal clan warfare and devastating drought. After her husband and children died in the violence, she was cast out as a widow. In the myrrh forests of the northern mountains, she gathered other outcast women and formed a warrior sisterhood. Arawelo trained her army to restore peace, believing that women must take power to end the endless cycle of male violence. She instituted a system where women held political and economic control, and men were judged by their contributions to the community. Her reign was both feared and revered — some accounts describe her punitive justice against violent men, while others celebrate her as a wise ruler who brought peace to the land. Her story is told across the Horn of Africa as a symbol of female empowerment.

title: Queen Crane
summary: A poor shepherd boy named Proud is befriended by a crane who is actually an enchanted queen, and through a series of magical transformations, he wins her hand and a kingdom. This very popular Northern tale features a seemingly witless hero with an unusual transformation motive.

title: Queen Makeda and King Solomon
summary: In the 10th century BCE, Queen Makeda of Ethiopia (known as the Queen of Sheba) heard of King Solomon's unparalleled wisdom and journeyed to Jerusalem with a magnificent caravan laden with gold, spices, and precious stones. Solomon was captivated by her beauty and intelligence. Through clever trickery, he persuaded her to stay, and she conceived his child. Before returning to Ethiopia, Solomon gave her a ring as a sign of their covenant. Makeda gave birth to a son, Menelik I (Bayna-Lehkem), who would later travel to Jerusalem as a young man. Solomon recognized his son and anointed him king of Ethiopia. According to the Kebra Nagast, Menelik then brought the Ark of the Covenant to Ethiopia, where it remains to this day in Axum. This legendary lineage established the Solomonic dynasty that ruled Ethiopia until 1974.

title: Quetzalcoatl
summary: Quetzalcoatl, whose name means Feathered Serpent, was one of the most important deities in the Mesoamerican pantheon.

title: Quetzalcóatl — The Feathered Serpent
summary: Quetzalcóatl, the Feathered Serpent, is the most important syncretic deity in Mexican and Mexican-American spiritual folklore. In Aztec tradition, he was the god of wind, knowledge, learning, and the priesthood — credited with creating humanity by descending to Mictlan (the underworld) and mixing his blood with the bones of previous generations. He is also associated with the morning star (Venus) and is the inventor of books and the calendar. The feathered serpent iconography appears throughout Mesoamerica from Teotihuacan (200 BCE) to the Aztec Empire, and his worship was centered at Cholula's great pyramid. In Chicano spirituality, Quetzalcóatl has been reclaimed as a symbol of indigenous identity, cultural resistance, and the profound wisdom of pre-Columbian civilizations. The legend of Quetzalcóatl's prophesied return was later conflated with Hernán Cortés's arrival, a complex historical narrative that continues to shape Mexican-American understanding of conquest and cultural survival.

title: Ra and the Hidden Name
summary: Isis, the great enchantress, desired power equal to Ra himself. As Ra aged, saliva dripped from his mouth and fell upon the ground. Isis gathered the saliva, mixed it with earth, and shaped it into a venomous serpent which she placed on Ra's path. When Ra was bitten by the invisible serpent, he suffered agonizing pain. Isis approached him and offered to cure him—but only if he would reveal his secret, hidden name—the name that gave him power over all gods and creation. Ra first listed his known names: 'I am Khepera in the morning, Ra at noon, Atum in the evening. I am the maker of heaven and earth, the creator of the gods.' But Isis insisted: 'Your name is not among those you have told me.' Finally, in agony, Ra consented. He asked Isis to leave him so he could pass his name from his heart to hers, and the secret power was transferred. Isis then commanded the poison to leave Ra's body, and he was healed. The myth explains how Isis gained her great magical knowledge and power.

title: Ra and the Secret Name
summary: Ra, the sun god, was the most powerful being in the Egyptian pantheon.. He created the world from the primordial waters of Nun.

title: Ra and the Snake
summary: In the golden age of the world, when the gods walked among men and the boundaries between heaven and earth were thin, Ra the sun god ruled over all creation.

title: Ragnarök: The End and Rebirth
summary: The seeress sat in the shadows, her eyes white as milk, her voice rising from a place deeper than mortal memory.

title: Rainbow Crow (Mànàka'has)
summary: In the time before fire, the world was cold and dark. The animals suffered, unable to keep warm or cook their food. Kishelamakank, the Creator, took pity on them and placed a great fire at the top of a high mountain, but only the birds could reach it. The crow, who in those days had a beautiful rainbow-colored song and iridescent feathers, volunteered to fetch the fire. Crow flew to the summit and seized a burning coal in his beak. The flames scorched his colorful feathers, turning them black, and the smoke choked his beautiful voice into a harsh caw. Despite the pain, crow carried the fire down to the people. The Creator honored crow's sacrifice by declaring that his black feathers would forever shimmer with the rainbow's ghost, visible when the sun catches them at the right angle — a reminder of his noble deed.

title: Rakshasa: The Shape-Shifting Demon
summary: Ancient demons from Hindu mythology who can change form, drink blood, and cause chaos—until smarter beings outwit them.

title: Rana Niejta: Daughter of the Green Earth
summary: Rana Niejta is the Sámi spring goddess, daughter of Radien-attje and Raedieahkka. Her name means 'the green' or 'the fertile fields.' She makes the southern slopes of mountains green so hungry reindeer have food after winter. She is one of three divine sisters: Sala Niejta (Sun's daughter) ends winter's cold, Rana Niejta brings forth vegetation, and Saivo Niejta governs the underworld. Together they control the seasonal cycle.

title: Rangi and Papa: The Separation of Sky and Earth
summary: In the beginning, Ranginui (Sky Father) and Papatuanuku (Earth Mother) lay locked in a tight embrace, leaving their children trapped in darkness between them. The children grew weary of the cramped darkness and debated how to gain freedom. Tane Mahuta, god of forests, proposed separating their parents. While Tawhirimatea opposed, Tane lay on his back and pushed upward with his feet, forcing Rangi upward and thrusting Papa down. Thus light entered the world. Tawhirimatea, enraged, joined his father in the sky and sent storms against his siblings, beginning the eternal conflict between wind, forest, sea, and land.

title: Rannamaari: The Sea Demon That Demanded Sacrifice
summary: In pre-Islamic Maldives, a terrible sea demon called Rannamaari rose from the ocean each month to demand a sacrificed virgin. The girls were dressed in fine clothes and left alone in a Buddhist temple on the eastern seafront of Malé; by dawn, they were found violated and dead. This terror continued until a Maghrebi Muslim traveler, Abu'l-Barakat al-Barbari (or Yusuf al-Tabrezi from Tabriz, Iran), volunteered to take the girl's place. He spent the night reciting the Quran, and when the demon appeared, the holy verses caused it to flee into the sea, never to return. The king, identified as Dhovemi, converted to Islam and took the name Sultan Muhammad ibn Abdullah in 1153 CE, and the Maldives became a Muslim nation. Historians note parallels with Buddhist tantric rituals, and folklorist Xavier Romero-Frias traces the name Rannamaari to a South Indian goddess.

title: Rapunzel
summary: Once upon a time, a married couple lived next to an old witch's garden.. The wife became pregnant and craved the rapunzel plants growing there.

title: Ravana
summary: Ravana, whose name means "He of the Terrifying Roar," was the most powerful demon king ever to rule the three worlds.

title: Raven and the Beaver (Tlingit)
summary: Near a bay near Kôts!ê'L! there was a seawater pond where a beaver lived. Raven very much wanted to catch and kill this beaver, so he dug two trenches to drain the lake at low tide. After the water ran out and the beaver was visible at the bottom, Raven lowered a hook and pulled the beaver up. After killing the beaver, Raven also killed a big whale and got his people to tow it to the place where the beaver had lived. He commanded four large canoes full of people to tow the whale up the rapids through one of the canals he had made. After they labored for many days and grew tired, Raven told them to take it easy. Finally, even Raven grew tired and said, 'Turn into stone.' All did so, and to this day you can see a large island shaped like a whale with a string of four smaller islands extending from it. This Tlingit etiological myth explains a distinctive geological formation near Sitka.

title: Raven and the First Men
summary: Raven, the trickster-creator, finds the first humans hiding in a clamshell on the beach and coaxes them out into the world.

title: Raven and the First Woman
summary: In this creation myth, the trickster god Raven wanders the shores of the world and finds a beautiful woman made of clay or shell. With a touch of his magic, he brings her to life, creating the first human woman. This story establishes Raven as the architect of human life and the source of the spark of consciousness in the Arctic world.

title: Raven and the Fog Woman (Tlingit)
summary: Raven wanted to marry and went to the chief called Fog-Over-The-Salmon, who had a young daughter. The chief agreed but made Raven promise to treat her with respect. They married and lived contentedly through summer and fall, but winter brought famine. Raven's wife began making a basket, and despite Raven's testy comments, she completed it. The next morning she washed her hands in the basket and salmon appeared, the first salmon ever created. Every day she did this and their house was soon full of drying salmon. But Raven forgot his good fortune and quarreled with his wife daily. In a rage, he hit her with a piece of dried salmon. She fled toward the water, and when Raven tried to catch her, his hands passed through her body as if through mist. All the salmon followed her into the sea. She disappeared into the fog, for she was Fog Woman herself. Raven went to his father-in-law to beg for her return, but Chief Fog-Over-The-Salmon refused, saying Raven had broken his promise.

title: Raven and the Moon Woman (Haida)
summary: Raven became the son of Moon Woman and cried incessantly, saying 'Boo-hoo, moon!' His mother, exhausted by his noise, stopped up all the holes in the house and untied the strings of a box containing the moon, letting Raven play with it. When she left, Raven turned into a raven and flew about the house with the moon in his beak. He then cried for the smoke hole to be opened, and when his mother obliged, he flew through it with the moon under his wing. He perched on a house top and called like a raven. Raven flew to the Nass River where fishermen were taking olachen in total darkness. He bargained with them, offering light in exchange for their spruce needles. When they mocked him, he let them see a sliver of the moon, and they gave him many olachen. He then flew to a high mountain, broke the moon in half, threw one half into the sky for the night and the other for the day, and scattered fragments as stars.

title: Raven Annoys Octopus (Nuu-chah-nulth)
summary: One morning as the tide went out, the old people came to sit and watch the ocean. They saw a woman walking along the beach with her hair long and strung into eight braids — she was Octopus, carrying a digging stick to look for clams. She sat down on a rock and began to dig. Soon another person came along the beach, tall with glossy black hair — it was Raven. The old people predicted he would bother Octopus, and they knew it was not a good idea. Raven walked right down to the rock where Octopus sat and began bothering her. He teased and pestered her while she tried to dig for clams. The story serves as a humorous cautionary tale about respecting others' boundaries and not interfering with people who are working. Raven's persistent meddling backfires, teaching him (and the listener) that pestering others leads to unpleasant consequences. The Nuu-chah-nulth version emphasizes Raven's trickster nature and his tendency to interfere in others' affairs.

title: Raven Becomes Voracious (Tsimshian)
summary: This Tsimshian myth explains how Raven acquired his insatiable appetite and voracious nature. Before this story, Raven was not known for his hunger. Through a series of events involving trickery, greed, and supernatural encounters, Raven's appetite grew beyond all bounds. He began devouring everything in sight, from salmon to berries, from seal meat to olachen grease. His hunger became so legendary that it defined his character. The story serves as an etiological myth explaining why ravens and crows are scavengers who eat constantly and are always hungry. It also carries a moral lesson about the dangers of greed and insatiable desire. Raven's voraciousness is both a humorous trait — he is constantly scheming to get food — and a serious warning about what happens when consumption becomes uncontrolled. The story is part of the larger Tsimshian Raven cycle that portrays Txamsem as both a world-creating culture hero and a deeply flawed, comic figure.

title: Raven Brings Light (Nuxalk - Qwaxw)
summary: In the beginning, when the world was covered in darkness, the people were in constant sadness and prayed to the Creator Alhkw'ntam for light. Alhkw'ntam held the sun in a box in his longhouse in Nusmata (the land above) and let no one see it. The Four Carpenters who made the world were sitting around a fire when the eldest, Yulm, grabbed a piece of charcoal and shook it in his hands. When he opened his hands, it was a bird. The second Carpenter made its wings, the third made its eyes, and the youngest gave it life. They asked the bird to say its name and it flew into the sky crying 'Qwaxw, qwaxw, qwaxw!' — they named it Qwaxw, Raven. The people begged Raven to get the light. He flew to Nusmata and observed Alhkw'ntam's granddaughter Skimina. He transformed into eagle down, then a hemlock needle, but she blew him away. Finally he muddied her drinking water, and she drank him in. She became pregnant and Raven was born as her child. Raven cried for the box holding the light until Alhkw'ntam gave in. Raven broke the globe against the wall, and light leaked through the smoke vent to become the sun, stars, and moon. The people were no longer sad.

title: Raven Mocker (Kâ'lanû Ahkyeli'skï) (Cherokee)
summary: Kâ'lanû Ahkyeli'skï, the Raven Mocker, is a malevolent Cherokee spirit that preys on the dying. These witches are said to be ordinary-looking people during the day who transform at night into raven-like spirits. They gather around the home of a dying person and torment them, stealing their remaining years of life for themselves. The Raven Mocker flies with a sound like rushing wind and can only be seen by medicine men. After a person dies, the Raven Mockers eat the heart of the victim. The only defense against a Raven Mocker is a medicine man who knows the proper rituals to drive them away. Raven Mockers are visible only to medicine men, who can identify them even in their human form by their sleepless, bloodshot eyes and their habit of appearing exhausted from their nighttime flights.

title: Raven Pulls the Salmon (Tlingit)
summary: After Raven brought light to the world and created rivers and lakes, there were still no salmon in the coastal waters. The salmon, herrings, and ooligans were kept in a magical house in the middle of the Pacific Ocean, where they spawned without ever coming to shore. Only rich chiefs could paddle out to catch them, leaving the poor hungry. Raven heard of Xanaax.atwaayaa, a mythical being who possessed an octopus-tentacle staff with supernatural powers. Raven tricked the being into trading the staff by demonstrating a magical bow and arrow (actually a magpie) that seemed to kill a mountain goat from impossible distances. With the staff, Raven went to the entrance of the Alsek River and latched it to the salmon house. He struggled mightily, and his nephew Crow urged him to sing a song about Xanaax.atwaayaa. When Raven sang, he easily pulled all the salmon into the bays and rivers. The tracks of Raven's struggle can still be seen at the Alsek River entrance.

title: Raven Steals the Light (Tlingit - Yeil)
summary: In the Tlingit version of this foundational myth, Yeil (Raven) was born as the son of Kit-ka'ositiyi-qâ and was instructed and trained in every way to make a world. At that time there was no light in the world, but Raven knew that far up the Nass River was a large house where a chief kept light just for himself. Raven turned himself into a pine needle and dropped into the drinking cup of the chief's daughter. She swallowed it and gave birth to Raven as a human baby. The grandfather loved the child and eventually gave him the bundles containing the stars. Raven scattered them across the sky. He cried for the moon and pushed it through the smoke hole. Finally he cried for the box of daylight, turned into his true raven form, and flew out with the daylight under his wing. The Tlingit version emphasizes Raven's dual nature as creator and trickster, and explains not only the origin of light but also the creation of human beings from leaves after the great flood.

title: Raven Steals the Sun (Nuu-chah-nulth)
summary: In the Nuu-chah-nulth version of this foundational myth, there was a time before sunlight when light was kept securely in a box guarded by a great chief sometimes called the Old Fisherman. Raven wanted this light and attempted various methods to release it. He transformed himself into a floating leaf that ended up in the teacup of the great chief's daughter. She accidentally ate the leaf and in due time gave birth to Son of Raven, who was actually Raven reborn. The child was doted upon by the chief, his grandfather. Son of Raven begged to see the box of light, and after persistent pleading, the chief relented and opened the box, releasing the light. Son of Raven immediately transformed back into Raven, seized the light, and flew high into the sky. He placed the light in the sky, creating the sun that shines down on all. This myth establishes Raven as the Nuu-chah-nulth's primary culture hero and explains the origin of day and night.

title: Raven Steals the Sun, Moon, and Stars (Haida)
summary: In the time before light, Raven (Nang Kilslas) was tired of living in darkness. He discovered an old chief who kept all the light of the universe hidden in a nested set of five boxes. Raven transformed himself into a hemlock needle and dropped into the river where the chief's daughter came to drink. She swallowed the needle and became pregnant, giving birth to Raven-child. The old chief adored his grandchild. Raven cried incessantly until the chief allowed him to open the boxes one by one. First the stars escaped, then the moon, then the northern lights. Finally Raven grabbed the sun in his beak and flew through the smoke hole, releasing light into the world forever. This core Haida myth explains the origin of all celestial light and establishes Raven as both a trickster and culture hero who brought essential gifts to humanity despite his selfish motives.

title: Raven the Creator (Nivkh Tradition)
summary: The Nivkh creation myth centered on the Raven, a central figure shared with neighboring Chukchi and Koryak traditions. In Nivkh mythology, the Raven (known as Kurka or similar names) created the world by diving into the primordial sea and bringing up earth on his beak. He shaped the land of Sakhalin Island and the Amur River estuary, and then created human beings from clay mixed with his own feathers. The Raven is both creator and trickster who taught the Nivkh people how to fish, build canoes, and conduct the sacred bear ceremony. The myths also explain how the Raven brought the sun and moon into the sky by stealing them from a powerful spirit. Nivkh folklore was first systematically recorded by Bronisław Piłsudski and later by Vladimir Sangi.

title: Raven Turns Himself into a Woman (Tlingit)
summary: Having lost his wife Fog Woman, Raven decided to marry again so people would look after him. Rather than finding a good wife, he turned himself into a woman and married a man from the Killerwhale people. As a wife, Raven was lazy and deceitful — she stole from the Killerwhale people. Eventually she decided to kill her husband and all the Killerwhales in the village. After this destruction, the story continues with Raven visiting Fish Hawk, promising to be a good partner and share work and food. But Raven never did any work; he ate and ate while Fish Hawk provided everything. Whenever Fish Hawk grew angry, Raven flattered him, praising his wealth and generosity. Finally Fish Hawk refused to feed Raven any longer and left him to find his own food. This comic story showcases Raven's laziness, deceit, and clever manipulation, using flattery to exploit others, while also serving as a moral lesson about the consequences of trusting flatterers.

title: Restoration of the Sun and Moon
summary: Through a combination of trickery, persistence, and magical songs, Wainamoinen and his companions manage to deceive Louhi into releasing the sun and moon, returning light and life to the world.

title: Rich Peter the Pedlar
summary: Peter, a humble pedlar, discovers a way to acquire wealth through honest trade and a touch of serendipity. The story follows his ascent from poverty to riches and the lessons he learns about the true value of money and friendship.

title: Rinkusteinar (The Rocking Stones of Oyndarfjørður)
summary: Two large boulders rest at the shore near Oyndarfjørður, constantly rocking back and forth with the rhythm of the waves. Legend says that a local sorceress (witch) saw pirate ships approaching her village after they had already attacked Fuglafjørður, robbing and killing. She rushed to the shore and cast a spell, transforming the pirate ships into stone. The two rocking stones are the petrified vessels, eternally rocking in the waves but never able to reach the village. Though often called Viking ships in modern sources, the raiders were actually Irish pirates. The natural phenomenon of their motion continues to baffle visitors.

title: Risin og Kellingin (The Giant and the Witch)
summary: Two giant sea stacks off the northern coast of Eysturoy, near Eiði. Legend says that giants in Iceland grew envious of the Faroe Islands and sent a giant and his wife (a witch) to drag the islands back to Iceland. The giant stood in the sea while the witch climbed the mountain Eiðiskollur with a heavy rope to tie the islands together. They struggled all night but could not move the islands. At dawn, sunlight struck them and turned them both to stone. The 71m stack (Risin/the Giant) and 68m stack (Kellingin/the Witch) remain visible from Tjørnuvík on Streymoy, staring longingly west toward Iceland.

title: River Mumma and the Golden Table
summary: River Mumma is a female water spirit who guards the sources of Jamaica's rivers. She is sometimes seen sitting by the river, combing her long hair with a golden comb, leaving the comb on rocks to entice victims whom she then draws into the water. Associated with her is the Legend of the Golden Table: a table of pure gold lies at the bottom of certain rivers, rising briefly to the surface at midday. Whoever sees it becomes mesmerized and obsessed with obtaining it, but efforts to procure the table always end in disaster as the river claims their lives. The legend likely arose from the Spanish quest for gold in Jamaica. In slavery times, sacrifices were offered to River Mumma in drought.

title: Robin and Blue-Jay (Chinook)
summary: Blue Jay and Robin, two brothers, were hungry. Blue Jay called a large fish (the sleeper) to come ashore through trickery and speared it. When they returned home, Robin asked for the tail, breast, and head, making Blue Jay angry. He said that the Q!têê'nse (a supernatural monster) would eat the fish instead. Robin cried and left. Blue Jay softened and called his brother back, giving him all the choice parts. Later, Blue Jay dreamed that people were sending for him to cure a sick person. Blue Jay and Robin journeyed to cure a duck who was choking, receiving payment of a lake's worth of roots. Next they cured a wolf girl who was choking on an elk's kneecap, receiving two canoes full of meat and grease. But Blue Jay's arrogance and greed in demanding excessive payment led to consequences. The story demonstrates the Chinook trickster cycle's typical structure: Blue Jay is boastful and selfish but ultimately provides for his family through his supernatural curing abilities, while long-suffering Robin represents patience and humility.

title: Robin Hood
summary: In the days when King Richard the Lionheart was away fighting in the Crusades and his brother Prince John ruled England with greed and cruelty, a young man from Locksley in Nottinghamshire was forced into the greenwood.

title: Roro Jonggrang and the Legend of Prambanan Temple
summary: A Javanese legend explaining the origin of Prambanan Temple. Bandung Bondowoso, a powerful prince with supernatural abilities and an army of invisible genies, fell in love with Princess Roro Jonggrang. When she rejected his proposal, he attacked her father's kingdom and conquered it. Forced to consider marriage, Roro Jonggrang set an impossible condition: Bandung must build 1,000 temples in one night. Using his supernatural army, he nearly completed the task. Desperate, Roro Jonggrang ordered her maids to light fires and pound rice, tricking the spirits into thinking dawn had arrived. Enraged by the deception, Bandung cursed Roro Jonggrang, transforming her into the 1,000th statue — which remains at Prambanan to this day.

title: Rostam and Sohrab
summary: The most famous tragedy of the Persian Shahnameh. Rostam, Iran's greatest hero, travels to Samangan where he marries Princess Tahmineh. He returns to Iran, leaving her pregnant with Sohrab. Years later, Sohrab, now Turan's mightiest warrior, leads an army against Iran, hoping to find his father. Unaware of each other's identity, father and son meet in single combat. After a grueling battle, Rostam throws Sohrab and stabs him. Only then does Sohrab show the armband amulet given by Tahmineh. Rostam discovers he has killed his own son. Despite desperate pleas for medicine, Kay Kavus withholds it. Sohrab dies in his father's arms, and Tahmineh burns all her possessions in grief.

title: Rostam's Seven Trials (Haft Khan-e Rostam)
summary: To rescue King Kay Kavus, captured by the White Demon (Div-e Sepid) in Mazandaran, Rostam undertakes seven impossible labors: (1) Killing Rakhsh's attacker, a ferocious lion; (2) Surviving a waterless desert with his horse Rakhsh; (3) Slaying a monstrous dragon; (4) Killing a powerful witch through divine discernment; (5) Capturing the warrior Olad to serve as guide; (6) Defeating the giant Arzhang Div; and (7) The ultimate trial — battling and killing the White Demon (Div-e Sepid) himself in the demon's cave, using the demon's own liver to restore the blinded king's sight. This epic is the Persian equivalent of Hercules' labors.

title: Rounce: The Forest Keeper
summary: A timber cutter who defies the old prohibition against felling trees in the deep forest encounters the Rounce, a nature spirit that punishes those who take more than they need and rewards those who leave offerings of respect.
themes: the cost of taking without giving

title: Rounces: The Night Riders
summary: A fisherman who mocks his grandmother's warnings about the Rounces discovers that the spirit-animals which ride the sleeping have their own terrible logic, and that the paralysis they bring is not cruelty but a test of the soul.

title: Ruwa and the Sacred Mountain Kilimanjaro
summary: Ruwa, the supreme god of the Chaga people, dwells upon the snow-capped peak of Kilimanjaro, the highest mountain in Africa. According to Chaga cosmology, Ruwa is associated with the sun and resides in the sky alongside his consort, the moon. From his celestial throne on Kibo peak, Ruwa watches over the Chaga people and all creation. The mountain is not merely a mountain but the physical manifestation of Ruwa's presence on earth — its glaciers are his crown, its forests his garments, its rivers his blessings flowing down to nourish the people. Sacrifices to Ruwa are performed at high noon, when the sun is at its zenith, in sacred groves on the mountain's slopes. The spirits of Chaga chiefs (Mangi) who have passed away join Ruwa on the mountain, interceding for their descendants. The Chaga believe that the mountain's glaciers will never fully melt, for as long as they remain, Ruwa's protection endures. Kilimanjaro is thus the sacred center of Chaga spiritual life.

title: Ryangombe and the Fire of the Hills
summary: Ryangombe, the great hero of the Rwandan hills, descends into the caverns beneath Mount Muhabura to reclaim the stolen fire that a jealous spirit has hidden from the people.

title: Rávga: The Undead Sea Creature
summary: Rávga is an undead sea creature in Sámi folklore, the soul of a drowned person whose body was never found and properly buried. It appears as a long-haired, large-mouthed creature in human form. It harasses sailors and people on shore by calling out and imitating the speech of the living. It can be driven away by reading the funeral service to it.

title: Sadko and the Sea King
summary: A gusli player from Novgorod is pulled beneath Lake Ilmen by the Sea King, who demands a song in exchange for safe return and a fortune in sea-stone.

title: Saint George and the Dragon
summary: A Roman soldier of unwavering faith slays a terrifying dragon to save a princess and leads a city toward a new spiritual awakening.

title: Samodiva: The Wood Nymphs of the Bulgarian Mountains
summary: Eternal beautiful forest spirits lure men to dance until they die in the mountains of Bulgaria.

title: Samudra Manthan — The Churning of the Ocean
summary: After sage Durvasa cursed Indra and the gods to lose all their strength, the demons (asuras) took over the universe. Lord Vishnu advised the gods to churn the Ocean of Milk with the demons to obtain amrita, the nectar of immortality. They used Mount Mandara as the churning rod and the serpent Vasuki as the rope. However, the mountain began to sink, so Vishnu took his Kurma (tortoise) avatar to support it on his back. As they churned, fourteen treasures emerged, including the deadly poison halahala, which Shiva drank to save creation, turning his throat blue (earning him the name Nilakantha). Finally, Dhanvantari emerged with the pot of nectar. Vishnu then took the form of Mohini to distract the demons and ensure only the gods received immortality.

title: Sang Kancil and the Crocodile
summary: The most famous fable from the Malay Archipelago features Sang Kancil, the clever mouse-deer, outsmarting a river full of hungry crocodiles. Wanting to cross the river to reach the fruit trees on the other side, Kancil tells the crocodiles that the king has ordered a headcount of all crocodiles, instructing them to line up across the river. The crocodiles oblige, and Kancil hops across their backs to the far shore. When the crocodiles realize they have been tricked, Kancil is already enjoying the fruits of victory. This tale, deeply embedded in Malay culture, celebrates wit over physical strength and appears in the coat of arms of Malacca with two mouse-deer supporting the shield.

title: Sang-ngag of the Hidden Temple
summary: A dragon named Sang-ngag guards a temple that appears only between breaths, and a young monk who has failed three times learns that the temple's real treasure is not what is inside it, but what it costs to reach it.

title: Sangkuriang and Mount Tangkuban Perahu
summary: A Sundanese legend from West Java telling of Sangkuriang, a young man who unknowingly falls in love with his mother Dayang Sumbi, a goddess-blessed princess who remains eternally young. When Dayang Sumbi recognizes her son by a scar, she sets impossible tasks to prevent their marriage: he must dam the Citarum River and build a lake with a boat before sunrise. With supernatural help, Sangkuriang nearly succeeds, but Dayang Sumbi tricks him by lighting the eastern sky with red cloth to mimic dawn. Enraged at the deception, Sangkuriang kicks the unfinished boat, which forms Mount Tangkuban Perahu (Upturned Boat), a volcanic mountain near Bandung.

title: Santa Muerte — Holy Death
summary: Santa Muerte (Holy Death or Saint Death) is a female folk saint and personification of death venerated primarily in Mexico and the US Southwest, with an estimated 12 million followers worldwide. She is depicted as a female skeleton wearing a long robe and carrying a scythe and a globe. Her origins blend pre-Columbian death deities such as the Aztec goddess Mictecacihuatl (Lady of the Dead) with the Spanish Grim Reaper (la Parca). Devotees pray to Santa Muerte for protection, healing, financial prosperity, love, and safe passage to the afterlife. Her statues are dressed in different colored robes depending on the petition: white for purification, red for love, gold for money, black for protection against enemies, green for justice. Though condemned by the Catholic Church, Santa Muerte's following exploded in the early 2000s and spread rapidly to the United States through Mexican immigration. Her shrines are found in botanicas and homes throughout Los Angeles, Houston, Chicago, New York, and other cities with large Mexican-American populations. She has particular appeal among those living on society's margins — taxi drivers, sex workers, police, soldiers, and prisoners — who face death's uncertainty daily.

title: Santhal Creation Myth — The World Born from Water
summary: The Santhal tribe, one of India's largest Adivasi communities, tells that in the beginning, the world was covered entirely with water. The supreme being Thakur Jiu (or Singbonga) sent the divine crow Marangbonga to find earth. The crow tried but found only water. Next, a tortoise and a crab attempted but failed. Finally, an earthworm brought up mud from the bottom of the primordial ocean. Thakur Jiu molded this mud into the first land. He then created the first human couple, Pilcu Haram and Pilcu Budhi, from clay. But they were imperfect, so he tried seven more times. The eighth attempt succeeded, but the couple was afraid of the cosmic darkness. Thakur Jiu then created the sun, moon, trees, and animals to accompany them. The bonga spirits, both benevolent and mischievous, inhabit all aspects of nature and must be honored through rituals led by the village shaman.

title: Saraswati
summary: In the deep waters of Scotland's lochs, where the surface is black as ink and the bottom has never been touched by human hands, there lives a creature more terrifying than any sea monster.

title: Sassi Punnun — Searching Across the Desert
summary: Sassi, a princess born to the king of Bhambore but abandoned at birth due to an astrological prophecy, was raised by a washerman. She grew into a woman of extraordinary beauty. Hearing of her, Punnun, a Baloch prince, traveled to Bhambore and fell in love with her at first sight. They married in secret, but Punnun's jealous brothers drugged him and carried him away across the desert while he slept. Waking to find her beloved gone, Sassi ran barefoot through the scorching Thar Desert, calling his name. Her delicate feet blistered and bled, but she pressed on until she collapsed and died of exhaustion. Punnun, upon waking and realizing what had happened, raced back toward her. Finding her body, he died of grief beside her. Their graves became a shrine for lovers in Sindh.

title: Savitri and Satyavan — Love That Conquered Death
summary: Princess Savitri chose to marry Satyavan despite the sage Narada's warning that he was destined to die within a year. On the fated day, Yama, the god of death, came to claim Satyavan's soul. As Yama carried the soul away, Savitri followed him through the wilderness. Impressed by her devotion, Yama granted her three boons — but not Satyavan's life. Savitri asked for her father-in-law's eyesight and kingdom to be restored, and then for a hundred sons for herself. When Yama granted the third boon, Savitri pointed out that she could not bear children without her husband. Bound by his word, Yama was forced to restore Satyavan to life. The story, from the Mahabharata, is a profound testament that love, wit, and determination can overcome even death.

title: Scheherazade
summary: The chronicles of the Sassanian kings tell of a monarch named Shahryar, who ruled an empire stretching from India to China.

title: Sea Maid, the Monacan Siren
summary: A beautiful siren of the French Riviera, the Sea Maid of Monaco lures sailors with her enchanting song beneath the waves.

title: Selkie
summary: On the rocky coasts of the Orkney and Shetland Islands, where the sea is never far and the storms come fierce in winter, there are tales of the Selkies—the seal folk, who can shed their skin and walk on land as humans.

title: Semetey: The Son of Manas
summary: After Manas's death, his treacherous younger brothers Abyke and Bobosh seized power and tried to kill Manas's son Semetey. Kanykey, Manas's widow, escaped with the infant Semetey to Bukhara, where her father ruled as khan. Semetey grew up unaware of his heritage until his mother revealed his identity. He returned to the Talas valley on the magical horse Taytoru to avenge his father's death. Semetey defeated his treacherous uncles in battle and beheaded the forty companions of his father who had betrayed Manas. He married the beautiful Ay-Chürök, a swan maiden, and continued his father's legacy of defending the Kyrgyz people. The second part of the Manas trilogy bears his name.

title: Seminole Creation: Breathmaker and the Earth (Seminole)
summary: The Seminole creation story begins with Breathmaker, the great Creator god, who existed before anything else. Breathmaker created the earth and all living things. In the Seminole version of the Muskogean creation tradition, the earth was formed from mud brought up from the primordial waters, similar to the Cherokee story. Breathmaker then created humans, animals, and plants, and taught the Seminole how to live properly. He gave them the Green Corn Ceremony and established the clans. Breathmaker also created the sun, moon, and stars to govern time and seasons. The Seminole believe that Breathmaker remains involved in the world and can be communicated with through prayer and ceremony. The creation story establishes the sacred relationship between the Seminole people and their land in Florida.

title: Serpan of the Deep Channel
summary: A serpent-like creature haunts the deep channel between two islands, dragging boats beneath the waves when sailors fail to toss a handful of salt into the sea.

title: Shahmaran, Queen of Serpents
summary: A young man discovers Shahmaran, the serpent queen who rules a hidden kingdom beneath the earth, and must choose between the world above and the world below.

title: Shahmaran: The Serpent Queen of Turkey
summary: A half-woman half-serpent queen rules an underground kingdom of snakes in Anatolian legend.

title: Shakuru and Pah: The Sun and Moon
summary: Shakuru (the Sun) and Pah (the Moon) were the last of all gods placed in the heavens by Tirawa. They are of relatively minor standing in Skidi Pawnee mythology compared to the star gods. The Sun and Moon produced a son, a boy who was placed on Earth to be the ancestor of the Pawnee people. The Sun is associated with warmth, light, and the daily cycle. The Moon governs the night and is associated with women's cycles. In Pawnee earth lodge construction, the door faces east to welcome the rising sun, and the smoke hole is aligned to observe the moon and stars.

title: Shango and the Dual Death (Yoruba)
summary: Shango was the fourth king of Oyo who deified himself as the god of thunder and lightning. According to legend, Shango was a powerful but tyrannical ruler who accidentally destroyed his own palace with lightning when his enemies provoked him. Overcome with grief and shame, he fled Oyo and hanged himself from an ayan tree. But rather than dying, Shango ascended to heaven and became an Orisha of immense power. His two wives, Oshun and Oya (who became the goddess of wind and death), followed him into the spirit world. Shango's sacred symbol is the oshe (double-headed axe), representing swift divine justice. His followers revere him for his fiery temper, his drumming, and his power to hurl thunderbolts at his enemies.

title: Shir the Holy Ram
summary: In the ages before the Ark came to rest on Ararat, a sacred ram carried the seeds of all living things through the floodwaters, guided by the light between its horns.
themes: the bond between creature and land

title: Shiva
summary: In the vast pantheon of Hindu deities, no figure is more complex, more paradoxical, or more awe-inspiring than Shiva.

title: Shortshanks
summary: A small boy named Shortshanks is underestimated by everyone due to his size. He embarks on a journey where he uses his exceptional cunning to outwit several ogres and trolls, eventually winning the hand of a princess and proving that size is no measure of capability.

title: Shteli Kherkher, the Mountain Guardian
summary: A nature spirit of the Hindu Kush mountains who protects the wild animals and punishes hunters who kill for sport.

title: Shurale the Forest Spirit
summary: Shurale is the most famous mythological creature in Tatar folklore — a forest spirit depicted as a hairy man with a horn on his forehead, one eye, and extremely long fingers. Shurale lures travelers into the forest, rides their horses at night, and tickles his victims to death. The most famous story, immortalized by Tatar poet Gabdulla Tukay, tells of a young woodcutter who outwits Shurale by tricking him into inserting his fingers into a split log, then removing the wedge to trap him. When Shurale screams in pain, other forest spirits ask what happened, and he tells them 'Byltyr kysty' (Last year pinched me) — so afraid of admitting he was fooled. The story teaches cleverness over brute strength and remains a cornerstone of Tatar cultural identity.

title: Shuten-Doji
summary: The sake-stealing demon who terrorized Kyoto until defeated by the hero Minamoto no Yorimitsu.

title: Si Bungsu and the Seven Brothers
summary: A traditional Bruneian folktale about the youngest of seven brothers who was underestimated and mistreated by his six elder siblings. While the elder brothers were strong, skilled, and proud, Si Bungsu (meaning 'the youngest') was gentle, humble, and assigned the most menial tasks. When the Sultan announced a challenge to retrieve a sacred kris (ceremonial blade) lost in the enchanted forest, the elder brothers set off confidently but failed — their arrogance angering the forest's guardian spirit. Si Bungsu, guided by humility and compassion, helped an old woman (the disguised forest spirit), who rewarded him with the kris and freed his spellbound brothers. He shared his reward with them, teaching that true strength lies not in skill but in kindness and compassion.

title: Si Tanggang (The Unfilial Son)
summary: A Malaysian folktale from Negeri Sembilan closely related to the Indonesian Malin Kundang. Tanggang, the son of a poor fisherman, leaves his mother to seek fortune overseas. After becoming a wealthy captain with a fine ship, he returns to his village. His elderly mother, overjoyed, wades into the water to greet him, but Tanggang denies knowing her, ashamed of her poverty-stricken appearance. His mother curses him for his ingratitude. A violent storm erupts, and Tanggang and his ship are petrified into stone. The rock formation known as Batu Belah Batu Bertangkup (Split Stone, Closing Stone) is said to be the remains of his ship, serving as a warning against filial disrespect in Malay culture.

title: Si'lat of the Old City
summary: A variant of the Si'lat said to haunt the ancient streets of Jerusalem, preying on those who stray from the path of righteousness.
