title: Si'lat, the Femme Fatale of the Levant
summary: A beautiful female jinn who seduces men and leads them to their doom, a cautionary figure in Palestinian folklore.

title: Sickness Spirits and the Noaidi's Healing
summary: A collection of legends about sickness spirits that cause disease. Illness was understood spiritually—either as soul-loss, as punishment for broken taboos, or as an attack by a hostile noaidi. The noaidi would use his drum to diagnose the cause, then journey in trance to retrieve the lost soul or confront the malevolent spirit. Sacrifices were promised to specific gods if healing was granted.

title: Sikakokuh and the Hunting Dog
summary: A Hopi story about a boy named Sikakokuh who had a remarkable hunting dog. The dog was no ordinary animal but possessed spiritual power, able to track game without fail and communicate with its master. Sikakokuh's success as a hunter made others jealous. Through the dog's guidance, Sikakokuh learned the proper rituals for hunting, including prayers and offerings to the spirits of the animals he killed. When enemies or jealous rivals tried to harm the dog, supernatural forces protected both boy and animal. The story teaches the sacred relationship between humans and animals, the importance of gratitude, and the proper conduct of hunters who must respect the spirits of the animals they take.

title: Silamaka and Pullori: The Fulani Epic Heroes
summary: The Fulani epic of Silamaka and Pullori recounts the adventures of two bound-by-friendship heroes from the Macina region of Mali. Silamaka, the saber-wielding warrior, is challenged to prove his temerity against the mighty Bambara king Da Monzon Diarra. He consults a geomancer who tells him that to become invulnerable, he must capture alive the sacred serpent Galamani that prowls the forest. With Pullori's help, Silamaka succeeds where many had failed, capturing the serpent and fashioning a protective belt. His fame spreads across Fulani villages. Da Monzon counterattacks with powerful magic, but Pullori, armed with Silamaka's enchanted lance, flees with their sons. As night falls, they all disappear, ascending to heaven. The epic symbolizes Fulani resistance against Bambara domination and remains a cornerstone of Fulani oral tradition.

title: Silverwhite and Lillwacker
summary: Two faithful brothers journey to rescue their sister from a sea troll who killed their father, overcoming enchanted forests, talking animals, and magical trials through unbreakable brotherly loyalty. The tale draws on an ancient Indo-Germanic cycle of faithful brothers.

title: Simbi: The River Spirits of the Kongo
summary: The Simbi are powerful water spirits who inhabit the rivers, streams, and sacred pools of the Kongo region. They are ancient beings who existed before humanity and witnessed the creation of the world. Simbi can appear as beautiful human figures, snakes, or shimmering reflections on the water's surface. They are guardians of esoteric knowledge and the natural balance of the forests and waters. Those who respect the Simbi and make proper offerings may receive visions, healing, or supernatural abilities. But those who pollute the waters or hunt excessively incur the Simbi's wrath — they may be dragged into the depths, never to be seen again, or afflicted with madness. The nganga (spiritual specialists) serve as intermediaries between the human world and the Simbi, conducting ceremonies at sacred river sites. The Simbi remind the Kongo people that water is not merely a resource but a living, spiritual force that sustains all existence.

title: Simurgh and Zal
summary: Sam of Zabulistan abandons his albino infant son Zal on Mount Alborz, ashamed of his white hair. The mythical bird Simurgh, a wise, benevolent creature resembling a giant dog-bird, finds the baby and raises him as her own. Zal grows into a handsome, powerful youth. Sam has a dream of reproach and seeks forgiveness. Zal returns to his father but receives three Simurgh feathers to burn when in need. Later, Zal marries the beautiful Rudabeh, but she nearly dies in childbirth. Zal burns a feather, and Simurgh appears to perform the first known cesarean section, saving both mother and child — the child being Rostam, Iran's greatest hero.

title: Sina and the Eel (Origin of the Coconut)
summary: The beautiful maiden Sina drew water from a pool where she discovered a young eel. She took it home as a pet and named it Tuna. The eel grew rapidly, outgrowing bowls, then pools, and becoming unnaturally large. Wherever Sina bathed, the eel appeared and encircled her. Frightened, she fled across multiple islands, but the eel always found her. Finally, the eel revealed itself as the King of Fiji transformed by magic, who confessed his love and asked Sina to bury his head. Though shocked, Sina complied. From the buried head grew the first coconut tree, its three dark pores representing the eel's eyes and mouth. When cracked, the coconut's shell resembles the eel's face.

title: Sinbad the Sailor (Seven Voyages)
summary: A wealthy Baghdad merchant known as Sinbad the Sailor recounts his seven extraordinary voyages to a poor porter named Sinbad the Landsman. Each voyage brings shipwreck, monstrous creatures (the giant bird Roc, gigantic serpents, whale-islands, cyclopean giants), and fantastic lands. Sinbad outwits cannibals, escapes the Valley of Diamonds, rides sea monsters, and encounters the Old Man of the Sea who clings to his shoulders. Through wit, courage, and Allah's mercy, he returns home each time richer, only to be driven again by wanderlust. The tales are a masterpiece of Arab maritime folklore.

title: Sint-Holo: The Horned Serpent (Chickasaw)
summary: Sint-Holo is a dragon-like horned serpent from Chickasaw mythology. This powerful water monster dwells in deep rivers, lakes, and underground springs. Sint-Holo has a serpentine body covered with scales, a horned or antlered head, and possesses supernatural powers. Unlike some malevolent serpents in neighboring tribes' mythology, Sint-Holo is sometimes ambivalent or even protective of the Chickasaw people. The serpent is associated with the underground water realm and represents the forces of nature that must be respected. Those who encounter Sint-Holo must show proper respect or face dire consequences. The horned serpent symbol appears in Chickasaw art and ceremonial objects and is one of the most widespread mythological figures across Southeastern Native American cultures.

title: Sinti Lapitta: The Horned Serpent (Choctaw)
summary: Sinti Lapitta is a great horned serpent from Choctaw mythology, a water monster with immense power. Described as a giant snake with a head like a panther or with two horns on its head, it dwells in deep rivers, lakes, and water holes. Unlike the malevolent horned serpents of some tribes, Sinti Lapitta was sometimes known to visit unusually wise young men, bestowing knowledge and power upon them. The serpent was both feared and respected, embodying the power of the water realm. It served as a symbol of the underworld and was associated with the chaotic forces that must be balanced against the order of the sky. Stories of Sinti Lapitta warn against disturbing sacred waters.

title: Sir Birre and the Trolls
summary: Sir Birre lives on a farm below the mountain where two trolls, Jock and Turing, dwell. When his sweetheart Tinka is kidnapped by the troll Domp-Domp-Dubbeldomp, Birre must ask Jock and Turing for help. In exchange, he teaches them to build a house and smelt iron. The trolls rescue Tinka, who traveled in Turing's furry ear, and they all become friends.

title: Sir Olof and the Elves
summary: A young knight riding to his wedding encounters the elf queen in the forest. She offers him her love, but he refuses — and her curse leads to tragedy on his wedding day.

title: Sisimito of the Blue Hole
summary: A Garifuna fisherman glimpses the Sisimito near the Great Blue Hole and learns that some creatures prefer the shadows between what is real and what is remembered.

title: Sisiutl the Double-Headed Serpent (Kwakwaka'wakw)
summary: The Sisiutl is a fearsome three-headed sea serpent whose glance can turn an adversary into stone. Typically depicted as a double-headed serpent with a central humanoid face representing Baxbaxwalanuksiwe' or Komokwa, it has horned heads, protruding tongues, and spiral noses that indicate supernatural power. The Sisiutl is closely associated with shamans, who mediate between natural and supernatural worlds, and warriors believed that its blood made them invincible in battle. It appears as a protective figure on clan house beams, war canoes, and ceremonial regalia. In some myths, the Sisiutl transforms into an invincible war canoe or a magic belt that protects the wearer against all dangers. The beach mineral mica was believed to be the scales of the Sisiutl and was incorporated into ceremonial traditions. The Sisiutl plays a dual role as both a terrifying monster and a powerful helper to ancestors who earned its favor.

title: Sita: The Abducted Queen
summary: In the ancient city of Ayodhya, Prince Rama was the beloved heir to the throne—brave, virtuous, and beloved by all.

title: Siyavash and Sudabeh
summary: Prince Siyavash, son of Kay Kavus, rejects the seductive advances of his stepmother Sudabeh. To prove his innocence, he rides through a mountain of fire and emerges unscathed. Despite this vindication, he cannot remain in Iran and voluntarily exiles himself to Turan, where King Afrasiab initially welcomes him and gives him his daughter Farangis in marriage. Suspecting conspiracy, Afrasiab orders Siyavash's execution, and the prince is beheaded. This unjust death becomes the casus belli for generations of war between Iran and Turan, and Siyavash's blood is avenged by his son Kay Khosrow. The story is one of the Shahnameh's most profound tragedies, exploring honor, betrayal, and fate.

title: Skunk Outwits Coyote
summary: Coyote came upon a prairie dog village and decided to catch himself a meal. He blocked all the holes except one and waited with his mouth open at the entrance. But Skunk saw what Coyote was doing and decided to teach him a lesson. Skunk approached Coyote and asked what he was doing. Coyote explained his plan, and Skunk offered to help by driving the prairie dogs toward Coyote's mouth. Instead, Skunk walked up to Coyote and sprayed him directly in the face. Coyote ran away howling, and the prairie dogs escaped. Skunk laughed at the trickster, proving that even the cleverest schemer can be outsmarted.

title: Sleeping Beauty
summary: The Erl-King is the darkest fairy tale that the Brothers Grimm collected, a poem of terror that has haunted German children for centuries.

title: Snow White and the Seven Dwarfs
summary: A beautiful princess escapes her jealous stepmother-queen and finds refuge with seven dwarfs. The queen tricks her with a poisoned apple, but a prince's kiss awakens her.

title: Snæbjørn (Snow Bear of Suðuroy)
summary: Snæbjørn was a powerful, brave, and proud servant working for a wealthy farmer in Hvalba on Suðuroy. He was secretly in love with a milkmaid. When a Dutch ship illegally traded luxury goods, Snæbjørn bought four silk scarves for her. The judge sentenced him to four years imprisonment on Bremerholm in Denmark for this crime. Enraged, Snæbjørn struck at the judge but accidentally killed the bailiff instead. He fled into the mountains where his speed, climbing skill, and knowledge of the terrain made capture impossible. Villagers secretly helped him with food and warned him of search parties. He became a folk hero—an outlaw who defied unjust Danish authority, reminiscent of Robin Hood.

title: Sodani the Great Shaman
summary: The Evenki epic tale of Sodani, the most powerful shaman who ever lived, who could journey between the Upper, Middle, and Lower Worlds. The story follows Sodani's initiation by spirits, his epic journey to the Lower World to retrieve a lost soul, and his battle against hostile spirits that threaten the Evenki people. He is aided by his animal spirit helpers including the reindeer, bear, and eagle. The tale illustrates the Evenki shamanic worldview where humans are but a small piece of the natural world and must maintain balance with all beings — animals, plants, rivers, mountains, and stars all have spirits that must be respected for harmony to prevail.

title: Sohni Mahiwal — Love Across the River
summary: Sohni, a beautiful pottery-maker's daughter, fell in love with Izzat Baig (later called Mahiwal), a wealthy merchant from another land who had come to trade. When her family married her to another man, Sohni still swam each night across the Chenab River using an earthenware pot as a float to reach her beloved Mahiwal on the opposite bank. Her sister-in-law, suspecting the affair, replaced Sohni's baked clay pot with an unbaked one. When Sohni jumped into the river, the pot dissolved in the water, and she drowned in the swirling currents. Mahiwal, seeing her body float downstream, jumped in and died beside her. One of the four classic tragic romances of Punjab, the story symbolizes love that defies social boundaries but meets a tragic end.

title: Sohni Mahiwal: The Tragic Lovers of Sindh
summary: A potter's daughter drowns crossing a river to meet her lover in one of South Asia's greatest love stories.

title: Son Tinh and Thuy Tinh
summary: In the mountains of Japan, where the bamboo forests rustle with secrets and the old Shinto shrines stand weathered by centuries of rain, there lives a yokai who is neither malevolent nor kind.

title: Songa Raudhat and the Lost Children
summary: When children vanish into the highland mist above Moroni, it is Songa Raudhat who leads them astray, and only the call to prayer can guide them home again.
themes: passing wisdom to the next generation

title: Songtsen Gampo and the Founding of Tibet
summary: The semi-legendary account of King Songtsen Gampo (7th century CE), the founder of the Tibetan Empire and the first Dharma King. According to Tibetan tradition, he was an emanation of the bodhisattva Avalokiteshvara, sent to bring civilization and Buddhism to the Tibetan people. He built the Jokhang Temple in Lhasa, subdued the demoness that lay beneath the Tibetan landscape by constructing 108 temples on her body's pressure points, and invented the Tibetan script by sending his minister Thonmi Sambhota to India. His marriage to Princess Wencheng of China and Princess Bhrikuti of Nepal is said to have brought Buddhism to Tibet. The story of Songtsen Gampo blends historical events with elaborate mythological elements that define Tibetan Buddhist identity.

title: Soria Moria Castle
summary: Halvor, a boy known for his laziness, leaves home to see the world. He travels to the legendary Soria Moria Castle, where he defeats three trolls and rescues three princesses, returning home with immense wealth and the love of the youngest princess.

title: Soucouyant, the Antiguan Fireball
summary: A fearsome vampire of the Caribbean, the Soucouyant sheds her skin by night and flies as a fireball to suck the blood of her victims.

title: Soucouyant: The Fire in the Dark
summary: A young woman who dismisses the old protective rituals of salt and garlic discovers the Soucouyant is real when she sees a ball of fire cross the yard and finds her baby's cribside stained with ash.

title: Soucouyant: The Fireball Hag of the Caribbean
summary: An old woman sheds her skin at night to become a ball of fire that hunts the blood of the living.

title: Spearfinger (U'tlun'ta): The Stone Witch (Cherokee)
summary: Spearfinger, also known as Nûñ'yunu'ï or 'Stone-dress,' is a fearsome Cherokee monster and witch who lives along the eastern side of Tennessee and western North Carolina. She has a long, sharp forefinger on her right hand like a spear or obsidian knife, which she uses to cut open her victims. She wears a dress made of stone that makes her nearly invulnerable. Spearfinger feeds on human livers, especially those of children. Her mouth is perpetually stained with blood. She can mimic the voices of loved ones to lure victims close. According to legend, she was eventually defeated by a group of Cherokee warriors who discovered that her only vulnerable spot was a small point on her palm. They shot arrows into her palm, and she fell from the mountain where she lived.

title: Sphinx
summary: The Sphinx is ancient—so ancient that she predates the pyramids themselves. Centers on Sphinx,  of royal power and wisdom in Egypt; symbol of dangerous knowledge in Greece..

title: Spider Woman and the Origin of Weaving
summary: In the Third World of Navajo tradition, Spider Woman and Spider Man, who lived near the Crossing of the Waters, taught the people the art of weaving. Spider Man showed them how to shape a spindle wheel and spin cotton thread from planted cotton seeds. First Woman declared that spinning must be done toward the body to attract beautiful goods, not away. Spider Man named the spindle 'turning around with beautiful goods' while Spider Woman called it 'turning around with mixed chips.' They constructed a rectangular loom frame, established the warp and weft, and created all parts of the loom. After teaching the people, Spider Man instructed that newborn girls should have spider web rubbed on their hands and arms so they would weave skillfully without tiring.

title: Splinter Foot Girl
summary: A childless Arapaho woman found a splinter embedded in her foot. To her amazement, the splinter grew and transformed into a baby girl. The girl grew rapidly and possessed supernatural abilities. She could communicate with animals and had the power to heal. She brought good fortune to her family and community, helping them find buffalo and warning them of danger. One day, a rival tribe kidnapped her, but she used her powers to escape and return home. The story teaches that blessings can come from unexpected places, and that even something as small as a splinter can hold great potential.

title: Sri Thanonchai: The Royal Trickster
summary: Sri Thanonchai is the legendary trickster figure in Thai folklore, a clever and witty commoner who used his sharp intellect to outsmart kings, nobles, and corrupt officials. Born with extraordinary cleverness, Sri Thanonchai could talk his way out of any situation and often turned the tables on those in power who sought to harm him. His stories, passed down through generations, involve elaborate wordplay, cunning schemes, and moral lessons about the power of wit over brute force. In one famous tale, he tricked a greedy official into believing a common pot was a magical fortune-telling device. Despite his mischief, Sri Thanonchai never used his tricks to harm the innocent — only to expose greed, hypocrisy, and abuse of power. His tales remain widely told in Thai oral tradition and have been adapted into television dramas, plays, and children's books.

title: St. Christopher and the Dog-Headed Men
summary: St. Christopher, depicted with the head of a dog in ancient Vatican iconography, encounters the Cynocephali and discovers they possess a faith purer than that of many Christians.

title: St. Joseph in the Forest
summary: An Austrian folk tale where St. Joseph tests three sisters by appearing as a beggar. Two sisters are cruel and are punished; the kind youngest is rewarded with a blessed life.

title: St. Peter and the Two Women
summary: St. Peter, disguised as a poor traveler, is turned away by a rich farmer's wife but welcomed by a poor widow. He blesses the widow so that whatever she starts doing she continues all day—she measures cloth that grows endlessly and becomes wealthy. The greedy rich woman demands the same blessing but begins pumping water and drowns.

title: Stagolee in Hell (Stagolee vs. the Devil)
summary: After Stagolee was hanged for murder, he arrived at the gates of Hell, still wearing his Stetson hat and carrying his .44 pistol. When the Devil tried to send him to his eternal punishment, Stagolee refused to submit. He pulled his pistol and challenged the Devil himself. The Devil, for all his power, found he could not control Stagolee. Stagolee kicked the Devil off his throne, sat down on it himself, and took over the running of Hell. In some versions, he set all the lost souls free; snip in others, he ran Hell more efficiently than the Devil ever did. The Devil eventually begged God to let Stagolee into Heaven, but Heaven refused as well, leaving Stagolee master of his own domain. This tale of a man so bad that Hell itself could not hold him became a cornerstone of African American 'toasts' (narrative poems), celebrating the ultimate rebellious figure who fears neither God nor Devil and answers to absolutely no one.

title: Stagolee Shoots Billy Lyons
summary: On Christmas night, 1895, in a St. Louis saloon, the notorious bad-man Stagolee (based on historical figure Lee Shelton) shot William 'Billy' Lyons after a dispute. In the folk tradition, the argument began when Billy Lyons snatched Stagolee's prized Stetson hat from his head and refused to return it. Stagolee warned him: 'I don't care what you do with me, but don't you mess with my Stetson hat.' When Billy laughed and refused, Stagolee drew his .44 pistol. Billy begged for his life, pleading that he had a wife and children, but Stagolee replied, 'I don't care about your wife and kids—you should have thought of them before you touched my Stetson hat.' He shot Billy dead. The song spread like wildfire across America, with each new version making Stagolee more mythic, transforming a common barroom murder into a foundational American outlaw legend—the quintessential 'bad nigger' who answered to no man and no law.

title: Stagolee's Funeral
summary: The folk ballad describes Stagolee's funeral as an event unlike any before seen. Thousands of people came from miles around to see the baddest man who ever lived laid to rest. A procession of mourners stretched for blocks—the women weeping, the men silent and respectful. His coffin was reportedly so fine it cost more than most men earned in a year. The ballad describes the funeral train, the flowers, the hymns sung over his grave. Yet even in death, Stagolee remained defiant. The women who heard of his death 'could not stay at home,' rushing to the funeral in droves. Verses describe how 'the women in the West' heard the news and lamented, cementing Stagolee's status as a tragic romantic figure. Stagolee's funeral became a set-piece in African American folk memory: the moment when the community paused to honor a man who, for all his violence, represented a kind of freedom—the freedom to be utterly oneself, without apology or compromise, in a world that demanded constant submission from Black men.

title: Stalo and Kauras
summary: This tale originates from the Sami people of northern Sweden (Lapland) and features a Stalo — a giant, man-eating troll-like creature from Sami folklore. Stalo is described as a large, evil being who wears impenetrable black iron clothing, hunts and devours people and reindeer, and terrorizes the region. He is rich, powerful, and ruthless, but also clumsy and unintelligent. In this story, a Sami boy named Kauras confronts the Stalo. Using his wits rather than strength, Kauras devises a clever plan to defeat the giant. He tricks Stalo into a head-butting competition against a tree trunk, rendering the giant unconscious. The Stalo's stupidity and vanity are his undoing — he cannot believe that a small boy could outsmart him. John Bauer's illustration for this tale depicts the moment of confrontation between the small, clever boy and the massive, armored Stalo. The story belongs to a broader tradition of Sami Stalo tales (including 'How the Stalos were Tricked' and 'The Tale of Njunje Paggas'), which serve as teaching tools about courage, resourcefulness, and the importance of maintaining Sami identity in the face of external threats. The Stalo figure in Sami folklore is sometimes interpreted as a symbolic representation of encroaching outside forces that the Sami people have historically had to resist.

title: Starkad and Bale
summary: The legendary hero Starkad — raised by Odin himself and the greatest warrior of the North — teams up with the sly trickster Bale to exact revenge through feats of impossible strength and clever deception against a treacherous king.

title: Stikini: The Owl Witches (Seminole)
summary: Stikini are dreaded owl-witches from Seminole folklore. During the day, Stikini appear as ordinary humans, but at night they transform into monstrous owls with supernatural powers. They are known to prey on humans, particularly those who are alone in the forest at night. A Stikini can be identified by its bloodshot eyes and unusual behavior. The owl-witches are associated with witchcraft and dark magic, and their appearance is considered an omen of death or misfortune. Seminole medicine men have the power to identify Stikini and perform rituals to protect against them. The legend serves as a warning against practicing evil magic and emphasizes the importance of staying within the protection of the community, especially at night.

title: Stompe Pilt
summary: A giant named Stompe Pilt terrorizes a parish until a brave little shepherd boy challenges him with a sling and a bag of tricks, proving that size is no match for wit. The tale is an entertaining parody of David and Goliath.

title: Stone Coat (Nûñ'yunu'ï): The Rock Giants (Cherokee)
summary: Stone Coat, also called Nûñ'yunu'ï, is a race of giant beings covered in stone-like skin that makes them nearly invulnerable. They dwell in the remote mountains and caves of Cherokee territory. These rock giants are cannibalistic and prey upon humans who venture too far into their domain. They are incredibly strong, capable of throwing boulders and tearing down trees. Stone Coat is also associated with Spearfinger, who wears a stone dress. The giants' only weakness is their vulnerability to certain spiritual practices. Cherokee medicine men knew rituals to confuse or drive away Stone Coats. The legend may have been inspired by encounters with the fossilized remains of prehistoric megafauna in the Appalachian region, and it serves as a warning against venturing into dangerous, unknown territory.

title: Storsjöodjuret
summary: A mysterious serpentine creature haunts the depths of Lake Storsjön in Sweden, appearing as a spectral guardian of the water.

title: Strigoi, the Undead of the Carpathians
summary: Restless spirits of the dead who rise from their graves to plague the living, the Strigoi are among the most feared creatures in Moldovan folklore.

title: Strigoi: The Undead Spirits of Romania
summary: Restless spirits rise from their graves to prey on the living in the land of Dracula.

title: Stuorra-Jouni and the Stállu on Áiligas Fell
summary: A legend from Talvadas on the Teno River. Stuorra-Jouni ('Big Jouni') is a legendary Sámi proto-hero, a wild deer hunter and storyteller. A noaidi from Varanger sent a Stállu to attack Jouni. Jouni met the Stállu on Áiligas fell and they fought according to the ritual pattern. The Stállu escaped on skis, leaving only its ski tracks on the fell, which remain visible to this day.

title: Stállo and Kauras
summary: The classic Sámi Stállo tale. The evil giant Stállo lived in Storfjellet and demanded reindeer sacrifices from the Sámi. He controlled all predators and would kill reindeer if not appeased. The brave Sámi boy Kauras decides to defeat him. After a head-butting contest where Kauras tricks Stállo by hiding his head in a hollowed tree trunk, Kauras survives Stállo's nighttime murder attempt. Terrified, Stállo pays Kauras silver and is expelled from the mountain forever.

title: Su Anasi: The Water Mother
summary: Su Anasi ('Mother of Water') is the Tatar water spirit, analogous to the Russian rusalka but with distinct Tatar characteristics. Long-haired and beautiful, she lives in rivers and lakes, with a golden comb that she uses to brush her hair while sitting on riverbanks. The most famous version, retold by poet Gabdulla Tukay, describes a village boy who finds Su Anasi's golden comb by the river and runs away with it. The water mother chases him all the way to the village until the village dogs drive her away. That night, she comes to his window, tapping and demanding her comb back. The boy's mother throws the comb out the window to appease her. The story teaches children not to take things that don't belong to them, as every object has a spirit owner ('iyäsi') who will reclaim it.

title: Sufax and the Founding of Tangier
summary: In the syncretic mythology that blends Berber, Greek, and Phoenician traditions, Sufax was the son of the Greek hero Heracles (Hercules) and Tinge, the Berber earth goddess. According to the legend, Heracles performed one of his labors in North Africa, where he met and married Tinge. Their son Sufax founded the city of Tangier, naming it after his mother (Tingis being the ancient name for Tangier). Sufax is also credited with founding parts of Mauritania. This myth demonstrates the cultural fusion characteristic of North African mythology, where Berber indigenous figures merged with Greek heroes from the time of the Greek colonies in Cyrenaica, and later with Roman interpretations. The story explains the founding of one of Morocco's oldest cities and illustrates how Berber mythology absorbed and transformed external influences while maintaining its indigenous core.

title: Sumpurnis, the Shapeshifter of the Birch Forest
summary: Sumpurnis, a terrifying shapeshifter wrapped in shaggy fur, roams the birch forests of Latvia, shifting form to lure or terrify those who stray from the path.

title: Sun Goat, the Chadian Steppe Sprite
summary: A legendary goat-like creature of Chadian folklore, the Sun Goat is a spirit of the Sahel that appears during droughts and leads herds to water.

title: Sundew and the Ghosts
summary: In the village of Skruväng, deep in the forests of Småland, there lived a girl named Sundew—called sårfot in the old tongue because her grandmother said she was as delicate and as keen as the tiny carnivorous plant that grew in the boggy meadows.

title: Sundiata: The Lion King of Mali
summary: A disabled prince who was exiled, returns to found the greatest empire in African history—the Mali Empire.

title: Supay, Lord of the Ujku
summary: Supay rules the underworld beneath the mountains, and the miners who descend into his domain must leave offerings at the entrance or face his wrath.

title: Supay, Lord of Uku Pacha
summary: The Aymara lord of the underworld Uku Pacha demands tribute from miners who dig too deep, and those who forget his offerings vanish into tunnels that have no end.

title: Swan Maiden
summary: A hunter captures a celestial swan maiden by stealing her feather cloak, leading to a marriage built on a secret that eventually reveals the cost of forced love.

title: Sweet Medicine and the Four Sacred Arrows
summary: Sweet Medicine (Motsé'eóeve) was the great prophet and law-giver of the Cheyenne people. He journeyed to Nóávóse (Bear Butte) in the Black Hills where Ma'heo'o (the Wise One Above) gave him the four sacred arrows—the Maahótse. Two arrows were for hunting, to ensure success in finding buffalo, and two were for warfare, to protect the people from enemies. Sweet Medicine also received the structure of Cheyenne government, the Council of Forty-Four peace chiefs, the military societies, and the system of legal justice. He predicted the coming of horses, white men, and the loss of the buffalo. He also invented the hoop-and-stick game (chunkey).

title: Sáráhkká: The Childbirth Goddess
summary: Sáráhkká is the most important birth goddess in Sámi mythology, daughter of Máttaráhkká. She lives under the hearth of the goahti. She places the fetus in the woman's womb. She protects both human women and reindeer during birth. Before birth, women drank 'Sáráhkká's booze' and after, ate 'Sáráhkká's porridge.' Wood was split for her to ease delivery. Female animals were sacrificed after successful births.

title: Símun of Kirkjubøur (Hulda-Símun and the Hidden Woman)
summary: Símun Símunarson, nicknamed Hulda-Símun or Troll-Símun, was a massive farmer at Kirkjubøur on Streymoy. A hulduman (hidden woman) lived on Kirkjubøur Felltop. The legend tells how Símun was kidnapped by the Huldufólk and taken to the cliffs near Kirkjubøur. After his encounter with the Hidden People, the Huldufólk were never seen in the village again. Símun was described as so large that his jacket required three lengths of double-width cloth, and none of his farmhands dared walk ahead of him on sheep round-ups. The story reflects Faroese beliefs about the Hidden People dwelling in the landscape and their ability to interact with humans.

title: Ta'aroa Creates the World from His Shell
summary: In the beginning, Ta'aroa, the supreme creator god of Tahiti, existed alone inside a great shell called Rumia, spinning through the endless void. Bored with his solitude, he shook himself and cracked the shell open. He threw pieces of shell outward to form the rocks, sand, and foundation of the world. From his backbone he shaped the mountains; snip from his tears he filled the oceans, lakes, and rivers. His scales became the fish and turtles, his blood colored the rainbow, and his feathers became the trees and bushes. Ta'aroa then created Tane, Ru, and Hina, who helped him decorate the sky with stars, hang the sun and moon, and populate the earth with humanity.

title: Tabaldak Creates Glooscap and Malsumis
summary: In Abenaki tradition, the Great Spirit Tabaldak first created the world and all the people. When he finished making humans, he wiped the dust from his hands, and from this divine dust were born twin brothers — Glooscap and Malsumis. Glooscap was given the power to create a good world, full of kind animals, sweet fruits, and gentle rivers. Malsumis, the wolf, was his opposite, creating only evil — dangerous animals, thorns, and crooked rivers that flooded the land. From birth, Malsumis resented his brother and plotted to destroy him. Glooscap discovered that his brother could only be killed by a blow from a fern root. Malsumis tricked the animals into revealing this secret and attacked Glooscap, but the good twin was saved by Grandmother Woodchuck. Glooscap eventually defeated Malsumis and turned him into stone, where he remains, the embodiment of all that is harmful in nature.

title: Taema and Tilafaiga: The Origin of Tattooing
summary: The twin sisters Taema and Tilafaiga, divine daughters of the god Tagaloa, journeyed from Fiji to Samoa carrying the sacred art of tattooing. They swam across the ocean holding a basket containing the tools and patterns for tatau. As they approached the Samoan shore, they began singing 'Fafafofoga o le tama' ('The tattoo fits the man'), establishing that body art was meant for men, not women. The sisters taught the Samoan people the intricate patterns, spiritual protocols, and practical techniques of traditional tattooing. Their gift of the pe'a (male tattoo covering from waist to knees) and malu (female leg tattoo) became a central pillar of Samoan cultural identity and rite of passage.

title: Tagaloa Creates the Samoan Islands
summary: In the beginning, only Tagaloa existed in the heavens above the endless waters. He looked down and decided to create a place to rest. He formed a great rock called Manu'atele, then divided it into pieces that became the stepping stones of the Pacific. The largest pieces became the islands of Savai'i and Upolu, while smaller ones scattered to form Tonga, Fiji, and other islands. Tagaloa then created the land, the forests, and the people, establishing the fa'a Samoa (Samoan way) of chieftainship, social order, and spiritual devotion. He sent his son to rule the earth, and from this lineage came the noble families of Samoa.

title: Tagaro and Suqe-Matua: The Creation of Good and Evil
summary: On Ambae Island in Vanuatu, the culture hero Tagaro is a creator figure pitted against his twelfth brother Suqe-matua. Tagaro and Suqe-matua shared the work of creation, but whatever Suqe-matua did was wrong. They always disagreed, but the word of Tagaro always prevailed. Tagaro created useful plants, gentle animals, and beneficial customs, while Suqe-matua created weeds, dangerous creatures, and harmful practices. Tagaro made ten human figures from mud and breathed life into them. He then threw a fruit at one of the figures, transforming the man into a woman, thus establishing the two sexes. The Tagaro figure is related to the Polynesian deity Tangaroa, showing the cultural connections across the Pacific.

title: Taktshang Palphug: The Tiger's Nest Monastery
summary: Paro Taktshang (Tiger's Nest) is Bhutan's most sacred monastery, clinging to a cliff-face 900 meters above the Paro Valley. In the 8th century, Guru Rinpoche (Padmasambhava) flew from Tibet to this location riding on the back of Yeshe Tshogyel, his consort, who had transformed herself into a tigress. At the cave known as Taktsang Senge Samdup, Guru Rinpoche assumed the wrathful form of Dorje Drolo and meditated, subduing malicious spirits and establishing Buddhism in Bhutan. An alternative legend says Tashi Kheudren, a local Bhutanese girl, was the disciple who transformed into the tigress. The monastery was built in 1692 by Gyalse Tenzin Rabgye, the fourth temporal ruler of Bhutan. Imprints of Guru Rinpoche's body remain on the cave wall. Tibetan saints including Milarepa, Machig Labdrön, and Thangtong Gyelpo later meditated at this holy site.

title: Taleju and the Origin of Kumari Worship
summary: Goddess Taleju Bhawani, a fearsome tantric form of Durga, served as the royal tutelary deity of the Malla kings of the Kathmandu Valley. Legend recounts that King Mahendra Malla dreamed of the goddess and built her the Taleju Temple in Kathmandu Durbar Square. The goddess would visit King Jayaprakash Malla nightly to play dice, appearing as a beautiful woman. One night, the king's daughter followed him and witnessed the goddess. Enraged by the broken taboo, Taleju vanished. When the king begged forgiveness, she appeared in a dream and declared she would return only in the form of a young virgin girl from the Shakya clan. This established the Kumari tradition. Her worship involves secret tantric rituals conducted by Rajopadhyaya and Karmacharya priests, centered on the Shri Yantra. Taleju represents both spiritual authority and the political sovereignty of Nepalese kingship.

title: Tales of the Trolls
summary: Three short tales of troll encounters: a peasant meets a troll at a spring, a girl is lured into a mountain by a handsome troll, and a farmer outwits a troll who steals his harvest. These tales reflect the Scandinavian belief in _bergtagning_ — being taken into the mountain by trolls.

title: Tam and Cam: The Vietnamese Cinderella
summary: Tam and Cam is a classic Vietnamese fairy tale with similarities to Cinderella, though with a distinctly Vietnamese character and a notably darker second half. The story follows Tam, a kind and hardworking girl whose mother dies, leaving her with a cruel stepmother and a lazy, jealous stepsister named Cam. After completing impossible tasks set by her stepmother, Tam receives magical help from the spirit of her mother, who appears as a goldfish. Tam's kindness is rewarded when she meets and marries a king. However, in a distinctly Vietnamese twist, Cam and the stepmother murder Tam and Cam assumes her identity. Tam's spirit transforms into an oriole, then later into a pair of golden apricot trees, and finally into a beautiful fruit — each time finding her way back to her husband. The tale features themes of reincarnation and transformation as Tam returns from death multiple times, ultimately achieving justice. Unlike Western Cinderella, the Vietnamese version emphasizes perseverance across multiple lifetimes.

title: Taming the Shrew
summary: A comedic and satirical story about a headstrong woman who believes she is superior to all suitors. A clever youth uses unconventional psychological tactics and persistence to win her respect and affection, eventually leading to a harmonious marriage.

title: Tangaroa and Tane: The War of Forest and Sea
summary: After the separation of Rangi and Papa, furious Tawhirimatea drove his brother Tangaroa, god of the sea, into the ocean depths. Tangaroa's descendants included Ikatere (fish) and Tu-te-wehiwehi (reptiles). When Tane Mahuta, god of the forest, offered shelter to Tu-te-wehiwehi and his reptile children, they abandoned the sea for the land. This betrayal enraged Tangaroa, who declared eternal war on Tane. To this day, the sea consumes the shores and forests, while Tane's creatures hide from the ocean. Fish and reptiles were divided—fish remained loyal to Tangaroa while reptiles joined Tane on land, creating the lasting enmity.

title: Tangaroa Creation Myth (Cook Islands)
summary: In the Cook Islands version of creation, Vari-ma-te-takere (the primordial mother) lived confined in a narrow space within Avaiki. She plucked pieces from her right side and left side to create six children. The first was Avatea (Vatea), a moon god with the right half of a man and left half of a fish. Avatea married Papa, and they bore twin sons: Tangaroa, god of the sea, and Rongo, god of agriculture. Tangaroa and Rongo shared dominion over all things—with Tangaroa taking everything red. Rangi, grandson of Rongo, later pulled Mangaia island up from Avaiki and became its first king, establishing the royal lineage. This creation cycle forms the foundation of Cook Islands cosmology.

title: Tangiia and Karika Divide Rarotonga
summary: Two great warrior chiefs, Tangiia and Karika, both arrived at Rarotonga claiming ownership of the island. They fought fiercely, neither able to defeat the other. Realizing their conflict would destroy the land they sought to rule, they agreed to negotiate. Tangiia and Karika divided Rarotonga between them, establishing boundaries through a sacred covenant. Tangiia took the northern and eastern districts while Karika claimed the south and west. Their treaty established the political structure of the island, and their descendants became the founding lines of the major Rarotongan tribes. The division they set has shaped Cook Islands society for generations.

title: Tantal, the Shapeshifter of the Gulf
summary: A shape-shifting spirit from Kuwaiti coastal folklore who appears as a beautiful woman to lure sailors to their doom.

title: Tao and the Mountain
summary: In ancient times, during the Warring States period, two great mountains stood between the southern part of Jizhou and the northern bank of the Yellow River.

title: Taotaomo'na, the Guamanian Ancestor Spirit
summary: The Taotaomo'na are the spirits of the ancient Chamorro people of Guam who inhabit the jungle and punish those who disrespect the old ways.

title: Tata Duende and the Lost Hunter
summary: A hunter who disrespects the deep forest is turned around by Tata Duende, the ancient guardian spirit who protects the wild places of Belize from those who take without giving thanks.

title: Tatar and the Little People
summary: In the mountains above the village of Szováta, in the匈牙利 (Hungarian) highlands, there lived a poor orphan boy called Tatar.

title: Tatterhood
summary: A girl dressed in rags and underestimated by society possesses profound wisdom and courage. Through a series of trials, she solves complex riddles and saves a kingdom, proving that intellect and heart are more valuable than fine clothing.

title: Tawa Creates the Worlds
summary: In the Hopi creation story, in the beginning only Tawa, the Sun Spirit, existed in endless space (Tokpella). Tawa formed the First World but its insect-like creatures lived unhappily in caves. To improve things, Tawa created Sotuknang, his nephew, who in turn created Spider Woman (Spider Grandmother) as a messenger and helper. Spider Woman was sent to lead the first creatures — then resembling insects — to the Second World, where they took on animal forms of wolves and bears. Still dissatisfied, Tawa created a Third World and Spider Woman guided the creatures there, where they finally became human. Spider Woman taught them weaving and pottery, and Hummingbird brought them the fire drill. This cycle of creation, destruction, and renewal through four worlds is central to Hopi cosmology, with humanity now living in the Fourth World.

title: Tek-ko-kui, the Bamboo Giant
summary: A giant nature spirit made of bamboo who protects the forests of Taiwan from those who would harm them.

title: Teke Teke: The Railway Ghost
summary: A woman who died on the railway returns as a vengeful spirit, her body sliced in half, hunting the living.

title: Tenali Raman — The Biggest Fool in the Kingdom
summary: Tenali Ramakrishna was the witty court jester and advisor in the court of King Krishnadevaraya of the Vijayanagara Empire. In this famous tale, a horse trader cheats the king by taking 5,000 gold coins as advance for three Arabian horses and never returns. When the king laments being tricked, Tenali presents him with a list titled 'The Biggest Fools in the Kingdom' with the king's name at the top. He explains that the king was a fool for trusting a complete stranger with so much gold. Through humor and clever reasoning, Tenali teaches the king a valuable lesson while exposing the trader's deceit.

title: Tengu: The Long-Nosed Goblin
summary: A proud monk is abducted by mountain spirits and taught that true wisdom begins with humility.

title: Thagyamin: The King of the Nats of Myanmar
summary: The highest spirit in Burmese folk religion rules over 37 nats from his heavenly throne.

title: Thanh Gióng the Giant Saint
summary: In the folklore of the Philippines, there is a creature that every child learns about before they can walk.

title: The Aasik of the Dog Pens
summary: The Aasik is a giant worm that dwells near dog pens where it feeds on puppies. While feared, it can be tamed by a strong-willed human and used as a mount or food source. Some legends describe Aasiks marrying humans, creating hybrid descendants.

title: The Abada of the Ubangi Forest
summary: A young BaAka hunter follows a trail of shimmering footprints deep into the equatorial forest, seeking the legendary Abada whose single horn holds the power to purify poisoned water.

title: The Abchanchu, Shapeshifter of the Road
summary: A shapeshifting vampire that appears as a beautiful stranger on the road, inviting travelers to share food and wine before revealing its true form — a skeletal figure that drinks the fat from human bodies.

title: the Acalica Water Spirits
summary: Tiny silver-skinned spirits that live in Lake Titicaca emerge at dawn to tend the reeds, and fishermen who see them must look away — or be drawn beneath the water to live among them forever.

title: The Afriq Demon: The Origin of Africa's Name
summary: According to Berber tradition, the name 'Africa' (Ifriqiya) derives from Afriq, a legendary demon or tribal deity worshiped by ancient North African peoples. The Afriq was a powerful spirit associated with the cave-dwelling peoples of Libya and Tunisia. Some accounts describe Afriq as a serpentine demon who demanded human sacrifice and terrorized the ancient Berber tribes. The Roman writer Pliny the Elder recorded that the name 'Africa' came from the 'Afri' tribe, but Berber oral tradition offers a mythological alternative: the demon Afriq was eventually defeated by a hero who sealed it in a cave beneath the Atlas Mountains. In another version, Afriq was a queen who founded a city that later gave its name to the continent. The root 'FRQ' in Berber languages relates to 'separate' or 'divide,' and some traditions say the demon Afriq was the spirit that divided the peoples of the earth. Whatever its true origin, the legend of Afriq as a primal demon-figure who gave the continent its name persists in Berber oral tradition, particularly among the Kabyle people of Algeria.

title: The Ahö'li and the Kachinas of Walpi
summary: In Walpi lived an old Ahö'li Kachina with his sister, the Kachin-mana, leading her because of his age and frailty. They planted in their field south of Walpi, depositing prayer offerings at a báho shrine. Meanwhile, the Ââ'ototo, Big-Horn Kachina, and others gathered and descended the mesa, marking shrines between villages. They encountered the Cóoyoko, a dangerous being with protruding eyes, a large knife, and rattles around his body, who killed and devoured children. The Kachinas negotiated safe passage, promising Cóoyoko could destroy only the bad. The Kachinas descended to a beautiful house in the valley where they sang all night, and the next morning rain poured. By noon, the fields were filled with corn, melons, and squashes. Big-Skeleton (Wokómásauwuu), who owns the earth, met them and told them to live on top of the mesa, where Walpi eventually moved.

title: The Aku-Aku Spirits of Rapa Nui
summary: The Aku-Aku are the powerful ancestral spirits of Rapa Nui, believed to inhabit the island's caves, cliffs, and sacred sites. These spirits could be both protectors and tricksters, guiding the living toward prosperity or leading them astray. The Aku-Aku were deeply connected to the moai statues—each moai embodied an ancestor's spirit, channeling their mana to protect the community. Oral traditions tell of spirit encounters in caves, where Aku-Aku would offer knowledge in exchange for offerings. The most powerful Aku-Aku was Ure, who taught the islanders the art of moai carving. Belief in Aku-Aku persists today, and many Rapanui still avoid certain caves and areas believed to be spirit dwellings.

title: The Akvan Div (The Demon of Madness)
summary: In the Shahnameh, the Akvan Div is a fearsome demon of madness who terrorizes Iran. King Kay Khosrow sends Rostam to destroy him. The demon finds Rostam sleeping and, instead of killing him outright, tosses him into the sea (a trick of his mad nature). Rostam swims ashore and, using cleverness, tricks the Akvan Div into revealing where he keeps his external soul. In a final confrontation, Rostam decapitates the demon, whose severed head continues to speak and curse. The Akvan Div represents the chaotic, irrational forces that threaten the civilized order of Iran, and his defeat demonstrates that brute force alone cannot overcome madness — cunning and intelligence are required.

title: The Al (Childbirth Demoness)
summary: In Persian folklore, the Al is a demonic being personifying puerperal fever, targeting women during and after childbirth. The name derives from Iranian 'al' meaning red, and she is described as a red-haired, stunted female creature with a rudimentary black humanoid form. She attacks mothers within the first six days after birth, causing sickness (al-zadagi) and death. Belief in the Al is widespread across Iran, the Caucasus, and Central Asia, with parallels in Jewish Lilith, Mesopotamian Lamaštu, and Armenian al traditions. Talismanic scrolls (hmayils) invoking saints are used to ward her off. She steals livers of newborn infants and must be neutralized by piercing her nose.

title: The Al and the Shepherd's Fire
summary: A band of shepherds on the high pastures of Ararat discover that the darkness between their campfires is not empty, and that the Al watches from the space between flames.

title: the Al-Mi'raj, the Desert Unicorn
summary: A yellow, rabbit-like creature with a single spiraling horn that can kill any beast — because in the deserts of Lebanon, the most dangerous thing is not the lion or the scorpion, but the thing you do not see coming.

title: The Altai Creation Myth
summary: The Altai creation myth is the foundational cosmology of the Altai Turks. In the beginning, there was only water — a primordial ocean covering everything. The supreme god Kayra Han (also Bai-Ulgen) sent a loon (or in some versions, a golden bird called galbingaa) to dive to the bottom of the ocean to bring up mud. From this mud, Kayra Han created the earth. He then planted the sacred tree Ulukayın (Bay-Terek), which grew with nine branches representing the nine heavens. From the roots of this tree, nine human ancestors emerged, forming the nine races of humanity. Kayra Han created the god Ulgen for goodness and Erlik for the underworld, establishing the dualistic balance between light and darkness. When Erlik tried to rival Kayra Han, he was cast down to the underworld where he rules as the god of death. The myth was recorded by Wilhelm Radloff in the 19th century.

title: the Amaru, Sacred Serpent of the Andes
summary: A massive winged serpent that lives in the deepest lakes of the Andes, carrying the bones of the dead between worlds — and when it surfaces, earthquakes split the mountains.

title: The Amur River Spirit
summary: A Nanai legend about the powerful spirit of the Amur River, known as the 'Dragon River' or Amur Father. According to tradition, the Amur is a living entity with its own will and consciousness. The river spirit can be generous or wrathful, providing abundant fish to those who respect it and drowning those who offend it. Shamans would perform rituals on the riverbanks to communicate with the Amur spirit, making offerings of millet, tobacco, and rings. The legend tells of the spirit appearing as a giant fish, a serpent-dragon, or an old man with a long white beard emerging from the river's waters. The Amur is considered the source of all life for the Nanai people, and it is taboo to speak disrespectfully of the river or to pollute its waters without making proper offerings.

title: the Anata, Spirit of the Carnival
summary: An ancient spirit of joy and chaos that wakes each February to ride through the streets on the backs of devils, scattering flowers and coins and madness — because the Aymara believe that grief must be drowned in celebration.

title: The Ancestor Who Guarded the Forest
summary: Ema, the ancestor-spirit, protects the mountain forests of Timor and punishes those who take more than they need from the land.

title: The Angara River's Escape
summary: A famous Buryat legend about the Angara River, the only river that flows out of Lake Baikal. According to the tale, Baikal had many sons (the rivers that flow into the lake) and one beautiful daughter named Angara. Baikal, a stern and possessive father, kept Angara imprisoned beneath a great rock to prevent her from leaving. But Angara fell in love with the hero Yenisei (the great river) and escaped. Enraged, Baikal threw a massive rock (Shaman Stone) after her, but she had already reached her beloved Yenisei. The shaman-stone still stands at the Angara's source. Baikal's tears from losing his daughter formed the lake's great depth. This legend is deeply embedded in Buryat cultural identity and is frequently retold in art and literature.

title: The Angel
summary: A literary fairy tale about a celestial being's interaction with humans, emphasizing themes of redemption, divine intervention, and the contrast between the earthly and the spiritual realms.

title: The Animal Dance
summary: The Animal Dance was a hunting ceremony received by Sweet Medicine at the Sacred Mountain (Bear Butte) to bring success to Cheyenne hunters. In this elaborate ceremony, men dressed as various animals—buffalo, deer, elk, antelope—while members of the Bowstring Society pretended to hunt them. Everything was done backwards for amusement: the animals chased the hunters, and all moved in reverse directions. The ceremony involved the entire community, with women preparing special foods and regalia. It was both a serious spiritual appeal for successful hunts and a joyful celebration that reinforced social bonds.

title: The Anqa (Mythical Bird of Arabia)
summary: The Anqa (or Anqa Mughrib) is a golden, fabulous female bird in pre-Islamic Arab mythology, described as very beautiful and colorful with a long neck, human face, four pairs of wings, and a whiteness in its neck. She lives alone on Mount Qaf, flies far away, and only appears once in ages. Created by God with all perfections, she became a scourge (hence the word 'anqa also means calamity) and was exterminated by a pre-Islamic prophet. She lives 1,700 years, mates at 500, and her chick stays in the egg for 125 years. Often identified with the Persian Simurgh and the phoenix, in Turkish she is called Zümrüdü Anka (the Emerald Anqa).

title: The Ants That Pushed on the Pine Tree
summary: A Pueblo story from Isleta about Kahp-too-óo-yoo (Corn-stalk Young Man), a famous hunter, warrior, and wizard who controlled the clouds and brought rain. After being bewitched by a false friend, he was imprisoned in the top of a giant pine tree that reached the sky. His family and village suffered from drought without his rain powers. The Little Black Ant discovered Kahp-too-óo-yoo in the tree and summoned all the armies of the Little Black Ants and Big Red Ants. They climbed the tree, placed a cup of cornmeal and honey at the top, and then — with the Black Ants pushing from above and the Red Ants pulling from below — drove the giant pine tree deep into the earth, freeing Kahp-too-óo-yoo. He returned home, playing his flute, and the rains returned. The story reflects Pueblo values of community, cooperation, and the power of even the smallest creatures to help.

title: The Apache Origin of the Animals
summary: After the Apaches emerged from the underworld, they traveled south for four days with only seeds to eat. A Raven brought a quiver with meat to a teepee, and when children ate the meat they became instantly fat. The Raven's meat was stolen, and he flew to his eastern mountain home. An Apache boy was transformed into a puppy to spy on the Ravens. Hidden in a young raven's blanket, the puppy watched as an old raven removed a flat stone, revealing an opening to the underworld. Each evening, a buffalo emerged and was eaten. After four days, the boy resumed human shape, descended into the underworld with white and black feathers, and claimed the buffalo. All the animals followed him to the Apache camp. But an old grandmother struck a deer's nose with a fire stick, leaving a white mark and decreeing that animals would avoid humans. Thus the harmony between humans and animals ended, and deer now use their noses to detect humans from afar.

title: The Ark of the Covenant at Axum
summary: After Menelik I was anointed king of Ethiopia in Jerusalem, the elders of Israel's tribes — jealous of Solomon's favor toward his Ethiopian son — decided that the firstborn sons of Israel's nobles should accompany Menelik back to Ethiopia. Before departing, Azariah, son of the high priest Zadok, stole the Ark of the Covenant from the Temple, replacing it with a replica. Guided by divine light, the Ark traveled to Ethiopia, where it was installed at Axum with great ceremony. The Ark, called Tabot Zion or Zion of the Holy of Holies, brought God's presence to Ethiopia. It is kept in the Church of Our Lady Mary of Zion, guarded by a single monk who spends his life in its service. The Ark's presence is believed to make Ethiopia the New Jerusalem, God's chosen nation on earth, and it remains the most sacred object in Ethiopian Orthodox Christianity.

title: The Artful Lad
summary: A clever servant lad helps a poor farmer by exposing his unfaithful wife who feeds the neighbor instead of her husband. The lad tricks the neighbor into giving him grain, repeatedly exhumes a spying old woman (the neighbor's mother-in-law) who dies in a chest, and manages three funerals before finally burying her for good.

title: The Aurora Spirits' Dance
summary: The Northern Lights are the spirits of the dead playing ball in the sky — and if you whistle to them, they will send you a gift.

title: The Awful Fate of Mr. Wolf
summary: Brer Wolf, determined to catch and eat Brer Rabbit, devises a plan to trap him in his own home. Brer Wolf hides in Brer Rabbit's house, planning to spring out when Brer Rabbit returns. But Brer Rabbit, always cautious, notices fresh tracks around the door and realizes something is wrong. He calls out, pretending to talk to himself: 'I wonder if Brer Wolf is in there. I'll just go ask my friend the cow if there's any fresh wolf tracks around.' Brer Wolf, thinking quickly, ties a string to a rock that he bounces to make it sound like he's not there. But Brer Rabbit sees through the trick and sets the house on fire. Brer Wolf burns to death inside, or in other versions, escapes with his fur singed and vows revenge. The story shows that Brer Rabbit's caution and intelligence allow him not just to escape but to turn the predator's own trap against him. Among African American audiences, the tale resonated as a message to the powerless: vigilance and cleverness can defeat even the most determined enemy.

title: The Awonawilona Creation (Zuni)
summary: In the Zuni creation myth recorded by Frank Cushing, only Áwonawílona, the All-Father, Maker and Container of All, existed in the beginning. He made himself into the Sun Father (Yatoka). The mist clouds formed into the Great Waters, from which Earth Mother (Áwitelin Tsíta) and Sky Father (Ápoyan Ta'chu) emerged. Together they conceived all men and creatures in the four-fold womb of the world. The Sun Father and Earth Mother brought forth the Twin Children of the Sun — the brothers Ko'wituma and Wats'usi (the Ahayuta twins) — who were given sacred knowledge, caps, bows, arrows, and shields to have dominion over all beings. The twins descended into the first underworld (Ánosin Téhuli) and formed a ladder for people to ascend to the second cave-world (Moss World, K'ólin Téhuli), then to the third (World of Mud, Áwisho Téhuli), and finally the fourth cave-world (Wing World, Tépahaian Téhuli), where the twins taught men the ways of life before they entered the Daylight World (Ték'ohaian Úlahnane).

title: The Baccoo and the Provisions
summary: A small, hairy, one-eyed trickster spirit sneaks into kitchens at night to steal food and tangle household work, punishing the lazy and rewarding the generous.

title: The Bakwa of the Morning
summary: The Bakwa, a great serpent of Kalinago legend, brings mist and rain to the island, and its appearance is both a blessing and a warning.
themes: the interconnectedness of nature and culture
the danger of dismissing ancestral knowledge

title: The Ball Game of the Hero Twins
summary: The Hero Twins Hunahpu and Xbalanque descend to Xibalba and challenge the Lords of Death to a ball game — with their own lives as stakes.

title: The Ballad of Mahua — Forbidden Love in Bengal
summary: One of the most famous ballads of the Maimansingha Gitika, Mahua tells the story of a young Brahmin man named Naderchand who falls in love with Mahua, a beautiful girl from the much lower Kaibarta (fisherman) caste. Despite the rigid social hierarchies of 18th-century Bengal, the two lovers pursue their forbidden romance. The ballad depicts the tension between individual desire and societal norms, with vivid scenes of Bengali village life. Mahua's beauty, the secret meetings by the river, and the ultimate tragic consequences of their cross-caste love resonate with universal themes of love against social convention. The ballad is notable for its lyrical beauty and its unflinching portrayal of the pain caused by caste discrimination in traditional Bengali society.

title: The Bamboo of a Hundred Sections
summary: A classic Vietnamese folk tale about a poor, hardworking orphan named Anh (or Khoai) who was taken in by a wealthy but cruel landlord. The landlord promised his beautiful daughter in marriage to Anh if he worked for three years without complaint. Anh faithfully completed his service, but the landlord refused to honor his promise and instead demanded that Anh bring him a 'bamboo of a hundred sections' as a final condition — an impossible task since bamboo naturally has continuous joints without divisions. Heartbroken, Anh went into the forest weeping, where a kind spirit (or a magical old man in some versions) took pity on him and taught him the magic words: 'Join together, join together, bamboo sections, join together.' Anh chanted the words, and the bamboo sections magically fused into one hundred-jointed stalk. When the landlord saw the miraculous bamboo and scoffed at it, Anh chanted the reverse spell: 'Separate, separate, bamboo sections, separate.' At this, not only did the bamboo separate, but the landlord himself was split into a hundred pieces. Anh then married the landlord's daughter, who had always loved him, and they lived happily. The tale is a classic Vietnamese story about the triumph of perseverance, kindness, and justice over greed and deception.

title: The Banshee
summary: A spectral guardian whose mournful wail heralds the passing of those from the ancient bloodlines of Ireland.

title: The Banshee: Weeping Woman of Ireland
summary: A spirit who wails before death, foretelling the end of a family line—the O'Brien clan is marked.

title: The Baobab Tree's Origin (Mande/Senegal)
summary: According to the Mande people, the baobab tree once grew in the heavens, and its fruits were reserved for the gods. A trickster spirit stole a baobab seedling and planted it on Earth so humans could enjoy its fruit and medicine. The gods were furious and pulled the tree upside down, leaving its roots exposed in the air as punishment. This is why the baobab looks like it is planted upside down, with its branches resembling roots reaching toward the sky. Despite this punishment, the baobab tree remained generous, providing food, water, medicine, and shelter to humans and animals. Its bark is used for rope, its leaves for medicine, its fruit for nourishment, and its hollow trunk for shelter. The baobab is considered the tree of life across West Africa.

title: The Barrel Bung
summary: Famine has struck the parish of Bolinge. All the cows have gone dry except for those belonging to the rich, elderly Lady Skinflint and her ugly daughter, who somehow have hundreds of cheeses and tubs of butter from only four cows. When Jerker, the eldest son of the poor farmer Jonson, discovers that his family's cow Star has stopped giving milk, he decides to investigate. He stays awake and catches the family tomte (house spirit), who tells him the answer lies in Lady Skinflint's storeroom. Jerker trades his Sunday clothes for food and offers himself as a farmhand at the manor. He breaks the lock on the storeroom and hides to observe. That night, he watches Lady Skinflint take out a large barrel bung (stopper), wedge it into a hole in the wall, and milk the udders of the villagers' cows that magically appear through the bung. Enraged, Jerker recites a rhyme that causes a cow's leg to kick out from the bung instead, beating the old woman and her daughter until they beg for mercy. Jerker forces them to hand over all the gold they earned from stealing milk and takes the magic bung. He returns the gold to the villagers, who share it equally, rewarding Jerker with a portion that allows him to buy a farm and marry his sweetheart. He destroys the bung in a fire so it can never harm anyone again.

title: The Basilisk in the Cistern
summary: When a basilisk takes up residence in the Vatican's ancient cistern, a young seminarian must descend into the dark to face the creature whose gaze alone can kill.

title: The Battle of the Mountains
summary: The mountains of the central North Island were once living warriors who fought for the love of the beautiful mountain Pihanga. Tongariro, the greatest volcano, won her heart. In jealousy, Taranaki (then located in the center) challenged Tongariro. During their terrible battle, Tongariro erupted in fury and Taranaki was defeated. Wounded and exiled, Taranaki carved a great path as he moved westward, forming the Whanganui River. He now stands alone near the west coast, his peak forever turned away from the central plateau where Pihanga lies. The story also includes Ruapehu and Ngauruhoe, Tongariro's faithful allies.

title: The Battle of the Noaidis
summary: A story about two powerful noaidi who engage in a spiritual battle using their drums and helping spirits. The noaidi could send their free souls into animals and control them to spy on enemies. The most powerful could create a Stállu from earth, wood, or turf, giving it part of their own life force, and send it to fight their enemies. This demonstrates the shamanic powers of the noaidi.

title: The Battle of the Twins
summary: Sapling and Flint's conflict over the world they had created came to a head when they agreed to settle their rivalry through combat. Sapling chose the branches of the giant crab apple tree as his weapon, while Flint preferred poisonous roots, monster's teeth, and serpent fangs. They fought for many days across the landscape. The battle ended when Sapling overthrew Flint. He sent his evil brother to live in the underworld, but could not destroy him entirely. It was agreed that the world would need both good and evil, light and darkness. Even in victory, Sapling decreed that his brother would continue to influence the world, bringing winter, darkness, and death to balance the good he had created.

title: The Bear Ceremony
summary: A 48-part antiphonal bear song recorded in 1775 that reenacts the Sámi bear ceremony. The bear was considered sacred, 'the only animal related to man.' The ceremonial hunt aimed to remove a fierce competitor while winning the bear's power and ensuring its reincarnation. The bear's death was celebrated with the bear participating symbolically. The yoik cycle covers from the felling to the feast days later.

title: The Bear Ceremony (Chakhlynd)
summary: The central Nivkh myth explaining the origin of the bear ceremony (chakhlynd), the most important ritual in Nivkh culture. The legend tells of a woman who married a bear in human form. She returned to her village with her bear-children, and the bear was killed by her relatives. Before dying, the bear promised that if people would honor bears in a special ceremony, the bear spirits would provide protection, good hunting, and prosperity. The ceremony involves raising a bear cub in a special enclosure for several years, treating it as an honored guest, before sacrificing it in a carefully ritualized manner. The bear's spirit is believed to return to the mountain god and report on how it was treated. The ceremony, which can last several days, includes elaborate singing, dancing, dog sacrifices, and feasting. It reinforces the sacred relationship between humans, animals, and the spirit world.

title: The Bear Mother (Haida)
summary: In this classic Haida narrative, a woman who mocked the bears was taken by a bear who made her his wife. She was led into the bear's den deep in the forest, where she lived among the bear people and bore children who were half-human, half-bear. Her human brothers eventually tracked her down and killed the bears in a great hunt, but the woman herself had been transformed by her time with the bears. This story, common across many Northwest Coast tribes including the Tlingit version known as Kaats' and the Bear, serves to explain the special relationship between humans and bears. The bear woman's children became powerful ancestors, and her story validates the bear as a crest figure for certain clans. It also teaches respect for all animal people and warns against the dangers of disrespecting the natural world.

title: The Bear Who Married a Woman (Tsimshian)
summary: A Tsimshian woman gathering berries in the forest encountered a bear who removed his bearskin and revealed himself as a handsome man. He took her to his village, where the bear people lived just like humans inside their lodges but appeared as bears to outsiders. The woman married him, learned the ways of the bear people, and gave birth to children who were half-human, half-bear. Her husband provided abundantly for her, bringing salmon and berries. She grew content with her bear husband, but when her human brothers came searching for her, she was forced to choose between her two families. The brothers killed the bear husband in a hunt, but the woman begged them not to harm her children. The children grew up with special powers of communication between humans and bears. Their descendants became the Bear Clan. This cross-cultural marriage story, found throughout the Northwest Coast, establishes the bear as a relative rather than an animal, requiring respect and proper protocol in hunting.

title: The Beaver Bundle Ceremony
summary: The Beaver Bundle is the most sacred medicine bundle of the Blackfoot people, said to have been given by the underwater spirits. According to legend, a Blackfoot man encountered beavers who taught him sacred songs, rituals, and the use of medicinal plants. The bundle contains various sacred objects including animal skins, pipes, and herbs, each with specific powers. The Beaver Bundle ceremony involves elaborate rituals, singing, and smoking the pipe. It is used for healing, ensuring good fortune, and maintaining the balance between the human and spirit worlds. The bundle is passed down through generations with great ceremony.

title: The Bell of the Morning
summary: The Sphinx of ancient Greece is one of the most famous monsters in all of mythology.

title: The Bell Witch
summary: Although the Bell Witch of Tennessee is one of America's most famous supernatural legends, its African American dimensions are often overlooked. Enslaved people on the Bell plantation near Adams, Tennessee, had their own interpretations of the entity that tormented the Bell family from 1817 to 1821. While white accounts describe the witch as the ghost of Kate Batts, African American oral traditions viewed the Bell Witch as a 'haint' connected to the horrors of slavery itself—a spirit born from the suffering of the enslaved on the plantation. Some accounts from formerly enslaved people describe the witch as a Boo Hag-like entity that could shed its skin and fly. The enslaved community used their own protective measures—salt, sulfur, haint blue paint, and conjure bags—to ward off the entity, often with greater success than the Bells' reliance on prayer and Christian ritual. The Bell Witch thus represents a convergence of African and European supernatural traditions on American soil.

title: The Bennu Bird and the Primordial Mound
summary: The Bennu bird—the inspiration for the Greek phoenix—was a self-created being associated with the sun god Ra and the city of Heliopolis. According to the Heliopolitan creation myth, before the world existed there was only the dark, watery abyss of Nun. From these primordial waters arose a mound of earth—the Benben—the first dry land. Upon this mound perched the Bennu bird, a heron-like deity who, with a cry, broke the primeval silence and initiated creation. The Bennu's call marked the beginning of time. Alternatively, the Bennu emerged from the flames of a sacred persea tree in Heliopolis. Each morning at dawn, the Bennu renews itself, representing the daily rebirth of the sun. It was associated with the cycle of life, death, and rebirth, and with Osiris as lord of resurrection. The Egyptian word for the Benben stone relates to the verb 'weben' (to rise), linking the Bennu to the rising sun. Later adapted by Greek writers as the phoenix, the legend spread throughout the Mediterranean world.

title: The Berber Creation Myth
summary: In the beginning, the universe was vast empty darkness. Within this void existed a supreme being known as Amun or Anzar, the embodiment of perfection with the power to create and destroy. First, the sky and earth were formed in perfect harmony—the sky personified as a male deity, the earth as a female. From their union, water was born, giving life to the barren world. The supreme being then created various deities to govern aspects of nature—the sea, mountains, wind, fertility, and war. Finally, humans were crafted from the earth itself, molded by the hands of the gods and given the breath of life. Humans were considered part of the natural world, living in harmony with the earth and venerating the gods who governed the forces of nature.

title: The Best Wish
summary: Three brothers each receive one wish. The elders wish for money, but the youngest wishes that every woman he sees falls in love with him, leading to a life of luxury and affection.

title: The Betrayal of Friends
summary: Two lifelong friends living in different parts of Greenland maintain a deep bond by exchanging gifts of seal and reindeer meat. However, jealousy grows in one friend, who decides to curse the other by rubbing seal fat with a piece of a corpse onto the food he shares. The betrayed friend, warned by his tornak (protective spirit), falls ill. The curse eventually consumes the betrayer, driving him to madness and a murderous hunger for his friend, ending in a tragic death in a cave.

title: The Bewitching of Sultan in the Desert
summary: A young Bedouin merchant traveling alone through the Empty Quarter encounters Umm Al Duwais, whose deadly beauty nearly claims his life before the adhan saves him.

title: The Bewitchment of Angutisugsuk
summary: A family is plagued by sudden, unexplained hatred and violence. It is revealed that they have been bewitched by a malevolent spirit, forcing family members to fight one another. The story serves as a cautionary tale about the power of external spiritual influence and the importance of shamanic intervention to restore harmony.

title: The Big Bird Dan
summary: A tale involving a giant bird named Dan who becomes an unlikely ally to a courageous protagonist. The story explores the relationship between humans and the mythical creatures of the wild, focusing on trust and the breaking of ancient curses.

title: The Big House Ceremony (Xinkwikaon)
summary: The Big House Ceremony is the paramount spiritual tradition of the Lenape people. According to oral tradition, the ceremony was given to the ancestors long ago when the people lived in the East. It is held in a special longhouse built to face the east, with carved faces on the center posts representing the Creator and the spirits. The ceremony lasts for twelve nights, during which the people pray, sing, and dance to fulfill their obligations to the spiritual forces of the universe. Participants use turtle-shell rattles and carved drumsticks, and each night a new fire is kindled with a fire-drill. The ceremony expresses gratitude to Kishelamakank, the four directions, and all of creation. The tradition declined during the forced removals but was revived through the dedication of elders who preserved the sacred songs and the original words.

title: The Big White Dog and the Sacred Pole (Chickasaw)
summary: In this Chickasaw origin story, a great white dog led the people on their migration and guided them with the sacred pole. The white dog was sent by Ababinili to protect the Chickasaw people during their long journey from the west. Each day, the dog would lead the way, and at night, the sacred pole was planted in the ground. The direction the pole leaned would indicate the path for the next day's travel. After many years, the pole finally stood upright at the site where the Chickasaw would settle. The great white dog then disappeared, its mission complete. The white dog is honored in Chickasaw tradition as a symbol of faithfulness, protection, and divine guidance. The story emphasizes the Chickasaw belief that animals are spiritual beings sent to assist humans.

title: The Bird Grip
summary: A king goes blind, and an old woman tells him that only the song of the magical bird Grip — kept in a cage by a king in another land — can restore his sight.
