His eldest son sets out to fetch the bird but stops at a merry inn and forgets his mission, drinking and gambling. The second son does the same. The youngest son, however, resists temptation and continues his journey. He stays at a sinister inn where the host murders guests who cannot pay. The prince pays the dead man's debt, arranges his burial, and escapes with the help of a captive maid. He then meets a talking fox who becomes his guide. The fox gives him magic grains to steal the bird Grip, but warns him not to stroke it. The prince succeeds in taking the bird but strokes it anyway, causing it to scream. Captured, he is put on trial and, following the fox's advice, answers 'Yes' when asked if he is a master thief. The king spares him on condition that he steal the world's most beautiful princess, then a golden horse. Each time the prince succeeds with the fox's help (though he nearly fails each time by breaking the fox's warnings). After rescuing the princess and horse, the prince finds his jealous older brothers about to be hanged for debt. He ransoms them, but they betray him, throwing him into a lion pit and claiming the treasures for themselves. The bird will not sing, the horse will not be ridden, and the princess weeps constantly. The prince escapes the lions (the fox was there protecting him), beheads the fox (which transforms into the dead man whose debt he paid), and disguises himself as a horse-shoer. He fits the horse with golden shoes and, by calling the bird by name, makes it sing, restoring the king's sight. The truth is revealed, the brothers are banished, and the youngest marries the princess.

title: The Birth of Changing Woman
summary: In the Navajo tradition, Changing Woman (Asdzą́ą́ Nádleehé) was the first human born in the Fourth World. She was originally born as Yoołgaii Asdzą́ą́ (White Shell Girl) and matured into Changing Woman, a central deity who represents the cycles of life, the seasons, and the earth itself. She later gives birth to the Hero Twins, Monster Slayer (Naayééʼ Neizghání) and Child of the Water (Tóbájíshchíní), who defeat the monsters plaguing the Navajo people. Changing Woman eventually departs to live in the west, where she resides in a floating house made of turquoise and abalone, creating the seasons as she ages and rejuvenates each year.

title: The Birth of the Twin Brothers: Sapling and Flint
summary: After Sky Woman's daughter Tekawerahkwa (Breath of the Wind) gave birth, the twin boys emerged in different ways. The right-handed twin, Sapling (Hahgwehdi-yu or Kanehtó:ton), was born naturally and became the creator of all that is good and beautiful in the world. The left-handed twin, Flint (Hahgwehdaetgah or Okarahtsikó:wa), forced his way out through his mother's armpit, killing her. From her buried body grew the sacred plants: tobacco from her heart and strawberries from her feet. The twins then set about completing the creation, each making their own contributions to the natural world, with Flint attempting to undo all of Sapling's good work.

title: The Biton Who Dwelt in the River
summary: A Biton spirit claimed a stretch of the White Nile as its own, flooding the banks each night in retribution for a fisherman's greed, until an elder brokered a fragile peace between the human and spirit worlds.

title: The Black Bull of Norroway
summary: A princess defies her family's wishes to follow a magical bull to a kingdom of wonder.

title: The Black-Necked Crane of Bhutan
summary: In Bhutan, the black-necked crane (Thrung Thrung Karmo) is revered as a sacred bird and believed to be the soul of virtuous monks returned to earth in elegant form. Legend says the cranes circle the Gangteng Monastery three times in a clockwise direction upon their arrival in the Phobjikha Valley each October — a traditional Buddhist circumambulation (kora) that is seen as a blessing. The Sixth Dalai Lama, Tsangyang Gyatso, wrote a famous poem: 'Oh white crane, lend me your wings, I'm not going far and away.' Local farmers believe that the arrival of healthy crane numbers promises good harvests, while a decrease foretolds leaner years. The cranes are thought to understand the traditional astrological calendar, timing their migration accordingly. The annual Black-Necked Crane Festival (November 11) features schoolchildren in black-and-white costumes performing the crane dance. Killing a crane carries a sentence of life imprisonment.

title: The Blackfoot Creation: Apistotoke, Na'pi, and the World
summary: Apistotoke (Ihtsipatapiyohpa), the Great Spirit, created first the Sky Beings: Naato'si the Sun, Ko'komiki'somm the Moon, and the stars including Aapisowaahs the Morning Star. He then created Ksahkomitapi (Earth) as mother to all creation. Apistotoke created Na'pi (Old Man), the first man and demigod who shaped the world with his wife Kipitaakii (Old Lady). Using mud collected by Turtle during a great flood, Na'pi designed the earth, then created men, women, animals, and plants. He taught the Blackfoot people which plants to eat and animals to hunt, especially the buffalo.

title: The Blind Men and the Elephant
summary: In a bustling city of ancient India, six blind men heard that a strange animal called an elephant had been brought to the town.

title: The Blue Belt
summary: A protagonist obtains a magical blue belt that grants superhuman strength and the ability to overcome impossible trials. Using the belt, they defeat monsters and solve the puzzles of a distant king to win a great reward.

title: The Blue Cap of Dalkeith
summary: A coal miner in the Dalkeith colliery befriends a Blue Cap spirit who shows him rich seams of coal, but warns that the gift comes with a price when greed overrides gratitude.

title: The Blue Caps
summary: In the coal mines of Scotland, deep beneath the earth where the daylight never reaches, there are helpers that the miners call the Blue Caps.

title: The Blue Lantern
summary: A ghost lantern leads travelers to ghostly villages in the Vietnamese mountains.

title: The Blue Wolf and the Fallow Doe: Ancestors of the Mongols
summary: According to the Secret History of the Mongols, the Mongol people descend from a blue wolf (Börte Chino) and a fallow doe (Göo Maral) sent by Tengri (Heaven). The wolf and doe crossed the Tengis Sea and settled near the source of the Onon River at Mount Burkhan Khaldun, where they gave birth to the first Mongol, named Batachiqan. This legendary origin story establishes the divine mandate of the Mongol ruling line and the sacred landscape of the Onon and Kherlen river region. The blue wolf ancestress myth was central to Genghis Khan's claim of heavenly authority to unite the Mongol tribes.

title: The Bluejay Cycle (Coast Salish)
summary: Bluejay is a prominent trickster figure in Coast Salish mythology, particularly among the Chemainus, Cowichan, and other Salish communities. He is generally a benevolent being who helps people, but he is also extremely foolish and careless, and stories about him are often humorous or slapstick. In one classic story, Bluejay boasted that he could steal the sun, but his lies got him into trouble when the people took him seriously and he had to deliver on his impossible promise. In another, he tried to imitate the skills of other animals and birds, with disastrously funny results. Bluejay often interacts with his long-suffering sister Ioi, who tries to keep him out of trouble but fails because Bluejay refuses to listen to good advice. Unlike Raven, who possesses genuine supernatural power, Bluejay's adventures typically stem from his foolishness rather than malice. The Bluejay stories serve as comic relief in the storytelling tradition while also teaching lessons about humility, honesty, and the dangers of boastfulness.

title: The Boiadeira of the Pantanal
summary: A phantom cattlewoman leads her ghostly herd through the mist of the Pantanal, and the cowboy who follows her into the swamp never returns.

title: The Boitatá Who Gave Sight
summary: A massive fire serpent guards the night fields, blinding the wicked with its gaze but lighting the way for those who walk with respect.

title: The Boo Hag
summary: In Gullah Geechee folklore, a young man named Emmet Fisher falls in love with a beautiful but mysterious woman who lives deep in the marsh. Against all warnings, he marries her. One night, Emmet pretends to be asleep and witnesses his bride remove her skin, hang it on a hook, and transform into a skinless red creature with bat-like wings. She flies out through the keyhole to ride her victims—sitting on their chests and stealing their breath while they sleep. Emmet confronts her the next morning, but she denies everything. He sprinkles cayenne pepper and salt around the room, and when she sheds her skin again that night, she cannot put it back on—the pepper burns her raw flesh. She flees into the night, forever skinless. The Boo Hag legend explains why Gullah people paint their doors and windows 'haint blue,' hang brooms by the entrance, and keep salt and pepper mixtures in corners: all ways to confuse, repel, or trap these night-visiting entities that drain the life force of the living.

title: The Book of the Dead: The Weighing of the Heart
summary: Central to ancient Egyptian funerary mythology is the judgment scene where the deceased's heart is weighed against the feather of Maat (truth and cosmic order) in the Hall of Two Truths. After death, the soul (the ba) journeys through the underworld (Duat), facing dangerous demons, fiery lakes, and gatekeepers. The climax is before Osiris, Lord of the Dead, enthroned with Isis and Nephthys behind him and the forty-two assessor gods before him. Anubis, the jackal-headed god of embalming, weighs the heart on a scale while Thoth, the ibis-headed scribe, records the verdict. If the heart balances with the feather, the deceased is declared 'true of voice' and is allowed to enter the Field of Reeds—a paradise of eternal life. If the heart is heavier with sin, it is devoured by Ammit, the 'Devourer of the Dead'—a composite creature with the head of a crocodile, the torso of a lion, and the hindquarters of a hippopotamus—and the soul ceases to exist. Spells from the Book of the Dead were placed in tombs to guide the deceased through this judgment.

title: The Bori Dance of Iskoki
summary: A Hausa healer undergoes the bori trance ritual to negotiate with the Iskoki spirits, discovering that the boundary between madness and divine knowledge is thinner than a drumbeat.
themes: the invisible world layered over the visible

title: The Boto Who Wore a Hat
summary: A pink river dolphin transforms into a handsome man to attend a village party, but a white hat cannot fully hide his true form.

title: The Bouda: Were-Hyenas of Ethiopia
summary: Certain clans are believed to possess the power to transform into hyenas at night.

title: The Boy and the Tomte Cap
summary: A burlesque story about a boy who borrows the tomte's invisibility cap and embarks on hair-raising adventures. With the cap's magic, he rescues an enchanted girl from a troll's power and wins both her hand and great riches. The tale follows the classic trickster-hero pattern common in Swedish folklore where a clever human outwits supernatural beings.

title: The Boy and the Trolls, or The Adventure
summary: An unnamed young lad packs his lunch, leaves the city, and heads into the woods in search of adventure. Meanwhile, in the kingdom, the young princess has gone missing, and her father the king has surrendered control of the realm to his second wife — a conniving woman suspected of orchestrating her stepdaughter's disappearance. On his journey, the boy encounters three troll brothers — Big Brother (with enormous ears), Medium Brother (with a huge chin), and Little Brother (with a prominent nose). Through his unfailingly polite manner, the boy treats them as he would any strangers, calling them 'uncle.' The trolls, who think the boy is hideous (to accentuate their own beauty), are heading home to their mother's mountain with treasures (silver, gold, precious stones) and delicacies (a garden snake, a frog, a toad) to court a captive princess. The boy follows them. Inside the mountain, the princess is being held captive by the troll mother until she chooses which son to marry. Benevolent elves bring fresh air and fruit, but cannot break the trolls' magic. The boy learns from the troll mother that the queen is actually her sister — a troll herself. The only thing that can defeat the trolls is a magic spell spoken by a fearless boy. The boy recites the words, rescues the princess, and they return to the city with the trolls' treasure. There, the evil queen is plotting to seal all windows and build a wall against the west wind. The boy exposes the queen as a troll, recites the magic words again, and the west wind blows the trolls away. The boy is rewarded, and the kingdom is saved.

title: The Boy Hunter Who Never Sacrificed to the Deer
summary: A Zuni story about a boy who was an excellent hunter but never performed the proper sacrifices or prayers to the spirits of the deer he killed. As a result, the deer spirits became angry. The boy's disrespectful hunting caused supernatural consequences — his kills became tainted, and he began to have bad luck. The spirits of the deer he had killed without proper ceremony confronted him. To make amends, the boy had to learn the proper rituals of the hunt, including making prayer sticks, offering cornmeal, and speaking words of gratitude to the deer's spirit. This story explains the origin of the Society of Rattlesnakes, which has the power to heal snakebites and conduct ceremonies that maintain balance between humans and animals. The story reinforces the Zuni teaching that all life is sacred and must be taken with gratitude and proper ceremony.

title: The Boy Who Ate with the Giant
summary: A clever little boy uses a series of tricks — a bag of porridge, a handful of bird feathers, and a stone — to convince a giant that he is stronger and hungrier than the giant himself.

title: The Boy Who Crossed the Great Water and Returned
summary: A Hopi tale of a boy who journeyed across the great waters and returned with knowledge and power. The boy's curiosity led him to leave his village and travel east toward the rising sun. He encountered various supernatural beings and overcame trials, including crossing a body of water that no Hopi had crossed before. Guided by Spider Grandmother, he learned sacred songs and ceremonies from the spirits on the other side. When he returned to his people, he brought new ceremonies, dance forms, and agricultural knowledge that benefited the Hopi. The story reflects the Hopi belief that spiritual power and knowledge can be gained through journeys to sacred places and that those who venture forth with pure hearts return to enrich the community.

title: The Boy Who Had an Eating Match with a Troll
summary: A small but hungry boy is challenged to an eating contest by a massive troll. Using a clever trick involving a hidden bag of food and a misunderstanding of proportions, the boy manages to out-eat the troll and win a great prize.

title: The Boy Who Never Feared
summary: A boy devoid of fear is sent on perilous tasks by his father to teach him caution, only to outsmart a mountain troll through sheer audacity and wit.

title: The Boy Who Strapped the Troll to the Sled
summary: A boy wanders deep into the forest and comes to the trolls' cave. Because he is not receptive to their temptations, the trolls have no power to hold him and are forced to bring him home. The tale illustrates the folk belief that trolls can only hold power over those who yield to their enticements.

title: The Boy Who Went to the Wind's Cave
summary: Little Mats sets out on a perilous journey to the end of the world to find his kidnapped sister. To reach the Wind's Cave and the magical realm where she is held, he must make terrible sacrifices along the way, giving up one ear, one eye, and one hand, each loss enabling him to pass through a different barrier. When he finally reaches the wind's domain, he confronts the forces that took his sister and rescues her from captivity. As a reward, his losses are miraculously restored, and he wins a princess and half the kingdom.

title: The Boy With Enormous Nostrils
summary: An abused boy is mocked for his enormous nostrils. However, he discovers that his condition allows him to hear secrets and distant conversations that others cannot. He uses this hidden power to outsmart his tormentors, demonstrating that what others see as a flaw can be a great strength.

title: The Breath of Mze Moya
summary: When the great storm deity Mze Moya turned away from the island, the coconut palms withered and the sea went still, teaching the Comorian people that even the mightiest powers must be entreated with reverence.

title: The Brewing of Beer
summary: A high-stakes contest of beer-brewing takes place, where the quality of the brew is used as a measure of a person's magical skill and social status. The winners gain immense prestige, while those whose brews fail are subjected to public shame and ridicule.

title: The Bride's Farewell
summary: The bride reflects on her transition from the familiar lands of Pohjola to the strange shores of Kalevala. She expresses the profound sadness of leaving her family and the anxiety and uncertainty associated with her new life in a foreign land.

title: The Bride's Farewell (Variant)
summary: A further reflection on the bride's journey and the emotional weight of the union between the two rival lands. It emphasizes the role of women in bridging the gap between opposing cultures through marriage.

title: The Brooms' Broom, King of All Brooms
summary: Jon, a poor broom-maker living in the forest, decides to bind a magical broom: Kvastarnas kvast, alla kvastars kung. He visits three forest hags for help — Vingmor (flight), Tassmor (bouncing), and Labbmor (striking power). At the Great Mountain, he confronts the troll king, commands his broom to steal his scepter, and rescues lost husbands from the trolls. The broom is sold for enough to build a dream home.

title: The Brothers: A Tale of Two Brothers
summary: Two brothers inherit a farm and discover that true fortune is found in the kindness of one's heart, not the wealth in one's purse.

title: The Brown Bull of Cooley
summary: One night in the royal bedchamber of Cruachan, the capital of Connacht, a conversation began that would lead to one of the bloodiest wars in Irish mythology.

title: The Brownie
summary: In the misty glens and rolling hills of Scotland, there lived a creature that was neither fairy nor ghost, but something in between.

title: The Brownies (Tomtar)
summary: In Swedish folklore, tomtar (also called brownies or nisses) are small, elderly-looking men about the size of a three- or four-year-old child, dressed in gray clothes with red caps. They live on farms, usually in barns or pantries, and work tirelessly to maintain the household. They wake servants for threshing, help in forges by signaling when to turn the iron, and watch over the cattle. Where there is order and prosperity, the tomte thrives; where there is disrespect or uncleanliness, he leaves. One story tells of a farmer whose harvest never ran out. Hiding in the barn, he saw a crowd of tomtar each carrying a stalk of rye, including one tiny tomte no bigger than a thumb carrying a straw. When the farmer asked why the smallest one puffed so hard under such a light load, luck left his house forever. Another story tells of a tomte who was offered Christmas porridge with honey. When the porridge was too hot and the honey melted to the bottom, he thought there was no honey and killed a cow in anger. Finding the honey at the bottom of the bowl, he bitterly regretted his haste and stole an identical cow from a neighbor to replace the one he killed. Yet another tale describes a housewife whose meal bins never emptied. Peeking through the door, she saw a tomte sifting meal tirelessly. Feeling grateful, she made him new clothes and left them on the bin. When he tried to sift while wearing his fine new suit, the meal made him dusty. He threw down the sieve and declared, 'Junker Grand is dusting himself. He shall sift no more,' and all his blessings ceased. These stories teach that one should never call attention to the brownies' work or try to reward them openly.

title: The Buda of the Lowlands
summary: A Tigre herdsman encounters a Buda, a shapeshifter who can take the form of any animal or person, and learns that the most dangerous monsters look exactly like you.

title: The Buda Woman of Asmara
summary: A Nara woman in Asmara is suspected of being a Buda when her neighbors notice her shadow does not match her body, forcing a community to confront the line between suspicion and justice.

title: The Buffalo Woman of the Mande (Mande)
summary: In the land of Dô, a buffalo terrorized the countryside, destroying crops and killing hunters. Two brothers, Oulamba and Oulani, discovered that the buffalo was actually a woman named Sogolon who transformed into the beast each night after being cursed by a rival. Following the advice of a wise hunter, one brother married Sogolon in her human form, breaking the curse. Sogolon was already pregnant with a child destined for greatness. This buffalo-woman gave birth to Sundiata Keita, the hero of the Mande people. The story explains Sogolon's mysterious origins, her hunchback appearance, and why Sundiata was prophesied to become a mighty king. It demonstrates the Mande belief that greatness often comes from humble or strange beginnings.

title: the Bukit Timah Monkey Man
summary: A half-man half-monkey creature that lurks in the dense forest of Bukit Timah, stealing fruit and scaring hikers, because even in a city of five million the jungle remembers.

title: The Bulgasari Who Ate the Iron
summary: A metal-eating beast born from the famine of the 1990s, devouring the iron fences and copper wires of a nation that locked its gates from the inside — because hunger makes beasts of everything.

title: The Bura of the Deep Waters
summary: Fishermen on the Kura River encounter a Bura, a water demon who demands a price for every fish pulled from the deep pools, and learn that some bargains are best left unmade.

title: The Buryat Earth-Diver Creation
summary: The classic Buryat creation myth — an earth-diver story similar to those found across Central Asia. In the beginning, the sky god Sombov looked down upon the primordial waters and saw the water bird Anghir. He commanded the bird to dive to the depths and retrieve material for making the earth. Anghir brought up black earth and red clay. Sombov made the earth from the black soil and humans from the red clay. These first humans were covered in wool. Sombov left a furless dog to guard his creations while he went to heaven for souls. The devil Shiktur (Erlik) approached the shivering dog, promised it a warm coat, and upon gaining access, spat on the humans — causing their wool to disappear except in certain places. This explains both human imperfection and why dogs still shiver despite their fur.

title: The Butterfly Lovers
summary: A young woman disguises herself as a man to study, falling in love with a fellow student, only to face a tragic end that transforms them into eternal companions.

title: The Bäckahästen – The Brook Horse of Åland's Waters
summary: The bäckahästen (brook horse) is a shapeshifting water spirit that appears as a beautiful, seemingly tame horse near streams, lakes, or the sea. When someone climbs onto its back, the horse gallops into the water and drowns its rider. The legend was particularly used to warn children away from dangerous waters. In some versions, the bäckahästen can be tricked by throwing a piece of steel or iron over its head, forcing it to revert to its true form. This creature overlaps with the Näcken tradition and is closely related to the Celtic kelpie. The countless inlets, streams, and shallow coastal waters of the Åland archipelago made this a particularly relevant cautionary tale for island children. The creature appears numerous times in the Sagenkartan entries from the Swedish-speaking regions of Finland.

title: The Böögg: The Swiss Bogeyman
summary: A mythical monster used to frighten children now burns every spring as a snowman effigy that predicts the summer weather.

title: The Cadejo at the Crossroads
summary: Two supernatural dogs — one white, one black — guard the roads of El Salvador at night, one protecting the faithful and the other preying upon the wicked.

title: The Cadejo Chico and the Children
summary: A small, mischievous variant of the Cadejo spirit haunts children who misbehave, appearing as a tiny dog that grows larger with each act of disobedience.
themes: small spirits that grow with neglect

title: The Cadejo Grande of the Coffee Roads
summary: The largest of the Cadejo spirits — a towering, spectral dog that guards the remote mountain roads where coffee pickers walk alone before dawn.

title: The Cadejo of the Dangriga Road
summary: A Garifuna woman walking home at dusk encounters both the white and black Cadejo on the road to Dangriga, and learns that good and evil travel the same path, differing only in intention.

title: The Cadejo of the Road
summary: Two spectral dogs — one white, one black — guard the roads of Central America, one protecting the righteous and the other preying on the wicked.

title: The Caipora and the Logger
summary: A hairy forest guardian rides a wild pig through the Atlantic rainforest, punishing loggers who take more than the jungle can bear.

title: The Calèche de Lallmatie
summary: Along the road to Lallmatie, a phantom horse-drawn carriage appears on moonless nights, its wheels soundless on the pavement, its passenger a figure no one dares look at twice.

title: The Cannibal Woman Society (Kwakwaka'wakw)
summary: Long ago when totemic beings walked the earth, there was Dzunukwa (Cannibal Woman), a gigantic female being with great wealth and powerful magic who ate people. The other beings became alarmed and decided only Raven could stop her. Raven flew to the North End of the World and recruited a flock of fearsome Cannibal Birds, becoming their leader. He returned with his flock to the great forest where Dzunukwa lived, and they danced and sang her praises. When the dance ended, Dzunukwa found herself bound by powerful magic and could no longer eat flesh — the only things she could eat were nuggets of native copper. This story establishes the origin of the Hamatsa (Cannibal Woman) Society, the most important secret society in Kwakwaka'wakw culture. The society's winter ceremonies reenact the capturing and taming of the cannibal spirit, transforming its destructive power into constructive social and spiritual energy for the community.

title: The Capelobo of the Interior
summary: A headless, ape-like creature with a gaping chest wound prowls the Brazilian backlands, and the traveler who encounters it must run or be devoured.

title: The Carver Who Gave Shetani Form
summary: A gifted Makonde carver discovers that the figures emerging from his ebony are not inventions of his imagination but true portraits of the shetani that haunt the forests, and that giving them form gives them power over the waking world.
themes: art as a conduit between worlds
the danger of giving form to the formless

title: The Cat of Norrhult
summary: The people of Norrhult are driven from their homes by trolls. A bear keeper arrives and his bear scatters the trolls then directs villagers to raise a cross on the mountain. A troll later asks if that vicious cat is still alive and upon hearing she has seven fierce kittens flees forever.

title: The Cat on the Dovrefjell
summary: A youth journeys to the Dovrefjell mountains where he encounters a magical cat. The cat, acting as a guide, leads the youth through perilous landscapes to a hidden treasure and helps him win the heart of a princess.

title: The Cat Ra
summary: In the land of ancient Egypt, where the Nile flows through golden sands and the pyramids pierce the sky, there lived a belief more powerful than any pharaoh's decree.

title: The Cave of Caguana: Taino Creation
summary: According to Taino mythology, all human life began in a sacred cave called Cacibajagua (Cave of the Jagua) on the island of Haiti (Hispaniola). The first humans emerged from this cave, while the gods dwelt in the Cave of the Serpent and the Cave of Coaybay. The deity Iguanaboína was among the first beings from the river. The Taino believed their ancestors originated from this cave system, with different groups emerging at different times. Those who emerged late were said to have been turned into stone by the morning sun — explaining certain rock formations. The cave of Caguana in Puerto Rico contains some of the most important Taino petroglyphs, depicting Atabey in her birthing position, marking it as a sacred ceremonial center for areítos (ceremonial dances and songs).

title: The Celestial Star Gods
summary: The Skidi Pawnee organized their entire society around the stars. Six major stars represented gods controlled by Tirawa: the North Star (watched over the people), Northeast Star (Big Black Meteoric Star, controlled animals and bison), Southeast Star (Red Star, regulated day and animals), South Star (ruled the land of the dead), Southwest Star, and Northwest Star (both female). The Milky Way contained paths that guided the dead to South Star's dominion. The sun (Shakuru) and moon (Pah) were the last gods placed in the heavens. The four villages of the Skidi were given by the four leading stars.

title: The Chains of Abu Al-Salasil
summary: A wealthy merchant who cheated his workers is visited by Abu Al-Salasil, the spirit of chains, who forces him to confront the weight of his injustices before dawn.

title: The Chameleon Who Carried God's Message
summary: When Chiuta needed a messenger to carry the word of immortality to humanity, he chose the Chameleon — slow, patient, and deliberate — but the Hare, sent second with the message of death, arrived first.
themes: the necessity of death for meaning and love
patience as a virtue superior to speed
the weight and responsibility of divine messages
delivery matters as much as content
the Mzimu spirit and ancestral continuity

title: The Chamos of the Underground
summary: Mischievous goblin-like creatures live in tunnels beneath Venezuelan cities, stealing small objects and playing tricks on anyone who wanders too close to their underground dwellings.

title: The Changeling
summary: A mother suspects her child has been replaced by a troll changeling and uses clever tricks — including brewing beer in an eggshell — to force the troll mother to return her real baby.

title: The Chickcharney of Andros Island
summary: The Chickcharney is a legendary creature from Bahamian folklore, specifically from Andros Island. It resembles a small, elf-like being with owl-like feathers, glowing red eyes, three fingers on each hand, and three toes on each foot. It walks upright and is said to whistle softly as it moves. According to tradition, how a person treats the Chickcharney determines whether luck or misfortune follows. Construction workers and lumberjacks on Andros Island would leave small offerings of food at the edge of their work sites as gestures of respect. Those who showed respect had safe workdays and found missing tools returned neatly nearby. Those who mocked the old warnings suffered accidents, illness, and misfortune. The Chickcharney embodies the principle that the forests hold memory, presence, and power deserving of respect.

title: The Child and the Cannibal (Nuxalk)
summary: This Nuxalk legend tells of a magical boy who defeats a man-eating monster that terrorized the people. A cannibal giant (Boqs) had been stealing children from a Nuxalk village, carrying them off to his remote mountain lair to devour. The people were helpless against the monster's supernatural strength and ferocity. A young boy, born with extraordinary powers and protected by supernatural helpers, volunteered to confront the cannibal. Using cleverness, courage, and his spirit-given abilities, he tracked the monster to its den. He outwitted the slow-witted giant, leading it into traps and finally killing it with the help of the forest spirits. He freed all the captured children and returned them safely to the village. The boy became a great chief and his descendants established one of the Nuxalk clans. This is part of a broader Nuxalk tradition of hero-child stories where young protagonists overcome powerful supernatural adversaries, demonstrating that age and size are less important than courage and spiritual power.

title: The Child-Snatcher of the Shore
summary: A cautionary tale about the Qalupalik, a scaly creature that lives beneath the ice and uses a pouch to kidnap children who wander too close to the water's edge. The story blends practical safety advice with supernatural fear to keep children safe from drowning.

title: The Children of La Llorona — The Weeping Children
summary: A poignant variant of the La Llorona legend tells that the spirits of the children she drowned did not pass on but remain as eternal, weeping children along the same waterways. Known sometimes as Los Hijos de la Llorona, these child spirits are said to appear as small, translucent figures playing near rivers and canals at dusk. Unlike their mother, who wails in anguish, the children are sometimes described as playful but sad, trying to lure living children to join them in the water. In some New Mexican versions, the children appear to warn other children away from dangerous waters. This variant transforms the story from one of pure horror into a tragedy of intergenerational trauma, where the sins of the mother echo through the spirits of the innocent. In Chicano literature and art, these children have been reclaimed as symbols of lost innocence and the enduring wounds of colonization.

title: The Children of Lir
summary: Long ago, in the mist-shrouded dawn of Ireland, when the Tuatha Dé Danann still walked among the hills and the land was alive with magic, there ruled a great king named Lir.

title: The Chiruwi of the Deep Forest
summary: Deep in the forests of southern Malawi, the Chiruwi — a shape-shifting forest spirit — tested the courage of hunters by leading them astray, teaching them that the forest gives only to those who respect its mysteries.
themes: respect for the power of the natural world
the danger of pride and overconfidence
forest spirits as guardians of ecological balance
grief as a vulnerability that spirits exploit

title: The Chudes Are Defeated by a Loon's Beak
summary: A humorous Sámi legend where Sámi outwit Chude raiders using minimal means—in this case, a loon's beak. The story illustrates the theme that superior force can be overcome by cleverness and that even small, humble tools can defeat powerful enemies.

title: The Chudes Are Tricked by a Boy Pathfinder
summary: A recurring Sámi legend type (Christiansen ML 8000). A band of Chude raiders attacks a Sámi settlement and captures a young boy, forcing him to guide them to other Sámi groups. The boy leads the raiders along a dangerous mountain path. He ties a rope around himself connected to the raiders, then at a critical moment on a steep precipice, he unties himself and cuts the rope, causing the Chudes to pull each other down the slope to their deaths.

title: The Chudes in Notozero
summary: A Skolt Sámi legend about Chude attackers in the Notozero region. The Sámi use their knowledge of the Arctic landscape and weather to evade and defeat the raiders. The story is part of the extensive cycle of Chude legends reflecting historical conflicts between Sámi and East Slavic raiders. The Chudes are always portrayed as cruel but ultimately outwitted by Sámi cunning.

title: The Chullachaqui and the Hunter
summary: A forest guardian with one human foot and one wooden foot punishes hunters who take more than they need from the jungle.

title: The Chureca, the Virgin Islands Beast
summary: A fearsome beast of the Virgin Islands, the Chureca is a monstrous creature that emerges from the forest to devour livestock and threaten villagers.

title: The Cipitío of the Volcanic Fields
summary: A small, mischievous trickster spirit born from the union of earth and fire, the Cipitío steals food and causes mischief among the villages near the volcanic highlands.
themes: the sacred nature of craft and art

title: The Circle Kachina and His Wife Become Stars
summary: In Hopi tradition, a maiden grinding corn was approached by the Póngo (Circle) Kachina, who danced at various kivas around the village. She agreed to marry him and went to the Kachina kiva where many different Kachinas gathered. She prepared their food while they prepared her bridal costume. They had two children, also Circle Kachinas. The Hotóto Kachina seduced the wife away to Shongópavi. The Circle Kachina, following her tracks, took his children to the Kachina house. After four days of flute playing at Kíba, the wife emerged from the water in her bridal costume. The Flute priests declared: 'You shall always follow each other this way.' The two ran westward and are still running — they became the stars that pursue each other across the sky, Nangö'sohu, one constantly overtaking and then falling behind the other.

title: The City of Brass
summary: Caliph Abd al-Malik sends Emir Musa and his party across the Sahara to find the legendary City of Brass, built by King Solomon to imprison rebellious jinn. They encounter a brass horseman statue that points the way, a chained Ifrit imprisoned in a pillar, and an ancient city with walls eighty cubits high and twenty-five gates, eerily preserved but inhabited only by corpses. Inside lies the embalmed princess Tadmurah of the Amalekites, her treasure guarded by animated statues. Greedy Talib ignores warnings and is decapitated by guardian statues. The party retrieves brass bottles containing imprisoned jinn and returns to Damascus.

title: The Clever Girl of Kairouan
summary: A Tunisian folktale from the ancient city of Kairouan about a poor man and his brilliant daughter. When famine strikes, the man seeks help from a corrupt judge who sets an impossible condition: 'You must come to me neither dressed nor undressed, neither walking nor riding, neither by day nor by night.' The man's daughter solves the riddle: she wraps herself in a fishing net so she is neither clothed nor naked, rides a donkey with her feet dragging so she is neither walking nor riding, and arrives at dawn—the moment between night and day. When the judge tries to swindle her father, she outsmarts him in court with her quick wit, exposing his corruption and securing justice for her family. The story became famous throughout Tunisia as a symbol of how intellect and moral courage can overcome corrupt authority, and is still told to emphasize the values of wisdom and justice in Maghrebi oral tradition.

title: The Cock and Hen a-Nutting
summary: A cock and a hen venture out to gather nuts in the forest, where they encounter a dangerous troll. Using their wit and coordination, they manage to trick the troll and escape his clutches, illustrating that intelligence and teamwork can overcome brute strength and predatory threats.

title: The Cock and the Crested Hen
summary: A vain little crested hen thinks herself too good for the other farmyard hens and goes off alone against the cock's warnings. A hawk swoops down and nearly catches her; she escapes but loses her finest feathers, learning humility.

title: The Cock and the Mouse (Zuni)
summary: A Zuni folktale of the hybrid type, combining Native and European story elements. The Cock (rooster) and the Mouse were friends living together. Mouse was industrious, gathering food and maintaining their home, while Cock was boastful and lazy. When danger came in the form of a cat or predator, Cock's crowing alerted everyone, but his bravado failed when actual confrontation occurred. Mouse, though small, used cleverness to escape danger. The story humorously contrasts the small, practical Mouse with the showy but ineffective Cock. It teaches that real value lies not in appearance or loudness but in practical skills and quiet diligence. Like many Zuni animal tales, it contains elements of social commentary, humor, and moral instruction wrapped in an engaging narrative.

title: The Cockatrice of the Garden
summary: In the Vatican Gardens, a basilisk born from a rooster's egg hatches under a serpent's care, and only the simplest act of faith — refusing to look — saves the gardener who must destroy it.

title: The Coming of Death
summary: In Navajo mythology, death came into being when one of the hermaphrodite twins (Nádleeh) stopped breathing after the first day of the Sun's journey. The people abandoned the body in fear, and the next day it was gone — a man looked down through the reed to the Third World and saw the twin sitting by the river. Coyote First Angry proposed a test: he threw a black rock into Black Water Lake, declaring that if it floated, spirits would return and there would be no death; if it sank, death would be permanent. The rock sank. The people learned that looking at the dead is dangerous when the two witnesses also died four days later. Coyote justified his decision by explaining that without death, the world would overpopulate, elders would remain trapped in infirm bodies, and there would be no room for new children.

title: The Comorian Dragon of Karthala
summary: Deep beneath Mount Karthala sleeps a dragon born from volcanic fire and ocean brine, and the Comorians know that the mountain's occasional tremors are merely the dragon turning in its restless sleep.
themes: balance between human ambition and ecological limits

title: The Comorian Jinn of the Clove Grove
summary: The Mashetani, Comoros' restless jinn, are said to inhabit the ancient clove groves, and a young bride learns that negotiating with spirits requires more courage than fleeing from them.
themes: the exchange economy of the supernatural
respect as a form of power

title: The Conjure Doctor Who Outwitted the Master
summary: On a Virginia plantation, the master hired a notorious slave driver to break the spirit of the enslaved people. Whippings and punishments only increased, and the people grew desperate. An old conjure doctor named Uncle Monday was called from a neighboring plantation. Uncle Monday walked through the quarters, speaking to the people and gathering roots and herbs from the forest. He prepared a special mojo bag and buried it at the crossroads near the plantation gate. That night, the slave driver could not sleep; snip he was tormented by nightmares of his victims. The next day, he was thrown from his horse for no reason. Within a week, he fled the plantation, claiming it was haunted. The master, furious, accused Uncle Monday of witchcraft and threatened to have him whipped. Uncle Monday calmly pointed at a tree stump, and it burst into flames. The master never touched him. Uncle Monday taught the people that conjure was their protection, passed from Africa, and that no master could ever truly break what the spirits protected. The tale embodies the power of conjure as a form of psychological and spiritual resistance against the violence of slavery.

title: The Contendings of Horus and Set
summary: The epic struggle between Horus, the son of Osiris, and Set, the murderer of Osiris, for the throne of Egypt is one of the most dramatic myths from ancient Egypt. After Osiris descended to the underworld, his son Horus came of age and demanded the kingship that was rightfully his. Set, Osiris's brother, refused to yield. The case was brought before the Ennead, the council of gods, presided over by Geb or Ra. The trial lasted eighty years. The conflict was both legal and violent: the gods debated endlessly while Horus and Set engaged in terrible battles. Set tore out Horus's eye; snip Horus castrated Set. Isis used cunning and magic to aid her son, at one point transforming into a beautiful woman to trick Set into condemning himself. Thoth served as scribe and mediator. Eventually the gods ruled in Horus's favor, and he became king of Egypt. The myth established the principle of divine kingship: every pharaoh was considered the living Horus. Set was not destroyed but was given dominion over the desert and foreign lands, representing chaos kept at bay by order.

title: The Corn Maidens (Zuni)
summary: In Zuni tradition, the Corn Maidens are sacred beings who embody the spirit of corn. They are associated with Paiyatuma, the god of the dawn and of music, and with the Kachina society. According to the myth, Paiyatuma courted the Corn Maidens, who were beautiful but shy. He played his flute for them, and they danced. Through this union, the sacred connection between corn and the people was established. The Corn Maidens taught the Zuni women how to grind corn, make piki bread, and prepare corn ceremonially. Each color of corn has its own maiden — Blue Corn Maiden, Yellow Corn Maiden, White Corn Maiden, Red Corn Maiden, Black Corn Maiden, and Speckled Corn Maiden. During ceremonies, the Corn Maidens are represented by Kachina dancers who carry ears of corn and bless the fields. The story of the Corn Maidens is central to Zuni agricultural ceremonies and reinforces the sacredness of corn as a gift from the spirit world.

title: The Corn Mother
summary: The Sluagh are the most feared of all Irish fairy creatures, and for good reason.

title: The Cosmic Egg Creation (Bon Tradition)
summary: The pre-Buddhist Tibetan Bon creation myth describing the origin of the universe from a cosmic egg. According to this tradition, in the beginning there was only emptiness. From the void emerged five pure lights, which condensed into a luminous egg. From this cosmic egg hatched the primordial being, who then created the world by separating sky from earth. The egg's white shell became the heavens, its yolk became the earth, and the liquid within became the oceans. Mountains, rivers, and all living beings arose from different parts of the egg's contents. This creation account is preserved in the Bon Kangyur and Tengyur sacred texts and represents Tibet's indigenous cosmology predating the introduction of Buddhism in the 7th century.

title: The Cougar Guardian's Two Heads
summary: A two-headed cougar spirit guards the boundary between the living world and the spirit world, and the traveler who passes without permission is dragged into the forest forever.

title: The Countess of Höjentorp
summary: When King Charles XI confiscates her property the Countess of Hojentorp greets him with a box on the ear. She feeds him only a herring's tail and oat cake. When the king asks for her gold she gives him a second slap, and the king retreats ordering she be left in peace.

title: The Cowherd and the Weaver Girl
summary: Star lovers separated by the Milky Way, reunited once a year on a bridge formed by thousands of magpies.

title: The Coyote and the Locust
summary: A Zuni trickster story about Coyote who heard Locust singing and playing his flute on a piñon branch. Coveting the song, Coyote demanded Locust teach it to him. Locust, wary of Coyote's intentions, tricked him by shedding his skin and placing a stone inside the empty shell on the branch. When Coyote returned and Locust refused to sing again, Coyote angrily bit the locust shell — but it was actually a stone wrapped in skin. Coyote broke his teeth, which is why coyotes have broken-looking teeth to this day. The story explains both the physical characteristic of coyotes and warns against anger, impatience, and not minding one's own business. Locusts, for their part, still sometimes shed their skins and leave their likenesses on trees to fool predators.

title: The Crane Guardian's Warning
summary: A sacred crane spirit warns the village of an approaching enemy, and the warrior who listens survives the battle while the others fall.

title: The Crane Wife
summary: In a small village in Korea, during the days of the Joseon dynasty, a poor woodcutter lived alone in a cottage at the edge of the forest.

title: The Crane's Repayment
summary: A wounded crane is rescued and repays the kindness with magic, only for the gift to be lost through a breach of trust.

title: The Creation of Earth and the Great Buzzard (Cherokee)
summary: In the beginning, all was water, and animals lived in the sky world above the stone vault. The water beetle Dâyuni'sï volunteered to explore below and brought up soft mud from the ocean floor, which grew into the earth. The earth was initially soft and flat. The Great Buzzard flew down to survey the land, and his wings striking the ground created the mountains and valleys of Cherokee territory. When the animals saw what the Buzzard had done, they feared he would make the earth too rough, so they called him back, leaving the Cherokee mountains steep and the valleys deep. The sun was set on a track to travel across the sky each day. This foundational myth explains the geography of the Southern Appalachian region and establishes the Cherokee cosmic order.

title: The Creation of Haida Gwaii
summary: Before the days of the grandfathers, there was nothing but water except a single reef where the supernatural beings lived crowded together. Raven flew about looking for a place to land but could alight nowhere. He flew up to the Sky Land, where he tricked a chief's family by taking the form of a baby. He caused mischief until a stone woman exposed him. The chief sang a magic song and Raven was dropped, falling onto the great waters in his cradle. A grebe appeared and summoned him to the underwater house of Sea-Gull Man. There, Raven was given two rocks: a small speckled one that became Haida Gwaii and a larger black one that became the mainland continent. Raven was instructed to spiral down from the sky, carrying the rocks, and when he reached the islands he made humans from the earth. This creation narrative establishes the sacred origin of Haida Gwaii and the Haida people's deep connection to the land.

title: The Creation of Lake Baikal
summary: A Buryat legend explaining the origin of Lake Baikal, the world's deepest and oldest lake. According to the myth, there was once a great earthquake — the mightiest ever seen — which created a massive crack in the earth's surface. Fire and lava erupted from the crack, threatening to destroy everything. The Buryat people cried out 'Bai Gal! Bai Gal!' meaning 'Stop Fire! Stop Fire!' and the flames ceased. Water then filled the vast depression, forming Lake Baikal. The Buryats consider Baikal a sacred living entity, calling it 'Baikal the Father.' The lake is home to countless spirits and is the dwelling place of powerful deities including the water spirit Usan Khatan and the great dragon-like Luus spirits.

title: The Creation of Lake Issyk-Kul
summary: An alternate legend describes the origin of Issyk-Kul ('Warm Lake') as the tears of the heavens. An old man and his beautiful daughter lived on the shores of a small river. When invaders came, the daughter prayed to Tengri for salvation. The sky god answered by sending a flood that drowned the invaders but also the old man. The daughter's endless tears of grief filled the valley, forming the vast lake that never freezes despite its altitude. The warm waters represent the mother's eternal love and the father's enduring protection. Even today, Kyrgyz herders say the lake's surface reflects the faces of those who died in the flood.

title: The Creation of the Faroe Islands
summary: Two folk explanations exist for the archipelago's creation. The first says the islands were formed from dirt that gathered under God's fingernails while He created the world and flicked away. The second, more dramatic myth connects to Norse mythology: after the World Serpent Jörmungandr (child of Loki) was defeated, a tooth fell from the dying serpent's mouth into the ocean and became the Faroe Islands. Both accounts are recorded in Faroese oral tradition. The Jörmungandr version connects Faroese identity to the great Norse mythological cycle, while the nail-dirt tale echoes a humble self-perception common in island folklore.

title: The Creation of the Karakum Desert
summary: According to Turkmen legend, the Karakum ('Black Sands') Desert was created by a battle between good and evil forces. The devil challenged the creator god to a contest — who could cover more land in one night. The creator god began covering the land with fertile soil, but the devil raised giant sandstorms. The creator god, realizing the devil's trick, scattered black stones across the sand to stop his advance. These stones became the desert's namesake 'black sands.' Another legend says that a giant serpent slept beneath the land, and when it turned in its sleep, it churned the earth into sand. The few oases that survive in the desert were created where the tears of angels fell, grieving for the land's desolation. The Bakhshi singers still perform tales of how the Turkmen people learned to thrive in this harsh environment.

title: The Creation of the Kathmandu Valley by Manjushri
summary: According to the Swayambhu Purana, the Kathmandu Valley was once a great lake called Nagavasahrada, inhabited by serpent beings (Nagas). On the lake floated a miraculous self-arisen flame (Swayambhu Jyotirupa) emanating from a thousand-petalled lotus. The Bodhisattva Manjushri, meditating on the Five-Peaked Mountain in China, became aware of the sacred light and travelled to the lake with his two wives, Kesini and Upakesini. Using his mighty sword Chandrahasa, Manjushri cut through the Chobhar Gorge, draining the lake and creating the fertile Kathmandu Valley. He persuaded Karkotaka, the King of Nagas, to remain in a smaller lake (Taudaha) as guardian of the valley's wealth. The lotus settled on Swayambhu Hill, where the great Swayambhu Stupa now stands. Manjushri then founded the first settlement, Manjupattan.

title: The Creation of the Niger River (Mande)
summary: Long ago, the Niger River flowed only underground. A heroic hunter named Fara Makan tracked a wounded antelope for seven days without water. When he was dying of thirst, he shot an arrow into the ground, and water burst forth, creating the Niger River. The river then wound its way across the Sahel, bringing life to the lands of Mali, Niger, and Nigeria. The Djoliba (the Mande name for the Niger) became the lifeblood of the Mali Empire, enabling agriculture, trade, and transport. Sundiata Keita's empire was built along this great river, and the river's annual flood is still celebrated as a gift from the spirits. To this day, fishermen and farmers along the Niger honor the river with offerings.

title: The Creation of the World (Fon/Dahomey)
summary: Before the world existed, there was only water, darkness, and the supreme deity Nana Buluku. Nana Buluku gave birth to twins: Mawu, the goddess of the moon and night, and Lisa, the god of the sun and day. Together, Mawu-Lisa created the world. They then gave birth to children who became the heads of the great vodun pantheons: Sogbo (thunder), Sagbata (earth), and Agbe (sea). Mawu created the first humans from clay and taught them how to live in harmony with nature. Lisa brought fire, metal, and civilization. Their androgynous union represents the balance of opposites that governs the universe. This creation story is central to the Vodun religion that spread from Dahomey (Benin) to Haiti, Brazil, and Cuba.

title: The Creation of the World (Yoruba)
summary: In the beginning, there was only water and chaos. Olodumare, the Supreme Being, sent Obatala down from the heavens with a calabash filled with soil, a rooster, and a palm nut. Obatala poured the soil onto the waters, and the rooster spread it to create dry land at Ile-Ife, the cradle of existence. He planted the palm nut, which grew into a great tree with sixteen branches, symbolizing the sixteen sacred Odù Ifá. Olodumare then breathed life into the clay figurines Obatala had molded, creating the first humans. Thus Ile-Ife became the sacred birthplace of Yoruba civilization and the dwelling place of the Orishas.

title: The Creek Flood Myth and the Dog's Sacrifice (Creek)
summary: The Muscogee Creek tell a flood story in which the Great Flood covered the entire earth. As the waters rose, the people prayed to the Creator for deliverance. A great dog appeared and offered to sacrifice himself by lying across a creek to dam the water. The dog's noble self-sacrifice allowed the people to cross to higher ground. In gratitude and mourning, the Creator set the dog's spirit in the sky, where it became a constellation. To this day, the Creek honor dogs for their loyalty and self-sacrifice. The myth shares elements with flood stories from many other Native American tribes but is distinctive in its focus on the selfless act of an animal rather than a human or divine hero, reflecting the Creek belief in the spiritual nobility of animals.

title: The Crocodile Who Formed the Island
summary: The great crocodile spirit Lafaek sacrificed himself to create the island of Timor, and his body became the land upon which the people live.

title: The Crossroads Spirit
summary: In African American conjure tradition, the crossroads is the most spiritually charged place—the intersection where the physical world meets the spirit world. The story tells of a young man who went to a crossroads at midnight seeking power. He was instructed by a rootworker to bring a black chicken, a bottle of whiskey, and nine silver dimes. At the crossroads, he was to draw an X on the ground, light a black candle, and wait. The spirits would test him with terrors, but he must not run. According to some accounts, a figure would appear—sometimes the Devil, sometimes an old man, sometimes a faceless presence—and offer a deal: power and fortune in exchange for his soul. The crossroads spirit could teach the secrets of conjure, give winning lottery numbers, or make an enemy sick. But the price was always steep. Those who succeeded at the crossroads gained power; snip those who failed lost their minds or their lives. The crossroads story blends African spiritual traditions (where crossroads are home to the trickster god Eshu-Elegba) with the American experience of desperate people seeking power in a world that denied them any.

title: The Crowing Cobra of Zambezia
summary: A boy who mocks the old warnings about the Crowing Crested Cobra learns too late that the wilderness holds creatures whose very names are meant to keep the unwary alive.

title: The Crystal Ball
summary: In a small German village at the edge of a dark forest, a poor boy was given a crystal ball by an old woman he met on the road.

title: The Curse of the Dolls — La Isla de las Muñecas
summary: The legend of the Island of the Dolls (La Isla de las Muñecas) in the Xochimilco canals near Mexico City is a modern legend that has spread widely through Mexican-American communities. According to the story, a man named Don Julián Santana found the body of a drowned girl in the canals and, haunted by her spirit, began collecting dolls and hanging them from trees to appease her soul. Over 50 years, thousands of decaying, mutilated dolls accumulated on the island, their blank eyes and torn limbs creating an atmosphere of profound unease. After Don Julián drowned in the same canal in 2001, the legend grew: visitors claim the dolls move their heads, blink, and whisper at night. The legend speaks to themes of death, childhood, and the thin boundary between the natural and supernatural worlds. For Mexican-Americans, the story resonates as a uniquely Mexican contribution to global horror folklore.

title: The Curse of the Raven's Eye
summary: A man steals a gemstone from the eye of a carved raven statue in an ancient temple. The gem gives him the ability to see the future, but it also attracts the attention of the raven's spirit, which slowly consumes his sanity until he returns the stone to its rightful place.

title: The Cursed Ring of the Highlands
summary: A traveler finds a gold ring in a mountain stream, only to discover it is cursed. The ring brings immense wealth but also attracts the attention of the Draugrs who previously owned it. The wearer is haunted by whispers and nightmares until they return the ring to the stream from which it came.

title: The Curupira and the City Boy
summary: A city boy visits the Amazon and ignores the warnings about the Curupira, whose backward feet lead him in circles until he learns to respect the forest.

title: The D'Sonoqua Who Became Wealth (Kwakwaka'wakw)
summary: In one Kwakwaka'wakw narrative, a clever boy was captured by D'Sonoqua and carried in her basket to her forest house. While she prepared to cook him, the boy noticed that D'Sonoqua was dim-witted with poor eyesight. He tricked her into showing him her treasures and then pushed her into her own cooking fire. As she burned, her wealth — copper shields, abalone shells, and blankets — spilled out. The boy took the treasures back to his village and became a great chief. But D'Sonoqua's ashes blew into the air and became mosquitoes, which is why mosquitoes bite humans — they carry D'Sonoqua's eternal hunger. This story also has versions where D'Sonoqua cannot truly die; she regenerates from any wound, and the only way to stop her is to burn her completely and scatter the ashes. Her association with wealth makes her a complex figure: she is a terrifying cannibal monster but also a source of great prosperity for those brave and clever enough to defeat her. At potlatches, a chief wearing the D'Sonoqua mask signals the end of the ceremony.

title: The Dahomey Amazons (Fon/Dahomey)
summary: The Dahomey Amazons (Mino, meaning 'our mothers') were an all-female military regiment of the Kingdom of Dahomey. According to legend, Queen Hangbe, who ruled briefly in the early 1700s, established the first female bodyguards. But the legend says that the Amazons were blessed by the vodun spirits, who gave them supernatural strength and courage in battle. These warrior women lived in the royal palace, wore men's clothing, and were forbidden from marrying or having children. They carried Danish muskets and machetes and were considered the elite shock troops of the Dahomean army. Their battle cry was 'We are invincible because we are mothers of the nation.' The Amazons fought fiercely against French colonial forces in 1890-1894, with many choosing suicide over capture. They remain a powerful symbol of African female power and resistance.

title: The Dakhanavars of the Mountain Pass
summary: Two vampires haunt a remote mountain pass in Armenia, draining travelers of their blood through their feet, until a clever monk devises a trap of iron and prayer.

title: the Dangun, Founding of the First Kingdom
summary: A bear and a god's son, transformed by patience and garlic and mugwort into the first humans — and from their line, a kingdom was born.

title: The Daughter of the Moon and the Son of the Sun
summary: A romantic Sámi folk tale. Niekia, the Moon's daughter raised by an elderly Sámi couple, had a face like cloudberries and hair of silver. When Peivalke (the Sun's son) fell in love with her, she refused him and fled. She found an empty house by the sea, cleaned it, and hid as a spindle. Northern Light warriors led by Nainas entered at dusk. The Sun pinned Nainas with a heat shaft. Niekia shielded him and was seized by the Sun. The Moon rescued her daughter.

title: The Day-Labourer and the Hidden People
summary: A poor youth is helped by magical hidden people after showing kindness to their dog.

title: The Death of Hun Hunahpu
summary: The father of the Hero Twins is summoned to Xibalba for playing ball too loudly, and the Lords of Death sacrifice him — but his blood gives rise to new life.

title: The Death of John Henry
summary: After defeating the steam drill, John Henry's heart, strained beyond its limit, gave out. With his hammer still in his hand, the mighty steel-driving man collapsed and died. His fellow workers gathered around as the man who had beaten the machine lay still. The ballad recounts that John Henry had a woman—Polly Ann, Mary Ann, or Julia Ann in various versions—who took up his hammer after his death. John Henry's funeral became a massive gathering where workers from every railroad line came to pay their respects. The ballad spread rapidly across the South, carried by itinerant workers, becoming one of the most recorded folk songs in American history. More than just a story, John Henry's death became a symbol of the human cost of industrialization and the struggle of Black workers against the dehumanizing forces of progress that sought to replace them.

title: The Death of Osiris
summary: Osiris was the ideal king of Egypt—good, fair, beloved by all who knew him. Centers on Osiris,  from Egypt mythology. Known for aquatic speed and soul sight and immortality..

title: The Death of the Sun's Daughter
summary: The Sun's daughter Njávisheatne lived a long and good life. When she felt death approaching, she ordered that she be buried atop the highest peak so she could watch over the people forever. She was wrapped in a shroud of njavvi (reindeer neck hair) and laid to rest on a mountain now called Sun Daughter's Mountain. Stones were placed at her head, feet, and arms, with a flat slab of rock covering the grave. An inscription was carved: 'The turf raised, read the memorial.'

title: The Deathless Horseman
summary: A headless rider known as the Dullahan wanders the night, heralding death with a single call of a name.

title: The Deer Stone Legends
summary: Across the Mongolian steppe stand ancient megalithic Deer Stones — carved monoliths dating back 3,000 years to the Bronze Age. Mongol legend says these stones are warriors turned to stone by the sky god Tengri for their arrogance. The deer depicted leaping across the stones represent the souls of fallen warriors ascending to the heavens. Another legend holds that the stones mark the graves of great shamans, with the deer serving as spirit animals to carry the shaman's soul across the sky. The most famous concentration is at the Uushigiin Uvur site in Khövsgöl Province, where over a dozen Deer Stones form a sacred ceremonial complex.

title: The Deer Who Became the River
summary: A sacred deer sacrifices itself to create the river that feeds the village, and its antlers become the trees that line its banks.

title: The Dekki H'd'rtna, Shadow Walkers of the Highlands
summary: In the Eritrean highlands, shadow spirits walk between the living and the dead, and a grieving widow who tries to speak with her dead husband learns that some doors should stay closed.

title: The Descent of the Tzitzimimeh
summary: When the gods grow weak and the cosmic order falters, skeletal star-demons descend from the sky to devour humanity — and only a solar eclipse can stop them.

title: The Destroyer, Guaraní Chieftain
summary: A fierce Guaraní war spirit who leads the souls of fallen warriors through the forest, and the hunter who hears his war cry must lie face-down or be driven mad.

title: The Destruction of Humanity by Sekhmet
summary: When the sun god Ra grew old, humanity rebelled against his rule. Ra assembled the gods and proposed to destroy mankind. Following their counsel, he sent his Eye—the goddess Hathor—in the form of the fierce lioness Sekhmet to punish humanity. Sekhmet descended upon the earth and slaughtered people with relish, wading in blood and destroying everything in her path. Ra watched the carnage with growing horror and repented his decision. He ordered 7,000 jars of beer to be dyed red with ochre to resemble blood and poured across the fields of Dendera. Sekhmet, mistaking the beer for blood, drank it until she fell into a drunken stupor, waking as the peaceful Hathor. This event explains why beer is consumed at the Festival of Hathor and why one of her epithets is 'Lady of Drunkenness.' After this, Ra ascended to the heavens, leaving humanity to govern itself and establishing the afterlife (the Field of Reeds) as humanity's ultimate destiny.

title: The Dev of the Iron Cave
summary: A giant Dev imprisoned in a cave beneath the Armenian highlands offers a miner riches beyond measure in exchange for his freedom, testing the limits of mortal greed.

title: The Devil's Dance at Bomarsund (Djävulsdansen)
summary: One of Åland's most famous legends, the Devil's Dance tells of a masked ball at the Russian military settlement of Skarpans near Bomarsund in the 1830s–1840s. A mysterious, elegantly dressed stranger arrived at the dance and asked which woman was the finest dancer. A priest's wife stepped forward. The stranger danced with her so wildly that blood came through her shoes. When the musicians stopped playing, the fiddles continued on their own. Finally, a clergyman named Prosten Sadelin was summoned. He confronted the stranger, who revealed a horse's hoof instead of a foot — the Devil himself. Sadelin drove the Devil out through a small hole in a window casement. The legend has inspired three theatrical plays and an opera performed at Alandica in Mariehamn in 2022.

title: The Devil's Golden Sword
summary: In medieval Germany, during the reign of the Saxon emperors, there lived a knight named Sir Hartmann von Aue.

title: The Diablada of Oruro
summary: Every year during Carnival, the devils of the mine emerge to dance through the streets of Oruro, wearing masks of hammered silver and carrying pitchforks of twisted ore — a reminder that the mountain never forgets.

title: The Div and the Fortress of Fire
summary: A Div, a powerful demon of ancient Zoroastrian and Turkic tradition, builds a fortress of black stone to block the sun, and only a fearless blacksmith can challenge it.

title: The Diving Duck Creation Myth
summary: The Yakut creation myth about a diving duck that brought the first earth from the bottom of the primordial sea. In the beginning, there was only water. The supreme deity sent a diving duck (or loon) down into the depths to retrieve mud from the ocean floor. The bird succeeded in bringing up a small piece of earth, which the deity then caused to expand and grow into the world as it exists today. This classic 'Earth Diver' myth is widespread among Siberian peoples and represents the Yakut variations on this ancient cosmogonic theme. The legend reflects the importance of waterfowl in Yakut culture and the deep connection between the people and their riverine environment.

title: The Djinn of the Aures Mountains
summary: Powerful spirits inhabit the mountains of eastern Algeria, testing the faith of those who cross their territory.

title: The Djinn of the Hollow Baobab
summary: A young Hausa herdsman discovers that an ancient baobab tree near the village well shelters a Toula djinn who tests the character of those who seek his aid.

title: The Djinn of the Sahara Well
summary: A Tunisian desert folktale about a lone traveler crossing the Sahara who discovers a hidden well. As he drinks from its cool water, a voice emerges from the darkness—a djinn, keeper of the well, bound to the place since ancient times. The traveler, driven by greed, demands riches. The djinn three tests: first, carry water from the well without spilling a single drop to a distant stone; snip second, sit by the well and hear what is not spoken; snip third, leave without looking back no matter what he hears. The traveler fails each test because of impatience, lack of awareness, and greed. The djinn spares his life but sends him away without treasure. The story warns against greed and teaches that humility and gratitude are greater treasures than gold. The well became a legendary landmark among Saharan nomads, its location passed from generation to generation—a reminder that the desert gives only to those who approach it with respect.

title: The Dodo and the Hunter's Fire
summary: Three Hausa hunters track a Dodo into the deep bush, only to discover that the monstrous shapeshifter feeds not on flesh but on fear, and the only weapon that defeats it is courage unmasked.

title: The Dog-Turks and the Sámi Women
summary: A story from Emilie Demant Hatt's collection featuring mysterious 'Dog-Turks' as attackers. Sámi women are the protagonists who outfox their attackers and save their people. The tale reflects the historical vulnerability of Sámi communities to various outside groups and highlights the agency and cleverness of Sámi women in these encounters.

title: the Dokkaebi and the Magic Club
summary: A mischievous goblin who can grant wishes with his magic club — but only to those who can answer his riddles — and if you steal his club, you become a goblin yourself.

title: The Dokkaebi Between the Fences
summary: A goblin who carries whispered messages across the DMZ for families separated by the war, slipping between barbed wire and landmines because even goblins know that some messages cannot wait.

title: the Dokkaebi Gam, the Medicine Goblin
summary: A goblin who lives in the market, stealing spices from greedy merchants and healing the sick with stolen herbs — because in Korea, even goblins have a sense of justice.

title: The Dokkaebi of the Erased Village
summary: A goblin who continues to play his games in a village that was demolished by the state, its houses torn down and its name removed from every map — because the Dokkaebi remembers what the state wants forgotten.

title: The Domovoi of Izba 17
summary: A house spirit who protects a peasant family tests their gratitude by disappearing for a week, and the chaos that follows teaches them never to forget his name.

title: The Donkey
summary: Once upon a time, in a small German village, there lived a young prince who found himself transformed into a donkey.

title: The Donkey Skin
summary: A princess flees an unwanted marriage to her father by wearing a donkey skin disguise. She works as a servant until a prince falls in love with her true identity.

title: The Doomed Prince
summary: In this ancient Egyptian tale, a king and queen are finally granted a son after long prayers. The Hathor goddesses arrive at the birth and prophesy that the child will die by either a crocodile, a serpent, or a dog. Desperate to protect his son, the king builds an isolated fortress in the desert where the prince is confined. The prince grows up but becomes determined to escape his fate. He takes his beloved dog and travels to the land of Naharin (Mesopotamia), where he wins the hand of a princess by climbing to the window of a tower seventy cubits high. He tells his wife of the prophecy. One night, a serpent attempts to bite him while he sleeps, but his wife kills it with beer and honey. Then a crocodile confronts him, but the story breaks off at this point due to the papyrus being damaged—the ending is unknown. The tale explores themes of fate vs. free will, the limitations of human protection against divine destiny, and the power of love to postpone or potentially alter fate.

title: The Douen: Lost Children of Trinidad
summary: Douen are the spirits of unbaptized children who died before receiving Christian names in Trinidadian folklore. They appear as small children wearing large straw hats that hide their faces, and they walk with their feet pointing backwards — making their footprints appear to go in the opposite direction. Douen are known to call out the names of living children, luring them into the forest to become lost. Parents warn children never to respond to a voice calling their name in the woods unless they can see the person. Once lured by a Douen, a child may wander into the wilderness and never return, becoming a Douen themselves. The legend serves as both a cautionary tale about wandering alone and a folk explanation for missing children in rural Trinidad.

title: The dragon and daughter
summary: A traditional tale involving a dragon and a princess, typically focusing on a hero's quest to rescue the maiden or a bargain made to save the kingdom from the dragon's wrath.

title: The Dragon Gate
summary: A story explaining how carp transform into dragons by leaping the Dragon Gate waterfall.

title: The Dragon of Babylon
summary: A simple shepherd saves a city from a terrifying dragon, proving that faith and wit are more powerful than the sharpest sword.

title: The Dragon of Belgrade
summary: Long ago, a fearsome dragon made its lair beneath what would become Belgrade Fortress, at the confluence of the Sava and Danube rivers.

title: The Dragon of Lopburi
summary: In the ancient city of Lopburi, there lived a powerful dragon beneath the great temple.

title: The Dragon of Mount Pilatus
summary: A dragon crash-landed on a Swiss mountain, and the healing stone from its blood is preserved in a museum to this day.

title: The Dragon of Wawel Castle
summary: A humble shoemaker saves the city of Kraków by defeating a terrible dragon through cunning rather than strength.

title: The Draugr's Treasure Guard
summary: Across the highlands, many burial mounds are said to be guarded by draugrs—corporeal undead who possess immense strength and magical abilities. These spirits protect their gold and jewelry, attacking any looter who dares disturb their slumber with a crushing grip and a frozen gaze.

title: The Dream Fast: The Boy Who Became a Robin
summary: An Ojibwe boy underwent his vision fast alone in the wilderness, seeking a guardian spirit as was traditional for young people. He prayed and fasted for many days without eating, asking the Creator for guidance. On the final day of his fast, a spirit appeared to him in a vision and promised that he would become a messenger between the people and the spirit world. When he returned to his village, his grandfather saw the change in him and understood that the fast had been successful. Later, the boy was transformed into a robin — the first robin — with a red breast that represents the fire and passion of his vision. From that day forward, the robin's song each morning reminds the people that the spirit world is close and that those who seek visions with a pure heart will be answered.

title: The Dreamtime
summary: The time before time when ancestral spirits created the world and all living things.

title: The Drekavac in the Cemetery
summary: A wailing spirit that rises from the graves of unbaptized children cries through the villages of Bosnia at night, and those who listen too closely hear the names of the children no one spoke aloud.

title: The Drowned Church
summary: In the Czech Republic, the golem is the most famous creature of Jewish folklore — a being made of clay and brought to life by the power of God's name.

title: The Drum of Thunder Calls Rain
summary: A humble drum maker is asked to make a sacred drum for the Thunder God—but pride leads to disaster.

title: The Duende of Machu Picchu
summary: A small forest spirit guards the hidden ruins of Machu Picchu, testing the worthiness of those who climb to the sacred city.

title: The Duppy of Brimstone Hill
summary: A young soldier stationed at Brimstone Hill Fort ignores the old guard's warning about duppies and is visited by a restless spirit in the dead of night.

title: The Dzin of the Bazaar
summary: A spirit bound to the old marketplaces of Bosnia, the Dzin grants fortunes to those it favors and misfortune to those who deal dishonestly, serving as an unseen guardian of fair trade.

title: The Dödning of Skåne
