summary: In the rich farmlands of Skåne, the southernmost province of Sweden, there was a farmer named Nils who was known for one thing: he never paid his debts.

title: The Eagle and Whale Husbands
summary: A legendary tale of Inuit women who find themselves married to powerful animal spirits — an eagle and a whale. These unions are fraught with difficulty as the women struggle to balance their human needs with the demands of their supernatural spouses. The story highlights the complexities of kinship and the influence of the spirit world on human destiny.

title: The Eland Creation: /Kaggen's Favorite Animal
summary: /Kaggen's wife /Hunntu!att!atten gave birth to the eland, and /Kaggen hid it near a secluded cliff to let it grow. His sons Cogaz and Gewi, not knowing their father's love for the animal, went hunting and killed it. Enraged, /Kaggen told Gewi to churn the eland's blood in a pot. Blood spattered onto the ground and turned into snakes, which displeased /Kaggen. When the blood scattered further it became hartebeests, still not what he wanted. Finally /Hunntu!att!atten cleaned the pot and churned fresh blood with heart fat, and when /Kaggen sprinkled this mixture on the ground, it turned into a great herd of eland, providing meat for his people to hunt. The eland's wildness is attributed to being killed before it was ready to be hunted.

title: The Elephant and the Sparrow
summary: In a lush forest of ancient India, there lived a great elephant named Channa.. He was massive and powerful, with tusks white as pearls and ears like great fans.

title: The Elk and the Lucky Reindeer
summary: A hunting legend from Emilie Demant Hatt's collection about an elk with supernatural qualities and the concept of 'reindeer luck.' The story describes a magical animal encounter and the propitiation that the hunter must perform. Luck in hunting was not random—it came from proper relationships with spirits, proper sacrifices at sieidis, and correct behavior toward animals.

title: The Eloko of the BaAka Forest
summary: A BaAka family traveling through the forest at dusk hears the laughter of an Eloko, a cannibal dwarf spirit, and must use their knowledge of ancient songs and forest lore to evade the creature.

title: The Eloko Who Wanted a Name
summary: A lonely Eloko spirit approaches a Gbaya village not to hunt but to ask for a human name, believing it will grant passage into the world of people, and learns a painful lesson about the boundaries between worlds.

title: The Elusive White Reindeer
summary: A Sámi nature myth about the white reindeer, considered a sacred and powerful creature. Seeing a white reindeer was considered an omen, and its appearance in dreams signaled major life changes. In the Pathfinder legend, Raste the noaidi seeing his spirit bull reindeer for the last time portends his death. The white reindeer is associated with Beaivi and the sun's power.

title: The Elves and the Shoemaker
summary: On the misty moors of Devon and Cornwall, where the fog rolls in from the sea and covers the land like a blanket, there is a light that leads travelers to their doom.

title: The Emadloti of King Sobhuza
summary: When a Swazi king is buried with his cattle, the spirit-emadloti rise as guardians of the royal lineage, protecting the bloodline from those who would seize the throne.

title: The Emergence (Jicarilla Apache)
summary: In the Jicarilla Apache emergence story, White God of the East made a mountain that grew toward the sky and caused reeds to stand in the center. Four girls twisted the reeds, stopping their growth. Four ladders were made — black, blue, yellow, and variegated — and placed at the mountain. Whirlwind went to the upper world and found much water. Beaver built dams, Badger followed him, and they reported the land was exposed. The people climbed the ladders, starting with black, then blue, then yellow, and finally variegated. After the last ladder wore out, an old woman and old man remained behind. 'You will come back here to me,' one called after the departing people, establishing that the dead return to the underworld. The people moved east along four parallel trails under four chiefs, and leadership alternated between fortunate and unfortunate. They finally settled near Taos. The two who remained became the rulers of the dead.

title: The Emperor's New Clothes
summary: There was an emperor in Denmark who was so vain—so obsessed with new clothes—that he spent all his money on the finest garments.

title: The Enchanted Deer
summary: In the sun-drenched hills of Italy, there once lived a poor hunter who spent his days tracking game through the dense forests that covered the mountainsides.

title: The Enchanted Duck
summary: A humble princess endures years of absolute silence to save her sisters from a magical curse.

title: The Enchanted Forest
summary: Two siblings lost in the enchanted forest of Tiveden must use their wisdom and purity of heart to solve riddles posed by mystical spirits to find their way home.

title: The Enchanted Mule
summary: In the hills of Andalusia, where Spain meets the Mediterranean sun, there lies a path that appears only at night—a road that leads to a place beyond human understanding.

title: The Epic of Ak-Kaan
summary: Ak-Kaan ('White Khan') is an Altai heroic epic telling of a shining white khan who brought justice to the Altai mountains. Born with a divine radiance, Ak-Kaan could see through deception and hear lies hidden in words. His quest was to defeat the dark shamans serving Erlik and restore balance between the upper and lower worlds. With his magical horse (argamak) that could fly between the three worlds, Ak-Kaan traveled to the court of Bai-Ulgen in the sky to receive divine weapons. He returned to defeat the seventy-seven demons of Erlik and establish the 'White Faith' (Ak Jang) — the Burkhanist religion that blends shamanism with Buddhist and Tibetan influences. The epic reflects the transition from pure shamanism to Burkhanism among the Altai people in the 19th and early 20th centuries.

title: The Epic of Alpamysh (Uzbek Version)
summary: The Uzbek version of Alpamysh (Alpomish) is the national heroic epic of Uzbekistan, with the largest recorded version by bard Fazil Yuldashogli containing 14,000 verses. The epic follows Alpamysh from his miraculous birth to elderly parents through his heroic courtship of Barchin, whom he wins in suitor contests. After marrying Barchin and returning home, he fights the usurper Ultantaz who has persecuted his father and tried to force Barchin into marriage. Alpamysh, returning after seven years in disguise as his old shepherd Kultay, comes to the wedding feast, frees his wife, and kills Ultantaz. The epic ends with reunification of the divided Kongrat tribe. The epic is performed by bakhshi (bardic artists) to the accompaniment of the dombra.

title: The Epic of Amir Timur's Rise
summary: According to Uzbek legend, the great conqueror Amir Timur (Tamerlane) was born with a clot of dried blood in his fist — a sign of his destiny as a warrior. As a young man, he was a sheep thief and a bandit until a vision from the spirit of his ancestor showed him his true path. After being wounded in battle, he limped through the mountains and took refuge in the cave of a holy man who prophesied that Timur would conquer from Damascus to Delhi. Timur's rise from obscure origins to ruler of the mightiest empire since Genghis Khan is seen as proof of divine favor. His construction projects in Samarkand, especially the Registan and Bibi-Khanum mosque, were said to be built with the help of jinn spirits.

title: The Epic of Dimdim (Kela Dimdimê)
summary: A Kurdish heroic epic based on the historical siege of Dimdim Castle (1609-1610) in the Bradost region near Lake Urmia. The Kurdish leader Emir Khan Lepzerin (Xanê Lepzêrîn, 'Gold-Arm Khan') rebuilt the ancient fortress of Dimdim on a 2,000-meter mountain. The Persian Safavid Shah Abbas the Great, seeing the growing Kurdish power, sent his grand vizier Hatem Beg to besiege the fortress. The Kurds held out for seven years against the Persian army. When Dimdim finally fell, the Persians massacred all defenders. The epic is sung by Kurdish dengbêj (traditional storytellers) and is considered the second most important Kurdish national epic after Mam and Zin. It symbolizes Kurdish resistance against foreign domination.

title: The Epic of Geser Khan
summary: Geser Khan is the central hero of one of the great Mongolian epics. Born as a runny-nosed, despised child on the Mongolian steppe, he is actually the son of the sky-deity Khürmasta Tengri, sent to earth to defeat the demons (mangus) that are devouring the world. Despite being mocked and rejected, Geser grows to defeat multi-headed ogres, rescue his mother from the underworld, marry the celestial princess Rogmo Goa, and subdue the entire universe including heaven and earth. The epic survives in Mongolian, Tibetan, Buryat, and Altai versions, with the earliest Mongolian printed edition from 1716 in Beijing.

title: The Epic of Jangar
summary: Jangar is a heroic epic of the Oirat Mongols (Kalmyks), comprising hundreds of thousands of lines. The epic describes the ideal kingdom of Bumba, ruled by the heroic Jangar and his twelve brave warriors (including the invincible Hongor, the swift Sabar, and the strong Mingyan). The heroes protect Bumba from monstrous invaders, capture magical horses and beautiful maidens, and embody the highest ideals of Mongol warrior culture — loyalty, courage, and hospitality. The epic is traditionally sung with tovshuur (lute) accompaniment during celebrations. The kingdom of Bumba represents a paradise on earth where there is no death, suffering, or old age.

title: The Epic of Maadai-Kara
summary: Maadai-Kara is one of the greatest Altai heroic epics, narrating a thousand-year struggle compressed into two generations. The epic begins with the hero Maadai-Kara and his people suffering under the oppression of the underworld lord Erlik. The central hero, Kögüdei Mergen (son of Maadai-Kara), undertakes a shamanic journey into the underworld to unlock the secret of life and death. He must bring his parents back from the dead, rescue his livestock and people from destruction, and defeat the dark forces of Erlik. The epic unfolds across three cosmic dimensions — the earth (middle world), the underworld (spirit realm), and the heavens (divine realm). The hero is aided by the sacred tree Bay-Terek, magical winged horses (argamak), and the supreme god Yuch-Kurbustan. Female shamanic figures like Abram Moos Kara Taaci (Erlik's daughter) play crucial roles as guides and challengers.

title: The Epic of Manas: The Birth of the Hero
summary: The Epic of Manas is the longest epic poem in the world (500,000+ lines), central to Kyrgyz national identity. Manas was born to the elderly and childless Jakyp in exile on the Altai. His birth was marked by supernatural signs — a mysterious light filled the tent, the earth trembled, and the sky thundered. Even as an infant, Manas showed extraordinary strength, weighing as much as a thirty-year-old man and greedily eating three sheep stomachs full of butter. From childhood, he gathered forty companions (kyrk choro) and began rallying the scattered Kyrgyz tribes against their Kalmyk and Chinese oppressors. The epic's reciters (manaschi) are believed to receive their calling through dreams, where Manas's spirit visits them.

title: The Epic of Sundiata (Mande)
summary: Sundiata Keita was the crippled son of King Naré Maghann Konaté and the ugly, hunchbacked woman Sogolon. A prophecy foretold that Sogolon's son would become a great king. After his father's death, Sundiata and his mother were persecuted by the king's first wife and forced into exile. During his exile in the Mema kingdom, Sundiata miraculously learned to walk by using an iron rod from a blacksmith, then a baobab branch. He grew into a powerful warrior. Meanwhile, the sorcerer-king Soumaoro Kanté conquered the Mandinka people. The oppressed called Sundiata back from exile, and at the Battle of Kirina (c. 1235), Sundiata defeated Soumaoro using a magic arrow tipped with a white cock's spur. He became the first Mansa (emperor) of the Mali Empire, establishing the Kouroukan Fouga constitution and building an empire that thrived for centuries.

title: The Erlking
summary: A father rode through the dark forest late at night, his feverish child pressed close against his chest.

title: The Eternal Chase of the Sun and Moon
summary: Aningaut (the Moon) and his sister Malina (the Sun) are locked in a perpetual race across the sky. The conflict began when Aningaut marked Malina's face with soot. Furious, Malina fled into the sky, becoming the bright sun. Aningaut continues to chase her eternally, though he occasionally descends to Earth to hunt seals, explaining the phases of the moon.

title: The Eternal Fool
summary: Once upon a time, in a quiet corner of Sweden, there lived a boy who was known to everyone as the Fool.

title: The Eternal Struggle: Quetzalcoatl
summary: Before the world as we know it existed, before the sun rose and set, before the first humans walked the earth, there were two brothers whose eternal struggle shaped the cosmos itself.

title: The Eternal Wisdom of Ifa Divination (Yoruba)
summary: Orunmila, the Orisha of wisdom and divination, received the sacred Odu Ifa from Olodumare at the beginning of time. The Ifa system consists of 256 sacred verses (Odu) that encode the entire knowledge of the universe—history, medicine, philosophy, and prophecy. Orunmila taught the Ifa to humanity through Babalawos (fathers of secrets), the priests trained to interpret the sacred palm nuts and divination chain. According to legend, Orunmila was present at the creation of the world and recorded everything that would happen. The first Babalawo was Ẹla, the son of Orunmila. Ifa divination is used for guidance on all aspects of life—health, marriage, travel, and spiritual matters. In 2005, UNESCO recognized the Ifa divination system as a Masterpiece of the Oral and Intangible Heritage of Humanity. The wisdom of Ifa continues to guide millions of Yoruba people worldwide.

title: The Evil One and Kitta Grau
summary: The Devil meets Kitta Grau, a sharp-tongued old woman, and she out-argues, out-cheats, and out-schemes him at every turn — proving that a clever woman can best even the Prince of Darkness. This tale from Halland shows that a wicked woman outdoes the Devil himself.

title: The Exodus from Notsie (Ewe)
summary: The Ewe people once lived under the tyrannical rule of King Agokoli (Togbe Agorkoli) in the walled city of Notsie (in present-day Togo). The king forced his subjects to build a massive mud wall around the city and worked them cruelly. The Ewe elders devised a clever escape plan: the women were told to wash their clothes in water and then soak them, creating a muddy slurry that they used to soften a section of the wall. While the drums played loudly to mask the noise, the Ewe people cut through the softened wall and escaped into the night. They walked backward away from the city to confuse pursuers who would see footprints pointing toward Notsie. The dispersed groups became the various Ewe clans found today across Ghana, Togo, and Benin. This story explains both Ewe unity and the existence of distinct Ewe subgroups.

title: The Eyes of Horus
summary: The battle between Horus and Set raged across the sky and earth for eighty years.

title: The Fairy of the Well
summary: In a small Polish village, there lived a girl called Złota—the golden one—not because she was wealthy, but because her hair shone like wheat in the summer sun.

title: The Fairy Ointment
summary: A young woman's curiosity leads her to use a forbidden fairy ointment, revealing a hidden world of both wonder and unsettling truth.

title: The Faithful Animals
summary: A poor woodcutter lived with his wife and children in a cottage at the edge of a great forest.

title: The Fanditha Sorcerer and the Demon of Fuvahmulah
summary: On the atoll of Fuvahmulah in the Maldives, legend tells of a kan'du fureytha (ocean demon) that emerged from the water as a 'pale, large flame looming over the rocks,' terrifying the islanders. The demon dragged people into the sea, and in despair, the inhabitants of one island sought help from Edhurutakkaange Mohamed Didi, a renowned fanditha veriyaa (sorcerer). Despite working his magic for many days at the reef, the demon kept claiming victims. Tormented by his failed attempts, Mohamed Didi cast one ultimate, all-powerful spell that trapped the evil demon forever within a deserted island. Shortly afterward, the island mysteriously vanished entirely, never to be seen again. A large reef rock called Fureytha Gaa (Demon Rock) now marks where the island was hidden. Local lore says that if you prod the stone with an iron rod, it still oozes blood, and will do so forever whenever struck.

title: The Farsakh Walker
summary: A giant who measured distances with his stride is said to have carved the great passes through the Pamir, leaving behind valleys that mortals still travel.
themes: the shaping of landscape by mythic forces
weariness and mortality of even great beings

title: The Fate of Aino
summary: Wainamoinen falls in love with the young Aino, but she is horrified by his advanced age and lacks any affection for him. Despite her desperate pleas, her parents force her to marry the old enchanter. In a final act of desperation to escape her fate, Aino leaps into the sea, where she is transformed into a mermaid-like creature.

title: The Ferocity of the Adlet
summary: The Adlet are a race of half-dog, half-human hybrids, possessing the lower body of a canine and the upper body of a human. They are known for their extreme speed and savage nature, frequently attacking human visitors to their territories. Most encounters with the Adlet result in brutal combat, though the humans usually manage to prevail through ingenuity and courage.

title: The Fiddler Who Got the Madonna's Golden Shoe
summary: A wandering fiddler (spelman) in medieval Sweden finds himself blessed by a miraculous encounter with the Madonna, who gives him one of her golden shoes as a reward for his devoted music. The tale draws on Catholic and folk motifs, blending Christian iconography with Scandinavian folk music tradition.

title: The Fig Tree Covenant
summary: When Ngai created Gikuyu and showed him the land, he made a sacred covenant beneath the wild fig tree (Mukuyu). Ngai said to Gikuyu: 'Descend from my home and establish your homestead among these fig trees. Whenever you are in need of me, make a sacrifice upon this tree and raise your hands to Kirinyaga, and I, the Possessor of Brightness, will come to your aid.' This covenant established the fig tree as a sacred altar where the Kikuyu communicate with Ngai. The elders offer sacrifices of meat, blood, and beer beneath its spreading branches, and these ceremonies mark every major life event — birth, initiation, marriage, and death. The mugumo tree is never cut down, for it is the living bridge between the people and their creator.

title: The Fire Keeper of the Gaucho Camps
summary: A spirit of the campfire who appears to gauchos in the wilderness, testing their hospitality and generosity.

title: The Firebird
summary: A humble prince embarks on a perilous quest for a magical bird, learning that kindness and integrity are the true keys to success.

title: The First Areíto Drum
summary: A Taíno legend explaining the origin of the sacred areíto drum. Before the drum, the Taíno remembered everything through spoken words alone, but as elders passed on and storms scattered villages, memories faltered and disputes arose over boundaries and promises. One night, a cacique (chief) prayed to the zemís asking how memory could be protected. From the forest emerged an old man carrying a hollowed log who taught the people to stretch animal hide across one end, creating the first drum. The drum would carry law, lineage, and story — guiding singers so words would not wander. Laws were sung with the drum's beat, agreements sealed through areíto performances, and the drum was never struck in anger. It belonged to the community, not any individual, and kept Taíno memory alive through rhythm.

title: The First Banana: A Baganda Legend
summary: According to Baganda tradition, the banana (matooke) was a gift from the gods to sustain humanity. In the time after Kintu, the people had grain but no fruit trees. One day, a woman named Nalongo was mourning the death of her twin children. She buried them in her courtyard and watered their graves with her tears. From one grave grew a banana plant, its leaves spreading like comforting arms. From the other grew a plantain. Nalongo tended the plants faithfully, and when they bore fruit, she discovered that cooking the green bananas produced a soft, nourishing food that could feed many people. She shared her discovery with the village, and the banana became the staple food of Buganda. The Baganda say that the banana plant's ability to produce offshoots (suckers) from its base is a reminder that life continues even after death, just as Nalongo's children continued to nourish their people. To this day, the banana garden is the heart of every Baganda homestead.

title: The First Corn
summary: The gods sacrifice themselves to feed humanity. Centers on Spirit,  human attempt to understand the soul, afterlife, and the unseen forces that govern existence..

title: The First Fire Stolen from the Sky
summary: An Evenki myth explaining how humans first obtained fire. In the beginning, the ancestors of the Evenki lived in eternal cold without fire. A brave shaman or culture hero transformed into a bird and flew up to the sky, where he stole a burning ember from the celestial realm. He brought the fire down to the frozen taiga, giving warmth, light, and the ability to cook food to humanity. The spirits of the sky were angered by this theft and sent storms and lightning to punish the earth. This myth belongs to the widespread 'stolen fire' tradition found across many northern cultures and emphasizes the Evenki value of bravery and sacrifice for the community good.

title: The First Hmong Shaman: How the Shaman Got His Power
summary: One of the most sacred Hmong myths explains the origins of shamanic power and the relationship between the human and spirit worlds. According to legend, there was once a man whose wife became gravely ill. Desperate to save her, he journeyed to the spirit world (yeeb ceeb), guided by a benevolent spirit. There he met the spirits of his ancestors and the king of the spirits (Ntuj), who showed him the sacred rituals, chants, and healing practices. The spirits taught him how to beat the drum to call spirits, how to swing the rattle bells (nyiaj cuam) to open gates between worlds, and how to sacrifice animals to pay the spirit debt. Upon returning to the human world, the man successfully healed his wife using the sacred knowledge. He became the first Hmong shaman (txiv neeb). A crucial element of the myth is the shamanic journey across a dangerous bridge or ladder connecting the worlds — a perilous crossing that only trained shamans can navigate safely. The legend includes the shaman's spirit helpers — particularly the tiger and the rooster — who guide and protect the shaman during soul-retrieval journeys. This myth establishes the shaman's role as the intermediary between the physical and spiritual realms, responsible for healing, soul-calling (hu plig), and maintaining cosmic harmony.

title: The First Navigator
summary: An ancient navigator discovers the secrets of the stars and the ocean's swells, guiding his people to new lands and establishing the art of wayfinding.

title: The First Prayer Flag
summary: A Tibetan legend explaining the origin of the iconic Tibetan prayer flags (Lungta or Wind Horse flags). According to the tradition, when the Buddha's teachings were first spreading in Tibet, harmful spirits and negative energies threatened the people. The great master Padmasambhava (Guru Rinpoche) used prayer flags as a technique to transform negative energy into positive blessings. The mantras and prayers printed on the flags, when touched by the wind, spread blessings across the land like a horse racing through the sky. The five colors of the flags — blue (sky), white (air), red (fire), green (water), yellow (earth) — represent the five elements of balance. The central Wind Horse symbol carries the wish-fulfilling jewel of enlightenment on its back.

title: The First Reindeer
summary: A Chukchi legend explaining the origin of the domesticated reindeer, essential to Chukchi survival in the Arctic tundra. According to the myth, Kuutkh created the reindeer from the scattered hairs of his own body or from the remnants of a celestial hunt. The reindeer was given to humanity as a gift from the sky spirits, providing transportation, food, clothing, and shelter in the harsh Arctic environment. The maritime Chukchi, who hunt sea mammals, have a different version where the first reindeer emerged from the sea, blending elements of coastal and inland traditions. The story reinforces the sacred bond between the Chukchi people and their reindeer herds.

title: The First Strawberries (Cherokee)
summary: The first man and the first woman quarreled, and the woman left their home in anger. The man, sad and remorseful, tried to bring her back. The Sun, taking pity on the man, created huckleberries along the path to tempt the woman to stop, but she paid them no mind. Next the Sun created blackberries, but she ignored them too. Finally, the Sun created strawberries — the first ever. When the woman saw the ripe, red berries, she stopped to taste one. The sweetness reminded her of happier times, and she began to gather them. As she looked back down the path, she saw her husband approaching, and she forgave him. They reconciled and returned home together. This Cherokee story explains the origin of strawberries and teaches the power of sweetness and forgiveness in mending relationships.

title: The First Sweat Lodge (Lakota)
summary: According to Lakota tradition, the sweat lodge was given to the people by the spirits as a means of purification and healing. A warrior who had been wounded in battle was near death when a spirit appeared and instructed him to build a framework of willow branches and cover it with buffalo hides. He was to heat stones in a fire, place them in a pit at the center, and pour water over them. The steam would purify his body and spirit. The warrior followed these instructions and was healed. The inipi (sweat lodge) ceremony became one of the Seven Sacred Rites, used for physical healing, spiritual cleansing, and preparation for other ceremonies.

title: The Fisherman and His Wife
summary: There was once a poor fisherman who lived with his wife, Ilsebill, in a miserable hovel by the sea — a place so small and filthy it was scarcely better than a pigsty.

title: The Fisherman and the Jinni
summary: A poor fisherman casts his net four times daily. On the fourth cast, he hauls up a copper jar sealed with Solomon's seal. Opening it releases an enormous Ifrit (jinni) who, having languished in captivity for centuries, has resolved to kill whoever frees him. The fisherman tricks the jinni back into the jar by questioning how such a mighty being could fit inside, rescaling it. After the jinni pleads and promises rewards, the fisherman releases him. The jinni leads him to a magical pond with talking fish, setting off a chain of revelations about an enchanted prince turned half to stone.

title: The Fisherman Sikur and the Troll Net
summary: Sikur the fisherman acquires a magical fishing net. When a troll steals the net, Sikur's three sons — one the fastest in the world, one the strongest, and one the wisest — team up to trick the troll and retrieve the net. Each son uses his unique gift to outwit the trollish foe in a classic trio-of-heroes structure.

title: The Flower of Happiness on Sunnymount Crest
summary: Deep in the Swedish forest, on the sun-drenched peak of Sunnymount Crest (Solberga klint), grows a magical flower that grants happiness to whoever finds it. Two young girls set out on a perilous journey through the deep woods where trolls, fairies, and witches keep their secrets. Their only hope of true happiness lies in reaching this elusive flower at the top of the mountain. Along the way, they encounter various supernatural beings from Swedish folklore — some helpful, some hostile. They must navigate enchanted forests, outwit dangerous creatures, and persevere through exhaustion and fear. The flower at Sunnymount Crest represents not just magical happiness but the idea that true fulfillment comes from the journey itself and the courage to pursue one's dreams despite all obstacles. The story, by Alfred Smedberg, was first published in the 1907 edition of 'Bland Tomtar och Troll' with illustrations by John Bauer. It reflects Smedberg's characteristic themes of love for the Swedish countryside, moral clarity, and the triumph of goodness and perseverance over adversity.

title: The Flying Canoe (Passamaquoddy)
summary: Three Passamaquoddy brothers, all skilled canoe-builders, competed to see who could build the finest canoe. The eldest two built large, sturdy vessels decorated with porcupine quills and painted designs. But the youngest brother, instead of building an ordinary canoe, consulted the spirits and built a magical canoe that could fly through the air as easily as it could glide across water. When the day of judgment came, the two older brothers mocked the youngest's strange craft. But when the youngest sang a special song, his canoe rose into the air and circled the village. The chief was so impressed that he gave his daughter to the youngest brother in marriage. The story celebrates innovation and the wisdom of seeking spiritual guidance rather than merely following tradition, a theme common to Wabanaki folktales.

title: The Flying Dutchman
summary: The Flying Dutchman is the most famous ghost ship in maritime history — a vessel condemned to sail the oceans forever, never making port, never finding rest.

title: The Flying Dutchman of the Cape
summary: A ghost ship doomed to sail forever around the Cape of Good Hope, appearing to doomed sailors as a warning.

title: The Flying Head (Kanontsistóntie)
summary: The Flying Head is a terrifying monster in the form of a giant disembodied head as tall as a man, covered in thick black hair with bat-like wings and long sharp claws. It comes to the homes of widows and orphans at night, beating its wings on the walls and issuing terrible cries, presaging death within days. According to one legend, the Flying Head was born from a massacre where a famine-stricken tribe decapitated their dead and sank the heads in the lake. The Seneca call it Takwánö'ë:yët, meaning whirlwind. One story tells of an old woman who defeated the Flying Head by sitting by her fire eating roasted acorns; the monster mistook the acorns for coals of fire and fled in terror, never to be seen again in that place.

title: The Flying Trunk
summary: A man acquires a magic trunk that allows him to fly. He uses this power to travel the world and eventually wins the hand of a princess by demonstrating his supernatural abilities.

title: The Forest Keeper of Mount Manengouba
summary: Deep in the forests of Mount Manengouba, the Boumba forest spirit protects the ancient trees and punishes those who would destroy what took centuries to grow.

title: The Forty Robbers of the Steppe (Kirk Kazak)
summary: The legend of the 'Forty Kazakhs' (Kirk Kazak) tells of forty exiled warriors who formed a brotherhood on the Kazakh steppe. According to tradition, the sons of a khan's younger wife, offended by their older brothers, fled to the steppe with thirty-three other exiles. They banded together as forty warriors, defending travelers on the Silk Road and fighting for justice. Their leader was a just and courageous batyr, and their code of honor required absolute loyalty to each other and protection of the weak. This legend is considered one of the foundational stories of Kazakh identity — the number forty appears throughout Kazakh symbolism, and the warriors' code influenced the Kazakh concept of heroism and justice.

title: The Foster-Child of the Deer
summary: A Zuni story about a child abandoned in the wilderness who was adopted and raised by deer. The deer taught the child to live in harmony with nature, to understand the language of animals, and to know the sacred plants of the forest. When the child grew up and encountered human hunters, a conflict arose between the human and deer worlds. The deer-mother bid farewell to her foster-child, who was torn between two worlds — the human world of their birth and the deer world of their raising. The story teaches respect for deer and the proper relationship between hunters and prey. It is connected to Zuni hunting rituals and the belief that deer willingly give themselves to respectful hunters who perform the correct ceremonies and prayers. The foster-child became a mediator between humans and deer, teaching people the rituals that honor the spirits of slain animals.

title: The Four Big Trolls and Little Peter Pastureman
summary: When the old Troll King dies, four enormous trolls — each as large as a mountain — vie for the throne. Their vicious rivalry threatens all magical folk in the kingdom, as their power struggles cause chaos throughout the land. Little Peter, a brave and lighthearted shepherd boy (called Vill-Vallareman in Swedish) who works as a pastureman for the four trolls, finds himself caught in the middle of their conflict. Despite his small size, Peter possesses quick wits and a courageous heart. While the four giant trolls argue, scheme, and battle one another, Peter uses his intelligence to outmaneuver them. He blows on a birchbark horn, which plays a key role in the resolution of the trolls' dispute. Through his bravery and clever thinking, Peter prevents what would have been a tragic outcome for all the magical folk. The story, richly illustrated by John Bauer with iconic images of the trolls and the small shepherd boy, demonstrates that size and strength matter less than intelligence and courage. It is a charming blend of adventure and folklore that teaches the triumph of good over evil through wit rather than force.

title: The Four Carpenters and the Creation of the World (Nuxalk)
summary: When the world was first created, the Creator Alhkw'ntam had help from Four Carpenters called the Masmasalanicw, who were like human beings with wings — angels. They carved the first ancestors from the cosmic tree Tcncniyaaq (the Milky Way). There were 45 original families, each with their own room in the House of Smayusta (the Creator's house in the upper world). The ancestors were given cwmnwas (spirit) placed in the bone of the back of their neck, and slhup'tsta (breath). They were given names, food, tools, a code of ethics, and protocols, all placed within a nuslhiixwta (treasure box). Hanging on the walls were animal, bird, and sea creature cloaks. Each ancestor chose a cloak — grizzly bear, raven, eagle, killer whale, wolf, mountain goat, heron — and danced with it. The Creator threw his sun blanket over himself and transformed into the sun. The ancestors did the same, transforming into their chosen animals. Guided by the eyelashes of the sun, they floated down to earth and removed their cloaks, which returned to heaven. This is the Nuxalk creation story, explaining the origin of all Nuxalk clans and their crests.

title: The Four White Umbrellas: The Burmese Creation of Kingship
summary: According to Burmese mythology, the institution of kingship began in the earliest age of the world when human society descended into chaos and conflict after losing its primordial harmony. The people, suffering from theft, violence, and disorder, gathered together and elected the most virtuous and handsome man among them to be their ruler. They named him Mahasamrat (the Great Elected One), and as symbols of his authority, they offered him four white umbrellas — one for each cardinal direction. The white umbrella (hti) became the supreme symbol of Burmese kingship and sovereignty. Mahasamrat established the first laws, formed armies for defense, created the caste system to organize society, and appointed officials to administer justice. This myth establishes the concept of the king as the people's chosen representative rather than a divine despot, and the four white umbrellas continue to be used in Burmese royal and religious ceremonies. The legend legitimizes the monarchy while simultaneously reminding rulers that their authority derives from the consent of the governed and their duty to maintain righteousness (dhamma).

title: The Fox as Herdsman
summary: A farmer hires a fox to be a herdsman for his sheep, believing the fox's promises of efficiency. However, the fox uses his cunning to deceive the farmer, stealing the sheep one by one while making the farmer believe the sheep are disappearing due to supernatural causes.

title: The Fox Spirit
summary: In the mountains and forests of Japan, where the bamboo sways in the wind and the shrines disappear into mist, there live foxes—yoko, the animal foxes.

title: The Fox Tricks the Bear
summary: A Sámi animal fable where the cunning fox outsmarts the bear. The fox uses clever words and deception to avoid being eaten. These tales parallel international trickster traditions but with distinct Sámi elements—the animals are those of the Arctic. The tales teach that intelligence is more valuable than brute strength.

title: The Frog Prince
summary: In the days when wishes still worked and magic was as common as morning dew, there lived a king whose youngest daughter was so beautiful that the sun itself stopped to stare when she stepped into the garden.

title: The Frog Princess
summary: A tsar commands his three sons to marry, and the youngest chooses a frog from the river who is really a princess under a spell.

title: The Frost Giant's Breath
summary: A village is plagued by a sudden, unnatural winter that kills all the crops. It is discovered that a Frost Giant has awakened from his sleep beneath the glacier. The villagers must travel to the heart of the ice and perform a ritual of fire and song to lull the giant back into a deep slumber.

title: The Frost-fiend
summary: The heroes face an encounter with the personification of winter, the Frost-fiend. They must rely on their wit, resilience, and magical songs to survive the killing cold and the oppressive environment of the extreme north.

title: The Fur Coat
summary: In a cold German winter, in a village nestled deep in the Black Forest, a poor girl was walking home through a forest when she found a fur coat lying in the snow.

title: The Gahe: Apache Mountain Spirit Dancers
summary: The Gahe (called Gaan by Western Apache) are the Mountain Spirits, powerful supernatural beings who live inside sacred mountains. The first Mountain Spirit ceremony originated when children of the Sun taught the Apache how to call and honor these spirits. The Mountain Spirits appear as masked dancers wearing distinctive tall, wooden-slat headdresses, with black-and-white body paint and black buckskin kilts. The Gahe ceremony is part of the Girls' Puberty Ceremony (Sunrise Ceremony), the longest and richest Apache ritual. Four Mountain Spirits typically dance together — one for each cardinal direction — along with a clown figure. The dancers move in a syncopated, swaying rhythm to singing and drumming, tracing sacred patterns in the dance ground with their feet. The Gahe are believed to possess healing powers and can cure illness, drive away evil influences, and bring blessings. Sierra Blanca (White Mountain) in New Mexico is considered the spiritual origin place of many Mountain Spirit dance groups.

title: the Gangsi, the Hungry Ghost
summary: A reanimated corpse that hops through the night with outstretched arms, draining the life force from the living — because in Korea, the dead do not always stay dead.

title: The Garamantes: Lost People of the Fezzan
summary: The Garamantes were an ancient civilization that flourished in the Fezzan region of southwestern Libya from approximately 1000 BCE to 700 CE. According to Herodotus, who first wrote of them in the 5th century BCE, the Garamantes were a 'very great nation' who cultivated date palms, bred cattle, and hunted cave-dwelling Ethiopians with four-horse chariots. They built a sophisticated underground irrigation system (foggaras) that tapped fossil water beneath the Sahara, enabling urban civilization in one of the harshest environments on earth. Their capital, Garama, housed thousands and was connected by trade routes to the Roman Empire, sub-Saharan Africa, and Egypt. The Garamantes were both raiders and traders—fighting wars against Rome while also supplying exotic animals, slaves, and gold to Mediterranean markets. The kingdom declined after over-extraction of fossil water and the collapse of Roman trade. Folk legends say the Garamantes were giants who lived for hundreds of years and that their ruins are haunted by the spirits of ancient kings. Their descendants are believed to include some Tuareg tribes.

title: The Garden of Paradise
summary: A contemplative story exploring themes of beauty, the unattainable nature of a perfect world, and the human desire for a paradise that exists only in dreams or the afterlife.

title: The Ghost Bride of the Sea Islands
summary: A young Gullah man named Joshua fell in love with a woman named Eloise, the most beautiful woman on the Sea Islands. They were to be married, but on the night before the wedding, Eloise fell ill and died of a sudden fever. Joshua was heartbroken. On the night of what would have been their wedding, Joshua sat alone on the beach, grieving. At midnight, Eloise appeared before him, dressed in white, her eyes glowing faintly. She said she had returned to claim her wedding. Joshua, driven by love, danced with her on the moonlit shore as the waves crashed around them. An old conjure woman saw them and rushed to intervene, throwing salt between Joshua and the ghost bride. The spirit vanished with a wail. The conjure woman explained that the ghost bride had come to take Joshua with her to the spirit world—if he had danced until dawn, his soul would have been hers forever. Joshua painted his door 'haint blue' and never went near the beach at night again. The story is a classic Gullah ghost tale, warning against the power of love to bind the living to the dead.

title: The Ghost Monk of Eynhallow
summary: The ghost of a medieval monk haunts the abandoned island of Eynhallow in Orkney, appearing each night to ring a bell that no living ear can hear.

title: The Ghost of the Lhamo (Tibetan Wrathful Deities)
summary: Tibetan legends of the Lhamo — powerful female wrathful deities who serve as protectors of the Buddhist teachings. The most famous is Palden Lhamo (Glorious Goddess), the principal female protector deity of Tibetan Buddhism. According to legend, she was a wild, blood-drinking demoness who was converted to Buddhism by the great saint Machik Lapdrön or by Padmasambhava himself. She rides a mule through a sea of blood, her saddle made from the flayed skin of her own son whom she killed to prevent him from betraying the dharma. The Lhamo traditions bridge Tibetan Buddhism and the earlier Bon animistic beliefs, representing the fierce, protective aspects of feminine spiritual power. Offerings and rituals to Palden Lhamo are performed to this day, especially during the New Year ceremonies in Lhasa.

title: The Ghost Torch
summary: In the islands of Fiji, where the jungle meets the coral reefs and the nights are thick with the songs of insects, the villagers tell a story about a flickering light that appears on the mountain paths after dark.

title: The Ghost Who Walked Between Worlds
summary: A family discovers their deceased grandfather still lingers at the edge of the village, walking the moonlit path between the living and the dead.
themes: the boundary between life and death

title: The Ghostly Monks of Trondheimsfjorden
summary: Three monasteries in the Trondheimsfjord left behind more than ruins — their ghostly monks still walk the shores.

title: The Ghostly Wedding of the Highlands
summary: Two lovers, separated by death, are said to meet every century in a hidden valley in the highlands. They hold a ghostly wedding feast attended by other spirits of the land. Those who stumble upon the feast are often entranced for days, waking up to find that a hundred years have passed in the human world.

title: The Ghoul of Kerak Castle
summary: A Crusader-era garrison at Kerak Castle discovers that the dungeons beneath the fortress house a ghoul older than the castle itself, and that it has been feeding on the fears of every army that has claimed these walls.

title: The Ghoul of Oualata
summary: A young widower in the ancient city of Oualata is stalked by a female ghoul who takes the form of his late wife, and must use the wisdom of a blind marabout to survive her embrace.
themes: the boundary between love and possession

title: The Ghoul of the Desert
summary: In pre-Islamic Arabic folklore, the ghul (ghoul) is a demonic, shape-shifting creature inhabiting deserts and graveyards. Usually appearing female to lure unwary travelers, the ghul has donkey-like hooves, a feline head, forked tongue, and hairy skin. It calls victims by name in the voice of a loved one, then devours them. The poet Ta'abbata Sharra famously boasted of killing a ghul in single combat. Described by al-Jahiz and in the Arabian Nights, ghouls are a type of jinn that feast on human flesh and corpse meat. The word entered English through William Beckford's 1786 novel Vathek.

title: The Ghoul of the Roman Road
summary: A merchant travelling the ancient Roman road near Jerash is lured from his path by a ghoul disguised as a woman selling bread, and learns too late that the desert's most dangerous predators take human form.

title: The Ghoula of the Date Palm Grove
summary: A young pearl diver encounters a shape-shifting Al Ghoula in the date palm groves near Riffa, and must outwit her to survive the night.

title: The Giant Cloud-Swallower
summary: A Zuni story about a giant being who swallowed clouds, causing drought and suffering among the people. With the clouds gone, no rain fell, and the crops withered. The people performed ceremonies and made prayer offerings, but nothing worked. The twin war gods took action, pursuing the Giant Cloud-swallower across the sky. They shot their lightning arrows at the giant, who was so large he could be seen against the horizon. The battle raged across the heavens. Finally, the twins struck the giant in the throat, causing him to release all the clouds he had swallowed. Rain poured down upon the parched earth, and the people rejoiced. The dying giant's body became the first rainbows and his scattered bones became the clouds that still drift across the sky. The story reinforces the Zuni understanding of weather phenomena as the actions of spiritual beings and the ongoing role of the war gods as protectors.

title: The Giant Maiden in Boråseröd Mountain
summary: A young peasant captures a beautiful giant's daughter by throwing his knife between her and the mountain. At the wedding feast the giant eats until half full, ensuring only half the couple's descendants become great. After years of abuse the wife reveals her supernatural strength, teaching her husband true humility.

title: The Giant of Dovrefjell
summary: Deep in the mountains of the north lives a giant king who rules over a court of trolls and mountain spirits. He is known for his immense size and his ability to manipulate the weather. In legends, he challenges brave heroes to riddles and tests of strength, often rewarding them with gold or cursing them with madness.

title: The Giant Puke
summary: The giant Puke lives in a mountain near Lofta church, tormented by church bells and holy water. His daughter throws a stone at the church but misses. She later finds human children at play and brings them to her father, who declares that the age of giants is past. Puke leaves for Götland and gives a ship captain a magical box to offer at the church, but the crew throws it overboard and sets an island ablaze.

title: The Giant Vrål of Bohuslän
summary: The giant Vrål of Bohuslän forces a farmer to give up his daughter in marriage, and she serves him a bowl of porridge laced with 24 horseshoe nails — which he eats without noticing until the last one.

title: The Giant Without a Heart
summary: The youngest prince, known as Boots, embarks on a perilous quest to save his six brothers who were turned to stone by a heartless giant with a hidden weakness.

title: The Gift of Fire (Comanche)
summary: Long ago, the Comanche people had no fire and ate their food raw. Coyote, always clever, decided to steal fire from the fire people who guarded it jealously. Coyote crept into their camp and, when they weren't looking, grabbed a burning branch and ran. The fire people chased him across the plains. Coyote threw the fire to the animals, who tossed it among themselves like a hot game. The fire singed the animals in passing—the badger still has black marks, the raccoon's tail was burned, and the coyote's nose was scorched. Eventually, the fire reached the Comanche people, and they have kept it ever since.

title: The Gifts From the Underworld
summary: An envious old bachelor seeks a way to surpass a younger, more successful hunter. Guided by his mother, he discovers a hidden path to the underworld. He is instructed to ignore the first boat he sees and take a piece of matak (whale-skin) from the second. The matak grants him incredible hunting luck, but when he tries to deceive the younger man by telling him to take from the first boat, the younger man is cursed with bad luck. Eventually, the path to the underworld is sealed, leaving the old man unable to retrieve more luck, a cautionary tale about greed and the perils of deceit.

title: The Girl and the Snake
summary: A girl lost in the forest meets a talking snake who offers to guide her home in exchange for a promise — a promise that leads to an enchanted romance beneath the earth. This tale from Södermanland shows distinctive Scandinavian features.

title: The Girl and the Spirit Drum
summary: In the heart of Sudan, where the sun beats down with a relentless intensity and the dust of the desert chokes the breath of the living, a terrible famine had descended upon the land.

title: The Girl Chenoo
summary: A beautiful Mi'kmaq woman was lost in the frozen north and suffered terrible hunger. To survive, she ate human flesh and was transformed into a Chenoo — a cannibalistic ice monster with a heart of ice and an insatiable hunger for human beings. Her family searched for her but when they found her, she had become a monstrous giant with claws and fangs, her heart visible through her translucent chest. The family's oldest grandmother did not abandon her. She sang the old healing songs and performed the sacred ceremonies to warm her granddaughter's frozen heart. Through love and prayer, the grandmother melted the ice around the Chenoo's heart and restored her to human form. The story teaches the Mi'kmaq understanding that even those who become monsters through tragedy can be healed through family love, community, and the power of traditional ceremonies.

title: The Girl Who Climbed to the Sky
summary: An Arapaho girl was picking berries when she saw a porcupine in a tree. She climbed after it, but the tree grew taller and taller, carrying her into the sky world. In the sky, she found a beautiful land populated by spirits. She married a sky spirit and was happy, but she missed her earthly family. The spirits taught her songs and ceremonies that she would bring back to her people. Eventually, a spider spun a web to lower her back to Earth, where she taught the Arapaho the sky ceremonies she had learned. She became a powerful medicine woman.

title: The Girl Who Had No Eyes
summary: In the wild and windswept Highlands of Scotland, where the mist rolls down from the mountains like a grey river and the heather stretches purple to the horizon, there lived a girl named Mhairi.

title: The Girl Who Married a Star
summary: A Crow girl gazed at the sky and wished to marry the Morning Star. Her wish was granted, and she was taken to the sky world where she became the wife of a star. She was happy but was told never to dig up a certain root. Lonely for her family, she eventually disobeyed and pulled the root, revealing a hole through which she could see her earthly home far below. Overcome with longing, she wove a rope to descend, but it was too short. She fell to Earth and survived, finding her way back to her people. The star husband, heartbroken, can still be seen in the morning sky.

title: The Girl Who Stood in the Door
summary: There was a little girl—her name was Lis, and she was the happiest, most content child in the village.

title: The Girl Who Understood Birds
summary: A quiet girl who can communicate with birds uses her unique gift to save a dying child and teach her village the value of listening to nature.

title: The Girl Who Was Not Satisfied
summary: This moral tale from the Iroquois tradition tells of a young girl who was never content with what she had, always wanting more and better things. She rejected the simple life of her village and the young men who courted her. One day she met a handsome stranger who was actually a great serpent in disguise. She went away with him, only to discover too late his true nature. The story teaches the importance of appreciating what one has and warns against the dangers of pride and dissatisfaction. It also reinforces the Iroquois value of community over individual desire, as the girl's isolation from her people made her vulnerable to the serpent's deceptions.

title: The Girls Who Wished to Marry Stars
summary: Two Ojibwe girls slept outside one summer night, gazing at the stars. They began to wish out loud — one wished to marry the brightest star, the other wished to marry the Morning Star. To their astonishment, the stars descended and took them to the sky world. At first, everything was wonderful beyond imagination, but the girls soon grew homesick. They missed their families and the familiar earth. Their star husbands warned them never to dig in a certain spot, but curiosity overcame them and they dug, creating a hole through which they could see the earth below. They wove a rope of basswood bark and tried to climb down, but the rope broke, and they fell. The first girl turned into a shooting star, forever falling between worlds. The second girl landed safely and returned to her people, but she was never quite the same, always gazing at the stars.

title: The Glass Mountain
summary: A brave youth overcomes an impossible ascent to rescue a princess from a crystal peak.

title: The Goblin and the Grocer
summary: A comedic tale about a goblin who attempts to trade his magic for human goods, resulting in a series of misunderstandings and mishaps between the supernatural creature and the practical grocer.

title: The Goddess Oshun and the Dried Riverbeds (Yoruba)
summary: When the Orishas were creating the world, they neglected to consult Oshun, the goddess of love, fertility, and rivers. Enraged by this disrespect, Oshun withheld her waters, causing the rivers to dry up and the land to become barren. The other Orishas grew desperate as crops failed and life became impossible. Obatala and Orunmila tried to intervene but failed. Finally, they recognized their error and sent a humble delegation to Oshun, offering her proper tribute. Oshun relented and released her waters, restoring life to the earth. The lesson became eternal: no endeavor can succeed without acknowledging the feminine principle of love and fertility. Oshun is associated with honey, sweet waters, peacock feathers, and the sacred Osun River in Nigeria.

title: The Goddess Pattini and the Burning of Madurai
summary: Pattini, revered by both Sinhalese Buddhists and Tamil Hindus, originates from Kannaki, the chaste heroine of the Tamil epic Cilappatikaram. Kannaki's husband Kovalan was unjustly executed in Madurai for allegedly stealing the queen's anklet. To prove his innocence, Kannaki revealed her ruby-filled anklet (the queen's contained pearls). Enraged by the injustice, she tore off her left breast and hurled it at the city, setting Madurai ablaze. The gods elevated her to goddesshood and resurrected Kovalan. King Gajabahu I (2nd century CE) is believed to have brought her cult to Sri Lanka, where she is worshipped as a guardian deity of fertility, healing, and protection against disease.

title: The Golden Cradle
summary: A ship carrying a golden cradle for Queen Elenor is wrecked off Tjorn and the islanders murder the crew and plunder the cargo. The cradle is buried in Stordal Heath where it remains hidden to this day. The dying peasant who concealed it tried to reveal its location but his final words were unintelligible.

title: The Golden Fish
summary: A humble fisherman releases a magical golden fish and discovers that true wealth lies in contentment.

title: The Golden Frog Creation Myth
summary: In the beginning, the earth was submerged in a boundless ocean. When the lord of the universe, Buddha Sakyamuni, flew over the ocean seeking to create land, he saw a golden-bodied frog swimming from north to south. Using his bow and arrows, he shot the frog's east side, turning it northward. Fire gushed from its mouth and water from its rump. Buddha threw golden sand on the frog, which became the earth. The arrow's protruding part became a forest, the arrowhead that passed through became a metal area. The fire from the frog's mouth made the north a region of fire, and the water from its rump made the south a watery area. When the frog moves its legs or shakes its head, earthquakes result.

title: The Golden Keys
summary: Lena, a humble meadow-maid, encounters three fairies who present her with a golden key that leads to a magical dream garden. This gift comes with a strict condition: the secret must never be revealed to anyone. Lena accepts and experiences the joy of the dream garden, but her loyalty is soon tested when the young king falls into grave danger. The only way to save him is to reveal the secret, breaking her promise. She chooses sacrifice over self-preservation, saves the king, and is rewarded with his hand in marriage.

title: The Golden Stool Descends from Heaven (Ashanti/Akan)
summary: During the reign of the Ashanti King Osei Tutu I, the great priest Okomfo Anokye summoned a golden stool from the sky in a cloud of dust and thunder. The stool, made of pure gold, descended onto the lap of the king, signifying that the Ashanti nation was united under his rule. The Golden Stool is believed to house the soul (sunsum) of the Ashanti people and is considered so sacred that no one has ever been allowed to sit on it. When British colonial forces demanded the stool in 1900, the Ashanti waged the War of the Golden Stool rather than surrender their sacred symbol. The stool was hidden and preserved, and to this day it remains the ultimate symbol of Ashanti unity, identity, and sovereignty, kept in the royal palace in Kumasi.

title: The Golden Time and How It Ended
summary: A southern Sámi creation myth. Jupmele (God) created a perfect world where mountains were clad in gold and silver, flowers bloomed everywhere, and there was no cold, night, or sorrow. Biejjie (the Sun) guarded this world. Two brothers lived: good Naevie and greedy Adtjis. Adtjis' wife came from the underworld with a sack of diseases. Adtjis murdered Naevie over land jealousy. Adtjis-ietnie released all diseases into the world. Jupmele overturned the mountain, hid gold and silver under stone, and promised good times would return when people became good like Naevie.

title: The Golden-Antlered Deer and the Thunder God
summary: A Sámi myth about a golden-antlered deer that tries to escape the thunder god Horagalles. The thunder god hunts the celestial deer across the sky—this is the Sámi interpretation of the constellation Orion pursuing the Pleiades. The Milky Way is the tracks of the skis of the mythic elk-hunter.

title: The Goose Girl
summary: There once lived an old queen whose husband had died years before.. She had one beautiful daughter, who was promised in marriage to a prince in a distant kingdom.

title: The Graveyard Dust Spell
summary: In Hoodoo tradition, graveyard dust is among the most potent and dangerous conjure materials. The tale tells of a woman whose husband was stolen away by a rival through love magic. Desperate, she went to a rootworker who instructed her to go to a graveyard at midnight, find the grave of someone who had been a faithful spouse, and collect dust from the center of the grave. She had to leave a silver dime as payment, walk backward away from the grave, and never look back. The graveyard dust was then mixed with the husband's personal effects and buried under the doorstep. According to the story, the husband returned within three days, unable to explain why he could not stay away. The rootworker warned that graveyard dust could be used for either love or hate, healing or harm, and that using it to harm an innocent would cause the dust to 'turn' on the user. The story teaches that the dead must be treated with respect and that conjure power requires not just knowledge but moral responsibility.

title: The Great Flood and the Origin of the Tides (Tlingit)
summary: Raven made a woman under the earth to have charge of the rise and fall of the tides. One time he wanted to explore everything beneath the ocean and commanded the tide woman to raise the water. She made the tide rise very slowly so the people had time to load their canoes and climb to the mountaintops. As the water lifted the canoes between the mountains, bears and other wild animals swam out to them, and those with dogs had good protection. Some people walled the mountaintops and tied their canoes inside. When the tide began to fall, the people followed it down, but the trees were gone and they had nothing for firewood, so they were destroyed by the cold. When Raven returned, he turned all the remaining people and animals into stone. He then made new human beings from leaves, which is why people die off rapidly in autumn when leaves fall. This Tlingit flood narrative explains both the origin of tides and the seasonal cycle of death, reflecting on human fragility and the consequences of curiosity.

title: The Great Flood and the Voyage to the Fourth World
summary: In the alternative Hopi emergence story, mainly told at Oraibi, Tawa destroyed the Third World in a great flood because of the people's wickedness. Before the destruction, Spider Grandmother sealed the more righteous people inside hollow reeds, which floated as boats. After the waters receded, the survivors found themselves on a small piece of dry land with nothing but water in every direction. They planted a giant bamboo shoot and climbed it to survey the land, but still saw only water. Spider Woman then instructed them to make boats from more reeds. Using island stepping-stones, the people sailed east until they reached the mountainous coasts of the Fourth World. The Hopi Water Clan's name (Patkinyamu) means 'dwelling-on-water,' preserving the memory of this ocean voyage. Different stories (sipapu vs. flood journey) coexist among different Hopi villages.

title: The Great Head and the Old Woman
summary: Cusick's story of the dispersion of the Great Heads recounts how an old Onondaga woman was sitting alone in her wigwam one evening, parching acorns over the fire, when a monstrous Flying Head appeared at her door. The head was enormous, with blazing eyes and long hair draping like wings. The old woman, showing no fear, continued calmly eating her roasted acorns. The Flying Head watched her crack the hard shells and eat what appeared to be red-hot coals from the fire. Terrified of a being who could eat fire itself, the Flying Head fled and none of its kind were ever seen in that region again. The story demonstrates the Iroquois value of courage in the face of supernatural terror.

title: The Great Horned Serpent (Oniare)
summary: Oniare is a dragon-like horned serpent of the Great Lakes region, deeply feared by the Iroquois and neighboring tribes for its habit of capsizing canoes and devouring people. It lives in the deepest parts of lakes and rivers, controlling the waters and causing storms. The serpent has a single horn or a crest of antlers and can grow to enormous size. It is the archetypal enemy of the Thunderers, who hunt it across the sky. In one legend, a great horned serpent appeared on Lake Ontario, killing many with its poisonous breath before the old women of the tribe prayed to the Thunderers to destroy it. The Thunderers hurled lightning bolts until the monster retreated to the depths, never to trouble the people again.

title: The Great Medicine Road
summary: The Pawnee believe that after death, the soul travels along the Milky Way, which they call the Great Medicine Road or the Path of the Dead. This celestial road leads the deceased to the land of the dead in the south, ruled by the South Star. Spirits must walk this path, and the journey is long. The stars in the Milky Way are the campfires of the dead. When a falling star streaks across the sky, it is a soul traveling to its final rest. The dead live in a world much like Earth, where they hunt, feast, and dance. The living honor their ancestors with prayers and offerings.

title: The Great Peacemaker (Deganawida / Skennenrahawi)
summary: The Great Peacemaker, known as Deganawida in the sacred language and Skennenrahawi in Mohawk, was a legendary leader who founded the Iroquois Confederacy, the oldest living democracy in North America. Born among the Huron, he crossed Lake Ontario in a stone canoe to bring peace to the warring Iroquois nations. With the orator Hiawatha and the Seneca chief Jigonsaseh (the Peace Queen), he converted the cannibal warrior Hiawatha and confronted the evil wizard Tadodaho at Onondaga, whose twisted hair was filled with snakes. They transformed Tadodaho and made him the first fire-keeper of the Confederacy. The Great Law (Kaianere'kó:wa) established the principles of peace, equity, and the power of the clan mothers.

title: The Great Race (Arapaho)
summary: Long ago, the animals decided to hold a great race to determine which would be the fastest and most powerful. All creatures gathered from across the plains. The two-leggeds and four-leggeds each chose their champion. The race was long and grueling, crossing rivers and mountains. The buffalo was winning for the four-leggeds, but the magpie—representing the two-leggeds—hitched a ride on the buffalo's back. Near the finish line, the magpie flew ahead and won. The Creator declared it a draw, ruling that two-leggeds would hunt four-leggeds for food, but must always show respect for their sacrifice. The Arapaho version emphasizes cooperation and cleverness over brute strength.

title: The Great Race of the Animals
summary: The Great Race is a Lakota legend about a competition between the four-legged animals and the two-legged birds to determine who would eat whom. The race was proposed by Ksapela the Wise One to settle conflicts among the creatures. Representing the four-leggeds was the buffalo, while the magpie represented the two-leggeds. As the race progressed, various animals helped their champion. The buffalo was winning until the magpie hitched a ride on his back, then flew ahead at the last moment. The Great Spirit declared the race a draw, decreeing that henceforth the two-leggeds would hunt the four-leggeds but must always show respect for their sacrifice.

title: The Great Turtle of the Pacific
summary: A cosmic turtle carries the islands of Tuvalu on its back, balancing the world against the rising tides through an ancient pact with the sea gods.

title: The Green Children of Woolpit
summary: Two green-skinned children appear from an underground world, leaving behind a land of perpetual twilight for a life in medieval England.

title: The Green Knight
summary: A tale featuring a mysterious Green Knight who challenges others to a contest of courage, honor, and strength, testing the character of the protagonists through a series of trials.

title: The Green Knight's Challenge
summary: On New Year's Eve at Camelot, an enormous green knight rides into the hall and issues a deadly challenge to any who would dare strike him, setting Sir Gawain upon a path of honor and terror.

title: The Green Lady and the Fisherman's Heart
summary: A grief-stricken fisherman climbs Mount Liamuiga at sunset and witnesses the Green Lady's flash, receiving a sign that love endures beyond loss.

title: The Green Traveller of Wadi Rum
summary: A Bedouin lost in Wadi Rum encounters Al-Khidr, the enigmatic green traveller, and discovers that the desert holds wisdom for those who surrender their pride.

title: the Gu, Guardian of the Crossing
summary: A sacred crocodile that guards the river crossing, granting safe passage to those who show respect — and dragging beneath the water those who do not.

title: The Guardian of the Basilica
summary: A humble Swiss Guard discovers that his guardian angel has walked beside him through every night watch, defending the Holy See from threats unseen.

title: The Guardian of the Hidden Valley
summary: Deep in the highlands lies a valley that remains green and warm even in the dead of winter. It is guarded by a massive white wolf who allows only those with a selfless heart to enter. Those who enter find a paradise where time stands still and all wounds are healed.

title: The Gumiho of the Demilitarized Zone
summary: A nine-tailed fox spirit trapped in the no-man's land between two Koreas, feeding on the grief of families who can never reunite — because some borders cut deeper than flesh.

title: The Gumiho Who Drank Belief
summary: A nine-tailed fox who abandoned feeding on souls and learned to feed on the belief of the faithful — and found the people of the hermit kingdom were the most nourishing meal she had ever tasted.

title: The Gumiho: Nine-Tailed Fox of Korea
summary: A fox spirit with nine tails seeks to gain immortality by stealing human hearts.

title: the Gyeong, the Vengeful Spirit
summary: A ghost born from the agony of a death by fire, its body twisted and burned, seeking justice in a world that has forgotten its name — because in Korea, some wrongs are never forgotten.

title: The Haetae of the Eternal Flame
summary: A fire-eating guardian that was commanded to protect not a palace but an ideology, feeding on the flames of propaganda — but the fire it swallows tastes different than the fire it remembers.

title: The Haetae That Guarded the Border Fire
summary: A fire-eating guardian that patrols the northern edge of the DMZ, swallowing the campfires of refugees who try to cross in the dark — because even the guardian has its orders.

title: the Haetae, the Fire-Eating Guardian
summary: A lion-like creature covered in scales that devours fire itself, protecting villages from conflagrations — and when the great fire came, only the Haetae stood between the palace and the flames.

title: The Hako (Calumet) Ceremony
summary: The Hako ceremony, also known as the Calumet ceremony, was a complex Pawnee ritual centered on the sacred pipe. It was a peace-making and adoption ceremony that created bonds between individuals, families, and even tribes. The ceremony lasted several days and involved singing, dancing, smoking the sacred pipe, and the exchange of gifts. A decorated pipe (the Hako) served as the central symbol of the ritual. The ceremony was dedicated to Atira (Mother Corn) and involved a corn symbol painted to represent the Rainstorm, Thunder, Lightning, and Wind. The Hako reinforced social ties and ensured the continuity of the community.

title: The Hamatsa Cannibal Spirit (Kwakwaka'wakw)
summary: Baxbaxwalanuksiwe' (Man-Eater at the North End of the World) is the most important supernatural being in Kwakwaka'wakw winter ceremonies. This cannibal spirit has mouths all over his body and can transform into various man-eating birds. His attendants include the Hamatsa bird-masks: Gwaxwgwakwalanuksiwe' (a man-eating raven), Galuxwadzuwus (Crooked-Beak of Heaven, a bird with a long, crooked beak), and Huxhukw (a supernatural crane-like bird who cracks skulls to suck out brains). The Hamatsa ceremony, the most prestigious of the T'seka (Red Cedar Bark Ceremonies), involves a four-day complex dance where initiates become possessed by Baxbaxwalanuksiwe'. The initiate goes into the woods for months, then returns to the village in a wild cannibalistic frenzy, calling 'Hap! Hap! (Eat! Eat!)'. He is gradually tamed by healers and society members through songs, dances, and rituals, finally emerging as a calm, respected member of Hamatsa society. The ceremony enacts the binding of cannibal forces for human benefit.

title: The Happy Hunting Ground
summary: The Lakota believe the soul journeys after death to the happy hunting ground, a realm resembling the living world with better weather and more plentiful animals that are easier to hunt. Some traditions say the soul travels along the Sky-Road (Milky Way) to reach this destination. At the entrance, the deceased must present proper tattoos to Hihankara (Owl-Maker). Those with correct tattoos are admitted; those without are pushed back to Earth to wander as restless ghosts. The dead may also travel along the Spirit Path, another name for the Milky Way, to reach their final resting place among the stars.

title: The Hare Trickster of the Tswana
summary: In Tswana folklore, the hare (mmutla) is a classic trickster figure who uses intelligence to overcome physically stronger opponents. In the well-known tale of 'The Lion and the Hare,' the hare repeatedly outwits the lion through clever schemes and quick thinking, teaching that wit and strategy can defeat brute strength. These stories belong to a wider cycle of hare trickster tales found across Bantu-speaking southern Africa, where the hare serves the same role as Br'er Rabbit in African-American folklore. The Tswana hare embodies the values of intelligence, resourcefulness, and the importance of community survival through cunning, providing moral education for children in an entertaining form.

title: The Heartman of Bridgetown
summary: A spectral figure walks the night streets of Bridgetown, searching for those whose hearts carry the heaviest burdens of guilt, and either absolves or claims them.

title: The Heavenly Camel: A Somali Creation Myth
summary: In the beginning, the sky was low enough to touch, and the Somali people lived in close communion with the stars. The creator god Waaq formed the first camel from the morning mist and gave it to the people as the most valuable of all animals — able to travel for days without water, carry heavy loads, and provide milk, meat, and shelter. The camel was so beloved that the people became distracted by its abundance and forgot to pray. Waaq grew angry and lifted the sky high out of reach, separating humanity from the divine realm. But he left the camel as a reminder of his generosity. To this day, the camel is central to Somali pastoral life, and the best camels are said to be those descended directly from Waaq's original creation. Somali poetry and song celebrate the camel's beauty, endurance, and loyalty, calling it the 'ship of the desert' and the foundation of Somali wealth and culture.

title: The Hermit Mitsina
summary: A Zuni story about Mitsina, a hermit who lived in seclusion with spiritual power. Mitsina had withdrawn from human society to live in a remote cave, where he communed with the spirits and gained deep knowledge of the sacred world. When the people faced a crisis, they sought him out for his wisdom and power. Mitsina, despite his isolation, felt compassion for his people and agreed to help. He used his spiritual knowledge to perform ceremonies and prayers that resolved the village's problems. Afterward, he withdrew again to his cave, teaching that spiritual power requires solitude and discipline to maintain. The story presents the Zuni concept of the shaman or medicine person who lives between worlds — part of the human community yet separate, possessing power that comes from sacrifice and isolation.

title: The Hero Twins: Monster Slayer and Child of the Water
summary: In Navajo mythology, Changing Woman gave birth to the Hero Twins, Monster Slayer (Naayééʼ Neizghání) and Child of the Water (Tóbájíshchíní), fathered by the Sun. The twins were born to rid the world of monsters (anaye) that terrorized the people. They journeyed to their father the Sun, passing tests of strength and courage. The Sun tried to kill them with a sweat lodge of stone knives, a heated stone bed, and poisoned smoke, but Spider Woman protected them. They received lightning arrows and armor before returning to earth. Monster Slayer killed the giant Yéʼiitsoh by striking his leg armor and then his head with arrows. He and his brother slew Déélgééd the Horned Monster by shooting arrows into his body and causing him to fall into the ocean. They disposed of other monsters including the giant birds, the monster who kicked people off cliffs, and those who caused hunger, poverty, cold, and old age. Some monsters were allowed to remain in diminished form as a balance for humanity.

title: The Hidden Paths of the Vittra
summary: The Vittra are invisible underground beings who live in parallel cities. They have their own cattle and roads that cross human lands. If a farmer builds a house over a Vittra-path, the invisible residents will cause accidents, make the cows sick, or drive the family out of the home through relentless noise.

title: The Hintha Bird Legend
summary: The Hintha bird — a mythical golden goose or Brahminy duck — is the sacred emblem of the Mon people and the symbol of Bago (Pegu) Region in Myanmar. According to Mon Buddhist legend, the Hintha bird was the Bodhisatta (a previous incarnation of the Buddha) in the form of a wise golden goose. In the Jataka tale of the Hintha Bird, a pair of Hintha birds lived on a golden lake in the Himalayas. The king of the birds taught the creatures of the lake important moral lessons about non-attachment and the dangers of pride. The Hintha tradition also tells the story of how the Mon people, guided by a pair of Hintha birds, found their homeland. Two birds — male and female — led the Mon king and his people across the sea to the shores of southern Burma, where they established the kingdom of Suvannabhumi (Golden Land). The two Hintha birds, forever together, became symbols of Mon identity, representing fidelity, prosperity, and the golden purity of the Buddhist faith. Their paired image adorns Mon state flags and Bago's official emblem.

title: The Hmong Creation Myth: The Flood and the Siblings
summary: The Hmong creation myth centers on a great flood that destroyed the world and the surviving sibling pair who repopulated it. According to the oral tradition passed down through generations, a great argument between the Sky Father (Saub) and the Earth led to a devastating flood that covered the entire world.
