Only two siblings — usually named as a brother and sister, known by various names in different clans — survived by taking refuge inside a large wooden funeral drum or a hollow gourd that floated on the waters. After the flood receded, they found themselves alone at the peak of a mountain. The brother proposed marriage to continue the human race, but the sister refused, believing it was wrong. After consulting with the spirit world, they were told to roll two millstones down opposite sides of the mountain; if the stones met at the bottom, they were meant to marry. The stones rolled and met, and the siblings married. The sister gave birth to a strange gourd-like egg or mass, which they cut open, releasing all the different peoples of the earth — including the Hmong, Chinese, and Lao. This legend explains Hmong ethnic identity and their relationship to neighboring peoples, while establishing the sacred bond between siblings and the role of divine guidance in human affairs.

title: The Holy Grail
summary: At the height of Camelot's glory, on the eve of Pentecost, the knights of the Round Table sat in the great hall at a celebration unlike any other.

title: The Honest Penny
summary: A poor boy finds a money box but throws it away, believing it contains stolen wealth, keeping only one silver penny that floats on water, which he deems 'honest.' This act of integrity leads him to a series of adventures and eventual immense wealth.

title: The Hopi Clan Migrations
summary: Upon arriving in the Fourth World, the Hopi divided and began great migrations across the land. Led by various signs and helped by Spider Woman, clans traveled to every direction, sometimes stopping to build towns, then abandoning them to continue their migrations. They left symbols on rocks to show that Hopi had been there. Clans were named after events or signs received during their journeys. Periods of harmonious living alternated with wickedness, contention, and separation — a pattern that began in the First World. The clans traveled to the farthest extremity of the land in every direction; far to the north was the 'Back Door' (possibly the Bering land bridge), but this was closed to the Hopi, though other peoples came through it. Eventually, guided by Masauwu, the Hopi were led to their permanent home in northeastern Arizona, where Masauwu gave them the land in exchange for their stewardship and service.

title: The Horned Women
summary: The night lay heavy over the Irish countryside, a winter's night so cold that the thatch on the cottage roofs crackled with frost and the breath of sleeping cattle rose in white clouds from the byres.

title: The How the Twins of War and Chance Fared with the Unborn-Made Men
summary: In this complex Zuni myth, Áhaiyúta and Mátsailéma, the Twins of War and Chance (or Morning Star and Evening Star), journeyed to the underworld to confront the Unborn-made Men. These were unfinished beings who had not yet been given their final form — they existed in a state of potential. The twins had to navigate the dark underworld, using their wits and divine weapons. They encountered various spirits and obstacles, including the guardians of the underworld. The story explores themes of destiny, free will, and the nature of creation — why some beings are completed and others are not. The twins' journey through the underworld mirrors the soul's journey after death and the process by which spirits become ancestors. The Unborn-made Men represent the untold potential that exists in every being before it takes its final form in the daylight world.

title: The Huanca, Stone Guardian
summary: A petrified warrior stands watch over the mountain passes, and the traveler who passes without offering a stone to the ground will lose their way forever.

title: The Huldra's Seduction
summary: The Huldra is a beautiful forest woman who lures lonely men into the woods with her singing and charm. While she appears human from the front, she possesses a long cow's tail which she carefully hides. If a man discovers the tail and treats her with kindness, she may become a loyal wife, but otherwise, she leads men to their doom.

title: The Huldufólk Nursery Rhyme: Hulda, Mulda, Tulda
summary: A traditional Faroese skjaldur (short nursery rhyme or tale) that invokes the Huldufólk. The rhyme 'Hulda, mulda, tulda' is a charm asking the Hidden People not to hide lost objects. It reflects the common belief that Huldufólk, being mischievous tricksters, enjoy hiding household items from humans. The rhyme tradition is one of the few surviving forms of Huldufólk interaction in the modern era—residents of Suðuroy claim the hidden people left with the introduction of electricity in the 1950s. These skjaldur, studied by linguist Stephen Pax Leonard, represent an endangered oral tradition unique to the Faroe Islands, blending pre-Christian and Christian elements.

title: The Hunger of the Amarok
summary: In this darker version of the wolf legend, the Amarok is a sinister force that hunts those who disturb the balance of nature. A man, consumed by grief, seeks out the Amarok to distract himself. After killing the wolf's young to lure the adult, the man is swiftly judged. The Amarok returns and takes the man's soul as punishment for his reckless cruelty toward the natural world.

title: The Hunter of the Sun (Choctaw)
summary: None of the Choctaw prophets or chief leaders could answer what happened to the Sun when it disappeared each night. A young man embarked on a mission to discover this mystery. He left his family, community, and country to dedicate his life to tracking the Sun's path. Many years passed — the young men became old, and the old men died — but the people continued to speak of him. Finally, he returned as an old man with the answer he had sought. He had journeyed to the great ocean and discovered that the sun sets and rises from the water. After sharing this profound knowledge with his people, the old man died, his life's purpose fulfilled. The story represents the Choctaw value of dedication to knowledge and truth.

title: The Huntress and the Great Serpent
summary: A brave huntress must defeat a great serpent that has been terrorizing her village—and discovers a unexpected truth.

title: The Huron Creation: Aataentsic and the Earth Diver
summary: In the beginning, the Wyandot people lived in the Sky Land. The shaman told the people to dig around the roots of the wild apple tree by the chief's lodge. As they dug, they broke through the floor of the Sky Land, and the tree and the chief's daughter Aataentsic fell through. Below was only water. Swans swimming on the water heard a thunderclap — the first thunder ever heard — and looked up to see the woman falling. They swam together so she could land on their backs. The animals held a council called by the Great Turtle. One by one the divers went down — Otter, Muskrat, Beaver — seeking earth from the tree's roots. Each drowned. Finally, Old Toad volunteered. The animals laughed at her smallness, but she dove and surfaced near death with grains of earth in her mouth. The Small Turtle spread the earth around the Big Turtle's shell, where it grew until it became the island of the world.

title: The Hyena Who Wanted to Be King
summary: In the golden, shimmering plains of the Sahel, where the acacia trees cast long, skeletal shadows across the scorched earth, the animals of the wild once gathered for a great council.

title: The Iatiku and Nautsiti Creation (Acoma Pueblo)
summary: In the Acoma Pueblo creation myth, two sisters named Iatiku (Life Bringer) and Nautsiti (Full Basket) emerged from the underworld through a sacred place called Shipapu, guided by Tsichtinako (Thought Woman). They were given two baskets containing seeds, animal figurines, and sacred objects. Tsichtinako instructed them to pray to the Sun (Uchtsiti), their father, who had created the world from a clot of his own blood. The sisters created the mountains, directions, plants, and animals. Iatiku created the Corn Mother and the Kachinas. Nautsiti introduced death into the world when she disobeyed a taboo. The sisters became the mothers of the Acoma people, with Iatiku's children becoming the Pueblo clans. The story explains the origins of ceremonies, clans, and the relationship between the people, the land, and the spirits.

title: The Ice Maiden
summary: There was once a boy named Rudy who lived in the Swiss Alps, near the foot of a great glacier.

title: The Ice-Maiden
summary: A youth becomes enchanted by a cold, ethereal Ice-Maiden. The story explores themes of love, frozen emotions, and the danger of being lured away from the warmth of human society.

title: the Imandwa, Spirits of the Hill
summary: Spirits that live in the tallest hills, appearing as balls of light at dusk — because in Burundi, every hill has a guardian, and the guardian demands respect.

title: the Imizimu, the Ancestors Who Walk
summary: The spirits of the dead who walk among the living, visible only in the flicker of a candle flame — because in Burundi, death does not end the conversation.

title: The Imugi Who Lost the Waterfall
summary: A giant serpent dreaming of dragonhood waits beneath a waterfall that was dammed by the state, coiling in the dark reservoir, waiting for a heaven that may never come.

title: The Inkanyamba of the Deep Pool
summary: A colossal serpent dwelling in a mountain pool summons devastating storms when angered, and only an old healer learns the secret of calming its wrath.

title: The Iron Pig
summary: A kind boy treats a mysterious iron pig with tenderness and discovers a hidden treasure.

title: The Isle of Refuge
summary: A poignant tale of seeking sanctuary during a time of war or political persecution. It explores the psychological toll of exile and the universal human search for a place of peace and safety away from conflict.

title: The Jack Ball: A Conjure Tale
summary: In Hoodoo tradition, a Jack Ball (sometimes called a 'follow-me-boy' or 'trick ball') is one of the most powerful conjure objects. The tale tells of a rootworker who created a Jack Ball from wax, graveyard dust, personal concerns of the target, and the rootworker's own blood, empowered by nine days of prayer and fasting. The Jack Ball was said to be able to 'follow' its target anywhere, bringing good luck to those it favored or misery to those cursed. The most famous Jack Ball story involves a man betrayed by his lover, who went to a conjure woman for justice. She created a Jack Ball that would ensure the unfaithful woman could not rest anywhere, her conscience tormenting her until she returned to make amends. The Jack Ball would roll by itself, knock on doors, and appear in unexpected places. Such stories reinforced the belief in the tangible power of conjure and the importance of honoring one's commitments. The making of a Jack Ball is one of the most secret and solemn rites in Hoodoo practice.

title: The Jade Emperor
summary: Long before the dynasties of China rose from the yellow earth, before emperors ruled from golden palaces, there was only the Jade Emperor—the ruler of heaven, the most powerful of all the celestial beings.

title: The Jengu Who Married a Fisherman
summary: A Sawa fisherman rescues a beautiful Jengu from a hunter's net, and she grants him a season of extraordinary catches in return, until the price of her love demands he choose between the river and the shore.

title: The Jenun of Chinguetti
summary: In the ancient library city of Chinguetti, a fqih discovers that the jenun who haunt the desert roads are not demons to be exorcised but forgotten scholars, bound to guard the books that no one reads anymore.
themes: jinn as guardians rather than demons
the death and rebirth of learning
the bond between spirit and purpose

title: The Jicarilla Apache Creation
summary: In the beginning there was nothing — no earth, no living beings, only darkness, water, and Cyclone the wind. Only the Hactcin (supernatural beings) existed. They made the earth as a woman facing upward and the sky as a man facing downward. Black Hactcin, the most powerful, created the first four-legged animal from clay, then made many animals from its body. He made birds from mud mixed with raindrops. When the animals and birds asked for a companion, Black Hactcin created the first man from turquoise, coral, opal, jet, abalone, and other precious materials brought by the animals. Four times Black Hactcin commanded the man to speak, laugh, and shout, and each time he did. Man dreamed of a woman when lice were placed on his head, and he awoke to find Ancestral Woman beside him. They had children and the people multiplied, living in darkness until the sun and moon were created.

title: The Jinn of Jerusalem
summary: A powerful jinn said to guard the holy places of Jerusalem, testing the worthiness of those who seek to enter.

title: The Jinn of the Asmara Market
summary: A Tigrinya merchant ignores the warnings about a jinn dwelling beneath the old market square in Asmara, and pays a price that no amount of coffee can undo.

title: The Jinn of the Dead Sea
summary: A fisherman on the Dead Sea encounters a jinn imprisoned in the salt flats since the time of the prophet Lut, and discovers that even a trapped spirit can bargain for freedom.

title: The Jinn of the Empty Quarter
summary: A Bedouin traveler encounters a powerful Jinn in the Rub' al Khali, engaging in a battle of riddles to secure safe passage across the shifting sands.

title: The Jinn Who Tended the Well
summary: Um Hmaar, a jinn bound to an ancient well in the Bahraini desert, tests the character of those who draw water from her domain.

title: The Jomala Runestone – Odin's Mark on Åland
summary: The Jomala runestone, located at Jomala Church — the oldest stone church in Finland — is one of the most significant Viking-age artifacts on Åland. The runestone bears inscriptions invoking Odin's guidance and names voyagers who once crossed the Baltic. Its serpent forms curl around the old Younger Futhark alphabet in the classic runestone style of 11th-century Scandinavia. The stone represents Åland's role as a crossroads between Sweden and Finland during the Viking Age, when the islands served as vital waystations for sea travelers. Local folklore holds that the stone possesses protective powers and that disturbing it would bring ill fortune. Jomala Church itself, built atop earlier pagan sacred ground, represents the layering of Christian and pre-Christian belief that characterizes so much of Åland's folk tradition.

title: The Journey to the Land of the Dead
summary: In Hopi tradition, the journey to the land of the dead begins at the sipapu in the Grand Canyon. The spirit travels westward, following the path of the setting sun, to the land of the ancestors. Along the way, the spirit encounters various challenges and must have the proper knowledge, gained through ceremonial instruction during life, to pass safely. The spirit is judged by Masauwu and the Kachinas who determine its fate. Good souls pass into a land of plenty, while those who lived badly face difficulties. The dead eventually become cloud people who can bring rain to their living descendants. The spirits of the dead are associated with the Kachinas and reside at the San Francisco Peaks. This cycle of life, death, and return as rain-giving spirits reinforces the Hopi connection between proper living, ceremonial participation, and the well-being of the community.

title: The Journey to the West
summary: Long ago in China, there lived a powerful monkey king named Sun Wukong. Centers on Sun Wukong,  to the West protagonist.

title: The Kabouter of the Belgian Forests
summary: A tiny forest spirit who helps those who respect nature and plays tricks on those who do not, found in the woods of Flanders.

title: The Kachina Spirits of the Pueblo
summary: Across Pueblo cultures, the Kachinas (Katsinam) are supernatural beings who are the spirits of ancestors, natural forces, and all things in the universe — rocks, stars, animals, and plants. They reside in the San Francisco Peaks (north of Flagstaff, Arizona) and come to the pueblos for six months each year during the winter season. The Kachinas bring rain, fertility, and other blessings through ceremonial dances. Each Kachina has a specific identity, mask, songs, and role in the ceremonial calendar: Crow Mother brings rain, the warrior Kachinas police behavior, and the clown Kachinas expose human pretension through comedy. When a man wears the Kachina mask, he becomes the spirit, not merely a representation. The tihu (Kachina dolls) given to children are teaching objects to help them learn to recognize each Kachina. The Kachinas emerged from the underworld with the people and taught them how to live properly.

title: The Kachina Tradition (Zuni)
summary: In Zuni tradition, the Kachinas (Kâkâ) originated from the search for itiwana, the Middle Place. The priest Ka'wimosa sent his sons in different directions to find the center of the world. Kiaklo went north, the Ánahoho áchi went south, and Síweluhsiwa and Síwiluhsitsa went east, where they had ten children from an incestuous union — the first Koyemshi (Mudheads), sacred clowns who speak idocies yet utter prophecies. Meanwhile, the Zuni divided into groups led by the Beloved Twins. Children who fell into the river during a crossing became lizards, frogs, turtles, and newts — the lost Little Ones who learned the Dance of Good (Kókokshi) from the god priests of Kóthluwalawan. Duck brought Kiaklo to the council hall where he learned the story of creation and the sacred dances. He returned to teach the Zuni the Kachina ceremonies, the masks, costumes, and rituals that connect the living with the spirits and the ancestors. The masks are considered so sacred that they guarantee the owner's admission to the dance house of the gods after death.

title: The Kachinas Bring Agriculture
summary: In Hopi tradition, during a great drought when the people were starving, they heard singing and dancing coming from the San Francisco Peaks (Nuvatukya'ovi). Investigating, they met the Kachinas — ancestral spirits and supernatural beings who inhabit the peaks. The Kachinas returned with the Hopi to their villages and taught them agriculture, including how to plant and care for corn, beans, and squash. They also taught the Hopi their ceremonial dances and songs, which are vital for bringing rain to the arid land. For six months each year (from winter solstice to July), the Kachina spirits leave the San Francisco Peaks and live in the Hopi villages. Men who put on the masks become the Kachinas — the mask is not a costume but a face that transforms the wearer. The Niman (Homegoing) ceremony in late July marks the Kachinas' return to the mountains.

title: The Kakamora: Elves of the Solomon Islands
summary: The Kakamora are mythical elf-like creatures in the folklore of Makira and Guadalcanal in the Solomon Islands. They are described as small, hairy beings with great strength, living in the deep forests and remote mountains. The Kakamora are known to be shy but mischievous, sometimes stealing food from villages or playing tricks on travelers. In some traditions they are considered forest guardians who protect sacred groves and punish those who disrespect nature. Their small size allows them to move through the forest undetected. Stories about the Kakamora serve as cautionary tales, warning children and adults alike to respect the boundaries between human settlements and the wild spirit-inhabited forests of the Solomon Islands.

title: The Kana-a Kachinas of Sunset Crater
summary: At old Mishongnovi lived a young maiden who refused all suitors. A Kachina youth from the San Francisco Peaks courted her through magical means — traveling by rainbow — and brought her across the desert to Palotsmo (Sunset Crater), home of the Kana-a Kachinas. There she underwent tests in the kiva, surviving four nights in an icy room with the North Wind, and passed. She married the Kachina youth. But a wicked man impersonated the Kachina husband and deceived the maiden. The Kana-a Kachinas at Sunset Crater took pity on the people suffering from the consequences of this deception. They brought sweet corn and food to the Hopi villages, dancing through the streets, asking each family to leave an ear of corn in their empty storage room. When the people awoke the next morning, their storage rooms were miraculously full of corn. The Kana-a Kachinas then entered a small butte near Mishongnovi, which remains their home.

title: The Kano Chronicle and the Founding of the Seven Hausa States
summary: The Kano Chronicle records the oral traditions of the Hausa people, tracing the founding of the seven legitimate Hausa states (Hausa Bakwai) to the sons of Bayajidda. After Bayajidda married Queen Daurama of Daura, their son Bawo fathered six sons who founded Kano, Katsina, Zaria, Gobir, Rano, and Daura itself, while Bayajidda's elder son Biram founded the seventh state. Kano grew into a major commercial hub of trans-Saharan trade, Katsina became a center of Islamic learning, and Zaria was later ruled by the legendary warrior queen Amina. This genealogy serves as a political charter that structured hierarchy, succession, and identity across Hausaland for centuries.

title: The Kapre
summary: A giant tree spirit of Philippine folklore that waits and watches from the branches.

title: the Karakondzola's Midnight Rite
summary: On Christmas Eve, the Karakondzola descends from the rooftops and enters the homes of the dead — because on this night, it does not call names, it remembers them.

title: the Karakondzola, the Night Walker
summary: A hunched creature with burning eyes that walks the rooftops at midnight, stopping at every house and calling residents by name — and whoever answers will never sleep again.

title: the Karanga, the Diviner's Secret
summary: A sorcerer who reads the future in the patterns of millet flour scattered on water — but the future he reads is not the one you want to hear.

title: The Kastelholm Witch Trials (1665–1668)
summary: The Kastelholm witch trials were the largest witch trials in Finnish history, held at Kastelholm Castle in Åland between 1665 and 1668. Governor Nils Psilander, educated at the University of Dorpat (Tartu) where witchcraft demonology was a major subject, conducted the trials. Unlike typical Finnish witch trials which involved single male defendants accused of sorcery, the Kastelholm trials were a mass trial modeled on continental European patterns. Several women were accused of attending a Witches' Sabbath and making a pact with the Devil. Six women were ultimately executed. The trials were unique in Finland for their scale and their focus on diabolical witchcraft rather than traditional folk magic. The first woman executed was Karin Persdotter, and the events have since inspired the 2016 Finnish film 'Devil's Bride' (Tulen morsian).

title: The Kazan Creation Myth
summary: The founding myth of Kazan explains how the city got its name. According to legend, a Bulgar prince was hunting on the banks of the Volga when his party stopped to prepare a meal. They put a copper cauldron (kazan in Tatar) on the fire to boil water. A serpent emerged from the water, warning the prince that a great city would rise on this spot but would face many trials. Frightened, the prince's men fled, leaving the cauldron behind. When they returned, the cauldron had filled with gold coins. The prince interpreted this as a sign from Tengri and founded the city of Kazan on the site. Another version connects the city's foundation to Queen Söyembikä, who threw a golden cauldron into the river while fleeing enemies, marking the spot where the city would be built.

title: the Keemse, Spirit of the River
summary: A water spirit that lives in the deep pools of the Volta River, granting fish to those who respect it — and drowning those who do not.

title: The Keepers of the Sacred Law
summary: The Lulik Spirits, guardians of Timorese sacred law, punish those who break taboos and reward those who uphold the ancient protocols.

title: The Kelpie
summary: The Rainbow Serpent is one of the most important and widespread figures in Aboriginal Australian mythology.

title: The Kidnapping of Angangujuk
summary: A traditional tale of a child, Angangujuk, who is kidnapped by supernatural beings and taken to a hidden realm. The story follows the desperate efforts of the parents to locate the child and the moral lessons learned about the dangers of wandering too far from the community and the strength of familial bonds in the face of spiritual abduction.

title: The Kikimora in the Walls
summary: A farmer's wife discovers that the mischievous spirit nesting in her home is not malicious but deeply offended, and must be appeased with respect rather than chased away with force.

title: The Kikimora Who Kept House
summary: A household spirit who appears to a widow as a tiny old woman, spinning flax by moonlight and keeping the house in order while the widow sleeps.

title: The King's Choice
summary: King Gustav must leave his country on a long journey and needs to choose one of his six councilors to govern in his absence — but each has a flaw: one is too bossy, another too young, one drinks too much, one is obsessed with money, another with his appearance, and the last is simply uninspiring. Riding through the forest, the king encounters a fairy who rises from the river mist. She transforms him into a woodcutter and places him in a cottage by the river. The fairy arranges for the six councilors' boat to be caught in a storm, forcing them to seek shelter at the woodcutter's cottage. Disguised as a poor woodcutter, the king invites them to dinner and observes their true natures when they believe no one of consequence is watching. Through this test, he discovers which councilor possesses genuine inner strength, humility, and wisdom. The story explores themes of leadership, the difference between appearance and reality, and the value of looking beneath the surface to find true merit.

title: the Kinkirsi, the Human Animal
summary: A being that is half-human, half-animal, born when a mother's craving during pregnancy crosses the boundary between species — and lives forever in the forest, caught between two worlds.

title: the Kintogou, the Fire Serpent
summary: A serpent made of fire that coils beneath the village, its heat warming the earth in winter and its rage burning the village in summer — because fire is a gift, but it is never free.

title: The Kishi at the Crossroads
summary: A seductive forest demon with two faces lures travelers from the path, offering them their heart's desire in exchange for a single step into the bush.

title: The Knight of Ellenholm
summary: A knight on his way to Christmas matins stops to rest by a mountainside, where a giantess forces him into the mountain to meet her husband. He refuses their food, and the giantess breaks his little finger as a warning against sleeping on the way to church.

title: The Knights of Ållaberg
summary: A peasant discovers a grand mansion in Allaberg where twelve golden-helmeted knights sleep in glittering armor. When he touches a bridle a voice asks "Is it time now?" and another answers "No, not yet!" He has glimpsed the warriors who will defend Sweden in its hour of greatest need.

title: the Koreisha, the Bear Woman
summary: A bear that was once a woman, or a woman that was once a bear — the boundary between them blurred by hunger, by faith, by the slow transformation of flesh into something that is neither and both.

title: The Kumiho and the Scholar
summary: A nine-tailed fox spirit who has lived a thousand years must collect one thousand human souls to become human herself — but the scholar she targets teaches her that some desires are worth more than transformation.

title: The Kumulipo: Hawaiian Creation Chant
summary: The Kumulipo is the sacred Hawaiian creation chant, a genealogical epic tracing the universe from its primordial origins. It begins in total darkness (Po) with the birth of coral, seaweed, and the first sea creatures. The chant follows the emergence of life from ocean to land, from the humblest plants to animals and finally humans. The chant connects the Hawaiian chiefly lineage directly to the gods, establishing mana through unbroken descent from the primal darkness. The Kumulipo was famously chanted in full at the birth of Kamehameha the Great, and later translated by Queen Liliuokalani. It stands as one of the greatest surviving works of Polynesian oral literature.

title: The Kurupí of the Forest
summary: A wild-haired forest spirit with impossibly long genitalia that he wraps around his waist ties women to trees in the deepest jungle, and only the smell of tobacco can drive him away.

title: The Lad and the Devil
summary: A clever lad tricks the Devil into shrinking himself and entering a nut, which the lad then seals with a pin. He later uses a blacksmith's hammer to destroy the nut, effectively defeating the Devil with wit.

title: The Lad and the Fox
summary: A lad on his way to church sees a fox sleeping on a stone and begins daydreaming about killing it, selling the skin, buying rye, and shouting at passersby to stay off his field—but he screams so loudly in his fantasy that he wakes the fox, which escapes.

title: The Lad Who Went to the North Wind
summary: A poor boy asks the North Wind to return flour it blew away. The North Wind sends him on a journey with magical objects that help him outwit a greedy innkeeper and the king.

title: The Lady of Pintorp
summary: A cruel noblewoman makes a pact with the Devil, and after a life of wickedness, her ghost returns to haunt Pintorp Castle in a spectral carriage on stormy nights. The lady may have been a historical figure — the wife of the royal counselor Erik Gyllenstjerna.

title: The Lady of the Lake
summary: The ethereal guardian of a mystical lake who provides King Arthur with his most powerful weapon and shapes the fate of Camelot.

title: The Lady Who Fell from the Sky
summary: Before the world was a world, before there were mountains or rivers or forests, there was only water.

title: The Lakhey: The Demon Guardian of Kathmandu
summary: A fearsome demon tamed by a goddess now protects the children of the Kathmandu Valley.

title: The Lakota Creation: Inyan, Maka, and the First Dawn
summary: In the beginning there was only Inyan (Rock) and the omnipresent spirit Wakan Tanka, the Great Mystery, and the darkness Han. Inyan wished to exercise his powers of compassion, so he created Maka (Earth) from himself, sacrificing much of his blood which became water. Inyan shriveled and lost his powers. The water gave birth to Skan, who became the supreme judge. When Maka complained of cold and darkness, Inyan created Anpo the Dawn and later Wi the Sun. Maka tried to separate from Inyan, but Skan ruled that rock and soil must remain bound together, explaining why rocks are embedded in the earth.

title: The Lame Dog
summary: A royal couple longing for a child trust a mysterious old woman who gives them a son with a terrible prohibition — if he ever sees the face of the one who loves him most, he will vanish like morning mist.

title: The Lame Warrior and the Skeleton
summary: A lame Arapaho warrior, unable to fight alongside his people, was left behind when the village moved. As he sat alone, a skeleton approached him. The skeleton offered to carry the warrior to battle if the warrior would promise to give the skeleton a proper burial afterward. They formed a pact. The skeleton carried the warrior into battle against their enemies, and the warrior's arrows struck true. They won a great victory. True to his word, the warrior gathered the skeleton's bones and performed the burial rites. The skeleton's spirit appeared in a dream, thanking the warrior and granting him the gift of healing. The warrior became a powerful medicine man.

title: The Lamia in the Archives
summary: A Vatican librarian discovers that the ancient Lamia has been feeding on the memories of scholars who venture too deep into the restricted archives beneath the basilica.

title: The Lamia of the Nursery
summary: A Lamia infiltrates the Vatican's ancient orphanage, luring children with the voice of their dead mothers, until a quick-witted nun discovers the creature's true nature.

title: The Land Otter Son (Kushtaka) (Tlingit)
summary: After their son was lost at sea, a grieving Tlingit couple living in poverty heard whistling outside their home at night. The wife called out, begging her son to come in. Without being seen entering, a figure appeared seated opposite them with his hands over his face. He only whistled by drawing in his breath. Toward midnight, the kushtaka (land-otter-man) revealed himself and brought them devilfish. The next morning he rowed his father to the halibut grounds with supernatural speed, catching fish effortlessly. He brought in a seal for them. The family decided to move to Sitka, and the land-otter son paddled with them, but as they rounded a point, his mother saw only his shadow — his body had disappeared. The kushtaka had returned to the forest, his true home. This story illustrates the Tlingit belief that those lost at sea become kushtaka, half-human, half-otter beings who can return to help their families but can never fully rejoin human society.

title: The Land-Diving Origin of Pentecost Island
summary: On Pentecost Island in Vanuatu, the tradition of land-diving (naghol) originated from a legend about a woman named Tamalie who was mistreated by her husband. She fled into the forest and climbed a tall banyan tree. When her husband followed, she tied liana vines to her ankles and jumped, surviving the fall. Her husband, thinking he could do the same, jumped without the vines and died. The ritual evolved into a test of courage and a rite of passage for young men, who dive from tall wooden towers with vines tied to their ankles, their hair brushing the earth. The land-diving ceremony is performed annually to ensure a good yam harvest and is believed to have inspired modern bungee jumping.

title: The Last Sunrise
summary: A man from the east coast of Greenland is so deeply attached to his homeland that he finds the sight of the sun rising over the ocean to be his greatest joy. His son eventually persuades him to travel to the west coast. However, seeing the sun rise behind the land instead of the ocean causes him great distress. Upon returning home, he awakens early to witness one final, familiar sunrise, and the overwhelming emotion of the moment causes him to pass away in a state of pure joy.

title: The Legend of Alasha Khan and the Three Zhuzes
summary: Long ago, a khan's son was born with a brindled (striped) appearance. Ashamed, the khan ordered the child abandoned in the steppe. An old woman collecting dung found the child and raised him. The boy grew into a young man of exceptional fairness, dexterity, strength, and wisdom. When the khan heard of his remarkable son, he sent a hundred warriors to bring him back, but they were so impressed by the young man that they stayed with him instead. This happened three times, with three hundred warriors choosing to serve him. They lifted him on white felt and proclaimed him Alasha Khan. He organized them into three groups, which became the three zhuzes (Senior, Middle, Junior) of the Kazakh people. This is why the battle cry of all Kazakhs is 'Alash!'

title: The Legend of Asan Kaighy and the Promised Land
summary: Asan Kaighy ('Asan the Sorrowful') is a legendary figure said to have lived during the reign of Kazakh Khan Janibek in the 15th century. A wise counselor and prophet, Asan searched across the entire Kazakh steppe for a promised land where there would be no suffering, hatred, or injustice — a paradise on earth where skylarks would nest peacefully among the sheep. He traveled on his swift camel, Jhelmaia, covering all the steppes, but could never find this utopia. Before dying, he promised to lead his people to unknown lands with better conditions, but death took him before he could fulfill his promise. His story embodies the eternal Kazakh yearning for justice and a better life.

title: The Legend of Banh Chung (Chung Cake)
summary: One of the most beloved Vietnamese legends explains the origin of the square sticky rice cake (banh chung) traditionally eaten during Tet, the Lunar New Year. The story dates to the reign of the 6th Hung King, who sought to choose his successor by asking his many sons to bring him the most valuable offering. While the princes scoured the land for rare treasures, the 18th prince, Lang Lieu — raised by a poor mother and skilled in farming — had a dream in which a spirit told him that nothing was more precious than rice, which sustains all life. Following the spirit's guidance, Lang Lieu created two types of cakes: a square cake made of sticky rice filled with mung beans and pork, symbolizing the Earth, and a round glutinous rice cake (banh troi) symbolizing the Sky. The square cake represented the people's gratitude for the earth's bounty. The king recognized the profound wisdom in Lang Lieu's humble offering and chose him as successor. Banh chung remains the essential food of Tet, embodying Vietnamese filial piety and agricultural heritage.

title: The Legend of Bibi-Khanum
summary: Bibi-Khanum, the favorite wife of Emir Timur (Tamerlane), decided to surprise her husband with a magnificent mosque while he was away at war. Thousands of architects and builders created a masterpiece of sapphire and turquoise. But the main architect fell madly in love with Bibi-Khanum and refused to complete the work unless she allowed him to kiss her. To finish the gift before Timur returned, she consented — but through her veil. The kiss was so passionate it left a trace on her cheek. Timur noticed the mark upon his return but said nothing until he brought her to the top of the mosque and pushed her to her death. He grieved deeply but named the mosque after her. Another version says the architect grew wings and flew to Mashhad to escape Timur's justice.

title: The Legend of Bodu Niyami Kalefanu and the Tuna Fish
summary: One of the most important Maldivian origin myths explains how the tuna fish — the nation's staple food — was brought to Maldivian waters. According to legend, a mythical seafarer named Bodu Niyami Kalefanu (literally 'Great Navigator') sailed close to the Dagas — the mythical cosmic tree at the end of the world — to bring this valuable fish back to the islands. The Dagas was believed to be the source of all marine life, standing at the boundary where the ocean meets the sky. Bodu Niyami Kalefanu, recognized as the greatest maalimi (navigator), used his exceptional knowledge of ocean currents, stars, and wind patterns to make this incredible journey. He successfully brought the tuna to the Maldives, ensuring the survival of the nation. Tuna fishing remains central to Maldivian economy and cuisine, and the traditional fishing dhow (masdhon) still uses techniques attributed to this mythic navigator.

title: The Legend of Boudhanath Stupa
summary: The great Boudhanath Stupa in Kathmandu is one of the largest spherical stupas in the world. Legend tells that after the Buddha's parinirvana, a widow named Samvari requested permission from King Dharmadeva to build a stupa. When the king refused, she asked for as much land as could be covered by a buffalo hide. The king agreed, and Samvari cut the hide into a single long, thin strip, encircling a vast area. The king recognized her wisdom and granted the land. After Samvari died, her four sons completed the massive stupa. Another tradition holds that the bodies of the four sons are buried at the four corners of the stupa. The eyes of the Buddha painted on all four sides of the spire — symbolizing the all-seeing wisdom of the Buddha — have become an iconic symbol of Nepal itself. The stupa was renovated by the Tibetan king Songtsen Gampo in the 7th century.

title: The Legend of Enriquillo and Anacaona
summary: The legend of Enriquillo and Anacaona is one of the most powerful stories of Taino resistance in Hispaniola (modern Dominican Republic and Haiti). Anacaona (Golden Flower) was a Taino queen and cacica (female chief) known for her poetry, music, and diplomacy. She ruled the province of Jaragua and initially sought peaceful coexistence with the Spanish. Despite her efforts, she was captured and executed by hanging in 1503 on false charges of conspiracy. Enriquillo, her nephew, led the most successful Taino rebellion in history from 1519 to 1533, using guerrilla tactics from the Bahoruco Mountains. He eventually secured a peace treaty that granted him and his followers land and autonomy. Both figures symbolize indigenous resistance against colonial oppression and remain cultural icons in the Dominican Republic.

title: The Legend of Gara Yakka
summary: Gara Yakka is a prominent demon in Sinhalese folklore, believed to be a Yaksha (demon) who was once a mortal wrongdoer transformed into a spirit. He is portrayed with fangs, bulging eyes, and a crown of flame, and is particularly associated with causing childhood illnesses, fevers, and nightmares. The Gara Yakka legends are central to the Daha Ata Sanniya (the eighteen maladies) — a group of eighteen diseases believed to be caused by demonic possession. Traditional exorcism rituals involve the Yak Deshiya or Devil Dance, where masked dancers embody Gara Yakka and other demons, performing complex choreography to the beat of drums (Geta Bera) to drive away the malevolent spirits. These rituals blend Buddhist, Hindu, and indigenous animist traditions.

title: The Legend of Hoan Kiem Lake and the Restored Sword
summary: One of Vietnam's most cherished legends tells of Emperor Le Loi and the magical sword of Heaven's Will (Thuan Thien). In the early 15th century, while fishing in a lake, Le Loi caught a magical sword that the Golden Turtle God (Kim Qui) had forged. With this sword, Le Loi led the Vietnamese resistance against the Ming occupation, driving out the Chinese invaders and founding the Later Le Dynasty. Years later, while boating on Luc Thuy Lake, a giant golden turtle suddenly emerged from the water and seized the sword, proclaiming that Heaven had lent it to defeat the enemy and now required its return. The emperor understood the divine will and surrendered the sword. The lake was renamed Hoan Kiem — Lake of the Restored Sword. The golden turtle became a symbol of Vietnam's independence and the legend explains the presence of rare softshell turtles in the lake, which are considered sacred descendants of Kim Qui.

title: The Legend of Igbo Ukwu (Igbo)
summary: The ancient kingdom of Igbo Ukwu in southeastern Nigeria was a center of sophisticated bronze and copper craftsmanship dating back to the 9th century CE. According to oral tradition, Eri, the divine founder of the Igbo people, descended from the sky on a chain and settled at the confluence of the Niger and Anambra rivers. The people of Igbo Ukwu were master smiths who learned metallurgy from the spirit world. Their elaborate burial ceremonies for kings (Eze Nri) involved elaborate bronze regalia, thousands of beads, and the ritual burial of royal attendants. The discovery of the Igbo Ukwu archaeological site in 1939 by Isaiah Anozie revealed a sophisticated civilization with trade networks stretching across West Africa. The artifacts include bronze ceremonial vessels, jewelry, and staffs that still hold spiritual significance in Igbo traditional religion.

title: The Legend of Inle Lake Spirits
summary: The floating villages and gardens of Inle Lake in Shan State are surrounded by ancient nat spirit legends. According to local lore, Inle Lake was formed from a great flood that consumed several villages as punishment for human arrogance. The lake is home to powerful water nats, chief among them the Spirits of the Five Pagodas who dwell on the lake's shores. The most famous legend tells of the Inle Lake Float — how the floating islands of vegetation were created by the nats to provide land for the Intha people who lost their homes. Each year during the Phaung Daw Oo Pagoda Festival, the four sacred Buddha images from the Phaung Daw Oo temple are carried on a royal barge across the lake, accompanied by leg-rowing Intha boatmen. The legend says that a nat once caused a storm to test the faith of the villagers carrying the images; when they refused to abandon the statues despite the danger, the storm miraculously calmed. The lake is also believed to be guarded by a powerful naga-serpent that lives in its deepest waters, surfacing only during the festival to pay homage.

title: The Legend of Kandaswamy and the Vel
summary: Lord Kandaswamy (Murugan/Skanda), the war god of Sri Lankan Tamils, is celebrated through the legend of the Vel (divine spear). According to tradition, Kandaswamy received the Vel from his mother Parvati to destroy the demon Surapadman. The Vel represents divine wisdom that pierces through ignorance. The Nallur Kandaswamy Temple in Jaffna, established in the 14th century, is the epicenter of this worship. The temple's annual festival features the Vel being carried in procession. Tamil folklore recounts that Kandaswamy wedded Valli, a Vedda tribal girl, at Kataragama in Sri Lanka — symbolizing the union between the Aryan and indigenous peoples. Kataragama remains a multi-religious pilgrimage site drawing Tamil Hindus, Sinhalese Buddhists, and Veddas alike.

title: The Legend of Kaujjagjuk
summary: A young boy possesses an unusual gift that leads him into conflict with the elders. Through his journey, he learns to harness his abilities to help his community, teaching a lesson about accepting those who are different and the hidden value of perceived weaknesses.

title: The Legend of Lake Issyk-Kul
summary: Lake Issyk-Kul, the second-largest mountain lake in the world, is the subject of numerous Kyrgyz legends. One legend tells of a cruel khan who fell in love with a beautiful shepherdess. When she rejected him, he kidnapped her. Her lover, riding a magical Tulpar (winged horse), rescued her but she was recaptured. Rather than submit to the khan, she threw herself from a tower. As punishment for her death, clear mountain water rushed down and flooded the entire valley where the khan's palace stood, creating the vast lake. Another legend says that Timur (Tamerlane) required each of his soldiers to place a stone at Issyk-Kul's shore to count his army, creating the Santash stone ridge. Some Kyrgyz legends even claim Genghis Khan is buried beneath the lake's waters.

title: The Legend of Lake Titicaca
summary: Before the sun ever rose, before the first Inca drew breath, Lake Titicaca lay still and sacred between the snow-capped peaks of Peru and Bolivia.

title: The Legend of Lake Toba
summary: A beloved folktale from North Sumatra about Toba, a poor fisherman who caught a magical golden fish that transformed into a beautiful woman. She agreed to marry him on the condition that he never reveal her fish origins. They had a son named Samosir, who was tasked with delivering food to his father in the fields. One day, Samosir ate the food meant for his father en route, enraging Toba who shouted, 'You son of a fish!' The wife, hearing her secret exposed, began to weep as the earth trembled. A massive flood engulfed the land, forming Lake Toba, while the boy became the island of Samosir in its center.

title: The Legend of Lal Shahbaz Qalandar — Sufi Saint of Sehwan
summary: Lal Shahbaz Qalandar, born Syed Muhammad Usman in Marand, Iran, was a 13th-century Sufi saint who settled in Sehwan, Sindh (present-day Pakistan). His name means 'Red Falcon,' referring to his crimson attire and spiritual stature. He belonged to the Qalandariyya order, known for rejecting orthodox religious formalism in favor of mystical love and ecstatic devotion. His shrine in Sehwan is one of Pakistan's most important pilgrimage sites, where daily dhamaal (ecstatic drumming and dance) brings together Hindus and Muslims. Countless folk stories attribute miracles to him, including healing the sick and protecting the needy. The poet Shah Abdul Latif Bhittai incorporated his legend into Sindhi Sufi poetry, and the iconic phrase 'Lal Meri Patth' (Red One, I am your devotee) resonates across Sindhi folk music.

title: The Legend of Lumut Lunting
summary: A Bruneian folklore centered around a small island in Brunei Bay called Lumut Lunting, named for its distinctive moss-covered appearance. The legend tells of a young couple deeply in love but separated by family conflict. The young man, a fisherman from a poor family, promised his beloved that he would prove himself worthy of her hand. He set out to sea during storm season, against all warnings, determined to catch the legendary golden fish that would bring wealth and respect to his family. His beloved waited on the shore for days, watching the horizon. When he never returned, she prayed to the spirits of the sea, and her tears turned into moss that spread across the island, giving it the name Lumut Lunting (Drifting Moss). The island remains a symbol of undying love and sacrifice in Bruneian culture.

title: The Legend of Manitou
summary: Among the Algonquian-speaking peoples of North America, whose territories stretched across the vast forests and lakes of what is now Canada and the northern United States, there exists a concept so profound it shapes their entire understanding of existence: Manitou.

title: The Legend of Manitou Springs
summary: A great battle once took place between the Comanche and the Shoshone near a sacred spring. Both tribes claimed the spring as their territory, and many warriors fell on both sides. The Great Spirit, seeing the bloodshed, caused the waters of the spring to bubble up with healing powers. The spring's mineral waters were said to have medicinal properties that could heal wounds and cure sickness. After the battle, the tribes agreed that the spring would be neutral ground where warriors from all nations could come to heal. The site, now Manitou Springs, Colorado, remains a place of spiritual significance.

title: The Legend of Maria Makiling
summary: Maria Makiling is the guardian spirit of Mount Makiling in Laguna, Philippines. Described as a breathtakingly beautiful woman with long dark hair and a white gown, she protects the mountain's forests and wildlife, rewarding those who respect nature and punishing those who harm it. According to legend, she was a mortal woman who fell in love with a hunter who never returned, and she now wanders the mountain eternally. Local stories tell of her guiding lost hikers, miraculously replenishing supplies, and appearing as a vision of serene beauty to those pure of heart.

title: The Legend of Matsyendranath (Karunamaya)
summary: Matsyendranath, also known as Karunamaya (the compassionate one) and Red Machindranath, is one of the most important deities in Nepali Buddhism and Hinduism. Legend says the Kathmandu Valley suffered a devastating 12-year drought caused by the demon Bhasmasur (or the Nagas withholding rain). Gorakhnath, a powerful yogi, trapped all the Nagas (serpent gods) in meditation, blocking rainfall. His guru, Matsyendranath, was meditating in the Himalayas. The people, led by the king, traveled to Assam and invited Matsyendranath to the valley. His arrival forced Gorakhnath to release the Nagas, bringing rain and restoring life. Matsyendranath is revered as an avatar of Avalokiteshvara (Padmapani) — the bodhisattva of compassion. The annual Red Machindranath chariot festival in Patan is one of Nepal's oldest and grandest processions.

title: The Legend of Maximón
summary: A K'iche' Maya man discovers an ancient stone effigy in the mountains and brings it to his village, only to learn that the spirit within demands offerings, loyalty, and respect.

title: The Legend of Mir Chakar Rind — Baloch Hero
summary: Mir Chakar Khan Rind (1468–1565) was the legendary Baloch chieftain who united the Baloch tribes into the Second Baloch Confederacy. Born in Makran, Balochistan, he became head of the Rind tribe at age 18 and led a thirty-year war against the rival Lashari tribe, a conflict that became central to Baloch oral epic tradition. After defeating the Lasharis, he migrated to the Punjab region with his followers. He later allied with Mughal emperor Babur and assisted Humayun, receiving territorial grants in Punjab. The epic of Hani and Sheh Mureed, centered on Mir Chakar, is one of the most important works of Balochi oral literature, exploring themes of honor, love, betrayal, and tribal loyalty. His octagonal mausoleum at Satgarha (Okara, Pakistan) remains a monument of Baloch heritage.

title: The Legend of Mount Mayon
summary: This Bicolano legend tells of the tragic love story between Daragang Magayon, the beautiful daughter of a tribal chief, and Panganoron, a brave warrior from a rival tribe. After Magayon's father rejected Panganoron's proposal, a war erupted between the tribes. Panganoron emerged victorious, and the two were finally united in marriage. However, Magayon's jealous suitor Pagtuga attacked them, killing Panganoron. Magayon died of grief clutching her husband's body. They were buried together, and the earth rose above their grave, forming the majestic Mount Mayon — its perfectly symmetrical cone symbolizing Magayon's beauty and the fiery eruptions representing Pagtuga's jealousy.

title: The Legend of Nan Madol
summary: Nan Madol, the ceremonial center of eastern Micronesia on Pohnpei, was constructed according to legend by twin sorcerers Olisihpa and Olosohpa from the mythical Western Katau. The brothers arrived in a large canoe seeking a place to build an altar to worship Nahnisohn Sahpw, the god of agriculture. With the aid of a flying dragon, they levitated enormous basalt columns across the sea and built the artificial islands connected by canals. Olisihpa died of old age, and Olosohpa became the first Saudeleur ruler. The dynasty produced sixteen other Saudeleur rulers of the Dipwilap clan. They ruled kindly at first, but later successors placed ever-increasing demands on the people. The city contains 92 artificial islets with walls made of columnar basalt, canals, and royal tombs, and is often called the Venice of the Pacific.

title: The Legend of Preah Vihear Temple
summary: The legend of Preah Vihear, the cliff-top temple designated as a UNESCO World Heritage site, tells of its divine origins and supernatural guardians. According to Khmer tradition, the site on the Dangrek mountain range was chosen by the gods themselves as a sacred threshold between the earthly and celestial realms. Local lore recounts that the temple was built by the devaraja (god-king) Suryavarman II — the same king who built Angkor Wat — but the site had been considered sacred since the earliest times. The legend tells of a hermit named Preah Vihear who meditated in a cave on the cliff and received visions from the god Shiva, instructing him to mark the spot as a place of pilgrimage. The temple's most unusual feature — its main entrance facing south rather than the traditional east — is explained by a story of two brothers who competed to build the temple; the younger brother built his section facing the ancestral Khmer lands. Local villagers believe the temple is protected by the powerful naga king who dwells beneath the cliff, and that anyone who tries to damage the sacred site will face supernatural consequences.

title: The Legend of Puran Bhagat — Penitent Prince of Punjab
summary: Prince Puran was the son of King Salwan of Sialkot in ancient Punjab. When Puran's stepmother, Queen Loona, developed an improper desire for him and was rejected, she falsely accused him of assault. The king ordered Puran's hands and feet to be cut off, and he was thrown into a well where he survived for twelve years through meditation and penance. The famous saint Gorakhnath eventually found and rescued him, making him a disciple. Through yogic practice, Puran regenerated his limbs and became a powerful yogi himself. He returned to the kingdom, forgave his father, and became a revered spiritual figure. The story is one of the most beloved Punjabi folk tales, highlighting themes of wrongful accusation, spiritual endurance, and the transformative power of forgiveness.

title: The Legend of Puteri Gunung Ledang
summary: From Johor comes the tale of a celestial princess who lived atop Mount Ledang. The powerful Sultan of Melaka, Sultan Mahmud Shah, hearing of her legendary beauty, sought her hand in marriage. The princess agreed — but only if the Sultan fulfilled seven impossible conditions, including building a golden bridge from Melaka to the mountain, constructing a silver bridge back, providing seven trays of mosquito hearts, a vat of virgin's tears, a bowl of his son's blood, and cups of the Sultan's own blood and semen. After much effort, the Sultan fulfilled six conditions but hesitated at the final, realizing the princess never intended to marry him. The mountain is now a protected national park, and the story is considered a timeless lesson in humility.

title: The Legend of Red Coulee
summary: The Blackfoot were told by the Snake First Nations about a powerful medicine stone located between McLeod and Fort Benton, Montana, near the Marias River. Years later, a group of Blackfoot men traveled to find the stone. When they discovered it, their leader laughed at the story, calling it a child's tale, and rolled the stone down the hill. On their return journey, they were ambushed in battle. All but one man were killed. The place became known as Red Coulee, and ever after the Blackfoot would leave offerings when passing it, to ensure safety and protection on their journey.

title: The Legend of Saman Deviyo and Adam's Peak
summary: Saman Deviyo (Sumana Saman) is the guardian deity of Adam's Peak (Sri Pada), the sacred mountain in Sri Lanka. According to the Mahavamsa, the Buddha, on his deathbed, entrusted the care of Lanka and Prince Vijaya to the god Sumana, who appeared to Vijaya's followers disguised as a wandering ascetic. Sumana Saman, one of the four guardian deities of Sri Lanka, protects the footprint of the Buddha atop Adam's Peak. The mountain itself is a multi-faith pilgrimage site — revered by Buddhists (Buddha's footprint), Hindus (Shiva's footprint), Muslims (Adam's footprint), and Christians (St. Thomas's footprint). The deity is associated with elephants, and pilgrims traditionally climb the mountain at night by torchlight.

title: The Legend of Sedna
summary: A girl cast into the sea by her own father becomes the goddess of marine animals, and only the shaman who braids her tangled hair can release the creatures she withholds.

title: The Legend of Sleepy Hollow
summary: In the year 1790, nestled along the eastern shore of the Hudson River in New York, there lay a secluded glen known as Sleepy Hollow.

title: The Legend of Tanit and Baal Hammon
summary: Tanit and Baal Hammon were the supreme deities of Carthage (in modern Tunisia), a civilization that blended Phoenician and Berber religious traditions. Tanit, the goddess of fertility, motherhood, and the moon, was the patron deity of Carthage—often depicted with a solar disc and crescent moon. Baal Hammon, the chief god, was a weather and fertility god who brought rain and controlled the storms, associated with the ram. According to tradition, the cult of Tanit and Baal Hammon involved child sacrifice (the 'tophet'), a practice that horrified Greek and Roman writers. Legend says that when Carthage was under siege, the citizens sacrificed their own children to Baal Hammon to gain his favor. Modern scholarship debates the extent of this practice, but the story became central to Carthaginian mythology in classical literature. Tanit's symbol—a circle atop a triangle with a horizontal line—is found on thousands of stelae across North Africa. After the fall of Carthage in 146 BCE, the cult persisted among Berber populations, with Tanit continuing to be venerated in various forms.

title: The Legend of That Phanom
summary: That Phanom — the most sacred stupa in northeastern Laos and Isan (Thailand) — is the subject of a powerful legend connecting the Lao people to the Buddha's lifetime. According to tradition, five Buddhas of the past (including Gotama Buddha) visited the site on the banks of the Mekong and predicted that a great reliquary would be built there. Five hundred years after the Buddha's parinibbana, five enlightened monks (arahants) from the Himalayas flew through the air carrying a relic — the Buddha's breastbone — to the site. King Phraya Phanom, the local ruler, built a small stupa to enshrine the relic. Over centuries, the stupa grew taller as successive kings enlarged it. In the 10th century, King Kuman Phaen from Luang Prabang visited the shrine and received a vision of the Nāga king, who revealed that the stupa was built directly above the Nāga's underground palace. The legend says that the Nāga king protects the relic and that each year during the That Phanom festival, he surfaces from the Mekong to pay homage. The stupa collapsed after a massive storm in 1975, and its restoration became a symbol of Lao cultural revival. The legend establishes That Phanom as one of the most powerful pilgrimage sites in the Lao Buddhist world.

title: The Legend of the Akhal-Teke Horse
summary: The Akhal-Teke horse, Turkmenistan's national treasure, is the subject of a creation legend. According to Turkmen tradition, the first Akhal-Teke was born from the union of a snake, a cheetah, and an eagle — explaining the horse's serpentine neck, cheetah-like speed, and eagle-eyed alertness. The breed's distinctive metallic golden coat came from the sun god's blessing. The horses were considered 'Heavenly Horses' by the Chinese, who believed they sweated blood (actually a trick of light on their thin skin). Legend says the Akhal-Teke can travel 300 miles through the Karakum Desert without water, guided by the spirits of their ancestors. The bond between horse and rider is so sacred that the horse is considered a member of the family, tied beside the yurt and fed bread soaked in mutton fat.

title: The Legend of the Amaru
summary: A great serpent-dragon guarded the sacred waters beneath the mountains, and those who showed reverence to the earth would be blessed with its power.

title: The Legend of the Bamboo Cutter
summary: In the ancient days of Japan, there lived an old bamboo cutter named Sanuki.. He was a man of simple means and a gentle heart, spending his days in the emerald depths of the bamboo groves that whispered secrets in the wind.

title: The Legend of the Bayon's Many Faces
summary: The Bayon Temple at Angkor Thom is famous for its 216 massive stone faces gazing in all four directions — and Khmer legend offers a mystical explanation for their origins. According to tradition, King Jayavarman VII, the great Buddhist monarch who built Angkor Thom, had a vision in which the bodhisattva Avalokiteshvara (the embodiment of compassion) appeared to him with faces looking in every direction. The bodhisattva told the king that these faces represented the all-seeing compassion of the Buddha, watching over the Khmer Empire to protect it from harm. Local folklore adds that the faces are the king's own features, and that he ordered his face carved on every tower so that his subjects would always feel his presence and protection. A darker legend tells of the architect who built the temple; after completing the towers, he was blinded so he could never duplicate the masterpiece. But when he touched the stone faces, his sight was miraculously restored, proving the divine power of the images. The faces remain one of Southeast Asia's greatest architectural mysteries and spiritual symbols.

title: The Legend of the Betel and the Areca
summary: An ancient Vietnamese legend explaining the origins of the betel nut chewing tradition and the deep bonds of brotherly love and marital fidelity. The story follows twin brothers Tan and Lang who were so identical that only their mother could tell them apart. When their mother died, Tan married a woman who could not distinguish between the brothers. To avoid impropriety, Lang departed secretly and traveled far away, eventually dying on a riverbank and transforming into a limestone rock. Tan searched for his brother in vain and finally died of grief by the same river, turning into an areca tree. Their wife searched for both men and died of sorrow, becoming a betel vine that wrapped around the areca tree. King Hung Vuong, hearing of this tale, tasted the combination of areca nut, betel leaf, and lime — finding the mixture produced a beautiful red juice and a warm sensation. He declared these three elements the symbol of faithful love and strong attachment. To this day, betel chewing remains central to Vietnamese weddings, ancestral offerings, and social customs.

title: The Legend of the Big Dipper (Crow)
summary: After the seven bison and their human companion defeated Bones Together and were healed by the first Sweat Lodge ceremony, the Creator raised the seven bison into the sky to become the Big Dipper (the Seven Bison). The human companion became the Little Dipper, following them eternally across the night sky. The Crow look at the Big Dipper and remember the sacrifice and healing of the first Sweat Lodge. The stars serve as a constant reminder of the power of prayer, purification, and the bond between humans and animals. This story connects the Crow people to the cosmos and their daily rituals.

title: The Legend of the Blacksmith's Daughter
summary: A beloved Tatar legend tells of a poor blacksmith's daughter whose kindness and skill saved her village. When a terrible drought struck the Volga region, all the wells dried up and the crops failed. The blacksmith's daughter, named Chulpan, prayed to Tengri for help. In a dream, she was shown a hidden spring beneath a sacred birch tree. The next day, she led the villagers to the tree, where they dug and found abundant water. The spring never ran dry, even in the driest summers. Grateful villagers believed that Chulpan was blessed by Su Anasi herself for her pure heart. A version of this legend attaches to the Kaban Lake in Kazan, whose name means 'Lake of the Boar' — from the wild boar that supposedly guarded the spring from the blacksmith's daughter's dream.

title: The Legend of the Bong Bong
summary: In the quiet barrios of the Philippines, where the nights are filled with the chirping of crickets and the distant croaking of frogs, there exists a legend that makes even the bravest villagers lock their doors and whisper prayers before sleep.

title: The Legend of the Cocoa Spirit
summary: A story of a spirit that guards the cocoa groves, rewarding those who tend the land with love and punishing the greedy.

title: The Legend of the Coquí
summary: In Puerto Rican folklore, the tiny coquí frog is beloved for its distinctive two-note call that fills the island's nights with song. One Taino legend tells that the coquí was once a vain and boastful frog who challenged the sun to a singing contest. The sun burned the frog so badly that he shrunk to a tiny size and was forced to hide in the shade by day, emerging only at night to sing. Another version speaks of the goddess Atabey creating the coquí as a symbol of resilience for the Puerto Rican people — the frog's song is a sacred balm that fills every Puerto Rican heart, reminding them that no matter how many times they fall, they can always rise again, just as the coquí sings on after every storm.

title: The Legend of the Desert Veil
summary: A Tuareg legend explaining why men of the Kel Tamasheq wear the indigo-dyed tagelmust (veil) that has earned them the name 'the Blue People.' According to oral tradition, when the Tuareg emerged as a distinct people after Tin Hinan led them into the Sahara, the desert spirits tested them with sandstorms that stripped away all protection. A powerful shaman prayed to the spirits of the ancestors, who revealed that blue cloth made from the indigo plant could protect the wearer from both the sun and evil spirits. The indigo dye, it was said, possessed protective properties because it was the color of the sky and the sacred Tuareg symbol. When a man dons the tagelmust, he is shielded from malevolent forces and his identity is concealed from enemies. The veil is worn only by men—women go unveiled—a reversal of many Islamic traditions. A man never removes his veil before elders or in-laws, and the most sacred veils are never removed at all. The indigo dye traditionally stains the skin blue, which is considered a mark of beauty and protection.

title: The Legend of the Dreamcatcher
summary: Long ago, when the forests east of the Great Lakes stretched endlessly and the waters shone like mirrors beneath the moon, the Ojibwe people lived close to the land.

title: The Legend of the Jade Mountain
summary: Deep in the Altai mountains lies a sacred peak called the Jade Mountain (or Mountain of the Green Stone). According to Altai legend, the mountain was once a giant jade serpent that protected the Altai people from invaders. When enemies massed at the foot of the mountains, the serpent raised itself and turned to stone, creating an impassable barrier of green jade. The spirit of the serpent still lives within the mountain, and the jade stones found in Altai rivers are fragments of its scales. Altai shamans use jade in their rituals, believing it connects them to the earth's power. The legend emphasizes the sacredness of the Altai landscape — every mountain, river, and spring has its own 'eezi' (spirit master) that must be respected through offerings of white ribbons tied to trees.

title: The Legend of the Kushite Kings
summary: The Kingdom of Kush, in what is now Sudan, was an ancient Nubian civilization that ruled over Egypt as the 25th Dynasty (c. 747–656 BCE). According to Kushite mythology, the god Amun (who had a major oracle at the sacred mountain of Gebel Barkal) chose the kings of Kush and bestowed divine kingship upon them. The most famous Kushite king, Piye, received a dream vision from Amun commanding him to unite Egypt under his rule. The Kushites believed their kings were the literal sons of Amun, born to restore maat (cosmic order) to the world. After the Kushites were driven from Egypt, they continued their kingdom in the Sudan, building more pyramids than the Egyptians—over 200 at the sites of El-Kurru, Nuri, and Meroë. The Kushite creation myth tells that Amun emerged from the primordial waters at Gebel Barkal, making the mountain the first land created. The lion-headed god Apedemak was the indigenous Kushite war god, distinct from the Egyptian pantheon. Kushite culture survived into the 4th century CE, and traditions of sacred kingship persist in Sudanese folklore to this day.

title: The Legend of the Mammoth (Great Underground Bull)
summary: A Yakut legend explaining the origin of mammoth tusks found in the Siberian permafrost. According to the myth, the mammoth is a great underground bull that lives beneath the earth and only emerges when it dies. The creature is so massive that its movements cause the earth to shake and create sinkholes. Yakuts believed that mammoths were giant creatures that had lived underground for millennia, shunning the sun's light. When their bones and tusks were uncovered by erosion, they were seen as evidence of these subterranean titans. The legend reflects the Yakut people's observations of frozen mammoth remains emerging from melting permafrost along riverbanks.

title: The Legend of the Morning Star
summary: In the ancient skies of Arnhem Land, where the Milky Way arcs across the darkness like a river of stars and the air is so clear that the heavens seem close enough to touch, the Yolngu people have watched the planet Venus for tens of thousands of years.

title: The Legend of the Origin of Corn
summary: A Timorese agricultural myth explaining the origin of corn (maize), a staple crop of the island. According to oral tradition, a severe drought struck the land, and a poor farming family was on the verge of starvation. The father, desperate to feed his children, prayed to the ancestors for help. In a dream, an ancestor appeared and instructed him to sacrifice his most prized possession — a single golden earring passed down through generations — and bury it in the driest part of his field. Following the instructions, he woke to find a strange new plant sprouting where he had buried the earring. The plant bore golden cobs that resembled the earring's shape, with kernels like drops of gold. Thus corn was given to the Timorese people by their ancestors, a gift born from faith and sacrifice.

title: The Legend of the Pineapple (Ang Alamat ng Pinya)
summary: A popular Filipino folktale explaining the origin of the pineapple. It tells of a lazy young girl named Pina who refused to help her mother with household chores. Her mother, frustrated by Pina's laziness, wished that her daughter would grow a hundred eyes so she could find things without asking. The next morning, Pina had vanished, and in her place grew a strange fruit covered in many eyes — the pineapple. This moral tale teaches children the importance of diligence, responsibility, and helping their parents, while also providing a cultural explanation for the pineapple's distinctive appearance.

title: The Legend of the Sacred Lake and the Crocodile Spirits
summary: Malagasy mythology tells of a prosperous village that once stood where Lake Antañavo now lies. The inhabitants angered the spirits through their arrogance, and as punishment, the entire village was submerged beneath the waters, transforming into crocodiles. To this day, the crocodiles of the lake are revered as the reincarnated inhabitants of the sunken village and are protected by fady (sacred taboos). Killing them is strictly forbidden. The lake is considered a sacred site where the boundary between the human world and the spirit world is thin, and offerings are made to the Razana (ancestors) who reside there. This myth illustrates the deep connection between nature, ancestors, and the sacred landscape of Madagascar.

title: The Legend of the Sacred Tooth Relic
summary: After the Buddha's cremation, his left canine tooth was preserved in Kalinga, India. When Kalinga was threatened, Princess Hemamali and Prince Dantha smuggled the relic to Sri Lanka by hiding it in the princess's hair. They landed during the reign of King Sirimeghavanna (301-328 CE), who enshrined the tooth at Meghagiri Vihara in Anuradhapura. The relic became the palladium of Sinhalese royalty — whoever held the tooth held the right to rule. It moved with successive capitals until finally enshrined in Kandy's Dalada Maligawa (Temple of the Tooth) by King Vimaladharmasuriya I. The annual Esala Perahera parades the relic casket on a caparisoned elephant.

title: The Legend of the Shwedagon Pagoda
summary: The most sacred Buddhist legend in Myanmar tells the story of the Shwedagon Pagoda's miraculous origins. According to tradition, two merchant brothers from the Mon kingdom of Okkalapa — named Tapussa and Bhallika — were traveling through India when they encountered the newly enlightened Buddha beneath the Bodhi Tree. The Buddha had just emerged from seven weeks of meditation and was still in his radiant spiritual state. Recognizing his divinity, the brothers offered him honey cakes and rice porridge. In gratitude, the Buddha gave them eight of his sacred hairs as relics. Returning to Burma, the brothers and King Okkalapa enshrined the relics on Singuttara Hill, where the Shwedagon now stands. However, the relics performed miracles: they multiplied into a dazzling radiance, emitted beams of light in six colors, caused the blind to see and the lame to walk, and raised a golden rain. A magnificent golden stupa was built to house them. The legend establishes Shwedagon as one of the world's most sacred Buddhist sites, predating even many Indian stupas, and the two brothers are venerated as the first Buddhist lay disciples in history.

title: The Legend of the Singing Sands of the Gobi
summary: In the heart of the Gobi Desert lies the Khongoryn Els — the Singing Sands. According to Mongol legend, these massive sand dunes were once a great city ruled by a cruel khan. The khan oppressed his people so terribly that the sky god Tengri cursed the city, burying it under mountains of sand. The souls of the buried inhabitants still cry out beneath the dunes, producing the deep, resonant hum that travelers hear when the wind blows across the sand. Mongol herders say the sands sing loudest before storms, warning travelers of danger ahead.

title: The Legend of the Singing Well of Khiva
summary: In the ancient city of Khiva, there is a well that is said to 'sing' when the wind blows across its opening. According to legend, a beautiful slave girl named Zulfiya was imprisoned in the well by a cruel khan for refusing his advances. She sang day and night, her voice echoing through the depths. Even after her death, her spirit continues to sing. Local tradition holds that the well's song changes according to the listener's fate — joyful melodies for those destined for happiness, mournful songs for those facing hardship. The legend is part of the rich oral tradition of Khorezm, the historical region that was once a center of Zoroastrian culture and later Islamic scholarship.

title: The Legend of the Sleeping Warrior
summary: In a deep cave beneath a mountain, a great warrior of old sleeps in a magical trance. Legend says that he will awaken only when Iceland is in its greatest hour of need, rising with his sword to defend the land from an overwhelming foe.

title: The Legend of the Squirrel Stick (Chickasaw)
summary: This Chickasaw legend tells of a young man who wished to marry a chief's daughter. The chief set an impossible task: the young man must catch a squirrel alive using only a specially carved stick — not a bow, trap, or snare. The young man prayed to Ababinili for guidance and spent days practicing with his stick in the forest. His persistence and faith were rewarded when a squirrel came to him without fear, and he caught it gently. The chief, impressed by the young man's patience, skill, and spiritual devotion, allowed the marriage. The squirrel stick became a symbol of the proper way to achieve one's goals: through preparation, faith, and respect for nature rather than through force or deceit.

title: The Legend of the Stone Monoliths
summary: The story of the ancient monoliths of Palau, created by spirits to mark the boundary between the human world and the realm of the ancestors.

title: The Legend of the White Elephant
summary: In Thai mythology, the white elephant (chang pheuak) is a sacred and auspicious symbol directly connected to royal power and Buddhist cosmology. The most famous legend tells how Queen Maya, the mother of the Buddha, dreamt of a white elephant offering her a lotus flower before she conceived — establishing the white elephant as a symbol of spiritual purity and royal legitimacy. In Thai folklore, the discovery of a white elephant was considered a divine sign that the reigning king ruled with righteousness (dharma). The legend of Phra Phutthabat (the Buddha's footprint) tells of a white elephant that knelt to show the sacred footprint at Saraburi province. White elephants were so revered that they were never forced to work, were given royal titles, and were considered members of the royal family.
