The current Thai national flag historically featured a white elephant on a red background, underscoring its cultural significance.

title: The Legions Beneath the Floor
summary: When Vatican excavators break through an ancient sealed chamber, they unleash a host of demons bound there since the age of Constantine, testing the faith of the modern Church.

title: The Leopard Spirit of the Bamenda Highlands
summary: In the misty highlands of Bamenda, a leopard spirit guarded the ancient forests, punishing hunters who took more than they needed and rewarding those who showed reverence for the land.

title: The Leshy Who Changed His Mind
summary: A forest lord captures a woodcutter's son, but the boy's clever sister bargains for his release by offering the Leshy something he wants more than a human soul.

title: The Light-Bearers
summary: In the frozen silence of a Finnish winter, a lost traveler is guided through a lethal blizzard by the ethereal, dancing lights of the forest spirits.

title: The Lipan Apache Killer-of-Enemies
summary: In Lipan Apache tradition, Killer-of-Enemies is the primary creator and culture hero, identified with the Sun. Killer-of-Enemies seems synonymous with Child-of-the-Water, and he is considered the child of Changing Woman (who is identified as the Moon and Thunder). The Lipan emergence story includes Killer-of-Enemies creating the world and fighting monsters. He has a younger brother called Wise One, who assists him. Killer-of-Enemies journeyed through the world, establishing the proper order of things, teaching the Apache how to hunt, conduct ceremonies, and live properly. He defeated powerful enemies including giant animals and spirits who threatened the people. His battles established the sacred geography of the Lipan Apache world. After completing his work, Killer-of-Enemies departed, promising to return if the people ever truly needed him. The Lipan version shares similarities with the Navajo Hero Twins tradition but emphasizes the role of the single Sun-figure more strongly.

title: The Little Girl Who Defeated the Windigo
summary: A Windigo as tall as a white pine tree approached a village, its approach signaled by a kettle swinging over the fire and trees cracking from the bitter cold. The villagers were terrified, but a wise old grandmother's granddaughter, a tiny girl, asked for two peeled sumac sticks as long as her arms. She told her grandmother to melt a kettle of tallow. When the Windigo came over the hill, the little girl ran out to meet it with her two dogs. She grew bigger and bigger with each step until she was as tall as the Windigo herself. She struck the Windigo with the sumac sticks, which had turned to copper, crushing its skull. Then she drank the hot tallow and shrank back to her normal size. The Windigo, when chopped up, was made of ice with a human body at its core. The village celebrated the little girl as their savior.

title: The Little Match Girl
summary: It was terribly cold and dark on New Year's Eve. Centers on Spirit,  human attempt to understand the soul, afterlife, and the unseen forces that govern existence..

title: The Little Mermaid
summary: A young mermaid princess sacrifices her voice for legs to win a prince's love. When he marries another, she faces a choice: kill him or become sea foam. She chooses sacrifice.

title: The Little People (Bohpoli/Kowi Anukasha) (Choctaw)
summary: The Choctaw believe in little people called Bohpoli ('the Thrower') or Kowi Anukasha ('Forest Dweller'). These are small beings about two feet tall who dwell alone in the thick, dark woods. They are mischievous but not malicious, often playfully throwing sticks and stones at travelers or hitting pine trees to create noise. All unexplained sounds in the forest are attributed to Bohpoli. They are never seen by common people, only by prophets and shamans. The little people are said to assist medicine men in creating their remedies. Sometimes Bohpoli would 'steal' children and take them into the woods to teach them about herbs and medicines, then return them to their homes. These children would grow up to become the tribe's doctors and healers.

title: The Living Goddess Kumari of Nepal
summary: The Kumari tradition venerates a prepubescent Newar girl as the living embodiment of the goddess Taleju Bhawani (a form of Durga). Legend holds that King Jayaprakash Malla of Kathmandu played dice nightly with the goddess Taleju, who visited him on condition of secrecy. When the king's daughter discovered them, the goddess vanished in anger, later appearing in a dream to instruct the king to worship a virgin girl of the Shakya clan instead. The chosen Kumari — selected through rigorous physical and astrological tests — lives in the Kumari Ghar palace in Kathmandu's Durbar Square, her feet never touching the ground outside. She is venerated by both Hindus and Buddhists until her first menstruation, when the goddess departs. Her expressions during public appearances are read as omens: tears mean death, laughter means national crisis, trembling means war.

title: The Lizard Deity of the Southern Cliff
summary: When a drought strikes the villages below the southern cliff, a monk descends to bargain with the ancient lizard deity who holds the rain locked beneath the stone — but the deity demands a price measured not in gold, but in years of life.

title: The Lizard Who Brought Sunrise
summary: An ancient highland Timorese tale from the mountainous interior of Timor-Leste. In a time before memory, the world existed in perpetual darkness because a giant lizard, coveting the sun's radiance, had dragged it deep into a mountain cave. The people suffered endlessly in cold and shadow until a young girl named Bui, inspired by her grandmother's stories of light, courageously climbed to the lizard's cave. Instead of fighting the enormous beast, Bui sang beautiful songs and danced — the ancient dances once performed to celebrate sunrise. The enchanted lizard emerged from the cave, mesmerized by her performance, allowing sunlight to flood the world. As the sun rose, the lizard shrank into the harmless house lizards found in Timorese homes today.

title: The Loogaroo and the Obeah Man
summary: When a loogaroo terrorizes a village through a series of unexplained attacks, only the village obeah man has the knowledge and courage to confront it.
themes: duality of human nature and monstrosity

title: The Lord of the Bears
summary: In a remote Austrian valley, where snow-capped peaks scraped the sky and forests of pine stretched for miles, there lived a young girl named Liesl.

title: The Lorelei
summary: Near the ancient town of Sankt Goarshausen, where the Rhine River narrows between towering cliffs of slate, there stands a rock that has haunted the imaginations of sailors and poets for centuries.

title: The Lost Bell
summary: In the old port city of Kołobrzeg on the Baltic coast, there is a legend that has been whispered for centuries.

title: The Lost City of Sijilmasa
summary: Sijilmasa was a legendary medieval city in southeastern Morocco, founded in 757 CE on the Ziz River near the Sahara. Once one of the most important trading hubs in the Islamic world, it controlled the gold and salt trade routes between West Africa and the Mediterranean. According to Moroccan folklore, Sijilmasa was a city of unimaginable wealth where the streets were lined with gold and the houses were decorated with precious stones. The city's wealth came from the gold of the Ghana Empire, which was traded at Sijilmasa's legendary markets. The city was destroyed in the 14th century during conflicts between the Marinids and the local Maghrawa tribe, and its location was lost to the sands. In Berber oral tradition, the ruins of Sijilmasa are guarded by djinn who protect a hidden treasure chamber beneath the old city. Today, archaeological excavations near Rissani have uncovered extensive ruins, confirming the historical basis of the legend. The story of the lost golden city of the Sahara continues to inspire treasure hunters and storytellers across Morocco.

title: The Lost Hunters of Orion
summary: The stars forming Orion's Belt are known as the Siagtut, representing a group of hunters who became permanently lost on the vast arctic ice. They remain in the sky as a celestial reminder of the dangers of the wilderness and the eternal struggle for survival, serving as a guide and a warning to hunters on Earth.

title: The Lost Treasure
summary: When enemies invaded Sweden, the people of Stenbrohult hid their treasure in a copper kettle sunk in Lake Möckeln, where it remains unreachable. A rich farmer buried his silver at Kalfhagsberg before dying suddenly. A poor cottager tries to retrieve it on a Thursday evening but fails when he breaks the silence by greeting a priest, and the treasure turns to birch-bark boxes.

title: The Lost Treasure of Montezuma — Aztec Gold in the Southwest
summary: The legend of Montezuma's hidden treasure is one of the most persistent treasure myths in the US Southwest, blending Aztec history with Spanish colonial folklore and Mexican-American oral tradition. The story claims that as Hernán Cortés approached Tenochtitlan in 1519, the Aztec emperor Moctezuma II ordered his vast treasure of gold, silver, and jewels to be hidden to prevent it from falling into Spanish hands. According to various versions, the treasure was transported northward by a chain of Aztec runners and hidden in a cave somewhere in the American Southwest — possibly in New Mexico's Sandia Mountains, the Superstition Mountains of Arizona, or the Sierra Madre Occidental. Spanish conquistadors spent centuries searching for it, and later Mexican and Anglo treasure hunters continued the quest. The legend intertwines with the Seven Cities of Cíbola myth and has inspired countless expeditions, some ending in death or madness. For Mexican-Americans, the legend speaks to the theft of indigenous wealth and the hope that what was lost might one day be recovered. The story remains part of Southwestern folklore, with occasional 'discoveries' reported in local news.

title: The Lougarou Who Wore the Moon
summary: On the sugar estates of Mauritius, a shapeshifting lougarou stalks the cane fields under a full moon, seeking the one person who knows how to send it back to the form it once held.

title: The Luison of the Uruguayan Pampas
summary: A cursed seventh son who becomes a werewolf-like creature roaming the pampas of Uruguay, feared by gauchos and villagers alike.

title: The Lukasa: The Luba Memory Board
summary: The Lukasa (memory board) is a sacred object in Luba tradition, a wooden board covered with beads and shells arranged in patterns that encode the entire history of the Luba people. According to legend, the first Lukasa was given to the Mbudye (memory specialists) by the founding heroes themselves. The beads represent kings, migrations, battles, sacred sites, and cosmic events. A trained Mbudye historian can 'read' a Lukasa like a book, reciting epics of the Luba kingdom that take days to complete. The Lukasa records the founding story of Mbidi Kiluwe and Kalala Ilunga, the list of all Luba kings, the sacred laws of kingship, and the secret knowledge of the realm. The Lukasa is not merely a record of the past but a living object charged with spiritual power. Before a reading, the historian offers prayers and kola nuts to the spirits of the ancestors. The Lukasa tradition ensures that Luba history and sacred knowledge survive across generations.

title: The Lungu of the Deep River
summary: A Bemba fisherman who overfishes a sacred river encounters the Lungu, a colossal serpent guardian who demands he restore what he has taken before the waters turn against the village.

title: The Lure of the Nykur
summary: The Nykur is a shape-shifting water horse that appears as a beautiful, grey stallion by the lakeside. When a weary traveler attempts to mount it, the horse's skin becomes adhesive, and it gallops straight into the deep water, drowning the rider in a cold, watery grave.

title: The Maasai and the Great Lion Hunt
summary: The lion has always held a sacred and complex place in Maasai culture — both a threat to livestock and a symbol of courage. According to tradition, the first lion was created by Enkai to test the bravery of Maasai moran (warriors). In ancient times, a pride of lions began terrorizing a Maasai village, killing cattle every night. The young moran, armed only with spears and shields, tracked the lions to their den. Their leader, a warrior named Sanket, faced the alpha male alone, singing his praise song. The lion charged, but Sanket stood his ground, driving his spear into the lion's chest at the last possible moment. He returned to the village carrying the lion's mane as a trophy. This act of courage became the model for Olmayian — the Maasai lion hunt, a rite of passage where young warriors prove their bravery by facing a lion in single combat. While lion hunting is now prohibited, the Maasai continue to honor lions as fellow warriors of the plains, and lion conservation programs employ former hunters as guardians.

title: The Maasai Origin of Fire
summary: Long ago, the Maasai lived without fire, eating their food raw and shivering through cold nights. The only fire in existence belonged to the mountain god who kept it hidden atop a great peak. A brave young moran (warrior) named Ole Nailor volunteered to steal fire for his people. He climbed the treacherous mountain for days, facing snow, ice, and fierce winds. When he reached the summit, he found the fire guarded by a great serpent. Using his wit rather than his spear, Ole Nailor distracted the serpent by singing a praise song, snatched a burning branch, and raced down the mountain. The serpent pursued, but Ole Nailor passed the fire to other warriors waiting in relay. Thus fire came to the Maasai people.

title: The Maboyo of the Layou
summary: A colossal serpent spirit guards the deepest pools of the Layou River, and those who offend the waters risk being dragged beneath the surface forever.
themes: ancient guardians of the natural world

title: The Magic Book
summary: A tale about a book endowed with supernatural powers that grants knowledge, secrets, or abilities to its owner, leading to both power and peril.

title: The Magic Guitar of Andalusia
summary: A poor musician discovers a magical guitar that brings uncontrollable joy and dance to all who hear it.

title: The Magic Scythe
summary: A day-laborer receives a magical scythe but loses it by not following instructions.

title: The Magician's Cape
summary: An evil magician lives in a mountain palace filled with frightened young girls he has stolen from their families. He forces them to dance and sing for him, and when one displeases him, he casts her into the forest to be devoured by bears and wolves. The magician possesses a black flying cape: when a maiden steps onto it, the cape turns into wings and he whisks her away. One day he discovers Alvida, a smith's beautiful daughter, combing her golden hair at a window. He tries to ensnare her with his cape, but she is clever and cautious. When a ram (summoned by the magician's whistle) charges at her, Alvida stumbles and tears the cape with the ram's horns. Feeling remorseful, she mends the tear using two thorns as a needle and a strand of her golden hair as thread. The magician then tricks her into stepping onto the cape, and she is carried away. As she cries for help, her golden hair catches on a tree branch and refuses to break. The magician is forced to release her. Enraged, he returns to his castle, but finds he cannot sleep—the golden thread sewn into his cape glows so brightly it fills every room with light. No matter how he tries to hide the cape, the radiance follows him. Desperate, he returns to Alvida's village and offers gifts, but she refuses to remove the thread, knowing trolls and magicians cannot enter Christian homes. Every good deed the magician performs dims the light slightly, and he is forced into a life of reluctant kindness. The golden thread represents the power of good deeds over evil ones.

title: The Magpie with Salt on Her Tail
summary: A poor boy named Olle (or Theo in some versions) is always wishing for things he cannot afford — a knife, a sled, a horse and carriage. An old man tells him an old legend: if you sprinkle salt on a magpie's tail and make a wish before the salt falls off, the wish will come true. Olle spends days trying to catch a magpie, but they are too clever. Finally, a magpie speaks to him, claiming to be an enchanted prince. The magpie agrees to let Olle sprinkle salt on her tail, but only if he first brings her increasingly extravagant gifts — first a fine knife, then a bicycle, then a sled, then a horse and carriage, then a castle, and finally chests of gold. Each time Olle acquires the item through his own hard work, the magpie demands something grander. Olle's frustration grows, but he persists. Finally, after years of labor, he has earned the castle, the gold, and everything the magpie demanded. When at last he sprinkles the salt on her tail and she asks him to make his wish, Olle realizes he already has everything he could ever want — all earned through his own efforts. The magpie flies away, having taught him the greatest lesson of all. The story is a Swedish folk tale variation on the theme that hard work, not magic, is the true path to achieving one's dreams.

title: The Maiden in the Castle of Rosy Clouds
summary: A poor, hardworking young man (named Cedric in some versions) collapses from exhaustion and dreams of a beautiful fairy maiden who walks out of rosy clouds and invites him to find her. When he wakes, he is determined to win her. But no one knows where the Castle of Rosy Clouds is, and people mock him for his quest. Finally, an old woman tells him a poem revealing three magical items he must obtain: a gray stallion who can find his way through the clouds, a red mantle to protect him from fire, and a sword named Gull to split the iron serpent's skull. The young man has no idea how to acquire these items. He returns to ordinary life, but over many years, he encounters three situations where people are in danger. Each time he selflessly helps — rescuing someone from a snake, saving a town, and so on — and each heroic act rewards him with one of the three magical items. But the quest takes so long that by the time he finally reaches the Castle of Rosy Clouds, he is an old man. As he ascends through the clouds on the gray stallion, wielding the sword Gull and wearing the red mantle, a giant appears. He charges and the giant vanishes. At the castle, the fairy maiden welcomes him and, looking at his reflection in the moat, he sees that he has been made young and handsome again. They live happily together as rulers of the castle. The story celebrates perseverance, selflessness, and the idea that true love is worth a lifetime of effort.

title: The Maiden of the Yellow Rocks
summary: A Zuni story about the beautiful daughter of the high priest of the Village of the Yellow Rocks. Despite her beauty, her pride and coldness drove away suitors. The twin war gods Áhaiyúta and Mátsailéma, living with their grandmother on Thunder Mountain, decided to court her. They appeared as ugly pygmies — boys who never grew to manhood. Meanwhile, the Field-mice, who were prolific and needed wool for their families, gambled with the gods. The mice lost everything, including the wool for their nests, and their babies died of cold. The war gods, despite their terrible nature, took the orphaned mouse babies to their grandmother, who raised them. The story teaches the Zuni value of caring for helpless children — if even the cruelest gods showed mercy, surely humans must care for abandoned infants and orphans.

title: The Maiden the Sun Made Love To
summary: A Zuni story about a maiden whom the Sun desired. The Sun came to her in human form and courted her, and she gave birth to twin boys — the ancestors of the Zuni war gods. The Sun's attention to the maiden brought both blessing and burden. The boys grew rapidly and displayed extraordinary abilities. They became the first culture heroes, teaching their people how to hunt, farm, and perform ceremonies. The story explains the origin of anger in the world — the maiden's anger at the Sun's departure (or at the gossip of the villagers) introduced this emotion to humanity. This origin myth establishes that both positive and negative emotions are part of the human condition and that even divine parentage does not exempt one from human struggles. The twins' journey to find their father the Sun and receive his blessing mirrors the Navajo Hero Twins tradition.

title: The Maiden Who Became a Bear
summary: A Navajo story about a young woman who transformed into a bear after being mistreated by her family or community. The maiden wandered into the wilderness in despair, and as she walked, her hands and feet slowly transformed into bear claws, her body grew fur, and she became a powerful bear. She later encountered hunters from her village, who recognized her by the remnants of her human appearance. The story serves as a cautionary tale about the treatment of others and carries ceremonial significance related to the Mountain Top Chant ceremony. Bear holds special power in Navajo tradition, and this story explains the deep spiritual connection between bears and specific healing ceremonies.

title: The Making of the Mojo Bag
summary: Mojo bags—small red flannel pouches filled with roots, herbs, coins, and personal objects—are central to Hoodoo practice, and their creation is surrounded by elaborate lore. One traditional story tells of a conjure woman named Aunt Polly who made mojo bags for her entire community. People came from miles around seeking her bags for luck in love, protection from harm, success in gambling, or revenge against enemies. The most famous story involves a young man about to gamble with a cruel white landowner who always cheated. Aunt Polly made him a mojo containing John the Conqueror root, a silver dime, and a petition written on brown paper. She told him to keep it in his left pocket and never let it touch the ground. At the gambling table, the young man won every hand. The landowner, enraged, accused him of cheating, but the mojo protected him from harm—the landowner's pistol would not fire. The young man escaped with his winnings and never gambled again. The mojo bag tradition reflects the African American belief that spiritual protection is carried with you, a portable connection to the power of the ancestors and the conjure tradition.

title: The Man and the Fox Wife
summary: A lonely hunter meets and marries a beautiful woman, only to discover that she is actually a fox in human form. The story explores the tension between the domestic world of humans and the wild nature of animals. Eventually, the woman must return to her own kind, leaving the man with a profound understanding of the boundaries between species.

title: The Man and the Girl at the Underground Mansion
summary: A surreal narrative describing a journey to a hidden subterranean world, exploring themes of the subconscious and the mysteries of the underground.

title: The Man and the Seven Rams
summary: A Crow man of immense ability and power once encountered the Seven Rams, magnificent creatures of the mountains. The man, confident in his strength, thought he could overpower them. But the Seven Rams taught him humility. Despite his great power, the man learned that he must respect the Sweat Lodge and its ceremonies, for the lodge's power was greater than any individual's. The Rams demonstrated that true strength comes from spiritual purity and connection to the Creator, not from physical prowess. The story emphasizes that even the most gifted individuals must submit to spiritual discipline and communal rituals.

title: The Man Who Carried Sickness Out of the Village
summary: A Sámi legend about a man who heroically carries a plague or sickness out of a village, stopping its spread. He removes the disease spirit from the community and ventures into the wilderness to save his people. The story reflects Sámi beliefs about disease as a spiritual entity that can be physically removed, and the role of individuals in protecting the community from supernatural harm.

title: The Man Who Died on Holy Innocents' Day
summary: A wicked man named Kalle Kula dies on Holy Innocents' Day and finds himself caught between Heaven and Hell, bargaining for his soul with a blend of humor and desperation. Part fairy-tale, part legend, this tale has a Danish variant and displays the innocently malicious humor of Gottfried Keller.

title: The Mantis Creates the Moon from an Ostrich Feather
summary: The San trickster god /Kaggen (the Mantis) broke an eland's gall, which blinded him. Crawling through the darkness, he felt his way to the place of the Ostrich, where he found a long white wing-feather. He threw the feather into the sky to become the Moon, lighting the ground so he could see. This story is one of many celestial creation myths among the /Xam San, explaining the origin of the moon and establishing /Kaggen as a demiurge who shaped the cosmos through his actions, both foolish and wise.

title: The Mapinguari of the Xingu
summary: A giant, foul-smelling beast with backward feet guards the deepest parts of the Amazon, and the hunter who pursues it finds the jungle turned against him.

title: The Mara's Heavy Breath
summary: The Mara is a spirit that visits people in their sleep, sitting on their chests to cause suffocating nightmares. This phenomenon, often associated with sleep paralysis, was believed to be the work of a malevolent entity that drained the energy of both humans and livestock, leaving them exhausted and broken.

title: The Marabout of the Stone Well
summary: A marabout with the power of baraka saves a drought-stricken village by descending into an ancient well to negotiate with the spirits who dwell in its darkness.

title: The Marquesan Hero Nukuhiva
summary: The legendary hero Nukuhiva emerged from the sacred valley of Taipivai and united the warring tribes of the Marquesas Islands. Gifted by the gods with extraordinary strength, courage, and wisdom, Nukuhiva traveled across Nuku Hiva, Hiva Oa, and Ua Pou, establishing peace through a combination of diplomacy and martial prowess. He codified the tapu system, defined territorial boundaries, and instituted the feast cycles that governed Marquesan society. His descendants became the island chiefs who maintained his laws long after his death. The story of Nukuhiva embodies the Marquesan values of warrior honor, tribal unity, and reverence for ancestral tradition.

title: The Marten's Wife
summary: A Cree hunter marries a woman who is secretly a marten spirit, and when she returns to the forest, he must choose between his world and hers.

title: The Master and His Apprentice
summary: A young apprentice endures seven years of absolute silence to master the secrets of magic.

title: The Master Thief
summary: A young man becomes a 'Master Thief' through his extraordinary cunning. He outwits a farmer, a priest, and a squire, eventually winning the hand of the squire's daughter by proving his skills.

title: The Master-Smith
summary: Once upon a time in Norway, there lived a smith who was the finest craftsman in all the land, but he was poor.

title: The Match Girl
summary: A poor girl sells matches in the freezing cold, seeing beautiful, hopeful visions in each flame before passing away in the snow.

title: the Mba-Katrè, Spirit of the Divination Bowl
summary: A spirit that lives in the diviner's bowl, speaking through the patterns of cast cowrie shells — but it only tells the truth, never what you want to hear.

title: the Mba-Soêmba, Spirit of the Granary
summary: A spirit that protects the village granary, ensuring that the harvest lasts through the dry season — but only if the grain is shared equally.

title: The Mbari Houses of Ala (Igbo)
summary: When the earth goddess Ala is displeased with a community, she demands that a Mbari house be built in her honor. Mbari houses are elaborate, open-sided clay temples that depict Ala surrounded by her children, Amadioha the thunder god, and everyday scenes of Igbo life. The construction of a Mbari house is a major communal undertaking: the entire village contributes labor, and specially initiated artists and priests design the sculptures. During construction, the artists live in seclusion and are forbidden from sexual contact. When the Mbari house is complete, a grand festival is held, and the house is left to decay naturally, never repaired—representing the cycle of life and death. Once the house crumbles back to the earth, Ala is satisfied and a new one may be commissioned. The Mbari tradition reflects the Igbo understanding of art as a spiritual act of creation and renewal.

title: The Mboreví, Sacred Jaguar
summary: The jaguar is the Guaraní's most sacred animal, a shapeshifting guardian who punishes hunters who kill without asking permission from the forest.

title: The Menehune Builders
summary: Before the first Polynesian canoes touched the shores of Hawaii, the islands were already inhabited.

title: The Menehune: Hawaii's Hidden Builders
summary: The Menehune are a legendary race of small but powerful people who inhabited Hawaii before the Polynesian voyagers arrived. They were master builders who worked only at night, constructing fishponds, temples (heiau), and irrigation systems across the islands. The Menehune could complete in one night what would take ordinary humans months. The Alekoko Fishpond on Kauai is said to be their work, built in a single night by a line of Menehune stretching from the mountains to the sea. If a human watched them work, the Menehune would stop and vanish. Today, the word Menehune is used to describe any mysterious or unexplained construction in the islands.

title: The Mercury Computer
summary: A modern folk legend about a sapient machine that hides within the global network, the Mercury Computer is a cryptid of the digital age.

title: The Mermaids Who Saved Saint Kitts
summary: During a great storm that threatens to destroy the fishing fleet, the Black Rocks Mermaids reveal that they are not only destroyers but protectors of those who respect the sea.
themes: the unexpected mercy of feared spirits

title: The Merman's Children
summary: A narrative focusing on the half-human children born to Agnete and the Merman, who were abandoned when Agnete returned to the human world, exploring the tragedy and longing of the aquatic offspring.

title: The Mi'kmaq Creation Story (Seven Levels of Creation)
summary: The Mi'kmaq creation story unfolds across seven sacred levels. First there was the Great Spirit Kji Niskam, who existed before all things. From the first spark of creation came Grandfather Sun and Grandmother Moon. The third level is Mother Earth, who bears the spirits of the ancestors. On the fourth level, the first man Glooscap was created when lightning struck the earth three times — the first strike gave him form, the second gave him seven sacred parts to his head, and the third freed him to walk. Glooscap lay on the earth for 365 nights with his head to the rising sun. On the fifth level, his grandmother Nogami was born from dewdrops on a rock. On the sixth level, his nephew Nataoa-nsen was born from the foam of the sea, created by Whirlwind. On the seventh level, Glooscap's mother appeared from dew collected on a leaf. Seven families were created from the sparks of the Great Fire, and the Mi'kmaq are one of these seven original families.

title: The Midsummer Bonfires – Ancient Solar Rites on Åland
summary: Every June, when the sun barely sets at this northern latitude, the people of Åland gather for Midsummer's Eve (Midsommar) — one of the most important celebrations of the year. Across the archipelago, bonfires blaze on hilltops and beaches, echoing solar rites far older than Christianity. These fires honor the eternal return of the sun, mark the height of fertility and growth, and ward off malevolent spirits. Couples dance around the midsummer pole (midsommarstång) decorated with birch leaves and wildflowers, while musicians play nyckelharpa, accordion, and fiddle in rhythms passed down through generations. In folk belief, Midsummer night was a time when the boundaries between worlds grew thin: the skogsrå and sjörå were particularly active, and magical plants gathered at midnight held special powers. Young women would pick seven different flowers and place them under their pillow to dream of their future husbands. The tradition remains one of the strongest living folk practices on Åland.

title: The Midsummer Night's Dance
summary: On the night of the summer solstice, the veil between worlds is thinnest. Humans are invited to dance with the Huldufólk in the mountain meadows. Those who dance until dawn are forever changed, possessing a lingering longing for the hidden world and a strange affinity for the nature of the land.

title: The Migoi: Bhutan's Yeti Legends
summary: The Migoi (from Tibetan 'mi rgod', meaning 'wild man') is Bhutan's version of the Yeti — a magical creature of the high Himalayan pastures. Unlike the Nepali Yeti, the Bhutanese Migoi possesses supernatural abilities: it can become invisible at will, its blood has magical qualities used for talismans, and it carries two enchanted objects — the dipshing (a juniper twig granting invisibility) and the sem phatsa (a satchel without which it loses all power). Bhutanese folklore describes two types: the mechume (a small, ape-like being with reddish-brown hair inhabiting deep forests) and the migoi/gredpo (a huge creature with grayish-black hair, said to have a hollow back — a feature associated with dangerous ghosts). The Migoi is considered a bad omen; only certain people can see it. Bhutan's Sakteng Wildlife Sanctuary was established in part to protect the Migoi's habitat.

title: The Mik'uji'w (Stone Giant)
summary: The Mi'kmaq encounter a stone giant in the deep forest — a creature older than the glaciers, made of the mountain itself.

title: The Milkman of Pieter Both
summary: On the winding road below the mountain named for a Dutch governor, a spectral milkman appears before dawn, offering his wares to travelers — but the milk he carries is not of this world.

title: The Milky Way (Seminole/Hitchiti)
summary: This Seminole and Hitchiti story explains the origin of the Milky Way. Long ago, a father was angry with his son and banished him from the village. The son, heartbroken, wandered the earth. A great dog took pity on the boy and decided to help him escape his sorrow. The dog ran through the sky, scattering sparkling dust from its fur across the heavens, creating a luminous path. This path — the Milky Way — would forever remind people of the dog's compassion. Another version tells that the Milky Way is the path of souls traveling to the spirit world. The story reflects the Seminole reverence for animals and the belief that the stars and sky are filled with the stories of compassionate beings who helped humanity.

title: The Minotaur
summary: A prince of Athens enters the impossible Labyrinth to slay the bull-headed monster and end a cycle of blood sacrifice.

title: The Mocko Jumbie of Sandy Point
summary: During the Christmas Carnival season, a master stilt walker in Sandy Point channels the spirit of the Mocko Jumbie to protect the village from duppies and ill fortune.

title: The Mokele-mbembe and the Rainmaker
summary: During a devastating drought, a BaAka rainmaker journeys to the Likouala swamp to bargain with the Mokele-mbembe, discovering the creature controls the rains and will release them only when humans prove their reverence for the water.

title: The Mokele-mbembe of the Sangha River
summary: A fishing village on the Sangha River is terrorized by a massive river creature that capsizes canoes, until a wise elder reveals the creature is an ancient guardian defending its spawning grounds.

title: The Molbo Stories
summary: A series of humorous tales about the inhabitants of the village of Molle, who are depicted as absurdly foolish. They attempt to solve simple problems using incredibly complicated and illogical methods, serving as a satire of human stupidity.

title: The Mongolian Death Worm: Olgoi-Khorkhoi
summary: A bright red worm that kills with venom and electricity lurks beneath the sands of the Gobi Desert.

title: The Monkey King
summary: At the beginning of time, on the Mountain of Flowers and Fruit, which stood at the edge of the Eastern Continent, there was a magic boulder.

title: The Monkey King's Wedding
summary: In ancient Sukhothai, at the edge of the great jungle, there lived a powerful monkey king named Hanuman—the greatest of all monkeys, able to leap mountains in a single bound.

title: The Monkey's Paw
summary: On a cold, wet night at Laburnam Villa, a small house somewhere in the English countryside, the White family gathered around a cheerful fire.

title: The Moon God's Guarani Warning
summary: The Guaraní Moon God sends dreams to the village chiefs, warning them of a flood that will come unless the people return to the old ways.

title: The Moon Rabbit of Korea
summary: A kind rabbit offers itself as food to a beggar, only to be rewarded with immortality on the Moon.

title: The Moose and the Sun
summary: An Evenki legend explaining the journey of the sun across the sky. The story tells of a celestial moose that carries the sun on its antlers as it runs across the sky each day. At night, the moose rests and the sun sinks below the horizon. However, every evening a great wolf or bear chases the moose, trying to devour the sun. When the predator catches the moose, a solar eclipse occurs. The Evenki shamans would perform rituals and make noise to scare away the predator and free the sun. This myth reflects the central importance of the reindeer and moose to Evenki subsistence culture while also providing a cosmological explanation for solar phenomena.

title: The Mora That Visited the Sleeper
summary: A young bride plagued by nightly visitations from a Mora discovers that only cunning and the old ways can drive the spirit away before it drains the life from her household.

title: The Morning Star Sacrifice Ceremony
summary: The Morning Star ceremony was a Skidi Pawnee ritual involving the sacrifice of a captive girl to ensure agricultural fertility and cosmic order. It was performed when a man dreamed that Morning Star commanded it. A captive girl was taken from an enemy tribe, treated with respect but kept isolated. In spring, she was ritually cleansed and painted, symbolically transformed into the Evening Star. At dawn on the final day, she was placed on a scaffold and shot through the heart with a sacred arrow while a priest opened her chest. Her blood fell to fertilize the earth. The ceremony reenacted the Morning Star's cosmic battle and marriage to the Evening Star that created humanity.

title: The Mossy Rock (Blackfoot)
summary: Na'pi (Old Man) was traveling across the plains when he came upon a large moss-covered rock. He stopped to rest and draped his robe over the rock to dry. When he tried to retrieve his robe, the rock refused to give it back. Na'pi grew angry and struck the rock with his stick. The rock split open and Na'pi retrieved his robe, but the rock's anger caused the earth to shake. Na'pi realized he should not have disturbed the rock's peace. The story teaches that one must respect all things in nature, even those that seem inanimate.

title: The Most Incredible Thing
summary: A philosophical tale about the nature of truth and the human tendency to argue over the impossible, concluding that the 'most incredible thing' is that the story itself is true.

title: The Mother of the Loom
summary: A weaver in a Bahraini village discovers that the mysterious spirit Um El Sa'af Wel Leef has been guiding her work, binding fate into every thread.

title: The Mother of the Toes and the Fisherman
summary: An aging pearl diver in Ras Al Khaimah is visited by Umm Al Duwais, whose backward feet betray her illusion, and must use his wits to escape her hypnotic gaze.

title: The Mother's Counsel
summary: Lemminkainen's mother warns her son against his reckless desires and the hidden dangers of the North. She serves as a crucial voice of reason and maternal caution, urging him to abandon his foolish quests for fame and forbidden love.

title: The Mount of the Golden Queen
summary: A poor cattle-tending lad discovers a hidden mountain hall where a golden queen holds court, and his kindness toward forest creatures earns him treasure and a royal bride. This distinctly visionary tale from Södermanland sends its hero on a world-wide quest.

title: the Mountain Giant, Keeper of the Peaks
summary: A giant made of stone and moss that lives on the highest peak of the Congo-Nile ridge, pushing the clouds aside with its hands — and when it rests, the fog covers the mountains for days.

title: The Mountain Top Chant
summary: The Mountain Top Chant (Dzil Naʼoodilii) is a major Navajo ceremony whose origin story tells of a maiden who encountered a bear during her puberty ceremony. A young Navajo woman, while gathering materials for her ceremony, was approached by a bear who taught her the sacred songs, prayers, and sandpaintings of the Mountain Top Chant. The bear spirit took her into the mountains where she learned the entire ceremonial cycle over several days. When she returned to her people, she taught them the ceremony, which is used to invoke the protection and power of the mountain spirits and to cure illnesses caused by animals. The nine-day ceremony features elaborate sandpaintings, songs, and dances that reenact the maiden's journey and transformation.

title: The Moved Coffins of Chase Vault
summary: Heavy lead coffins inside a sealed stone vault in Christ Church shift and rearrange themselves overnight, defying every explanation that rational men can offer.

title: The Muki in the Mine
summary: A dwarf-like spirit with enormous feet and a hat of silver lives in the deepest mines of Bolivia, guiding miners to rich veins — if they remember to share their coca.

title: The Muladi of the Recife Slums
summary: A spectral figure born of unrequited love haunts the alleys of Recife, seeking the one who rejected it and punishing those who mock the lonely.

title: The Myling at the Crossroads
summary: In the province of Värmland, near an old crossroads where the main road meets the path to the church town, there have always been strange sounds at night.

title: The Mysterious Inn
summary: In the cold, creeping dark of a Danish winter night, a weary traveler found himself far from any town, his horse lame and his provisions nearly spent.

title: The Mysterious Traveler
summary: In the dusty roads of old Mexico, where the agave fields stretch silver under the moon and the hills echo with the songs of coyotes, there travels a figure who appears in times of need and disappears like morning mist.

title: The Myth of the Djinn of the Hoggar Mountains
summary: The Hoggar (Ahaggar) Mountains of southern Algeria are believed in Tuareg and Berber tradition to be inhabited by powerful spirits—ancient djinn who dwell in the volcanic peaks and hidden valleys. According to legend, these spirits predate human habitation in the Sahara and guard the secrets of the mountain, including hidden oases, ancient treasures, and magical caves. Travelers in the Hoggar must never anger the spirits by taking more than they need or disrespecting the mountain sanctuary. Some stories tell of djinn who lead lost travelers to water, while others speak of spirits who punish arrogance with madness or eternal wandering. The highest peak, Mount Tahat, is considered particularly sacred—a meeting place between the earthly and spirit worlds. The Hoggar spirits are sometimes identified with the Isabaten, a legendary pre-Tuareg people who, according to oral tradition, lived in the mountains and spoke an archaic Tamasheq language. The discovery of Tin Hinan's tomb in this region reinforced the belief that the Hoggar is a place where the boundaries between the human and spirit worlds are thin.

title: The Nahurac: Spirit Animal Lodges
summary: Tirawa conferred miraculous powers on certain animals who would act as his messengers and servants. These spirit animals, called nahurac, could intercede with Tirawa on behalf of the Pawnee. The nahurac had five sacred lodges: Pahuk (hill island on the Platte River), Lalawakohtito (dark island in the Platte), Ahkawitakol (white bank on the Loup River), Kitzawitzuk (a sacred spring on the Solomon River), and Pahur (guide rock hill). These five lodges were places of spiritual power where the nahurac gathered. The Pawnee would visit these sites to seek guidance, healing, and blessings from the animal spirits.

title: The Nanan of the Gullies
summary: A small nature spirit lives in the deep gullies of Barbados, tending the old trees and punishing those who cut wood without asking permission from the land.

title: The Natchez Great Sun and Tattooed Serpent (Natchez)
summary: The Natchez were ruled by two paramount chiefs: the Great Sun, who had supreme authority over civil and religious affairs, and the Tattooed Serpent, who oversaw matters of war, peace, and diplomacy. Both were hereditary positions within the Sun lineage, the royal clan. The Great Sun was considered a living deity, a direct descendant of the sun itself, and was carried on a litter so that his feet never touched the ground. When the Tattooed Serpent died in 1725, the funeral was a spectacular and solemn event. Two of his wives, one of his sisters, his first warrior, his doctor, his head servant and the servant's wife, his nurse, and a craftsman of war clubs all chose to die with him through ritual suicide, believing they would accompany him to the spirit world. The practice reflected the absolute authority of the Sun dynasty and the Natchez belief in an afterlife where rank and status persisted.

title: The Natchez Sacred Fire (Natchez)
summary: The sacred fire was the heart of Natchez religion and governance. A perpetual fire was kept burning in the temple atop the main platform mound at the Grand Village of the Natchez. The fire was guarded by temple priests and was never allowed to go out. Only the Great Sun and his family could enter the inner sanctum where the fire burned. The fire represented the sun on earth and the continuing presence of the divine among the Natchez people. When the temple fire was ritually extinguished and rekindled each year, it marked the most important ceremonial occasion. The story of 'Polluting the Fire' warns of a time when someone defiled the sacred flame by bringing unclean objects near it, angering the spirits and causing misfortune to fall upon the people until the fire was ritually purified.

title: The Nav and the Weaver
summary: A jealous night demon descends on women who weave beautiful cloth, tangling their threads and spoiling their patterns, because the Nav cannot bear to see anything more perfect than itself.

title: The Neck's Violin
summary: A determined young violinist makes a dark bargain with Näcken, the water spirit, trading his most beloved animals for the ability to play music that can move the world.

title: The Necken's Enchanted Violin
summary: Deep in the forests of Sweden, where the pine trees grow so thick that sunlight filters through the needles like light through stained glass, there runs a river called the Silverån.

title: The Ngoma Drums of the Swahili Coast
summary: The ngoma drum is sacred along the entire Swahili coast, serving as both musical instrument and spiritual vessel. According to legend, the first ngoma was given to the people by sea spirits (pepo) who rose from the Indian Ocean during a storm. The drum's voice could summon rain, heal the sick, and communicate with ancestors. In Zanzibar, it is said that the ngoma drums of the old sultans still beat beneath the sea on moonlit nights, played by the spirits of drowned musicians. The Baganda of Uganda trace their royal lineage to the ngoma, calling themselves 'children of Ngoma.' Among the Swahili, the drum is also a symbol of authority — no chief could rule without his royal ngoma, and the drum's rhythm dictated the pace of life from birth ceremonies to funerals. When a master drummer dies, his drum is buried with him so he may continue playing in the spirit world.

title: The Night Marchers
summary: In Hawaii, when the sun dips below the Pacific and the shadows of the volcanic peaks stretch across the land like dark fingers, the wise ones stay indoors.

title: The Night Marchers of Hawaii
summary: The Huaka'i Po (Night Marchers) are ghostly processions of ancient Hawaiian warrior spirits who march along traditional pathways on moonlit nights. Led by fire-wielding priests and accompanied by the sound of conch shells and war chants, they travel to sacred sites and battlefields. They can appear as torches floating in the darkness, with only the sound of marching feet. According to legend, anyone who looks directly at the Night Marchers will be killed, but those who lie face down and show proper respect will be spared. The procession includes the spirits of great chiefs, alii, carrying their divine mana through the landscapes they once ruled.

title: the Night-Walker, Shadow of the Savanna
summary: A shadow that walks the savanna at night, taking the shape of anyone who has ever died — and if you see it, it will take your shape next, so that someone, someday, will see you walking where you have never been.

title: The Nightingale
summary: An emperor prefers a mechanical, jeweled bird over a real nightingale, only to realize the true, irreplaceable value of natural beauty and song.

title: The Nisse and the Christmas Porridge
summary: A house spirit (Nisse) demands his Christmas porridge with a pat of butter on top. When a farmer skimps on the butter, the Nisse plays terrible tricks until properly fed.

title: The Nisse's Barn Revenge
summary: Every traditional farm is said to have a Nisse, a small wight who protects the animals and the property. If the farmer treats the Nisse with respect and provides a bowl of porridge with butter on Christmas Eve, the farm prospers. However, if insulted, the Nisse will sabotage the barn and terrorize the livestock.

title: The Nix of the Millpond
summary: A miller's daughter must outsmart a malevolent water spirit to save her brother from a desperate bargain made by her father.

title: The Nixie's Song
summary: By the old millpond on the edge of the Black Forest, where the water lay still and dark under the shadow of the willows, there lived a nixie.

title: The Nommo Descend in the Ark of Sirius
summary: After the Pale Fox disrupted creation, Amma sent the Nommo, twin amphibious beings half-human and half-fish, to restore order. They descended from the star Sirius (Sigi Tolo) in a spinning copper ark that traced a spiral path to Earth. The ark landed at the Bandiagara Escarpment in Mali, where the Nommo stepped out carrying the eight first ancestors of humanity. They brought every cultivated seed, the techniques of pottery and weaving, and most importantly the sacred word. The Nommo taught humans speech, agriculture, and ritual. Their descent established the spiral as the fundamental pattern of Dogon life, reflected in dance, architecture, and village layout, with every granary built to replicate the shape of the original ark.

title: The Nun's Priest Tale
summary: In the bustling streets of 14th-century Florence, where merchants hawked their wares and the scent of fresh bread mingled with the aroma of roasting meat, there lived a priest whose appetite for earthly pleasures far exceeded his devotion to spiritual matters.

title: The Nunnehi: Cherokee Spirit People (Cherokee)
summary: The Nunnehi, meaning 'The Travelers' or 'Those Who Live Anywhere,' are a race of invisible spirit people who dwell in the mountains and forests of Cherokee country. They are friendly toward humans and often appear as regal Cherokee warriors. The Nunnehi are said to be great dancers and musicians; travelers sometimes hear their singing and drumming coming from inside hollow mountains. They have saved Cherokee war parties from defeat by magically enlarging their numbers or by confusing enemy forces. The Nunnehi are known to invite favored humans into their underground dwellings, where time passes differently — a visitor may spend what seems like a single night only to return home and find that years have passed. They are generally benevolent but withdraw from contact if treated with disrespect.

title: The Nutcracker and the Mouse King
summary: The Monkey King, Sun Wukong, is the greatest trickster in all of Chinese mythology.

title: The Nuxalk Origin of the Sun (Nuxalk)
summary: The Nuxalk people tell that before the sun existed, there was only the dim light of copper-colored darkness. The people prayed constantly to Alhkw'ntam, the Creator, for light. In Nusmata, the house of the gods in the upper world, the Creator's granddaughter Skimina lived. The Four Carpenters created Raven (Qwaxw) from a piece of charcoal to answer the people's prayers. Raven, after being born as Skimina's child, cried persistently for the box containing the globe of light. When Alhkw'ntam finally relented, Raven rolled the globe back and forth until he smashed it against the wall. Light poured out through the smoke hole, flooding the world with brightness. The breaking of the globe created the sun for daytime, the moon for night, and the stars scattered across the sky. The people's sadness ended, and they celebrated the gift of light. This myth emphasizes the cooperative work of the carpenters, Raven's role as mediator between heaven and earth, and the Nuxalk belief that the sun is a living being with whom they maintain a spiritual relationship.

title: the Nyonyose, Spirit Behind the Mask
summary: When the mask dancer puts on the Nyonyose mask, the human disappears and the ancestor speaks — because in Burkina Faso, the dead do not leave, they wait behind the mask.

title: The Näcken – Water Fiddler of Åland's Lakes and Streams
summary: The Näcken (Näkk in Finnish Swedish) is a male water spirit who sits naked among the reeds or under waterfalls, playing hauntingly beautiful violin music. His playing is irresistibly seductive, luring listeners — especially children and young women — toward the water, where they drown. However, the Näcken can be outwitted by those who know the proper countermeasures: if someone learns to play a tune the Näcken cannot match, or if a priest thwarts him with prayer, the spirit can be driven away. In some versions, the Näcken teaches his art to those who bring him a stolen offering. In the Åland context, with its thousands of lakes, inlets, and streams, the Näcken was a powerful cautionary figure used to keep children away from dangerous waters. The figure is closely related to the Norwegian Fossegrim and the Finnish Näkki.

title: The Näckens Violin
summary: By the dark lake in Hälsingland, where the water is black even in daylight, there lived a fiddler named Anders who could play as no other in the village.

title: The Nāga Fireballs of the Mekong
summary: An enduring Thai legend surrounding the mysterious Nāga fireballs (Bang Fai Phaya Nak) that rise from the Mekong River each year during the full moon of the 11th lunar month (October). According to tradition, the serpent king Phaya Nāga who dwells beneath the Mekong releases these glowing red orbs — ranging from tiny sparks to basketball-sized spheres — to honor the Buddha's return from heaven. Thousands gather annually in Nong Khai province to witness the phenomenon. Local lore tells that the Nāga also created Nong Han lake (the 'Sea of the Nāga') near Sakon Nakhon, where his serpentine body carved the lakebed into existence. The event symbolizes the deep connection between the Mekong River's spiritual guardians and Theravada Buddhist tradition.

title: The Nāga of the Mekong: Guardian Serpent of Laos
summary: In Lao mythology, the Nāga (Ngueak in Lao) is the most powerful and revered supernatural being — a great serpent deity that dwells in the Mekong River and serves as the guardian spirit of the Lao people. According to legend, the Mekong River was created by the Nāga king as he slithered across the land, carving the riverbed with his massive body. Every village along the Mekong has its own Nāga legends. The Nāga are believed to protect boatmen from drowning, ensure good fish catches, and guard treasures hidden beneath the river. They can appear in human form, often as handsome men who marry mortal women. The most famous Lao Nāga legend tells of a young woman who married a mysterious man from the river who was actually a Nāga prince; their child became a powerful ruler. During the annual Rocket Festival (Bun Bang Fai), villagers launch homemade rockets to signal the Nāga to bring rain for the rice fields. The Nāga is also central to the Boat Racing Festival, where longboats carved in the shape of Nāga serpents race to honor the river spirits. The Nāga fireball phenomenon at the Mekong is as significant in Laos as in Thailand, deeply woven into Lao spiritual geography.

title: The Obambo That Would Not Cross
summary: When a man dies before completing his life's work, his Obambo ghost lingers at the river crossing between the world of the living and the dead, unable to move on until his unfinished task is completed.

title: The Ocean Spider's Gaze
summary: A skilled kayaker paddling near Godthaab notices the sea floor is unexpectedly shallow. He recalls warnings about the Ocean Spider, a massive creature that lurks beneath the waves. Just as he realizes the danger, he sees a giant eye staring back at him from the depths. Thanks to his agility and quick reactions, he manages to paddle away from the creature's reach, narrowly avoiding becoming its next meal.

title: The Octopus Spirit of the Coastal Waters
summary: The Octopus Water-Spirit of the Cameroonian coast taught the Douala people the art of diving and gathering shellfish, but demanded they never harvest from the coral beds where her children slept.

title: The Ogbanje Spirit (Igbo)
summary: The Ogbanje is a malevolent reincarnating spirit in Igbo cosmology that deliberately plagues a family by being born, dying young, and then being reborn to the same mother repeatedly. These spirits cause endless grief to families, with children dying before puberty in each cycle. The Igbo believe that each Ogbanje buries an iyi-uwa, a special stone that serves as the connection between the spirit world and the physical world and allows it to find its way back to the same family. To break the cycle, a dibia (priest-diviner) must discover and destroy the iyi-uwa. Once the stone is destroyed, the Ogbanje cycle is broken, and the child can live a normal life. The concept of Ogbanje has been explored in Chinua Achebe's novel 'Things Fall Apart.'

title: The Old Dame and her Hen
summary: An old woman's hen is stolen by a Man of the Hill. Her three daughters search for it; the first two are killed, but the youngest outwits the ogre and rescues her sisters.

title: The Old Troll of Big Mountain
summary: A poor cottager and his wife own little more than a small cottage, two goats, and their five-year-old son Olle. While they work as day laborers, they lock Olle in the cottage with bread and milk, letting the goats graze in an enclosure. One evening, they return to find both goats gone — the evil old troll of Big Mountain (Storberget) has stolen them. The loss is devastating, and Olle now gets only water instead of goat milk. Worse, they fear the troll might return for Olle himself. Determined to recover what was taken, Olle sets out despite his young age. Armed with a board with a nail and a wooden sword, he ventures into the forest to confront the troll. The old troll of Big Mountain is a fearsome creature — described in Swedish folklore as a pipe-smoking, flute-playing giant who steals livestock and children. Olle's courage in facing this terrifying being demonstrates that even the smallest and weakest can stand against oppression. The story, originally published in the magazine Tummeliten in 1900 with illustrations by Jenny Nyström, presents a classic tale of a child's bravery against a supernatural adversary, with the troll representing the harsh and unpredictable dangers of the natural world that rural Swedish families had to contend with.

title: The Old Woman and the Fish
summary: An old woman catches a talking pike that grants three wishes: that her pails fetch water by themselves, that whatever she strikes breaks right off, and that whatever she pulls becomes long. Each wish backfires—she slaps her knees in delight and breaks her legs off, then blows her nose and it grows terribly long.
themes: be careful what you wish for

title: The Old Woman and the Origin of the Sea
summary: Among the Baining people of New Britain, Papua New Guinea, a myth explains how the sea was created. In the beginning, the sea was only a tiny waterhole from which an old woman extracted saltwater to flavor her food, keeping it hidden under a cover of tapa cloth. One day, her sons became curious and tore open the cover. The farther they tore, the larger the waterhole grew. Terrified by the expanding water, they fled, each carrying a corner of the cloth, which caused the water to spread until it became the vast ocean. In desperation, the old woman hastily planted twigs along the edge of the shore, creating the first coastline and preventing the ocean from destroying all things. This story is found in variants throughout Melanesia.

title: The Old Woman and the Tramp
summary: A clever tramp talks a stingy old woman into giving him shelter, then tricks her into contributing ingredients one by one to make 'nail broth'—starting with a nail and adding oatmeal, beef, potatoes, barley, milk, and brandy until they feast together.

title: the Orang Bunian, the Hidden People
summary: A race of invisible beings who live alongside humans in the same forests and villages, visible only to those with the gift, because in Singapore the world is wider than you can see.

title: The Origin of Breadfruit
summary: During a terrible famine in Tahiti, the people prayed to the gods for deliverance. The god Rongo, moved by their suffering, transformed himself into a great breadfruit tree. The tree bore fruit that tasted like fresh bread when roasted, saving the people from starvation. Each part of the tree proved useful—the fruit as food, the sap as glue and medicine, the leaves as plates, and the wood for building canoes. Rongo also taught the people how to cultivate the tree through cuttings rather than seeds, ensuring the breadfruit would follow them wherever they voyaged. The story explains why breadfruit was carried by Polynesian settlers across the Pacific and remains a staple food across the islands.

title: The Origin of Corn
summary: The gods create humans from corn after failing with mud and wood, establishing maize as the sacred foundation of Maya civilization.

title: The Origin of Corn (Pueblo)
summary: In Pueblo mythology, corn was a gift from the Holy People. The origin story varies between communities but commonly involves a culture hero or deity who obtained corn from the underworld or from supernatural beings. In one version, the Corn Maidens (Blue Corn Maiden, Yellow Corn Maiden, etc.) brought corn to the people. In another, a boy discovered corn growing in a hidden place and brought it to his village. The sacred nature of corn is reflected in its inclusion in nearly every Pueblo ceremony. The different colors of corn (white, yellow, blue, red, black, and speckled) each have spiritual significance and are associated with the six directions. The successful growth of corn depends not only on farming skill but on the proper performance of ceremonies and the people's moral conduct. Corn is understood as a sentient being with which humans have a reciprocal relationship — humans care for corn, and corn nourishes humans.

title: The Origin of Corn: First Mother's Sacrifice
summary: In the time of the first people, the Abenaki were hungry. Gluskabe's grandmother Nokomes taught the people to survive on wild plants, but food was scarce. First Mother, the first woman created by Gichi Niwaskw and Gluskabe, saw her children starving. She told her husband to kill her and drag her body across a clearing. Weeping, he obeyed. Where her body passed, corn sprang up — tall green stalks bearing golden ears. Where her heart lay, beans grew to climb the corn. Where her feet lay, squash spread across the ground. First Mother had given her life so her children would never starve. The Abenaki honor her sacrifice in every planting season, and the Three Sisters — corn, beans, and squash — are always planted together, as First Mother intended, supporting each other just as the people must support each other.

title: The Origin of Death in Ambrym
summary: On the island of Ambrym in Vanuatu, a myth explains how death came into the world. After the creation of humanity, the good deities proposed that humans should shed their skin like snakes, preserving their youthful appearance forever and living eternally. However, the evil deities disagreed, arguing that when humans grew too old, they should be buried in the ground forever. Because the one who speaks last prevails in the councils of the gods, the evil deities had the final word, and death became the fate of all humanity. This story belongs to a widespread Melanesian mythological theme explaining why humans die while snakes shed their skins and appear renewed.

title: The Origin of Disease and Medicine (Cherokee)
summary: Long ago, all plants, animals, and humans lived together in harmony, and animals were larger and stronger. As the human population grew, they began killing animals without respect. The animals held councils to decide how to protect themselves. The Deer council decreed that any hunter who killed a deer without asking forgiveness would develop rheumatism. The Birds, Insects, and smaller animals created diseases to afflict humans. But the Plants heard of the animals' plans. Since plants had always been friends with humans, they vowed that for every disease the animals created, they would provide a cure. This is why every plant has medicinal purpose, and why medicine men must learn from the spirits of plants which herbs to use. The story establishes the Cherokee understanding of balance between humans, animals, and plants.

title: The Origin of Fire
summary: How fire first came to the world, stolen from the gods for the benefit of humanity.

title: The Origin of Fire (Motu People)
summary: Among the Motu people of southern Papua New Guinea, a myth tells that the ancestors originally ate all food raw because they had no fire. One day, smoke was seen rising far out at sea. A dog volunteered to investigate the source, swimming across the water. The dog reached an island where women were cooking with fire. Seizing a blazing brand in its mouth, the dog swam safely back to the mainland, bringing fire to the people. Another version from the Massim people of southeastern Papua tells of an old woman named Goga who possessed fire from her own body but kept it for herself, eating cooked food while serving raw food to others. When a man discovered her secret and stole a firebrand, the fire spread rapidly, eventually reaching a tree where a snake lived, setting its tail permanently ablaze as the source of fire for humanity.

title: The Origin of Ganesha's Elephant Head
summary: Goddess Parvati, longing for a son, created a boy from sandalwood paste and turmeric from her own body, breathed life into him, and appointed him as her guardian while she bathed. When Lord Shiva returned and tried to enter, the boy — who had never met his father — stopped him, obeying his mother's command. Enraged by this defiance, Shiva severed the boy's head. When Parvati emerged and saw her son dead, her grief and fury threatened to destroy the universe. To pacify her, Shiva sent his attendants to fetch the head of the first creature they found facing north, which was an elephant. He placed the elephant's head on the boy's body, restoring him to life and declaring him Ganesha, leader of his celestial hosts and remover of all obstacles.

title: The Origin of Hmong New Year (Noj Peb Caug)
summary: The Hmong New Year legend explains the origins of the most important celebration in Hmong culture — Noj Peb Caug (Eat Thirty), marking the end of the agricultural cycle. According to Hmong oral tradition, in ancient times the spirit of the New Year (Xyoo Tshiab) was a powerful deity who traveled through the villages bringing blessings, prosperity, and renewal. But the New Year spirit could only visit if invited through proper rituals and offerings. The legend tells of a poor Hmong family who forgot to prepare offerings for the New Year spirit and suffered a year of misfortune — failed crops, illness, and death. A kind shaman taught the people the proper way to welcome the New Year spirit: cleaning the house, preparing special foods, performing soul-calling ceremonies, and releasing the old year's spirits. The celebration lasts for three days and includes the tossing of the ball (pov pob) — a courtship ritual where young men and women throw cloth balls to one another, practicing the movements of catching blessings from the spirit world. Another key tradition is the hu plig (soul-calling ceremony), where the head of household calls the souls of family members to return home for the New Year. The legend emphasizes that the New Year is not just a social celebration but a spiritual renewal — a time when the boundary between worlds thins and blessings can flow from ancestors to the living.

title: The Origin of Kava
summary: A Tongan chief and his wife prayed to the gods for a child. Their prayers were answered with a son, but he was born with leprosy. The grief-stricken parents buried the child, and from his grave grew two plants—a tall, branching plant (the kava) and a shorter broad-leafed plant (the sugarcane). A wandering spirit discovered these plants and instructed the people on how to prepare them. The kava root was chewed and mixed with water to create a ceremonial drink that brought peace, unity, and connection to the ancestors. Thus kava became the sacred beverage of Tongan ceremony, used to seal agreements, welcome visitors, and commune with the gods.

title: The Origin of Kava in Fiji
summary: In Fijian oral tradition, the origin of kava (yaqona) is tied to a sacred ritual. According to legend, a chief and his followers were instructed by the gods to perform a ceremonial planting. From a specific plant, the roots were discovered to produce a potent drink that connected the drinker to the spirit world. The preparation and drinking of kava became central to Fijian ceremony, used to honor ancestors, settle disputes, and communicate with deities like Degei. The kava ceremony remains the most important cultural ritual in Fiji, with strict protocols governing its preparation, serving, and consumption as a bridge between the human and spiritual realms.

title: The Origin of Lake Victoria
summary: Long ago, the land where Lake Victoria now sits was a lush valley filled with prosperous villages. But the people grew greedy and forgot to honor Were with sacrifices. Were sent a great flood as punishment, but one old woman named Nyanjala was warned by a spirit. She gathered her family and a few animals and climbed to the highest hill. The waters rose for days, drowning the valley and everyone who had not listened. When the waters finally settled, the valley had become a great inland sea. Nyanjala and her family became the ancestors of the lakeside Luo. To this day, fishermen make offerings before launching their boats, and elders say the water spirits (nyawawa) still guard the depths, descendants of those who drowned in the great flood.

title: The Origin of Maple Sugar (Wenebojo and the Maple Trees)
summary: Long ago, when Wenebojo was wandering the earth, he discovered that the maple trees produced thick, sweet syrup that flowed freely from their trunks. The people had only to collect it and drink their fill. Wenebojo, being lazy and greedy, drank so much that he became sick. Angrily believing the trees had tricked him, he diluted the syrup by throwing water into the trees so that only a thin sap remained. Then he took his spear and stabbed the birch tree full of holes (the marks are visible on birch bark to this day), declaring that in the future people would have to work hard to get maple sugar — gathering wood, boiling the sap for many hours, and it would take forty barrels of sap to make one barrel of sugar. Thus Wenebojo made life harder for his people through his own fault.

title: The Origin of Sedna
summary: Sedna, once a mortal girl, is betrayed by her father after fleeing a bird-husband. As she clings to the side of her father's kayak during a storm, he cuts off her fingers to save the boat. As her fingers fall into the sea, they transform into the first whales, seals, and walruses. Sedna sinks to the bottom of the ocean, becoming the powerful goddess of the sea who controls the availability of marine animals, requiring shamans to comb her hair to appease her when food is scarce.

title: The Origin of the Apsara Dancers
summary: According to Khmer mythology, the Apsaras are celestial dancers born from the churning of the Ocean of Milk — a Hindu creation myth adopted and deeply embedded in Cambodian culture. The story tells of the devas (gods) and asuras (demons) who churned the cosmic ocean using Mount Mandara as a churning rod and the serpent Vasuki as a rope. From the churning waters emerged countless treasures, including the Apsaras — exquisitely beautiful celestial maidens whose purpose was to entertain the gods with their heavenly dance. The most famous Apsara in Khmer tradition is Mera, from whom the name 'Khmer' is believed to derive — combining 'Kambu' (the legendary founder) and 'Mera' to form Kambuja (Cambodia). The Apsara dance tradition was considered so sacred that only the royal court could perform it, and the dancers were believed to be earthly embodiments of the celestial Apsaras. The bas-reliefs of Angkor Wat depict over 1,800 distinct Apsara carvings, each with unique hairstyles, jewelry, and gestures. The royal ballet of Cambodia continues this tradition, with Apsara dance remaining a symbol of Khmer cultural identity and spiritual devotion.

title: The Origin of the Chaga People
summary: According to Chaga tradition, the first Chaga people emerged from the sacred caves on the slopes of Kilimanjaro. Long ago, a great famine drove people from the surrounding plains to seek refuge on the mountain's fertile slopes. There, Ruwa led them to hidden caves where underground rivers flowed and the soil was eternally rich. The first Chaga clans divided the mountain among themselves — those who settled on the eastern slopes became one clan, those in the west another, and so on. Each clan was given a sacred grove where they could communicate with Ruwa and the ancestors. The mountain's volcanic soil, enriched by ancient eruptions, provided such abundant harvests that the Chaga never went hungry. The ancestors taught them how to build irrigation channels from mountain streams, how to terrace the steep slopes for farming, and how to brew banana beer for ceremonies. The Chaga believe that as long as they honor Kilimanjaro and its spirits, their people will thrive.

title: The Origin of the Coconut Tree in the Maldives
summary: Maldivian mythology explains the origin of the coconut tree — the nation's most vital resource — through a poignant legend. When the first settlers arrived on the barren coral islands of the Maldives, they found no plants and struggled to survive. Many died, and tragedy struck nearly every family. A sorcerer (fandita man) among the settlers, desperate to save his people, brewed a magical potion and poured it on the growing pile of corpses in the graveyard. After several weeks, green shoots began sprouting from the mouths of the dead. The shoots grew into coconut trees — large dark trees from the bodies of big men, smaller fairer trees from women and children. The sorcerer taught the survivors how to use every part of the tree for food, water, shelter, and oil. The coconut tree spread across the islands, saving the Maldivian people. To this day, Maldivians believe that removing the husk of a coconut reveals a face — a hallmark of their anthropomorphic origin.

title: The Origin of the Horsehead Fiddle (Morin Khuur)
summary: A shepherd named Namjil the Cuckoo from eastern Mongolia was drafted into military service on the western border. He sang so beautifully that people called him Namjil the Cuckoo. During his service, he fell in love with a local prince's daughter, who gave him a magical winged horse to cross the vast distances to meet her. A jealous woman discovered the horse's wings and cut them off, causing the horse to fall from the sky and die. The grieving Namjil made the first horsehead fiddle from the horse's skin, tail hair, and bones, using it to play poignant songs about his beloved horse and lost love. The instrument became the national symbol of Mongolia.

title: The Origin of the Hummingbird
summary: In the time of the Maya, before the great cities fell to jungle, there lived a young warrior named Utz that was the finest in his tribe—strong, swift, brave in battle.

title: The Origin of the Medicine Pipe
summary: A beautiful woman appeared to a Blackfoot man who had gone on a vision quest. She gave him a pipe decorated with eagle feathers and taught him the prayers and songs that went with it. She told him the pipe would be a mediator between the people and the spirit world. When he returned to camp, the elders recognized the pipe's power and established the Medicine Pipe society. The pipe is central to Blackfoot ceremonies, used for healing, making peace, and communicating with Apistotoke. Its keeper must follow strict taboos and conduct annual renewal ceremonies.

title: The Origin of the Stars
summary: A myth explaining the placement of stars in the night sky. It describes a celestial event where fragments of a great spirit or cosmic object were scattered across the heavens. These stars serve as a map for the Inuit, linking the physical world to the ancestral realm and providing direction for navigation across the ice.

title: The Origin of the Sun Dance (Cheyenne)
summary: The Sun Dance was given to the Cheyenne by the culture heroes Sweet Medicine and Erect Horns. Sweet Medicine brought the Sacred Arrows and the structure of the Sun Dance from his journey to the Sacred Mountain. The Sun Dance is held each summer when the tribe gathers to renew their connection to Ma'heo'o. Dancers fast and dance for four days, blowing eagle bone whistles and gazing at the central pole. In the Cheyenne version, dancers are pierced with thongs through their breast muscles as a sacrifice. The ceremony renews the earth, ensures the return of the buffalo, and maintains the harmony of all creation.

title: The Origin of the Thunderbird (Wabanaki)
summary: In the Wabanaki tradition, the Thunderbird was once a great chief who loved his people so much that after his death, the Great Spirit transformed him into a giant bird whose wings make the thunder and whose eyes flash lightning.
