He was given dominion over the sky and tasked with hunting the great horned serpent Weewillmekq (Jipijka'm), who lurked in lakes and devoured people. Whenever the horned serpent rose to attack, the Thunderbird descended from the clouds and struck it with lightning. The Thunderbird had a nest on the highest peak of the mountains, and its eggs were made of solid lightning. The Wabanaki honored the Thunderbird with offerings of tobacco, asking it to bring rain for the crops and to protect them from the underworld monsters.

title: The Origin of the Tiki
summary: In the timeless era before the world was fully awakened, when the heavens and earth were still locked in a cold, silent embrace, there existed a longing for life.

title: The Origin of Throat Singing (Khöömei)
summary: The Tuvan legend explaining the origin of khöömei throat singing, the unique overtone singing technique of the Tuvan people recognized by UNESCO as Intangible Cultural Heritage. According to the myth, long ago a young Tuvan hunter became lost in the Sayan Mountains during a blizzard. Desperate and alone, he began to mimic the sounds of his surroundings — the howling wind, the rushing rivers, and the calls of animals. He discovered that by manipulating his throat and breath, he could produce multiple sounds simultaneously. The mountain spirits were so pleased that they blessed him with this gift to share with his people. Another version says that throat singing was first taught to humans by the spirits of the mountains themselves, who sang the songs of the earth, wind, and water through the human voice. Historically, the practice is deeply connected to Tuvan animism and pastoral life.

title: The Owl Husband (Passamaquoddy)
summary: A beautiful young Passamaquoddy woman was visited each night by a mysterious man who came to her lodge after dark. He was kind and gentle, and she grew to love him, though she had never seen his face clearly. Her parents warned her to discover his identity. One night, she placed ashes near the doorway. When the man left, his footprints showed the marks of an owl's claws. The next night, she hid and watched, and saw her husband transform into a great horned owl and fly away. Heartbroken but determined, she followed him into the forest. The owl tried to keep her as his wife in his tree-home, but she longed for her human family. Finally, the owl released her, but she was never the same — she had seen the spirit world and could not fully return to human life. The story teaches that love between different kinds of beings cannot overcome the fundamental boundaries of nature.

title: The Owl Wife
summary: A young hunter finds a beautiful woman sleeping under an owl skin, but when he steals the skin, she is trapped in human form — and the owls come looking for her.

title: The Painted Skin
summary: In Taiyuan, during the Ming Dynasty, there lived a scholar named Wang. Centers on Demon,  the concepts of absolute evil, temptation, and the consequences of moral failure..

title: The Pale Fox and the Divination Grid
summary: Yurugu the Pale Fox (Ogo), the first being of Dogon creation born from Amma's flawed act, limps across the Sahel on uneven legs as the living embodiment of disorder. Despite his chaotic nature, Yurugu serves a vital purpose in Dogon society through divination. Each night, Dogon diviners draw a rectangular grid in fine sand at the village's edge, placing kola nuts at specific intersections according to the question being asked. The pale fox walks the grid at night, and in the morning the diviner reads the paw-prints to interpret the future. Because Yurugu is the original wound of creation, he knows everything that has gone wrong since, making his tracks truthful. This paradox lies at the heart of Dogon spirituality: disorder, read correctly, becomes a map of truth.

title: The Panchatantra: The Lion and the Rabbit
summary: In a great forest of India, there lived a mighty lion named Dhandara. Centers on Gwyllion,  mountain folklore. Causes disorientation and getting lost - represents dangerous mountain paths..

title: The Panther Deity of the Chaco
summary: A black panther spirit guards the western Chaco, and the farmer who clears its land without offering will find his crops burned by invisible fire.

title: The Papa-Figo of Salvador
summary: A ghoulish figure in a top hat devours the figs — the vital organs — of the living, and only the protection of the orixás can ward it off.

title: The Parikhan Lantern
summary: A ghost who carries a lantern through the mountain fog is said to guide lost travelers home, though those who follow too eagerly may never find their way back.
themes: tests of character in the wilderness
the danger of grasping for salvation

title: The Parson and the Clerk
summary: A miserly parson who refuses charity disguises himself as a tramp to turn away beggars. The clever clerk, also in disguise, torments the parson all night by pretending his corn has been spilled and his cattle let loose, while impersonating the parson to his wife. The terrified parson reforms and becomes generous.

title: The Patasola
summary: A one-legged forest creature lures men into the jungle with the voice of their loved ones.

title: The Pathfinder — Aigin's Revenge
summary: The famous Sámi legend adapted into the 1987 Oscar-nominated film. Circa 1000 AD in Finnmark, a young Sámi man named Aigin returns from hunting to find his family massacred by Chude raiders. He escapes to another Sámi community, but the Chudes follow. The noaidi Raste hides with Aigin but is tortured. Aigin reveals himself, guides the Chudes onto treacherous mountain terrain, tricks them into binding themselves, then cuts free, causing them to fall to their deaths.

title: The Pawnee Capture of the Sacred Arrows
summary: Around 1830, the Cheyenne attacked a Skidi Pawnee hunting party in central Nebraska, carrying their most sacred possession—the Maahótse (Four Sacred Arrows) bundle. During the battle, the Pawnee captured the sacred arrows, described as the greatest disaster in Cheyenne history. The Cheyenne made replica arrows and desperately tried to recover the originals. They recovered one arrow directly from the Pawnee; the Lakota captured another and returned it for horses. The replicas were ceremonially returned to Bear Butte. This loss was believed to have been caused by the people's failure to properly honor the arrows, and it foreshadowed the misfortunes that would come to the Cheyenne.

title: The People Could Fly
summary: In this beloved African American folktale collected by Virginia Hamilton, enslaved Africans secretly retained the magical ability to fly—a power brought from their homeland. One day, as an old man named Toby worked in the cotton fields under a cruel overseer's lash, he began to whisper ancient words in a language the other slaves had forgotten. One by one, the enslaved people remembered the magic of flight. Sarah, carrying her baby on her back, rose into the air. Young Jesse and his mother lifted off. The overseer watched in disbelief as worker after worker soared into the sky. Toby himself flew last, calling the magic words until all who remembered were gone. They flew across the ocean back to Africa, leaving their chains behind. But some chose to stay, their wings clipped by the harshness of bondage, and their descendants tell the story still. The tale expresses the deepest longing of the enslaved: that freedom meant not just escape but miraculous, transcendent return to the ancestral home.

title: The Peri (Fairy Spirits of Persian Myth)
summary: Peris are beautiful, benevolent winged spirits in Persian mythology, originally fallen angels in Zoroastrian tradition who later became more benign in Islamic Persian folklore. They are depicted as exquisite beings who dwell in the lower heavens and enchant humans with their beauty. Peris are locked in eternal conflict with the malevolent Divs (demons), who often capture and imprison them in cages. Unlike divs (who are male), peris are usually female and friendly to humans. Queen of Sheba (Bilqis) is considered offspring of a Chinese emperor and a Peri. The word 'peri' entered English through Thomas Moore's 1817 poem 'Lalla Rookh' ('Paradise and the Peri').

title: The Peri and the Poet
summary: A grieving poet is visited by a Peri, a celestial spirit of Persian-Azerbaijani myth, who offers him a choice between forgetting his sorrow and learning its deeper meaning.

title: the Phujku, the Harvest Demon
summary: A skeletal figure wrapped in dead corn husks stalks the fields at harvest time, draining the life from crops — and only the sound of bells and singing can drive it back to the earth.

title: The Piath of the Baobab Grove
summary: A monstrous Piath haunted the baobab grove near Renk, stealing children who wandered too far from the village, until a clever girl turned its own hunger against it and banished it to the dry wastes beyond the river.

title: The Pied Piper of Hamelin
summary: In the year 1284, the German town of Hamelin suffered a plague unlike any other.

title: The Pig King
summary: A princess must break the enchantment of a pig-like king, learning that true beauty lies within.

title: The Pipe of Peace Treaty
summary: The sacred pipe given by White Buffalo Calf Woman serves as the ultimate symbol of peace among the Lakota. When two warring tribes wished to end hostilities, they would smoke the pipe together. The pipe bowl, made of red stone, represents the earth; the wooden stem represents all that grows upon the earth. The smoke rising carries prayers to Wakan Tanka. To smoke the pipe in ceremony is to pray with and for all the universe. The pipe is pointed to the sky (for the Creator), to the earth (for Grandmother Earth), and to the four directions before smoking. The pipe ceremony remains central to Lakota spirituality.

title: The Pishtaco of the Mountain
summary: A white-skinned stranger with a silver knife appears in mountain villages at night, draining the fat from sleeping farmers — because fat, in Aymara belief, is the substance of the soul.

title: The Plague
summary: In Swedish folk tradition, the devastating plagues were personified as a boy with a rake and a girl with a broom, wandering from village to village. Where the boy raked, some were spared; where the girl swept, death left an empty house. On Soller Island, the plague spirits strewed gold along the roads, but the treasure was so infected that anyone who touched it died before the next sunset.

title: The Plat-Eye
summary: The Plat-Eye is a malevolent, shapeshifting spirit in Gullah Geechee folklore, believed to be the restless ghost of a person who was wronged in life and died with unfinished business. The Plat-Eye takes various forms—an animal with one large glowing eye, a ball of light, or a shadowy figure—and haunts the place of its death or burial. It is intensely territorial and will attack anyone who intrudes upon its domain. Unlike the Boo Hag, which enters homes, the Plat-Eye stays outdoors, lurking in swamps, crossroads, and graveyards. To ward off a Plat-Eye, Gullah people carry a small burlap sachet filled with equal parts gunpowder and sulfur, whose strong smell offends the spirit and drives it away. The Plat-Eye tradition reflects African beliefs in ancestral spirits who require proper burial rites to find peace, combined with the harsh reality of the many enslaved people who died unjustly and were buried in unmarked graves along the Sea Islands coast.

title: The Polar Bear Son
summary: A woman, unable to have children, adopts a polar bear cub. As the cub grows, it develops human intelligence and speech, becoming a protector and companion to the woman. The story emphasizes unconventional family bonds and the deep respect the Inuit hold for the polar bear as a sentient being.

title: The Polkan at the Ridge
summary: A shepherd boy encounters the Polkan shapeshifter on a mountain ridge and survives by offering it neither fear nor aggression, but a riddle it cannot answer without revealing its true form.
themes: the power of riddles and ancient bargains
the boundary between nature and spirit

title: The Poludnitsa in the Wheat
summary: A noonday spirit in a white dress haunts the wheat fields at midday, and the reaper who works through the heat will meet her and never work again.

title: The Pond Spirit Who Danced
summary: A water spirit who lives in a forest pond teaches a lonely boy to dance, and the dance becomes the boy's gift to the village.

title: the Pontianak of the Coast
summary: A Pontianak who haunts the coastal roads of eastern Singapore, appearing as a woman with a baby, because in Singapore the sea and the dead are never far apart.

title: the Pontianak, the Vampire Bride
summary: A beautiful woman in white who appears on lonely roads at night, her long black hair hiding a face that is not a face, because in Singapore beauty is the deadliest weapon.

title: The Poor Devil
summary: When a peasant prays for his cow's protection, God and the Devil argue over who truly controls fate — leading to a wager that reveals the Devil's limitations and God's grace. This tale from Småland is at once humorous and philosophical.

title: The Poor Turkey Girl
summary: A Zuni Cinderella-like story about a poor girl who was mistreated by her community and found companionship among the wild turkeys. The turkeys, taking pity on her, transformed her appearance with beautiful clothing and feathers so she could attend a sacred dance at the village. She danced beautifully and won the heart of a young man, but had to flee before dawn to return the turkeys' gifts. She lost one of her turkey-feather garments, which the young man used to find her. However, when the turkeys discovered she had not properly thanked them or kept her promises, they abandoned her and took back their gifts. The girl was left with nothing, learning that ingratitude and broken promises have consequences. The story teaches Zuni values of humility, gratitude, and keeping one's word.

title: The Porcupine and the Beaver (Tsimshian)
summary: This Tsimshian myth from the William Beynon collection tells of a time when animals spoke like human beings and possessed great powers to change the weather. Porcupine and Beaver, two animal-people, had a contest of abilities that determined their roles in the world. Porcupine demonstrated his cleverness and defensive capabilities, while Beaver showed his industrious nature and engineering skills. The story carries important teachings about using one's natural gifts wisely and respecting the different abilities of others. It is also an etiological tale explaining the physical characteristics and behaviors of both porcupines and beavers. Porcupine's quills and Beaver's tail receive supernatural explanations in the narrative. Recorded by William Beynon, a Tsimshian ethnographer who worked with Franz Boas, this story represents one of the many animal-person tales that convey moral teachings while explaining the natural world.

title: The Prairie-Dogs and Their Priest the Burrowing-Owl
summary: A Zuni story about a village of Prairie-dogs who were suffering from a drought. They held a council and decided to ask their grandfather, the Burrowing-owl who lived on top of their mountain, for help. The Burrowing-owl, a powerful priest, agreed to intercede with the rain gods. He collected a foul-smelling beetle and instructed his wife to cook beans. He placed the beetle and beans in a bag and climbed to the top of his mountain. As the storm clouds gathered, the Owl struck the bag with a stick, releasing such a terrible odor that even the Rain-gods themselves fled in retreat. The clouds scattered and the sky cleared. The Prairie-dogs emerged from their holes and cheered their grandfather, the Burrowing-owl. The story explains why burrowing-owls make their nests in prairie-dog holes — they have been friends ever since. The Burrowing-owl's control over the weather demonstrates the Zuni belief that spiritual power can reside in unexpected beings.

title: The Prince and the Princess in the Forest
summary: A romantic tale of two lovers separated by tragic circumstances and reunited through magic and enduring love in a mystical forest setting.

title: The Princess and the Glass Mountain
summary: A princess sits atop a treacherous glass mountain, and the man who can ride to the top wins her hand — a poor boy with a magic horse succeeds where knights fail. The princess is a relative of Brunhilde of Germanic heroic legend, and the tale is very popular across the North.

title: The Princess and the Pea
summary: Once upon a time, in a kingdom of rolling green hills and turreted castles, there lived a prince who searched the world for a true princess to marry.

title: The Princess in the Chest
summary: A tale of a princess hidden away in a chest for her safety, and the subsequent quest by a brave hero to find and rescue her.

title: The Princess on the Glass Hill
summary: A determined young man seeks to win the hand of a princess who resides atop an impenetrable glass hill. Through his bravery, wit, and the help of magical entities, he overcomes the obstacles and ascends the hill to claim his bride.

title: The Psoglav of the Unmarked Graves
summary: A monstrous hound with a human face and a single eye in its forehead feeds on the forgotten dead buried without crosses, and those who hear its digging at night know which graves the village tried to erase.

title: the Psoglav, the One-Eyed Dog
summary: A creature with a dog's body, a human face, and a single eye in the center of its forehead that feeds on the dead in unmarked graves — because in Montenegro, some graves are unmarked for a reason.

title: The Pueblo Emergence from the Underworld
summary: A central Pueblo creation theme across multiple Pueblo tribes (Acoma, Zuni, Hopi, Laguna, etc.) involves the emergence of the first people from the underworld through a sacred opening called the sipapu. In the beginning, the people lived in darkness beneath the earth. Guided by spirits, culture heroes, or twin war gods, they climbed up through four underground worlds, each representing a stage of development. They used a giant reed, spruce tree, or ladder to ascend. As they climbed, they transformed from insect-like or unfinished beings into fully formed humans. The last people to emerge were often an old man and woman who became trapped, becoming the rulers of the underworld — establishing that all must return there after death. The sipapu is often identified with the Grand Canyon or a specific location within each Pueblo's traditional territory.

title: The Pueblo Hero Twins
summary: In Pueblo mythology, the Twin War Gods (Masewi and Oyoyewi in some traditions) are the most important heroic figures. They were born to a virgin mother who conceived from the Sun, much like the Navajo Hero Twins. These twins are credited with creating the world and all living creatures, as well as slaying a giant monster that terrorized the Pueblo people — a beast so large it could eat entire villages in one bite. The twins tracked the monster and killed it with their magical weapons, which included lightning arrows and shields. They established the directions, brought order to the world, and taught the people how to live. After completing their work, they returned to the underworld but continue to watch over the Pueblo people. They are often celebrated in ritual performances and dances, reinforcing their cultural significance as protectors and culture heroes.

title: The Qalupalik
summary: A humanoid sea creature with green skin and long fingernails drags children who wander too close to the ice edge beneath the water.

title: The Queen
summary: Queen Adelgunda possesses a remarkable gift: she can see into the hearts of men. This power makes her a wise and just ruler, but it also creates complications. When the noble Sigmund — whom the queen secretly loves — is accused of dishonorable intentions, the queen's gift suggests his guilt. To save Sigmund from the dishonor that her veiled judgment implies, Adelgunda must make a painful choice: reveal her own love for him, risking her reputation and position, or allow an innocent man to be condemned. The story follows the queen's internal struggle as she balances her public duty with her private heart. In a climactic moment, she chooses love and truth over safety and appearances, baring her soul to save the man she loves. The story is notable for its psychological depth and focus on a female protagonist who holds real power and must navigate complex emotional and political terrain. Anna Wahlenberg, who wrote over 200 fairy tales, was known for embedding social commentary and feminist themes in her stories. 'The Queen' exemplifies her ability to combine traditional fairy tale enchantment with nuanced human emotion, portraying a ruler whose supernatural gift becomes a burden that only love can truly overcome.

title: The Queen Bee
summary: Two kings' sons once set out on a grand adventure, but they fell into wild and reckless ways and never returned home.

title: The Queen's Necklace
summary: The cruel King Hendrik possesses a necklace of one hundred perfect pearls. He forces his nephew to find him a wife, and the kind Blanzeflor is chosen. On their wedding day, the king fastens the pearls around her neck with a threat: the day she is found without them will be her last. Blanzeflor, trapped in a cold marriage, gives away the pearls one by one to help the needy. When the king discovers the necklace is gone, he sentences her to death, but the birds she befriended rescue her and tear the wicked king to pieces.

title: The Quilting Party Ghost
summary: A classic Gullah ghost story set in the Sea Islands of Georgia. A group of women gathered for a quilting party at an old cabin on St. Helena Island. As they worked on the quilt by lantern light, they told stories to pass the night. An old woman named Sarah, whose grandmother had been enslaved on the plantation before the Civil War, told them about the cabin's history. It was said that a young enslaved woman named Liza had died there, waiting for her husband who had been sold away. As Sarah finished the story, the women heard footsteps on the porch. The door creaked open, and a young woman in an old-fashioned dress stood there, looking at the quilting frame. The women froze, recognizing the description Sarah had just given. The ghost smiled sadly, touched the quilt, and vanished. After that night, the women always left a piece of blue fabric—haint blue—in the quilt pattern to protect the cabin. The story reflects the Gullah belief that ghosts are often not malevolent but are ancestral presences who remain connected to the places and activities they loved in life.

title: The Rabbit Trickster (Chickasaw)
summary: Chukfi (or Chokfi), the Rabbit, is the trickster figure in Chickasaw folklore. Rabbit is clever, mischievous, and always getting into trouble, but he also uses his wits to benefit the people. In one story, Rabbit outwits the wolves by pretending to be dead and then escaping when they are not looking. In another, he tricks the larger animals into letting him share their food. Rabbit's adventures explain many natural phenomena, such as why Rabbit has a short tail, why the possum's tail is bare, and why the deer has antlers. Though Rabbit is often selfish and deceitful, his cleverness is admired, and his stories teach important lessons about the consequences of pride, greed, and dishonesty. Listeners are encouraged to laugh at Rabbit's antics while learning from his mistakes.

title: The Rabbit Trickster of the Kongo
summary: Among the Kongo, the rabbit (sometimes called Nsumunu) is the greatest of all tricksters, smaller than nearly every other creature but cleverer than them all. In the most famous tale, Rabbit grew tired of drinking from muddy puddles while the great elephant and hippo drank from the clear river. Rabbit challenged them to a tug-of-war, tying one end of a rope around elephant's trunk and the other around hippo's tail, then hiding in the bushes and shouting 'Pull!' The two giants pulled against each other for hours, each believing Rabbit was on the other end, until they collapsed from exhaustion. Rabbit then calmly walked to the river and drank his fill. Chief Leopard, furious at Rabbit's trickery, tried to catch and eat him, but Rabbit always escaped — hiding in thorn bushes Leopard could not enter or using honey to glue Leopard's paws together. The Rabbit stories teach that intelligence and wit will always overcome brute force.

title: The Race of Good and Evil
summary: After the world was made, Good and Evil existed as two brothers. Evil constantly spoiled Good's work, making stony places and poisonous fruits. Good decided to destroy Evil. He proposed a race, and each brother had to reveal his greatest fear. Evil feared buck's horns; Good feared braided Indian grass. Evil filled Good's path with braided grass, which Good chewed for strength when he tired. Good filled Evil's path with deer antlers. Evil struggled badly, tripping and falling. When Evil begged to stop, Good refused. Toward evening, Evil collapsed. Good took buck's horns and killed him. But Evil's spirit returned and spoke with their grandmother, who loved Evil. Evil declared he would go to the northwest land where those who follow him never return, condemning death upon the world. From that day, Good ruled the living and Evil ruled the dead, and the cycle of life and death was established forever.

title: The Rain Princess of the Sotho
summary: Sotho oral tradition tells of a rain princess who possessed the power to control the weather and bring fertility to the land. In times of drought, the Sotho people would perform ceremonies to honor the rain princess and her connection to Modimo, the supreme god. The princess was both a spiritual figure and a political leader, embodying the link between the people and the divine forces that governed their agricultural existence. Her ability to summon rain was tied to strict ritual observances, and any breach of tradition could result in devastating drought. This figure reflects the central importance of rain in the semi-arid highlands of southern Africa, where water determined survival.

title: The Rainbow Serpent and the Creation of the Land
summary: The Rainbow Serpent (known by many names across Australia including Julunggul, Kunmanggur, and Wagyl) is one of the most widespread and significant creator beings in Aboriginal Australian mythology. In the Dreamtime, the great Rainbow Serpent traveled across the land, creating rivers, gorges, mountains, and waterholes as she moved. She emerged from the ground after sleeping beneath the earth and her journey shaped the landscape into its present form. She gave life to plants and animals, established the laws for human society, and taught the people how to live properly. The Rainbow Serpent is associated with rain, water, fertility, and regeneration, but also with danger. She can punish those who break the law with floods, lightning, and storms. The Rainbow Serpent remains present in deep waterholes and continues to protect sacred sites.

title: The Rainbow Snake
summary: The great creator serpent of Aboriginal Australian mythology who shaped the land and rivers.

title: The Rainmaker of the Kalahari
summary: In the shimmering, amber expanses of the Kalahari, where the horizon trembles in the heat and the earth is a mosaic of cracked clay, rain is not merely weather—it is the difference between existence and extinction.

title: The Raven and the Whale
summary: A Chukchi story from the Kuutkh cycle describing how the Raven creator interacted with the primordial whale. In this tale, Kuutkh encounters a giant whale that threatens the newly created world. Through a combination of trickery and negotiation, the Raven convinces the whale to accept boundaries for its territory, establishing the separation of sea and land. The whale becomes the ruler of the ocean while the Raven takes dominion over the land and sky. This myth establishes the cosmological order of the Chukchi world, explaining why whales remain in the ocean and ravens on land. It reflects the importance of both reindeer herding (inland) and sea mammal hunting (coastal) in Chukchi subsistence.

title: The Re-Creation of the Sacred Mountains
summary: After emerging into the Fourth World, First Man, First Woman, Water Sprinkler, and Black God re-created the six sacred mountains from dirt First Man had brought from the Third World. They placed Sisnaajiní (Blanca Peak) in the East, decorated with white shells, white lightning, white corn, and dark clouds for male rain. They placed Tsoodził (Mount Taylor) in the South, adorned with turquoise, dark mist, animals, and light clouds for female rain. Dookʼoʼoosłííd (San Francisco Peaks) in the West received abalone shell and yellow corn. Dibé Nitsaa (Hesperus Mountain) in the North was covered with black beads and heavy rain. At each mountain they created resident deities — Rock Crystal Boy and Girl at Sisnaajiní, Turquoise Boy and Corn Girl at Tsoodził, and others at each sacred peak.

title: The Red Cloak
summary: In the old days of the Crusades, when Christian knights traveled to the Holy Land to fight what they were told were enemies of the faith, there was a knight of Brittany called Sir Guillaume le Rouge—William the Red.

title: The Red Headband of Grande Comore
summary: A fisherman discovers that the forest spirits wear crimson headbands to mark those they have chosen to protect, and learns that the boundary between the human world and the spirit world is thinner than the strand of a fishing net.

title: The Red Robin of Wales
summary: A small bird endures the fires of hell to bring comfort to suffering souls, becoming an eternal symbol of compassion and hope.

title: The Red Shoes
summary: There was once a little girl named Karen, pretty and delicate, but so poor that she wore wooden shoes in winter that chafed her ankles raw.

title: The Release of the Buffalo (Arapaho)
summary: In the time before buffalo roamed the plains, all the buffalo were confined in a cave beneath a mountain, guarded by a powerful spirit. The Arapaho people had only small game and were often hungry. A young man on a vision quest learned from a mouse spirit that the buffalo were hidden underground. With the help of various small animals, he found the cave entrance. Using songs given by the mouse spirit, he opened the cave. The buffalo stampeded out, covering the plains. The guard spirit, angry at the release, cursed the Arapaho to always need the buffalo, but also blessed them that the buffalo would always provide.

title: The Release of the Wild Animals
summary: In the beginning, all wild animals were confined in a great underground cavern by a spirit who wanted to protect them. The Comanche people had only dogs and horses. A brave warrior followed a trail to the cavern entrance and heard the stamping and snorting of many animals within. With the help of the wind spirit, he opened the cavern door. Out rushed deer, antelope, elk, bears, wolves, and mountain lions, spreading across the plains. The warrior was nearly trampled but survived. The spirit, angry at the release, caused some animals to become dangerous to humans, while others remained gentle.

title: The Riddle of the Mountain Troll
summary: A traveler is captured by a mountain troll who agrees to let him go only if he can solve three impossible riddles. The traveler uses his wit and knowledge of the natural world to outsmart the troll, proving that intelligence is more powerful than brute strength.

title: The Ride of the Wild Hunt
summary: During the darkest nights of winter, the sky is filled with the screams of the Wild Hunt. Led by a ghostly chieftain or Odin himself, the hunt consists of spirits and hounds that gallop across the clouds. Those caught in the path of the hunt are swept away to the spirit realm forever.

title: The Ring
summary: A young prince rides out in the moonlight and finds a tiny ring by the shore — a delicate band with blue stones arranged like a forget-me-not flower. He picks it up and puts it in his pocket. The ring belongs to a captive princess who, as a child, was taken from her mountain castle when a foreign conqueror killed her father and imprisoned her. Now, the foreign prince wants to marry her, but he is a coarse, giant-like brute. Desperate to escape, the princess had thrown the ring into the river as a plea for help, following a spell her mother taught her. The ring leads the prince to her. Meanwhile, a mountain troll has also been pursuing the princess, intending to eat her (keeping her fattened up for years). When the prince discovers the princess imprisoned in the troll's mountain domain, he must face both the mountain troll and the foreign prince to free her. He and the princess escape on his horse, with the mountain troll bellowing after them like a pack of wolves. They ride through forests and across rivers until they reach the prince's castle. The story is notable for its romantic opening (described as having 'a perfect fairy tale first line') and its layered conflicts — the innocent ring, the captive princess, the hungry troll, and the prince's steadfast pursuit of love and justice. John Bauer's illustration of the knight riding with the princess is one of his most famous works.

title: The Riri Yaksha and Suniyam Sorcery Legends
summary: The Riri Yaksha (Blood Demon) is one of the most feared demonic figures in Sinhalese folklore, central to the Bali and Tovil exorcism traditions. According to legend, Riri Yaksha was born from the blood of a slain demon, possessing enormous power and an insatiable thirst. The Suniyam demon, associated with sorcery and black magic, is believed to be a Yaksha who once served the god Vishnu but was cursed. Sinhalese folklore describes Suniyam as the chief of all demons governing disease, misfortune, and madness. The Tovil ritual, involving elaborate masks, drumming, and dances, is performed to exorcise these malevolent spirits. These Yakshas are neither purely evil nor good — they can be both disease-bringers and protectors when properly propitiated.

title: The Rise of the Kraken
summary: Sailors in the north often reported seeing a massive island of skerries emerging from the sea. In reality, this was the Kraken, a colossal cephalopod. The creature creates massive whirlpools as it sinks back into the depths, dragging entire ships down with it in a swirl of tentacles and foam.

title: The Rival Suitors
summary: Several heroes of Kalevala, including Wainamoinen and Lemminkainen, compete for the hand of the Daughter of Pohjola. The competition is characterized by a mixture of physical strength and magical ingenuity, as each hero attempts to prove themselves the most worthy suitor.

title: The River-Shutter of Delagoa
summary: When a greedy fisherman begins taking more from the bay of Delagoa than he returns, the great water spirit Kambujanu rises to teach him the difference between harvest and theft.

title: The Roc
summary: There are birds, and then there is the Roc. Centers on Roc,  from Saudi Arabia mythology. Known for nature manipulation and animal communication and wind control..

title: The Rolling Calf
summary: One of Jamaica's most feared duppies, the Rolling Calf appears as a massive jet-black bull with blazing red eyes that gash fire, dragging heavy chains that clank and spark as it moves. It haunts lonely roads, bridle paths through cane fields, and crossroads at night. The Rolling Calf is believed to be the restless spirit of a wicked person — often a cruel butcher or a brutal plantation overseer from slavery days. To escape, one must lie flat in a ditch off the road, scratch a cross in the earth, throw a garment as a decoy, or carry protective herbs like vervain. The legend transforms the chains of slavery into a supernatural symbol of guilt that can be outwitted.

title: The Rolling Calf of St. Joseph
summary: A monstrous bull with a chain of fire around its neck roams the roads at night, chasing down those who break their word or cruelty to animals.

title: The Rolling Stone Legend (Cheyenne)
summary: A Cheyenne boy was left in camp while the adults went hunting. A mysterious rolling stone appeared and began chasing him. The boy ran for his life, but the stone rolled faster and faster, crushing everything in its path. The boy encountered various animals who tried to help—a magpie pecked at the stone, a badger dug a hole for the boy to hide—but none could stop the pursuing boulder. Finally, a wise old turtle advised the boy to climb a certain tree. When the stone rolled under the tree, a branch caught it and held it fast. The boy was saved, and the stone remains there to this day.

title: The Rooster of Barcelinhos
summary: On the West African coast, in the dense mangrove swamps and lagoons of Nigeria, there is a spirit that every fisherman knows.

title: The Rooster, the Hand-Mill and the Swarm of Hornets
summary: A poor peasant trades a pig for three seemingly worthless gifts — a rooster, a hand-mill, and a hornets' nest — but each proves invaluable when he outwits a greedy innkeeper. The gold-laying rooster is a widely known international folktale motif.

title: The Rusalka of Lake Ilmen
summary: A drowned maiden haunts the waters of Lake Ilmen, singing songs that lure fishermen to their deaths during the green weeks of spring.

title: The Russian Fortress of Bomarsund – A Cursed Ruin
summary: The unfinished fortress of Bomarsund, built by Russia between 1832 and 1854, is one of Åland's most evocative historical sites. Local folklore holds that the fortress was cursed from the start — built on ground that was never meant to be fortified. Thousands of laborers, prisoners, and soldiers worked on the project, which was to be the largest construction in Åland's history. But in August 1854, during the Crimean War, an Anglo-French fleet destroyed the fortress in just three and a half days. The defeat led to the demilitarization of Åland (which remains in effect today). Folk tradition speaks of strange lights seen among the ruins, ghostly Russian soldiers still marching their posts, and the phantom sounds of construction echoing from the hills. The nearby hilltop Djävulsberget ('Devil's Mountain') takes its name from the folklore surrounding the site. The Bomarsund legend exemplifies how a historical event became woven into the supernatural fabric of Åland's folk tradition.

title: The Saci Who Stole the Wind
summary: A one-legged trickster with a red cap steals the wind from a village, and only a clever grandmother with a pair of scissors can catch him.

title: The Sacred Drum of the Luba Realm
summary: According to Luba tradition, the first sacred drum was given to the people by the spirit of the forest. It was said to have the voice of the ancestors, and its beat could be heard across the entire kingdom. The drum contained the soul of the Luba nation — as long as it beat, the kingdom would endure. The Luba kings (mulopwe) kept the sacred drum in a special house guarded by initiated priests. The drum was played only during coronations, royal funerals, and times of great crisis. Its rhythm was a coded language that announced the king's health, the coming of war, or the death of a ruler. When the Belgians colonized the Congo, the last sacred drum was hidden in the forest to prevent its capture. Some say it still beats deep in the Katanga forest, preserving the spiritual heartbeat of the Luba kingdom. The drum represents the continuity of Luba royal power and the connection between the living rulers and their ancestral predecessors.

title: The Sacred Groves of the Chaga
summary: The Chaga people maintain sacred groves (mshitu) on the slopes of Kilimanjaro, patches of virgin forest that are never cut or farmed. According to tradition, these groves are the dwelling places of the mountain spirits (warimu) who protect the Chaga people. The largest and most sacred grove is said to be where Ruwa himself first touched the mountain. Within these groves, the trees are never felled, the animals are never hunted, and only initiated elders may enter. The groves serve as the burial grounds for chiefs (Mangi) and as sites for the most important ceremonies. When a child is born, a tree is planted in the family's grove; when a person dies, their spirit returns to the grove to join the ancestors. The Mangi (chief) is responsible for ensuring the groves remain untouched. The Chaga believe that if the sacred groves are ever destroyed, Ruwa's protection will leave Kilimanjaro and the mountain's glaciers will finally melt, ending the Chaga people's special bond with the great mountain.

title: The Sacred Pipe (Blackfoot)
summary: The Blackfoot believe the sacred pipe was given to them by the Thunder spirit, who taught them the songs and rituals for its use. A man once heard thunder and saw a lightning-struck tree. Where the lightning had struck, he found a beautifully carved pipe. The Thunder spirit spoke to him, instructing him to form a society of pipe keepers. The pipe would be used for healing, peace-making, and communicating with the spirit world. The Blackfoot Medicine Pipe ceremony involves elaborate rituals, the smoking of the pipe, and the offering of prayers to Apistotoke for the well-being of the people.

title: The Sacred Sieidi Stones
summary: Legends about sieidis—unusual rock formations considered sacred dwelling places of spirits. Each family had its local sieidi. Offerings of reindeer meat, antlers, and fish were made for hunting luck and protection. The Storjunkare were stones resembling humans or animals, set up on mountain tops. They had power over all animals, fish, and birds. Reindeer were sacrificed at these sites.

title: the Saka, the Possessing Spirit
summary: A spirit that attaches itself to a family line, growing stronger with each generation, demanding offerings that escalate from flowers to blood, because in Singapore some debts are inherited.

title: The Saltvik Runestone – Serpent of the Norse Sea
summary: The Saltvik runestone is a second significant Viking-age monument on Åland, located in the Saltvik parish north of Mariehamn. Like the Jomala stone, it is carved with runic inscriptions in the Younger Futhark, its serpentine bands curling like waves around the ancient alphabet. The stone marks the connection between Åland's Viking-era settlers and the wider Norse world, commemorating voyages, kinship, and courage. In local folk belief, runestones were not mere memorials but living objects with spiritual power. Some Åland traditions held that runestones could speak at midnight, or that they protected the land from evil spirits. The Saltvik stone, in particular, is associated with the legend of the Devil's Dance — the parish church at Saltvik being the home of the priest's wife who allegedly danced with the Devil at Bomarsund.

title: The Sampo Lost In the Sea
summary: During the fierce struggle to escape Pohjola, the Sampo is broken into pieces and falls into the sea. While the main machine is lost, fragments of the Sampo wash ashore, continuing to bring wealth and luck to the land of Kalevala.

title: The Sand Jinn and the Lost Son
summary: A young Soninke boy separated from his family during a sandstorm is found by a sand jinn who offers him safe passage in exchange for a piece of his memory.

title: The Sausage
summary: A mysterious lady borrows a woman's brewing pan and grants her three wishes in return. Eager to please her hungry husband, the woman wishes for a sausage—then her angry husband wishes it stuck to her nose. Their last wish must be used to remove it.

title: The Sayona Who Watched from the River
summary: A beautiful woman lures unfaithful men to the riverbank at dusk, then tears away her skin to reveal a white skeleton that demands they confess their sins before dawn.

title: The Scorpion Spirit of the Chokwe
summary: A scorpion spirit punishes a greedy chief who hoards the harvest, teaching the Chokwe people that generosity is the price of leadership and sting is the cost of selfishness.

title: the Sea Beast of Raouche
summary: A creature that lurks in the caves beneath the Raouche Rocks, emerging only during storms to pull fishermen beneath the waves — because Beirut's most famous landmark hides Beirut's most dangerous secret.

title: The Sea Draugr – Ghost of Drowned Sailors
summary: In the Nordic maritime tradition that extends to Åland, the draugr or sea draug is the restless spirit of a drowned sailor. It appears as a figure in oilskins with a head of seaweed, sailing in half a boat. The sea draugr serves as an omen of impending drowning: if a fisherman sees the draug or hears its cries, his own vessel is likely to be lost. The draugr could be placated with offerings — in the old Christmas tradition, beer was left out as 'draug-beer' to keep these spirits from becoming malicious. For Åland, where seafaring has been the backbone of life for thousands of years and where entire communities have lost men to the sea, the draugr legend gave voice to collective grief and the ever-present danger of the Baltic. The tradition of leaving offerings at sea cairns on islands like Eckerö and Geta connects to this belief in appeasing the drowned.

title: The Sea Draugr's Warning
summary: The Sea Draugr is the spirit of a man who drowned at sea, appearing as a pale, bloated corpse with a head made of seaweed. He wanders the coastlines during storms, calling out to sailors and attempting to lure them into the surf to join him in the freezing depths of the ocean.

title: The Sea Island Creation Frog
summary: In Gullah Geechee creation folklore, the frog was one of the first creatures and played a crucial role in shaping the Sea Islands. The story tells that in the beginning, there was only water everywhere. The Creator needed someone to dive to the bottom and bring up mud to make land. All the big animals tried and failed—they could not hold their breath long enough to reach the bottom. Finally, the little green frog volunteered. The big animals laughed at him, but the frog dove down, down, down, past the fish, past the whales, to the very bottom of the ocean. He scooped up a mouthful of mud and kicked his way back up. When he surfaced, the Creator took the mud from the frog's mouth and formed the Sea Islands. As a reward, the frog was allowed to live both in water and on land and to sing the loudest song of any creature at dawn. This pourquoi tale explains both the origin of the Gullah homeland and why frogs sing so loudly at daybreak, connecting the Gullah people's deep sense of place with the natural world around them.

title: The Sea Nymph
summary: One night on the northwest shores of the island of Gotland, fishermen sleeping in a hut see a white, dew-besprinkled woman's hand reaching through the door. They recognize it as a sea nymph seeking to destroy them, and pretend to be asleep. The next day, a young, newly married man from Kinnar in Lummelund joins them. He boasts that had he been present, he would have taken the hand. That night, a plump white arm with a beautiful hand reaches in. True to his word, the young man seizes it. Instantly, he is drawn silently out through the door and disappears. Despite an extensive search, he is not found. Three years pass, and his wife, having mourned him as dead, is persuaded to remarry. On the evening of her wedding, a stranger enters the cottage — it is her first husband, returned. He explains that he was dragged down to the sea nymph's pearly halls, where he forgot his former life completely. Only that morning, the sea nymph told him 'There will be a dusting out in Kinnar this evening,' meaning his wife's wedding. His memory returned, and he begged to see her. The sea nymph allowed him to go but forbade him from entering the house. Unable to resist, he entered anyway. A great tempest immediately rose, tearing off half the roof. The man fell sick and died three days later. The legend, collected by Herman Hofberg in 'Swedish Fairy Tales' (1890), is a classic cautionary tale about the dangers of supernatural beings, the consequences of arrogance, and the irrevocable nature of bargains made with otherworldly powers.

title: The Sea Spirit Tolk
summary: A Nivkh legend about Tol (or Tolk), the powerful sea spirit who governs the waters around Sakhalin Island and the Sea of Okhotsk. Tolk is a massive creature that controls the movement of fish, the intensity of storms, and the success of sea mammal hunts. Before embarking on sea voyages, Nivkh hunters and fishermen would make offerings to Tolk — throwing tobacco, food, and sacred objects into the sea to ensure his favor. Tolk could appear as a giant sea serpent, a whale of impossible size, or a terrifying humanoid figure rising from the waves. If angered, Tolk would capsize boats, hide fish from nets, and send storms to punish the community. The spirit is associated with the cycle of the seasons, as Tolk's moods shift with the ice and currents of the northern Pacific. Shamanic rituals were performed to divine Tolk's will.

title: The Sea Wolf (Wasgo) (Haida)
summary: Wasgo the Sea Wolf is a powerful supernatural being in Haida mythology, a creature that combines the features of a wolf and a whale. He possesses the strength of both land and sea animals and serves as an important crest figure for Haida clans. In the narratives, Wasgo descends from a supernatural lineage and mediates between the ocean and forest worlds. He appears in Haida art as a composite creature with a wolf's head and body but with the fins and tail of a killer whale, often depicted with exaggerated features indicating supernatural power. Wasgo stories teach about the fluid boundaries between animal species in the Haida worldview and the power that comes from understanding both the land and sea. The sea wolf is considered one of the most potent supernatural helpers a person could receive.

title: The Secret World of the Huldufólk
summary: The Huldufólk, or Hidden People, are a race of elegant and powerful beings who live inside the rocks and mountains. They are generally peaceful but can be vengeful if their homes are disturbed. Many roads in Iceland are diverted to avoid disturbing these unseen neighbors and their dwellings.

title: The Sedna Hunter's Wife
summary: A Cree hunter's wife is taken by the wind and must navigate the spirit world to return home, aided by the animals she once cared for.

title: The Selkie Bride
summary: A man steals the skin of a seal-woman to make her his wife, but learns that a love born of theft can never truly hold a spirit of the sea.

title: The Selkie Wife
summary: A solitary man captures a selkie's skin to force her into marriage, discovering that love built on captivity can never truly replace the pull of the ocean.

title: The Selkie's Stolen Skin
summary: A group of selkies, seal-people who can shed their skins to become human, visit the shore to dance. A man steals one of the skins, preventing a female selkie from returning to the sea. He forces her to marry him, and though she lives as a human for years, she eventually finds her skin and returns to the ocean.

title: The Separation of the Hmong Clans
summary: According to Hmong oral tradition, in the earliest times all Hmong people belonged to a single clan and lived together in harmony. But as the population grew, disputes arose, and it became impossible for everyone to live under one roof. The ancestors sought divine guidance and were told in a vision that the people must separate into different clans (xeem), each with its own name, taboos, and responsibilities. The myth recounts the founding of the original 18 Hmong clans, including the most prominent ones: Vang, Yang, Her, Lee, Xiong, Moua, Thao, Vue, Chang, Kue, Kong, Fang, Hang, Cheng, Cha, Chue, Vue, and Lor. Each clan was assigned a specific totem or animal taboo — for example, some clans must not eat the meat of a particular animal associated with their origin. The separation was marked by a sacred ceremony where each group took a piece of the ancestral hearth fire to start their own. The clans were also given their original surnames, which remain patrilineal in Hmong society. The myth establishes the clan system as divinely ordained, explains the exogamous marriage rules (Hmong cannot marry within their own clan), and provides the foundation for Hmong social organization. The 18 clans spread across southern China, Laos, Vietnam, and Thailand, maintaining their distinct identities while remaining one people through the shared clan system.

title: The Separation of Women and Men
summary: In Navajo mythology, First Woman boasted that women could live without men, claiming she thanked her vagina for the deer First Man brought. Enraged, First Man led all men and the two hermaphrodite twins across the river to the north bank. For four years, the sexes lived apart. Women tried to satisfy themselves with bones, feathers, and long stones, while men used animal livers. The people suffered and longed for each other. Owl warned that the separation was wrong and that monsters would be born from it — and indeed, from the women's unnatural acts, monsters were conceived that later terrorized the people. Finally, First Man called across the river, they reconciled, and the people reunited on rafts, resuming their lives together with restored harmony.

title: The Seri Gumum Dragon of Tasik Chini
summary: Malaysia's answer to the Loch Ness Monster: Seri Gumum is a legendary dragon (naga) said to dwell in the depths of Tasik Chini in Pahang, a pristine lake surrounded by ancient rainforest. According to Orang Asli legend, the dragon was once a princess transformed into a serpentine guardian of the lake's mystical waters. Fishermen speak of seeing a massive serpentine creature with golden scales breaching the surface, especially during storms. The dragon is considered a protector rather than a menace — harming the lake's ecosystem is believed to invoke its wrath. Local stories tell of the dragon surfacing on full moons and during times of great change or crisis in the region.

title: The Serpent of the Sea (Kolowisi)
summary: A Zuni legend about Kolowisi, the great horned water serpent that lives in the sacred lake. A maiden from Zuni went to the lake and was seen by Kolowisi, who took her as his bride beneath the waters. She lived with the serpent in his underwater home, where there was no light but she was treated well and given abundance. The people mourned her loss and held ceremonies to bring her back. Eventually, Kolowisi allowed her to return to the surface, but she was transformed and carried spiritual power from her time in the serpent's realm. She brought knowledge of healing ceremonies and water-songs back to the Zuni people. Kolowisi is generally a benevolent figure, associated with water, fertility, and the life-giving forces of the natural world. The serpent's horn symbolizes power, and offerings are made to Kolowisi during ceremonies asking for rain.

title: The Serpent Rainbow Ayida-Weddo (Fon/Dahomey)
summary: Ayida-Weddo is the rainbow serpent, the androgynous cosmic serpent who supports the world. According to Fon cosmology, the universe is held up by Ayida-Weddo, who coils beneath the earth and stretches into the sky as the rainbow. When the serpent moves beneath the ocean, it causes earthquakes and tidal waves. Ayida-Weddo is also known as Damballa in Haitian Vodou, where it is revered as the ancestral spirit of wisdom and the connection between heaven and earth. The serpent sheds its skin as a symbol of rebirth and eternal renewal. In Dahomean art, Ayida-Weddo is often depicted as a double rainbow serpent, representing the union of the celestial and earthly realms. Offerings of white cloth and eggs are made to appease the great serpent.

title: The Seven Foals
summary: Three brothers attempt to win a princess by watching seven magical foals for a day. While the elder brothers are lazy and fail, the youngest, Boots, discovers the foals' true identity as princes and helps them break a curse.

title: The Seven Hanging Poems (Mu'allaqat)
summary: A collection of seven long pre-Islamic Arabic poems considered the finest examples of ancient Arabian poetry, traditionally said to have been written in gold on Coptic linen and hung from the Kaaba in Mecca. The seven poets are Imru' al-Qais, Tarafa, Zuhayr, Labid, Antarah, Amr ibn Kulthum, and Harith ibn Hilliza. Each poem exemplifies the qasida form with themes of love (nasib), desert journeys, tribal boasting, and moral wisdom. The Mu'allaqat represent the pinnacle of pre-Islamic oral tradition and served as the linguistic and literary benchmark for subsequent Arabic poetry.

title: The Seven Reindeer of the Sky
summary: A Nenets celestial myth about seven magical reindeer that traverse the sky, forming the constellation that guides Nenets reindeer herders on their seasonal migrations. According to the legend, the seven reindeer were originally earthly animals belonging to a great shaman who could fly. When the shaman ascended to the sky to negotiate with Num for better conditions for his people, the reindeer followed him and were transformed into stars. Their yearly path across the heavens marks the seasons for the Nenets — when they appear in the east, spring is coming; when they are overhead during the longest nights, winter has reached its peak. The story also emphasizes the sacred status of the number seven in Nenets culture.

title: The Seven Sacred Rites
summary: White Buffalo Calf Woman gave the Lakota people the Seven Sacred Rites that would guide their spiritual life. The rites are: 1) Keeping of the Soul (preserving the spirit of the deceased for a year before release); 2) The Purification Rite (sweat lodge ceremony for cleansing); 3) Crying for a Vision (vision quest for guidance); 4) The Sun Dance (annual renewal ceremony with sacrifice and dancing); 5) The Making of Relatives (adoption ceremony); 6) The Girls Coming of Age (womanhood ceremony); and 7) The Throwing of the Ball (symbolizing the Creator's love). Each rite uses the sacred pipe given by the White Buffalo Calf Woman.

title: The Seven Sisters (Pleiades) Dreaming
summary: The Seven Sisters is a widespread Aboriginal Australian Dreaming story found across many language groups. The story tells of seven sisters who fled across the land and into the sky to escape a persistent pursuer, often a man named Wurrurrumbi or a hunter who wanted to take one of the sisters as his wife. As they fled, the sisters created landmarks, waterholes, and important sites across the Australian landscape. Finally they leaped into the sky, becoming the Pleiades star cluster. The pursuing man became the star Orion or the Moon, still chasing them across the heavens. In different regional versions, the sisters are associated with the arrival of the monsoon season or with ceremonies for girls' initiation. The story encodes practical knowledge about seasonal changes and the movements of celestial bodies crucial for survival.

title: The Seven Wishes
summary: Olle Niklasson is a thirteen-year-old boy who is exceptionally ugly, lazy, and stupid. His hair resembles a dried juniper bush, his cheeks like swollen fly agaric mushrooms, and he is so lazy he barely moves when he falls. Even the magpies laugh at him. One day in the forest, Olle sees a viper staring down a frog that is slowly crawling toward the snake's open mouth. Too stupid and lazy to intervene with a stick, he nonetheless shouts at the frog for being foolish. This breaks the snake's spell, and the frog escapes. The frog is revealed to be a fairy queen who had been punished for mocking a frog in danger — she was transformed into a frog for twenty-four hours. Grateful for her rescue, she grants Olle seven wishes. Olle uses his wishes foolishly — his first wish makes his bundle of sticks fly wildly through the village, destroying crops and frightening animals. He wastes wish after wish on trivial, selfish things. But after using up six wishes with nothing to show for it, he finally wishes, almost accidentally, that he could learn to read. The fairy queen grants this wish, but tells him that true wisdom comes only through his own hard work. Olle discovers that reading opens his mind. He becomes diligent, studious, and kind, eventually growing into a good and handsome man whom everyone loves. The story teaches that laziness and ignorance are the true sources of ugliness, while knowledge and hard work bring beauty and happiness.

title: The Shadow
summary: A wise man lived in a northern land, and he was content with his life—except that he was always overshadowed by other men.

title: The Shaman's Canoe Journey to the Underworld
summary: A Nanai shamanic epic describing a powerful shaman's journey in his spirit-canoe to the underworld (buni) to retrieve a dying person's soul. According to Nanai tradition, the underworld is a mirror of the world above but reversed — the rivers flow backward and the seasons are opposite. The shaman must navigate treacherous waters in his magical canoe, defeat hostile spirits, pass through a narrow strait guarded by monstrous creatures, and bargain with the lord of the underworld for the soul's release. The journey takes many days and the shaman must leave his physical body in a trance state. If the shaman fails, he may die himself or become trapped in the underworld. The tale illustrates the Nanai concept of soul dualism — a person has multiple souls, one of which can wander during dreams or be stolen by spirits.

title: The Shaman's Journey to the Spirit World
summary: Altai legend tells of the first shaman, named Jaangara, who was taught the art of kamlanie (shamanic journeying) by Erlik himself. According to the story, a nobleman fell ill and called upon Jaangara to heal him. As Jaangara drummed and entered a trance, his spirit traveled up the sacred tree Bay-Terek to the sky world, where he spoke with Bai-Ulgen, and then descended its roots to the underworld court of Erlik. Erlik offered him the power to heal in exchange for a sacrifice. Jaangara accepted but was forever bound to serve both worlds — bringing healing from the upper gods and knowledge of death from the lower spirits. The Altai people say that real shamans (kamlars) still make this journey today, guided by their spirit-helpers (ongons) and accompanied by the sound of the topshuur (two-stringed lute).

title: The Shark as Provider
summary: A mother and daughter are abandoned by their kin and left to starve. Their fortunes change when a dead seal washes ashore, followed by a talking shark that rises from the deep. The shark promises to protect and provide for them, eventually carrying them and all their possessions on its back to a safe, remote island to escape the predatory Inuarutligaks. This tale highlights unexpected protection from the natural world.

title: The Sheep and the Pig Who Set up House
summary: A sheep and a pig decide to partner up and create a household. The story follows their comedic attempts at domestic management, showcasing the friction and eventual cooperation required to maintain a home.

title: The Shipwrecked Sailor
summary: An ancient Egyptian literary tale from the Middle Kingdom (c. 2000 BCE), the Shipwrecked Sailor tells of a sailor who survives a storm that sinks his ship, killing all his companions. He washes ashore on a magical island filled with food, fruit, and fish. After offering thanks to the gods, he hears a thunderous noise and a giant serpent appears, covered in gold and lapis lazuli, thirty cubits long. The serpent carries the sailor to his lair and questions him. The serpent reveals that the island is enchanted, and that he and his family (seventy-five serpents) once lived there until a falling star destroyed them all, leaving him the sole survivor. The serpent prophesies that a ship will come to rescue the sailor in four months and warns him that he will never see the island again. The rescue ship arrives as predicted, and the serpent gives the sailor precious gifts. When the sailor returns to Egypt and reports to the Pharaoh, he is rewarded. The tale contains themes of survival, divine providence, and the fragility of fortune.

title: The Shtriga: The Vampire Witch of Albanian Folklore
summary: An ancient witch feeds on the life force of infants, escaping through keyholes in the form of a flying insect.

title: The Siguanaba and the Lovesick Boy
summary: A beautiful woman with a horse's face appears to young men walking alone at night, seducing them with her beauty before revealing her true monstrous form.

title: The Silversmith and the Moon
summary: A beloved Hmong folktale tells the story of a master silversmith who created the most beautiful silver jewelry in all the land. His work was so exquisite that the Moon herself, looking down from the sky, fell in love with his craftsmanship. Each night, the Moon crept closer to earth to admire the silversmith's work. The Moon whispered to the wind, asking it to carry her longing to the silversmith. Touched by the Moon's appreciation, the silversmith decided to create his masterpiece — a silver ornament so beautiful that it would capture the Moon's radiance forever. He worked for a year, hammering silver thinner than a butterfly's wing, chasing patterns of flowers and dragons into the metal. When he finished, he held up the silver piece, and the Moon saw her own reflection in it. Delighted, the Moon cast a beam of light to earth, and where it touched silver, it left an eternal glow — explaining why Hmong silver seems to shine with an inner light. The silversmith's creation became the first traditional Hmong silver necklace, which Hmong women have worn ever since as a connection to the Moon and the divine. The tale explains the cultural importance of silverwork in Hmong tradition and the moon motifs that adorn Hmong jewelry and embroidery.

title: The Simorgh and the Prince
summary: A Persian prince is saved by a magical bird, the Simorgh, who teaches him the value of promises.

title: The Simurgh and the Burning Garden
summary: The great Simurgh descends from Mount Qaf to heal a garden scorched by divine fire, teaching a village the difference between destruction and renewal.

title: The Sipapu Emergence
summary: In one version of the Hopi emergence story, the people of the Third World grew wicked and corrupt. With the help of Spider Grandmother or bird spirits, a hollow bamboo reed grew at the opening between the Third World and the Fourth World. This opening, called the sipapu, is traditionally located at the Grand Canyon. Only the people with good hearts — those who showed kindness — were able to make the journey through the sipapu to the Fourth World, the world of the present. In the Fourth World, they encountered Masauwu, the Spirit of Death and Earth God, who wore a hideous but also beautiful mask. Masauwu gave them their land and four sacred tablets outlining their way of life and their future wanderings. He taught them to worship properly and ensured the dead would return safely to the underworld.

title: the Sisimito of the Rainforest
summary: A hairy ape-like creature that guards the deep rainforest, punishing those who hunt too greedily and rewarding those who respect the balance.

title: The Six Initiation Societies of the Bambara
summary: Bambara spiritual life is organized through six initiatory societies: N'domo, Komo, Nama, Kono, Tyiwara, and Kore. Each society represents a stage of knowledge and spiritual development, guiding members from childhood through full spiritual maturity. The Komo society, one of the most powerful, preserves esoteric knowledge about the cosmos, medicine, and divination. The N'domo society deals with circumcision and the transition to manhood. The Kore society represents the highest level of initiation, conferring 'mastery of speech' and complete understanding of cosmic order. Together these societies provide the complete intellectual, moral, and religious education of the Bambara people, with ceremonies held at key agricultural and astronomical intervals.

title: The Six Servants
summary: A prince travels with six extraordinary servants who each possess unique abilities (super hearing, super sight, super strength, etc.). Together they overcome impossible challenges to win a princess.

title: The Six Swans
summary: A silent princess endures hardship to save her brothers from a wicked enchantment.

title: The Sjörå – Lady of the Baltic Sea
summary: The sjörå (sea spirit) is a guardian entity of the Baltic waters surrounding the Åland archipelago. She appears as a beautiful woman, sometimes described as hollow-backed like the skogsrå, who can calm storms or raise tempests depending on how she is treated. Fishermen and sailors traditionally greeted her with respect before setting out. Those who showed her reverence were rewarded with calm seas and good catches, while those who disrespected her faced endless wind and perilous voyages. The sjörå embodies the deep bond between the Åland islanders and the sea that has sustained them for millennia. Stone cairns along the shores of Eckerö, Finström, and Geta mark ancient graves of seafarers — each a monument to lives carried across these treacherous waters. Even today, some islanders speak of her presence when the tide falls silent and the horizon blurs.

title: The Skalunda Giant
summary: A giant who fled Skalunda mountain because of church bells meets shipwrecked sailors from his homeland, tests their blood with a red-hot iron bar, and sends a magical girdle home that uproots an oak tree.

title: The Skin Satchel
summary: Hunger and need have fallen upon Niklas's village. He accidentally witnesses a troll take six grains from a leather satchel and in minutes grow an entire field of wheat. He resolves to obtain the magic satchel, but the treasure is hard to find and even harder to keep. The satchel can only be found at night but must be retrieved by sunrise. During this time the trolls cause such terror that one might lose the treasure by letting go of the satchel or speaking a single word.

title: The Skitters
summary: In the remote glens of Scotland, where the mist lingers between the hills and the old ways still hold sway, there are tales of creatures so small and so terrible that they make the bravest men tremble.

title: The Skogsrå and the Hunter
summary: In the deep forests of Västmanland, where the trees grow so thick that summer days are dim, there lived a hunter named Erik who was the pride of his village.

title: The Skogsrå – Forest Spirit of Åland's Woodlands
summary: The skogsrå (forest spirit) is a female nature spirit found throughout Swedish-speaking regions including Åland. She appears as a beautiful woman from the front, but seen from behind she has a hollow, rotten back and often a cow's tail or one horse foot. She lures men deep into the forests, leading them astray into swamps or wilderness. Men who follow her may lose their health or sanity after repeated visits. However, she is known to be kind to charcoal burners and woodcutters, and can reward hunters with good fortune. In the Christian reinterpretation common to Åland and the Nordic region, the skogsrå and similar rå spirits were said to be angels who fell from heaven with Lucifer — those who landed in forests became skogsrå, those in water became sjörå. The Åland archipelago, with its blend of pine forests and rocky shores, is considered a natural home for these borderland spirits.

title: The Slave Who Became a Buzzard
summary: A Gullah version of the Flying Africans legend, recorded by the Federal Writers' Project in the late 1930s. Wallace Quarterman, a Gullah man born in 1844 on Sapelo Island, Georgia, recounted that the Igbo people who drowned at Dunbar Creek did not die at all. According to the oral tradition passed down through generations, the Igbo 'rise out of the water and turn into buzzards and fly back to Africa.' In Gullah belief, the buzzard is not a carrion eater but a sacred bird that carries the souls of the dead back across the Atlantic. This story reflects the deep spiritual connection between the Gullah people and their West African ancestors, and the belief that death by water was not an end but a transformation. The buzzard's circling flight over the Georgia coast is seen as the lingering presence of those who refused to be slaves, forever watching and waiting.

title: The Slaying of Déélgééd the Horned Monster
summary: After defeating Yéʼiitsoh, the Hero Twins faced Déélgééd, the Horned Monster, a creatures described as having one horn and living in the water. In some versions the monster was a giant water creature with a single horn. Monster Slayer and Child of the Water tracked it to its lair. Monster Slayer shot the creature multiple times; its blood gushed out and it plunged into the ocean. As it floated on the surface, both twins shot arrows into it until it was dead. The head of Déélgééd floated to the shore where people later used its horn for ceremonies. This victory was one of several that cleared the world of the monsters that had been devouring the people since the time of the separation of men and women.

title: The Slaying of Yéʼiitsoh
summary: Monster Slayer's greatest feat in Navajo tradition was killing Yéʼiitsoh, the Big Giant, who wore armor of flint knives on his legs. The Hero Twins approached him after their father the Sun had weakened the giant by striking him four times. Monster Slayer shot an arrow into the giant's leg armor but it shattered; a second arrow broke through. The giant collapsed face-down, and Monster Slayer shot a third arrow through his head. Child of the Water also shot the giant's head. When Yéʼiitsoh began to rise again, Spider Woman warned the twins. Monster Slayer shot a fourth arrow which pinned the giant's hair to the ground. As Yéʼiitsoh died, rivers of blood flowed from his wounds. Monster Slayer used the giant's own stone knife to cut off his head and returned home carrying it as a trophy.

title: The Snatcher of the Dubai Alleyways
summary: When children begin vanishing from the lanes of old Dubai, a grandmother traces the disappearances to Khattaf Rafai, the demon who steals children with whispered promises.

title: The Snegurochka Who Melted
summary: A girl made of snow falls in love with a shepherd, but when she tries to kiss him, she melts into a puddle of spring water.

title: The Snow Leopard of Mount Kailash
summary: A wandering pilgrim lost on the slopes of Mount Kailash encounters a spectral snow leopard who guides him through a blizzard — but the path she chooses leads not to the monastery, but to the place within himself he has spent a lifetime avoiding.

title: The Snow Queen
summary: A courageous girl journeys to the frozen ends of the earth to rescue her friend from the Snow Queen's icy grip.

title: The Son of the Sun's Courting in the Land of the Giants
summary: The epic origin myth of the Sámi people. Beaivvi bárdni (the Son of the Sun) sails beyond the easternmost star to the land of the giants to seek a bride. He wins the giant's daughter through strength and cunning. The giant's daughter ties three knots in the wind to help them escape her pursuing brothers—untying each knot releases stronger gales. The brothers are turned to stone by the rising sun. The Son of the Sun marries the giant's daughter on a bearskin and reindeer hide, and she gives birth to the Gállábártnit (the hunting sons), the legendary ancestors of the Sámi people.

title: the Sonangi, the Rain Child
summary: A child-shaped spirit that appears in the rain, following travelers on mountain paths — and if you turn to look at it, you will hear its voice calling your name until the rain stops.

title: The Song of the Forest Sprite
summary: In the rare forests of the north, a sprite is said to play a flute that can put any human to sleep. Those who fall asleep to the melody enter a dream world where they are tempted with riches and power, but they can only wake up if they find the strength to ignore the sprite's promises.

title: The Song of the Mermaids of Black Rocks
summary: A young fisherman ignoring his grandmother's warnings sails past the Black Rocks at twilight and hears the mermaids' song, nearly meeting his doom on the volcanic stones.

title: The Sorceress of Oyndarfjørður
summary: The Rinkusteinar legend in its more detailed form. Long ago, when Irish pirates attacked Fuglafjørður, they killed, robbed, and terrorized the village before setting sail for Oyndarfjørður. An old witch (sorceress) living in Oyndarfjørður saw them coming and rushed to the shore. She raised her arms and cast a powerful curse, transforming the pirate ships into stone. The two rocking stones (rinkusteinar) are the pirate vessels, forever rocking in the waves near Oyndarfjørður, eternally prevented from reaching their destination. The witch's name has been lost to history. The story is one of the best-known witch legends in the Faroe Islands.

title: The Soucouyant of Chalky Mount
summary: An old woman sheds her skin at night, becomes a ball of fire, and flies through the darkness to feed on the blood of infants, leaving telltale marks on their sleeping bodies.

title: The Soucouyant of Roseau
summary: An old woman sheds her skin each night to become a fireball that preys on the blood of sleeping villagers, until a clever young woman discovers her secret.
themes: the power of observation and courage

title: The Soucouyant of Vieux Fort
summary: An old woman suspected of being a soucouyant is exposed when a clever girl discovers the jar of fire where the creature hides its skin at night.

title: The Soucouyant, the Vampire of Trinidad
summary: The Soucouyant is one of the most feared beings in Trinidadian folklore — a vampire-like creature who appears by day as a harmless old woman living alone in a shack with shuttered windows. At midnight, she sheds her human skin, hiding it in a wooden mortar, and transforms into a searing ball of fire that slips through keyholes and cracks to hunt. She targets sleeping infants and children, slowly draining their blood and leaving them pale and weak with tiny pinprick marks. To repel her, scatter uncooked rice or salt at the threshold — she is compelled to stop and count every grain until dawn. To destroy her permanently, find her hidden skin during the day and fill it with salt or pepper; when she tries to reclothe herself at dawn, the burning will destroy her spirit in the sunlight.

title: The Soungoula and the Sleeping Children
summary: A vampiric spirit called Soungoula slips into homes at night to drain the breath from sleeping children, leaving them pale and listless until a healer performs the right ceremony.

title: The Specter in Fjelkinge
summary: An innocent man is wrongly executed, and his ghost appears to the true murderer night after night until justice is done and his soul can finally rest. The tale is founded on the ancient belief that innocent blood calls for atonement.

title: The Spider Trickster and the Sugar Kings
summary: When the sugar planters of Mauritius grew too wealthy and too cruel, the Spider Trickster wove a web of illusions that turned their fortune against them.

title: The Spirit of Kilimanjaro
summary: A Chaga legend tells of a poor hunter named Mushi who lost his way in the dense forest on Kilimanjaro's slopes. After days of wandering, starving and exhausted, Mushi came upon a clearing where an old woman sat beside a fire. The old woman was the spirit of the mountain, though Mushi did not know it. She gave him food and shelter, asking only that he not look back when he left at dawn.
