In the morning, Mushi walked away without looking back, and found himself at his own village in an instant, his pack heavy with blessings. When others heard of his fortune, a greedy man from a neighboring village climbed the mountain seeking the same favor. The old woman also fed him, but his greed got the better of him and he looked back before leaving, reducing his blessings to ash. The mountain spirit teaches that those who approach Kilimanjaro with humility and gratitude receive its bounty, while the greedy and disrespectful are left with nothing.

title: The Spirit of the Black Sands
summary: On the shores of the south, a spirit is said to appear as a small child guiding travelers away from the dangerous sneaker waves. However, if the traveler is greedy or unkind, the spirit leads them directly into the crashing surf, where the ocean claims them as a sacrifice.

title: The Spirit of the Great River
summary: A young Fang hunter must navigate the secrets of the forest and appease the river spirits to save his village from a devastating drought.

title: The Spirit of the Sacred Cloth
summary: A weaver discovers that the spirit Lei inhabits the finest tais cloth, guarding the patterns that carry ancestral memory.

title: The Spring Awakening Ceremony
summary: The most important Pawnee ceremony was the Spring Awakening, meant to awaken the earth and prepare it for planting. The timing was determined by celestial observation: the priest would track 'two small twinkling stars known as the Swimming Ducks in the northeastern horizon near the Milky Way.' When these stars appeared and the first rolling thunder was heard from the West, the ceremony began. The ritual involved songs, prayers, and the renewal of sacred bundles. The Skidi Pawnee performed this as the Thunder ceremony, focusing on corn renewal, while the South Bands performed the White Beaver ceremony, which revitalized hibernating animals.

title: The Star Husband (Arapaho)
summary: Two Arapaho women lay outside their tipi at night. One pointed at a bright star and said she wished to marry it. The next day, a handsome young man appeared at their camp. He was the star in human form, come to claim his bride. The woman went with him to the sky world, where she lived among the star people. But she grew homesick and was told she could return to Earth if she did not eat certain food. She broke the taboo and immediately found herself back on Earth. Her star husband appeared no more, but she gave birth to a son who became a legendary Arapaho hero.

title: The Star Woman (Blackfoot)
summary: A Blackfoot chief's daughter married a star and went to live in the sky world. Each day she was given the task of digging roots, but she was forbidden from digging up one particular turnip. Curiosity overcame her, and when she pulled the turnip, she saw the Earth far below. Overcome with homesickness, she wove a rope of sinew to lower herself back. But the rope was too short and she fell, landing safely but finding herself alone. Following a stream, she found her way back to her people, forever changed by her time among the stars. Her story became a lesson about obedience and the bond between Earth and sky.

title: The Stars and Constellations
summary: First Man, First Woman, Great Coyote, and the Holy People gathered pieces of rock-star mica to create the night sky in Navajo tradition. First Man drew a plan in the dirt to arrange stars like a woven rug. Black God placed the North Star (Sǫʼtsoh). First Man placed the Big Dipper (Náhookǫs bikąʼí) and First Woman the Little Dipper (Náhookǫs baʼáádí). First Man placed the Pleiades (Dilyéhé), which Black God claimed represented parts of his body. They placed Orion's belt (Coyote's Feather), the Rabbit Tracks, and many others. First Angry Coyote, excluded from the careful arrangement, grew impatient and snapped the blanket, scattering the remaining mica chaotically across the sky — explaining why stars appear scattered rather than neatly ordered.

title: The Steadfast Tin Soldier
summary: There were once twenty-five tin soldiers—all brothers, cast from the same old tin spoon.

title: The Steel Donkey of St. Lucy
summary: A monstrous donkey of living metal haunts the northern parishes, guarding hidden treasure and trampling anyone foolish enough to dig where they should not.

title: The Stone Breaker
summary: In the deep forests of Serbia, where the oaks grow thick enough to block the sun and the wolves howl at the edge of every village, there is a creature that haunts the nightmares of every Serbian child.

title: The Stone City of Great Zimbabwe
summary: The ruins of an ancient city in Zimbabwe hold secrets—and a legend about a buried treasure guarded by spirits.

title: The Stone Giant's Challenge
summary: A heroic Iroquois warrior once issued a challenge to a fearsome Stone Giant who had been terrorizing villages. The giant accepted and the two met in battle. The warrior discovered that ordinary weapons could not pierce the giant's stone skin. Using his wits, he lured the giant onto treacherous ground where a rockslide buried him, then climbed to the giant's head and found the vulnerable soft spot. This story was recorded in multiple versions by anthropologists in the 19th century, including by Erminnie Smith among the Onondaga and by Arthur C. Parker among the Seneca. It belongs to a cycle of legends about the extermination of the Stone Giants, which the Iroquois believed once ruled the land before humans were created.

title: The Stone Giant's Wife
summary: This legend tells of a human woman who was taken captive by a Stone Giant. Against all expectations, she survived in the giant's lodge by learning his habits and discovering the secret weakness of his kind — the soft spot on the crown of the head. She eventually escaped and returned to her people with the critical knowledge that would allow them to defend themselves against the stone-coated monsters. The story reflects the Iroquois belief that even the most terrifying adversaries have vulnerabilities, and that courage and observation can overcome seemingly insurmountable threats. It was one of the most popular tales told around winter fires, and versions appear in the early ethnographic collections of the Bureau of American Ethnology.

title: The Stone Giants (Otneyarhed / Stone Coats)
summary: The Stone Giants, also known as Stone Coats, were a race of cannibalistic giants whose skin was as hard as stone, making them nearly invulnerable to weapons. They were the mortal enemies of humans and the constant antagonists in Iroquois hero tales. According to legend, they were exterminated through the cunning and bravery of heroes who discovered that their only weakness was the soft spot on the top of their heads, where a special stone or arrow could pierce their otherwise impenetrable hides. Tales include the Stone Giant's wife, who helped humans, and the story of a young warrior who challenged a Stone Giant in personal combat. Their threat was so great that it required the intervention of the Thunderers to finally drive them away.

title: The Stone Statue
summary: A man who blasphemed in a churchyard was turned to stone. After many parsons failed to save him, a new parson brings the statue into his study and prays daily. The statue laughs during evening prayers and explains that the parson's quarrels with his wife invite imps into the house. The parson reforms, the imps leave, and the statue finds peace.

title: The Storm-Witches of Kastelholm
summary: Åland folklore tells of storm-witches who possessed the secret art of 'tying the wind' into knots of rope. These women could sell sailors a favorable breeze or calm at sea by selling them a knotted rope: untying one knot released a light wind, untying two filled the sails, but untying all three would awaken a devastating tempest. The practice is associated with the maritime culture of Kastelholm Castle, the 14th-century fortress at the heart of the main island. Even today, some islanders refuse to throw rope knots into the sea without cutting them first, for fear of stirring what should sleep. This legend reflects the deep folk belief in weather magic, a tradition found throughout the Nordic coastal regions but with a distinctly Åland character rooted in the archipelago's dependence on safe sea passage.

title: The Story of Ablai Khan
summary: Ablai Khan (1711-1781) was one of the greatest Kazakh khans, who united the three Kazakh zhuzes (hordes) and led the struggle against the Dzungar invaders. According to legend, as a thirteen-year-old orphan named Abulmansur, he worked as a shepherd disguised as a beggar called 'Sabalak' to avoid his father's rivals. His destiny was revealed when he miraculously defeated a Dzungar champion in single combat, earning the title 'batyr' (hero). He was a master diplomat who played Russia against China to maintain Kazakh independence. Legend says he was blessed by the spirit of his ancestor Genghis Khan and commanded the loyalty of all the steppe tribes through a combination of military genius and sacred charisma.

title: The Story of Asdiwal (Tsimshian)
summary: Asdiwal is one of the most important Tsimshian hero narratives, recorded in multiple versions by Franz Boas. The story begins with a mother and daughter dying of starvation during a winter famine in the Skeena River region. A supernatural being named Hatsenas (a bird of good omen) appears, provides food, and fathers Asdiwal with the younger woman. Hatsenas gives his son magical objects including a never-missing bow, invisible-making hat, and inexhaustible food basket. Asdiwal's adventures include hunting a magical bear up to the sky, where the bear transforms into Evening-Star, daughter of the Sun. He marries her after passing deadly trials set by the Sun. Returning to earth, Asdiwal marries a Tsimshian chief's daughter and becomes wealthy through potlatches. He competes with his brothers-in-law in sea-lion hunting but is abandoned on a reef during a storm. His father saves him. Eventually Asdiwal goes mountain hunting without his snowshoes, gets lost, and is turned to stone with his dog and lance — a transformation that can still be seen on a mountain at Ginadâos Lake.

title: The Story of Bernardo Carpio
summary: Bernardo Carpio is the Filipino equivalent of Hercules — a legendary giant with superhuman strength believed to be trapped between two great rocks in the mountains of Montalban (Rizal province). According to folklore, he was a Spanish-Filipino of immense size and power who single-handedly fought entire armies. When the Spanish authorities could not defeat him, they tricked him into entering a cave where a magical spell trapped him between two massive boulders. Every time he struggles to free himself, the earth trembles, causing earthquakes in the Philippines. The legend became a symbol of Filipino resistance against colonial oppression.

title: The Story of Ista (Nuxalk)
summary: Ista is the name of the First Woman who descended to Nuxalknalus (King Island) in Nuxalk tradition. She came down to earth and decorated her crest on a blanket with abalone shell and danced up the coast. Ista was greatly admired for how she chose to show her connection to the Creator. Her story is part of the Nuxalk understanding of how the first ancestors established territories and rights to the land. Traditional family names are handed down and validated at potlatches. The Ista story also includes the tale of Patsallht (First Born), who thought he was the only one on earth. He was given a medicine box containing a 'mukw' of shame, stubbornness, and jealousy. He met the Sisawk people (Society of Chiefs) but was ashamed he was not a member. Later, he met a beautiful woman wearing a red blanket who proposed marriage. She was a grizzly bear woman who built him a home from hemlock. When she left him, First Born refused to leave the house. People followed his puppy to find him and convinced him to feast with them by offering to paint their faces black. The Ista people were ultimately wiped out by a cannibal raiding party from far away.

title: The Story of Kannagi and the Chera King — From Vengeance to Divinity
summary: After the burning of Madurai, Kannagi left the destroyed city and journeyed west into the Chera kingdom (modern-day Kerala). The Chera king Senguttuvan, learning of her story, recognized her as a divine incarnation of chastity. He built a temple for her and established the cult of Pattini (the chastity goddess). Kannagi is worshipped as a goddess in Kerala (as Kodungallur Bhagavati) and among Tamils in Sri Lanka. This portion of the Silappadikaram records a historic expedition by Senguttuvan to the Himalayas to bring a sacred stone for Kannagi's idol, making her one of the few mortals in Indian tradition to be elevated directly to goddess status through the power of her own righteous fury and unwavering virtue.

title: The Story of Noqoilpi the Great Gambler
summary: In Navajo tradition, Noqoilpi was a powerful gambler who challenged and defeated all who came to him, taking their possessions and even their freedom. He was said to live at the base of Chʼóolʼį́ʼí (Great Spruce Mountain or El Capitan). Noqoilpi gambled with entire nations, winning their wealth and enslaving their people. The Holy People decided he had grown too powerful and needed to be stopped. They sent a challenger who gambled with Noqoilpi in a series of contests. The challenger, aided by the Holy People, finally beat Noqoilpi at the moccasin game and other gambling games. Defeated, Noqoilpi was forced to leave the Navajo world. He departed eastward, taking his gambling implements with him, and was never seen again, though his influence lingered in the form of gambling as a human vice.

title: The Story of Saint Yared and the Birth of Ethiopian Music
summary: In the 6th century, a young boy named Yared was sent to study at the holy city of Axum. But he was a slow learner and often ran away to play in the fields. One day, while hiding under a tree, Yared saw a caterpillar climbing a stalk. The caterpillar fell but climbed again — and again — until it reached the top. Inspired by its perseverance, Yared returned to his studies with renewed dedication. He mastered the scriptures and became a deacon in the Ethiopian Orthodox Church. One day, while praying, Yared received divine inspiration and created the five-note scale system (zema) that became the foundation of Ethiopian liturgical music. He composed the Deggua (hymn book) and invented musical notation for the Ge'ez language. Three birds — representing the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit — are said to have guided his voice, and his music was so beautiful that angels descended from heaven to listen.

title: The Story of the Girl Who Was Never Seen
summary: A mysterious invisible girl whose presence is known only through her voice and actions.

title: The Story of the Moccasin Game
summary: The Moccasin Game is a traditional Navajo story explaining the origin of a sacred winter game. In the mythological account, the animals gathered to play the moccasin game, which involves hiding a stone or yucca ball under one of four moccasins while the opposing side guesses its location. The game was played between the day animals and the night animals, with the stakes being control over light and darkness. Through trickery and strategy — particularly from Coyote who cheated by using a yucca ring instead of a stone — the night animals won, establishing that darkness would have its place in the world. This story is traditionally told only during winter months and is considered sacred, teaching lessons about balance, trickery, and the boundaries between day and night, summer and winter.

title: The Striga of the Mountain Pass
summary: A traveling priest encounters a Striga in the High Tatras and learns that some curses cannot be broken by faith alone, only endured with courage and sacrifice.
themes: the making of monsters by human cruelty
the failure of exorcism against injustice

title: The Stállu's Christmas Meal
summary: A Sámi Christmas legend from Kautokeino. While parents were away at church, a Stállu came to the camp and began killing and eating children one by one. A quick-witted maid saved the youngest child, tricked Stállu with her traveling cape, and escaped on skis behind the fastest reindeer. The reindeer burst into pieces in the Kautokeino River from exhaustion. All reindeer in the camp were turned to stone. The stones remain in the Kautokeino River as a reminder of Stállu's anger.

title: The Sultan of Pate and the Liongo Proclamation
summary: When Oromo emissaries came to visit the Sultan of Pate, they heard tales of the legendary hero Liongo. Curious, they asked the Sultan about him. The Sultan sent for Liongo, who packed his bag and hung three great horns about his waist. The journey that took the messengers two days, Liongo completed in half a day. Arriving at the edge of town, he blew his first horn with such force that it split in two. The courtiers were startled, but the Sultan recognized the blast: Liongo had arrived. A second horn blast at the city gates, and a third before the palace announced his presence. When Liongo entered the court, his immense height and strength awed the Oromo visitors. He recited a praise poem celebrating his bow, the Song of the Warrior (Sifu Uta Wangu), and the Oromo delegates left with new respect for the Swahili kingdom. This story illustrates Liongo's role as the protector and symbol of Swahili identity.

title: the Sumbo, Spirit of the Fallow Field
summary: A spirit that inhabits the fields left fallow, protecting the land while it rests — and destroying anyone who plows a field before its rest is complete.

title: The Sun and the Moon
summary: A celestial tale of sibling rivalry that explains the origin of the day and night cycle and the necessity of cosmic balance.

title: The Sun Dance Lodge Symbolism
summary: The Crow Sun Dance lodge (Ashé Isée) is built as a microcosm of the universe. The central forked pole, representing God, faces east. A white flag tied to one branch represents Earth; a blue flag represents the sky. Three charcoal rings on the pole symbolize the three days of the dance and the three worlds of Crow cosmology. A buffalo head and eagle body are hung on the pole as patrons. Twelve cottonwood posts form the lodge boundary, representing the twelve months and the circle of life. For contemporary Christian Crows, the twelve posts also symbolize the twelve apostles and the three rings represent Christ's three days in the tomb.

title: The Sun Dance Wheel
summary: The Arapaho Sun Dance, known as the Offerings Lodge, is a central spiritual ceremony. Unlike other Plains tribes that practiced self-torture, the Arapaho version involved donating personal items, space, or land to the community as sacrifice. The sacred Flat Pipe was central to the ceremony, symbolizing the Arapaho's connection to the Creator. The Sun Dance lodge was built with a central pole representing the Creator, surrounded by a circle of posts representing the community. The ceremony lasted four days and included dancing, prayer, singing, and offering. The wheel symbolism represents the cycle of life and the interconnectedness of all things.

title: The Sun Tests His Son-in-Law (Nuxalk)
summary: In this Nuxalk myth, the daughter of the Sun married a human man known as Salmon Boy. The Sun was not pleased with his daughter's choice and subjected his new son-in-law to a series of deadly tests. The Sun took Salmon Boy to a mountain of unparalleled steepness where mountain goats climbed, commanding him to kill one. Salmon Boy succeeded with the help of his wife. Next, the Sun required him to draw water from a spring whose walls closed in on anyone who approached. Again his wife helped him. The Sun tried to bake him in a supernaturally hot sweat lodge, burn him on hot stones, and crush him with a falling tree. Each time Salmon Boy survived through his wife's guidance and his own growing supernatural power. Finally recognizing his son-in-law's worth, the Sun accepted him and bestowed upon him the gift of bringing salmon to the people. Salmon Boy returned to earth as a powerful being who taught the Nuxalk people how to properly catch, prepare, and honor the salmon, establishing the sacred relationship between the people and the salmon runs.

title: The Sun's Daughter
summary: A cycle of myths about Beaivvi nieida, the Sun's daughter, who descended from the sky to teach the Sámi people to tame reindeer, as well as beauty, handicraft, and hunting yoiks. After her death, she was buried on a mountain peak with reindeer neck hair as bedding. Her spirit wanders all of Sápmi with her reindeer herd—visible only when she sleeps. He who discovers her and awakens her with a kiss will gain her and her herd, but must prove himself worthy by following her instructions precisely.

title: The Sun, Moon and Firmament
summary: A Chukchi astral myth describing the origins and relationships of celestial bodies. The Sun is considered the most important celestial being, spoken of as an individual spirit with great power. The Moon is seen as a male figure, often described as the 'evil spirit' counterpart of the Sun. Chukchi reindeer herders still seek the influence of specific constellations when making important sacrifices. The myth includes stories of the North Star (a central pillar of the sky), Betelgeuse, and other celestial bodies that guide hunters and herders across the featureless tundra. The firmament itself is envisioned as a solid dome connected to the earth at the horizon, with holes through which spirits and celestial beings pass.

title: The Sure Shot
summary: A watchman in Göinge boasts of his marksmanship and wagers he can shoot a roe on Halland's Mountains from his doorstep. He fires into the dark and kills a magnificent stag, proving to his horrified companions that he is in league with the Evil One.

title: The Swaichen of the Salt Flats
summary: A Bedouin herder loses his way on the salt flats of Bahrain and encounters the Swaichen, a monstrous creature that feeds on the disoriented and the desperate.

title: The Sweat Lodge Origin: Seven Bison and Bones Together
summary: Seven Bison and their male human companion fought against the angry bison Bones Together, whose pure bone armor was impenetrable. As each bison charged, they broke their legs against Bones Together. Finally the human companion, blessed by an eagle with the power to transform into a feather, faced Bones Together. The monster charged four times, but the man turned into a feather and wafted out of harm's way. On the fourth charge, the man shot an arrow into Bones Together's rectum, piercing his heart. Though victorious, the bison were grievously injured. Together they performed the first Sweat Lodge ceremony, which healed all the bison. Afterward, the Seven Bison rose into the sky to become the Big Dipper, and the man became the Little Dipper.

title: The Swineherd
summary: In the snow-covered forests of northern Japan, where the winter temperatures drop so low that your breath freezes before it leaves your lips, there is a yokai that haunts the blizzards.

title: The Sword in the Stone
summary: After the death of Uther Pendragon, the kingdom of Britain fell into turmoil. Centers on Spirit,  human attempt to understand the soul, afterlife, and the unseen forces that govern existence..

title: The Sámi Boy Who Married a Háldi Girl
summary: A Sámi boy falls in love with a háldi girl from the hidden underground people. Despite being from different realms, they find a way to marry. The story explores the boundaries between the visible human world and the invisible world of the háldi, a recurring theme in Sámi folklore. Such marriages come with strict taboos that, if broken, cause the supernatural spouse to disappear forever.

title: The Tabudo of the Motagua
summary: A water spirit dwelling in the rivers of eastern El Salvador lures the unwary with the scent of copal incense, dragging them beneath the current to serve in its underwater kingdom.

title: The Tale of Kagsagsuk
summary: Kagsagsuk is a mistreated orphan boy who suffers extreme cruelty from his foster mother and the village men. Seeking strength, he journeys to the mountains to encounter the Amarok, a giant solitary wolf spirit. Through a series of grueling trials where the Amarok repeatedly throws him down, Kagsagsuk sheds his weaknesses and gains superhuman strength. He eventually returns to the village, defeats three bears, and takes revenge on those who tormented him, though he remains a lonely figure of legend.

title: The Tale of Njunje Paggas
summary: A Stállu tale collected by P. A. Lindholm and illustrated by John Bauer. Njunje Paggas is a Sámi hero who faces the Stállu in a battle of wits. The Stállu is a large, human-like creature who eats people. The Sámi hero wins through cleverness rather than strength. The Stállu's own knife must not be used against him, or he gains strength.

title: The Tale of the Aluxob
summary: Small, elf-like spirits called Aluxob protect cornfields and forests, but they demand respect — and they love to dance.

title: The Tale of the Bak Bak
summary: In the islands of the Philippines, where the coconut palms sway against turquoise skies and the sea stretches endlessly in every direction, the elders tell stories of the Bak Bak — a mysterious creature that lives in the deepest parts of the forest.

title: The Tale of the Bamboo
summary: A boy is born from bamboo and embarks on adventures that reveal his divine origins.

title: The Tale of the Black Duck
summary: In the tradition of the First Nations peoples of Canada, particularly among the Algonquian and Ojibwe communities, the black duck holds a special place as a teacher of survival and adaptation.

title: The Tale of the Cowherd and the Weaver Girl
summary: A celestial weaver and a mortal cowherd fall in love, only to be separated by the Milky Way, meeting once a year on a bridge of magpies.

title: The Tale of the First Fire
summary: In the beginning, when the world was young and the animals spoke with human voices, there was no fire on earth.

title: The Tale of the Fisherman and the Little Fish
summary: A magical golden fish grants an old fisherman's wishes, but the greed of his wife leads them back to where they started.

title: The Tale of the Lost Man (Tuareg)
summary: A classic Tuareg teaching tale from the rich Imayen oral tradition. A man becomes lost in the vast Sahara desert during a sandstorm. His water runs out, his camel collapses, and he resigns himself to death. As he lies on the sand, a mystical camel appears—a creature that seems to be made of light and shadow, with eyes that glow like stars. The camel carries him to a hidden oasis where a Tuareg elder lives. The elder nurses him back to health and teaches him the ways of the desert: how to read the stars, how to find water in dry wadis, how to respect the wind. When the traveler is ready to leave, the elder tells him that the camel was not an animal but a benevolent desert spirit (an 'akal' spirit) that tests humility. The lesson: the desert gives life only to those who approach it with humility and gratitude. The traveler returns to his tribe a changed man, and the story is told by Tuareg mothers to teach children the importance of humility and respect toward nature, especially the precious bond between nomad and camel.

title: The Tale of the Silver Salmon
summary: A fisherman catches a shimmering silver salmon that can speak. The fish promises to grant him one wish in exchange for its freedom. The man asks for the ability to understand the language of all animals, which allows him to uncover a plot to overthrow the local chieftain.

title: The Tale of the Three Apples
summary: A classic murder mystery from the Arabian Nights. Caliph Harun al-Rashid orders his vizier Jafar to solve the murder of a young woman found dismembered in a chest. The investigation leads to her husband, who confesses after returning home to find a strange apple in her possession and killed her in jealous rage. However, the actual chain of events involves a slave who had taken the apple from the caliph's own palace. Jafar is given three days to find the killer or face execution. The story is notable as an early example of the 'locked room' mystery structure and detective fiction.

title: The Tale of the Three Sisters
summary: Three sisters become corn, beans, and squash — the Three Sisters crops that sustain life.

title: The Tale of the Two Brothers
summary: In ancient Egypt, two brothers ruled the land. Centers on Osiris,  from Egypt mythology. Known for aquatic speed and soul sight and immortality..

title: The Tale of the Völva
summary: A powerful Völva, or seeress, is summoned to a chieftain's court to predict the future of the land. Through a ritual of chanting and trance, she reveals a vision of coming wars and natural disasters, reminding the people that the threads of fate are woven by the Norns and cannot be undone.

title: The Tallow Candle
summary: A poetic story told from the perspective of a tallow candle, reflecting on the fleeting nature of life, light, and the inevitable end.

title: the Tanganyika Serpent, the Lake's Guardian
summary: A massive serpent that lives in the deepest waters of Lake Tanganyika, stirring the currents that bring fish to the shore — and when it sleeps, the lake goes still and the fishermen catch nothing.

title: The Tashka and Walo: Brothers Who Followed the Sun (Choctaw)
summary: Two brothers named Tashka and Walo followed the sun every day from childhood to adulthood. One day, the sun rested over a great expanse of water, and the boys swam into it, emerging in the home of the sun. The sun's wife, the moon, and the stars all lived there. The sun asked why they had followed him for so many years, and they replied they only wished to see where he died each evening. The sun agreed to send them home but warned them not to speak for four days after returning, or they would surely die. A giant buzzard flew them home. Their frightened mother made them speak, and they told of their journey, knowing they would now die. After telling all they knew, they died and entered the spirit world.

title: The Tell-Tale Heart
summary: Guilt makes a man hear a heart. Centers on Spirit,  human attempt to understand the soul, afterlife, and the unseen forces that govern existence..

title: the Tenga, Spirits of the Earth
summary: The Mossi people believe the earth is alive with spirits called Tenga who must be consulted before every harvest — and those who ignore them find their fields barren and their children sick.

title: The Terror of the Yule Cat
summary: The Yule Cat is a giant, monstrous feline that prowls the Icelandic countryside during the winter solstice. It is said that the cat eats anyone who has not received a new piece of clothing for Christmas, a legend that historically encouraged the completion of wool production before the end of the year.

title: The Tertön (Treasure Revealer) Traditions
summary: Tibetan legends of the tertöns — treasure revealers who discovered hidden spiritual texts and sacred objects (terma) concealed by Padmasambhava and his consort Yeshe Tsogyal in the 8th century. According to tradition, Padmasambhava foresaw the persecution of Buddhism that would occur in Tibet centuries later and hid thousands of teachings, ritual objects, and sacred images in lakes, caves, rocks, and the minds of future disciples. These hidden treasures would be discovered at the prophesied time by specially destined tertöns, who would have been the original disciples of Padmasambhava in a previous life. Major tertöns include Nyangrel Nyima Ozer, Guru Chöwang, and the famous Jamyang Khyentse Wangpo. The terma tradition remains active in Tibetan Buddhism today.

title: The Theft of Daylight
summary: In a time of eternal darkness, the world was cold and blind. Raven, the cunning trickster, discovered that a powerful being held the light of the world captured in a box. Through a series of disguises and tricks, Raven managed to steal the light and release it into the sky, creating the sun, moon, and stars, and bringing warmth and visibility to the Inuit people.

title: The Theft of Light (Tsimshian - Weeget)
summary: On Raven's first journey, Weeget (Giant/Raven) flew inland toward the east carrying a stone his father the chief had given him. When exhausted, he dropped the stone on the sea, where it became a large rock. At that time there was always darkness — no daylight existed. Weeget put on his raven skin and scattered salmon and trout roe into every river and creek, declaring that all waters should have fish. He then flew up through a hole in the sky to reach heaven. Near the chief of heaven's house, he found a spring where the chief's daughter drank. He turned into a floating object, was swallowed, and was born as a human child. He stole the light (called maa) and escaped back to earth. When the Frog people at the Nass River mocked him while fishing for olachen and refused his requests, Weeget broke the maa, releasing daylight. The north wind drove the Frogs away, and they froze onto a rock where they remain as stone to this day. Thus the Tsimshian explain the origin of daylight.

title: The Three Aunts
summary: A story about a young man who inherits a strange set of rules from his three aunts. To claim his inheritance, he must spend a year following their eccentric whims, leading to a series of surreal events and personal growth.

title: The Three Dogs
summary: A king falls under the spell of an evil witch-queen, and only his faithful queen and three magical dogs — with powers of strength, speed, and music — can break the enchantment. From Västergötland, this tale emphasizes the magic of music against trolls.

title: The Three Little Pigs
summary: There was once an old sow who had three little pigs, but times were lean and she could not keep them.

title: The Three Princesses of Whiteland
summary: A brave youth journeys to the distant kingdom of Whiteland to win the hand of one of three princesses. He must pass three impossible tests of courage and wisdom, aided by the guidance of a mysterious forest spirit.

title: The Three Sisters: Corn, Beans, and Squash
summary: In Iroquois tradition, the Three Sisters are the agricultural spirits Corn (Onatah), Beans, and Squash. They are inseparable companions who grow best when planted together. According to legend, the Creator gave these three plants to the people as a sacred gift. Corn provides a stalk for the beans to climb, beans fix nitrogen in the soil for the corn, and squash spreads its broad leaves to shade the ground, preventing weeds and retaining moisture. The sisters represent the principle of mutual support and cooperation that underlies Haudenosaunee society. Ceremonies honor them throughout the growing season, especially the Green Corn Festival when the first corn ripens.

title: The Thunder Beings (Aniyvdaqualosgi) (Cherokee)
summary: The Cherokee believe in the Thunder Beings, known as Aniyvdaqualosgi or Ani-Yuntikwalaski. The Great Thunder and his two sons, the Thunder Boys, live in the land of the west above the sky vault. They dress in lightning and rainbows. Unlike many tribes where thunder spirits take bird form, Cherokee Thunderers are human in form — powerful and dangerous but generally friendly to humans. The priests pray to the Thunder beings for rain and blessings. Some lesser thunder beings live closer to the Earth's surface in cliffs, mountains, and waterfalls, and these are more mischievous, sometimes causing harm. Thunder is said to be the sound of the Great Thunder's wings or his voice rolling across the sky. Lightning is the fire from his eyes.

title: The Thunderbird and the Whale
summary: The Thunderbird, lord of the sky, wages eternal war against the Great Whale, lord of the sea — and their battle is the storm.

title: The Thunderbird Wakinyan
summary: Wakinyan is the great Thunderbird of Lakota mythology, a powerful sky spirit associated with thunder, lightning, and storms. His flapping wings create thunderclaps and his eyes flash lightning. When Unhcegila emerged from the primordial waters to flood the land, Wakinyan flapped his wings to dry the earth and shot lightning to destroy the serpent's heart. The Thunderbird represents the destructive yet renewing power of storms and is considered one of the most potent spirits. Wakinyan is also associated with the west direction and is a protector of the Lakota people against chaos and disorder.

title: The Thunderers (Hadiwennoda:dye's)
summary: The Thunderers are powerful storm spirits who live in the sky and cause thunder and lightning. They are described as giant warriors who hunt and kill the great horned serpents and other monsters that threaten humanity. In the Seneca tradition, they are led by the great chief Hino. Their gaze can bring death to mortal men, yet they are generally benevolent and play a protective role in Iroquois legends. They are the eternal enemies of the Great Horned Serpent Oniare and maintain the balance of the world by ensuring no monster grows too powerful. The Thunderers are honored with tobacco offerings, and their rumbling voices are heard whenever they pursue evil spirits across the sky.

title: The Tickling Demon Mahaha
summary: Mahaha is a thin, ice-blue demon who tickles victims with long nails until they die from lack of breath. However, the story concludes that Mahaha can be outwitted by the clever, who eventually trap him in a water hole.

title: The Tide-Keeper of Abu Dhabi
summary: A young diver who disrespects the Gulf earns the wrath of Baba Dariah, Father of the Tide, and must learn to honor the sea before it claims him entirely.

title: The Tie Snake and the Horned Serpent (Creek)
summary: The Tie Snake and the Horned Serpent are powerful underwater serpents in Muscogee Creek mythology. The Tie Snake has immense strength and can drag humans underwater to drown. The Horned Serpent is even larger, with antlers or horns, and represents the chaotic forces of the Lower World. According to legend, these creatures were once humans who ate prohibited food, causing them to transform into snakes overnight. A hunter who broke a taboo could become a Tie Snake, signaling the importance of respecting the cosmic balance between the three worlds. These serpents serve as guardians of the boundary between the Middle World and the Lower World. Their stories warn against violating sacred prohibitions and emphasize the consequences of disrupting the natural order.

title: The Tiger and the Three Brothers
summary: In an old Korean village during the Joseon dynasty, three brothers lived with their mother in a cottage at the foot of a great mountain.

title: The Tikoloshe in the Guest House
summary: A visiting trader encounters the mischievous tikoloshe in a roadside inn and learns that some spirits feed on the arrogance of strangers.

title: The Tinderbox
summary: A soldier finds a magic tinderbox that allows him to summon three powerful dogs made of precious metals, leading him to wealth and a princess.

title: The Tlanuwa Bird (Natchez)
summary: The Tlanuwa is a giant mythological bird of prey known to both the Natchez and Cherokee. This enormous raptor has feathers made of impenetrable metal that it can launch like arrows at enemies. The Tlanuwa was large enough to carry away humans and even deer. It nested in the highest cliffs and mountains. The Natchez tell stories of the Tlanuwa battling the great water serpents such as the Olobit and the Tie-Snake, representing the conflict between the sky and the underworld. Heroes in Natchez legends sometimes sought the feathers of the Tlanuwa for their protective properties. The bird was feared but also respected as a powerful spirit being. The name Tlanuwa is Cherokee — the original Natchez name for this creature was never recorded, though the stories survived.

title: The Toad and the Snow Kachinas
summary: In Oraibi, the Snow Kachinas were practicing for a dance in the Chórzhovi kiva. North of the village at Katcínavala lived Toad Woman with her son. The boy often went to listen to the Kachinas sing. On the dance day, the Toad Boy painted his face and wore a wildcat robe. Children laughed at him and took him to an anthill because he liked ants. He ate the ants and returned to the plaza to enjoy the dance. When the children gave him red piki (paper bread) from the Kachinas, he brought it home to his mother. She was happy, and they ate it together. This story teaches about the inclusion of even the lowliest creatures in Kachina celebrations and demonstrates the Hopi value of kindness to those who are different.

title: The Tokoloshe of the Umfolozi
summary: A cunning water sprite terrorizes a riverside village until an elderly sangoma devises a way to banish it back to the depths.

title: The Tomtarna
summary: The boy Andreas has left his childhood farm to seek fortune in the city. His aging parents miss him terribly. The farm tomte takes pity on them and sets out to find the boy. Andreas works as a guard in the troll prison until a troll bites off his fingers. In despair, he runs into the forest. The tomte finds him, produces the mother's apron, and tucks it into the boy's hand. Andreas dreams his mother is leading him home. When he wakes, the tomte has enchanted his hand with 'troll fingers' that work better than ever.

title: The Tomte and the Christmas Porridge
summary: A farmer learns to respect the farm spirit and the importance of keeping traditions.

title: The Tomtegubbe – Åland's Household Guardian
summary: The tomte (or gårdstomte) is a household spirit who lives on farms and in barns, watching over the family and livestock. On Åland, as in the rest of the Swedish-speaking world, the tomte was both protector and disciplinarian: he rewarded hard work and good management with prosperity, but punished laziness, drunkenness, and night work with mischief or outright harm. The tomte expected to be fed — typically a bowl of porridge with butter on Christmas Eve. If neglected, he would cause accidents, make the cows go dry, or leave the farm entirely. The tradition is preserved in the annual children's anthology 'Bland tomtar och troll' (Among Gnomes and Trolls), first published in 1907 and still going today, which features stories collected from across the Swedish language area including Åland. The tomte represents the moral code of the traditional Åland farming community, where hard work and respect for the unseen were paramount.

title: The Tomten's Christmas Vigil
summary: In the deep of a winter night, the Tomten — the ancient guardian spirit of the farm — makes his silent rounds while the household sleeps, watching over all creatures and reflecting on the mysteries of life.

title: The Tortoise and the Cracking Shell (Igbo)
summary: Mbe the Tortoise was once a bird with a beautiful smooth shell, but his greed and vanity led to his downfall. When the birds of the sky were invited to a great feast in heaven, Tortoise persuaded them to lend him feathers so he could fly and join them. At the feast, he tricked the heavenly hosts into giving him the choicest foods by claiming the name 'All of you' was his. When the hosts served food 'for all of you,' Tortoise ate everything. The angry birds retrieved their feathers from Tortoise and left him stranded in heaven. Tortoise convinced the heavenly hosts to throw him down to earth, but his fall shattered his shell into pieces. The story explains why tortoises have cracked, patched shells and serves as an Igbo warning against greed and deception.

title: The Tortoise and the Hare
summary: In the sun-baked valleys where the dusty trails wound between olive groves and dry riverbeds, the animals of the district had gathered for their usual morning disputes.

title: The Tortoise and the Hyena
summary: The clever tortoise tricks the greedy hyena in this traditional African folktale.

title: The totem Pole
summary: Animals mark family history, telling the story of a clan through carved symbols.

title: The Touni Minwi of Port Louis
summary: In the narrow streets of Port Louis, a restless spirit known as the Touni Minwi drifts through shuttered windows and locked doors, carrying a lantern that burns with a light no fire can produce.

title: the Toyol and the Jeweler
summary: A jeweler in Kampong Glam who used a Toyol to steal diamonds from his competitors, until the Toyol stole the one thing the jeweler treasured more than gold, his reflection.

title: the Toyol, the Thief's Spirit
summary: A small green goblin summoned by black magic to steal for its master, but the Toyol steals not just gold, but the master's humanity, one theft at a time.

title: The Transformation of Raven
summary: An origin story explaining why the Raven is black. Originally, Raven had beautiful shimmering feathers, but through a series of mishaps and his own trickery, he was scorched by fire or covered in soot. This transformation serves as a permanent mark of his trickster nature.

title: The Transformer Who Became the Mountains (Coast Salish)
summary: The Coast Salish tell of a Transformer (Xe'las) who walked through the land making the world right for the coming humans. Near Lake Chelan, he encountered people who had become corrupted by greed and selfishness. He transformed them into stone, their canoes becoming islands in the lake. Near the Fraser River, he found a woman with a vagina full of teeth who emasculated men — he turned her into a rock formation that still guards the river. In the San Juan Islands, he found two sisters fighting over a man and turned them into a pair of islands called The Sisters. The Transformer also created Mount Rainier (Tacobud) as a refuge during the great flood, and the mountain still bears the scars of the waters. Every rock, island, and mountain in Coast Salish territory has a story of transformation, creating a landscape that serves as a permanent record of moral teachings. The land itself is a library of stories that instruct people in proper behavior and remind them of the consequences of their actions.

title: The Treasure in Säby Creek
summary: A miserly gentleman sinks his gold-laden wagon in Saby Creek rather than let it fall to others. A farmer raises white calves on skimmed milk to drag the treasure out but one calf is weakened by watered milk. The wagon slips back as a voice taunts about the calves.

title: The Treasure of Skógafoss
summary: Legend tells of a wealthy man named Þrasi Þórólfsson who buried a chest filled with gold and valuables behind the curtain of water at the Skógafoss waterfall. For centuries, people have searched for the treasure, and it is said that only those with a pure heart can find the spot where the gold remains hidden.

title: The Treasure Seekers
summary: In Swedish folk belief, those who seek buried treasures must maintain absolute silence or the search will be in vain. Four men form a party to unearth treasures in Josäterdal. As they dig, supernatural illusions appear — an officer, soldiers firing at them, a red calf, a gallows. One digger wears a red shirt that catches the spirits' attention. When a voice cries out 'Shall we begin with him wearing the red shirt?' the man flees in panic.

title: The Trial of Lovers: Maiden of Matsaki
summary: A Zuni folk tale about the beautiful Maiden of Matsaki, desired by many suitors. After the war god Áhaiyúta and his brother courted her, they discovered she was cruel — she had let the children of Field-mice die of cold while she gambled. The gods punished her but also showed compassion for the helpless mouse children, taking them to their grandmother who raised them. The story teaches that even gods can be cruel, but those who find helpless children must care for them. The Maiden of Matsaki's story illustrates Zuni values about compassion, the consequences of cruelty, and the duty to care for orphans and vulnerable children. It also demonstrates that even divine beings are subject to moral judgment and that mercy can follow justice.

title: The Trickster Hare and Bouki the Hyena (Wolof)
summary: Leuk the Hare is the clever trickster of Wolof folklore, constantly outwitting Bouki the Hyena, who is greedy, stupid, and easily fooled. In one famous tale, Bouki and Leuk found a calabash of milk. Leuk wanted it all for himself, so he convinced Bouki that the milk was poisoned and offered to run and fetch an antidote. While gone, Leuk drank all the milk. When he returned, he pretended to have taken the antidote himself and told Bouki he was now ill. Bouki, believing the milk was poisoned, was too afraid to drink it. In another tale, Leuk tricked Bouki into holding up a rock to keep it from rolling away—a rock that was actually Leuk's trick to trap Bouki in place all day while Leuk feasted. Leuk represents intelligence triumphing over brute strength, a central theme in Wolof culture that values wit over power.

title: The Trickster Scorpion and the Merchant
summary: A greedy merchant crossing the Sahara encounters a talking scorpion who offers to guide him to a hidden caravansary in exchange for a promise he never intends to keep.

title: The Troll Ride
summary: Peder Lars, a farmer's son, is riding to town to buy a new jacket before courting the beautiful and wealthy Lisa that evening. He is confident she will accept his proposal. But on the way through the forest, he encounters a hideous troll-woman lying injured in a ditch. She begs him to collect resin from seven pine trees to heal her wounded leg, offering gold coins in return. Peder Lars is repulsed by her appearance and initially refuses, but the haunting cries of the troll-woman's mother calling for her drive him to collect the resin. He tosses it at her in irritation and rides on. The delay causes him to be late: while en route, his brother meets him with terrible news — the rich miller Jonas has also come to propose to Lisa. With only minutes to spare and miles to go, Peder Lars' horse suddenly gains supernatural speed. Unseen, the grateful troll-woman rides behind him, her magic urging the horse forward at breakneck speed through the dark forest. Though his jacket is torn and his hair is wild, Peder Lars arrives at Lisa's house at the very last moment. Lisa, seeing his determined and disheveled appearance, finds him handsome and rushes into his arms. Peder Lars wins her hand, and from that day forward, he is never late again — because the troll-woman's magic ensures he always arrives on time.

title: The Troll Shoes
summary: An old witch prepares to fly to Blakulla by greasing her enchanted shoes. A weary traveler accidentally puts on the witch's shoes and is dragged head-downward through the night. A passerby knocks off one shoe which instantly vanishes and the weakened witch falls into what becomes the Troll Woman's Pit.

title: The Troll Son Who Had Sun Eyes
summary: Humpe, the red-haired son of a troll mother, has large clear eyes with a gleam of sunlight in them, marking him as different from troll-kind. His unnatural affinity for daylight makes him an outcast. Filled with daylight's vigor, he leaves troll society and ventures into the forest. He encounters a birch maiden who, when he kisses her tree, transforms into a beautiful woman made of light. She accepts him despite his trollish appearance, and his love for sunlight transforms him, making him lose his troll-grey skin and become a handsome human forester.

title: The Troll Who Captured a Princess
summary: A classic Faroese folk tale collected by Jakob Jakobsen tells of a troll who lived in a cave and captured a princess to pick lice from his hair. Three brothers set out to rescue her. The elder two brothers failed, but the youngest—helped by the princess who threw him a ball of yarn to track the cave entrance—confronted the troll. The troll tried to trick the boy but was outwitted. When the troll gained entry to the king's house by picking the Faroese wooden lock (hvölpalás), the boy killed him. The treacherous brothers claimed credit, but the princess revealed the truth. The youngest brother married the princess and became king. Faroese trolls are creatures of darkness, large and ugly but easily outwitted.

title: The Troll's Daughter
summary: A story about a human's interaction with the daughter of a troll, exploring the tension and attraction between the human and supernatural worlds.

title: The Trolls and the Youngest Tomte
summary: In the world of Swedish tomtar (house gnomes), the youngest and most curious tomte listens with wonder as the older tomtar tell stories of their adventurous visits inside the trolls' mountain. The older tomtar warn of the dangers, but the youngest tomte's curiosity gets the better of him. He decides to venture into the trolls' mountain himself, despite the warnings. Inside the mountain, he discovers an open treasure chest guarded by two terrible trolls. The young tomte must use all his wits and courage to navigate the perilous troll realm and escape with his life. He narrowly avoids being captured and uses clever tricks to outsmart the trolls, who are large and powerful but not very intelligent. The story, beautifully illustrated by John Bauer (whose artwork for this tale is among his most celebrated), captures the tension between youthful curiosity and the wisdom of experience. The youngest tomte's adventure teaches respect for the dangers of the world while also celebrating the bravery required to explore the unknown. He eventually escapes with barely his life intact, learning a valuable lesson about the importance of heeding the warnings of elders.

title: The Trolls in Resslared
summary: Trolls in Resslared sabotage church bells until the Bishop of Skara consecrates one. The trolls then live in harmony with villagers borrowing food and repaying double. When new niggardly residents refuse a troll woman's requests their own provisions vanish and they are forced to leave.

title: The Trolls of Reynisdrangar
summary: Two trolls attempted to pull a great three-masted ship to the shore of the black sand beach of Reynisfjara. However, they were too slow, and as the sun rose over the horizon, the sunlight hit them, instantly turning them into the towering basalt sea stacks that still stand today as a warning against the power of the sun.

title: The Trolls of the Lava Fields
summary: The vast lava fields of the south are said to be the remains of trolls who were caught by the dawn. These creatures spent their nights carving the land and building fortresses, but the first light of the sun turned their skin to basalt, leaving them as permanent, frozen monuments in the stone.

title: The Trow's Fiddle
summary: A musician is lured into the hillside by the haunting music of a Trow, learning that the beauty of the spirit world comes with a heavy price.

title: The Trung Sisters Rebellion
summary: The legend of the Trung Sisters — Trung Trac and Trung Nhi — is Vietnam's most celebrated story of female heroism and national resistance. Born in the 1st century CE to a Lac lord in Me Linh, the sisters were educated in martial arts and military strategy by their father. When Trung Trac's husband Thi Sach was brutally executed by Chinese Han officials for plotting rebellion, the sisters raised an army of over 80,000 soldiers, many of them women, led by female generals. They stormed 65 Chinese-held citadels and drove the Han occupiers out of Vietnam, establishing an independent kingdom with Trung Trac as queen. They ruled for three years before the Han Emperor dispatched General Ma Yuan with a massive invasion force. Facing defeat, the sisters chose death over capture, drowning themselves in the Hat Giang River. Their sacrifice transformed them into national martyrs, and temples throughout Vietnam honor them as heroines. They are remembered as the embodiment of Vietnamese resistance against foreign domination and the spirit of Vietnamese womanhood.

title: The Tunche of the Jungle
summary: Deep in the Amazon, a shape-shifting spirit called the Tunche lures the unwary into the jungle with familiar voices, and those who follow are never seen again.

title: The Twelve Brothers
summary: A princess is born after twelve brothers who are cursed to become ravens if she speaks before her twelfth birthday. She must remain silent for twelve years to save them.

title: The Twelve Dancing Princesses
summary: Twelve princesses secretly dance every night in an enchanted underground kingdom, their secret revealed by a clever soldier.

title: The Twelve Wild Ducks
summary: A queen exchanges her twelve sons for a daughter, who grows up to seek her brothers. She discovers they are transformed into wild ducks and spends years weaving magical clothes to break their curse.

title: The Two Little Ones and Their Turkeys
summary: A Zuni story about two orphaned children who were cared for by a flock of wild turkeys. The turkeys provided them with feathers for warmth, eggs for food, and protection from danger. The children lived in harmony with the turkeys, learning the ways of the forest and the language of birds. When the children grew older, they faced pressure to return to human society, but the turkeys warned them about the dangers of human greed. Eventually, the children had to choose between the freedom of the wild and the community of humans. The story explores themes of adoption — being raised by non-human caretakers — and the tension between wild and civilized life. The turkeys, like the deer in other Zuni stories, represent the generosity of the natural world and the reciprocal obligations between humans and animals.

title: The Two Step-Sisters
summary: A kind-hearted girl is mistreated by her cruel stepmother and step-sisters, who force her to do all the hard work. Through her perseverance and the help of magical elements, she manages to overcome their malice, proving her inner beauty and virtue, and eventually finds her rightful place of happiness and honor.

title: The Two-Men-Who-Changed-Things (Coast Salish)
summary: The Coast Salish people of the Olympic Peninsula tell of Ho-ho-e-ap-bess, the Two-Men-Who-Changed-Things, who were the brothers of the Sun and the Moon. When the world was very young, there were no people, birds, or animals — only grass and sand and creatures that were neither animal nor human. The Two-Men-Who-Changed-Things came to earth to make it ready for a new race of people. They called all the creatures to them and transformed them: a thief became Seal, with shortened arms and tied legs so he had to catch his own fish; a creature with a long fishing spear and a white cape became Great Blue Heron, his spear becoming his bill and his cape becoming white neck feathers; a huge appetite couple became Raven and Crow, given strong beaks to tear food; Bluejay's uncooperative son became Mink, living on land and eating fish from the shore. They also created the yew tree to provide tough wood for bows. This cycle explains the origins of all Pacific Northwest animals through transformation.

title: The Two-Mouthed Woman of Fotouni
summary: A woman with a hidden second mouth behind her head feasts on her stepdaughter's hair each night, until the girl discovers the truth and turns the curse back upon its source.

title: The Ugly Duckling
summary: It was summertime, and the countryside was beautiful.. A mother duck was sitting on her nest, waiting for her eggs to hatch.

title: The Ulda's Old Mother
summary: A Sámi story about the matriarch of the Ulda. The underground people are rich, beautiful, and well-dressed, with reindeer of exceptional colors. All gold and silver under the earth belongs to them. They care for the bear in his winter den, feeding him invisibly. They sometimes swap their children for human babies. If you throw a metal object over a herd of Ulda reindeer that leave no tracks in snow, the herd becomes yours.

title: The Universal Basilisk
summary: A legendary serpent or dragon, the Basilisk is known as the king of serpents, with a gaze and breath so venomous it can kill anything it encounters.

title: The Universal Demon
summary: Demons are malevolent supernatural beings found in virtually every religious and mythological tradition, representing the forces of evil and chaos.

title: The Universal Dragon
summary: The dragon is the most widespread mythical creature, appearing in cultures from Europe to Asia as a powerful serpentine being associated with elemental forces.

title: The Universal Dwarf
summary: Dwarfs are small, skilled humanoid beings from Germanic and Norse mythology, master craftsmen who live underground and hoard treasure.

title: The Universal Fairy
summary: Fairies are nature spirits found in folklore worldwide, beings of great beauty and capricious nature who inhabit the spaces between worlds.

title: The Universal Ghost
summary: The ghost is a universal belief found in every culture: the spirit of a deceased person that remains among the living, usually due to unfinished business.

title: The Universal Giant
summary: Giants appear in the mythology of nearly every culture, representing the raw, untamed forces of nature and the primordial world.

title: The Universal Gryphon
summary: A hybrid creature with the body of a lion and the head and wings of an eagle, the Gryphon is a guardian of treasure and a symbol of divine power.

title: The Universal Kelpie
summary: A shapeshifting water spirit that appears as a horse, the kelpie lures riders onto its back before diving into the water to drown them.

title: The Universal Mermaid
summary: Half-woman, half-fish, the mermaid appears in seafaring cultures worldwide as a symbol of the ocean's beauty, danger, and mystery.

title: The Universal Nisse
summary: A household spirit of Scandinavian tradition, the Nisse is a small, bearded being who helps with chores but punishes laziness or disrespect.

title: The Universal Nix
summary: A water spirit of Germanic and Slavic folklore, the Nix is a shape-shifting being that lures people to their deaths in rivers and lakes.

title: The Universal Phoenix
summary: A mythical bird that cyclically regenerates by being consumed by fire and rising from its own ashes, symbolizing renewal and immortality.

title: The Universal Roc
summary: A colossal bird of prey from Middle Eastern legend, the Roc is so large it can carry an elephant in its talons.

title: The Universal Selkie
summary: A shapeshifting seal that sheds its skin to become human, the Selkie appears in the folklore of northern seafaring cultures.

title: The Universal Sphinx
summary: A mythical creature with a human head and a lion's body, the Sphinx is a guardian of mysteries who poses riddles to those who seek passage.

title: The Universal Spirit
summary: A generic spirit that embodies the animistic belief that all things in nature possess a spiritual essence, from rocks and trees to rivers and mountains.

title: The Universal Troll
summary: The troll appears in folklore across cultures as a giant, brutish being that dwells under bridges and in caves, a universal symbol of the wild and untamed.

title: The Universal Vampire
summary: Vampires are undead beings who feed on the blood of the living, appearing in the folklore of many cultures around the world.

title: The Universal Werewolf
summary: A human with the ability to transform into a wolf, the werewolf appears in folklore across Europe and beyond, representing the wildness within.

title: The Universal Witch
summary: Witches are practitioners of magic found in folklore worldwide, wielding supernatural power for good or ill through spells, potions, and communion with spirits.

title: The Unwelcome Guest
summary: A story exploring the laws of hospitality and the consequences of betrayal. A guest arrives unexpectedly and proceeds to cause chaos and distress, testing the patience, virtue, and generosity of the hosts in a challenging social dynamic.

title: The Urko of North Wij
summary: In the mountain of Urberg dwells the Urko a monster cow whose plowing created Lake Sommen. She is fettered by a horseshoe eating one hair from a cowhide each Christmas until the hairs run out and the world ends. If a king crosses Ydre she will break free having already killed King Frode.

title: The Valiant Chanticleer
summary: A childless woman is given an egg to hatch in her bosom, but out comes a cockerel. He grows enormous, ploughs the fields with a single ox, then sets off to win the king's daughter. He gathers a fox, wolf, bear, and lake as companions, defeats the king's geese, cattle, and horses, survives being roasted, and finally the princess wrings his neck—releasing a handsome prince.

title: The Valraven
summary: The Valravn is a Danish supernatural raven that can transform into a knight. It appears on battlefields, feasting on the dead, and can be bound by oaths.

title: The Vedda Creation Myth and Kande Yakka
summary: The Vedda people, Sri Lanka's indigenous inhabitants, trace their origin to the children of Prince Vijaya and Kuveni — a son and daughter abandoned in the wilderness who married each other and became the first Veddas. Their central deity is Kande Yakka, the chief of the ancestral spirits (Yakku), who governs hunting success. Before a hunt, Veddas invoke Kande Yakka and Bilindi Yakka; after a successful kill, a portion of meat is offered to them or bad luck follows. The Nae Yakka (spirits of recently deceased ancestors) inhabit hills, caves, and rocks. The Vedda shaman (kapurala) performs the Kiri Koraha ritual dance to become possessed by these spirits, who promise abundant yams, honey, and game.

title: the Veshtitza, the Witch of the Mountain
summary: A witch who lives in the highest mountain caves, stealing the milk from cows and the breath from children — and the only way to stop her is to leave a scissors open on the windowsill.

title: The Vila of Maglić
summary: A winged mountain spirit dances on the summit of Maglić in storms, and the shepherd who follows her song into the clouds returns with impossible knowledge — or does not return at all.

title: the Vila's Healing Song
summary: A Vila who fell in love with a mortal shepherd and healed his wounds with her song — but her song could only heal the body, not the loneliness of loving someone who would grow old and die.

title: the Vila, the Mountain Nymph
summary: A beautiful winged woman who dances on the mountain peaks at dawn, her song carrying across the valleys — and the shepherd who hears her dance will never love a mortal woman again.

title: The Village Magician
summary: A traveling magician arrives in a Yorkshire village performing impossible feats, only to be revealed as a mortal man whose greatest trick is convincing others to believe.

title: The Vishap on the Mountain of the Ark
summary: A primordial dragon guards the deepest waters beneath Mount Ararat, dreaming of a second Flood that will return the world to the chaos it once commanded.
themes: the balance between destruction and renewal

title: The Visiting Animals
summary: A grieving old man lives near a fjord to stay close to his son's grave. He is visited by three mysterious men of varying sizes and nose shapes. After he shows them hospitality and provides them with sole leather and walrus tusk, the visitors reveal their true natures and transform into a reindeer, a fox, and a hare, leaping away into the Arctic wilderness. The story emphasizes the value of kindness toward the unknown.

title: The Vittra – The Hidden People of Åland
summary: The vittra (singular: vitter) are an underground-dwelling people who live in a parallel civilization beneath the hills and meadows of Åland. Invisible to most humans, they have their own farms, livestock, and churches. They are known to do favors for humans who treat them with dignity and respect, but can become vengeful if their homes are disturbed — for example, by building a structure on their invisible property. The vittra are closely related to the Swedish 'de underjordiska' (the underground ones) and the Scandinavian 'huldrefolk' (hidden folk). Offerings of food, particularly porridge, were traditionally left for them. In the Sagenkartan records from Åland, many entries describe encounters with vittra who borrowed tools from farmers or requested that specific areas be left undisturbed. The tradition reflects a deep-seated belief that the land is shared with unseen inhabitants who must be respected.

title: The Vittra's Path
summary: A hardworking farmer discovers his prosperity is tied to the unseen world when he must move his entire house to avoid blocking the ancestral path of the vittra.

title: The Vodnik of the Mountain Stream
summary: A fisherman who has grown too greedy learns a lesson from the Vodnik, the water spirit who guards the mountain streams and punishes those who take more than they need.
themes: the Vodnik as judge and keeper

title: The Vodyanoy of the Volga
summary: A bearded water spirit with green skin drags the unwary beneath the Volga, and the only way to escape is to throw a black rooster into the river.

title: The Voice of the Witz
summary: A young Maya priest enters a sacred cave to seek a vision from the mountain spirit, but the Witz demands a price he did not expect.

title: The Voyages of Kiviuk
summary: The epic adventures of Kiviuk, a supernatural hero who travels across the Arctic encountering spirits, monsters, and divine beings. His journeys involve solving riddles and completing impossible tasks. Kiviuk represents the ideal of Inuit resilience, courage, and curiosity.

title: The Wail of Nya-Nya Bulembu
summary: A forest monster that mimics the cries of lost children lures travelers into the deep woods, where the boundary between the living and the dead grows thin.

title: The Wandering Jew
summary: A man cursed to wander the earth until the Second Coming after taunting Christ, becoming a timeless witness to human history.

title: The Warrior Suitor of Moki (Hopi)
summary: A Zuni story about a warrior from Zuni who traveled to the land of the Hopi (called Moki in Zuni) to win a bride. The warrior had to prove his worth through feats of strength, courage, and skill. He faced challenges set by the Hopi elders, including hunting dangerous game, competing in races and games, and demonstrating his knowledge of proper ceremonial conduct. Through his bravery and skill — and with the help of the war gods — he succeeded in all the trials and won the maiden. The marriage between the Zuni warrior and the Hopi woman established ties between the two nations. The story reflects historical relationships between the Zuni and Hopi peoples, who share similar cultural roots and maintain trade and marriage connections. It also illustrates the Zuni values of courage, perseverance, and cross-cultural respect.

title: The Water Dragon of Kupa
summary: In the silver days of old Croatia, along the winding Kupa River where the waters whispered through valleys of green, there lived a family of seven children.

title: The Water Goblin of the Vltava
summary: An ambitious fiddler trades his soul for the secret of perfect music, only to become a permanent trophy of a river spirit.

title: The Water Serpent of Tornedalen
summary: A mythical water serpent from the Tornedalen region, known in both Sámi and Meänkieli traditions as Čáhcegearpmaš. This huge serpent lives in lakes and rivers and frightens people away from fishing. It embodies the dangers of Arctic waters. The tradition is preserved in contemporary Sámi children's radio programs.

title: The Waters of Aral
summary: A young shepherd discovers that the mountain lakes harbor ancient water-spirits who guard the balance between the highland villages and the lowland deserts.

title: The Weaving of Ix Chel
summary: The moon goddess Ix Chel weaves the fabric of fate on her backstrap loom, but when she unravels her work in grief, the world nearly drowns.

title: The Wee Wee Man
summary: A traveler meets a tiny man who shows him a different world, teaching him the value of secrets.

title: The Weeping Nun
summary: A nun who committed suicide now wanders a church, weeping for her unborn child—her spirit will rest only when someone acknowledges her.

title: The Weeping Stones
summary: In the remote Isles of the Hebrides, particularly upon the wild shores of Skye and the distant Outer Islands, there are stones that weep.

title: The Weeping Sword
summary: Kitsune — the fox spirit of Japanese folklore — is one of the most complex and contradictory creatures in world mythology.

title: The Weeping Woman
summary: A spectral woman in flowing white haunts the Danish coastline, appearing as a sorrowful omen of impending shipwrecks and oceanic tragedies.

title: The Weeping Woman of Lake Atitlán
summary: A Tz'utujil woman, betrayed by her husband, drowns her children in Lake Atitlán and is condemned to wander its shores forever, weeping for what she destroyed.

title: The Wendigo
summary: The cannibal spirit of Algonquian legend, a gaunt creature of insatiable hunger.

title: The Wendigo Hunt
summary: A hunting party in the deep winter forest encounters a wendigo — and learns that the real monster is not the spirit, but the hunger that made it.

title: The Wendigo: Cannibal Spirit
summary: A frozen spirit of greed—it possesses humans who resort to cannibalism, turning them into monsters of hunger.

title: The Werehyena of Bangui
summary: In the growing city of Bangui, a man discovers his quiet neighbor is a werehyena who shifts form at the new moon, and must decide whether to expose the creature or honor the old compact that keeps the peace.

title: The Werewolf
summary: A prince cursed to become a werewolf roams the wilderness until a princess's self-sacrificing love and courage break the spell. Rooted in the ancient Teutonic belief in werewolves, this tale from Uppland emphasizes redemption through love.

title: The Werewolf Transformation
summary: A Sámi shape-shifting legend where people are turned into wolves. The transformation can be reversed only if the werewolf does not taste the blood of a reindeer, or if they are given cooked food. This reflects Sámi beliefs about the permeability between human and animal identities, and the importance of reindeer in maintaining one's humanity.

title: The Whale Who Sang the World Awake
summary: Before the island existed, a Great Whale sang a song that called the land up from the deep, and its echo still guides fishermen home.

title: The Whistle of El Silbón
summary: A giant spirit wanders the llanos at night whistling a tune that rises and falls with the wind, carrying a sack of bones on his back and hunting the men who have wronged their fathers.

title: The White Bead Maiden's Marriage to the Sun
summary: In this Navajo story, White Bead Maiden (Yoołgaii Asdzą́ą́) was sought in marriage by the Sun. The Sun, disguised as a handsome warrior, courted the maiden. After many trials, she agreed to marry him and traveled to his house in the eastern horizon. The Sun's house was a square room of turquoise and white shell with the four directions represented. White Bead Maiden bore the Sun's children, who became the Hero Twins. However, the Sun already had another wife, and tensions arose in their celestial household. White Bead Maiden eventually returned to earth, where she was transformed into Changing Woman, the central female deity of Navajo religion who governs the cycles of life, seasons, and time itself. This story establishes the sacred lineage from the Sun to the Navajo people and the deep connection between celestial and earthly realms.

title: The White Beaver Ceremony
summary: Among the Chawi band of the Pawnee South Bands, the White Beaver ceremony served the same purpose as the Skidi's Spring Awakening ceremony—renewing life and ensuring fertility. However, instead of focusing on corn, the White Beaver ceremony revitalized hibernating animals. The white beaver was a sacred animal associated with the water spirits. The ceremony involved elaborate rituals, songs, and the use of sacred bundles. This difference between the Skidi (celestial-focused) and South Bands (animal-focused) reflects the two approaches to Pawnee spirituality: the Skidi looked to the stars while the South Bands relied on animal spirits as intermediaries.

title: The White Dove
summary: A tale of purity, hope, and peace represented by a white dove, set within a traditional folk context of kindness and reward.

title: The White Mountain Apache Creation
summary: In the White Mountain Apache creation myth from Noze (recorded in 1910), a maiden went to the top of a high mountain where the rays of the rising Sun first struck. She raised her skirt and the breath of the Sun entered her. She went up the mountain four mornings, and four times the Sun's breath entered her. This unmarried girl became pregnant, and the people gossiped about her. She gave birth to Naiyenezgani (Monster Slayer) and Tobatc'istcini (Child of the Water). The twins grew rapidly and were given weapons by their father the Sun. They killed the monsters threatening the people, including Naiye' who devoured humans. After proving their power by cutting a tree in half with a thrown weapon, they assured the people that no more monsters would trouble them. They established that a messenger would circle the earth in one day to keep them informed. The twins then resumed their roles as protectors of the people and warriors against evil.

title: The White Snake
summary: A white snake spirit transforms into a beautiful woman and marries a human man. A Buddhist monk discovers her true nature and traps her under Thunder Peak Pagoda.

title: The White Stag
summary: In the deep forests of Hungary, where the Carpathian Mountains rose like the bones of ancient giants, there lived a white stag unlike any other.

title: The Wicked Prince
summary: A tale of a prince whose inherent cruelty and lack of empathy lead to his eventual downfall and isolation from others.

title: The Widow's Son
summary: The youngest son of a widow is underestimated by his brothers and father, but possesses a kindness and curiosity that leads him to magical discoveries. He eventually saves his family from ruin through his generosity and bravery.

title: The Wild Swans
summary: Far away, in a land where swallows fly when winter comes, there lived a king who had eleven sons and one daughter named Elisa.

title: The Will-o'-the-Wisp
summary: A mysterious floating light that leads travelers astray in bogs and marshes, serving as a warning against following false promises.

title: The Windigo Baby
summary: A newly married couple had a baby boy who seemed normal until one day, while still in his cradleboard, he spoke to his parents saying he would visit the Sky Spirit. That night, the baby vanished from his cradleboard. The parents found tiny tracks leading to the lake, then enormous footprints beyond. The child had transformed into a Windigo, a cannibalistic ice monster. The creature walked across the lake toward the Sky Spirit's home, which was protected by fifty Thunderers who threw lightning bolts at approaching threats. When the Windigo approached, the Thunderers fought it with lightning, finally striking it dead. It fell like a great tree. When the people chopped it up, they found it was made of ice, and in the center was a tiny infant six inches long — the original baby — with a hole in its head where the lightning had struck.

title: The Wise Fool of Somali Folklore
summary: Somali folklore features a beloved character known as the 'wise fool' — a simpleton whose apparent foolishness conceals profound wisdom.
