In one popular tale, a poor man was mocked by villagers for talking to rocks. 'Stupid man,' they laughed, 'rocks cannot hear!' When a terrible drought came, the wise fool walked to a great boulder and asked it where water could be found. Following a strange impulse, he dug beneath the rock and found an underground spring that saved the village. When others tried to imitate him and dug under other rocks, they found nothing. The wise fool explained: 'The rock did not speak with words, but with silence. I listened to what was around the rock — the green moss, the damp earth, the birds that gathered there.' The story teaches that wisdom comes not from imitating others but from observing nature with patience and humility.

title: The Witchcraft Spirits of Lipangula
summary: A young Makonde girl discovers that the inherited witchcraft flowing through her bloodline is not a curse but a responsibility, when the spirits of uchawi choose her to restore balance to a village torn by fear and suspicion.
themes: balance between seen and unseen worlds
the nature of witchcraft as neutral force
coming of age through spiritual initiation

title: The Wolf and the Seven Kids
summary: There was once an old mother goat who lived with her seven little kids in a cozy cottage at the edge of a great forest.

title: The Wolf's Wedding: The Moroccan Rainbow Legend
summary: A North African folk explanation for the rainbow that is widespread across the Maghreb, among both Arabic and Berber-speaking populations. When a rainbow appears in the sky—especially when rain falls while the sun shines—it is said to be 'the marriage of the jackal' or 'the wolf's wedding' (tameγra bbuššen in Berber, 'ers ed-dib' in Arabic). According to the legend, a wolf once promised his family he would marry, but on condition that it take place on a stormy day during which the sun shines in defiance of rain, forcing the 'sky's bride' (the rainbow) to appear. The wolf believed this was impossible, but one day the paradoxical conditions coincided, the rainbow appeared, and the wolf was forced to honor his promise. In some Berber versions, the rainbow is the scarf of the jackal's bride. In Tunisia (among the Matmata), children sing during rain-calling rituals: 'When the sun is at its zenith, it rains without a cloud. O my aunt the rain, falls, falls... It's the marriage of the Jackal.' The story beautifully encodes ecological knowledge in mythological form.

title: The Woman Who Fell from the Sky
summary: In the Sky World above the earth, a pregnant woman named Atsi'tsaká:ion (Mature Flower) fell through a hole created when the Great Tree of Life was uprooted. As she descended, she grasped seeds from the tree. Water birds saw her falling and caught her, placing her on the back of the Great Turtle. The muskrat dove to the ocean floor and brought up mud, which she spread on the turtle's back. She danced in a circle, and the mud grew into the land known as Turtle Island. She planted the seeds from the Sky World, and the first plants grew. This is the Haudenosaunee account of how the earth was formed on the back of the Great Turtle.

title: The Woman Who Married a Buffalo
summary: A Lakota woman was picking berries when a buffalo bull approached her. To her surprise, he spoke and asked her to be his wife. She agreed and went to live with the buffalo people, where she learned their ways and language. She gave birth to a son who was half-human, half-buffalo. One day, her human brothers came hunting and nearly killed the buffalo people. The woman pleaded with her buffalo husband to spare them. In return, she agreed to return to her human family. Before leaving, she gave her son a sacred buffalo robe that would protect him. The story explains the special relationship between the Lakota and the buffalo.

title: The Wonderful Horns of the Orphan Boy
summary: A Xhosa boy whose mother had died was mistreated by his stepmothers and decided to leave home, riding on his father's ox. The ox fought and defeated a fierce bull from a passing herd. Later the ox told the boy it would die fighting another bull and instructed him to break off its horns. After the ox's death, the boy discovered that striking the right horn produced food and drink, while the left horn could store it. A greedy man tried to steal the horns but failed. The boy eventually reached a village where the chief's daughter married him, and the horns never ceased to provide abundance. This story teaches about perseverance, resourcefulness, and the rewards of kindness despite adversity.

title: The Wonderful Tar-Baby
summary: Brer Fox fashions a doll made of tar and turpentine and sets it in the road to trap Brer Rabbit. When Brer Rabbit greets the silent Tar-Baby and receives no reply, he grows angry and strikes it, getting his paw stuck. He strikes with the other paw, then kicks, and finally butts with his head—each limb becoming hopelessly ensnared in the sticky tar. Brer Fox emerges from hiding, delighted at his capture, but Brer Rabbit's clever pleading ultimately allows him to escape when he begs not to be thrown into the briar patch—the one place he was born and bred to thrive.

title: The Xan of Mountain Passes
summary: A shepherd encounters a Xan, a restless mountain ghost, and learns why the dead sometimes refuse to leave the high places they loved in life.

title: The Xtabai of Temptress Creek
summary: A beautiful woman lures men into the jungle on moonlit nights, but those who follow the Xtabai discover too late that her beauty is a veil over ancient hunger, and the jungle keeps what she claims.
themes: the jungle as a living force

title: The Yacumama of the Río Napo
summary: A massive water serpent dwells in the deepest pools of the Amazon, swallowing canoes whole and guarding the jungle's hidden treasures.

title: The Yacuruna and the Fisherman's Wife
summary: A water people abduct a fisherman's wife, and he must journey to their underwater city to bring her back before she forgets the surface world.

title: The Yaguarón's River Curse
summary: A cat-like river monster with glowing eyes drags livestock and children beneath the brown waters of the Paraguay River, and only the medicine man's song can release them.

title: the Yagwanggwi, the Night Watcher
summary: A shadowy figure that watches over sleeping villages, its glowing eyes visible from the hilltops — because in Korea, someone must guard the night.

title: The Yap Stone Money Origin
summary: Yapese legend tells of the origin of rai stones, the massive stone money for which Yap is famous. According to oral tradition, a legendary navigator named Anagumang led an expedition by raft and canoe to the islands of Palau, where the Yapese discovered limestone. Anagumang had his men carve the limestone into circular discs resembling the moon. The largest stones weighed several tons and required risky voyages of hundreds of kilometers across the open ocean. The stones were brought back to Yap on rafts, and many were lost at sea during storms. The value of each stone was determined not only by its size but by the difficulty of the voyage and the number of lives lost in its transport. These stone discs served as currency and are still used today for ceremonial exchanges, with ownership transferred verbally while the stones remain in place.

title: The Yara-ma-yha-who: The Vampire Spirit
summary: The Yara-ma-yha-who is a vampiric spirit from Aboriginal Australian Dreaming legends, particularly in the mythology of the Yuin people of southeastern Australia. This creature is described as a small, red-skinned being standing about four feet tall with an oversized head, large mouth, and long skinny limbs. Each of its hands and feet ends in suckers like those of an octopus. The Yara-ma-yha-who lives in fig trees and drops down on unsuspecting travelers, using its suckers to drain their blood. After feeding, the creature swells up and then drops the victim, who wakes up weaker but alive. The process repeats each time the victim passes beneath the tree, and with each encounter the victim grows shorter and redder until eventually becoming a Yara-ma-yha-who themselves. The legend reinforces the dangers of traveling alone through unfamiliar bush territory and serves as a moral warning about the consequences of foolish behavior.

title: The Yeti (Migoi) Legends
summary: Tibetan legends of the Yeti (Migoi or Migyur, meaning 'wild man'), a powerful apelike creature said to inhabit the high Himalayas. In Tibetan folklore, the Yeti is not merely a physical creature but a spiritual guardian of the mountains, often associated with mountain gods like Nyenchen Thanglha. Some traditions describe it as a flesh-and-blood being, others as a supernatural creature that can become invisible at will. Stories tell of encounters with the Yeti by pilgrims, herders, and travelers in remote mountain passes, where it must be appeased with offerings. Buddhist lamas have traditionally performed rituals to pacify the Yeti's potentially dangerous nature. The legend has been adopted into Western popular culture but remains a living part of Tibetan Himalayan folklore.

title: The Yeti: Abominable Snowman of the Himalayas
summary: The Yeti (from Sherpa 'yeh-teh', meaning 'cliff dweller') is a legendary ape-like creature said to inhabit the Himalayan mountains of Nepal, Tibet, and Bhutan. In Sherpa and Tibetan Buddhist tradition, Yetis are more than cryptids — they are spiritual beings that act as protectors of sacred valleys. Ancient Tibetan texts like the Mani Kabum recount that humans and Yetis share a common ancestry, born from the union of a compassionate monkey (Avalokiteshvara) and a mountain ogress. Some descendants became humans, others remained wild as Yetis. The Khumjung Monastery in Nepal's Khumbu region preserves a famous Yeti scalp, said to have belonged to a creature that served the lama Sangwa Dorje by bringing water and firewood. In 1974, a Yeti reportedly attacked a yak herder in Machermo Valley, killing livestock.

title: The Yeti: The Abominable Snowman of the Himalayas
summary: A mysterious ape-like creature haunts the high Himalayas, seen only by those with pure hearts.

title: The Youth and His Eagle
summary: A Zuni story about a young boy who raised an eagle and developed a deep spiritual bond with the bird. The eagle became his protector and provider, bringing him gifts from the sky world. However, jealous members of the village conspired against the boy and his eagle. The eagle, being a sacred creature connected to the Sun Father, possessed supernatural powers and could communicate with the spirit world. Through his relationship with the eagle, the boy learned important spiritual lessons about power, responsibility, and the consequences of greed. The eagle eventually returned to the sky world, but it left the boy with sacred knowledge that benefited his people. The story emphasizes the Zuni belief in the spiritual power of birds and the importance of maintaining proper relationships with animal spirits.

title: The Yule Lads' Mischief
summary: Thirteen brothers, the sons of Grýla the ogress and Leppalúði, descend from the mountains each December. Each Lad has a unique personality and a specific prank, such as stealing sausages or licking windows, terrorizing children and farmers before Christmas Eve.

title: The Yule Stállu (Juovlastállu)
summary: A terrifying Christmas tradition from Finnmark and northern Troms. Juovlastállu is the Yule giant who punishes children who misbehave at Christmas. He drives a sled pulled by mice or lemmings. Families must sweep the area around the home clean so the sled doesn't get stuck, and must leave water outside for him. If he doesn't get water, he becomes enraged and may suck blood from humans. He whistles sharply in the wind. His pipe or whistle can be dangerous to hearing.

title: The Yumboes: The Fairy Spirits of Senegal
summary: Small, silver-skinned fairy beings dance under the moonlight on the coast of Senegal.

title: The Zambur of the Valley
summary: An ancient animal-spirit that haunts the warm valleys of southern Tajikistan teaches hunters the difference between taking what is needed and taking what is wanted.

title: The Zana: Benevolent Fairies of the Albanian Mountains
summary: Beautiful mountain fairies protect lost travelers and bless newborns with gifts of beauty and talent.

title: The Zar of the Red Sea Coast
summary: A woman in the coastal town of Massawa is possessed by a Zar spirit who demands music, dance, and recognition, and her family must learn that some illnesses cannot be cured by medicine alone.

title: The Zar Queen of Keren
summary: In the western city of Keren, the Zar spirits are led by a queen who selects her court from among the living, and a Tigre man who refuses her summons discovers that pride is the most dangerous offering of all.

title: The Zar Spirit Possession Cult
summary: The Zar cult is a widespread spirit possession tradition found throughout Sudan, Egypt, and the Horn of Africa, blending pre-Islamic African beliefs with Islamic Sufi practices. According to tradition, zar spirits are invisible beings created from smokeless fire who can possess humans, causing illness, infertility, or psychological distress. The spirits are organized into 'nations' reflecting historical periods: Darawish (Sufi holy men), Pashawat (Ottoman nobility), Khawajat (Europeans), Habbash (Ethiopians), Arabs, and Zirug (Black African warriors). Each spirit has specific demands for clothing, perfumes, colors, and foods. The possessed person must undergo a initiation ceremony (usually involving drumming, dancing, and trance) to appease the spirit and establish a lifelong relationship of mutual accommodation. The cult is predominantly female and has been interpreted by scholars as a form of resistance to patriarchal structures, allowing women to make demands through their possessing spirits that would otherwise be socially impossible. Despite condemnation by orthodox Islamic authorities, zar remains widely practiced.

title: the Zduhać's Battle in the Clouds
summary: Two Zduhaći from rival villages battle above the clouds during a hailstorm, their punches becoming thunderbolts — and the villagers below can only pray and wait for the sky to choose a winner.

title: the Zduhać, the Weather Warrior
summary: A man who can leave his body while sleeping to fight storms in the sky, battling other Zduhaći to protect his village from hail and lightning — because in Montenegro, the weather is not natural, it is earned.

title: The Zin Who Married a Fisherman
summary: A Songhai fisherman on the Niger River falls in love with a Zin, a water spirit of terrible beauty, and must choose between the world of water and the world of men.

title: The Zombi: The Living Dead of Haitian Vodou
summary: A bokor sorcerer raises the dead to serve as mindless slaves in Haitian folklore.

title: The Zombie Creation Myth of Haitian Vodou
summary: The zombie (zonbi) originates from Haitian folklore, where it is a dead body reanimated through magic by a bokor sorcerer. In Vodou belief, a person has two souls: the ti bon ange (little good angel) and the gros bon ange (big good angel). The bokor captures the ti bon ange, the essence of personality and consciousness, bottling it while the body becomes a soulless slave. The Bizango secret societies are said to have used zombification as social control, poisoning individuals who transgressed codes and then providing antidotes to leave them in a pliant, obedient state. The zombie metaphor reflects the terror of enslavement — being alive but without will or identity. The word comes from Kikongo 'nzumbi' meaning spirit of a dead person.

title: The Zuni People Emerge into Daylight
summary: In Ruth Benedict's version of the Zuni emergence, people dwelt in total darkness deep in the fourth world. Awonawilona, the Sun, took pity on them. His two sons, the bow priests, located the opening to the fourth world in the southwest and led the people upward. They planted seeds that grew into pine, spruce, silver spruce, and aspen. Each tree became a prayer stick stretched to the next world. The people climbed through four worlds, each time finding themselves still incomplete. They had no mouths, anuses, or fingers; their hands and feet were webbed, and they had horns and tails. In the first world (the one below daylight), they could finally see — they were covered in filth and slime. The bow priests cut mouths into their faces with a knife sharpened on a red whetstone, then cut anuses with a soot-blackened knife. They cut fingers and toes, and finally removed the people's horns and tails. When the people emerged into sunlight at last, they cried from the brightness, and sunflowers grew where their tears fell.

title: The Älvor – Meadow Elves of the Åland Archipelago
summary: The älvor (elves) are beautiful, otherworldly female beings who dance in the meadows and misty fields of Åland, particularly at dawn and dusk. Their dancing leaves behind 'älvringar' (fairy rings) — circles of flattened grass or mushrooms where the ground is forever enchanted. Humans who interrupt their dances may be lured into their realm, losing all sense of time and place. Those who step into an älvring may become invisible to other humans or fall into a sleep from which they cannot wake. In Swedish-speaking Åland tradition, the älvor are skilled in magic and illusions. They are sometimes described as half-transparent spirits, closely linked to the coastal mists that roll in from the Baltic. The figure of the älva is related to the pre-Christian female deities called dís (plural dísir), powerful spirits associated with fate and protection. Even today, the word 'dis' remains a synonym for mist or very light rain in Swedish.

title: Theyyam — The Dance of the Gods in Kerala
summary: Theyyam is an ancient ritualistic performance tradition of northern Kerala where performers transform into living deities through elaborate makeup, costumes, and trance-dance. Each Theyyam tells a specific mythological story. Among the most famous is the legend of Muchilottu Bhagavathi, a goddess born from the fire of a warrior's fury who had to be tamed by a Brahmin. Another central legend is that of Kathivanoor Veeran, a low-caste man who attained divinity through his valor and devotion. The most popular Theyyam, Vishnumoorthy, reenacts the story of the Brahmin Kannappan who offered his own eye to the god Shiva's lingam when he saw it weeping. Theyyam embodies the Dravidian spiritual tradition where deities emerge from the community itself, often from marginalized castes, challenging the hierarchies of temple-based Brahminical Hinduism.

title: Thoth
summary: In the grand hall of judgment that lies at the heart of the Duat, the Egyptian underworld, there sits a figure of profound importance.

title: Three Billy Goats Gruff
summary: Three billy goat brothers use their wits and varying sizes to outsmart a hungry troll guarding a bridge, proving that cleverness can overcome brute strength.

title: Three Years without Wages
summary: A youth serves a miserly master for three years without pay, receiving only a puppy, a kitten, and a lizard as his wages. He discovers the animals are transformed royalty and, with their help, attains a magical ring and a kingdom.

title: Thumbelina
summary: There once lived a woman who wanted a tiny child more than anything in the world.

title: Thunderbird and Whale (Kwakwaka'wakw)
summary: The epic struggle between Thunderbird (Tseiqami) and Whale is one of the most important myths of the Pacific Northwest, found across Kwakwaka'wakw and Nuu-chah-nulth traditions. Thunderbird is a massive supernatural bird whose wingbeats cause thunder and whose eyes flash lightning. He hunts whales for food, plunging from the sky to seize them in his talons. In the Kwakwaka'wakw version recorded by Franz Boas, the battle takes place between Thunderbird and the leader of the animals, who retaliates against Thunderbird for carrying away one of his sons. The leader raises an army carried in an artificial whale. In the great battle at the village, Thunderbird's four children (named One-Whale-Carrier among them) are drowned, and Thunderbird himself is killed, survived only by a nine-month-old infant in the cradle. Some versions tell of Thunderbird dropping the whale to create thunder, or of the whale escaping and causing earthquakes and tidal waves. Geologists believe this myth may describe the 1700 Cascadia earthquake and tsunami.

title: Ti Lobo and Chibinho
summary: The cunning little goat Chibinho repeatedly outsmarts the greedy wolf Ti Lobo, proving that wit is more powerful than appetite.

title: Ti Malice and Bouki: The Trickster and the Fool
summary: Ti Malice and Uncle Bouki are paired characters in Haitian folklore, representing the split of the Anansi trickster archetype. Ti Malice is smart, cunning, and guileful, while Uncle Bouki is hardworking but greedy and foolish. In one classic tale, Bouki hears an old woman cry 'Ay-yai!' after biting her lip, and mistakes it for the name of a delicious food. He rushes to the market asking for 'ay-yai' and is laughed at. Ti Malice then fills a bag with random items and sells it to Bouki as 'ay-yai,' teaching him a lesson. The characters originated in West African oral traditions where Bouki is a hyena (from Fulani/Wolof 'bouki') and Malice is a hare called Leuk in Senegal.

title: Tiddalik the Frog
summary: The greedy frog who drank all the water, and had to be made to laugh to release it.

title: Tiddalik the Thirsty Frog
summary: In an Australian Aboriginal Dreamtime story attributed to the Gunaikurnai people of Gippsland, Victoria, Tiddalik the frog awoke one morning with an insatiable thirst and drank all the fresh water in the world. Lakes, rivers, and waterholes dried up, and creatures and plants everywhere began to die. The other animals conspired to make Tiddalik release the water. A wise old owl coordinated their efforts, and Nabunum the eel performed comical dances, tying himself in ridiculous shapes. Tiddalik began to laugh, and as he laughed, all the water rushed out of his mouth, replenishing the lakes, swamps, and rivers. In the original versions, the resulting flood caused many to drown, with others stranded on islands until Borun the pelican rescued them, and the pelican's feathers changed from all-black to black-and-white as a result.

title: Tiggak the Shaman
summary: Tiggak is a powerful angakkoq (shaman) who becomes lazy and neglects his duties, causing friction with his brothers-in-law. During a harsh winter, the group becomes stranded on dangerous ice floes. Tiggak's supernatural foresight and magical abilities become the group's only hope for survival. By invoking charms and navigating the treacherous landscape with mystical guidance, he saves his companions, proving that his wisdom is indispensable despite his personal failings.

title: Tikta'Liktak's Journey Home
summary: A young hunter becomes stranded on a drifting ice floe. The story chronicles his struggle for survival and encounters with Arctic spirits. His return home is a testament to navigation skills and the spiritual connection between a hunter and his homeland.

title: Timun Mas (The Golden Cucumber)
summary: A Javanese folktale about a childless couple who pray desperately for a child. An ogre-like giant named Buto Ijo grants their wish by giving them a magical cucumber seed, which grows into a cucumber containing a baby girl named Timun Mas (Golden Cucumber). The giant promises to return when she is seventeen to claim her as his meal. As the deadline approaches, a kind hermit gives the parents four magical items: cucumber seeds, needles, salt, and shrimp paste. When the giant comes for Timun Mas, she flees, scattering each item behind her — they transform into a cucumber forest, bamboo thicket, ocean, and a boiling sea of shrimp paste. The giant drowns, and Timun Mas lives freely.

title: Tin Hinan, Mother of the Tuareg
summary: Tin Hinan—meaning 'she of the tents' or 'mother of us all'—is the legendary ancestress and queen of the Tuareg people. According to oral tradition, she was a 4th-century princess who fled north Africa with her servant Takamat, riding a white camel across the Sahara. Near perishing in the wilderness, they stumbled upon grain in desert anthills, which saved their lives. Tin Hinan settled in the Hoggar Mountains of southern Algeria, where she became the first queen (Tamenokalt) of the Tuareg. She had three daughters who became the ancestral mothers of the Tuareg nobility, while Takamat's descendants became the commoners. Her monumental tomb was discovered in 1925 at Abalessa, Algeria, containing the skeleton of a woman buried with gold and silver jewelry—bridging legend and historical reality. The Tuareg still honor her as the matriarch of their people.

title: Tin Hinan: The Queen of the Tuareg
summary: A legendary Berber queen fled Roman persecution and established the matrilineal traditions of the Tuareg people.

title: Tippafossur and the Killing of Jógvan
summary: A grim legend within the Ormur cycle. Jógvan, a farmer from Oyri, caught Ormur of Skála stealing his sheep and attacked him. Miraculously, Jógvan overpowered the huge Ormur and held him down, calling for his son to bring a knife. But the son, terrified of Ormur, fled and hid at the Tippafossur gorge. Ormur, pinned and fearing death, promised the devil a piece of his little finger in exchange for strength. Suddenly gaining supernatural power, Ormur broke free and killed Jógvan. He then found the boy at Tippafossur and killed him too. Later, in his sleep, Ormur muttered: 'The clothes lie under the corn and the bodies under Tippafossur.' His farmhands heard, found the evidence, and informed the authorities.

title: Tiramakhan Traore Conquers Kaabu (Mande)
summary: General Tiramakhan Traore, Sundiata Keita's greatest military commander, was sent to conquer the Senegambia region after the king of Jolof insulted Sundiata by confiscating his horses and sending him a skin to make shoes. Tiramakhan marched his army through the Gambia River valley, defeating kingdom after kingdom. The greatest battle was against King Kikikor of the Bainuk people in Kaabu (Guinea-Bissau). Kikikor was a powerful sorcerer who could turn into a beast, but Tiramakhan was protected by his Mandinka gris-gris (protective charms). After a fierce battle, Tiramakhan killed Kikikor with a spear blessed by Sundiata himself. Kaabu was annexed into the Mali Empire and became a Mandinka kingdom ruled by Tiramakhan's descendants, the Ñaanco dynasty, for over 600 years until 1867.

title: Tirawa Creates the Universe
summary: Tirawa (Atíʼas Tirawa), 'Our Father Above,' was the supreme creator god of the Pawnee. He created the universe and placed the Morning Star in the East and the Evening Star in the West. The Morning Star, a male warrior god, was created first. The female Evening Star resisted the divine plan to create humankind, so Morning Star fought and overcame forces in the western sky with his fireball to mate with her. The first human thus created was a girl. Tirawa taught the Pawnee tattooing, fire-building, hunting, agriculture, speech, clothing, religious rituals, and sacrifice. His wife was Atira (Mother Corn), goddess of the Earth.

title: Tizan the Illness Bringer
summary: A restless spirit called Tizan wanders the villages at dusk, laying curses of sickness on those who have wronged their neighbors or spoken ill of the dead.

title: Tlanuwa: The Giant Raptor (Cherokee)
summary: Tlanuwa is a giant mythological bird of prey with feathers made of impenetrable metal. This massive raptor could carry off humans and even small deer in its talons. Its feathers were said to be sharp as knives and could be launched as projectiles. The Tlanuwa lived in the highest mountain peaks and remote cliffs. In Cherokee legend, the Tlanuwa sometimes battled the Uktena serpent, their ancient enemy. The birds were also known to fight against humans who invaded their territory. The Tlanuwa appears in stories from many Southeastern tribes including the Creek and Natchez, suggesting it was a widespread figure in the regional mythology. Some accounts describe it as a benevolent protector spirit of the Cherokee people.

title: To-Kabinana and To-Karvuvu: The Twin Gods of New Britain
summary: Two divine brothers create the world through wisdom and folly, explaining the origins of good and evil.

title: To-Kabinana and To-Karvuvu: The Wise and Foolish Brothers
summary: In the mythology of New Britain (Papua New Guinea), the two culture hero brothers To-Kabinana (wise) and To-Karvuvu (foolish) were created when an old woman scratched her arms with pandanus strips while wading in the sea, and the two bloodied strips swelled into boys. To-Kabinana created good things for humanity while To-Karvuvu's attempts went wrong, bringing evil and harmful things into the world, including cannibalism. To-Kabinana climbed a coconut tree and threw two unripe coconuts to the ground, which burst and became his wives. When To-Karvuvu tried to imitate this he threw the nuts point-downward, creating women with flat ugly noses. Their stories explain the origin of many of the world's imperfections.

title: Tobacco Society: Chief No Vitals Discovers Tobacco
summary: The Crow people believe that tobacco was first discovered by Chief No Vitals at Devils Lake in eastern North Dakota. The Creator instructed him to seek the sacred plant, telling him that the worship of tobacco would help the Crow honor God and maintain their connection to the spirit world. Chief No Vitals found the plant and brought it back to his people, establishing the Tobacco Society (Bacu'sua). The society ensures that all rites and rituals for cultivating tobacco are performed correctly. Smoking tobacco is believed to carry prayers directly to God, as the smoke ascends to the heavens. The sacred pipe society uses tobacco daily to maintain closeness with the Creator.

title: Tokoloshe: The Mischievous Water Trickster
summary: The Tokoloshe is a dwarf-like water sprite in Zulu mythology, a small hairy humanoid summoned by witches and sorcerers to carry out evil deeds. It can become invisible at will and causes illness, bad luck, and misfortune. Many South Africans still believe in the Tokoloshe and take precautions such as raising their beds on bricks to prevent the creature from reaching them at night. The Tokoloshe embodies the fear of witchcraft and unseen malevolent forces, serving as a warning against meddling with dark powers.

title: Tokoloshe: The Water Imp
summary: A mischievous, malevolent water spirit that can only be seen by certain people—and is used to frighten children.

title: Tom Thumb
summary: In the days of the great King Arthur, there lived a poor ploughman named Thomas and his wife.

title: Tom Totherhouse
summary: A clever youth enters into a wager with a woman who is having an affair with a neighbor while her husband is deaf. Through a series of ingenious tricks and psychological manipulations, he forces the woman to confess her infidelity, winning the wager and exposing the truth.

title: Tomte's Christmas Porridge
summary: A greedy farmer attempts to steal the Christmas porridge meant for the farm's protector spirit, the Tomte, only to face the devastating consequences of his disrespect.

title: Tonantzin and Our Lady of Guadalupe — The Sacred Syncretism
summary: The story of Our Lady of Guadalupe is the most profound example of indigenous-Hispanic syncretism in the Americas. According to tradition, in December 1531, the Virgin Mary appeared to Juan Diego, an Indigenous Chichimec peasant, on Tepeyac Hill in what is now Mexico City. Speaking to him in Nahuatl, she asked that a church be built on the site. When Juan Diego relayed this to Archbishop Zumárraga, the bishop demanded a sign. The Virgin instructed Juan Diego to gather Castilian roses blooming miraculously on the frozen hilltop, and when he opened his tilma (cloak) before the archbishop, the flowers fell to reveal the image of the Virgin imprinted on the fabric. Crucially, the apparition site was the former temple of Tonantzin, the Aztec mother goddess — making the Virgin of Guadalupe a direct continuation of indigenous earth-mother worship within a Catholic framework. For Chicanos and Mexican-Americans today, the Virgin of Guadalupe transcends religion to become a cultural symbol of Mexican identity, maternal protection, and the resilience of indigenous spirituality within a colonial context. She is venerated as the Empress of the Americas and the Patroness of the Unborn.

title: Tongue-Cut Sparrow
summary: A kind woodcutter's compassion for a wounded bird is rewarded with wealth, while his greedy neighbor's calculated kindness leads to disaster.

title: Torre Jeppe
summary: A mummified corpse named Torre Jeppe sits in a church night after night until a brave sexton discovers that the ghost cannot rest because of an ancient wrong that must be righted. A ghost-story founded on the belief that wrongdoing torments the guilty even after death.

title: Trolls in Church
summary: In the mountains of Norway, where the trolls have their halls in the great stone halls, there live creatures who see humans as pests—annoying, but sometimes useful.

title: Trollvaskers of Dovre
summary: A shepherd discovers the secret rhythms of the Dovre mountain trolls, who gather weekly to wash their garments in a thunderous, rhythmic display of nature.

title: True and Untrue
summary: Two brothers, True and Untrue, leave home. Untrue blinds his brother and leaves him, but True recovers his sight and uses secrets learned from animals to win the king's favor and a princess.

title: Tróndur í Gøtu (Tróndur the Viking Chieftain)
summary: Tróndur í Gøtu was a powerful 10th-century Viking chieftain who lived in Gøta on Eysturoy. He is the central figure in the Færeyinga Saga, which recounts his fierce opposition to the Christianization of the islands. He led pagan resistance against Sigmundur Brestisson, who was sent by King Olaf Tryggvason of Norway to convert the Faroese. After a series of battles, Sigmundur ultimately won and killed Tróndur. However, in folklore, Tróndur is often portrayed as a tragic hero—a symbol of Faroese independence and resistance against foreign domination. His burial mound is said to exist near Gøta.

title: Trøllanes and the Troll House Party
summary: The settlement of Trøllanes on Kalsoy Island takes its name from ancient trolls who would come ashore once a year to wreak havoc—eating all available food, drinking, dancing, and behaving like wild party-goers. Terrified villagers would flee to Mikladalur every year, leaving their homes to be ransacked. One year, a woman was unable to escape and hid under a table as the trolls danced and feasted above her. In terror, she exclaimed 'Christ!' The trolls, hearing the holy name, fled from the village in panic and never returned. The route to the Kallur lighthouse begins in Trøllanes, offering some of the most dramatic views in the Faroe Islands.

title: Trøllkonufingur (The Troll Woman's Finger)
summary: A giant troll-woman from Iceland came to Vágar Island with the same plan as Risin and Kellingin: to steal the Faroe Islands and drag them to Iceland. Like the giants, she could only work at night. Caught by sunrise, sunlight turned her to stone. She toppled from the cliff into the sea—and was so enormous that her head became the island of Koltur (inhabited by only two people, Bjørn and Lukka Patursson), while one finger remained above water as the rock formation Trøllkonufingur near Sandavagur. Visible from the airport, it is a popular climbing spot. In 1844, a member of the Royal Danish entourage climbed it, descended, realized he'd dropped a glove, climbed back up—and was never seen again.

title: Tselane and the Cannibal Dimo
summary: A beloved Sesotho folktale about Tselane, a young girl who refused to leave her beautiful forest home when her mother wanted to migrate. They agreed that Tselane would stay, locked safely in the house, and her mother would visit daily, singing a secret call-and-response song as their code. The cannibal Dimo watched and learned, but his first attempts to mimic the song failed because his voice was too hoarse. He consulted a medicine woman who advised him to thrust a red-hot iron rod down his throat to clear his voice. Dimo succeeded in imitating the song, and Tselane opened the door. He captured her, put her in a bag, and carried her away. On his journey home, Dimo stopped at a tavern, and local children discovered Tselane in the bag, replacing her with a swarm of bees. When Dimo opened the bag at home, the bees attacked and stung him to death.

title: Tsichtinako Teaches the Sisters
summary: In the Acoma Pueblo creation story, Tsichtinako (Thought Woman) appeared as a voice guiding the sisters Iatiku and Nautsiti from within the earth. She couldn't be seen because she was a spirit without a human body. Tsichtinako instructed the sisters in all aspects of life: how to plant seeds from their baskets, how to make prayer sticks (pahos), how to conduct ceremonies, and how to organize their society into clans. She explained that Uchtsiti (the Sun, their father) had created the world but it was not yet complete, and the sisters were to complete it. Tsichtinako also taught them language, naming each plant, animal, and feature of the landscape. She established the four sacred directions and the relationship between the people and all beings. Tsichtinako continues to guide the Acoma people invisibly, representing the power of thought and the spiritual foundation of existence.

title: Tsui-Goab and //Gaunab: The Khoikhoi Supreme Being and the Evil One
summary: In Khoikhoi mythology, Tsui-//goab is the supreme being, creator, and guardian of health, associated with the east, the moon, and good fortune. His eternal adversary is //Gaunab, a malevolent being who causes sickness and death. Tsui-//goab's name means 'wounded knee,' stemming from a myth where he was injured in his battle against //Gaunab. The Khoikhoi traditionally prayed at dawn facing east, offering supplications to Tsui-//goab for rain and prosperity. The moon was seen as his visible manifestation, and its cycles were deeply tied to Khoikhoi religious observance.

title: Tsunki, the Water Spirit
summary: A powerful water spirit from Shuar tradition who lives in the rivers of the Ecuadorian Amazon and controls the fish and the currents.

title: Tuamotu: The Voyage of Kiwa
summary: The great navigator Kiwa sailed across the Pacific guided by the stars, discovering the Tuamotu Archipelago. According to Tuamotuan tradition, Kiwa was sent by the gods to find new lands for the growing population of the central islands. He followed the flight paths of seabirds and the patterns of ocean swells to locate the low coral atolls hidden on the horizon. At each island, Kiwa planted coconuts, released breeding pairs of fish into the lagoons, and established the tapu that would protect the fragile atoll ecosystems. His voyages mapped the Tuamotu chain, and the navigational knowledge he passed down—star paths, wave patterns, and bird signs—remained the foundation of Tuamotuan seafaring for generations.

title: Tunda, the Shapeshifter of the Coast
summary: A shape-shifting spirit from Ecuador's coastal region who leads men into the wilderness and abandons them, leaving them lost and mad.

title: Turtle Island: The Lenape Earth Diver
summary: In the Lenape creation account, before land existed, all the animals lived in deep water. They grew weary of swimming and wanted dry land. One by one the animals dove to retrieve earth from the bottom — the otter, the beaver — but each failed, gasping for air. Finally the humble muskrat took his turn. He was under the water so long the others thought he had drowned. At last he surfaced, near death, with a tiny clump of mud in his paw. He Who Creates Us By Thought summoned Turtle to the surface and placed the mud on Turtle's back. The Creator caused the mud to grow and spread across Turtle's shell, forming Turtle Island, the North American continent. From a tree growing on this new land sprouted the first man and woman, the ancestors of all people.

title: Twigmuntus, Cowbelliantus, Perchnosius
summary: A clever farmer's lad determines to win the king's daughter by outwitting the king and his seven learned professors. On his journey, a twig hits him (Twigmuntus), a cow bellows (Cowbelliantus), and a perch bites his nose (Perchnosius). When the professors finish their learned gibberish, he stumps them with these three nonsense words.

title: Two Friends: Coyote and Bull Snake Exchange Visits
summary: Coyote and Bull Snake were friends who decided to visit each other's homes. Coyote visited Bull Snake first and found his burrow beautiful and comfortable. Bull Snake then visited Coyote's den. During the visit, Coyote played a trick on Bull Snake, or vice versa, depending on the version. The story humorously explores the nature of friendship across differences, the expectations of hospitality, and the consequences of deception between friends. It also incorporates elements of Hopi social values, including proper guest behavior and the responsibilities of hosts. The story ends with the two friends parting ways, each having learned something about trust and respect for different ways of living.

title: Tórur Rami and the Three Gifts of Mykines
summary: A giant named Tórur Rami tried to conquer the island of Mykines. The native inhabitant Óli Rami opposed him. When the giant approached, Óli Rami used magic to split Mykineshólmur from the main island, creating the islet now reached by a narrow metal bridge. The giant jumped across and they fought. Óli Rami won and spared the giant's life in exchange for three gifts: (1) a great whale would appear annually in Hvalagjógv bay—but the people complained and it stopped; (2) a giant magical tree—but the people complained it was shabby and it withered; (3) gannets (seabirds) that still nest only on Mykineshólmur. The condition was that the people must never complain about the gifts.

title: Udea and Her Seven Brothers
summary: A Libyan fairy tale collected by Hans Stumme in Tripoli. A woman with seven sons gives birth to a daughter, Udea. The seven brothers are driven away from home by a rival female spirit and set out into the world. The mother promises them a sign when Udea is born: a red flag for a daughter, a white one for a son. The rival spirit arranges for a white flag to be raised instead of red, tricking the brothers into thinking they have another brother. Years later, Udea grows up, learns of her brothers, and sets out to find them. She travels through dangerous territory and eventually locates them, but her sister-in-law becomes jealous and sets impossible tasks for her, including fetching a magical bird and finding a singing tree. With supernatural help, Udea completes each task. Eventually, the truth is revealed, the jealous sister-in-law is punished, and Udea is reunited with her family. The tale includes themes of sibling loyalty, jealousy, and the triumph of perseverance over supernatural obstacles.

title: Uekera: The Tree of Knowledge
summary: In Kiribati legend, Uekera is a sacred tree that reaches to the heavens, known as the tree of knowledge. It was planted in Buariki village in North Tarawa by the goddess Nei Tekanuea. According to tradition, Uekera's roots extend deep into the earth while its branches reach into the sky world, making it a bridge between the human and divine realms. The tree is said to possess great wisdom and those who approach it with respect can gain knowledge and insight. Uekera inspired the name of Kiribati's weekly newspaper, Te Uekera. The tree symbolizes the connection between the people of Kiribati, their land, and their ancestors, representing the transmission of cultural knowledge from generation to generation through oral tradition.

title: Uksáhkká: Guardian of the Door
summary: Uksáhkká (Door Woman) is one of the daughters of Máttaráhkká, living under the door of the goahti. She protects people entering and leaving the dwelling, receives the newborn child into the world during birth, and protects children as they learn to walk. Drinks were poured under the door as offerings. Christian influence equated her with Virgin Mary. She was known only among Scandinavian Sámi.

title: Uktena: The Horned Serpent (Cherokee)
summary: Uktena is a massive horned serpent covered in shining scales, with a single blazing crystal in its forehead that grants supernatural vision. The first Uktena was once a man who attempted to kill the sun. He failed and was transformed into the monstrous serpent as punishment. Uktena dwells in deep rivers, lakes, and under mountains. Its gaze alone can paralyze or kill. Only the bravest medicine men and heroes dare to hunt Uktena, seeking the Ulûñsû'tî, the diamond-like crystal from its forehead, which grants great power to whoever possesses it. The most famous story involves a hunter who stalked an Uktena to its lair and, after a great battle, retrieved the crystal. The stone brought power but also danger, and was eventually hidden away in a sacred place.

title: Um Al Duwais, the Mother of Toes
summary: A terrifying female jinn who steals children at night, known for leaving only a single toe behind as her signature.

title: Umar Marvi — The Faithful Woman of Sindh
summary: Marvi was a beautiful peasant woman from the Thar Desert village of Malir in Sindh. The local ruler, Umar Soomro, became obsessed with her and had her kidnapped and brought to his palace. He offered her wealth, jewels, and queenship if she would marry him, but Marvi refused steadfastly, remaining faithful to her betrothed, a simple farmer. She endured years of captivity and torture, never wavering in her loyalty. Eventually, Umar Soomro was so impressed by her unwavering virtue that he released her. Marvi returned to her village and married her true love. The story, immortalized in Shah Abdul Latif Bhittai's Shah Jo Risalo, is one of the seven tragic romances of Sindhi folklore and is celebrated as a symbol of truth, loyalty, and the unbreakable connection to one's homeland.

title: Umm Al Duwais of the Abandoned Fort
summary: A group of children exploring an old Portuguese fort encounter the terrifying Umm Al Duwais, whose eerie laugh echoes through the ruins to this day.

title: Unhcegila the Serpent Monster
summary: Unhcegila was a gigantic serpent monster who wreaked havoc upon the land, devouring anyone who stumbled upon her. A red crystal in the seventh spot on her head functioned as her heart and granted its bearer great power. In one version, a warrior from the Bear Clan, guided by a Weasel spirit, allowed himself to be devoured then cut his way out, freeing other victims. In another, two brothers—one blind—killed her with arrows from a medicine woman. A third version tells of Unhcegila emerging from primordial waters, only to be struck down by Wakinyan the Thunderbird whose lightning shattered her heart, scattering her bones across the Badlands.

title: Unkulunkulu: The First Man Who Broke from the Reeds
summary: In the beginning there was only darkness and Uthlanga, the primordial reed bed. The god Umvelinqangi created a seed that grew into a massive reed, and at the end of one reed grew a man named Unkulunkulu, the 'old old one.' He grew so large that he snapped off from the reed and walked across the land, where he found men and women sprouting from other reeds. He picked them and they became the first ancestors of all nations. He gathered fish and flung them into rivers, harvested birds and antelope, and plucked cattle for humans. He threw a ball of fire and a glowing stone into the sky, creating the Sun and Moon. He also sent the chameleon with the message that men should not die, but the slow chameleon was beaten by a fast lizard carrying the opposite message, and so death entered the world.

title: Urashima Taro: The Fisherman and the Sea Kingdom
summary: A kind fisherman is rewarded with a visit to the underwater Dragon Palace, only to return to a world where centuries have passed in a heartbeat.

title: Ursitoare, the Weavers of Destiny
summary: Three fate-weaving spirits who appear at a child's birth to determine the course of its life, found in Moldovan and Romanian tradition.

title: Vasilisa and the Doll
summary: A girl with a magical doll discovers that the love of a mother can protect her and guide her through the darkest trials.

title: Vatnsdæla Saga - The Haunted Pastures
summary: The saga depicts a landscape where the boundary between the living and the dead is thin. It features episodes where ancestral spirits and ghosts return to warn their descendants of impending doom or to settle old scores, reflecting the deep belief in the enduring presence of the dead in the Icelandic countryside.

title: Viejito del Monte: The Little Old Man of the Mountain
summary: The Viejito del Monte is a small, ancient nature-spirit of the Nicaraguan highlands who rewards those who respect the forest and punishes those who despoil it.

title: Vikram and Betaal (Baital Pachisi) — The King and the Vampire
summary: King Vikramaditya of Ujjain is challenged by a sorcerer to capture a mischievous spirit called Betaal (Vetala) who hangs from a tree in a cremation ground. Each time Vikram tries to carry Betaal back to the sorcerer, the spirit tells a riddle-like story ending with a moral question. If Vikram answers correctly (which he cannot help but do), Betaal escapes back to the tree. This cycle of 25 tales forms a frame story that tests the king's wisdom, justice, and self-control, weaving complex moral dilemmas about loyalty, duty, truth, and the nuances of right action in impossible situations.

title: Vishnu
summary: When the forces of evil threaten to overwhelm the world, when dharma—the cosmic order—crumbles and chaos threatens to consume all that is good, a presence stirs in the highest heavens.

title: Vodnik, the Slovenian Water Sprite
summary: A mischievous water sprite of Slovenian folklore, Vodnik lives in rivers and lakes, drowning the unwary but also helping those he favors.

title: Vorvong and Sorvong: The Two Princes of Khmer Legend
summary: Two princes banished by their father overcome giants and treachery to reclaim their kingdom.

title: Wainamoinen and Youkahainen
summary: Youkahainen, a young and arrogant singer, challenges the elderly Wainamoinen to a singing match to prove his superiority. Wainamoinen uses his deep knowledge of the origins of things and his superior magical songs to sing Youkahainen into a swamp, demonstrating that ancient wisdom far outweighs youthful arrogance.

title: Wainamoinen Finds the Lost-word
summary: Wainamoinen seeks the 'lost words' of creation, ancient incantations that provide total mastery over nature. He journeys to the deepest parts of the ocean or the underworld to retrieve this forbidden knowledge, emphasizing the theme of knowledge as the ultimate source of power.

title: Wainamoinen's Boat-building
summary: Wainamoinen decides to sail to Pohjola and spends immense effort building a magnificent boat. However, he fails to complete it because he forgets a small but crucial piece, the cross-beam. This story serves as a lesson on the importance of attention to detail and the dangers of pride.

title: Wainamoinen's Hapless Journey
summary: Seeking a new bride to end his loneliness, Wainamoinen sails to distant and strange lands. During his journey, he encounters numerous obstacles and faces various trials that test both his physical endurance and his magical prowess, often finding himself in precarious situations that require his ingenuity to survive.

title: Wainamoinen's Harp-songs
summary: The songs played on the kantele are used to preserve the history of the world and the legendary deeds of the heroes. This process establishes the harp as a central tool for cultural memory and divine communication.

title: Wainamoinen's Lamentation
summary: Overcome with grief after Aino's death, Wainamoinen wanders the world, mourning the loss of the woman he loved. Through his songs, he reflects on the nature of love, the pain of loss, and the inevitability of fate, while continuing to refine his magical abilities and search for meaning in his solitude.

title: Wainamoinen's Rescue
summary: While on his journeys, Wainamoinen is captured or trapped in a foreign land, often within the depths of the sea or a dark cave. Through a combination of his own magical songs and the unexpected help of allies, he is eventually rescued, continuing his endless quest for a suitable partner.

title: Wainamoinen's Sailing
summary: Wainamoinen organizes a final, daring voyage to retrieve the Sampo from the fortress of Pohjola. He coordinates with other heroes of Kalevala, combining their strengths for one last great effort to secure the source of prosperity.

title: Wainamoinen's Sowing
summary: Wainamoinen attempts to sow the earth, but the land remains barren. He is challenged by powerful winds and storms that seek to prevent the growth of life. Using his profound magical songs, he calms the elements and prepares the land for agriculture, establishing the first signs of order and sustenance in the world.

title: Wainamoinen's Wedding-songs
summary: Wainamoinen performs a series of magical wedding songs, using his voice to bless the union of Ilmarinen and the Daughter of Pohjola. His songs provide wisdom to the couple and attempt to instill harmony between the two conflicting nations.

title: Walu: The Sun Woman
summary: The Sun Woman who lights the world each day — a powerful Dreamtime ancestor whose daily journey across the sky sustains all life on Earth. In the Dreamtime, Walu was chosen by the sky spirits to carry the great fire across the heavens, and her golden hair became the rays that warm the land. She rises each morning from the eastern sea and descends each evening into the western waters, and the seasons turn according to her will. The Aboriginal peoples honor her with songs at dawn and ceremonies at solstice.

title: Walumbe: The Origin of Death
summary: Walumbe, whose name means 'death' in Luganda, was the brother of Nambi who followed her and Kintu to earth when they forgot the millet. Ggulu had warned them not to return, but Walumbe insisted on accompanying them on their way back. Once on earth, Walumbe demanded one of Kintu and Nambi's children as his servant. Kintu refused, and Walumbe began killing the children one by one. Kintu tried to hide his children in a deep trench, but Walumbe's power was inescapable. Kintu appealed to Ggulu, who sent his other sons to capture Walumbe. They caught him and were dragging him back to the sky, but Walumbe tricked them by crying out and startling them into letting go. He escaped into a deep hole in the earth from which he emerged periodically to claim his due. And so death became permanent in the world. Yet Ggulu decreed that Walumbe could only take one person at a time, and that new life would always replace the old, ensuring the continuation of humanity.

title: Wandjina the Cloud Spirits
summary: The Wandjina (also Wanjina, Wondjina) are powerful cloud and rain spirits in the beliefs of the Wanjina Wunggurr cultural bloc of northwestern Australia, including the Worrorra, Wunambal, and Ngarinyin peoples of the Kimberley region. According to Dreamtime legends, the Wandjina created the landscape and its inhabitants and continue to influence both. When the spirit beings found the place where they would die, they painted their images on cave walls and entered a nearby waterhole. The paintings, which date back about 4,000 years, show figures with large upper bodies, eyes and noses but typically no mouths (because they are so powerful they do not need speech, and if they had mouths rain would never cease). The Wandjina can punish lawbreakers with floods, lightning, and cyclones. Aboriginal people repaint these images annually to regenerate their life-force and ensure the coming of monsoon rains.

title: Well Done and Ill Paid
summary: A man tricks a bear into being bound to a sledge, but the fox who helped him is betrayed by the man's own wife, who sends hounds to hunt the fox.

title: Wenebojo and the Dancing Geese
summary: Wenebojo, hungry and lazy, saw a flock of geese dancing on the shore. He convinced them to teach him their dance, saying he had seen a more beautiful dance in his dreams. The geese agreed, and Wenebojo joined them, singing and dancing with his eyes closed as he had been instructed. As they danced, Wenebojo began to wring the necks of the geese one by one, still keeping his eyes shut. A young goose opened its eyes and saw what was happening, crying out a warning. The remaining geese flew away. Wenebojo was left with a pile of dead geese, but his treachery was discovered and he faced the consequences. This trickster tale teaches both humor and the lesson that dishonesty will eventually be exposed.

title: Wenebojo Creates the Earth (After the Great Flood)
summary: In the Algonquian creation story, the trickster-transformer Wenebojo (Nanabozho) caused a great flood through his battle with the underwater serpents who killed his brother. After the waters covered everything, Wenebojo floated on a log with the surviving animals. He asked the loon, then the otter, then the muskrat to dive to the bottom of the flood waters and bring up a pawful of earth. One by one they tried; each failed until the humble muskrat dove so deep he nearly died, but surfaced with a tiny bit of mud in his paw. From this mud, Wenebojo created a new earth, placing it on the back of a great turtle. The turtle grew and grew, becoming Turtle Island, the North American continent. The muskrat's sacrifice is remembered as proof that even the smallest can achieve the greatest.

title: Were and the Creation of the World
summary: Were, the supreme god of the Luo, created the world from the primordial waters. First, Were created the sky and the earth, then the sun, moon, and stars to give light. He fashioned the first man and woman from clay and breathed life into their nostrils. Were gave them cattle, goats, and seeds to plant, teaching them how to live. But the first people disobeyed Were's command not to eat from a certain tree, and death entered the world. Were withdrew from direct contact with humanity but left the ancestral spirits (juogi) as intermediaries. The juogi watch over their descendants, guiding them and protecting them from harm. To this day, the Luo honor Were through prayers and offerings made at dawn and dusk, when the boundary between the physical and spiritual worlds grows thin.

title: What Shall Baby's Name Be?
summary: A well-to-do couple's daughter Peggy finally gets a suitor, but when she goes to the cellar for beer she becomes so preoccupied with what to name her future first baby that she, her mother, and her father all become lost in thought, causing the impatient suitor to leave forever.

title: When Mother Troll Took in the King's Washing
summary: Troll Mother and her son Drulle live in a forest cottage where she does laundry for travelers. When a king builds a nearby castle for his queen and newborn princess, the lady-in-waiting hires Troll Mother to wash the royal clothes cheaply so she can pocket the difference. Troll Mother becomes enchanted by the beautiful baby clothes and begins stealing them, using a troll rhyme her son recites during counting to conceal the theft. An orphan girl named Inga, who mends clothes at the castle, is blamed for the missing garments and sent away. She wanders to the trolls' cottage and is taken in, where Drulle becomes infatuated with her. Inga meets the queen's young page in the forest, who believes in her innocence and asks for her hand, but she refuses out of shame. When Troll Mother reveals the stolen baby clothes and her tail becomes loose, Inga realizes she is living with trolls and flees. She marries the page, while Drulle's misery causes him to forget the counting rhyme, leading to exposure of the theft. The trolls abandon their cottage, and years later return the remaining baby clothes. Inga and the page live happily, becoming the royal forester and his wife.

title: White Buffalo Calf Woman and the Sacred Pipe
summary: During a time of great famine, two Lakota scouts encountered a mysterious woman in white buckskin. One scout approached her with lustful intent and was reduced to bones. The woman instructed the remaining scout to prepare the tribe. She gave the people the chanupa (sacred pipe) made of red stone carved with a buffalo calf, taught them the Seven Sacred Rites including the Sun Dance and vision quest, and showed them how to pray to Wakan Tanka. Before departing she transformed through four colors—black, red, brown, and white—becoming a white buffalo calf who promised to return when the people needed her most.

title: White Painted Woman and Child of the Water (Chiricahua Apache)
summary: In Chiricahua and Mescalero Apache tradition, the creation begins not with an emergence from the underworld but with a great flood that destroyed a malevolent world. After the flood, White Painted Woman (Changing Woman) appeared. She conceived Child of the Water (also known as Killer-of-Enemies in Lipan tradition) from the rays of the Sun. Child of the Water became the dominant culture hero who rids the world of monsters. He is sometimes described as the Sun himself in some versions, and his younger brother is the Wise One. White Painted Woman is identified with the Moon and Thunder. The Girls' Puberty Ceremony reenacts White Painted Woman's first menstruation, when she received her power from the Sun. The ceremony lasts four days and includes the Mountain Spirit dance, blessing the young woman with health, fertility, and a long life, just as White Painted Woman was blessed.

title: Whowie: The Monster of the Murray
summary: Long ago, before the old grandfathers' time, there lived a creature in the Murray River that was more terrible than anything that has lived since.

title: Why Leaves Change Color in Autumn
summary: According to Wyandot legend, the changing colors of autumn leaves are the result of a great battle between the summer spirits and the winter spirits. Every autumn, the giant who rules the North Wind comes down from his cold kingdom and fights with the spirit of summer. During the battle, the leaves are bruised and battered, turning yellow, red, and orange from the struggle. The frost giants paint the remaining leaves with ice colors before stripping them from the trees entirely. Another version says that when the Thunders retreat south for the winter, their departing tears fall on the leaves, staining them red and gold. The fallen leaves cover the ground as a blanket to protect Mother Earth during her winter sleep. When spring returns and the Thunders come back north, new green leaves sprout, and the cycle begins again.

title: Why Men Commit Evil at Night (Ashanti/Akan)
summary: Nyame the Sky God had three sons: Esum (Darkness), Osrane (Moon), and Owia (Sun). He wanted to make Owia a chief and proposed that the son who could guess the name of a secret yam would inherit his royal stool. Anansi discovered the name 'Kintinkyi' and revealed it to Owia, who won the contest. Nyame punished Esum by decreeing that evil deeds would happen in his time (night). He told Osrane that only children would play during his time (moonlight). And he blessed Owia (daytime) as the time for settling disputes and doing good work. Nyame gave Owia the rainbow as a promise of protection from his brothers, and he made Anansi his messenger for knowing his thoughts. This story explains the division of day and night and why light and dark have different moral qualities in Akan cosmology.

title: Why Mr. Possum Has No Hair on His Tail
summary: A pourquoi tale explaining the possum's hairless tail. Brer Possum once had the most beautiful, bushy tail in the animal kingdom. He was so proud of it that he spent all his time grooming and displaying it, neglecting to gather food for the winter. When winter came, Brer Possum was starving. He went to Brer Rabbit and begged for food. Brer Rabbit, always the trickster, offered him a deal: if Brer Possum would let Brer Rabbit cut off his beautiful tail, Brer Rabbit would give him food for the entire winter. Brer Possum refused at first, but as hunger grew, he reluctantly agreed. Brer Rabbit cut off the bushy tail and gave Brer Possum food. But the tail never grew back, and only a thin, hairless, rat-like tail remained. Brer Possum was so ashamed that he learned to play dead whenever anyone looked at him, so they wouldn't see his shameful tail. To this day, possums have hairless tails and play dead when frightened, eternally reminded of the price of vanity.

title: Why the Bear Is Stumpy-Tailed
summary: In this origin story, a cunning fox tricks a gullible bear into believing he can catch fish by leaving his tail in a frozen pond overnight. The bear's tail freezes solid, and when he tries to pull it out, it snaps off, explaining why bears have short, stumpy tails today.

title: Why the Executioner is Called Assessor
summary: An executioner on his way to an execution discovers a robbers' den in the forest. After completing his duty, he tells the king, who disguises himself as a tramp and together they defeat twelve robbers. In gratitude, the king decrees that executioners shall be called 'Assessor' and treated with respect.

title: Why the Negro Is Black
summary: An African American origin tale explaining skin color, collected by Joel Chandler Harris. According to Uncle Remus, in the beginning, all people were the same color. The Lord was making people and set them out to bake in the sun, like bread. He planned to bake them different shades—some light, some dark, some in between. The first batch was put in the oven, but the Lord became busy with other matters and left them too long. When he took them out, they were burnt quite black. That was the Negro. The second batch, watched more carefully, came out just right—a nice golden brown. That was the Indian. The third batch, watched too nervously, was pulled out too soon and came out pale and undercooked. That was the white man. The story is told with characteristic humor and is typical of African American 'why' tales that use wit to explain natural phenomena, often with a subtle commentary on racial hierarchy. While using self-deprecating humor, the tale subtly subverts racist ideologies by suggesting racial difference is mere accident of timing in the divine kitchen.

title: Why the Ocean Is Salty
summary: In the days when the world was young, there were two brothers. Centers on Spirit,  human attempt to understand the soul, afterlife, and the unseen forces that govern existence..

title: Why the Salt is Far Away
summary: A Hopi legend explaining why the Hopi must travel long distances to obtain salt. Long ago, salt was close to the Hopi villages. But a woman or a group of people violated a taboo involving salt — either by being wasteful, disrespectful, or by using salt improperly during a ceremony. The Salt Woman (or salt spirits) became angry and moved the salt deposits far away, to the Grand Canyon and other distant locations. Ever since, the Hopi have had to undertake long, dangerous journeys to gather salt, a sacred substance used in ceremonies and daily life. The story teaches respect for natural resources and the consequences of taking blessings for granted.

title: Why the Sea is Salt
summary: A man possesses a magical mill capable of producing any item on command. A curious sailor steals the mill and, not knowing the command to stop it, asks for salt. The mill produces salt relentlessly, filling the ocean and explaining why the sea remains salty to this day.

title: Why the Spider Has a Bald Head (Ashanti/Akan)
summary: Anansi attended his mother-in-law's funeral wearing a fine hat made of leopard skin. During the mourning, Anansi became infatuated with the chief's daughter and boasted that he could perform a magical dance. The chief agreed, but warned that if Anansi failed to impress, he would lose his head. Anansi danced wildly, and the hat flew off, revealing his bald head. The chief's daughter laughed at him, and everyone realized his boasting was empty. In shame, Anansi tried to hide but his hat was gone forever. To this day, spiders are bald because of Anansi's vanity and empty boasting. The story teaches the dangers of pride and the importance of humility in Akan culture.

title: Wihio the Spider Trickster
summary: Wihio is the Cheyenne trickster figure, a spider-like being similar to Iktomi of the Lakota. He is clever but greedy, often getting into trouble because of his selfishness. In one story, Wihio tried to kill some ducks for a feast by tricking them into a dance with their eyes closed. A loon peeked and exposed the trick, and Wihio was shamed. In another tale, Wihio's greed caused him to be trapped inside a hollow log by his own scheme. Wihio stories serve as cautionary tales, teaching Cheyenne children about the consequences of selfish behavior and the importance of community values.

title: Will Scarlet
summary: Will Scarlet was the most hot-tempered of Robin Hood's Merry Men, a man who wore his anger like a cloak and held a grudge like a treasured possession.

title: Wolf Clan and the Salmon (Tsimshian)
summary: This Tsimshian legend tells of a volcanic eruption caused by disrespect for the salmon. The Wolf Clan, one of the four major Tsimshian clans, had specific protocols for harvesting and honoring the first salmon of the season. One year, a member of the Wolf Clan failed to follow the proper rituals — he did not welcome the salmon chief properly, did not prepare the first salmon with the required ceremony, and showed disrespect to the salmon people. In response, the supernatural forces beneath the mountains grew angry. A great volcanic eruption occurred, devastating the land and reminding all Tsimshian people of the sacred obligation to honor the salmon. The story reinforces the fundamental Northwest Coast principle that humans and salmon are in a reciprocal relationship: humans must treat salmon with respect or face catastrophic consequences. It also explains volcanic activity in the Nass and Skeena River regions through the lens of spiritual cause and effect.

title: Wolf Spirit and the Warrior's Vision
summary: A young Comanche warrior went on a vision quest alone in the mountains, fasting for four days without water. On the fourth night, a Wolf appeared to him in a vision. The Wolf said, 'I am your brother. I will give you strength, courage, and the ability to track your enemies. But you must never kill my kind, for we are connected.' The warrior returned to his people with Wolf as his guardian spirit. He became a great hunter and warrior, always guided by Wolf's wisdom. This story reflects the Comanche belief in animal spirit guides who grant powers to individuals through vision quests.

title: Wunzh and the Origin of Indian Corn (Mon-Daw-Min)
summary: A young boy named Wunzh went into the forest to fast and pray for guidance, as was the custom of his people. After many days of fasting, a spirit appeared to him dressed in green and yellow, with feathers on his head. The spirit challenged Wunzh to wrestle him. Though weak from fasting, Wunzh fought with all his strength. The spirit returned every day, and each day Wunzh grew stronger. Finally, the spirit revealed himself as Mon-Daw-Min, the gift of the Creator. He told Wunzh to kill him, bury his body in the ground, and tend the grave. Wunzh obeyed, and from the spirit's body sprouted the first corn plant. The kernels were his teeth, the silk his hair, and the stalk his body. Wunzh brought this sacred knowledge to his people, who have cultivated corn ever since.

title: Xnifs, the Goblin of the Megaliths
summary: A small, hairy goblin who haunts the ancient megalithic temples of Malta, sometimes helpful and sometimes malicious.

title: Yamal Creation from the Mammoth
summary: A Nenets creation myth from the Yamal Peninsula, whose name means 'End of the Land' in the Nenets language. The legend tells that the world was formed from the body of a giant mammoth that emerged from the primordial sea. The great sky god Num sent the mammoth to create dry land for humans and reindeer. When the mammoth died, its massive body became the Yamal Peninsula, its bones became the Ural Mountains, and its great tusks formed the rivers. Ice spirits (Yul-Chyn) emerged from the mammoth's frozen breath. The Nenets traditionally believed that earthquakes were caused by the mammoth stirring beneath the permafrost. This myth explains the origin of frozen mammoth carcasses that periodically emerge from melting tundra.

title: Yamm, God of the Deep
summary: The sea god who was defeated by Baal but never destroyed, because the sea cannot be destroyed — it can only be held back by the strength of the storm.

title: Yanauluha Brings Medicine and Agriculture
summary: In Zuni mythology, Yanauluha is the benevolent culture hero who brought the arts of medicine and agriculture to the people. Unlike trickster figures in some traditions, Yanauluha is a dignified, wise teacher. After the emergence into the daylight world, the people were struggling to survive. Yanauluha appeared among them carrying seeds, digging sticks, and sacred objects. He taught them which plants were edible and medicinal, how to plant corn, beans, and squash together in hills, when to plant by observing the stars and the position of the sun, and how to prepare and store food. He also taught them how to use plants for healing — which roots, leaves, and barks cured various illnesses. Yanauluha established the pattern of the agricultural year and the ceremonies that accompany planting and harvest. He is associated with the directions and with the sacred mountains that surround the Zuni world. After teaching the people, Yanauluha departed, but his knowledge continues through Zuni farmers and medicine people.

title: Yara-ma-yha-who: The Little Red Men
summary: In the old times, children were told: 'Do not wander alone in the bush.. Do not rest beneath the fig trees.

title: Yemayá, Mother of the Ocean
summary: Yemayá (Yemoja) is the great mother orisha of the ocean, maternity, and the moon in Cuban Santería, syncretized with the Virgin of Regla. She is the goddess of living waters, the salt sea, and is considered the mother of all life and the protector of women and children. Her colors are blue and white, her number is 7, and her symbol is a fan. A famous patakí tells how Yemayá gave her long magical hair to her sister Oshún as a gift of generosity, binding their realms of salt and fresh water forever. Yemayá is depicted as a mermaid or a beautiful woman emerging from the waves. She represents the maternal, protective, and sometimes fierce aspect of the divine feminine. Her domain is the ocean's depth and mystery.

title: Yemoja and the Waters of Life (Yoruba)
summary: Yemoja, the mother of all waters and the goddess of the Ogun River, is said to be the mother of many of the Orishas. According to legend, when her waters burst forth, they created the oceans and rivers of the world. Yemoja is the patroness of pregnancy, childbirth, and all nurturing aspects of womanhood. In one tale, when the world was threatened by drought, Yemoja emerged from the depths carrying the moon in her womb, bringing the tides and the rains. Women pray to her for fertility and safe delivery. Her devotees dress in blue and white and offer her rice, fish, and gourds. She represents the maternal essence of the universe, the primordial ocean from which all life emerged, and her name literally means 'Mother whose children are the fish.'

title: Yewe, the God of Thunder (Ewe)
summary: Yewe (also known as So or Hevioso) is the Ewe god of thunder, lightning, and rain. Yewe is a trɔwo (lesser deity) descended from Mawu, and is considered one of the most powerful and feared spirits in the Ewe pantheon. Those who offend Yewe may be struck by lightning, and special priests (Yewe priests) are needed to intercede. The Yewe cult has elaborate initiation ceremonies in which new initiates spend months in seclusion learning sacred songs, dances, and rituals. The sacred drumming tradition called Sowu is performed exclusively for Yewe ceremonies. Yewe's sacred color is red, and his shrine typically holds a carved wooden figure holding an axe, reminiscent of the Yoruba Shango. During annual festivals, Yewe's priests dance in possession trance, channeling the god's power for the community's blessing.

title: Ysatters-Kajsa, the Wind-Troll of Narke
summary: A Swedish legend about Ysatters-Kajsa, a powerful troll-woman who controls the winds over Narke province. She creates storms and blizzards when angered.

title: Yuki-Onna: The Snow Woman
summary: A snow spirit spares a young man's life on one condition: that he never reveal the secret of their encounter, a promise that will one day be tested by love.

title: Yuletide Specters
summary: A woman riding to Christmas mass encounters witch-trolls at a bridge and finds the church filled with headless specters and a headless priest, barely escaping with scraps of her mantle scattered on every grave. This ghostly Christmas legend is common throughout Scandinavia.

title: Yunwi Tsunsdi: The Little People (Cherokee)
summary: Yunwi Tsunsdi are the Cherokee Little People — small, child-sized nature spirits who live in caves, under rocks, and in the dense forest. They are usually invisible but sometimes reveal themselves to humans they trust. They possess powerful magic and are said to have taught medicine to certain shamans. The Little People can be helpful to those who respect them, leading lost hunters to safety or granting blessings. However, they are easily angered by disrespect and punish those who bother them excessively with confusion or misfortune. They are known to borrow tools from villagers, always returning them with small gifts of thanks. The Yunwi Tsunsdi are not to be spoken of lightly; those who encounter them rarely discuss the experience directly.

title: Zahhak: The Serpent-Shouldered Tyrant
summary: Zahhak (Aži-Dahāk) was a prince seduced by Ahriman (the devil) who kisses his shoulders, causing two black serpents to sprout. They demand daily sacrifices of young men's brains for sustenance. Zahhak overthrows the just king Jamshid and rules Iran for a thousand years with cruelty. The blacksmith Kaveh, having lost several sons to the serpents, leads a revolt and raises his leather apron on a spear (the Derafsh Kaviani flag) as a symbol of resistance. The noble Feraydun ultimately defeats Zahhak, chains him in Mount Damavand, where he remains imprisoned until the end of the world. The legend originates in Zoroastrian texts (Avesta) and is central to the Shahnameh.

title: Zanahary and Ratovantany: The Creation of Humanity
summary: In Malagasy mythology, the supreme sky god Zanahary and the earth god Ratovantany collaborated to create humanity. Ratovantany shaped the physical bodies from clay, but they remained lifeless. Zanahary, dwelling in the sky, breathed souls into the clay forms, animating them with divine essence. This division established Malagasy cosmology: upon death, the soul returns to Zanahary in the heavens, while the body returns to Ratovantany in the earth. This myth underpins the deep Malagasy reverence for ancestors (Razana), who are believed to dwell in the sky realm near Zanahary, serving as intermediaries between the living and the divine.

title: Zin Kibaru and the Stolen Children
summary: When children vanish near the river at night, a Zarma grandmother confronts the Zin Kibaru, a fearsome water spirit who steals the young to serve in his underwater kingdom.

title: Zmaj, the Kosovan Dragon
summary: A dragon of Kosovo legend, Zmaj is a powerful serpentine being who brings rain and guards the sacred sites of the Albanian and Serbian peoples.

title: Zmeu, the Dragon of Moldovan Skies
summary: A great dragon-like creature with three heads that terrorizes the Moldovan countryside, often serving as the ultimate test of a hero's courage.

title: Zmeu: The Dragon of Romanian Folklore
summary: A dragon-like giant kidnaps maidens and battles heroes in the mountains of Romania.

title: Zmey, the Macedonian Dragon
summary: A dragon of Macedonian folklore, the Zmey is a wise and powerful serpent who controls the weather and protects the land from foreign invaders.

title: Zmey: The Benevolent Dragon of Bulgarian Folklore
summary: Unlike Western dragons, the Bulgarian Zmey is a protective guardian that controls the weather and ensures good harvests.

title: Zonbi of the Coconut Grove
summary: A dead plantation worker rises as a zonbi to haunt the coconut groves, driven by unfinished labor, until a Creole healer performs the rite that finally sets him free.

title: Zuleikha and the Forty Maidens
summary: The legend of the Forty Maidens (Kirk Kiz) is a Central Asian heroic tale found among Turkmen, Kazakh, and Karakalpak peoples. A beautiful and brave maiden named Zuleikha leads a band of forty warrior women who defend their people against invading forces. Rather than submit to forced marriage to an enemy khan, Zuleikha trains herself and her forty companions in martial arts, horseback riding, and archery. The forty women fight with the ferocity of lions and the cunning of wolves. When the enemy surrounds their fortress, Zuleikha leads a night raid that scatters the invaders. The stone monument 'Forty Girls' exists in multiple locations across Central Asia, believed to be the petrified remains of these warrior women who chose death over dishonor. The legend celebrates female heroism and resistance against oppression.

title: Átahsaia the Cannibal Demon
summary: A Zuni legend about Átahsaia, a giant cannibal demon who terrorized the people. Átahsaia is described as a huge, monstrous being with burning eyes and an insatiable hunger for human flesh, especially children. The demon would descend from the mountains to raid villages, carrying off victims in a large basket on its back. The twin war gods Áhaiyúta and Mátsailéma confronted Átahsaia to save their people. They used their divine weapons and cunning to defeat the demon. In some versions, they tricked Átahsaia into falling into a pit of fire or into a canyon. The battle between the divine twins and the cannibal demon represents the eternal struggle between good and evil, order and chaos. After Átahsaia's defeat, the people were safe, but the story reminds Zuni children to be cautious and to respect the boundary between the civilized pueblo and the wild lands where dangerous spirits dwell.

title: Čáhcerávga: The Water Wraith
summary: Unlike the Rávga (believed real), Čáhcerávga (Water Wraith) was known to be a fictional creature used to scare children away from dangerous waters. It was described as a long-necked, scary creature that might carry a child away. It was said to appear in all bodies of water where children were not supposed to go, including wells.

title: Čázevulošnieida: The Underwater Girl
summary: A Sea Sámi legend from Unjárga on the Varangerfjord, Norway. Čázevulošnieida (the Underwater Girl) is the daughter of Čáhceháldi (the Sea Guard). She lives in a parallel underwater world. When a fisherman boy encounters her, their meeting reveals how perspectives are turned upside down when two different worlds meet.
